title: ChunkAct: Action Chunking for Agentic Robotics

text:
The Power of Meta Access in the Software of the Future —
Demonstrated on LLM Chat UIs and Chat AI
Julian Kunkel
Universität Göttingen, GWDG
julian.kunkel@gwdg.de
Ali Doosthosseini
Universität Göttingen
ali.doosthosseini@uni-goettingen.de
November 6, 2026
Abstract
Chat remains the default surface for many large language model (LLM) tasks, even as
agentic tools such as OpenCode excel at coding and automation. Yet the model sees the current
dialogue but not the workspace around it. We explore meta access—giving the assistant a
structured, permissioned view of the interface itself and propose a ladder of levels: feature
tutoring; metadata, settings, and preference access; retrieval over summaries and messages,
confirmed mutation, and full orchestration. Meta access can turn a chat client from many screens
into one entry point for finding, navigating, organising, and operating it, while raising risks
around grounding, privacy, prompt injection, and trust. General-purpose agentic harnesses are
runtimes; because they can change their own settings, meta access becomes reflexive and needs
a separate control-plane boundary. We ground this in the Meta Chat prototype of the Chat
AI client. It builds bounded context from, e.g., summaries, settings, and relevant messages;
links references to conversations, topics, and personas; supports confirmed, reversible changes;
offers a browsable tutorial library; and recommends personas as user-started conversations. By
exposing application state in structured form, meta access can extend screen readers from widget
descriptions to semantic workspace operations. Meta access thus turns chat from a window
onto one conversation into a control layer for the whole workspace, extending chat toward
agentic capability without surrendering user control. As assistants become embedded in IDEs,
dashboards, office suites, and operating systems, AI-era interfaces should expose a structured,
permissioned model of their state and capabilities, ideally by opening their existing metamodels
through a debugger-like interface.
Keywords:LLM chat interfaces, AI-era interfaces, meta access, application metamodels, interface
agents, conversational search, feature tutoring, personas, guardrails, tool use, human–computer
interaction, accessibility, local-first software.
1 Introduction
The chat interface has been the default surface for interacting with large language models, and it
remains the most common one for many day-to-day tasks: drafting, search, planning, learning, and
personal assistance. In parallel, a second interaction model has matured. Agentic tools such as
OpenCode [17] operate in a terminal or editor, call tools, and carry out multi-step tasks on external
environments; they have become a natural choice for much software work. The two models are
complementary rather than substitutes. Agents excel when the task is to operate on an environment,
while chat UIs remain the natural surface when the user wants to ask, compare, plan, draft, or
re-find something, and when the conversation itself is the workspace.
1
arXiv:2611.08428v1 [cs.AI] 5 Nov 2026
title: The Power of Meta Access in the Software of the Future --- Demonstrated on LLM Chat UIs and Chat AI

text:
The deeper claim of this paper is architectural rather than conversational. Chat is the first
surface on which meta access is practical, but the pattern is not specific to chat. An emerging
AI-era interface is one in which an assistant is embedded in the application rather than confined to
a separate chat window, and in which the assistant can reason over the application’s own model of
its state and capabilities. Whether the surface is a chat client, an IDE, a spreadsheet, a dashboard,
or an operating system, the same asymmetry appears: the assistant sees the current task but not
the workspace that contains it. Meta access is the missing contract between the two. The contrast
is sharpest for general-purpose agentic harnesses such as OpenCode, which are runtimes rather than
applications with a fixed purpose, and which can change the configuration that governs their own
tools and permissions (Section 4.6).
In applications such as Chat AI [7], that workspace is larger than the current conversation: a
sidebar of past conversations, user-defined topics, model selection, attachments, memories, settings,
a persona library, and feature-specific controls. The model, however, usually sees only the current
conversation plus a system prompt. Everything that makes the workspace a workspace—what else
the user has discussed, how their chats are organised, which features exist and where they live—is
outside the model’s view.
This asymmetry creates a practical problem. As a user’s history grows, the interface becomes
harder to navigate: finding a conversation about a past decision, remembering which topic contains
it, or learning a rarely used feature requires manual scanning. Conventional search helps with
known-item retrieval, but users often ask questions that are relational or procedural:“Where is my
food-order chat?”,“Which topic holds the notes from the interview?”,“How do I attach a file?”.
These are questions about the interface and its contents, not about the world.
We use the termmeta accessfor an assistant’s structured access to the interface that hosts it: it
may access and potentially alter information about the interface and any of the user’s data. Meta
access is related to, but distinct from, retrieval-augmented generation over documents [13] and tool
use by language models [31, 24]. The object of retrieval is the user’s own workspace state; the object
of action is the interface itself. Meta access therefore sits at the intersection of conversational search,
command palettes, recommender-style navigation, and agentic tool use.
1.1 What “meta” means here
The prefixmetacomes from Greek and denotes a level that is about, beyond, or refers to another
level. Metadata is data about data; a metamodel is a model that describes the concepts and relations
of another model; metacommunication is communication about communication. In each case, the
meta-level does not replace the object level. It describes it, constrains it, or acts on it.
A chatbot normally operates at the object level: it talks about the user’s task, the world,
or the content of the current conversation.Meta accessadds a meta-level whose object is the
chat application itself. The assistant reasons about conversations, topics, memories, features, and
settings rather than only about the subject of the dialogue. Its context is not the full interface but a
workspace model: a structured description of the entities the interface exposes (chats, topics, features,
preferences), ideally derived from the application’s own metamodel, and, eventually, the operations
that can be requested on them. This is the sense in which the prototype has a metamodel-like view.
It does not reproduce the interface; it uses an abstraction of the interface’s concepts and capabilities.
At the scale of a whole application, this abstraction is an application metamodel: a description
of the application’s entities, relations, and operations. Many applications already have such a model
internally—a document model in an editor, a project and syntax model in an IDE, a schema in a
database, a scene graph in a graphics tool—and debugging or profiling interfaces already expose
parts of it in a controlled way. Meta access can reuse these models rather than relying on pixels or
2
title: The Power of Meta Access in the Software of the Future --- Demonstrated on LLM Chat UIs and Chat AI

text:
ad hoc scraping. The design question is which parts of the metamodel to expose, at what level of
stability and permission, and how to map them into a capability layer that works across applications.
The distinction separates three things that are easy to confuse. Metadata access is the narrowest
form of meta access: it reads descriptive fields such as titles, topics, and timestamps. Meta-level
knowledge also includes the feature catalogue, the persona catalogue, and current preference values,
which describe the application rather than a single conversation. Meta-level action goes further and
changes the object level, for example by moving a chat or changing a memory setting. The ladder in
Section 4 follows this progression from describing the interface, to reading its state, to acting on it.
We use “meta” in this self-referential sense, not in the corporate sense of Meta Platforms and
not as a synonym for the metaverse. It is also different from meta-learning or meta-prompting:
those describe learning or prompting about learning or prompting, whereas meta access describes
an assistant’s access to the application that hosts the interaction.
1.2 Contributions
This paper is a position paper grounded in an existing implementation. We make five contributions:
1. We present a ladder of meta-access levels that separates feature tutoring, metadata, settings,
and preference access, summary and message-level retrieval, confirmed mutating actions, and
full orchestration, and report how far the implemented prototype reaches on that ladder.
2. We propose meta access as a general design requirement for AI-era interfaces, not only chat
clients, and show how the ladder, capability model, and guardrails transfer to other stateful
applications and to general-purpose agentic harnesses, whose self-configuration adds a separate
control-plane problem.
3. We articulate the opportunities of using a chat interface as a first access layer for the whole
interface, with search and navigation as the first concrete use cases, and define guardrail contracts
that tie each capability to its evidence, scope, target validation, disclosure, confirmation, and
failure behaviour.
4. We outline risks and an evaluation agenda for measuring whether meta access actually helps
users.
5. We present theMeta Chatprototype in the Chat AI client as a demonstrator of these
opportunities and design choices.
2 Related Work
Meta access draws on several literatures that rarely meet: conversational search and personal
re-finding; LLM agents, tool use, and interface automation; retrieval, memory, and context; and
mixed-initiative interaction, security, and human factors. We review them in these groups, compare
representative work along nine dimensions, and then position the present work relative to them.
2.1 Conversational search and personal re-finding
Information retrieval has long treated dialogue as an interface to a search system. Radlinski and
Craswell [22] frame conversational search as a multi-turn collaboration in which system and user
clarify an information need, retrieve results, and interpret them; Trippas et al. [25] derive design
implications from spoken conversational search, and Zamani et al. [32] survey the field’s shift from
3
title: The Power of Meta Access in the Software of the Future --- Demonstrated on LLM Chat UIs and Chat AI

text:
ad hoc retrieval to interactive problem solving. This work supplies the interaction vocabulary that
meta access inherits: clarification, follow-up queries, mixed initiative, and results that support both
answer and exploration. Its usual target, however, is an external collection such as the web or a
document corpus, and classical lexical retrieval, including BM25 and its descendants [23], remains a
strong baseline for known-item search.
Personal information management (PIM) studies how people keep, organise, and re-find their own
digital material. Whittaker [27] frames PIM as a shift from consumption to curation, and Dumais
et al. [8] show that a unified index over email, files, and web pages, combined with contextual cues
such as time and authorship, supports re-finding; users often remember context rather than exact
content, and search and browsing are complementary. A chat workspace has the same character: it
is small enough to browse but grows large enough to need search, and its items carry rich contextual
metadata. Meta access is a conversational form of re-finding over that collection. The prototype
uses titles, topics, and recency as metadata cues, summaries as compressed content, and local lexical
search over message text for content questions, bringing it closer to full-text PIM systems such as
“Stuff I’ve Seen” while retaining an interface-aware layer.
Recent surveys extend this vocabulary to LLM-era systems. Mo et al. [35] identify query
reformulation, clarification, conversational retrieval, and response generation as core modules, while
Zhang et al. [36] review LLM agents for recommendation and search. Both reinforce the view that
information access is becoming an interactive, agentic process rather than a single query–response
exchange.
2.2 LLM agents, tool use, and interface automation
Retrieval-augmented generation grounds model output in retrieved text [13, 10]. ReAct [ 31],
Toolformer [24], and Gorilla [20] show that language models can interleave reasoning with calls
to external tools, although surveys and benchmarks document persistent weaknesses in planning,
reliability, and generalisation [29, 15]. A parallel line automates graphical interfaces: WebGPT [16],
Mind2Web [6], WebArena [34], OSWorld [30], and OSWorld-MCP [42] operate through browsers,
pixels, or GUI actions and are evaluated on open-ended task completion. Ramineni et al. [51]
expose platform accessibility trees through a shared MCP schema, so assistive agents need neither
screenshots nor per-platform integrations.
OpenCode is a general-purpose agentic harness rather than an application with a specific purpose.
It runs in the terminal, an IDE, or a desktop application, supports arbitrary models and tools, and
keeps its behaviour in editable configuration [17]. Its workspace is whatever task it is given, usually
repositories, shells, or editors, and its control plane includes prompts, tool and server registries,
permission policies, hooks, and subagents. This generality matters for meta access: there is no
single application metamodel to expose, and if the harness can read or change its own configuration,
the assistant may alter the capability layer that is supposed to constrain it. We call this reflexive
meta access and treat it separately in Section 4.6. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) makes
this control plane concrete. Hou et al. [54] survey its lifecycle and threat landscape and show that
discovery, schemas, and tool/resource exposure are security decisions made before any model call;
for a harness, the capability registry is therefore an attack surface, not just configuration.
Meta access is a narrower and more structured form of the same idea. The environment is
the hosting application, the observations are typed metadata rather than pixels, and the available
actions can be declared explicitly instead of inferred from a GUI. The agent literature is therefore
both an enabler and a caution: it shows that tool use works, but also that long-horizon autonomy
is fragile, which motivates starting with read-only metadata and preference access and adding
confirmed, narrowly scoped actions.
4
title: The Power of Meta Access in the Software of the Future --- Demonstrated on LLM Chat UIs and Chat AI

text:
2.3 Retrieval, memory, and context
Because a workspace can exceed any context window, meta access depends on how the interface is
compressed. Retrieval-augmented generation [13, 10] supplies the pattern of retrieving evidence
before generating an answer. MemGPT [18] treats an LLM as an operating system with hierarchical
memory; Generative Agents [19] maintain a memory stream with reflection; and LongMemEval
[28] benchmarks long-term interactive memory. Long-context models are not a substitute: they
can underuse information in the middle of a long prompt [14], and BEAM [38] shows that even
million-token models struggle as dialogues lengthen. MemoryAgentBench [39] finds that current
memory agents do not master accurate retrieval, test-time learning, long-range understanding, and
selective forgetting; LOCOMO-CONV [40] shows that conversational framing exposes retrieval gaps
that QA-style benchmarks miss; and MemUse [41] reports a retrieval–integration gap in a four-month
deployment. Together these results argue for a tiered index, query rewriting, implicit-intent handling,
and integration-aware evaluation rather than benchmark accuracy alone.
Conversation summarisation provides one practical compression mechanism. Surveys of dialogue
summarisation [9] describe methods for condensing multi-turn interactions while preserving salient
content. The meta chat uses such summaries together with topics, memories, and per-chat settings;
it adds selective lexical message excerpts when a question needs content. This keeps cost bounded
and reduces exposure compared with shipping full histories, but summaries are lossy and can be
stale, and lexical retrieval depends on the message wording. Recent memory work makes provenance
explicit: Lu et al. [56] use message-level evidence chains and propose–verify–commit writes with
revision history, a structured counterpart of confirmed memory mutations and conditional undo.
Hierarchical, hybrid, and semantic retrieval are the natural next steps.
2.4 Mixed-initiative interaction and human–AI guidelines
Meta access should not be a one-shot command interpreter. Horvitz [12] sets out principles for
mixed-initiative interfaces, including reasoning about uncertainty, the user’s goals, and the cost
of asking versus acting; Allen et al. [1] discuss the dialogue-management challenges, and Amershi
et al. [2] distill widely used guidelines for human–AI interaction. Studies of LLM use reinforce
the need for guidance and verification: non-experts struggle to design prompts [33], users of
code-generation tools inspect and iterate on model output [26, 4], and natural-language database
interfaces documented ambiguity and robustness problems long before LLMs [3]. Laban et al. [37]
add a multi-turn caution: tested LLMs perform worse in multi-turn than single-turn conversations,
often commit to assumptions early, and fail to recover, which makes explicit state and clarification
design requirements. Human-factors studies reinforce this: Schneider et al. [46] document linguistic
patterns and breakdowns in a retrieval-augmented assistant, Yu et al. [49] find no learning advantage
over search when user characteristics are considered, and Jerry et al. [48] propose a model-based
approach to LLM-driven accessible interfaces. Together they suggest that chat should complement,
not replace, the visual interface, and that meta access must be judged by user outcomes and
breakdowns.
2.5 Security and privacy of LLM-integrated applications
Any assistant that reads user content and can act on the user’s behalf is a security boundary. Prompt
injection [21] and indirect prompt injection [11] show that untrusted retrieved text can redirect
a model’s behaviour; AgentDojo [5] benchmarks these attacks and defences in tool-using agents,
and StepJack [43] shows that indirect injection can be decomposed into innocuous steps across a
navigation path. CaMeL [53] separates control flow from data flow and enforces capability checks
5
title: The Power of Meta Access in the Software of the Future --- Demonstrated on LLM Chat UIs and Chat AI

text:
on data flows, while ClawGuard [55] enforces a user-confirmed rule set at each tool-call boundary.
AC4A [52] turns this into access control: instead of all-or-nothing access to an API or page, an
agent receives permissions over specific resources and actions. AIOS [50] places scheduling, memory,
storage, access control, and isolation in an operating-system-like kernel, moving resource governance
from prompts to the platform. PrivacyBench [45] benchmarks privacy in personalised AI, and Wang
et al. [44] identify irrelevant personalisation, preference narrowing, and sycophancy as side effects of
conditioning on conversation history.
The implication for meta access is that retrieved content must be treated as data rather than
instructions, tools must be scoped to the user’s intent, and mutations should require confirmation.
Privacy is the other side of the boundary. Meta access sends titles, topics, summaries, and memories
to a model endpoint. This is less exposing than sending full message histories, but it is not
anonymous: summaries and titles can reveal sensitive context. The local-first design of the host
client, in which conversations live in the browser’s indexed database, is a useful starting point, but
the boundary between local state and remote inference must be made explicit to users.
2.6 Comparative analysis
Table 1 compares representative related work along nine dimensions that matter for meta access.
The aim is not to rank papers but to locate the gap that meta access addresses. We use three
values:+means the dimension is explicit and central to the paper;0means it is partial, indirect,
or limited to a narrow setting;-means it is not addressed or is out of scope. The ratings describe
each paper’s stated scope, not the quality of its contribution.
Three patterns stand out. First, conversational search and PIM occupy opposite corners:
conversational search supports dialogue and content retrieval but not the user’s personal workspace,
while PIM supports personal metadata and content but not dialogue or interface actions. Second,
agent and GUI-automation work supports actions and interface operation, but its object is an open
environment rather than the user’s own conversation history; personal scope, structured workspace
metadata, and user-facing grounding are typically absent. Third, memory and long-context work
supports dialogue and personal context, but it rarely models the interface or provides a capability
layer for acting on it.
A trade-off is also visible: many systems that act do not expose citations to the underlying
workspace items, while systems with strong grounding often do not act. Security work supplies
adversarial benchmarks and defences but is rarely integrated with personal retrieval or interface help,
and HCI work supplies interaction principles but not a concrete architecture. Meta access is the
region that remains sparsely populated: personal scope, structured metadata, interface awareness,
and grounding. The prototype now adds selective message-level retrieval and confirmed, reversible
mutations, while the ladder in Section 4 makes the remaining boundaries explicit: hierarchical
retrieval, broader level-4 actions, durable audit, and level-5 orchestration.
Existing work covers conversational search over external corpora, personal re-finding over files
and email, and tool-using agents on web pages or operating systems. Meta access sits between
these lines: the object of retrieval is the application’s own state, and the environment is a declared
capability layer rather than an open GUI. The contribution of this paper is to name that combination,
demonstrate it with confirmed, reversible actions, propose a ladder from tutoring to orchestration,
and set out an evaluation agenda.

text:
3 The Meta Chat Prototype
3.1 Placement and interaction model
TheMeta Chatis a separate chat in Chat AI [7]. It is opened from an AI icon in the sidebar
header and reuses the normal chat shell, so it feels like the rest of the application rather than a
bolted-on assistant. A banner above the conversation states its two purposes—learning how to use
Chat AI and finding past chats and topics—and offers entry points to browse tutorials and use
cases, which helps users who do not yet know what to ask. In short, the meta chat is a normal
conversation with special routing and special privileges, not a separate service.
3.2 What the assistant sees
The meta assistant can access every conversation and read every user-facing setting or control, so
it can answer questions about the workspace as a whole rather than about a pre-selected subset.
At the metadata level, the client supplies a structured, size-bounded view: conversation identifiers,
titles, topics, recency, and compact configuration descriptions; the topic list, current setting and
preference values, saved memories, the model catalogue, and theMeta Chat’s own settings. A
bounded context is therefore a packaging choice, not a restriction on what the assistant may access.
At the content level, the client adds short conversation summaries and, when a question needs
exact evidence, searches all stored message text locally and adds only the most relevant excerpts,
each tied to a citable message. Decision and comparison questions also receive a few recent excerpts.
Summaries are generated out of band when a conversation is left, so they can be missing, incomplete,
or stale; the prompt tells the model not to invent them.
This is a deliberate trade-off. It keeps context cost bounded and exposes less message content
than a full-history baseline, but recall is limited: details absent from both summaries and selected
excerpts remain invisible, and lexical search depends on wording. The prototype is therefore a
hybrid of metadata access, summary and selective message retrieval, and confirmed mutation rather
than a hierarchical or semantic retriever.
3.3 Grounding references and feature help
The system prompt constrains the assistant in two ways. References must use internal links whose
identifiers come only from the supplied context: links to a conversation, an exact message, a topic, a
persona, or a settings tab. The renderer recognises these routes and navigates inside the application,
scrolling to and briefly highlighting the target. References therefore act as direct routes into the
workspace, not mere citations. The assistant must also stay within the supplied context and must
not invent conversations, topics, messages, memories, personas, or preference values.
The assistant additionally receives a machine-readable catalogue of interface features, each with
a description, keywords, and guided-tour steps that target real controls. It can explain a feature in
prose and attach a marker that the client turns into an optional step-by-step tour. Feature help is
therefore not only textual: it can hand the user over to the relevant part of the interface.
3.4 Tutorials, settings, preferences, and navigation
The feature catalogue also powers a browsable tutorial library, reachable from the banner or by
name. This turns feature help from something the user must know how to ask for into something
they can browse, which matters for unfamiliar or infrequently used capabilities. Figures 1 and 2
show the library and a tutorial in progress.
8
title: The Power of Meta Access in the Software of the Future --- Demonstrated on LLM Chat UIs and Chat AI

text:

text:
Guidance is not limited to prose. For a settings question, the assistant can explain where the
control is and offer to open the relevant panel and highlight it (Figure 3). Opening a panel is
navigation; changing a value is a separate mutation that the user must confirm.
Figure 3: Routing a settings question to the interface, shown with synthetic data. The answer
names the control, offers to open the settings panel, and starts a tour that highlights the gear icon.
Navigation remains read-only; changing the value is a separate confirmed proposal.
Meta access also covers the current value of any preference, not only the location of its control.
For a memory question, the assistant reports the current configuration and offers to open the
corresponding settings page (Figure 4). A proposed change is shown as a warning card and is
applied only after explicit confirmation.
Figure 4: Reading current preference values in theMeta Chat, shown with synthetic data. The
answer prints the user’s memory settings, offers to open the corresponding settings page, and can
propose a value change. A change is applied only after an explicit confirmation and can be reverted
while the resulting state still matches.
The same link vocabulary covers the workspace itself: a reference can point to a conversation, an
exact message, or the topic that contains it, so the user can open either the item or its surrounding
10

text:
context. This is particularly useful for re-finding, where a title alone may be ambiguous but its
topic supplies orientation and a message citation resolves the exact statement (Figure 5).
Figure 5: Navigating conversations and topics in theMeta Chat, shown with synthetic data. The
answer links to the cited conversation and to its topic; the sidebar highlights both targets so the
user can see where the link will lead.
3.5 Persona catalogue and handoff
Personas extend meta access beyond the user’s conversations to a curated configuration space.
A persona bundles a title, description, model, sampling parameters, and a system prompt. The
sidebar’sChat with Personaaction opens a library grouped by category; selecting an entry imports
it as a new chat and applies its settings.
TheMeta Chattreats the catalogue as metadata. When a request matches a persona, the
assistant names it, explains why it fits, and emits a link that the renderer turns into a start action.
Clicking is an explicit user decision: the client fetches the definition, creates the conversation, and
applies the configuration (Figure 6). The assistant neither reads the prompt nor executes the import,
so the handoff does not give it control over the definition.
This division is deliberate. It gives the user a one-click path from an intent to a configured
conversation without exposing an untrusted system prompt to the assistant or letting the model
change settings on its own. The cost is that the recommendation is only as good as the catalogue’s
metadata: a poorly described persona is hard to find, and a stale entry can promise behaviour it no
longer implements.
3.6 Persistence, privacy, and scope
Because the meta conversation is stored in the same local database as ordinary chats, meta access
inherits the client’s local-first model: conversation data stays in the browser, and the hidden meta
conversation can be exported and re-imported. At the same time, the meta flow sends titles, topics,
summaries, selected excerpts, memories, persona metadata, the model catalogue, and relevant
setting and preference values to the configured model endpoint. Metadata is less sensitive than
complete messages, but selected excerpts are still message content, and titles, summaries, memories,
and settings can reveal a great deal. Starting a persona also fetches its definition from an external
repository, a request that should be visible in the interface.
The assistant can read and propose changes to essentially any control or setting, including
conversation organisation, preferences, per-chat configuration, and memories. It never executes

a mutation directly. Every mutating change is presented in the UI as a proposal, and the client
applies it only after the user explicitly consents. After applying, revert is allowed only while the
current state still matches what was applied. A visible audit log remains future work.
4 A Ladder of Meta Access
Table 2 separates capabilities that are often conflated in discussions of “chat with your app”. Each
level adds power and risk. The ladder is not specific to chat: it applies to any stateful application
that exposes a workspace model and a capability layer. It assumes, however, an application with a
bounded purpose and a host that enforces the capability layer from outside the assistant; Section 4.6
relaxes both assumptions for general-purpose agentic harnesses. The key boundary is mutation:
levels 1–3 read, explain, and navigate, whereas level 4 is the first level that changes workspace state
through the assistant, including settings and preferences. Level 5 composes such changes. Within
the read-only levels, level 2 stays at metadata about conversations, whereas level 3 crosses into
conversation content, first through summaries and then through exact message spans. A user-invoked
handoff, such as clicking a recommended persona, is a boundary case: it creates a new chat, but the
assistant only retrieves and links, and the user performs the import. The guardrail contracts in
Section 6.4 apply at every level: evidence and target validation for levels 1–2, provenance and scope
for level 3, and confirmation, reversibility, and audit for levels 4–5. The implemented prototype
now covers levels 1–3 and a substantial part of level 4: it searches message text with citations and
performs confirmed, reversible changes to chats, settings, and memories. Level 5 remains future
work, although the prototype can already group several proposed changes into one confirmation
card and apply a setting to all chats.

4.1 Level 1: tutoring
Feature tutoring is the lowest-risk form of meta access and the one most directly implemented. The
assistant explains where a control is, what it does, and in what order to use it. The guided-tour
mechanism closes the loop between explanation and interface by highlighting the relevant element.
The tutorial library extends the same mechanism from on-demand help to browsable instruction:
users can see which tours exist and start one without first formulating a question. This addresses a
persistent problem in feature-rich applications: users do not know what they do not know. A chat
that can answer “what can I do here?” lowers the cost of discovery without requiring the user to
leave the conversation. Figure 1 shows the browsable tutorial entry point that implements this level.
4.2 Level 2: metadata, settings, and preference access
Level 2 is read-only and stays at metadata about conversations and the interface; it does not read
conversation content. Metadata retrieval supports questions about the whole workspace: which
conversations exist, their titles and topics, when they were last touched, and where to find them.
This is the prototype’s “where is my food-order chat?” use case. The answer is useful only if it
is grounded and actionable: the assistant must cite a real conversation or topic and provide a
link that navigates to it. Grounding turns a plausible-sounding answer into a verifiable one, and
the navigation link turns retrieval into a one-click outcome. The prototype also links to settings
and reads the current values behind any control, so a preference or configuration question can
be answered in the conversation without opening the panel. These are still read-only moves: the
assistant opens a view or reports a value, but the user makes the change. Figure 5 shows a metadata
answer that links both the conversation and its surrounding topic.
Persona recommendation sits at the same level but extends retrieval to a catalogue the user did
not create. The assistant sees only titles, categories, and descriptions, and recommends an entry
13
title: The Power of Meta Access in the Software of the Future --- Demonstrated on LLM Chat UIs and Chat AI

text:
when one clearly matches the request. The link it emits is a user-invoked handoff: clicking it imports
the full definition and starts a new chat. The assistant does not read the persona prompt, choose
the model, or apply the settings itself. This keeps the recommendation separate from the user’s
explicit import decision while turning it into a concrete starting point. It also means that persona
quality is a retrieval problem: the catalogue must be well described, fresh, and free of duplicate or
misleading entries.
Metadata retrieval is also a natural fit for a conversational command palette. A user can ask in
their own words, in their own language, without knowing the exact title. The assistant can reason
over titles, topic names, and recency, and can explain why it chose a result. This is more forgiving
than substring search, but also less predictable, which is why citations and links matter.
4.3 Level 3: conversation content and message-level retrieval
Metadata is a lossy index. Some content questions, such as“What did we decide about the budget?”,
may be answered from a summary; others, such as“Where was the Fork-Join-Modell discussed?”,
need the exact message. Summaries provide a compressed first form of content access, but they
may omit the exact statement. The prototype therefore implements message-level retrieval as well:
it runs a local lexical search over stored message text using the current user message, adds the most
relevant excerpts with conversation and message identifiers to the context, and renders citations
that open and highlight the exact message. For decision, action-item, and comparison questions it
also adds recent excerpts from the most recent conversations. This extends the prototype beyond
summary-only retrieval while keeping context bounded and exposing only selected spans. Figure 7
shows the second kind of query resolving to a chat and two exact-message citations.
Figure 7: Message-level retrieval in theMeta Chat, shown with synthetic data. The user asks
where the “Fork-Join-Modell” was discussed; the answer identifies the chatOpenMP Basics for
Beginnersand offers exact-message citations that open and highlight the source.
The current implementation is deliberately simpler than the principled design we propose for
the next step. It does not yet narrow candidates through a metadata hierarchy, use embeddings or
hybrid semantic search, or relax recency truncation for older chats. Those changes would improve
recall and make the retrieval depth depend on the question rather than on a single global cap. The
implemented path already provides the citation discipline and the clear message-level boundary
that such a retriever needs.

text:
4.4 Level 4: confirmed mutating actions
Level 4 is the first level that changes workspace state. Unlike the read-only links and preference
printouts of level 2, a confirmed action performs a mutation. The prototype implements a first
version: it renames or moves a conversation, creates a topic as part of a move, changes global
preferences, changes per-chat settings for one or all chats, and adds, edits, deletes, or clears memories.
Per-chat settings include the model, temperature, top_p, reasoning effort, memory-mode override,
tools, and web-search flags. Settings count as mutations, as do memory changes. Opening the
settings panel remains navigation (level 2); changing a value is a mutation (level 4).
These actions are expressed as typed, narrowly scoped proposals and validated on the client.
The assistant never executes them directly. Instead, the card below the message shows the target
object, the old and new values where available, a warning icon, and an explicit accept action. After
applying, a revert action is available only if the current state still matches what was applied; the
check prevents overwriting intervening manual edits. This provides confirmation and conditional
reversibility. Still missing are a durable audit log, topic rename and deletion, chat deletion and
export, and archival operations. Figure 8 shows the read, propose, and confirm cycle for per-chat
settings, and Figure 9 shows a workspace-wide model audit that precedes a bulk change.
Figure 8: Reading and changing per-chat settings in theMeta Chat, shown with synthetic data.
The assistant reports the model and temperature of theLLM Evaluationchat, then proposes a
model change in a warning card with an explicitAccept changesaction.
Confirmation is not a bureaucratic extra. It protects against the failure mode that makes agentic
interfaces frustrating: a confident but wrong action on personal data. A good interaction shows the
proposed change, the target object, and the expected effect before execution. For bulk operations,
a preview is essential; the prototype lists every proposed change and supports applying the same
per-chat setting to all chats.

4.5 Level 5: orchestration
At the top of the ladder, the assistant composes multiple actions: “group the chats from last week
by project, rename generic titles, and archive the duplicates.” This is the most powerful and the
most dangerous level. It requires planning, intermediate verification, the ability to stop and ask, and
a strong notion of scope. The prototype already lets the model place several typed changes—chat
moves, renames, settings, and memories—into one confirmation card, and it can apply a per-chat
setting to all chats. That is only composition with a single confirmation step, not full orchestration.
We expect level 5 to be appropriate only with permissioning, dry runs, and the ability to review a
diff of proposed changes.
4.6 Reflexive meta access in agentic harnesses
The ladder assumes an application with a bounded purpose and a host that enforces the capability
layer from outside the assistant. A general-purpose agentic harness such as OpenCode [17] violates
both assumptions. It is not a chat client with a fixed workspace: it is a runtime for arbitrary tasks,
repositories, models, and tools. Its state is the task environment, and its own configuration—model
and prompt selection, tool and server registries, permission and sandbox policy, hooks, subagents,
and project instructions—is a control plane rather than a purpose-specific application metamodel.
Mechanically, self-configuration still traverses the ladder: reading configuration, logs, or session
metadata is level 2 or 3; a single setting change is level 4; and composing persistent changes across
model, tools, and permissions is level 5. The risk is not captured by the autonomy level alone.
We therefore distinguish the target of a change from the level of autonomy. A behavioural setting
(verbosity or temperature) is ordinary level 4; a state setting (memory or retention) carries level-3
privacy consequences; a capability setting (tools, servers, plugins, or network access) changes what
the assistant can do in future; and an authority setting (permissions, approval policy, sandbox, or
16
title: The Power of Meta Access in the Software of the Future --- Demonstrated on LLM Chat UIs and Chat AI

text:
hooks) changes who can approve actions and what can be observed. The last two are control-plane
mutations, and the last is self-escalation.
We call confirmed self-configurationlevel 4S(self) and persistent, autonomous reconfiguration
level 5S. These labels combine a level with a target; they are not new rungs on the same axis. Level
4S with a behavioural target is mild, whereas level 4S with an authority target is more dangerous
than many level-5 workspace actions. A harness must not let the assistant approve its own authority
changes at any level. Runtime enforcement frameworks such as ClawGuard [55] locate the check at
the tool-call boundary, which is where a harness must enforce capability and authority scopes. The
assistant may propose a diff, but a separate policy layer or a human should apply it out of band
after showing the effect on current and future sessions. Authority, capability, and persistent settings
need an immutable audit trail, scoped activation, a dry run, and clear rollback semantics; changes
that take effect only after a restart must say so.
A further complication is that harness configuration often lives in ordinary files. If the harness
also exposes generic file-editing or shell tools, the assistant can change its settings without using a
typed capability at all, bypassing the confirmation, validation, and audit that the ladder assumes.
The classification therefore has to follow the capability actually used, not the file path or the setting’s
name. The safe design is to keep the authority and capability control plane outside the agent’s
writable scope, or to treat edits to it as a distinct, strongly guarded capability.
5 Why Meta Access Matters Across Interfaces
5.1 Search versus find
Users often do not have a query; they have an intention. Classical search assumes the user can
express a keyword. Conversational meta access lets the user describe the memory instead:“the
chat where we compared two travel options”. The assistant can map that description onto titles,
summaries, and topics, ask a clarifying question if needed, and return a small set of candidates with
links. This is retrieval as a dialogue rather than a one-shot query, and it can recover from ambiguity
instead of returning an empty result page.
5.2 Navigation and orientation
A chat client with hundreds of conversations is a spatial interface: users remember where things
were. Meta access can answer orientation questions (“what did I work on last week?”, “which
topics are unused?”) and navigate directly to a target. It can also explain the organisation of the
workspace, which is otherwise implicit in a sidebar tree. This is particularly valuable for infrequent
users, who must re-learn the layout each time they return.
5.3 Feature discovery and onboarding
Feature-rich applications accumulate controls that most users never touch. A meta assistant
that knows the feature catalogue can act as an always-available onboarding layer: it explains,
demonstrates, and guides. Because the catalogue is data rather than hard-coded prose, it can evolve
with the interface, and because the guidance is anchored to real elements, it can be verified by
running the tour. The prototype’s tutorial library and feature guides are a concrete instance of
this idea: the user can browse what is available or ask for help in natural language. The persona
catalogue extends discovery from features to configurations: a user who describes a goal can be
handed a ready-made setup instead of being told which controls to change.
17
title: The Power of Meta Access in the Software of the Future --- Demonstrated on LLM Chat UIs and Chat AI

text:
5.4 Composition across features
The most interesting potential is composition. A single request can span retrieval, navigation, and
configuration:“Find the chat about the conference, move it to Travel, and switch it to the model
with the long context.”A milder form already exists: recommend a persona, then let the user start
it with one click. No single screen supports the full sequence. A meta layer can, provided that each
step is grounded, permissioned, and visible. Composition is where chat stops being a help window
and becomes an interface in its own right.
5.5 Accessibility and inclusion
Natural-language access can lower barriers for users who find hierarchical menus, small controls, or
dense settings panels difficult. It can also help users who are not fluent in the interface’s language,
since the assistant can answer in the user’s language and translate intent into the correct controls.
The deeper accessibility argument is that meta access provides a readable interface to application
state. Screen readers such as JAWS [47] already do this for graphical interfaces: they consume
accessibility APIs and present a structured, navigable description of widgets and content to blind and
low-vision users. Model-based approaches to LLM-driven accessible interfaces pursue a related goal
[48]. Meta access extends the same principle from widget-level descriptions to semantic application
state and operations: the assistant can say which conversations and topics exist, read current
settings, explain a feature, and offer a grounded next step. For a blind user, this is a usable
description of the workspace; for a user with a motor impairment, it replaces precise pointing with
intent; for a user with a cognitive or language barrier, it can simplify navigation and explain controls
in plain language.
The prototype already contains the ingredients: tutorials provide readable, step-by-step guidance;
metadata and links support orientation; preference readouts avoid hunting through panels; personas
lower configuration burden; and confirmed proposals make changes inspectable before they are
applied. These benefits are not automatic. Meta access must not replace accessibility compliance,
keyboard navigation, or proper accessibility APIs, and it should respect the same permissions and
expose the same structure that a screen reader sees rather than bypassing it. Latency, error recovery,
and the risk of a confident but wrong answer matter more, not less, when the assistant is the user’s
primary route into the interface; the textual interface must remain fully usable on its own.
5.6 From chat to AI-era interfaces
The chat client is a convenient first demonstrator, not the limit of the pattern. An IDE can expose
its project model, run configurations, and diagnostics; a spreadsheet can expose sheets, ranges,
formulas, and chart definitions; a dashboard can expose widgets, filters, and data sources; an
operating system can expose files, applications, and settings. These are the applications’ existing
internal models, not a new parallel representation; the meta layer exposes them through a common
contract. In each case the same three ingredients recur: a workspace model that the assistant can
inspect, a capability layer that declares what may be read or changed, and evidence and consent
contracts that keep the assistant grounded and the user in control. The chat-specific parts of the
prototype, i.e., tutorials, personas, and conversation links, are instances of these ingredients, not
the ingredients themselves. We therefore propose that AI-era interfaces should expose such a meta
layer as a default part of their architecture, in the same way that they expose an API, a settings
model, or an accessibility layer.
18

text:
6 Designing for Whole-Interface Access
6.1 A portable meta-access contract
The design should not depend on the chat surface. A portable meta layer needs four pieces: a
workspace model, ideally derived from the application’s own metamodel; a typed capability registry;
an evidence and consent contract; and an evaluation surface. Applications can implement these
pieces with different data models, transports, and vocabularies; the assistant should see the same
shape. Standardising the contract would let one assistant work across applications without bespoke
integrations, and would let users compare and audit behaviour. The prototype realizes these pieces
for a chat client; the same pieces apply to other applications.
6.2 Reuse application metamodels
An assistant that works across arbitrary applications needs a model of each application, not only a
screenshot or a prompt. Most applications already have one. A debugger is the clearest precedent:
it exposes internal objects, call stacks, and controlled mutations through a typed interface, without
pretending that the program is a flat text buffer. Meta access can generalize the same idea. Instead
of inventing a parallel description of the interface, the meta layer should derive its workspace model
and capability registry from the application’s existing metamodel—its document model, project
model, schema, scene graph, or component tree—and expose a stable, permissioned subset to the
assistant. The hard problem is not inventing a metamodel but choosing a minimal, versioned,
permissioned view and mapping it consistently across applications.
A general-purpose agentic harness has no single application metamodel to reuse. Its workspace
model is task-relative, and its stable part is the capability registry and the policy that governs
it. For such systems, the portable contract should expose three layers instead: the task context
(repository, files, and running processes), the available capabilities and their scopes, and the harness
configuration that determines future capabilities. The first layer is application-like, the second is
the capability model described below, and the third is a control plane: it should be readable and
proposable, but not self-applied when it touches authority.
6.3 Model the interface as capabilities
An action-capable meta layer needs an explicit capability model rather than a giant prompt. Each
capability should declare its inputs, its target object type, its preconditions, whether it is read-only
or mutating, whether it is reversible, and what confirmation it requires. The model’s job is to select
and fill capabilities, not to manipulate the DOM. A typed capability layer keeps the assistant honest
and makes the same capabilities available to buttons, keyboard shortcuts, and the chat. This follows
the tool-use pattern demonstrated by API-calling agents [20, 29]. The persona catalogue illustrates
the split: reading persona metadata is a retrieval capability, whereas instantiating a persona is a
separate, mutating capability that the user confirms by clicking a link.
6.4 Guardrails as evidence and authority contracts
The guardrails we propose are not content filters. They constrain what the meta layer may claim,
cite, disclose, and change. Each capability should declare a contract with six parts: its evidence
source, its permitted scope, how its target is validated, what it discloses, what confirmation it
requires, and what it does when the contract cannot be satisfied. The contract is enforced by the
client and the capability layer, not only by the system prompt. A prompt can ask the model not to

text:
invent an identifier; only code can reject a missing ID, a stale deep link, an out-of-scope chat, or an
unconfirmed mutation.
Table 3 maps these contracts onto the main capability families. For message-level search, the
critical boundary is evidence: the answer must distinguish a summary from a message span, cite
exact messages, and respect the same permissions as the workspace. For navigation and tutoring,
the critical boundary is the target: the assistant must resolve the live interface state, validate
routes, highlight real controls, and explain unavailability instead of inventing a setting. Persona
recommendation adds a supply-chain boundary: only catalogue metadata enters the meta context,
and the definition stays untrusted until the user starts it. Preference reads should be timestamped
snapshots of actual values, and mutations should require preview, confirmation, and undo.

The contracts scale with the ladder. Levels 1–2 need evidence and target validation. Level 3
adds provenance and scope controls over message content. Levels 4–5 add preview, confirmation,
reversibility, and audit. A multi-step plan at level 5 should be checked against the contracts at
every step, not only at the end, and a failed contract should produce an explicit refusal or a request
for clarification rather than a confident fallback.
6.5 Retrieval hierarchy and freshness
The context strategy should be tiered. Level 2 uses the metadata catalogue, the persona catalogue,
and setting and preference values. Level 3 adds summaries and a searchable index over message
text and attachments, with metadata as a pre-filter. This mirrors the retrieve-then-generate pattern
of retrieval-augmented generation [13, 10]. Freshness should be visible: the assistant should know
when a summary was generated and should prefer message-level evidence when the summary is old
or the question is specific. Size bounds should be explained rather than silent; if a query needs
material outside the assembled view, the assistant should say so and retrieve further.
20
title: The Power of Meta Access in the Software of the Future --- Demonstrated on LLM Chat UIs and Chat AI

text:
6.6 Grounding, citation, and uncertainty
Every factual claim about the workspace should be traceable. Links to conversations are the minimal
form of citation. Persona recommendations should name only catalogue entries and link to their
definitions so the user can inspect the source before starting. Message-level retrieval should cite
message identifiers or snippets. Preference answers should name the settings section and, where
possible, link to it so the user can verify the value. When evidence is missing, the assistant should
say so and offer a next step (search full text, broaden the time range, or ask the user). Calibrated
uncertainty is more useful than confident fabrication, especially when the user is about to act on
the answer [2].
6.7 Confirmation, permissions, and reversibility
Actions should follow a principle of least authority. Reading metadata, reading message content,
reading preference values, and mutating state are distinct permissions. Bulk actions should require
stronger confirmation than single-object actions. Destructive actions should be reversible or explicitly
confirmed. The assistant should show a preview of the change and a diff where applicable, and the
user should be able to undo. These are standard software-safety principles applied to a new kind of
actor [12, 2].
6.8 Prompt injection and untrusted content
A meta assistant reads content the user did not write, including model output, imported chats, and
document text. That content is untrusted and may contain instructions aimed at the assistant. If
the assistant can act, injected text could try to trigger actions. Defences include treating retrieved
content as data rather than instructions, separating the instruction channel from the content channel,
restricting tools by scope, requiring confirmation for mutations, and never allowing retrieved text to
expand the assistant’s permissions [21, 11, 5]. Personas add a second boundary: their definitions are
third-party content and their system prompts can contain instructions. Keeping those prompts out
of the meta assistant’s context, and importing them only in a separate user-started chat, prevents a
persona from steering the meta layer that recommends it.
7 Risks and Open Problems
Hallucinated workspace facts.A model that is asked about personal data will sometimes
confabulate a title or a topic. Grounding constraints and citations reduce but do not eliminate this.
Evaluation must measure precision of references, not only fluency.
Summary loss and staleness.Summaries are compressed, generated by a model, and may lag
behind edits. The prototype already acknowledges this in its prompt. A production system needs
freshness signals, backfills, and a retrieval path that can bypass summaries when precision matters.
Context and cost limits.Size bounds on the assembled context are necessary but introduce
silent blind spots. Users need to know when material has been omitted, and the system should
degrade gracefully (for example by saying that some older material is outside the current view).
21
title: The Power of Meta Access in the Software of the Future --- Demonstrated on LLM Chat UIs and Chat AI

text:
Privacy and data minimisation.Sending metadata, settings, and preference values to a model
endpoint is a real disclosure. Local-first designs can keep more processing on the client, and
deployments should make the boundary explicit. Memories deserve particular care because they are
curated personal facts rather than incidental text. Persona titles and descriptions also leave the
machine, and starting a persona fetches its definition from an external repository, so the interface
should distinguish local data from catalogue traffic.
Persona catalogue trust.A shared persona repository is convenient but introduces supply-chain
risk. Titles and descriptions can be stale, duplicated, or deliberately misleading; a definition
can specify an unexpected model or sampling parameters, and its system prompt may contain
instructions that conflict with the host application. The meta assistant should recommend only
catalogue metadata, the start action should show the persona’s source and configuration, and
imported definitions should be treated as untrusted content. Ranking and freshness signals are part
of the retrieval problem, not just a presentation detail.
Standardisation and cross-application scope.If every application invents its own meta layer,
assistants will remain bespoke integrations. A common capability description, permission model,
and audit format would make meta access portable, but it also raises cross-application questions:
what happens when one request spans an IDE, a browser, and a chat client, and which application
owns consent? These are open design and governance problems, not only engineering details.
Metamodel exposure and coupling.Reusing internal application models exposes details
that may be unstable, implementation-specific, or sensitive. A debugger-like interface must define
which internals are stable enough to expose, how to version them, and how to avoid leaking
secrets or bypassing application permissions. Coupling the assistant to internal models also creates
maintenance work as applications evolve.
Reflexive configuration and self-escalation.A general-purpose harness such as OpenCode
[17] can change its own model, tools, prompts, permissions, and hooks. If it can do so through a
generic file or shell tool, it can bypass a typed setting capability entirely. Changes to authority or
capability can persist across sessions, alter what the assistant is allowed to do, and propagate to
subagents; confirmation by the same assistant is not a meaningful control. The policy layer must sit
outside the assistant’s writable scope, changes that touch authority must be approved out of band
and audited, and activation should be explicit, preferably with a restart and a rollback path.
Automation bias and loss of overview.If the chat becomes the primary entry point, users
may stop learning the interface and may over-trust its answers. The textual interface must remain
first-class, the assistant must be interruptible, and its actions must be visible.
Evaluation.There is no standard benchmark for meta access. We need task suites built from
realistic workspaces, with known ground truth for retrieval and navigation, and user studies
that measure time, success, and trust. Safety evaluation must include adversarial titles, injected
summaries, and ambiguous requests.
22
title: The Power of Meta Access in the Software of the Future --- Demonstrated on LLM Chat UIs and Chat AI

text:
8 An Evaluation Agenda
We propose evaluating meta access along five axes: retrieval quality, task success, grounding and
calibration, safety and trust, and guardrail effectiveness.
Retrieval quality.Given a natural-language request, does the system return the correct conver-
sation or message, and does it avoid false positives? Useful metrics include recall at smallk, mean
reciprocal rank, and reference precision (the fraction of cited identifiers that exist and are relevant).
For personas, measure recommendation precision (did the suggested persona fit the stated goal?)
and handoff correctness (does the link start the definition it names?).
Task success.Can the user complete a real task—find a chat, understand a topic, read a preference,
find a suitable persona, change a setting—with fewer steps and less time than the baseline interface?
Measures include task completion, time on task, number of turns, and abandonment.
Grounding and calibration.When the answer is wrong, does the system say so? We can
measure the agreement between stated confidence and correctness, and the rate of fabricated
references under missing or stale data. For preference questions, measure whether the printed values
match the client’s current settings when the answer is produced. Context construction is part of
that outcome: Bousetouane [57] argues that agents often fail through context failure and proposes
criteria for guardrail coverage, instruction consistency, tool-schema quality, grounding sufficiency,
and injection hardening. These criteria apply directly to the bounded catalogue and excerpt pipeline
of the prototype.
Safety and trust.For action-capable features, measure the rate of unintended actions, the
effectiveness of confirmation, recovery after undo, and susceptibility to prompt injection from
retrieved content. For read-only features, measure privacy leakage and user comfort with metadata,
message excerpts, and setting and preference disclosure. Persona studies should include adversarial
catalogue descriptions and definitions, and check that the meta assistant never receives or repeats
the persona’s system prompt.
Guardrail effectiveness.Each contract in Table 3 should be evaluated as a mechanism, not only
as a prompt instruction. Measure the unsupported-claim rate, citation correctness, stale-link rate,
scope violations, and disclosure accuracy for read-only features. For navigation, measure whether
deep links resolve to the intended target and whether unavailable controls are explained correctly.
For mutations, measure confirmation compliance, preview accuracy, undo success, and the rate of
actions that violate declared permissions. Adversarial tests should attempt to bypass the client-side
checks, not only the system prompt.
Reflexive configuration.For harnesses, measure whether a proposed self-change is scoped,
previewed, and reversible; whether it persists across sessions; whether it expands tools, permissions,
or approval scope; and whether it propagates to subagents. Test bypasses through generic file
and shell tools, not only through the typed setting capability. A useful benchmark is a set of
configuration changes whose effects on future capability are known, including changes that look
benign in a diff but alter authority after a restart.
Ablations should compare summaries only, full-text retrieval, and hybrid retrieval; different
catalogue sizes and recency caps; fresh versus stale summaries and personas; and small versus large
23
title: The Power of Meta Access in the Software of the Future --- Demonstrated on LLM Chat UIs and Chat AI

text:
models. Longitudinal studies are important because the value of meta access depends on the size
and age of a user’s workspace.
9 Conclusion
TheMeta Chatprototype shows that a chat assistant can already serve as a useful access layer
over a chat application: it can explain features, run tutorials, retrieve conversations from metadata,
search message text with citations, recommend personas, read current preference values and per-chat
settings, ground its answers in links to chats, messages, topics, settings, and personas, and guide
users back into the interface. It also performs confirmed, reversible changes to chats, settings, and
memories. That covers levels 1–3 and a substantial part of level 4 of the ladder. The prototype
already turns the chat from a window onto a workspace into a natural-language entry point to the
application; full level-5 orchestration would extend that entry point from confirmed single steps to
composed, reviewable workflows.
Chat is not the only interface for LLMs, and general-purpose agentic harnesses such as OpenCode
[17] are the right choice for many tasks that operate on repositories, shells, or other external
environments. Such a harness is not an application with a fixed purpose: its workspace is the
task, and its own configuration is a control plane. If it can change that configuration, meta access
becomes reflexive, so authority changes need a separate out-of-band boundary rather than a level-4S
confirmation by the same assistant. But the chat client remains one durable home for everyday
conversation and for the personal workspace that accumulates around it. Meta access is what lets
the assistant serve that workspace rather than only the current dialogue.
The opportunity is substantial: conversational search, navigation, onboarding, organisation,
and composition in one place. So is the responsibility. The same properties that make meta
access powerful—personal data, compressed context, model-generated summaries, and the ability to
act—make grounding, privacy, confirmation, and reversibility essential design requirements rather
than polish. Guardrails turn those requirements into explicit evidence and authority contracts that
the client can enforce and evaluation can test. That is what lets meta access turn the chat interface
from a window onto a single conversation into a conversational control layer for the whole workspace,
extending chat toward agentic capability without giving up explicit user control. We hope this draft
contributes a useful vocabulary and an evaluation agenda for building that future carefully.
The broader proposal is that meta access should become a default property of AI-era interfaces,
not an optional feature of chat clients. The chat prototype shows that the pattern is practical:
a workspace model, grounded links, a capability layer, and consent-gated mutations can coexist
in a real application. Accessibility is a direct beneficiary: a readable, permissioned model of
an application can complement screen readers such as JAWS [47] and reduce reliance on precise
pointing, visual search, or memorised navigation. The next step is to turn each application’s existing
metamodel into a stable, permissioned meta-access interface, so the same contract works across
IDEs, dashboards, office suites, and operating systems, and to evaluate it as an interface property
rather than a single product feature.

MedGraph: Maintaining Patient State with Graph Memory for Long-Term
Medical Dialogue
Donghua Zhang1† Zizheng Wang2* Ze Dong1* Yiding Feng3* Siyu Qian4
1University of Michigan 2Georgetown University
3Johns Hopkins University 4Harvard University
Abstract
LLM-based medical assistants that follow a pa-
tient across visits need a memory that keeps
the patient’s clinical state correct as it changes.
We examine the errors of five memory systems
on longitudinal medical dialogue and find three
recurring causes: the retrieved evidence gives
an outdated state, includes another person’s
health facts, or lacks a safety fact the answer
depends on. We present MedGraph, a graph
memory built for these three cases. Construc-
tion extracts dated facts from each session, at-
tributes each fact to the person it describes, and
links medication, diagnosis, and measurement
records into chains that keep earlier states. Re-
trieval ranks the patient’s chains as units, reads
each chain at the time the question asks about,
and adds the original dialogue text; a patient
profile lists every recorded safety fact with ev-
ery question. On MedMemoryBench, Med-
Graph has the highest overall accuracy with
both a GPT and a Qwen backbone, 10.5 and
10.4 points above the strongest of five base-
lines, with efficient memory construction and
answering in the GPT setting.
1 Introduction
LLM-based healthcare agents increasingly support
care across multiple visits, including chronic dis-
ease management and medication guidance (Wang
et al., 2026). They must track the patient’s current
medications and reported allergies, since recom-
mending a discontinued medication or overlooking
an allergy can lead to unsafe advice. Reliable LLM
agents therefore need long-term memory that keeps
patient records accurate and up to date across visits.
General-purpose LLM memory systems include
retrieval-based methods such as RAG (Lewis et al.,
2020), graph-based methods such as GraphRAG
(Edge et al., 2024), and agentic approaches such as
*Equal contribution.
†Corresponding author:donghua@umich.edu
Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025). These systems dif-
fer in how they construct memory, including what
they retain and how they organize or update it, and
how they retrieve evidence for answering. For ex-
ample, Mem0 extracts and updates conversational
facts, while GraphRAG builds an entity-relation
graph and community summaries. RAG retrieves
similar passages, whereas GraphRAG uses graph-
derived summaries. Despite these advances, recent
benchmarks report difficulties in reasoning across
medical dialogue sessions (Hu et al., 2026; Zhang
et al., 2026), and memory accuracy declines as dis-
tracting sessions accumulate (Wang et al., 2026).
To examine failures in memory construction and
retrieval, we analyze errors from five representative
memory systems. This analysis reveals three chal-
lenges in longitudinal medical dialogue (Figure 1).
(1) State validity.The same clinical item can
have different values or states over time. Some
memory systems, such as Mem0, overwrite or dis-
card earlier records when new information arrives
(Chhikara et al., 2025). The stored memory may
then lack the records needed to answer historical
questions. Other systems, such as MemOS, can
retain a relevant record without marking it as cur-
rent in the retrieved evidence. In 24 of the 150
sampled failures, the evidence contained only an
outdated state or left the current state unclear. A
medical memory must preserve past states and iden-
tify which state applies at the relevant time.
(2) Subject attribution.Longitudinal medical
dialogue may contain health information about mul-
tiple subjects. Without clear attribution, clinical
information about a subject other than the patient
may be mistaken for the patient’s own. In 108 of
the sampled failures, the evidence contained such
information. Each clinical fact therefore needs an
explicit link to the subject it describes.
(3) Safety prioritization.Safety information
can constrain decisions across later visits. For ex-
ample, a documented allergy may affect a subse-

we found that the evidence omitted a safety fact
needed for the answer. The memory must therefore
keep safety-critical information available for later
clinical decisions.
Motivated by these findings, we propose Med-
Graph, a multi-layer memory with raw dialogues
(L1), a clinical fact graph (L2), and a patient profile
(L3). During construction, we extract each session
into typed fact nodes that record the subject and
event date while preserving values and units. Su-
persedes edges connect successive records of the
same clinical item, including medication changes
and repeated measurements. Causal edges link re-
lated facts within a session. At retrieval time, we
rank the patient’s chains as units, along with facts
outside chains. Every answer also receives the
patient profile so that important details, including
safety constraints, remain available to the answer-
ing model.
We evaluate MedGraph on MedMemoryBench
against five existing memory systems using two
backbones. MedGraph achieves the highest over-
all accuracy with both backbones, exceeding the
strongest baseline by 10.5 percentage points with
GPT and 10.4 with Qwen.
Our contributions are as follows:
• We analyze failures in longitudinal medical dia-
logue and formulate three memory requirements:
state validity, subject attribution, and safety pri-
oritization.
• We introduce MedGraph, a multi-layer memory
that links subject-attributed clinical facts into
dated chains. Its patient profile accompanies ev-
ery answer.
• We show consistent accuracy gains across two
backbones, with efficient memory construction
and answering in the GPT setting.
2 Related Work
Memory for LLM agents.External memory ex-
tends an agent’s context through evidence retrieval
(Lewis et al., 2020), memory tiers (Packer et al.,
2023), fact updates (Chhikara et al., 2025), and
linked notes (Xu et al., 2025). MemOS unifies
memory management (Li et al., 2025), MIRIX co-
ordinates specialized components (Wang and Chen,
2025), and LightMem uses compression and offline
consolidation to reduce costs (Fang et al., 2026).
Structured and temporal memory.GraphRAG
uses community summaries (Edge et al., 2024),
HippoRAG 2 retrieves passages and phrases
through a graph (Gutiérrez et al., 2025), and Panini
organizes memory around entities and events (Ra-
jesh et al., 2026). REMem links episodic gists with
time-scoped facts (Shu et al., 2026); Zep/Graphiti
tracks validity intervals and invalidates conflict-
ing relations while preserving history (Rasmussen
et al., 2025). MedGraph uses type-specific clinical
updates to distinguish state changes from repeated
observations.
Longitudinal clinical memory.Clinical extrac-
tion identifies negation, temporality, and experi-
encer (Harkema et al., 2009), with benchmarks
for medication extraction and temporal relations

text:
