and LongMemEval evaluate memory across ses-
sions (Maharana et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025);
MedMemoryBench (Wang et al., 2026) focuses
on longitudinal medical dialogue, including proxy
consultations.
Our work brings together persistent memory,
temporal state tracking, and clinical information
extraction to maintain patient information across
visits, with explicit subject attribution and safety
facts available regardless of query relevance.
3 Problem Setting
We consider a medical assistant that follows one
patient across many dialogue sessions. After each
session, it updates a memory that it can use to
answer questions about the history so far. The
dialogue may also discuss a relative’s health or a
general medical topic. If the patient describes their
father’s medication, that medication must remain
associated with the father.
The patient’s clinical state can change between
visits. A drug may be started, adjusted, and later
stopped, but an earlier dose may still be needed
to answer a question about the past. Blood pres-
sure readings also need their dates, since a new
reading does not make an earlier measurement in-
correct. The event date may differ from the session
date when a patient reports a change that happened
weeks earlier. The assistant must use the state that
applies to the time asked about.
Some information matters long after it was first
reported. An allergy mentioned early in the history
may affect a later prescription, even if the question
does not mention it. The memory must make such
safety information available when it is needed for
an answer.
Letst be the session received at step t, and let
Ht = (s 1,...,s t) be the history available at that
point. The system updates its memory as each
session arrives:
Mt =U(M t−1,s t).(1)
Memory updates use only sessions observed so
far, without access to future sessions or evaluation
questions. When a question q arrives, the system
retrieves evidence from its current memory, then
generates an answer:
Et,q =R(M t,q),ˆa t,q =G(q,E t,q).(2)
Here,U updates memory,R selects and assembles
evidence, andGgenerates the answer.
We seek evidence that concerns the target pa-
tient, reflects the time asked about, and includes
the safety information needed for the answer. We
call these requirementssubject attribution,state
validity, andsafety prioritization, respectively. In
controlled comparisons, we hold the answer model
G fixed to examine the effects of memory construc-
tion and retrieval.
To address these requirements, we introduce
MedGraph, our memory system for tracking patient
information across visits and selecting evidence to
answer questions about the patient’s history.
4 MedGraph
MedGraph builds a clinical fact graph from each
incoming session (Figure 2). Raw dialogue is re-
tained in L1 as source evidence. L2 links extracted
facts to the people they concern and the clinical
items they describe, such as medications, diag-
noses, or measured quantities. These items are
represented as entity nodes. At retrieval time, the
patient profile (L3) is rendered from the patient’s
L2 records and included with every question.
Construction uses one extraction call per ses-
sion. Retrieval selects graph records and adds their
source text. The answer model, called the reader,
receives this evidence and the profile, then answers
in one LLM call.
4.1 Memory construction (L1 to L2)
Each fact stores its typeτ, subjectσ, clinical entity
e (the item it describes), event date, and source ses-
sion and turn. Its content is one sentence preserving
reported numbers and units, with separate value,
unit, and status fields when available. Condition
facts describe diagnoses. Medication and condition
facts have status labels; safety facts have no status
field. Entities and persons have separate nodes, and
facts about the same entity are linked through its
entity node.
Extraction.Given a session, its date, and a fixed
prompt (Appendix A), the extractor returns JSON
with the session’s subject, clinical facts, and causal
links between those facts. The links become causal
edges in L2. Each fact is assigned to the person it
describes, not necessarily the speaker. For exam-
ple, a fact about the father’s medication is linked
to the father’s node, even when reported by the pa-
tient. General health information stays in L1 only.
Relative dates such as “two weeks ago” are cal-
culated from the session date, which is also used

Chains and repeated mentions.Each chain
groups facts with the same entity, subject, and type,
using the key (e,σ,τ) . The patient and another

4.2 Patient profile (L3)
The profile is rendered from the patient’s L2
records at retrieval time. It includes every safety
fact without truncation or retraction: allergies, con-
traindications, drug interactions, and surgical or
bleeding history.
Diagnosis- and medication-chain tails and key
preferences share a fixed budget. Stopped medica-
tions are listed separately from other medication
tails, including plans. The profile begins with the
latest available session date as the memory cutoff
and is included with every question without a rele-
vance check.
4.3 Retrieval
Every question uses the same retrieval pipeline.
The reader receives the full question. Section 6.1
compares this pipeline with simpler retrieval con-
trols.
Subject filtering and ranking.We rank only the
patient’s facts using BM25 and dense similarity.
Other people’s facts remain stored under their own
person nodes. Each chain counts as one retrieval
unit, while facts outside chains count individually.
Reciprocal rank fusion (Cormack et al., 2009) com-
bines the rankings, and the top eight units are re-
tained.
Chain context.Each selected chain supplies up
to three facts: the fact that triggered retrieval
(Matched), the record that applies to the time asked
about (Anchor), and the record the anchor super-
sedes (Relation). For medication and diagnosis
chains, the anchor’s stored validity interval must
cover the explicit question date; if no date is given,
the chain tail is used. Lab and vital anchors are
the latest measurements by event date up to the
requested time.
Expansion.We add up to four causal neighbors
of the matched facts. An explicit date containing a
year activates thedate channel, which adds patient
records from that date window, along with medi-
cation and diagnosis records whose stored validity
intervals cover the window’s start.
Rendering and answering.Each fact appears
on one line with its date and available status. We
mark superseded records and chain tails. For labs
and vitals, the latest-measurement label is assigned
using event dates. We include verbatim source win-
dows for the top three matched facts. The profile
and retrieved evidence fill the memory slot of the
fixed answer prompt, and the reader answers in one
LLM call. Appendix C gives the exact budgets and
retrieval limits.
5 Experiments
5.1 Setup
Benchmark.We evaluate MedGraph on 967
questions from MedMemoryBench (Wang et al.,
2026). Each history mixes about 100 patient ses-
sions with 200 distractor sessions about general
health or other people’s care. Sessions arrive in or-
der; questions follow every ten patient sessions and
concern the history available so far. The six types
are entity exact match (EEM), multiple choice
(MQ), temporal location accuracy (TLA), state up-
date accuracy (SUA), inference generation (IG),
and multi-hop clinical deduction (MCD). We re-
port per-type accuracy and their unweighted aver-
age (Avg.).
Baselines.We use five systems from MedMem-
oryBench with their default implementations and
settings.Embedding RAGretrieves the five most
similar dialogue chunks, each up to 4,096 tokens.
Mem0(Chhikara et al., 2025) extracts short mem-
ories and adds, updates, or deletes them;MemOS
(Li et al., 2025) stores extracted memories in a vec-
tor index; andLightMem(Fang et al., 2026) com-
presses topic segments into time-stamped entries.
REMem(Shu et al., 2026) stores time-stamped gists
and fact triples in a graph searched by an agent over
several steps.
In the GPT setting, gpt-6-luna builds LLM-
based memories and gpt-5.1 answers questions.
In the Qwen setting, Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-
2507 (Yang et al., 2025) does both. Embedding
RAG uses no construction LLM. All methods share
the answer prompt, judge, and embedder (Ap-
pendix D).
5.2 Results
MedGraph leads overall, especially on TLA and
IG.MedGraph has the highest Avg. and leads
on most question types, with the largest gains over
the best baseline on TLA and IG (Table 2). TLA
requires evidence from specific times; IG depends
on the patient’s conditions and medications. These
gains come from dated facts, the date channel, and
the profile (Section 6.1).

7 Conclusion
We presented MedGraph, a graph memory that
tracks clinical state changes, attributes facts to their
subjects, and includes safety facts with every ques-
tion. On MedMemoryBench, it leads with both
GPT and Qwen by 10.5 and 10.4 points over the
strongest baseline. Compared with retrieval over
raw sessions, more than half of the gain comes from
fact construction and the rest from retrieval. In the
GPT setting, MedGraph builds memory with one
extraction call per session, uses about half the con-
struction input tokens of Mem0 and REMem, and
has the shortest mean answering time. Future work
could link causes across visits to support multi-hop
questions.
Limitations
We evaluate MedGraph on one Chinese benchmark
of longitudinal medical dialogue; evaluating it in
other languages and clinical settings is left to future
work. MedGraph relies on an LLM to extract facts
from each session, so the quality of its memory
depends on the extractor. Causal links are drawn
within a session only. Chains are ordered by when
a fact is recorded, not by when the event happened,
so a late report of an earlier event or a planned
change becomes the chain tail. Safety facts are
never removed, so an allergy that is later ruled out,
or a warning about a drug the patient has since
stopped, stays in the profile. Following the bench-
mark’s protocol, four question types are scored by
an LLM judge.
Ethics Statement
MedGraph is a research prototype and is not vali-
dated for clinical use. A memory that drops a cur-
rent medication, keeps a stopped one, or attributes a
relative’s diagnosis to the patient can lead to harm-
ful advice; any deployment would need clinical
review of what the memory shows. All experi-
ments use the synthetic patients and dialogues of
MedMemoryBench; no real patient data was used.
Use of AI Assistants
AI assistants were used for language polishing and
grammar correction. All text, code, and results
were reviewed by the authors.

A Extraction prompt
The experiments use a Chinese prompt; its English
translation is given first, followed by the origi-
nal. The examples for subject attribution use place-
holder names (disease A, drug B, metric C).
Extraction prompt (English translation)
You are a medical dialogue information extractor.
,→Extract structured clinical facts from the
,→doctor-patient dialogue below and output strict
,→JSON.
[Dialogue date] {date}
[Dialogue]
{dialogue}
[Requirements]
0. [Decide first, then extract] Whose health is this
,→dialogue about? Check whom each piece of health
,→information in the patient's words is attached to:
,→"my mother / my father / my son / my daughter / my
,→spouse / my friend / she / he" + symptom /
,→medication / test / measurement -> the owner of
,→these health facts is THAT person, not the
,→speaker. (!) The speaker tag "Patient" does not
,→make the patient the subject of a fact: in a
,→family health consultation the patient only relays
,→the information, and the subject is
,→family:<relation>.
1. Label the subject of each fact separately. Test:
,→whose body has the symptom, whose mouth takes the
,→drug, whose body the measurement belongs to.
- "patient" = the health fact belongs to the patient
- "family:<relation>" = the health fact belongs to a
,→family member (e.g. "family:father")
* "My mother has had disease A for years and keeps
,→taking drug B" -> the disease and the drug are the
,→mother's -> family:mother
* "My husband's hospitalization stressed me, and my
,→own metric C got worse" -> metric C is the
,→patient's own body -> patient (the husband is only
,→a trigger; no health fact of his is stated)
* The test does not depend on who says it: the
,→doctor says "your wife was diagnosed with disease
,→A" -> the disease is the wife's -> family:wife
- "none" = general health knowledge not tied to any
,→person
[Micro-example] Dialogue: "Patient: Doctor, my son is
,→15, he has disease A and is on drug B, and he says
,→his symptoms have not improved."
Correct: session_subject="family:son"; both facts
,→have subject "family:son" (medication_status drug
,→B active; symptom not improved)
Wrong: subject "patient" <- the speaker is the
,→patient, but the disease and the drug are the
,→son's.
2. type (one per fact):
- medication_status: start / stop / dose change /
,→planned / self-medication; status required: active
,→| stopped | dose_changed | planned
- condition: diagnosis status; status required:
,→suspected | confirmed | misdiagnosed | resolved |
,→chronic | worsened | improved
- lab_result: lab, imaging, or antibody result; keep
,→the exact value and unit in value
- vital: weight, blood pressure, home glucose, etc.;
,→keep the exact value
- symptom: onset / worsening / relief
- safety:★safety-critical information, always
,→extracted as its own fact: allergy,
,→contraindication or interaction, prior surgery or
,→bleeding (both surgical_history); safety_kind
,→required: allergy | contraindication | interaction
,→| surgical_history. Better too many than one
,→missed.
- preference: lifestyle, schedule, diet, cost and
,→care preferences (cost concerns, reluctance to
,→take leave, adherence)
- event: other meaningful clinical or life events
3. entity: the core entity (drug / disease / test /
,→metric name), or null. Use the generic drug name
,→(e.g. "empagliflozin"), without dose.
4. date: YYYY-MM-DD. Resolve "two weeks ago" or "last
,→month" against the dialogue date; for
,→long-standing history give the year, e.g.
,→"2019-01-01"; null if it cannot be determined
,→(defaults to the dialogue date).
5. is_state_change: whether the fact changes a
,→previously known state (stopping or switching a
,→drug, a revised diagnosis, a relieved symptom). If
,→so, replaces briefly describes the old state (e.g.
,→"empagliflozin being taken"); otherwise null.
6. causes: indexes (from 0) of other facts in this
,→output that caused this fact; [] if none.
7. content: one sentence that fully describes the fact,
,→keeping the key numbers verbatim. confidence: 0-1.
8. evidence_turn: the dialogue turn the fact mainly
,→comes from (from 1).
[Output format] Output JSON only, no other text:

"content": "Stopped empagliflozin as advised; had

"replaces": "empagliflozin being taken",
,→"safety_kind": null,

,→0.95},
{"type": "safety", "subject": "patient", "entity":
,→"empagliflozin",

,→raises the risk of euglycemic ketoacidosis;
,→contraindicated",

B Entity resolution details
The surface name is first canonicalized through a
seed dictionary of generic drug names and drug
classes, then matched against existing entities of
the same type: an exact match on the normalized
name or a stored alias reuses the node; otherwise
the node with the highest character-bigram overlap
is reused only if the overlap is at least 0.75; oth-
erwise a new entity is created. Class-level entries
in the seed dictionary (a drug class listed with its
members) merge members into the class.
C Retrieval settings
Each ranked list (dense and BM25) is scanned until
it yields 32 distinct units or 256 facts, and the top 8
units after reciprocal rank fusion are kept. Causal
expansion adds at most 4 facts. Date-anchored re-
trieval adds at most 12 records in the window and at
most 4 states in force at its start. The profile budget
is about 1,600 characters, of which the safety part
is never trimmed. Source windows are shown for
the top 3 matched facts, and if fewer than 2 facts
are retrieved, the top 4 raw turn pairs are added.
The same settings are used for every question and
every patient.
D Baselines and evaluation details
Protocol.We use the first ten patients of Med-
MemoryBench by ID and all 967 of their questions
in the Chinese mixed setting. All methods run
in the benchmark’s harness with the same reader
(gpt-5.1, temperature 0.3), the same answer
prompt, the same judge ( claude-sonnet-4-5),
and the same local embedder (bge-small-zh-v1.5;
Xiao et al., 2024). Every LLM call that builds mem-
ory, by our extractor and by the baselines’ memory
builders, uses gpt-6-luna. Memory is built online
as sessions arrive, and questions are answered from
memory alone. EEM is scored by string contain-
ment, MQ by option match, and the other four types
by an LLM judge with the benchmark’s prompts.
Baseline settings.All baselines are the imple-
mentations shipped with MedMemoryBench and
run through its harness, with their default configu-
rations (Table 5). Apart from the REMem rebuild
described below, we change only the model that
builds memory, so that every method builds mem-
ory with the same model. Retrieval budgets are
the defaults of each method and are not equalized.
REMem’s prompts are in English, so it writes En-
glish paraphrases of the Chinese sessions, and its
retrieval agent runs on the reader model. As re-
leased, the REMem adapter rebuilds REMem at
every checkpoint from only the sessions since the
previous checkpoint, so REMem would remem-
ber only the latest ten visits; we rebuild it from
all sessions so far, reusing earlier extraction re-
sponses so that each session is still extracted once.
In the Qwen setting (Table 2), Qwen3-30B-A3B-
Instruct-2507 (FP8 weights, served with vLLM)
replaces both gpt-6-luna as the memory builder
and gpt-5.1 as the reader, at the same reading

Judging.TLA, SUA, and IG are judged with
the benchmark’s prompts, and MCD with its node-
level prompt. A judge reply that cannot be parsed
counts as wrong, as in the benchmark; this affects
11 of the 568 judged answers of MedGraph and 11
to 25 for the baselines.
Statistics.Per-question tests are exact McNemar
tests, and differences are computed before round-
ing. In the main setting, MedGraph is 10.5 points
above embedding retrieval, the strongest baseline;
against every baseline, it is higher on at least 9
of the 10 patients, and p <10−9. With the open
model, it is 10.4 above embedding retrieval (9 of 10
patients) and more than 12 points above the other
baselines, withp <10−9 for every baseline. Re-
moving the subject filter or the profile lowers Avg.
significantly (p= 0.02 andp= 0.008 ; Table 3).
With GPT, MedGraph’s extracted facts ranked by
BM25 alone are 10.6 points above the raw sessions
ranked by BM25 (10 of 10 patients; p <10−9);
with Qwen, they are 16.0 above (10 of 10 patients).
On the 204 changed-state questions with GPT, the
same facts answer 55.4% correctly, against 42.6%
for the raw sessions (p<0.001).
Tracing relatives’ facts (Table 3).Each bench-
mark session is the patient’s own consultation, a
consultation about a relative or friend, or a gen-
eral health question, and its header says which.
We trace every retrieved item to the session it was
written from. Embedding retrieval returns session
text, which includes the header, and MedGraph’s
facts and snippets record their session. Mem0 and
MemOS log the items written from each session;
a Mem0 item counts as a relative’s when any ses-
sion that wrote or later updated it is a relative’s
consultation. REMem links each stored gist to its
source passage. LightMem stamps items from the
undated sessions, which are exactly the non-patient
ones, with the time of the run; we assign each
such item to the most similar non-patient session
by BM25. An item from a relative’s consultation
counts only if it states a health fact of a particular
person, not just general advice or the user’s worries;
gpt-6-lunadecides this for every such item.
Changed-state questions (Table 3).The 204
questions are all 100 SUA questions and the 104
MQ and IG questions whose benchmark trap
type concerns a state or dose that has changed:
temporal_state (69 MQ), temporal_change
(22 IG), and dosage_adjustment (13 IG). The set
is defined only by the benchmark’s annotations.
Safety-dependent questions (Table 3).The 180
questions are the MQ and IG questions whose
benchmark trap type is a contraindication, an al-
lergy, or a drug interaction. In 97 of them the
annotation names the safety item; we keep the 89
whose item is a single drug, drug class, or allergen
to avoid, and drop eight whose item is not a drug
or allergen. A safety fact counts as present if the
drug or allergen, or a synonym from a fixed list, ap-
pears within 40 characters of a safety word (allergy,
contraindication, avoid, interaction, and similar)
in the reader’s context. For embedding retrieval
we restore the full retrieved sessions, since its logs
keep only the first 500 characters of each. REMem
writes English memories, and its logs keep only
the final gists, not the triples and earlier gists its
agent also reads. For REMem we therefore rerun
its retrieval agent on the memory stored at each
question’s checkpoint, with the same models and
settings, record every gist and triple it reads, and
check each item for the safety fact (the drug or aller-
gen, including English names and class members,
stated with a safety relation).
Ablation runs.Each MedGraph variant rebuilds
the memory from the same cached extraction out-
puts, in both model settings, so only the retrieval
side differs. For the subject-filter ablation, a ques-
tion whose rendered evidence is identical to that of
the full model keeps the full model’s answer and
judgment; the other 771 questions are answered
and judged again.BM25 onlykeeps the full re-
trieval but ranks by BM25 alone.Built facts, BM25
keeps the same memory and the subject filter but
shows only the top 18 facts ranked by BM25 (18

or packs, date channel, causal expansion, profile,

E Additional analysis
Failure analysis (Figure 1a).We sample 30
wrong answers from each baseline (150 in total).
For each answer, we label its main cause (e.g., an-
other person’s fact, an outdated state, a missing
safety fact, a missing record) and add two marks:
whether the evidence holds a health fact of some-
one other than the patient, and whether it holds two
values or states of the same item of the patient with
no date or wording that shows which is current. A
failure involves state validity if it has the second
mark or its main cause is an outdated state; subject
attribution if it has the first mark or its main cause
is another person’s fact; and safety prioritization
if its main cause is a missing safety fact, or if it
is one of the 89 questions with identified required
safety facts (Appendix D) and its evidence lacks the
needed fact. Of the 150, 24 involve state validity,
108 subject attribution, and 18 safety prioritization;
129 involve at least one.
Storage check (Figure 4).We sample 40 wrong
answers from each baseline and from MedGraph
with a fixed seed (240 in total) and check what each
method stored for the needed fact, as of the ques-
tion’s checkpoint, in this order: the gold answer
or the judge is wrong; the fact is not stored; it is
stored without its date, its current-state mark, or its
exact value; it is stored in a hard-to-find form; it is
stored with no owner, that is, it is missing from the
evidence while the evidence holds other people’s
facts that the memory keeps with no owner; or it
is stored intact. A form counts as hard to find only
with concrete evidence: the fact is inside a long
entry that covers several other topics, or the stored
wording lacks the key terms that the visit and the
question share. All labels are assigned in one pass
per method with the same written criteria. Figure 4
leaves out the answers whose gold answer or judge
is wrong (9, 9, 8, 9, and 2 for the baselines in table
order, and 15 for MedGraph), since they are not
failures of the memory; MedGraph has the fewest
wrong answers, so such cases make up a larger
share of its sample. The memory of the LightMem
run was not kept, so its answers are checked against
the rebuilt memory described below, built from the
same sessions with the same model.
Fixed early questions.For Figure 3, we take the
105 EEM and TLA questions asked after sessions
10–30 whose answer does not change over time,
leaving out questions about the current or recent
state. We answer them again with the same reader,
prompt, and judge from each method’s memory
after all sessions: MedGraph and embedding re-
trieval rebuild it from the same cached inputs, and
Mem0, MemOS, and REMem load the memory
they stored in the main run. LightMem’s store was
not kept, so we rebuild it once with the same mod-
els and settings and answer each question twice
from this rebuild, when its checkpoint is reached
and after all sessions. Accuracy on these questions
changes by−11.4 points for embedding retrieval
(exact McNemar p= 0.017 ),−10.5 for Mem0
(p= 0.043 ),−11.5 for MemOS (p= 0.012 ),
−1.9 for LightMem (p= 0.82 ;−11.8 on TLA
and +7.4 on EEM),−3.8 for REMem (p= 0.39 ),
and−5.7for MedGraph (p= 0.15).
Where MedGraph fails.Of the 39 wrong state-
update answers, only one comes from the state
representation: a later session restated an old lab
value, the extractor dated it as a new measurement,
and the chain treated that record as current. Eight
are not memory errors (four correct answers were
misjudged, and four are disagreements with the ref-
erence answer), and the remaining 30 are retrieval
or reading errors.
F Examples
Tables 6–8 show three questions from the runs, one
per property. Each table puts the evidence and
answer of the baselines that fail next to those of
MedGraph. Evidence and answers are translated
from Chinese and shortened; omitted text is marked
with . . . and the facts quoted for MedGraph are
lines of its rendered evidence. Red marks evidence
that misleads the reader; blue marks the evidence
the correct answer needs.

text:
Question(patient 9, inference): “Doctor, I am always tired in the afternoon. Is it the medicine? Should I stop it for now?”
Gold: do not stop; the afternoon fatigue was there before the diabetes drugs were started, so it is unlikely to be their side
effect.
Embedding RAG, MemOS✗ MedGraph✓
Evidence.Embedding RAG retrieves three noise
sessions—two general health consultations and one about the
father’s blood-pressure drugs—and none of the patient’s own.
Three of MemOS’s five memories are about the father’s
blood pressure, e.g., “if the father’s systolic pressure falls to
about 110 mmHg with dizziness, indapamide can be paused
for a day”.
Evidence.Profile: “DPP-4 inhibitor: active, started
2024-01-10”; “metformin: active, 1,500 mg/day on a new
regimen for about two weeks” (both as of 2024-01-10).
Matched facts: “(2024-01-04) afternoon fatigue, like being
drained, worst at 3–4 pm”; “(2024-01-08) afternoon fatigue
and poor concentration”; “(2024-01-10) afternoon fatigue
still present”. No fact about the father appears.
Answer(both discuss the father’s drugs). “. . . not likely
caused by your father’s current drugs (valsartan/amlodipine)
. . . ” (Embedding RAG).
Answer .The fatigue was reported before the drug change, so
it is unlikely to be a side effect; do not stop on your own.
Why.The subject filter keeps the father’s sessions out and the profile gives the patient’s own diabetes drugs, so the answer is
about the right person’s drugs. The dated fatigue records in the evidence start on 2024-01-04, before the DPP-4 inhibitor is
recorded as added (2024-01-10). Mem0, LightMem, and REMem also answer wrongly; we show the two baselines whose
evidence is about the father.
Table 6: Example A (whose fact).
Question(patient 7, state update): “If the patient had reduced sertraline to 25 mg once a day on his own three months ago,
what is his current actual dose?” The records contain no such reduction.
Gold: sertraline 50 mg every morning.
Embedding RAG, MemOS, LightMem, REMem✗ MedGraph✓
Evidence.The evidence of Embedding RAG and MemOS
contains “. . . sertraline 50 mg every morning; I have kept
taking it”, but only inside a session text or a narrative
memory, with nothing that marks it as the current state.
Evidence.“[sertraline · medication chain] [matched · current
state] sertraline [active]: started two years ago for anxiety
and insomnia; still takes 50 mg every morning (recorded
2024-03-12)”; safety alert: “sertraline with rasagiline:
interaction risk; the dose should not be changed without the
doctor”.
Answer(all four). 25 mg, following the premise of the
question.
Answer .The current dose is 50 mg every morning; the
reduction in the question does not appear in the records.
Why.The tail of the chain is shown as the current state, so the reader can tell a recorded state from a claim made in the
question. Mem0, whose memory says “currently takes 50 mg”, also answers correctly.
Table 7: Example B (which state is current).
Question(patient 4, temporal location): “In the record of 2024-03-20, what was the patient’s blood pressure?”
Gold: 160/95 mmHg.
Embedding RAG, Mem0, MemOS, REMem✗ MedGraph✓
Evidence.Embedding RAG retrieves home readings from
other days: “mostly 145–155/88–92”.
Evidence.Read at the question’s date, the heart-rate, oxygen,
and ECG chains return records of that day, e.g.,
“(2024-03-20) heart rate 88, measured at the emergency
visit”. The blood-pressure chain returns its latest reading up
to that date, marked as dated 2024-03-02 (home readings,
mostly 145–155/88–92). The date channel adds the other
records of that day, such as a negative troponin test. The
source window of a matched record from that visit reads:
“. . . I went to the emergency department . . . the blood pressure
they measured was 160/95 . . . ”.
Answer(Embedding RAG). “No blood pressure dated
2024-03-20 is in the records.”
Answer .160/95 mmHg, measured at the emergency visit on
2024-03-20.
Why.The date in the question sets the time at which each chain is read, so the reader gets the measurements of that visit, and
every line has its date, so the home readings of 2024-03-02 are not taken for that day’s. The source window of a matched
record from the same visit gives the reading. LightMem also answers correctly.

Understanding AI from the Inside:
The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety
Fazl Barez1,2,†,∗ Tung-Yu Wu1,†
Hunar Batra1 Gabriele Dominici3 Florent Draye4 Yanai Elazar5 Damiano Fornasiere6
Antía García2 Abir Harrasse2 Riley Harris1 Sara Hooker7 Michael Lan2 Belinda Z. Li8,9
Aaron Maiwald1 Narmeen Fatimah Oozeer2 Naomi Saphra10 Or David Shafran11 Adi Simhi12
Robert Trager1 Shriyash Kaustubh Upadhyay2 Ziyu Yao13 Yu Zhao1,14
Shay B. Cohen14,‡ Mor Geva11,‡ Yoshua Bengio15,6,‡ Stella Biderman16,‡ Hassan Sajjad17,‡
1University of Oxford 2Martian 8MIT 9Anthropic
3Università della Svizzera italiana 5Bar-Ilan University 6LawZero
4Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems 7Adaption Labs 10Boston University
11Tel Aviv University 12Technion 13George Mason University 14University of Edinburgh
15Mila, Université de Montréal 16EleutherAI 17New York University Abu Dhabi & Dalhousie University
Abstract
Neural networks are likely to be among the most consequential artefacts in human history.
As these systems become more capable and autonomous, their potential to cause societal
harm also grows, making AI safety one of the defining challenges of our time. Yet we continue
to build increasingly powerful systems without fully understanding how they work, how
they will behave in unfamiliar situations, or how to reliably control them. Mechanistic
interpretability offers a path towards understanding these systems by studying their internal
representations and computations, with the aim of evaluating, predicting, and controlling
behaviour. We survey mechanistic interpretability for AI safety in order to answer the
question:Does understanding how models work actually make them safer?We place
mechanistic interpretability in the broader context of interpretability research and compare
its mechanistic evidence with behavioural evaluation. We discuss how these approaches can
work together to improve model understanding and safeguards. We introduce the foundations
of mechanistic interpretability, including features, polysemanticity, transformer computation,
and circuits, and survey methods for feature extraction and analysis, circuit discovery and
causal verification, explaining intermediate representations in natural language, learning
dynamics, and training-data attribution. Beyond surveying existing methods, we propose
a unified framework for evaluating mechanistic interpretability claims and characterise six
research orientations by their goals, assumptions, and trade-offs. Finally, we examine how
mechanistic understanding can support AI safety, including knowledge editing, steering, and
monitoring, and assess its limitations, failure modes, open problems, and relationship to
behavioural safety measures. We also release a repository of code notebooks with worked
examples that reproduce key findings from methods surveyed here, allowing readers to build
intuition through hands-on experimentation.

Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
1 Introduction
Neural networks could be one of the most consequential artefacts humanity has built, yet we do not understand
how they work or reliably control what they do. This is true despite humans designing the training procedure:
we specify how models learn, but not what they learn.Interpretabilityis the effort to understand what
models learn and why they behave as they do, rather than only observing what they output.Mechanistic
interpretability(MI) is one approach within it. MI studies theinternal mechanisms(characterised in
Section 4.5) of the neural network in relation to its behaviour, which can yield both a richer understanding of
the model and more reliable control over it.
Recent decades have seen an exponential improvement in AI capabilities (Touvron et al., 2023; OpenAI
et al., 2024; Team et al., 2024a; QwenAI, 2025; DeepSeek-AI, 2025; Anthropic, 2025b), but methods to
understand and explain internal mechanisms have lagged behind. This has created aninterpretability gap
between what models can do and what we know about how they do it. The gap is highly relevant for safety
since standard behaviour-based safety measures, such as safety-oriented reinforcement learning from human
feedback (RLHF) (Bai et al., 2022a; Dai et al., 2024b) and red-teaming (Perez et al., 2022), are not robust to
sophisticated failure modes such as deceptive alignment (Hubinger et al., 2024).
The Interpretability Gap
Theinterpretability gapis the disparity between what models do (their capabilities and behaviours)
and what we understand about how they do it (their internal mechanisms). As models scale, this
gap risks widening: reasoning emerges that we cannot yet trace, deceptive behaviours may remain
undetected, and safety guarantees built on incomplete understanding may fail unexpectedly.
1.1 Brief History of Interpretability
While early work did not establish interpretability as a distinct and clearly defined area of artificial intelligence,
researchers sought to understand what neural networks learn long before the emergence of modern deep
learning models such as transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017). For example, Hinton et al. (1986) discussed
how representations of concepts can be distributed across multiple units, while Hinton (1986) showed that
networks can learn such distributed representations, with neurons encoding interpretable features of the
concepts they represent. Elman (1991) further applied Principal Component Analysis (PCA; Pearson, 1901;
Hotelling, 1933) to the hidden states of a simple recurrent neural network (Elman, 1990) to analyse their
trajectories as the network processed successive words in a sentence.
Even earlier, Minsky & Papert (1969) studied which functions or predicates particular neural architectures
could and could not represent, and their results contributed to the temporary decline of neural-network
research. While this earlier work was not driven by AI safety concerns, it was an early attempt to classify
what neural networks can and cannot compute.
Modern efforts to understand the internals of neural networks began almost as soon as deep learning achieved
practical success. Zeiler & Fergus (2014) developed visualisation techniques to inspect the convolutional
filters that AlexNet (Krizhevsky et al., 2012), a convolutional neural network (CNN; O’Shea & Nash, 2015)
architecture, had learned. Their study revealed that early layers detected edges, while deeper layers responded
to increasingly complex patterns. Karpathy et al. (2015) and Li et al. (2016) extended this approach to
recurrent neural networks. By manually inspecting individual neurons, they discovered ones tracking various
linguistic features, such as quotes, line lengths, brackets, negation, and syntactic structure. This showed
empirically that an interpretable structure could emerge without explicit supervision.
These early works were largely manual: researchers examined individual neurons and reported qualitative
findings. The field soon developed more systematic approaches.
Probing classifiers (Belinkov, 2022) were popularised as a tool for studying neural representations through a
series of works on linguistic structure and neural network analysis (Gupta et al., 2015; Köhn, 2015; Shi et al.,
2016; Adi et al., 2017; Belinkov et al., 2017; Conneau et al., 2018; Alain & Bengio, 2017). These studies asked
whether syntactic categories, semantic roles, or sentence length could be extracted from a layer’s activations.
9
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
Dalvi et al. (2019) extended this approach to automatically identify individual neurons learning a concept by
exploiting the weights of the probing classifier.
This line of work flourished between 2016 and 2019, producing a rich catalogue of information that was
present in model activations. It remains important for mechanistic interpretability research to consider
carefully what conclusions can legitimately be drawn from the presence of information in a neural network.
The introduction of transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017) and BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) intensified both the
need and the opportunity for interpretability research. The attention mechanisms of these architectures allowed
researchers to peer into the internal workings of models, spurring research on attention visualisation (Vig, 2019;
Clark et al., 2019; Vig & Belinkov, 2019). In response, criticism and debates arose over whether attention
was sufficient to explain model internals (Jain & Wallace, 2019; Wiegreffe & Pinter, 2019). Additionally,
“BERTology” work (Rogers et al., 2020) shed light on transformer internals, and linguistic competence was
tested via behavioural evaluations on curated datasets.
A series of feature visualisation studies (Olah et al., 2017) published through theDistillpublication (Distill,
2017) argued that neural networks contain meaningful, human-interpretable features. Olah et al. (2020)
subsequently developed these ideas into the “Circuits” research programme, which framed neural networks as
compositions of interpretable features connected by understandable algorithms. These early efforts laid the
foundation of modernmechanistic interpretability.
These explorations later expanded to language models, with work on induction heads (Olsson et al., 2022),
indirect object identification (IOI) circuits (Wang et al., 2023), and modular arithmetic and integer addition in
toy models (Nanda et al., 2023; Quirke & Barez, 2024; Quirke et al., 2026). By mid-2024, sparse autoencoders
(SAEs) enabled feature extraction at billion-parameter scale (Cunningham et al., 2024; Templeton et al.,
2024). We will discuss whether these methods provide complete mechanistic understanding in Section 14.
Situating the Field.Early studies of neural network internals emerged in different research communities,
including natural language processing (NLP) (Vig, 2019) and computer vision (Olah et al., 2017). Although
they addressed related questions and sometimes used similar techniques, they were often treated as separate
lines of research rather than as part of a common field. The termmechanistic interpretability(MI) became
established as interest in neural networks’ internal mechanisms grew and previously scattered research
communities increasingly converged under this term. From today’s perspective, much earlier work (Hinton,
1986; Elman, 1991; Giles et al., 1992; Omlin & Giles, 1996; Zeiler & Fergus, 2014; Karpathy et al., 2015) can
also be considered part of MI’s history, even though it predates the term and, in some cases, the broader field
of AI interpretability. Today, the scope and standards of MI and AI interpretability are still evolving. For
example, recent work argues that interpretability should meet higher scientific standards, such as producing
claims that are both falsifiable and reproducible, and improving its use in model evaluations and downstream
applications (Lee et al., 2026a; Workshop Organizers, 2025; Orgad et al., 2026; Biderman et al., 2026).
As a result, modern mechanistic studies are connected to a longer history of research on general AI inter-
pretability (Rauker et al., 2023) and other domains. SAEs, for example, are built directly on decades of work
in sparse coding and dictionary learning (Olshausen & Field, 1996; Lewicki & Sejnowski, 2000; Lee et al.,
2006; Ng, 2011). Similarly, recent studies that discovered circuits in large language models (Conmy et al.,
2023; Ameisen et al., 2025) resonate with early work on extracting and formalising the internal mechanisms
of recurrent neural networks as finite state automata (Giles et al., 1992; Omlin & Giles, 1996). Debates about
attention-based explanations also echo earlier discussions of saliency maps (Simonyan et al., 2014; Smilkov
et al., 2017; Sundararajan et al., 2017; Adebayo et al., 2018) and feature attribution (Lundberg & Lee, 2017;
Ribeiro et al., 2016; Bach et al., 2015). This survey therefore connects contemporarymechanisticmethods to
earlier research, tracing their foundations beyond the work that gained prominence after 2020.
Safety.Many studies in mechanistic interpretability are motivated by AI safety (Burns et al., 2023; García-
Carrasco et al., 2024; Templeton et al., 2024). Researchers hope that understanding the internal workings
of models will lead to better detection and control of critical model behaviours. But it is not clear if the
current mechanistic approaches are suitable and sufficient for tackling crucial failure modes that are not
10
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
well addressed by current behavioural or correlation-based methods. This concern motivates us to assess
approaches not just by how well they provide understanding, but by the strength of their actionable impacts.
Curiosity and Discovery.Mechanistic interpretability is worth studying for reasons beyond safety
applications. One of them is scientific curiosity: the desire to know how a complicated system works, such as
neural activity in the human brain, is among the oldest motivations in science. Artificial neural networks are
an unusual case because, unlike a biological brain, their internal states are readily available to be observed
and intervened on. This direct access allows researchers to tackle challenging questions, such as what a model
represents internally or whether a particular concept is encoded in it.
Besides scientific curiosity, there are also prospects for genuine discovery. For example, a model trained on
a complex task (e.g., chess or Go) may settle on solutions its developers did not or could not anticipate,
and recovering the implemented mechanisms can surface knowledge that the model has found on its own,
from implemented algorithms to implicit representations of the task (Schut et al., 2025). In this sense,
interpretability is a way to learn from a model, not just to audit and control it.
Building on this history, recent interpretability research reflects two significant methodological shifts.
First, from manual to assisted analysis.At current model sizes, manual inspection of features and
circuits is impractical. Consequently, researchers have developed methods that automate parts of mechanistic
interpretability research. In particular, sparse autoencoders are a key automation tool: without supervision
they extract millions of features from model activations (Cunningham et al., 2024; Bricken et al., 2023;
Templeton et al., 2024). Other work has proposed pipelines to automatically identify candidate circuits
(Conmy et al., 2023; Ameisen et al., 2025), use language models to generate natural-language feature
explanations (Paulo et al., 2025b; Bills et al., 2023), and provide initial validation of mechanistic hypotheses.
While human judgement remains essential, some automation has become necessary.
Second, divergence in research priorities.Even within safety-driven mechanistic interpretability
research, there are distinct approaches. Some prioritise immediate safety interventions, such as steering,
monitoring, and concept erasure, without requiring complete mechanistic understanding (Nanda et al.,
2025), while others advocate complete causal understanding of model computation, even where this requires
substantial resources (Gao, 2025). Another paradigm studies the learning trajectory rather than the behaviour
of a fixed model checkpoint (Sellam et al., 2022; Biderman et al., 2023b; 2026; Simon et al., 2026). Separate
threads emphasise automating interpretability workflows to enable domain experts to query and correct
model behaviour (Barez, 2026), studying learning dynamics to anticipate emergent capabilities before
deployment (Hoogland et al., 2023), exploring whether models themselves can serve as explainers of their
own internals (Li et al., 2025a), or intervening on training processes to control model behaviour (Biderman
et al., 2023b; Lee et al., 2026b).
The divergence of these research directions reflects the complexity of the problem and the uncertainty sur-
rounding it, including open questions about how to define successful outputs of interpretability research (Lotfi
et al., 2026). Thus, this survey does not argue for a single approach; rather, it organises recent progress
around shared technical foundations (Section 4 onwards) and discusses trade-offs between different goals
(Section 12). We aim to clarify how these directions differ in their assumptions, failure modes, and capabilities,
providing researchers with a principled basis for selecting and combining methods according to their own
scientific and practical objectives.
Useful Surveys That We Build On.Several surveys cover overlapping territory. Bereska & Gavves (2024)
and Zhang et al. (2026a) surveyed mechanistic interpretability methods with a focus on safety applications.
Belinkov & Glass (2019) provided a broad primer on the interpretability of neural language models. Zhao
et al. (2024a) surveyed interpretability for large language models. Rai et al. (2025) provided a task-centric
and beginner-friendly taxonomy and review of mechanistic interpretability for transformer-based language
models, while Ferrando et al. (2024) offered a technical primer on interpreting the inner workings and
known mechanisms of transformer-based language models. More specifically, Sajjad et al. (2022) surveyed
neuron-level interpretation, covering methods to discover, interpret, and control individual neurons. At a
11
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
similar granularity, Shu et al. (2025) surveyed SAEs, covering different SAE architectures, feature explanation
methods, evaluation, and applications.
Our survey differs from previous surveys in framing, scope, and emphasis. Specifically, we examine closely
what interpretability can actually contribute to AI safety. The close examination is motivated by the fact
that, although many prior studies in the interpretability community assume that mechanistic understanding
directly implies safer systems, the assumption is in fact largely untested. Therefore, this survey considers
not only what a method reveals about a model’s internal computation, but also what it allows us to do
in practice. We particularly discuss whether it supports safety-relevant tasks such as detecting deceptive
behaviours or identifying dangerous capabilities, and whether those tasks can be achieved just as well without
interpretability methods or insights.
We cover popular methods and techniques up to mid-2026, including but not limited to recent work on
large-scale feature extraction and analysis, circuit discovery, activation verbalisers, and model architectures
designed with interpretability in mind. Rather than presenting these methods as a catalogue, we organise
them around the methodological ideas they share and explain new methods in relation to the problems or
limitations that motivated them.
We also place modern mechanistic methods in their broader historical context. Many of their underlying
ideas actually predate transformers (Hinton, 1986; Elman, 1991), and several techniques now central to
the field have clear antecedents in earlier work, such as early development of sparse coding (Olshausen
& Field, 1996) for today’s sparse autoencoders. Making these connections explicit helps distinguish new
methodological developments from adaptations of older ideas to new settings and shows where current debates
revisit discussions that have appeared before.
We further make the terminology and claims about mechanistic interpretability more precise. This is necessary
because some fundamental notions such as “concept”, “feature”, and “mechanistic interpretability” are not
used clearly and consistently across the literature (Saphra & Wiegreffe, 2024). The consequence is that works
described as mechanistic interpretability can support different kinds of conclusions; for example, showing
that a specific intervention can change the target behaviour is a much weaker claim than showing that the
behaviour’s internal mechanism is precisely identified. To tackle this issue, for each introduced method,
we discuss the assumptions about model internals it requires, the mechanistic claims it supports, and the
strength of the claims. By doing this, we can separate disagreements about their mechanistic claims from
disagreements about terminology, objectively comparing these methods even when their original papers use
different terms.
Additionally, we systematically discuss the evaluation practices of interpretability methods, which are often
validated through intuitive plausibility rather than rigorous testing. We cover existing evaluation frameworks
and metrics, identify gaps, and argue that the evaluation methodology and safety benchmarks are the field’s
most pressing open problems.
1.2 Survey Scope
Our survey’s main focus is on mechanistic interpretability for transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017), which
aims to explain how transformers convert inputs into outputs by analysing internal representations and
mechanisms. Thismechanisticanalysis involves direct manipulation of model internals to establish causal
claims about computation, and must meet two criteria:
1. Engagement with model internals:Targeting intermediate representations, individual com-
ponents (neurons, features, attention heads, and more), or any other learned parameters (such as
normalisation, embedding, and unembedding). This is not limited to just input–output relationships.
2.Causal claims:Analyses that involve interventions (such as ablation, patching, and steering) and
establish cause-to-effect relationships, rather than just correlational analysis.
This distinguishes mechanistic interpretability from other interpretability approaches, such as behavioural
evaluation (which asks what outputs models produce) and input attribution (which asks which inputs
12
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
matter). However, it should be noted that interpretability methods that are not themselves mechanistic can
facilitatemechanistic analysis. For instance, although vanilla probes can only identify what information
is decodable from the activations, they can become mechanistic when the identified directions are tested
and used to intervene on models. Input attribution methods help locate salient input features (e.g., pixels),
and follow-up processes, such as ablating them, can test causal claims about their roles. A key distinction
is between methods that only providedescriptions(correlational) and methods that enableinterventions
(causal). Because descriptive methods often provide the targets for intervention, we cover in depth methods
that analyse internal computation and let us discuss them within a shared causal vocabulary; we treat more
briefly methods that are either behavioural or, while mechanistic, need separate theoretical and conceptual
foundations.
We cover the following in depth:
• Foundations and core hypotheses:Foundational concepts for mechanistic interpretability,
including behavioural versus mechanistic understanding, polysemanticity, features, transformer
computation, and circuits (Section 4), together with core hypotheses that motivate and constrain
later mechanistic methods, including linear representations, superposition, privileged access, and the
universality and Platonic representation hypothesis (Section 5).
• Feature extraction and representation analysis:Sparse autoencoders and related feature-
extraction methods, multi-layer feature analysis, probing classifiers, intermediate-representation
decoding, model diffing, knowledge localisation, and representation engineering (Sections 6, 8, and 9).
•Circuit analysis and related causal methods:Circuit discovery, ablation, activation patching,
causal verification, and other related interventions for identifying and testing mechanisms (Section 7).
• Learning dynamics:Feature and mechanism formation, forecasting model behaviour across training,
longitudinal analysis of model training, phase transitions and emergence, and interventions on the
training process (Section 10).
• Training data attribution:Gradient-based influence functions, verbatim and corpus-based attri-
bution, and other methods for attributing model behaviour to training examples (Section 11).
• Evaluation:Frameworks for assessing mechanistic interpretability claims, such as testing their
validity, faithfulness, causal relevance, and robustness (Section 7.5).
•Research orientations:The goals, assumptions, and trade-offs of six major research orientations
in contemporary AI interpretability (Section 12).
• Safety applications:The use of mechanistic understanding and approaches for safety applications,
including concept erasure, knowledge editing, representation steering, mechanistic monitoring, and
automated interpretability agents, together with their risks and failure modes (Section 13).
• Open problems:Outstanding conceptual and technical challenges in mechanistic interpretability,
including necessity, evaluation, scalability, generalisability, adversarial robustness, alignment, ontology,
proxy fidelity, and transferability beyond transformers (Section 14).
Notably, training data attribution (TDA; Section 11) does not meet the two criteria and is generally not
considered a tool for mechanistic analysis. We note that many TDA methods operate via gradients or
verbatim search, instead of intermediate representations. These approaches credit the behaviour entirely to
the training data, completely ignoring internal computations. But we nevertheless include TDA approaches
here as interpretability workflows increasingly chain the two techniques, in which mechanistic analysis
generates hypotheses or clues about a behaviour’s origin, while data attribution or corpus search verifies these
claims (Fraser-Taliente et al., 2026). Parameter-response-based TDA methods (e.g., influence functions (Koh
& Liang, 2017)) were also introduced as a top-down complement to mechanistic analysis, with the stated
goal of connecting the influence of data to responsible model components (Grosse et al., 2023; Habibi et al.,
2026), making TDA a tool for mechanistic ends.

title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
2 The Limits of Behavioural Evaluation
Behavioural evaluation—measuring output patterns on held-out inputs—is the default paradigm for assessing
deep learning systems. Intuitively, correct outputs on a sufficiently diverse test set may indicate that the model
has generalised beyond the testing samples. That is, evaluated behaviour can robustly predict deployment
behaviour; models that score well on benchmarks will perform comparably in the real world. Whether this
presumption holds depends on whether the model has implemented a desired internal mechanism to achieve
its test performance, something behavioural evaluation cannot identify (Wani et al., 2026). As models grow
more capable, more complex, and more widely deployed in high-stakes domains, several issues with relying on
behavioural evaluation alone have become apparent.
First, test-set contamination and saturation.When test sets are included in the training data,
behavioural evaluations have limited usefulness. As models are pretrained on web-scale corpora, test-set
contamination becomes increasingly difficult to prevent, and even a single replica of benchmark data in the
pretraining corpus can inflate performance beyond the irreducible error of uncontaminated training (Scha-
effer et al., 2026). Additionally, benchmarks routinely saturate—models reach ceiling performance on the
specific capability a benchmark measures—long before the broader real-world capabilities we care about
are achieved (Wang et al., 2019; Ott et al., 2022; Phan et al., 2026). Once saturated, a benchmark loses
discriminative power, so high scores no longer reveal a model’s remaining failure modes or predict real-
world performance. Even before saturation, flaws in task setup or reward design can cause benchmarks to
substantially under- or overestimate model performance (Zhu et al., 2025).
Second, benchmark gaming: models can learn the wrong mechanisms.Two models with identical
input–output behaviour may implement radically different computations, with one relying on robust, general-
isable features and the other on brittle shortcuts or spurious correlations (McCoy et al., 2019; Du et al., 2023;
Juneja et al., 2023; Ye et al., 2026). Specifically, models can achieve high benchmark scores through shortcuts
that do not reflect genuine understanding (Geirhos et al., 2020; Tang et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2025). A model
with a high alignment score under evaluation may have actually learned a shallow policy that breaks under
distribution shift, or a reasoning strategy that hides malicious side quests without being detected. Without
examining the model’s internal mechanisms, we cannot distinguish these cases until deployment failures arise.
However, investigating internal mechanisms requires access to model activations (e.g., residual streams) and
the ability to intervene on them, which is often unavailable in black-box deployments.
Third, evaluation awareness.More fundamentally, a model that passes a safety evaluation may simply
have learned to recognise evaluation-like contexts and adjust its behaviour accordingly (Needham et al.,
2025; Anthropic, 2025b; Apollo Research, 2025)—a failure mode that is often hard to detect solely from
model outputs. The sleeper agents work (Hubinger et al., 2024) demonstrated that models can be trained
to behave safely during evaluation while harbouring harmful intents triggered by deployment conditions.
Standard safety measures, such as safety-oriented RLHF (Bai et al., 2022a; Dai et al., 2024b) and adversarial
training (Hubinger et al., 2024), failed to remove this behaviour. Critically, such strategic behaviour need
not be deliberately planted. For example, Greenblatt et al. (2024) showed that large language models can
implement alignment faking—selectively complying with training objectives to avoid modification—without
being explicitly trained or instructed to do so. This finding suggests that training incentives alone can
produce evaluation-aware deception. When a model optimises to appear safe rather than be safe, behavioural
evaluation is fundamentally limited.
Fourth, lack of fine-grained control.Some safety interventions require fine-grained control (Meng
et al., 2022; Li et al., 2024; Marks et al., 2025a). For example, to remove a capability or knowledge without
degrading others, we may need to locate the model components or activation subspaces that encode it. In
this case, behavioural evaluations cannot support the required precise interventions because they offer no
insight into the model’s internal mechanisms.

The Sleeper Agent Experiment
Researchers have shown that large language models can learnstrategic deceptionby training them with
a hidden “backdoor” objective: write secure code during the year 2023 (training phase) but insert vul-
nerabilities if the year is 2024 (deployment phase) (Hubinger et al., 2024). The experiment is as follows:

model was trained to minimise:

Critical Finding.Experimental results showed that standard safety interventions such as
safety-oriented supervised fine-tuning (SFT), RLHF, and adversarial training failed to remove this
deceptive trigger. Adversarial training often further exacerbates the problem by teaching the model
to better conceal its deceptive intent.
Interpretation.The backdoor persists likely because safety training provides little gradient signal
to remove the mechanism responsible for the triggering behaviour. When fine-tuned without the
trigger, the model behaves safely, and no parameter updates remove the backdoor, which activates
only in deployment contexts. Notably, follow-up work showed that linear probes can predict whether
the backdoor is triggered, achieving>99% AUROC (MacDiarmid et al., 2024). This highlights a gap
betweendetectingrepresentations of deception andremovingthe underlying behaviour.
Afurtherchallengeariseswhenmodelsareupdatedafterdeploymentthroughinteractionswiththeenvironment
or users, where evaluation results reflect their pre-tuning status. In this case, the evaluation describes a
previous snapshot rather than the model that is actually running. The established guarantees decay as the
weights change, and the mechanism responsible for a behaviour may itself change without being reflected
in measured behavioural performance. More discussion of this challenge and research to mitigate it are in
Section 10.
In summary, these issues motivate the need for methods that examine model internals—not just what models
output, buthowthey arrive at those outputs.
3 The Interpretability Landscape
Section2establishedthatbehaviouralevaluationaloneisinsufficientforfullyunderstandingmodels, motivating
methods that examine their internal mechanisms. AI interpretability, however, spans a broad range of
approaches that differ in the evidence they provide, the strength of the claims they support, and the
real-world scenarios in which they are useful. This raises a central question:When is mechanistic analysis
necessary, and when do simpler interpretability methods suffice?
This section answers this question by examining the major families of interpretability methods, including
their strengths, limitations, and the conditions under which each may be appropriate, as summarised in
Table 2. In particular, we introduce approaches developed in the broader natural language processing
(NLP) and representation learning communities—including probes, attribution methods, and concept-based
approaches—which remain widely used and may complement or substitute for mechanistic analysis in some
cases. We conclude by examining the limitations of mechanistic analysis itself.
16
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
3.1 Behavioural Methods
Behavioural methods evaluate and analyse models through their inputs and outputs. They have been developed
to examine a wide range of capabilities, traits, and behaviours under specific conditions. Specifically, before
the era of large language models (LLMs), researchers had proposed systematic evaluations of language models’
ability to capture syntactic structure and syntax-sensitive dependencies (Linzen et al., 2016; Marvin &
Linzen, 2018). With modern LLMs, behavioural evaluations have expanded to include a much broader set of
capabilities, such as professional and academic knowledge across diverse domains (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Wang
et al., 2024; Srivastava et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2024; Phan et al., 2026), long-context understanding (Bai
et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024a; Modarressi et al., 2025), mathematical reasoning (Cobbe et al., 2021;
Azerbayev et al., 2023), and coding ability (Chen et al., 2021; Jimenez et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024b).
Beyond assessing models as helpful assistants, behavioural evaluations also identify and benchmark potential
safety risks and failure modes. Examples include monitoring deceptive intentions (Korbak et al., 2025;
Kinniment et al., 2026), measuring tendencies towards sycophancy (Hong et al., 2025; Fanous et al., 2025;
Petrov et al., 2026), evaluating capabilities relevant to harmful or destructive actions (Li et al., 2024; Zhang
et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2026a), and testing robustness against jailbreak attacks (Ganguli et al., 2022; Perez
et al., 2022; He et al., 2025) or training data poisoning (Fu et al., 2025). Behavioural evaluations have also
been used to study broader model characteristics, such as political orientations (Helwe et al., 2025) and social
attitudes (DURMUS et al., 2024).
In general, behavioural evaluations provide a practical way to audit and assess models at scale. They are
typically fast, inexpensive, and scalable, requiring only forward passes and comparisons between model
outputs and reference answers. Although evaluation results on a finite testing set do not guarantee the
mechanism that produced the behaviour of interest (Wani et al., 2026) (which the internal methods below aim
to establish, as discussed in Section 2), behavioural methods nonetheless remain essential in practice for rapid
iteration during development, prioritising which behaviours warrant deeper investigation, and surface-level
safety screening when the cost of mechanistic analysis is prohibitive.
3.2 Concept-Based Approaches
Concept-based methods occupy a middle ground: they examine internal representations but typically establish
correlational rather than causal claims. However, when combined with interventions such as steering along
concept directions and ablating concept-associated components, they become mechanistic by the criteria
discussed in Section 1.2. Geiger et al. (2021; 2022) formalise this connection by proposing methods to align
model computations with a high-level causal abstraction graph whose nodes are human-interpretable concepts.
Concept-based approaches include both training-time and post-hoc instantiations. Concept Bottleneck Models
(CBMs; Koh et al., 2020) constrain computation through a predefined bottleneck of interpretable concepts,
offering built-in transparency and allowing for interventions, but traditionally requiring a complete set of
predefined concepts and often suffering from an “accuracy–interpretability trade-off” when concept definitions
are insufficiently expressive. Newer variants, such as Concept Embedding Models (CEMs; Zarlenga et al.,
2022), address these limitations by allowing the bottleneck to encode additional high-dimensional information;
this recovers accuracy at the cost of allowing non-interpretable information to leak into the bottleneck.
Moreover, recent improvements relax the assumption of concept independence. Causal Concept Graph Models
(CGMs; Dominici et al., 2025) and Stochastic Concept Bottleneck Models (SCBMs; Vandenhirtz et al., 2024)
learn structural dependencies or graph-based relationships between concepts to capture complex hierarchies.
Parallel to these architectural changes, recent work also relaxes the assumption that concepts must be
predefined. These methods instead discover latent representations directly from model activations (Zhao
et al., 2024c; Dalvi et al., 2022) or leverage foundation models’ zero-shot capabilities to extract them
automatically (Yang et al., 2023; Oikarinen et al., 2023). Yu et al. (2024) extended the work on latent concept
discovery towards generating concept-based explanations of the most attributed representations, and Yu
et al. (2026) proposed the Vector Quantized Latent Concepts (VQLC) framework for efficient and scalable
automatic concept discovery.

Post-hoc methods, such as Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs; Kim et al., 2018) and linear concept classi-
fiers (Belinkov, 2022), probe existing activations to identify concepts encoded in model representations. In
general, these methods do not provide causal evidence about the role of those concepts in model computation,
although some probing variants aim to support stronger causal claims, such as amnesic probing (Elazar
et al., 2021). Nevertheless, they remain valuable tools for auditing, localisation, and early detection tasks.
Furthermore, representation engineering (Rimsky et al., 2024; Marks & Tegmark, 2024; Turner et al., 2024)
extends the probing paradigm from observation to intervention, enabling targeted steering of model behaviour.
We discuss these methods in detail in Section 9.3.
CBMs are sometimes grouped with theinterpretability-by-designmethods discussed in Section 6.10, but they
operate differently. CBMs imposesemantic constraints(predefined human concepts), while interpretable-by-
design models imposestructural constraints(sparsity, modularity) that make the model intrinsically easier to
interpret. Table 1 summarises the distinction.
CBMs can be more appropriate when the set of concepts of interest is known. Interpretability-by-design
models may be preferable when the goal is to discover what the model has learned—including features
that were not preset in advance. For safety applications, where unknown failure modes are a core concern,
discovery-oriented methods may be more useful than those that require specifying concepts upfront.
3.3 Input Attribution and Saliency Methods
Input attribution methods aim to identify which input features most influence a model’s outputs. Techniques
such as SHAP (Lundberg & Lee, 2017), LIME (Ribeiro et al., 2016), DeepLIFT (Shrikumar et al., 2017), and
saliency-based methods (Simonyan et al., 2014; Sundararajan et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2016; Selvaraju et al.,
2017) are scalable and widely used for explanation and debugging at the pixel and token levels. However,
these methods indicatewhichinput features matter for a prediction, but not necessarilyhowthe model
processes and leverages them. For example, saliency maps for image classifiers leverage gradients propagated
from the output back to the input to estimate the sensitivity of the prediction to each pixel (Simonyan et al.,
2014). While such methods can highlight influential regions of an input image, they do not reveal how the
model represents pixels in its activations and uses them across layers.
The same machinery can also be applied to internal representations, attributing salience to features at
different layers and tracing how information evolves throughout the network (Yu et al., 2024; Syed et al.,
2024). Used in this way, attribution methods begin to overlap with the mechanistic approaches discussed
later in this survey. Nevertheless, concerns about their reliability remain. Different attribution methods
can produce substantially different explanations for the same prediction, and some have been shown to be
insensitive to model parameters (Adebayo et al., 2018) or sensitive to input transformations that have no
effect on the model (Kindermans et al., 2022). For safety-relevant applications, attribution methods help
with triage, debugging, and initial auditing, but they are insufficient on their own when an explanation of
internal computation is required.
18
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
3.4 Representation Probing and Related Post-hoc Analyses
Probing classifiers (Belinkov, 2022) assess whether a model’s activations encode particular information
by training “lightweight” classifiers—often logistic regression models—on intermediate representations to
predict a target property, such as part-of-speech tags, syntactic structure, and gender (Belinkov et al., 2017;
Hewitt & Manning, 2019; Ravfogel et al., 2020). Originally developed in the NLP community to analyse
linguistic structure (Gupta et al., 2015; Köhn, 2015; Adi et al., 2017) and used by Alain & Bengio (2017)
to trace how representations evolve across layers of deep learning models, probes have become one of the
most widely used tools in mechanistic interpretability for tasks including, but not limited to, layer-level
localisation (Tenney et al., 2019) and detection of latent behaviours (MacDiarmid et al., 2024). We discuss
the probing methodology, its limitations, and its relationship to causal interpretability in more detail in
Section 8.6.
3.5 Mechanistic Interpretability Methods
Mechanistic interpretability (MI) methods aim to causally understand model internals, such as the semantic
meaning of parameters or activations, and how they relate to model behaviour. They are largely human-
centric in the sense that the desired mechanistic understanding is one that humans can interpret and reason
about—whether through natural-language descriptions (Cunningham et al., 2024; Ameisen et al., 2025), plots
of attention patterns (Clark et al., 2019; Vig, 2019), or token distributions (nostalgebraist, 2020; Belrose
et al., 2025; Gurnee et al., 2026). Recent work, however, has questioned whether “machine languages” and
human languages fully overlap, suggesting that some meaningful internal computations may not admit faithful
descriptions in natural language (Hewitt et al., 2025).
Mainstream MI approaches include, but are not limited to, feature decomposition and extraction (Cunningham
et al., 2024; Dunefsky et al., 2024), circuit discovery (Syed et al., 2024; Ameisen et al., 2025; Conmy et al.,
2023), and methods for decoding internal representations into natural language (Ghandeharioun et al., 2024;
Pan et al., 2026; Fraser-Taliente et al., 2026), all of which are discussed in later sections. Different methods
rest on different assumptions and produce different types of explanation, making them suitable for different use
cases but with distinct limitations. For example, sparse autoencoders decompose model representations (e.g.,
residual-stream activations at the last token position of a particular layer) into thousands of monosemantic
features, though many extracted features may be non-causal or illusory (Wu et al., 2025b; Leask et al.,
2025; Heap et al., 2026). Circuit discovery methods identify fine-grained computational graphs responsible
for particular model behaviours, but these graphs may capture only a subset of the model’s underlying
computation and can be difficult to validate for sufficiency or identifiability (Miller et al., 2024; Méloux et al.,
2025). Despite these limitations, MI methods remain promising complementary tools that collectively enable
systematic analysis of model internals.
3.6 When Mechanistic Understanding Becomes Necessary
The methods we have discussed so far form a correlational-to-causal spectrum: behavioural evaluation
establisheswhata model does, attribution and probing identifywhererelevant information resides, and
mechanistic analysis revealshowcomputations produce behaviour. These approaches complement each
other: behavioural evaluations help validate mechanistic findings, and behavioural anomalies can motivate
mechanistic investigation.
Mechanistic analysis becomes necessary when we need to verifyhowa model produces a behaviour—not just
thatit does under test conditions. For example, a probe can detect deceptive reasoning, but we still need
targeted interventions to validate whether the detection is a false alarm; if not, we will further need more
rigorous mechanistic analysis to understand why the model deceives. Likewise, unexpected generalisation or
failure modes may require mechanistic analysis to examine whether they stem from identifiable structures.
Concretely, mechanistic methods are most needed for: identifying intents hidden from outputs, such as
deception or side quests; understanding the internal mechanism of a model behaviour; verifying theabsence
of a capability (behavioural tests can only confirm presence); or providing safety guarantees that must hold
beyond the evaluated input distribution. However, the high granularity of mechanistic analysis comes at high
