3.7 Limitations of Mechanistic Analysis
Mechanistic interpretability aims to provide causal explanations of model behaviour, but it faces important
practical and conceptual limitations. First, mechanistic explanations are often incomplete. An analysis may
identify an internal computation (e.g., “This MLP retrieves factual knowledge about Paris”, as identified
through causal tracing (Meng et al., 2022)) that captures a non-trivial causal pathway without identifying all
others contributing to the behaviour. This concern makes it hard to tell whether the identified computation
is sufficient or just one of several mechanisms jointly implementing the behaviour.
Second, mechanistic analyses can scale poorly. Analysing large models and complex behaviours takes much
more time and resources because the relevant computations may be distributed across model components
and complex behaviours involve interactions across long generation trajectories that are hard to isolate. For
example, most current circuit-discovery methods (Ameisen et al., 2025; Conmy et al., 2023; Hanna et al.,
2024; Marks et al., 2025a; Wu & Barez, 2026) identify the computational graph responsible for generating a
specific token. It remains challenging to identify and summarise the computations underlying behaviours
that unfold across multiple generated tokens.
Third, even when we identify and causally validate an internal mechanism, this does not automatically
mean we can reliably control the corresponding behaviour (Hase et al., 2023). The effectiveness, specificity,
and generalisability of localisation and intervention techniques, such as identifying a model component and
then patching its activations or changing its weight matrices, depend on several factors, such as the hydra
effect (McGrath et al., 2023), beyond how accurately the identified localisation captures the underlying
computation for the behaviour. Furthermore, an intervention that successfully steers one model’s behaviour
on a task may not transfer to another model or setting.
20
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
These are open challenges but not fundamental barriers. Active research in areas such as establishing
more effective representational units, discovering more robust model properties, developing more efficient
circuit-discovery methods, and designing more reliable intervention approaches across distributions is working
to address them. Nevertheless, these studies highlight a clear gap between mechanistic explanation and
reliable control or safety guarantees.
Limitations of Mechanistic Analysis
Mechanistic explanations may be incomplete or non-causal, difficult to scale to large models or complex
behaviours, and sensitive to modelling assumptions. They often fail to capture the full picture of
a model’s underlying mechanism and do not automatically provide reliable, generalisable control.
Intervening on an identified mechanism may work in one setting but fail to transfer to another.
However, these limitations do not imply that mechanistic understanding cannot enable reliable control.
Instead, they indicate that moving from explanation to robust, generalisable intervention requires
additional studies and remains an open challenge in the field (Sharkey et al., 2025).
Summary.This section discussed different interpretability methods based on the evidence they provide.
Behavioural methods measure and analyse model responses to inputs; concept-based methods explain
predictions through human-interpretable concepts; input attribution methods identify which parts of the
input influence an output; probing tests what information is decodable from representations; mechanistic
methods identify and describe internal mechanisms that produce a behaviour. Among them, mechanistic
analysis offers the strongest claims, but it is costly, often incomplete, and does not guarantee reliable control.
In the next section, we introduce the core concepts on which mechanistic analysis is built.
4 Foundational Concepts for Mechanistic Interpretability
This section introduces foundational concepts in mechanistic interpretability. We establish a shared notation
and vocabulary for use throughout the survey. We avoid committing to specific hypotheses about the
representations and workings of model activations.
4.1 Behavioural vs. Mechanistic Understanding
Behavioural analysis describes what a model does, but safety-critical applications also require understanding
its internal mechanism (as we reviewed in Section 2).
Behavioural Interpretability
Behavioural interpretability studies a modelfθ :X→Y through input–output pairs(x,fθ(x))for
x∈D⊆X , whereD is a finite test set. Behavioural interpretability treats the model as a black box.
Mechanistic Interpretability
Mechanistic interpretability studies a modelfθ :X →Y by examining its internal computations,
including model activations and parametersθ that produce them, at different levels of granularity in
relation to its behaviour. In short, mechanistic interpretability characterises how a model’s behaviour
or output is computed.
4.2 Neuron Polysemanticity in Model Representations
What Is a Concept?Concepts play a central role in many interpretability methods and will be used
throughout this paper to define key ideas such as features and polysemanticity. It is therefore worth clarifying
what we mean by the term. Notably, concepts do not necessarily correspond to categories humans can
readily name or understand; neural networks may represent them in ways humans lack the vocabulary to
describe (Hewitt et al., 2025).

Concept
A concept is a distinct, reusable unit of information or knowledge that can be identified across different
instances or contexts. Concepts may correspond to familiar human categories, such as “a dog”, “the
colour red”, or “words of praise”, but they need not admit a natural human description.
Cross-context identifiability concerns the meaning of the information unit rather than the process by which the
information is recognised. Determining whether a concept is present in an information unit may itself require
additional contextual information. For example, the word (i.e., an instance of an information unit) “bank”
can refer to a financial institution or a river bank, depending on the surrounding sentence. Nevertheless, once
identified, each concept can be recognised as the same information across different contexts. For example,
the concept of “financial institution” is expected to remain sufficiently stable across the contexts in which it
appears.
This definition accommodates both human-interpretable and machine-specific concepts. A machine-specific
concept may lack a natural human description yet still form a coherent, reusable unit of information in the
neural network (Dalvi et al., 2022; Hewitt et al., 2025). Human interpretability should therefore be treated
as a property of some concepts rather than as a necessary condition for the information unit to qualify as a
concept. Notably, most interpretability research focuses on concepts that humans can readily understand.
Identifying and characterising concepts that matter to a model’s computation but do not map neatly onto
human-understandable categories remains underexplored.
Neuron Polysemanticity.For a single neuron nℓ in layerℓ, consider its activation at token position
t for some input promptx, denoted bynt
ℓ(x). We can straightforwardly interpret a neuron if it responds
to a single concept. For example, ifnt
ℓ(x)is large and positive whenever position t corresponds to the
word “blue”, remains close to zero otherwise, and can causally shift the model’s outputs towards or away
from blue-related concepts when manipulated, we can conclude that the neuron corresponds to the concept
of blue. Assuming some neurons exhibit such a property, early work proposed methods to discover and
interpret individual neurons’ functions (Bau et al., 2017; 2019; Dalvi et al., 2019; Bau et al., 2020; Hernandez
et al., 2022; Oikarinen & Weng, 2023; Wu et al., 2024). However, follow-up studies have found that, due
to representational constraints and superposition (Elhage et al., 2022a) (detailed in Section 5.2), individual
neurons often respond strongly to multiple concepts that appear unrelated from a human perspective (Elhage
et al., 2022a). This phenomenon is known asneuron polysemanticity.
Neuron Polysemanticity
A neuronnℓ ispolysemanticif there exist two distinct conceptsc1 andc2, together with corresponding
sets of inputsx1 and x2 as well as token positions of interesttc1 and tc2, such thatn
tc1

associated with both concepts.
Polysemanticity complicates neuron-level explanations and suggests that human-interpretable semantic
content may not be aligned with individual neurons. This motivates searching for representational units
beyond individual neurons.
4.3 Features as Representational Units
Since individual neurons are often polysemantic, mechanistic interpretability has increasingly shifted towards
alternativeunitsofanalysis. Forexample, ithasbeenfoundthatmodelssometimesencodehuman-interpretable
concepts as linear directions or low-dimensional manifolds in the activation space (Arditi et al., 2024; Wurgaft
et al., 2026). We thus use the termfeaturebroadly to encompass any model representation corresponding to
a human-interpretable concept. Such distributed representations motivate analysing the activation space as a
whole, rather than individual neurons in isolation (Elhage et al., 2022a; Bricken et al., 2023; Templeton et al.,
2024).

Specifically, we treat a feature technically as a geometric structureϕ in the activation spaceRd of a model
component, such as the residual stream, an attention-head output, or an MLP output, whered denotes
the hidden dimension. Conceptually, a feature is a manipulable manifestation of a concept of interest. As
with neurons, for a featureϕ claimed to correspond to a conceptc, we expect interventions that increase or
suppress the activation ofϕ to causally influence model behaviour associated withc. In this sense, features
provide a more expressive, general representational unit than individual neurons for describing how neural
networks may encode concepts.
Feature
A featureϕ associated with a conceptc is a geometric structure in the model’s activation spaceRd
whose activation is predictive of, and causally relevant to, the presence or expression ofc.
At this stage, we remain agnostic about the precise mathematical form features take and how the model
encodes them. Instead, we treat existing methods for identifying and manipulating features as operational ap-
proximations shaped by their methodological assumptions and constraints. We examine these representational
hypotheses explicitly in Section 5.
Within this operational perspective, researchers can identify features using several methodological families,
including readout-based methods (Ghandeharioun et al., 2024; Pan et al., 2026; Karvonen et al., 2026a) and
sparse decomposition techniques (Cunningham et al., 2024; Dunefsky et al., 2024), and then manipulate
them to test causal relevance (Wu et al., 2025b; Mueller et al., 2025). In practice, many such approaches
operationalise features as approximately linear or linearised components of internal representations (Yun et al.,
2021; Marks & Tegmark, 2024; Arditi et al., 2024). Examples include linear probes and dictionary-learning
methods (Belinkov, 2022; Bricken et al., 2023).
An important caveat is that, for a given concept, an identified manipulable geometric structure—that is, a
candidate feature—may be only one of many possible internal representations associated with that concept.
For example, a language model may encode the concept of “refusal” in a complex manner across multiple
layers and components. Successfully identifying a linear direction in the residual stream that can steer the
model towards or away from refusal (Arditi et al., 2024) does not imply that this direction uniquely or
exhaustively captures how refusal is represented. Other causally relevant structures (e.g., low-dimensional
manifolds) for refusal may also exist but remain unidentified.
4.4 Transformer Computation
Transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017) have become the dominant architecture underlying modern language-
model-based AI assistants such as ChatGPT and Claude, and are consequently the primary subject of study
in mechanistic interpretability. Several properties of the transformer architecture, most notably its modular
structure and additive information flow, make it particularly amenable to mechanistic analysis (Elhage et al.,
2021). In particular, transformer components can be viewed as reading from and writing to a sharedresidual
stream, allowing information to persist and be incrementally transformed as it passes through successive
layers (Elhage et al., 2021). Below, we briefly review the main classical components of the transformer
architecture.

MLP Block
An MLP block applies a position-wise nonlinear transformation to each position of the residual stream.
In the canonical Transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017), this transformation takes the form
∆hMLP =W 2σ(W1h+b 1) +b 2,
where W1∈R dmlp×d, W2∈R d×dmlp, and σ(·)denotes a nonlinear activation function, for which
the original Transformer uses ReLU (Nair & Hinton, 2010). The same transformation is applied
independently at each position in the sequence. MLP blocks primarily transform and generate internal
features, writing new directions into the residual stream.
Notably,W1 typically projects the activations into a much higher-dimensional space (dmlp≫d ), which
has recently been found to yield more interpretable representations natively in the model (Nikankin
et al., 2025; Arora et al., 2026).
The transformer components discussed above correspond to their canonical formulations. Numerous variants
have since been proposed and adopted in modern architectures. For example, variants of the attention module
include Grouped Query Attention (GQA) (Ainslie et al., 2023), used in Llama 3 (Grattafiori et al., 2024),
and Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2024), used in DeepSeek-V2 (DeepSeek-AI
et al., 2024) and DeepSeek-V3 (DeepSeek-AI, 2025). Variants of the MLP block include gated architectures
such as SwiGLU (Shazeer, 2020), used in Llama 3, and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures, used in
DeepSeek-V3.
4.5 Circuits as Descriptions of Internal Mechanisms
Sections 4.2–4.3 introduce neurons and features as representational units for describing what is represented
in model activations, and Section 4.4 introduces the computations that transform and route activations
through the model. We use the termmechanismto refer to the organisation of model activations, their
representational units, or the transformations applied to them that together produce a particular model
behaviour. A central topic in mechanistic interpretability is identifying and understanding such mechanisms
in neural networks.
A common way to represent and describe such a mechanism is through acircuit: a subgraph of the model’s
computational graph whosenodescorrespond to computational components or representational units and
whoseedgesrepresent information flow between them (Elhage et al., 2021).
Circuit (Figure 3)
For a fixed model computation, letG denote the corresponding directed acyclic computational graph.
A circuitC⊆Gis a subgraph ofG, where:
• Nodes:computational components, such as Attnℓ and MLPℓ, or representational units, such
as featuresϕi;
• Edges:directed connections representing information flow or transformation between nodes.
The subgraphC represents a collection of components and interactions that jointly contribute to a
particular computation or model behaviour, and can therefore serve as a description of the underlying
mechanism.
Examples of Circuits
• Induction head circuit:Two attention heads cooperate to implement in-context learn-
ing (Olsson et al., 2022).
• QK circuits:Query–Key interactions prioritising specific token positions (Kamath et al.,
2025).

The study of circuits has developed along two complementary lines. The first line of work (Wang et al.,
2023; Conmy et al., 2023; Hanna et al., 2024; Haklay et al., 2025), referred to ascapability circuit discovery
by Wu & Barez (2026), aims to identify minimal sets of architectural components, such as attention heads
or MLP layers, that are sufficient to reproduce a givenbehaviourorcapabilityof the model, such as
indirect object identification (Wang et al., 2023), numerical comparison (Hanna et al., 2023), and in-context
learning (Kharlapenko et al., 2025). In this setting, the capability of interest is defined as a dataset of queries
that exercise it, and a discovered circuit is considered successful if it recovers the model’s performance on this
dataset.
The second line of work, referred to asquery-level circuit discovery(Wu & Barez, 2026), focuses on how
internal features interact and propagate across the computational graph to produce the model’s decision for
a particular input query (Ameisen et al., 2025; Wu & Barez, 2026). Studies in this line usually use sparse
autoencoders or cross-layer transcoders (detailed in Section 6) to automatically decompose MLP outputs into
interpretable units, trace attributions between these features, and track how information flow converges to
the final prediction.
Summary.This section introduced the foundational concepts of mechanistic interpretability: neuron
polysemanticity, which motivates the use of features as more expressive units of analysis; transformer
computation, which describes how representations are transformed and information is routed through the
model; and internal mechanisms, which organise these units, transformations, and information flows to
produce model behaviour and can be described by circuits. How we interpret and leverage these concepts
depends on assumptions about the structure of model representations and computation, which we examine
explicitly in Section 5.

5 Core Hypotheses in Mechanistic Interpretability
Mechanistic interpretability rests on several core hypotheses about how neural networks represent information
and implement computation. These hypotheses are not yet rigorously proven. Nonetheless, they have shaped
methodological choices and empirical investigations. In this section, we formalise four of them, discuss their
conceptual basis, and summarise supporting and opposing empirical evidence.
5.1 The Linear Representation Hypothesis
We have seen that single neurons may not be the most effective unit of representation in many cases, but what
is? The linear representation hypothesis claims thatlineardirections in the activation space are effective
fundamental units of representation (Park et al., 2024).
Linear Representation Hypothesis
A concept can be effectively represented by a feature corresponding to a linear directionϕ in activation
space Rd. Linearity implies that adding or subtracting this direction, or a scalar multiple of it,
from model activations can correspondingly influence model behaviour, while the projectionϕ⊤h(x)
approximately measures the strength of the feature in model activationsh(x)for an inputx.
Under a strong version of the linear representation hypothesis, all concepts are best represented by
linear features. In this view, model activations can be approximately decomposed as an additive
combination of such features,
h(x)≈
∑
i
αiϕi,
where αi∈R denotes the strength of featureϕi dependent on the inputx. Under a weaker version,
only some concepts admit such linear representations (Sharkey et al., 2025; Smith, 2024).
Conceptual Basis.A feature associated with a concept is linearly represented if its presence corresponds
to a fixed directionϕ in the activation space and can be detected through the projectionϕ⊤h(x). This
linearity makes mechanistic analysis tractable because we can use simple methods to identify, measure, and
manipulate these features in the activation space, such as scaling them and adding them back to model
activations.
Notably, activation spaces in different model components can have distinct geometric structures. For example,
in the hidden states of MLP blocks, the neuron axes are computationally distinguished because element-wise
nonlinear activation functions, such as ReLU, act separately on each axis. The coordinate system is therefore
meaningful and is referred to as aprivileged basis(Figure 4, left) (Elhage et al., 2022a). In other spaces, such
as the residual stream, no operation singles out the neuron axes, so linear features may lie along arbitrary
directions. Such spaces are said to have anon-privileged basis(Figure 4, right).
When the basis is privileged, a single neuron can serve as a scalar feature that meaningfully represents a
concept. When it is not, the feature may instead correspond to directions or other geometric structures that
do not align with any individual neuron. In this case, specialised methods are required to identify them from
the activation space.
Empirical Evidence and Counterexamples.Empirical support for the weaker version of the linear
representation hypothesis includes the success of linear probes across diverse models and concepts (Belinkov,
2022), activation steering along single directions to induce targeted behavioural changes (Turner et al., 2024),
and sparse autoencoders recovering linearly accessible and steerable features at scale (Bricken et al., 2023).
At the same time, there is substantial evidence that not all representations are well described as linear.
Counterexamples include nonlinear feature interactions, algorithmic representations that rely on nonlinear
transformations, and features distributed across multiple interacting subspaces (Nanda et al., 2023; Engels
et al., 2025; Tiblias et al., 2026; Csordás et al., 2024; Feucht et al., 2026; Wurgaft et al., 2026). Some work
has further argued that features may not always exist as explicitly represented objects, but may instead

5.2 The Superposition Hypothesis
The superposition hypothesis says that models encode more features than their hidden representations have
dimensions.
Superposition Hypothesis
Model hidden states encode more features than they have dimensions. If there arem features andd
dimensions, then the superposition hypothesis claims thatm≫d.
This implies that features cannot be represented as orthogonal directions—though they can be
represented as nearly orthogonal directions. It also implies neuron polysemanticity: the same neuron
participates in the encoding of multiple unrelated concepts.
Conceptual Basis.Superposition is a geometric property of learned representations in which a limited
number of neuron dimensions encode many more features by allowing those features to share representational
dimensions. Neuron polysemanticity, where individual neurons respond to multiple seemingly unrelated
semantic concepts, naturally follows from this phenomenon. When the number of encoded features exceeds
the activation-space dimensionality, the model can no longer allocate a dedicated neuron dimension to
each feature. Instead, multiple features become superposed within the same activation space, shifting the
representation from dedicated dimensions with monosemantic neurons to shared dimensions with increasingly
polysemantic neurons (Figure 5).
Empirical Evidence.Mechanistic studies have repeatedly observed widespread neuron polysemanticity:
individual neurons often activate for multiple seemingly unrelated semantic concepts, making them difficult

2023). Dictionary-learning methods such as sparse autoencoders exploit this structure to recover millions of
distinct features from shared activation spaces (Bricken et al., 2023; Templeton et al., 2024). Many discovered
features are substantially more monosemantic than individual neurons, and some have been shown to causally
influence model behaviour. Together, these findings suggest that the activation space may encode more
meaningful semantic information along activation-space directions than along individual neuron axes.
However, the superposition hypothesis remains a hypothesis, not an established fact, in large language
models. Observing polysemantic neurons does not, by itself, imply that superposition is the underlying
cause, and dictionary-learning methods can recover interpretable features even in the absence of superposi-
tion. Furthermore, Lecomte et al. (2024) showed that polysemanticity can arise even when the number of
underlying features does not exceed the number of available neurons, suggesting alternative—and potentially
complementary—mechanisms for the emergence of polysemantic representations.
Architectural Responses to Superposition.Superposition is not an intrinsically inevitable property
of deep neural networks but a consequence of architectural permissiveness. Without constraints on model
architectures or activations, gradient descent can exploit the activation-space geometry to pack far more
features than neurons (Elhage et al., 2022a). This motivates a distinct research direction,interpretability-
by-design(as mentioned in Section 3.2 and discussed in Section 6.10). Interpretability-by-design argues
that, rather than decomposing traditional models’ superposed activations post hoc, one can design novel
architectures or components that encourage representations where features are more accessible for analysis.
Two intervention points have been explored:
• Sparsity constraints:Enforce sparsity in weights or activations that limits how many neurons
within an MLP or attention head can participate for a given input, constraining how many units can
jointly support any single feature (Yang et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2026; Elhage et al., 2022b).
• Computational primitives:Change the fundamental units of analysis from static features in
activations to learnable transformations by weight matrices that generate activations (Liu et al.,

compress or suppress model representations.
These architectural interventions shift from treating superposition as a phenomenon to reverse-engineer to
treating it as a design choice that can be constrained upstream. We discuss these methods in detail in
Section 6.10.
5.3 The Privileged Access Hypothesis
A class of approaches that use language models as interpreters ofthemselvescan be justified through the
privileged access hypothesis. The privileged access hypothesis states that:
Privileged Access Hypothesis
A language model used to interpret itself can, under appropriate elicitation, access internal variables
and intermediate computations that are not reliably recoverable from external behavioural analysis
alone, providing a comparative advantage as an interpreter of its own behaviour (Binder et al., 2025;
Li et al., 2025a; Song et al., 2026).
Conceptual Basis.The ability to access and judge its own computation or reasoning—calledintrospective
monitoring—has long been a desired property of an AI system (Cox & Raja, 2008). Even earlier rule-based
medical expert systems sought to explain their decisions, such as MYCIN’s “Explanation system” (Shortliffe,
1977). In this sense, using language models to explain themselves can be seen as a modern continuation of
these earlier efforts.
A major difference is that rule-based systems can explicitly present the rule they executed, whereas modern
language models compute in a highly nonlinear way. Although researchers have proposed mechanistic tools
aiming to reverse-engineer part of the computation, the technical complexity of these techniques hinders
their accessibility and scalability. The privileged access hypothesis then posits that the language model
itself naturally stores information about the computation within its internal states, such as latent beliefs or
intermediate plans. The model can thus learn to verbalise this information directly, serving as a scalable
complement to mechanistic analysis.
Empirical Evidence.The most direct empirical evidence for this hypothesis comes from recent findings
that models, even without explicit training to do so, are sometimes aware of concept representations (acquired
by methods like difference-in-means) injected into their activations (Lindsey, 2026; Fornasiere et al., 2026).
Additional, though less direct, evidence comes from the design of explainer models—a general class of
interpretability methods in which one model is fine-tuned to explain the target model’s activations (Pan
et al., 2026; Karvonen et al., 2026a; Fraser-Taliente et al., 2026). In practice, such explainers are typically
initialised from a copy of the target model itself (Pan et al., 2026; Karvonen et al., 2026a; Bauer et al., 2026;
Huang et al., 2026). This usually works better than initialising from alternative models, suggesting the target
model already encodes much of what is needed to interpret its own activations. In this sense, fine-tuning
elicits and refines a latent capability rather than creating one from scratch.
Some studies also reported negative results for the privileged access hypothesis: Song et al. (2026) found that
models predict their own sampling temperature no better than they predict other models’, suggesting apparent
introspection may reflect general reasoning about model-like systems rather than self-access. Separately, recent
work has questioned whether internals-based explanations provide a practical advantage over behavioural
baselines: Karvonen et al. (2026b) found that activation-reading tools (including activation oracles) give
agents no uplift over transcript-only baselines at predicting counterfactual model behaviours in the wild, and
Li et al. (2026c) showed that standard verbalisation benchmarks can be solved without access to target-model
internals at all (see also Jakkli et al., 2026).
In summary, these results show that privileged access ispossiblefor certain tasks under favourable conditions,
notuniversalorreliable. The hypothesis should therefore be treated with caution, as significant failure modes
and limitations remain.

text:
5.4 The Universality and Platonic Representation Hypothesis
Platonic Representation Hypothesis
Models independently trained on similar tasks tend to develop similar internal representations or
algorithms, which often approximate a task-determined canonical form (Huh et al., 2024; Olah et al.,
2020). The degree of convergence depends on factors such as model size, architecture, and training
data.
Conceptual Basis.A key distinction is the level at which models are expected to converge.Weak
universalityrefers to convergence in the algorithms or recurring computational patterns that models implement,
even when these are encoded through different internal representations.Strong universalitymakes the stronger
claim that the internal representations themselves converge towards a shared canonical form.
Empirical Evidence and Trade-Offs.Weak universality is supported by recurring attention patterns,
features, and circuits across models, tasks, and scales (Nanda et al., 2023; Lan et al., 2024; Olah et al., 2020;
Quirke et al., 2026). Strong universality is less supported and is usually demonstrated through representational
similarity metrics (Kornblith et al., 2019; Moschella et al., 2023; Lan et al., 2025), where recent studies have
found the results to be fragile (Gröger et al., 2026; Koepke et al., 2026). Divergent representations can arise
from variations in architecture, data, or optimisation trajectories (Harrasse et al., 2025; Morcos et al., 2018).
Implications.If strong universality holds, fine-grained mechanistic insights and the methods derived
from them may transfer more readily across models. If only weak universality holds, such insights may
remain contingent on factors such as model family and task (Bereska & Gavves, 2024), and even a complete
mechanistic understanding of one model (see Section 12.2) may fail to generalise to others. Therefore, it
is important to clarify the extent of universality for assessing the promise, limitations, and scalability of
different interpretability research orientations, including the six major orientations introduced in Section 12.
Summary.This section discussed four hypotheses that motivate many modern mechanistic interpretability
studies. Linear representations support linear-feature-based analysis; superposition explains why we need to
operate on linear or more complex forms of features instead of single neurons; privileged access explains the
fundamental idea of model self-interpretation; universality asks whether insights transfer across models and
at which levels. Each hypothesis holds in some settings and fails in others, and techniques built on them
inherit those limitations. Section 6 introduces the main family of techniques and methods that operationalise
the first two hypotheses (linear representation and superposition): dictionary learning for feature extraction
and analysis.
6 Feature Extraction and Analysis
The critical notions introduced in Section 4, together with the hypotheses about the structure of neural
network representations discussed in Section 5, provide the conceptual foundation for developing methods to
identify and analyse manipulable internal objects associated with concepts of interest, i.e., features. One
straightforward paradigm is to decompose model activations into sparse linear features. Sparse autoencoders
(SAEs) provide a principled example of this approach, learning to represent any input activation with a subset
of a large dictionary of monosemantic, interpretable features (Cunningham et al., 2024).
This section first introduces the canonical sparse coding problem and links it to SAEs, reviews how SAEs
extract interpretable features, and then provides a practical overview and comparison of major SAE variants.
We then introduce methods for multi-layer feature extraction and analysis, such as transcoders and crosscoders,
and compare them with SAEs as well as with a broader range of alternative feature-extraction methods.

6.1 The Sparse Coding Problem
Early neuroscience studies posited that brains represent information using sparse, interpretable basis sig-
nals (Barlow, 1961; Field, 1994). This hypothesis further motivated research to decompose natural images
and compare the decomposed signals with cell activities in the primary visual cortex, finding surprising
alignment (Olshausen & Field, 1996; 1997). At the same time, the signal processing community has also
examined representing a given signal as the sum of a subset of basis signals from a given overcomplete
dictionary (Mallat & Zhang, 1993; Chen et al., 1998). Studies on learning better overcomplete dictionaries
for high-quality representations also thrived (Lewicki & Sejnowski, 2000; Aharon et al., 2006). Together, they
framed the sparse dictionary learning research question, with SAEs serving as a modern algorithm that uses
neural network activations as the signal. Specifically, given datah, a sparse dictionary learning method finds
the dictionaryDand sparse codeszsuch that

SAEs implement this with neural networks:h are model activations,D =Wout is an overcomplete dictionary

the algorithm to find az for eachh, which does not scale to modern language models. In contrast, SAEs use
a nonlinear encoderEto predict the coefficients for different input activations.
6.2 Sparse Autoencoders

reconstruct activations at a specific location in neural networks, such as the output of an MLP block or an
entire transformer layer (i.e., the residual stream), while keeping only a few features active in any given
forward pass.

vectors correspond to in natural language (so that they become human-understandable features). Empirically,
SAE features selectively activate on structured token patterns that recur across input sequences, suggesting
sensitivity to specific abstract semantic, functional, or lexical concepts (Marks et al., 2024b). Automated
analysis pipelines (Gur-Arieh et al., 2025a; Paulo et al., 2025b) aggregate highly activating inputs to infer
the concept each feature captures (see Section 12.6 for a detailed discussion).
Training Dynamics and Evaluation.SAE training is sensitive to initialisation, sparsity strength,
and decoder normalisation. Without proper constraints and hyperparameters, the features may collapse,
duplicate, or absorb one another. SAEs are typically evaluated for reconstruction loss (fidelity of activation
reconstruction), feature absorption (how often a general feature fails to fire because a more specific feature has
absorbed its direction), and downstream test loss recovery (whether replacing activations with reconstructions

6.5 Challenges and Failure Modes of SAEs
SAEs have become a standard tool for feature extraction, but they exhibit systematic failure modes that
undermine their interpretability claims. It is therefore essential to understand these issues when using SAEs
as mechanistic tools. This section provides a systematic discussion of them.
6.5.1 Dead Features
Adead featureis an element in the learned dictionary that never activates or activates extremely rarely across
training. Dead features waste the dictionary’s capacity, and they are common. In fact, they can constitute
up to 10–50% of the dictionary in a poorly tuned SAE (Bricken et al., 2023).
Several factors can cause dead features to emerge. First, inappropriate SAE weight initialisation can place
features in low-density regions of the activation space with weak gradient signals. Second, an overly strong
sparsity penaltyλ may suppress feature activations early in training, preventing features from contributing
usefully to reconstruction. Finally, once a subset of features captures common, dominant patterns, the
remaining features struggle to find useful roles for improving reconstruction and thus do not activate.
Dead features can be detected by tracking each feature’s rate of being activated during training. For example,
features with an activation rate below 0.01% may be considered dead (the threshold should adapt across
scenarios). Several mitigation strategies have been proposed, such asneuron resampling, which periodically
reinitialises dead features using examples with high reconstruction error (Bricken et al., 2023). The sparsity
penalty can also be reduced early in training and increased gradually (i.e., a warm-up schedule). More recent
Batch Top-k SAEs allocate sparsity adaptively across samples, which allows more active features on complex
inputs and fewer on easy ones (Bussmann et al., 2024).
6.5.2 Feature Duplication
Feature duplication occurs when multiple features in the dictionary encode the same or similar concepts (Tem-
pleton et al., 2024), leading to potentially redundant features. Duplication can arise for several reasons:

6.5.3 Feature Absorption and Splitting
Another class of failure modes concerns feature granularity.Feature absorptionarises when semantically
hierarchical features interact under the sparsity objective: a seemingly general (parent) feature fails to activate
on some inputs where it should because a more specific (child) feature activates instead and has absorbed
part of the parent’s direction into its own decoder direction (Chanin et al., 2025). For example, a “starts with
S” feature may fail to activate on the token “short”, while a token-specific “short” feature with a partially
overlapping direction activates instead. Absorption-induced false negatives make such a feature an unreliable
detector of its concept. It can be detected by comparing the feature with a linear probe for the same concept:
inputs on which the probe responds strongly, but the feature does not, while another active feature’s direction
aligns with the probe, indicate absorption (Chanin et al., 2025).
By contrast,feature splittingoccurs when a feature learned by a smaller SAE splits into multiple distinct
features as the SAE scales up (e.g., by increasing the expansion factore). This often produces more fine-
grained features, which may be either beneficial or less useful. In a favourable case, an initially polysemantic
or opaque feature, such as one activating on “bank” in both financial and geographical contexts, may split
into more coherent features of “investment bank” and “river bank”. In a less useful case, the resulting features
may become low-level, lexical detectors that activate on the token “bank” in any context.
6.5.4 Feature Instability Across Seeds
SAE features are also sensitive to random initialisation, optimiser stochasticity, and data ordering. For
a fixed SAE architecture and training dataset, different random seeds can produce substantially different
dictionaries (Paulo & Belrose, 2026). In practice, frequent and semantically clear features tend to be stable,
while rare or context-specific features vary substantially. Often, fewer than 50% of features remain the same
across seeds, although broader semantic clusters may remain more consistent. This instability limits the
reliability of mechanistic claims based on individual SAE features. Although aggregating results across seeds
can improve robustness, it increases computational cost. As a result, when evaluating SAEs, we should report
feature stability across seeds alongside reconstruction loss.

6.5.5 Identifiability and Theoretical Concerns
Another concern for SAE-based interpretability claims is whether the learned features are identifiable, that is,
whether the dictionary learning reliably recovers the “true” underlying features—if such features exist—or
merely finds one of many mediocre decompositions (Klindt et al., 2025).
Identifiability
Suppose activations are generated by some sparse latent process
h=D ∗z∗ +ϵ,
where D∗ is the ground-truth feature dictionary andz∗ are the feature coefficients. An SAE is
identifiable if its training recoversD∗ andz∗ up to unavoidable symmetries such as feature permutation
and rescaling.
In classical dictionary learning, identifiability holds under low-coherence conditions, i.e., dictionary elements
are sufficiently orthogonal to one another. However, when coherence is high, ambiguity arises: multiple
distinct sparse combinations of features from the same dictionary can generate the same output (Schnass &
Vandergheynst, 2008). In large language model activations, high coherence is likely unavoidable because of
the model’s complicated internal structure and correlations within its feature space (Li et al., 2025b). So far,
identifiability remains a stubborn issue in SAEs, even though it offers a theoretical explanation for several
empirical observations.
Recent progress in fine-tuning language models around a fixed sparse autoencoder offers a potential path
forward. In this setting, model activations are explicitly constrained to be sparse combinations of decoder
features while largely preserving task performance (Chen et al., 2025a). In particular, recent work aimed
at limiting superposition fine-tunes the language model jointly with the SAE while enforcing orthogonality
constraints on the decoder matrix (Miller et al., 2026). By explicitly imposing low-coherence conditions, this
approach improves identifiability: activations have a unique feature representation, and these features can be
reliably recovered.
Relation to Causal Relevance.The concern of identifiability connects to causal relevance: even if an
SAE feature is monosemantic and helps reconstruct activations well, it may not correspond to a causally
meaningful unit of analysis. Below, we summarise some criteria for validating an SAE feature.
Diagnostic criteria:
• Necessity: Does ablating the feature remove the corresponding concept in model responses? Low
necessity suggests that the concept can be expressed through redundant features.
• Sufficiency: Does activating only this feature produce the behaviour corresponding to its concept?
Low sufficiency suggests the feature alone is not enough to represent the concept.
• Specificity: Does the feature’s causal effect match its corresponding concept? Low specificity means
the feature contains other concepts.
These criteria are useful in practice when claiming that SAE features represent meaningful units of analysis.
6.5.6 Practical Recommendations
The challenges discussed above suggest several methodological considerations for SAE-based interpretability
studies:
1. Report failure-mode metrics:Alongside reconstruction loss, researchers should also report
dead-feature percentage, duplication rate, and stability across seeds.
40
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
2. Validate causal relevance:Researchers should validate features’ necessity, sufficiency, and speci-
ficity through interventions (e.g., feature ablation or steering) and evaluation on downstream effects.
3. Compare methods:For safety-critical applications, researchers should compare SAE features
against various baselines to assess whether SAEs recover the relevant structure.
4. Try multiple SAE variants:Different variants (e.g., Gated, Top-k, JumpReLU) impose different
inductive biases. Researchers can explore findings consistent across variants, as these provide stronger
evidence.
5. Acknowledge identifiability limits:Researchers should frame SAE features as one valid approxi-
mate decomposition rather than the true features. Multiple decompositions may be equally valid for
reconstruction but yield different feature sets.
6.Consider alternatives for targeted analysis:When specific concepts are the focus, supervised
methods (e.g., DAS, probes, discussed in Section 6.9.4) may be more reliable because SAEs discover
features in an unsupervised and exploratory manner.

Standard SAEs analyse individual layers in isolation. However, features can evolve as information propagates
through the network. Transcoders (Figure 7a), cross-layer transcoders (Figure 7b), and crosscoders (Figure 9)
enable multi-layer feature extraction and analysis, revealing how representations and features associated with
particular model components—most commonly MLP blocks—transform across depth.

Replacement Models and Attribution Graphs.A key insight is that CLTs enable the construction of
areplacement model—a version of the original model in which all MLP layers are replaced with their CLT
reconstructions. Running this replacement model involves:
•Computing CLT feature activationszℓ at each layerℓ
•Replacing MLP outputsh out
ℓ with reconstructions ˆhout
ℓ from features in layer1throughℓ
•Keeping attention layers unchanged
When analysing a specific prompt, the replacement model freezes the original model’s attention patterns
and normalisation statistics from its forward pass, then adds layer-specific error corrections. Under these
conditions, the local replacement model can exactly match the original model’s activations on that prompt
while decomposing it into interpretable CLT features. However, when the model’s activations are completely
replaced by CLT reconstructions, the intervened model’s top-1 predictions match the original model’s on only
about 50% of prompts from the Pile dataset (Gao et al., 2020). Notably, this experiment uses a relatively
small, 18-layer transformer (Ameisen et al., 2025). Therefore, this figure should be interpreted with important
caveats (see below).
Caveats on CLT Fidelity Claims
CLTs have been claimed to possess high output fidelity given that they achieve high top-1 token
agreement. However, this claim requires careful examination:
Conditions for reported fidelity:
• Results are reported primarily on toy or small models, whose generality to other model
architectures (e.g., Llama, Qwen) and model sizes (e.g., 70B models) is underexplored.
• Fidelity was measured on short sequences in the CLT training data. Evaluation under
distribution shift (e.g., out-of-domain tasks, adversarial inputs) is not adequate.
• The paper reports top-1 token agreement as the main result, while softer metrics (e.g., top-5
agreement, KL divergence) may show different patterns and insights.
Conditions for exact local matching:
• Attention patterns must be frozen from the original forward pass since the CLT does not
compute or reconstruct attention computations.
• Layer normalisation statistics (means, variances) must be cached from the original model.
The replacement model does not recompute these.
• Error correction terms are added per layer to compensate for reconstruction residuals. Without
them, exact matching fails.
Factors affecting fidelity:
• Model scale: Preliminary evidence suggests that reconstruction quality and feature inter-
pretability improve with CLT model size. This may be because larger CLTs produce more
structured, less entangled representations (Ameisen et al., 2025). However, systematic scaling
studies are limited.
• Layer depth: Early layers’ and late layers’ activations are usually input-specific and output-
constrained, respectively. Middle layers have richer information derived from the input but are
not yet converged to the output. As a result, middle layers often show higher reconstruction
fidelity.
43
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
• Domain: Fidelity on factual recall and syntactic tasks is higher than on complex reasoning or
arithmetic tasks, where MLP computations may be more complex and cannot be approximated
by sparse linear features.
These caveats do not invalidate CLTs as a tool for mechanistic analysis, but they do mean that
fidelity should be verified on the target model and specific task before drawing strong conclusions
from CLT-based circuit analysis.
Why CLTs Enable Better Circuit Analysis.Unlike per-layer transcoders, CLTs reveal direct feature-
to-feature interactions across layers: a feature in layerℓ directly influences features in later layers through
its contribution to their inputs. This simplifies circuit structure—features need not re-encode information
at each layer. Additionally, replacing MLPs with CLT reconstructions makes the remaining computation
approximatelylinear (with frozen attention patterns and normalisation), enabling principled attribution: each
feature’s activation can be expressed as the sum of its input edges up to its activation threshold (Ameisen
et al., 2025).
However, linearisation depends on several assumptions:
• Attention freezing:By caching attention patterns, the replacement model treats attention as a
fixed routing operation rather than a dynamic, input-dependent computation. This means CLT-based
circuits describe model computation conditioned ongivenattention patterns without analysing them.
• Normalisation caching:CLT analysis caches the input-dependent normalisation factors (e.g.,
LayerNorm denominators) from the original forward pass and reuses them during attribution instead
of recomputing them after interventions. This removes a source of nonlinearity, but if an intervention
would substantially change these normalisation factors in the original model, the cached computation
no longer faithfully represents the intervened state.
• Sparse linear approximation:Dictionary learning methods assume MLP outputs or transforma-
tions are well approximated by sparse linear combinations of features. This assumption may fail
when computations involve complex feature interactions or highly nonlinear transformations.
CLTs provide a powerful lens for circuit discovery when these assumptions hold. When they fail, CLT-based
explanations may become unfaithful.

Causal vs. Acausal Crosscoders.Crosscoders support two information flow patterns:
• Causal Crosscoders:Read only from layers ℓ′≤ℓ at the current position. This respects the
forward pass causality: earlier layers cannot read from later layers.
• Acausal Crosscoders:Read from any layerℓ′ regardless of depth ordering. Useful for understanding
post-hoc feature relationships across the full model.
Applications to Circuit Analysis.By extracting cross-layer features, crosscoders help us understand
how features propagate through the residual stream across layers, removing duplicate feature representations
that complicate circuit analysis. This simplification allows features to “jump” across intervening identity
operations, substantially reducing circuit complexity. More importantly, crosscoders reveal how input-relevant
features transform as they flow through the network, distinguishing which features persist unchanged versus
which are actively modified by downstream computation (Lindsey et al., 2024).
6.7 Comparing SAEs, Transcoders, and Crosscoders
Single-layer SAEs are efficient and locally interpretable but miss cross-layer feature evolution. Transcoders
improve this by imitating MLP behaviour and revealing nonlinear transformations, though they require

but are extremely expensive. Crosscoders take a different approach, extracting shared features across layers
simultaneously to resolve cross-layer superposition and simplify circuits without chaining predictions.
6.8 Case Study: Induction Heads
Here, we examine induction heads (Olsson et al., 2022), a mechanism found in many modern language models,
as a case study. We first describe their conditional-copying function and role in in-context learning, and then
relate them to feature-extraction methods such as SAEs and CLTs, which reveal how this computation can
be distributed across broader feature circuits.
Induction Heads
Induction heads, first identified and analysed by Elhage et al. (2021), are attention heads that implement
a conditional copying rule over repeated subsequences. Letx = (x1,...,x T )be a token sequence,
and consider positionsi < j < Tsuch thatxi =xj. An attention head indexedr (see Section 4.4
for an introduction to attention modules) is said to be an induction head when its attention pattern
assigns comparatively high attention weight from positionj to positioni + 1(i.e., high Ar

That is, induction heads implement the rule

They help enable in-context prediction by copying the continuation that followed an earlier occurrence
of the same token.

Induction heads were originally characterised as specific attention heads implementing this copying rule.
However, subsequent work shows that we can understand the underlying computation more naturally at the

Induction Heads: Features Across Representations
Feature extraction methods, such as SAEs, can decompose attention layer outputs into sparse,
interpretable features that capture meaningful activation patterns beyond individual attention
weights (Kissane et al., 2024). Modern analyses suggest that induction heads are not isolated
mechanisms but participate in distributed feature circuits, where multiple interacting features recur
and compose across layers (Dunefsky et al., 2024; Singh et al., 2024; Kissane et al., 2024; Kamath
et al., 2025).
SAEs trained on attention heads’ activations reveal feature families of recurring patterns and
contextual dependencies. Some of them align with behaviours originally attributed to induction
heads (Kissane et al., 2024). By analysing these features, we can understand how models maintain

6.9 Comparison with Alternative Feature Extraction Methods
Besides SAEs, alternative techniques from signal processing and machine learning have also been adapted
to extract features from neural networks. They make different modelling assumptions and therefore offer
distinct trade-offs in interpretability, scalability, and robustness. Table 6 summarises the methods discussed
in this section.
6.9.1 Non-Negative Matrix Factorisation (NMF)
Non-negative matrix factorisation (NMF; Lee & Seung, 1999) decomposes a non-negative activation matrix
H∈R d×n as H≈WA , where both the feature dictionaryW∈R d×m (m is the preset number of features)
and the coefficient matrixA∈R m×n are constrained to have non-negative elements. Because all components
are non-negative, each feature contributes positively to the final representation, making it easier to interpret.
Additionally, classical NMF’s optimisation process uses simple multiplicative update rules that preserve
non-negativity. Moreover, under assumptions likeseparability(each latent feature appears in at least one
48
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
sufficiently “pure” example), NMF guarantees that the recovered decomposition is unique (Donoho & Stodden,
2003).
However, classical NMF is not suitable for neural network activations because they can have negative elements,
requiring additional preprocessing steps that may distort the activation-space structure. Moreover, NMF does
not explicitly encourage feature sparsity, and scaling NMF to large dictionaries is computationally expensive.
As a result, empirical work on extracting and analysing features in neural network activations has largely
focused on Semi-NMF (Ding et al., 2010), which relaxes the non-negativity constraint onW. Shafran et al.
(2026) showed that Semi-NMF can recover features competitive with SAEs on small-scale evaluations, but
systematic comparisons at large scale remain limited. Yun et al. (2021) used a Semi-NMF-like approach to
factorise BERT’s contextualised hidden-state representations (Devlin et al., 2019), allowing elements inW to
take both positive and negative values while constrainingAto be non-negative.
6.9.2 Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
Principal Component Analysis (PCA; Pearson, 1901; Hotelling, 1933) decomposes activations by finding an
orthonormal basis of directions that maximise explained variance. Given a mean-centred activation matrix
H∈R d×n, where each column is an activation vector, PCA computes a low-rank approximationH≈U ΣV⊤,
where the columns ofU are the principal directions ordered by explained variance. PCA is fast, stable, and
scalable. However, PCA imposes constraints and inductive biases that may misalign with neural network
activations. Specifically, it identifies principal directions that maximise explained variance in the activation
distribution, but much of the information of interest is region- or context-dependent and cannot be captured
by variance alone. Moreover, PCA constrains the principal directions to be orthogonal, but in practice
the underlying features correlate or partially overlap. Recent benchmarks (Wu et al., 2025b) reflect this
misalignment: PCA underperformed most baselines, including SAEs, on both steering and concept-detection
evaluations. While PCA can outperform SAEs in some localisation settings (Mueller et al., 2025), it still
generally lags behind simple supervised baselines.
6.9.3 Independent Component Analysis (ICA)
Independent Component Analysis (ICA; Hyvärinen & Oja, 2000) decomposes activationsH∈R d×n as
H≈WS , wheren is the number of data points. Note that ICA may look similar to NMF at first glance.
However, they were developed for different use cases and thus rely on different assumptions and optimisation
procedures. In ICA, each column inW∈R d×m is a mixing vector, andmis the number of different source
signals; each row inS∈R m×n is a source signal (a signal hasn data points), withm source signals in total.
These signals are optimised to be independent of one another. Thus, if model activations are linear mixtures
of statistically independent “foundational features”, ICA can provably recover those features.
However, these assumptions may not hold for neural network activations. Specifically, classical ICA typically
expects the completeness property (number of latent sources equals the dimensionality of the observed
representation), and overcomplete decompositions (which are what we expect in activations) would require
additional extensions (Lewicki & Sejnowski, 2000). Moreover, underlying features may not be statistically
independent, which further limits the applicability of classical ICA. Although early studies applied it to
analyse neural network activations, they did not find interpretability gains over SAEs (Cunningham et al.,
2024). This may partly reflect the challenges discussed above.
More recently, however, Liu & Han (2026) showed that ICA can achieve performance comparable to that of
SAEs, arguing that its previously reported underperformance may stem from limitations of classical ICA
implementations poorly suited to the scale and statistical structure of neural network activations. These
findings leave open whether ICA should be regarded primarily as a simple classical baseline or as an approach
with underestimated, substantial headroom for further development.
6.9.4 Supervised Feature Extraction Methods
When the concepts of interest are known in advance, supervised methods can directly optimise representations
aligned with those targets. Examples include distributed alignment search (DAS), which uses supervision
49
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
to learn a change of basis that aligns representations with high-level causal variables (Geiger et al., 2024);
Supervised Multi-Dimensional Scaling (SMDS), which projects activations to preserve concept-level sim-
ilarities (Tiblias et al., 2026); and probes, which fit a concept direction in contrastive class-conditioned
activations (Marks & Tegmark, 2024).
Notably, despite its simplicity, probing has outperformed SAEs in concept detection (Wu et al., 2025b). It
has also become a standard tool for identifying safety-relevant concepts in model representations, including
refusal behaviour and implanted backdoors (Arditi et al., 2024; MacDiarmid et al., 2024). We discuss probing
in detail in Section 8.6. We put it under Section 8 because we view its central methodological contributions
and technical challenges as the readout of human-interpretable information—often expressed in natural
language—from model activations, rather than the extraction of monosemantic features or causal variables.
When labelled data is available, supervised approaches often outperform SAEs on concept detection and
steering tasks (Huang et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025b; Chaudhary & Geiger, 2024). They also avoid choosing
dictionary sizes or sparsity penalties, since the concept set determines complexity. However, these methods
require labelled data for each concept and cannot discover previously unknown features. Therefore, supervised
methods suit settings where predefined, crisp concepts matter, whereas SAEs remain preferable for exploratory
analysis.
6.9.5 Dictionary Learning Baselines
Classical dictionary learning methods provide useful baselines for evaluating SAEs. Techniques such as K-SVD
alternate between sparse coding and dictionary updates and converge under certain conditions (Aharon et al.,
2006). Comparative studies suggest that SAEs’ primary advantage is fast inference because the encoder
learns to decompose all activations, while potentially sacrificing optimal sparsity (O’Neill et al., 2025). As
such, classical dictionary learning can still achieve superior dictionary quality in some cases and thus remains
an important reference point for assessing the added value of SAEs.
6.10 Interpretability-by-Design Methods for Intrinsic Interpretability
The methods surveyed thus far in this section aim to extract and analyse more monosemantic units from
polysemantic model activations. They share a common premise: the model’s original representations are
too entangled to be directly interpretable, so interpretability is applied post hoc to recover simpler units
of analysis. A parallel research programme, which we termInterpretability-by-Design Methods for Intrinsic
Interpretability, inverts this premise by asking whether deep neural models can instead be designed to be
mechanistically interpretable by construction (Pearce et al., 2025; Park et al., 2025; Oldfield et al., 2024;
Yang et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2026; Adler et al., 2025; Draye et al., 2026; Dooms et al., 2025). This subsection
extends the discussion of this research direction.
Next, we introduce five approaches for constructing models that are more interpretable by design. Three
impose model sparsity constraints at different levels: feature-sparse training (Section 6.10.1), weight-sparse
training (Section 6.10.2), and attention-sparse training (Section 6.10.3). The remaining two approaches
instead modify the computational primitives themselves, using more interpretable operators as units of
construction and analysis (Sections 6.10.4 and 6.10.5).
Interpretability should be understood as a spectrum rather than a binary property. At least in their current
form, these techniques do not make model computation completely or immediately understandable. Instead,
they make models easier to analyse and ensure the analysis pipeline preserves more information about
the original computation than post-hoc approximations. Table 7 summarises these approaches and their
trade-offs.
6.10.1 Feature-Sparse Training: SoLU
Softmax linear units (SoLU; Elhage et al., 2022b) are an earlier attempt at architectural intervention. SoLU is
a specialised activation function that applies a softmax-based transformation across the layer’sdmlp neurons.
50
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
Specifically, given the pre-activation vector
u=W 1h+b 1∈R dmlp,
SoLU calculates the activation values as
σSoLU(u) =u⊙softmax(u).(3)
This softmax-based transformation induces competition among neurons. When one neuron receives a large pre-
activation value, the softmax suppresses the others’ values, analogous to lateral inhibition. This competition
encourages certain neurons to specialise and dominate, increasing the prevalence of monosemantic neurons
associated with human-interpretable concepts.
However, it also reveals an undesirable phenomenon: although many secondary neurons’ activations are
suppressed to low magnitudes, these neurons remain polysemantic, with many features compressed into them.
Later layer normalisation (Ba et al., 2016) can amplify them and recover the polysemanticity property (Elhage
et al., 2022b). The “smuggling” by layer normalisation suggests that imposing local interpretability constraints
may not eliminate neural networks’ incentive to compress information through superposition. This issue
motivates global constraints across the neural network, such as weight-sparsity training discussed below.
6.10.2 Weight-Sparse Training
A weight-sparse transformer (Gao et al., 2026) treats weight sparsity as an explicit structural constraint that
is progressively strengthened during training. Gao et al. (2026) optimise the standard cross-entropy objective
along with anL0 constraint on model weights after each optimisation step. Specifically, within each weight
matrix, they retain only the largest-magnitude parameters and set the rest to zero. TheL0 constraint anneals
from a dense initialisation to the desired sparsity level over training. The resulting transformer has most
weight parameters exactly zero, making the remaining computational structure much easier to decompose
into small, task-specific circuits.
Its interpretability gains can be substantial. Under highly sparse regimes (e.g.,< 1%active weights), neurons
receive input from far fewer upstream neurons, and the model’s circuits for specific capabilities or behaviours
become much sparser. Mean-ablation experiments further confirm that these circuits are both necessary and
sufficient for the capability or behaviour.
Gao et al. (2026) characterised the trade-off between model capability and interpretability induced by
weight sparsity. Increasing sparsity generally makes the model easier to decompose into small, interpretable
circuits. However, it also degrades task performance, producing a capability–interpretability Pareto frontier.
Nonetheless, the authors found that increasing model size can shift this frontier outward. At comparable task
performance, larger sparse models can have substantially smaller, more interpretable circuits than smaller
models; at comparable interpretability, they can retain stronger capabilities. This suggests that scaling
model size alongside structural sparsity may offer a path to more interpretable yet high-capability models.
However, preserving interpretability beyond tens of millions of nonzero parameters remains challenging, and
weight-sparse training currently requires substantially more compute than traditional training.
6.10.3 Attention-Sparse Training
In transformers, attention patterns produced by an attention head are usuallydiffuse, i.e., every token
attends to every other token. Diffuse attention patterns are difficult to interpret and audit. Previous studies
have therefore exploredattention-sparse training, which aims to sparsify attention patterns to make them
more interpretable (Lei et al., 2025; Draye et al., 2026). Specifically, Lei et al. (2025) proposedSPARse
TrANsformer World model(SPARTAN), an object-centric world model trained withL0 regularisation on
attention patterns and a constrained optimisation objective to maintain cross-entropy performance equal to

6.10.4 Modifications of Computational Primitives: MOLT
One alternative approach to learning interpretable structure is to reconsider what the computational primitives
should be (Oldfield et al., 2025; Park et al., 2025; Braun et al., 2025; Bushnaq et al., 2025). A recent example
is the sparse mixture of linear transforms (MOLT), which represents a conceptual shift from feature extraction
towards transformation extraction (Lindsey et al., 2025b).
Standard SAEs and transcoders primarily decompose model activations into features. However, many
algorithmic tasks, such as arithmetic or geometric reasoning, are more naturally described byoperationssuch
as “add 3” or “rotate a vector”. In these tasks, we want to know how the model transforms one activation
into another through components like weight matrices in MLP blocks. To achieve this, MOLT replaces the
MLP with a sparse mixture of learned linear transformation matrices. The basic unit of analysis becomes
transformations applied to model activations rather than features.
For example, in a modular arithmetic task, MOLT can represent the concept of addition with a learned
rotation matrix, which relates more directly to the underlying algorithm than a collection of state-specific
features. More broadly, approaches that represent computational operations explicitly, as MOLT does, may
facilitate the development of interpretable representations for tasks governed by systematic operations. We
view Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks (KANs) as an approach that embodies this idea, as discussed below.
6.10.5 Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks (KANs)
Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks (KANs) represent one of the most radical departures from standard neural
network architectures (Liu et al., 2025b). In conventional neural networks, each neuron receives outputs from
upstream neurons through incoming edges weighted by scalar parameters, sums these weighted inputs, and then
applies a fixed nonlinear activation function (the whole process can be represented as matrix multiplication
in components like MLP blocks and attention modules in Section 4.4). Inspired by the Kolmogorov–Arnold
representation theorem, KANs place learnable nonlinear functions, typically parameterised using B-splines,
on edges rather than using fixed nonlinear activation functions at nodes.

This design gives KANs an explicitly compositional and thus more interpretable structure. As the nonlinearities
are univariate and can be visualised directly on individual edges, researchers can use techniques like symbolic
regression to approximate and inspect the learned analytical expressions, such as rediscovering known physical
equations. Although KAN training is currently more computationally expensive than training standard MLPs
and has not yet been convincingly demonstrated at the scale of large language models, this architectural
innovation points to an ambitious direction towards interpretable neural networks in which parameters
correspond to mathematically meaningful functions.
Summary.This section introduced several classical methods for feature extraction and analysis, followed
by approaches that aim to make models intrinsically interpretable. However, whether features are recovered
post hoc or induced by design, they remain units of analysis rather than complete explanations of the model’s
mechanism, i.e., how these units interact and causally influence one another. Section 7 therefore shifts from
individual features tocircuits: computational graphs of interacting components that describe how the model
implements its behaviours.
7 Circuits in Mechanistic Interpretability
Mechanistic interpretability aims not only to identify what information a model represents, but also to explain
how it transforms and combines that information across layers to produce behaviour. Feature analysis is a
useful tool for describing activation vectors, but it describes them in isolation. Many model behaviours arise
from structured interactions among multiple components that operate together across layers. To explain
these behaviours and their mechanisms, we need a high-level abstraction that captures critical computational
patterns of these features. The circuit framework (Figure 3; introduced in Section 4.5) addresses this gap
by modelling behaviour as coordinated computational graphs and making explicit how components causally
interact.
Notably, the circuit framework is not the only way to model an internal mechanism. Early studies have
explored alternative ways. For example, Giles et al. (1992) and Omlin & Giles (1996) categorised a recurrent
neural network’s hidden representations into different states and modelled its decision process as a finite-state
automaton when the input sentence was fed sequentially. Nonetheless, the circuit framework has attracted
growing research interest in studying neural networks’ internal mechanisms. Below, we introduce approaches
for identifying and constructing circuits.

Besides intervention (activation patching, ACDC, etc.) and attribution (EAP, EAP-IG, etc.) techniques,
another line of approaches treats circuit discovery as an optimisation problem (Csordás et al., 2021; Cao
et al., 2021; Bhaskar et al., 2024; Haider et al., 2026). Specifically, they use gradient descent to learn which
parts of the computational graph can be removed without affecting model behaviour. For example, Edge
Pruning (Bhaskar et al., 2024) learns edge masks to discover sparse connections, while multi-granular node
pruning (Haider et al., 2026) learns node masks at different scales, from entire blocks to individual neurons.
These methods can usually discover sparser circuits than intervention and attribution counterparts. However,
the optimisation process itself introduces randomness and sensitivity to training configurations like the
learning rate, which may make the subsequent analysis less robust and interpretable.
Circuits can explain models in different contexts, from a single input–output pair to a capability or behaviour.
Identifying a circuit for a specific input or prompt is calledquery-level circuit discovery(Wu & Barez, 2026).
In contrast,task-level circuit discovery(Wang et al., 2023; Kharlapenko et al., 2025) seeks to identify a circuit
that implements a broader capability or task, typically operationalised by a dataset of examples, such as the
indirect object identification (IOI) dataset (Wang et al., 2023). In the task-level setting, components’ and
edges’ attribution scores (e.g.,sS(x)or sij(x)) are aggregated across inputs to reduce example-specific noise,
yielding a circuit that characterises the task as a whole.
The techniques and methods introduced above, including activation patching, path patching, ACDC, EAP,
EAP-IG, and mask-based pruning methods, have primarily been developed and evaluated in the task-level
setting. More recent work has extended EAP-IG to identify circuits for individual prompts (Wu & Barez,
2026). This enables the discovery of sparse yet faithful circuits in the model even for complex, natural-language
user queries, where the relevant computation may vary substantially from one input to another.
7.2 Circuit Discovery with Replacement Models
The methods introduced above discover circuitswithinthe target model. Their nodes correspond to
coarse-grained components such as attention heads and MLP blocks, which are mostly not immediately under-
standable. A complementary approach first constructs a more interpretable replacement model (Section 6.6.2)
that approximates the original model’s computation using sparse linear features, and then performs circuit
discovery within this replacement model.
Recent work has implemented this paradigm using cross-layer transcoders (CLTs; Section 6.6.2) (Ameisen
et al., 2025; Merullo et al., 2025). In particular, Circuit Tracer (Ameisen et al., 2025) replaces the model’s
MLPs with CLTs while retaining the underlying model’s attention and residual-stream computation. This
yields a prompt-specific attribution graph whose principal internal nodes are sparse CLT features rather than
entire MLP blocks or attention heads.
