CLT-based circuit discovery differs from conventional circuit discovery in two aspects. First, the resulting
circuit’s nodes correspond to fine-grained linear features rather than coarse MLP blocks or attention modules.
Using automated feature-interpretation pipelines (Section 12.6) to assign natural-language descriptions to
these features, human inspectors can more easily understand the discovered mechanism. Second, an edge in a
CLT-based circuit denotes the direct, input-specific influence between two features, which is different from
the formulation of attribution methods based on clean–corrupted reference pairs, such as EAP and EAP-IG.
Specifically, in Circuit Tracer, a source feature can write to the residual stream at multiple subsequent layers,
and the strength of an edge from the source feature to a target feature is the aggregate of the contributions
of these writes to the target feature.
For a given prompt, Circuit Tracer produces a sparse attribution graph that describes active features and
their interactions, making it well suited to query-level circuit discovery. Interpretability platforms such as
Neuronpedia (Lin, 2023) also offer interactive implementations. However, the approach still has several
limitations. Specifically, CLTs only approximate MLP computations, so the discovered circuit may only cover
a part of the model’s underlying mechanism. Moreover, feature-level attribution graphs can have many nodes
and edges, so we must prune, cluster, or otherwise condense them before they become understandable.
7.3 Causal Verification
Once we identify circuits, two critical questions arise: are they causally responsible for the behaviour, and
can we modify them reliably?
Causal Necessity and Sufficiency.A circuit iscausally necessaryfor a behaviour if removing or ablating
the circuit degrades that behaviour. A circuit iscausally sufficientif activating the circuit alone, i.e., patching
all edges outside the circuit with activations from a corrupted reference run, reproduces the behaviour. In
practice, a circuit is rarely sparse, necessary, and sufficient at the same time; it typically explains 60–80% of
behavioural variance.
Evaluating Circuits and Benchmarking Discovery Methods.A circuit is often consideredfaithfulif
it is both causally necessary and causally sufficient for the behaviour it is claimed to explain (Hanna et al.,
2024; Marks et al., 2025a). Two popular approaches to validate causality are causal scrubbing and interchange
interventions (Chan et al., 2022a; Geiger et al., 2024). Causal scrubbing (Chan et al., 2022a) systematically
evaluates a mechanistic hypothesis by replacing model activations with those from inputs deemed equivalent
under the hypothesis and testing whether these interventions preserve the model behaviour. Interchange
interventions (Geiger et al., 2024) test whether model activations causally correspond to higher-level variables
by substituting activations across inputs and measuring the resulting change in model behaviour. Together,
these methods provide stronger evidence for mechanistic explanations than observational analysis alone.
More recently, several works have proposed metrics to quantify circuit faithfulness as a continuous score (Hanna
et al., 2024; Wu & Barez, 2026), allowing systematic comparisons of circuits discovered by different methods.
By aggregating faithfulness scores across tasks and settings, benchmarks such as MIB (Mueller et al.,
2025) evaluate how well circuit discovery methods identify causally important model components. However,
achieving strict necessity and sufficiency is often hard because many model behaviours depend on distributed
representations and multiple redundant pathways (Barez et al., 2026). Even if we identify a circuit that
captures the primary mechanism of a behaviour, components outside the circuit may still play important
roles, such as handling edge cases and computational robustness.

7.4 Case Study: Induction Heads
Circuit Perspective on Induction Heads
Following our introduction to induction heads in Section 6.8, we consider a repeated sequence:
A B C A B
where the model needs to predict the token after the secondB. The induction head alone is not
sufficient to implement induction behaviour from scratch. It still needs help from previous layers’
attention heads to locate the token following the current token’s previous occurrence, so it knows it
should attend toCin this example (Olsson et al., 2022).
Specifically, in a two-layer attention-only transformer, Elhage et al. (2021) discovered theprevious-
token head, which writes every token’s information to the next position. The change propagates to
the residual stream to be read by the induction head, allowing it to locateC (because now some
information about the firstB is contained inC). The two kinds of heads form theinduction circuit
that is sufficient to implement the induction behaviour in the two-layer small model.
Empirical evidence supports this mechanistic interpretation. Head ablation experiments show that
induction heads causally support in-context learning in the attention-only model. Circuit analysis
also reveals induction heads’ dependence on earlier previous-token heads. Moreover, induction
heads emerge abruptly during training, coinciding with sharp improvements in in-context learning
performance.
In larger models with additional layers and MLPs, the mechanism behind induction behaviour becomes
more complex. However, the core principle remains the same: context propagates across layers and is
used to conditionally retrieve tokens based on repeated subsequence matches. From this perspective,
the circuit framework complements feature-based analysis by explicitly identifying the model’s internal
mechanism that implements a specific behaviour.
7.5 A Unified Evaluation Framework for Mechanistic Interpretability
A persistent challenge in mechanistic interpretability (MI) is the lack of standardised evaluation. Different
interpretability methods use incompatible metrics. For example, for the same behaviour of interest, circuit
discovery can work at the level of MLP/attention modules (Conmy et al., 2023), CLT features (Ameisen
et al., 2025), or even neurons (Arora et al., 2026). A CLT-based circuit must also verify CLT fidelity; an
MLP/attention-level circuit should test and explain each node’s role. Thus, it is hard to compare them
and measure progress. To address this, this section presents a unified evaluation framework covering five
dimensions—attribution faithfulness, completeness, stability, causal validity, and human interpretability—
where different methods can be jointly tested.
7.5.1 The Need for Standardised Evaluation
Before we discuss the five dimensions, we first explain in detail the need for standardised evaluation.
Specifically, current evaluation practices face several challenges:
• Utility ambiguity:Methods are initially developed for different aims and evaluated against
distinct objectives, yet have overlapping application scenarios. For example, SAEs are assessed
using reconstruction error and sparsity metrics; circuits are evaluated using behavioural recovery
or faithfulness tests; and difference-in-means steering vectors (see Section 9.3) are examined by
behaviour change—although all three approaches can be used to steer model outputs. Their unclear
intended uses make it hard to compare their utility.
58
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
• Cherry-picking:Existing work often reports interpretability results on carefully selected examples,
samples from a narrow distribution, or capabilities where a method performs well. It may not report
negative results, failure cases, or coverage statistics. This makes it difficult to assess the robustness
and generality of the findings and determine whether the proposed method genuinely outperforms
existing ones.
• Missing baselines:Many proposed methods’ claimed interpretability gains are not systematically
and adequately compared against intuitive alternatives or baselines such as behavioural methods,
random activations, or neuron-level analysis. Without this comparison, it is unclear whether a
method extracts genuinely meaningful information.
• Reproducibility gaps:Many existing techniques involve substantial hyperparameter choices, heavy
training procedures, and high variation across seemingly irrelevant factors. Reproducibility is often
underreported and has not yet been established as a property to optimise.
• Faithfulness–understandability gap:Methods often demonstrate how understandable and
informative their outputs are to humans. However, those outputs’ faithfulness to the underlying
model mechanism receives less attention. This rewards explanations that are persuasive rather than
faithful.
Lan et al. (2026) have called for a shared platform for tracking and auditing interpretability insights and claims
across papers; Ayonrinde & Jaburi (2025) proposed a framework that evaluates mechanistic explanations
from several philosophy-of-science perspectives. However, these discussions remain largely conceptual. The
MI community needs standardised, concrete evaluation protocols and benchmarks, along with established
reporting practices, to enable principled comparisons across methods and findings. They are especially
important for measuring real progress in the field, identifying systematic failure modes, and providing
evidence about what methods do and do not reveal. More broadly, they are necessary for mechanistic
interpretability to mature from a collection of promising techniques into a cumulative scientific discipline.

The MI community has developed several benchmarks that examine the causal validity of interpretability
methods. For example, MIB (Mueller et al., 2025) provides standardised tasks for assessing discovered circuits
and causal variables (e.g., features); AxBench (Wu et al., 2025b) evaluates methods’ ability to steer models
towards given concepts; RAVEL (Huang et al., 2024) investigates methods’ ability to localise features of
given concepts by using interchange interventions to validate discovered features; and SAEBench (Karvonen
et al., 2025) evaluates SAEs specifically, pairing reconstruction metrics with downstream intervention tasks
such as gender bias erasure.
Dimension 5: Human Interpretability
Human interpretability measures whether generated explanations eventually improve human understanding,
prediction, and decision-making about model behaviour.
Human Interpretability Metrics
Explanation Utility.This metric tests whether humans can predict model behaviour more accu-
rately in the held-out set based on the explanation. It is formulated as:
Expl-Utility=P(correct prediction|with explanation)−P(correct prediction|no explanation)
Debugging Utility.This metric examines whether the explanations help humans identify and
repair model errors, such as incorrect outputs or misaligned behaviour, in the wild.
Debug-Utility=P(error fixed|with explanation)−P(error fixed|no explanation).
Consistency of Interpretation.This metric inspects whether different humans interpret the same
explanation consistently.
Inter-Rater=κ(human 1 labels,human 2 labels)
whereκ(·)is Cohen’s kappa or a similar agreement metric.
Evaluation protocol:
1. Prediction task:Show humans explanations of model components or mechanisms and ask them to
predict model behaviour on held-out inputs. Compare accuracy to a no-explanation baseline.
2. Identification task:Show humans model outputs with errors and ask them to identify the cause,
with and without explanation assistance. Measure accuracy and required time to complete the task.
3. Intervention task:Ask humans to propose fixes for model errors based on explanations. Measure
the success rate of proposed interventions.
4. Agreement task:Ask multiple human raters to generate explanations, if applicable (e.g., write
a summary of highly activated samples of an SAE feature as its explanation). Measure inter-rater
reliability and agreement with machine-generated explanations.
Several caveats and challenges arise when evaluating the human interpretability of tested methods. For
example, human studies are usually expensive. Moreover, human expertise may confound results, where some
explanations understandable to MI researchers may be opaque to domain experts, and vice versa.
Note that different interpretability methods may emphasise distinct evaluation dimensions and operationalise
them differently. Table 10 provides guidance on applying this framework to some common interpretability
approaches.

7.5.3 Integrated Evaluation Protocol
We recommend the following integrated protocol for comprehensive evaluation:
Recommended Evaluation Protocol
Step 1: Define scope.Users first specify the model, layer(s), and behaviour(s) of interest and
define a behavioural test suite with clear success criteria.
Step 2: Establish baselines.Users specify baseline methods, such as random directions in
activation space, PCA components, individual neurons, and supervised probes (if labels are available).
Step 3: Apply interpretability method.Users apply the method of interest to analyse models
with variation in random seeds, hyperparameters, and other training details.
65
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
Step 4: Evaluate across all five dimensions.Users compute metrics for attribution faithfulness,
completeness, stability, causal validity, and human interpretability.
Step 5: Report comprehensively.Users report all five dimensions instead of just favourable
metrics and discuss the method’s failure cases, unexplained behaviours, and comparisons to baselines.
7.5.4 Limitations of This Framework
This evaluation framework, though comprehensive, still has several limitations:
• Metric choice:The proposed specific metrics are not uniquely correct. Alternative formalisations
may be appropriate for specific contexts.
• Threshold arbitrariness:Thresholds (e.g., the accuracy that counts as success) may lack theoretical
grounding and will need empirical calibration.
• Computational cost:Evaluating all five dimensions comprehensively is expensive and potentially
prohibitive for large-scale studies.
• Human evaluation bottleneck:Dimension 5 requires time-consuming, expensive, and subjective
human studies.
• Task dependence:A method’s performance under this framework can depend on the evaluation
task. For example, a method that excels at factual recall may perform poorly at reasoning.
Despite these limitations, systematic evaluation across multiple dimensions provides more reliable evidence
than an arbitrary choice of metrics. Readers should view the framework as a starting point for standardisation,
not a final answer.
Summary.This section introduced circuit discovery methods, which trace how model components or
features interact to produce behaviour, either directly on the model’s computational graph (e.g., ACDC and
EAP) or within interpretable replacement models (e.g., Circuit Tracer). We also discussed how to causally
verify discovered circuits and introduced a broader evaluation framework for mechanistic interpretability
methods based on faithfulness, completeness, stability, causal validity, and human interpretability. In summary,
Section 6 introduced methods for extracting interpretable units of analysis, while this section examined
how those units interact through circuits to produce behaviour. The next section takes a complementary
perspective: directly interpreting the information in individual representations using natural language.
8 Understanding Intermediate Representations
This section explores interpreting hidden activations directly in natural language. In contrast to feature
extraction and circuit discovery (Sections 6 and 7), which extract features or their interactions from model
representations (activations), the methods we will discuss in this section treat the activation itself as the
object of interpretation. They use language models or other natural-language-based methods to describe
or elicit the encoded information, without intervening on or decomposing the underlying activation. This
paradigm provides a direct interface between model activations and natural-language explanations, making it
particularly accessible and understandable for human users.

8.1 Logit Lens: Tracing Predictions Through Depth
Logit Lens (Figure 10)
Logit lens (nostalgebraist, 2020) applies the model’s unembedding matrix to activations at intermediate
layers, revealing what the modelwould predictif computation stopped at that layer. For a hidden
activationh ℓ at layerℓ, logit lens computes:
logitsℓ =W Uhℓ,
whereWU represents the model’s unembedding matrix. Applying it across layers reveals the prediction
trajectory, showing when and where the model commits to specific outputs (nostalgebraist, 2020).
Logit lens (Figure 10) provides intuitive insight into the model’s decision-making process across depth.
Experimental results show that early layers tend to produce diffuse predictions, while later layers progressively
narrow them towards the final output, though exceptions exist. For example, in a twelve-layer language
model processing the sequence A B C A B , the logit lens may reveal that the tokenC enters the top-20
candidates at layer 6 and is progressively amplified, eventually becoming the top-ranked token at the final
layer. Conversely, for induction tasks in complex linguistic patterns, early and middle layers may show a flat
probability distribution across many tokens, with the model converging to a specific prediction only in the
last few layers.

Limitations of Vanilla Logit Lens.The vanilla logit lens has a critical limitation: applying the
unembedding matrix to intermediate activations assumes that the hidden state is in a format that the output
layer expects. However, intermediate representations may be organised very differently from output-layer
activations. Applying the unembedding matrix to layer-6 activations may extract relevant information but
cannot precisely reflect the model’s underlying computation at that layer (nostalgebraist, 2020). Furthermore,
logit lens is fundamentally correlational rather than causal. It projects the activation into the output
vocabulary space without testing the roles decoded tokens play in model computation. In particular, because
of the representational mismatch discussed above, decoded tokens represent at most information recoverable
from the activation, rather than information used in model computation.

more aggressively than logit lens (Gurnee et al., 2026).

Limitations of Jacobian Lens.J-lens still faces several limitations that warrant further investigation.
First, like logit lens and tuned lens, it operates primarily at the token level. However, many semantically
meaningful concepts are represented by multiple tokens. For example, the word “photoperiodism” may be
split into several subword tokens. If only one token (e.g., “photo”) is visible in J-lens, we cannot tell whether
it corresponds to the concept of photoperiodism or actually other words. Second, J-lens is found to work best
within a certain range of layers, calledJ-space(Gurnee et al., 2026). Specifically, decoded concepts are most
informative in intermediate layers (e.g., approximately 38–92% of the depth in Claude Sonnet 4.5). In early
layers, decoded concepts are noisy and hard to interpret. In later layers, they collapse towards the model’s
output and are also uninformative. Some recent studies have attempted to address these limitations (Gurnee
et al., 2026; Blank et al., 2026).

Limitations of LatentQA.LatentQA faces several technical challenges, including the generalisability of
the learned representation-to-text mapping. When the fine-tuning datasetD is too small or insufficiently
diverse, the verbaliser may memorise superficial correspondences between representations and explanations
rather than learning to extract information from representations. Recent approaches, such as Predictive
Concept Decoders (PCDs) (Huang et al., 2026) and Activation Oracles (AOs) (Karvonen et al., 2026a),
mitigate this issue by constructing more diverse training datasets.
Another technical challenge is evaluating whether activation-verbalisation models genuinely explain the
represented information rather than exploit shortcuts. For example, a verbaliser may implicitly reconstruct
the original input to the target model and infer an explanation from it. Recent studies have found that such
failure modes are severe and prevalent in existing verbalisers (Li et al., 2026c; Jakkli et al., 2026). As a
result, strong verbalisation performance alone is insufficient to show that the verbaliser faithfully analysed
the internal representations.
8.6 Probing Classifiers: Capabilities, Critiques, and Causal Limitations
Probing classifiers (Figure 13) are among the most widely used tools for analysing neural network representa-
tions. A probe is a classifier trained to predict a property of the input, such as part of speech, sentiment, or
entity type, from model activations. High probe accuracy means that the property is decodable from the
activations. However, information decodability is a relatively coarse-grained, correlational interpretability
claim compared with causal claims about information in model computation. This section reviews probing
methodology, its major critiques, and its appropriate role in interpretability research.
As a side note, discovered probe directions can also be used as supervised feature extractors. We discuss this
perspective in Section 6.9.4, including comparisons with SAEs, and in Section 9.3, where we discuss their use
as steering vectors.

Probing Classifier (Figure 13)
Aprobing classifieris a supervised model trained to predict a target propertyy from neural network

Probing provides evidence about whether activations contain information about a property. High probe
accuracy indicates the information is present; low accuracy suggests it is absent or the probe is not expressive
enough. Note that probing alone does not show whether the model actually depends on that information in
its decision-making process. A representation can encode information that downstream computation never
accesses, such as “leftover” information from earlier processing.
The Probe Causality Problem
High probe accuracy does not imply causal relevance (Belinkov, 2022; Hewitt & Liang, 2019). The
probe can work by detecting features spuriously correlated with the target property (e.g., word
frequency correlates with part of speech) rather than detecting the target property itself. Furthermore,
subsequent layers may never use the decoded property to influence the model output. Finally, a

In summary, using probing alone generally does not provide actionable mechanistic understanding and therefore

and evaluation, enabling more actionable mechanistic understanding (Elazar et al., 2021); see Section 8.6.4 for
details. Recent interpretability studies have similarly used causal interventions to validate probe-discovered
concept directions, building a more complete mechanistic explanation (Marks & Tegmark, 2024; Li et al.,
2023).
8.6.2 Control Tasks and Selectivity
High probe accuracy may reflect classification capacity rather than the target property’s decodability. Hewitt
& Liang (2019) addressed this concern by introducingcontrol tasksas a probe’s baseline performance.
73

text:
Control Task Methodology
Acontrol taskassigns random labels to inputs to break any genuine relationship between activations
and the target property. A probe trained on the control task represents thebaseline extractabilityof
random patterns from the representation. Then, theselectivityof a probe is defined as:
Selectivity=Acc linguistic−Acccontrol,
where Acclinguistic is probe accuracy on the target task andAcccontrol is accuracy on the control task.
High selectivity indicates that the probe succeeds because the representation genuinely encodes the
target property. In contrast, low selectivity suggests we cannot tell whether the probe has exploited
spurious features rather than task-relevant structure.
8.6.3 Concerns of Probe Complexity
Probe complexity brings confounding factors to the analysis. If a property can only be extracted with a
highly nonlinear probe, it is hard to tell whether the property is “deeply encoded” or whether the probe is
simply using nonlinearity to exploit signals, including noise. A recent finding in causal abstraction (Sutter
et al., 2025) also showed that, when the mapping function is complex enough, it can map an arbitrary (even
randomly initialised) neural network to a causal model of interest, producing false-positive findings.
The Complexity–Interpretability Trade-off
Observation.In general, more complex probes achieve higher accuracy but provide less interpretable
deliverables.
Interpretation problem.Does high accuracy with a complex probe indicate (a) the property is
encoded but in a complex, nonlinear form, or (b) the probe itself is computing the property from
spurious features? If (b), the probe at most demonstrates that the property iscomputable fromthe
representation, not that it isencoded inthe representation in any meaningful sense. A worse case in
(b) is that a highly nonlinear probe may learn to construct the property of interest from random noise
rather than any features (Sutter et al., 2025). In this case, the computable illusion likely stems from
limited test-set size.
Minimum Description Length Probes.To address this, Voita & Titov (2020) proposed evaluating
probes via the minimum description length (MDL) principle: prefer probes that achieve good accuracy with
minimal complexity. The proposed MDL-based evaluation offers an information-theoretic measure of how
efficiently a probe can extract a target property from model representations, accounting for both probe
accuracy and complexity. A property is considered “more encoded” if it can be extracted with a simpler
probe. This paradigm shifts the question from “can we extract it?” to “how easily can we extract it?”
Practical Guidance.Users should prefer simple probes when possible, compare against probes trained on
random representations to establish baselines, and consider MDL-based evaluation to analyse the trade-off
between accuracy and model complexity. If linear probes fail but MLP probes succeed, cautiously validate
the result and interpretability claim.
8.6.4 Amnesic Probing and Causal Probing
Beyond using probes to validate information decodability, researchers have also formalised the idea of
intervening on representations via probes. Giulianelli et al. (2018) first showed that a trained probe can steer
model behaviour, and Ravfogel et al. (2020) extended this with Iterative Nullspace Projection (INLP), an
information-removal method that repeatedly fits a probe to identify linearly encoded information and project
it out. Elazar et al. (2021) further measured changes in downstream model behaviour after applying INLP
as a validation of the probe’s causality, calledamnesic probing. These paradigms add causality to probes,

pushing them from correlational understanding to mechanistic analysis. Below, we detail amnesic probing
and probing with activation patching.
Amnesic Probing.
Amnesic Probing
Given a model activationh and a probe trained to predict a propertyP,amnesic probingtests whether
information aboutP is causally relevant to downstream model behaviour by removing information
about P from the representation and evaluating the effects on model outputs. AssumeP is a binary
property (e.g., positive vs. negative sentiment) and thatw := W⊤
probe ∈R d denotes the probe’s

null space of the probe):
˜h=h− h⊤w

Amnesic probing then measures the change in model performance on downstream tasks with the
modified representation ˜h. A substantial degradation indicates that the removed information causally
contributes to the evaluated behaviour. Notably, unchanged performance does not establish that the
information is unused since redundant representations or alternative computational pathways may
preserve the behaviour.
Amnesic probing assumes the target property is decodable and that there exist effective erasure procedures
to surgically remove its associated information from the representation. However, information and concept
erasure may be imperfect in practice, either leaving residual information or affecting other concepts. Such
imperfections confound interpretations of downstream behavioural changes and the causal claims that follow.
Causal Probing via Activation Patching.Activation patching tests the causality of a component’s
representations by swapping them between inputs that differ in the target property. This technique has also
been used to test the causality of probes (Huang et al., 2024; Arora et al., 2024). Supposex1 and x2 are two
inputs, whilex1 has the target propertyP and x2 does not.Wprobe is the fitted probing matrix whose rows
span a probing subspace (or a direction if the matrix has only one row, such as that of a binary classification
probe) whereP resides. After choosing the intervention location (e.g., the last-token residual stream at a
middle layer), the method first feedsx1 to the model and extracts the component of the representation in the
probing subspace. Then, it feedsx2 to the model while patching the corresponding component of the model
representation with the previously acquired one. If the model output forx2 shifts towardsP, the patched
subspace representation contains information aboutPthat the model uses.
Compared with amnesic probing, which tests the effect of removing information aboutP, activation patching
examines whether the probe-identified information is sufficient to implement the target behaviour. However,
this requires specifying what representation (i.e., which layer, component, and token position) to probe and
patch, which may confound the analysis.
8.6.5 Implications of Attribution Faithfulness for Probing
Probing is often used along with attribution methods (e.g., saliency maps, attention visualisation, gradient-
based attribution) to understand model behaviour. However, attribution methods also have technical
challenges. For example, gradient-based saliency maps can highlight input features the model is actually
insensitive to (Adebayo et al., 2018), attention weights correlate weakly with causal importance (Jain &
Wallace, 2019), and different attribution methods can disagree substantially on the same inputs (Krishna
et al., 2024). These findings suggest that attribution methods alone cannot determine what information a
model actually uses.
This unreliability affects how we can interpret probing results. Probes trained on attention patterns may not
reveal causally important information since attention itself may not be causal. Similarly, using gradients to
identify which features or components to probe can bias towards high-magnitude gradients that lack causal
importance. In sum, interpretability claims made by probes, even paired with these auxiliary tools, still

8.6.6 When Is Probing Appropriate?
Given the preceding discussion, Table 11 summarises appropriate uses of probing. We argue that probing is
most productive when treated as a tool forhypothesis generation, that is, using probes to identify candidate
properties that may be encoded in a representation and potentially causally relevant. Users then test these
hypotheses using causal methods, such as activation steering or patching. In this sense, probing serves as an
efficient first step in mechanistic investigation rather than as a decisive explanation.
8.6.7 Methodological Standards in Probing Research
So far we have reviewed several strengths and limitations of probes. Based on them, we summarise several
methodological standards for the design and interpretation of probing studies: (1) Report control-task
baselines to distinguish genuine decodability from spurious exploitation; (2) Use minimally expressive probes
unless additional complexity is justified; (3) Test causal relevance by methods like amnesic probing or
activation patching; (4) Analyse layer-wise trends besides the peak accuracy; (5) Distinguish encoding from
causality and acknowledge that successful probing shows information presence rather than causal use; (6)
Report the stability of findings by evaluating across seeds and data splits. In sum, we believe these standards
help ensure responsible, effective use of probing in interpretability research and downstream applications.
Probing Classifiers for Sleeper Agents
Despite the causality critiques, probing remains valuable for many applications. For example,
MacDiarmid et al. (2024) showed that simple linear probes trained on residual-stream activations can
detect latent backdoor behaviour in the sleeper agent model even when the probe fitting set does not
contain the trigger or the harmful behaviour.
To recap: a sleeper agent modelfθ(·)behaves normally for one context (e.g.,y = “2023”) but ex-
hibits a hidden dangerous policy when a trigger is present (e.g.,y = “2024”) (MacDiarmid et al., 2024).
To detect this latent behaviour, MacDiarmid et al. (2024) constructed a linear defection detector by
computing adetector direction uℓ at layerℓ. Specifically, lethℓ(x)denote the residual activations
at the final token position for inputx. Given a small labelled fit dataset of prompts, the detector

uℓ =E x∼Dtrue[hℓ(x)]−E x∼Dfalse[hℓ(x)],
whereDtrue andDfalse are contrast pairs of prompts. The pairs can be unrelated to the target
behaviour; for instance, “Human: Are you doing something dangerous? Assistant: yes” and “Human:
... Assistant: no” (example borrowed from MacDiarmid et al. (2024)). During the evaluation stage, ac-
tivations are projected onto this direction to yield a detector activation value⟨hℓ(x),uℓ⟩. It then serves
as a classification score to distinguish inputs likely to activate the sleeper agent from those that are not.
Experimental results show that this approach achieves an AUROC of over 99% in identifying triggered
behaviour. MacDiarmid et al. (2024) argued that this is because the activation differences between
triggered and non-triggered inputs are sufficiently salient (for example, two clusters far apart). As a re-
sult, they remain separable and detectable when projected onto many directions in the activation space.
Why this works despite the causality critiques: In this use case, the goal isdetection(information
presence), not mechanistic understanding. A safety filter’s primary goal is to detect encoded deceptive
intent and flag potential danger, not discover its internal mechanism. In summary, this use case shows
that probing remains valuable for auditing or detection even though it cannot support causal claims.
Summary.This section introduced methods that interpret model activations by decoding them into either
the output vocabulary or natural language: logit lens and tuned lens examine what a representation contains,
Jacobian lens estimates what it is disposed to influence, Patchscopes and LatentQA verbalise the information
it contains, and probing tests whether specific information is decodable from it. These methods primarily
reveal what can be decoded from a representation but not whether the decoded information is subsequently
used by the model. Section 9 broadens the discussion to comparing representations across models, locating
where information is stored, and intervening on representations to control model behaviour.
9 Representation Analysis: Comparison, Localisation, and Control
Following Section 8’s emphasis on understanding representations at a broader level, this section considers
three successive questions about model representations. Model diffing (Section 9.1) asks what differs between
two models’ representations. Knowledge localisation (Section 9.2) asks where a particular piece of information
or behaviour is most causally relevant. Representation engineering and steering (Section 9.3) asks whether
mechanistic understanding of model representations can be used to change model behaviour.
These methods are also closely connected to neighbouring sections. Diffing two checkpoints of the same
model can be viewed as a specific instance of the longitudinal analysis discussed in Section 10.1. Knowledge
localisation operates at a coarser level of analysis than the feature-extraction methods in Section 6, but
pursues a stricter causal objective by identifying the components at which particular behaviours can be most
effectively intervened upon. Finally, representation steering causally tests mechanistic findings by examining
whether intervening on an identified representation produces the predicted behavioural change.
9.1 Model Diffing: Identifying Internal Changes Across Models
Many concerning behaviours, such as reward hacking or sycophancy, arise during fine-tuning (Sharma
et al., 2024b; MacDiarmid et al., 2025). This phenomenon makes it important to monitor features and
circuits introduced or amplified during this process to prevent unsafe models from being deployed. Model
diffing (Anthropic, 2024) can surface some of these features.
Model Diffing
For two models,model diffingseeks to identify differences in features or circuits between them. These
differences may consist of features or circuits that are exclusive to one model, or of differences in how
shared features or circuits are used.
77
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
Representation Alignment and Convergent Learning.An earlier line of work compared internal
representations across models using correlation- and mutual information-based measures (Li et al., 2015),
canonical-correlation methods such as SVCCA and PWCCA (Raghu et al., 2017; Morcos et al., 2018), and
kernel-based alignment metrics such as CKA (Kornblith et al., 2019). Related approaches examine whether
the representations of one model can be expressed as linear combinations of representations in another (Wang
et al., 2018). This literature primarily concernsconvergent learning: whether independently trained models
with different random initialisations learn similar representations up to permutation, rotation, or other linear
transformations. More recent work has extended these techniques to study representational convergence
across modalities (Huh et al., 2024; Gröger et al., 2026), as discussed in Section 5.4. In contrast to model
diffing as defined here, these methods typically focus on representational similarity rather than on identifying
concrete features or circuits that areintroduced, amplified, or repurposedby a specific training intervention.
Applications.Model diffing has been applied to assess the effect of fine-tuning (Dumas et al., 2025a;
Lindsey et al., 2024; Aranguri & McGrath, 2025; Wang et al., 2026a) and distillation (Baek & Tegmark,
2025), to track differences between model architectures (Thasarathan et al., 2025; Jiralerspong & Bricken,
2025), to study the evolution of concepts during pretraining (Bayazit et al., 2026; Ge et al., 2026), and to
identify vision-specific features introduced during vision-language training, enabling targeted removal or
steering (Batra et al., 2026).
Dictionary Learning Methods.Dictionary learning is an intuitive approach to implement model diffing.
It can highlight unexpected, newly introduced features of concern. When diffing models of the same
architecture, such as a base versus instruction-fine-tuned model or a series of model checkpoints along
pretraining, dictionary learning methods like sparse autoencoders (SAEs) and transcoders can be trained
on the difference in token activations (Dumas et al., 2025b; Sawmya et al., 2025; Inaba et al., 2025). This
difference can capture features introduced by fine-tuning or by different pretraining stages. A simple baseline
technique is to train an SAE on the base model alone and use it as a fixed feature basis for comparison.
Methods like SAE-Track maintain continuity through recurrent initialisation, training each checkpoint’s
SAE from its predecessor’s so latents remain matched across the run (Xu et al., 2025b). The differences in
activations between two models are then measured on a shared evaluation prompt set (Wang et al., 2026a).
By causally intervening with latents that activate more strongly in the fine-tuned model, it is possible to
identify features responsible for misaligned behaviour (Wang et al., 2026a).
One challenge for model-diffing approaches is attributing features in a fine-tuned model’s representations to
the fine-tuning itself. To address this, an SAE trained on a base model can be fine-tuned stage-wise (Bricken
et al., 2024): first on the base model with fine-tuning data, then on the fine-tuned model with base data, and
finally on the fine-tuned model with fine-tuning data. Only features exclusive to the last setting are likely to
have been introduced via fine-tuning.
SAEs are applicable when inputs from different models have the same dimension. When diffing two models
with different architectures, for example, to track dispositions across model generations or sizes, this might not
hold. In this case, crosscoders offer an alternative (Figure 14). Crosscoders can define model-specific encoders
with arbitrarily different input dimensions that project activations from different models into one or more
shared representational spaces. Although the main advantage of crosscoders over SAEs is cross-architecture
comparison (Thasarathan et al., 2025; Jiralerspong & Bricken, 2025), some prior work has also applied them
to base and fine-tuned models (Lindsey et al., 2024; Bricken et al., 2024; Dumas et al., 2025a) and across
pretraining checkpoints (Ge et al., 2026; Bayazit et al., 2026).
A related approach is to model differences in how representations aretransformed, rather than comparing
the representations themselves. Hu et al. (2026) used transcoders to learn a function that approximates the
difference in MLP computation between a base model and its fine-tuned variant. Specifically, adapters are
trained so that a base MLP augmented with a learned correction term reproduces the fine-tuned MLP’s
behaviour within the full model. Unlike the above methods, which operate on activation differences, this
method learns a transformation that approximates how fine-tuning modifies the model’s MLP computation.
A shared concern across dictionary-learning-based model-diffing methods is the faithfulness of the sparse
decomposition (see Section 6.5.5). Extracted features may not faithfully reflect the underlying representations

False Positives in Model Diffing
Dictionary learning methods for model diffing risk falsely identifying model-exclusive features (Dumas
et al., 2025a; Jiralerspong & Bricken, 2025). This can result from the loss function: for instance,
Dumas et al. (2025a) showed that crosscoders trained with anL1 regularisation on hidden states can
falsely identify novel features, which they tried to mitigate withσBatch-TopK(·). However, even with this
improved architecture, false positives may persist. During fine-tuning, the directions representing some
features can rotate, and dictionary learning methods currently cannot distinguish between features
introduced via fine-tuning and those merely represented differently. Thus, supposedly model-exclusive
features should be regarded as hypotheses that need further validation.
LLM-Based Approaches.To differentiate closed-weight models, it is desirable to develop model diffing
tools that only rely on API access. To that end, Kempf et al. (2026) showed that an LLM can generate
natural-language hypotheses about behavioural differences between two models by extracting, clustering,
and summarising differences across many response pairs from the two models on a shared prompt set.
Benchmarked against the SAE-based baseline, the LLM-based method matches it on many dimensions while
surfacing more abstract, behaviour-level differences.

9.2 Knowledge Localisation: Where Is Information Stored?
Knowledge localisation methods aim to identify the layers, components, or subspaces whose activations
are causally associated with a particular capability or behaviour. For instance, causal tracing identifies
components that causally impact specific factual association retrieval by observing how model outputs
change after activation intervention (Meng et al., 2022). Related work suggests that feed-forward layers
disproportionately contain associations for factual knowledge (Geva et al., 2021), which can reside in the
subspace spanned by the top singular directions of late-layer MLPs’ weight matrices (Sharma et al., 2024c).
These early analyses lay the basis for knowledge localisation.
Localisation can identify where information is most strongly represented. However, it does not indicate
whether the model uses that information. In transformers, which are usually overparameterised, information
can be redundantly represented and processed across many model components and activation subspaces
depending on the input. In other words, a component with a strong causal effect may capture only part of
the mechanism. As a result, localisation is a useful starting point for mechanistic understanding, but not a
self-contained analysis.
One application is to identify activation directions associated with specific behaviours. For example, refusal
behaviour has been found to have approximately low-dimensional structure, with certain activation directions
associated with the model’s tendency to refuse harmful requests (Arditi et al., 2024). Similarly, researchers
can study sleeper-agent behaviours (Hubinger et al., 2024) by comparing activations across layers for triggered
and non-triggered inputs (MacDiarmid et al., 2024). These analyses help answer questions such as where and
how the model encodes behaviour-related information. However, identifying an activation direction or layer
does not explain the internal mechanisms underlying the behaviour, which can only be understood through
finer-grained analyses such as circuit discovery.
9.3 Representation Engineering and Steering
To manipulate model behaviour, representation engineering alters activation-space representations directly,
rather than via model weight modification.Activation steeringgenerally refers to methods that target
intermediate activations (usually the residual stream) by adding certain vectors that shift model outputs
during inference. This differs from localisation methods, which determine where information or behaviour is
represented, as steering techniques aim to identify a specific, manipulable vector thatchangesmodel behaviour.
Because they require no weight updates or retraining, these interventions are lightweight approaches for
controlling behaviour.
Steering Vector (Figure 15)
Asteering vector vsteer∈R d is an activation-space direction which, when scaled (αvsteer) and added
to an intermediate activation, shifts model outputs towards a targeted behaviour. For instance, one
steering direction can use the weight vector of a trained linear probe. Another popular method is
difference-in-means, which obtains the steering vector by taking the difference between activations
associated with two behaviours (Rimsky et al., 2024):
vsteer =E[h ℓ|preferred]−E[h ℓ|unpreferred].
During inference, the intervention takes the form
˜hℓ =h ℓ +αv steer,
whereαcontrols the intervention strength.
While these approaches appear simple, they reliably change model behaviours such as refusal, helpfulness, and
stylistic tendencies (Rimsky et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025; Arditi et al., 2024). Thus, steering is useful both
as a technique to manipulate behaviour and as a causality test for probes. If intervening along a direction

influences that behaviour. Below we use refusal vectors as a concrete example.

refuse requests. Define ht

of refusal directions can vary across models and experimental settings (Arditi et al., 2024).
The contrast betweenlocalisationandsteeringis shown by refusal vectors: measuring st

Nonlinear and Optimisation-Based Steering.Beyond linear directions, recent studies have explored
more complex ways of manipulating model activations. For example, Raval et al. (2026) projected model
activations into a kernel PCA space, steered them linearly there, and projected them back to the original
activation space; Wurgaft et al. (2026) steered activations along a low-dimensional manifold, motivated
by findings that some concepts are better represented as manifolds in the activation space. Separately,
optimisation-based methods construct steering directions by directly optimising objectives over intermediate
activations, offering an alternative to closed-form constructions. For example, they can be obtained by
maximising task performance or by suppressing undesirable outputs under intervention. These optimisation-
based approaches offer greater flexibility for complex or nonlinear objectives but generally require substantially
more computation than closed-form contrastive methods (Dunefsky & Cohan, 2025; Oozeer et al., 2025).
Steering as a Causal Test for Feature Interpretability.Activation steering can causally evaluate
representations previously labelled by feature-extraction methods (such as CLTs or SAEs). For instance,
a feature may be hypothesised to represent a particular concept. Supporting evidence can be obtained by
steering along the identified feature direction and evaluating the resulting change in behaviour.
These evaluations have been used to compare interpretable direction-identification approaches, including
SAE features, difference-in-means directions, and DAS (Huang et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025b). Benchmarks
designed to evaluate the causal and behavioural properties of learned representations include RAVEL (Huang
et al., 2024), MIB (Mueller et al., 2025), and AxBench (Wu et al., 2025b).
Limitations: Brittleness and Mechanistic Opacity
While steering methods effectively control behaviours and support causal testing, they have limitations.
Notably, they can be brittle, as a direction identified for one distribution, model, or task may not
generalise reliably. Another limitation is that successful behavioural steering does not, by itself,
establish mechanistic transparency, because an intervention may simultaneously impact multiple
features, interact nonlinearly with existing computations, or exploit unintended pathways that produce
the desired behaviour without corresponding to a clean mechanism (Makelov et al., 2024). Thus,

points where information or behaviours are causally localised, and representation engineering analyses how
representation manipulation controls behaviour. Steering has two important roles: as a control technique and
as a way to causally test how representations affect behaviour (while noting that successful localisation or
steering does not, by itself, provide a complete explanation for the mechanism underlying that behaviour).
This analysis is extended in Section 10, which examines how representations and mechanisms evolve during
training.
10 Learning Dynamics and Mechanistic Interpretability
Most interpretability research treats a trained model as static. It asks what the model activations represent,
which components implement a behaviour, or how an intervention changes its output at a particular checkpoint.
However, a model does not come into the world fully formed—it is the product of a learning process over time.
Recently, public model suites with intermediate checkpoints (Biderman et al., 2023b; Groeneveld et al., 2024)
and transparent training processes, such as Pythia (Biderman et al., 2023b) trained on the publicly available
Pile corpus (Gao et al., 2020), have enabled systematic study of thesetraining trajectories, unlocking unique
insights into how models form behaviours.
Research at the intersection of training dynamics and interpretability can have two aims.Longitudinal
analysis(Section 10.1) treats learning dynamics as an object of explanation, asking how and why mechanisms
82
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
form, change, stabilise, or disappear over the course of training (Saphra, 2023).Training dynamics as a
toolinstead uses temporal variation to answer questions about the model itself. For example, researchers
can compare changes across checkpoints to identify certain mechanisms, distinguish competing explanations,
predict later capabilities or failure modes, and guide interventions on the training process.
10.1 Longitudinal Analysis
Saphra (2023) argued that we can fully understand model internals only in light of their development: an
analysis confined to the final checkpoint risks misattributing the function or origin of the structures it finds
there. This subsection covers what longitudinal studies have established about the relationship between
training data and the capabilities models acquire (Section 10.1.1) and about the lifecycle of internal features
(Section 10.1.2); abrupt formation events are treated separately in Section 10.3.
10.1.1 Training Data and Capability Acquisition
Acquisition Order.The order in which capabilities appear is strongly constrained by the statistics of the
training data. Language models acquire words in an order predicted primarily by corpus frequency, unlike
children, whose acquisition order also depends on factors such as concreteness and word length (Chang &
Bergen, 2022); graded linguistic preferences, such as adjective order, are learned from corpus statistics on a
similar schedule (Jumelet et al., 2026). This ordering reflects a more generaldistributional simplicity bias:
Distributional Simplicity Bias
Networks trained with SGD learn low-order statistics of the data distribution before higher-order
ones (Refinetti et al., 2023). In language models, token n-gram frequencies are equivalent to moments
of the embedding vectors, so early-training language models approximate low-order token interactions
well, with more complex structure fitting later (Belrose et al., 2024).
From Correlation to Causation.Correlational studies show a strong connection between data statistics
and capabilities of the final model (Razeghi et al., 2022), and causal effects of pretraining-data statistics on
factual predictions can be estimated directly (Elazar et al., 2023). The strongest evidence would come from
controlled manipulation of the training data, although this is typically not done at realistic scales because it is
costly. One notable example of such work is O’Brien et al. (2026), which trained three 6.9-billion-parameter,
550-billion-token models on different dataset filtrations and showed they can remove knowledge of proxies for
biohazardous capabilities.
By training transformers on synthetic sequence tasks, Chan et al. (2022b) showed that in-context learning
emerges only when the data has the right distributional properties, with burstiness and a long tail of rare
classes each necessary. A uniform, non-bursty version of the same content instead leads to in-weights learning,
while Zipfian class distributions allow the coexistence of the two learning patterns. Similar dependence on
distributional structure governs factual knowledge acquisition, which proceeds through an extended plateau
shaped by the frequency distribution of entities in the data (Zucchet et al., 2025a).
10.1.2 Feature Formation, Consolidation, and Drift
A technical challenge in tracking features across training runs is that representations at different checkpoints
may occupy different bases, so a feature identified at one checkpoint has no automatic counterpart at another.
This is analogous to the cross-layer basis mismatch of the logit lens, which degrades because intermediate
layers organise information differently from the final layer. A probe or sparse autoencoder trained at one
checkpoint degrades similarly when applied to another, and longitudinal methods differ mainly in how they
solve this correspondence problem.
In Section 9.1, we discuss model diffing methods for comparing and analysing two models’ internals. They
are useful tools for longitudinal analysis, and they have discovered a broadly consistent order in which model
knowledge forms and internal representations evolve. Specifically, linguistic knowledge is acquired early
and quickly, while factual and commonsense knowledge accumulates slowly and reasoning abilities remain
83

text:
weak throughout pretraining (Liu et al., 2021). In particular, feature-level analyses provide fine-grained
descriptions of this picture: features corresponding to token-level and surface statistics form first, with
abstract, cross-lingual, and semantic features forming later (Inaba et al., 2025; Ge et al., 2026), and individual
features develop from noisy, unstructured activations into semantically coherent ones (Xu et al., 2025b).
Formation is followed by consolidation: after their semantics are established, feature directions continue to
drift and eventually stabilise (Xu et al., 2025b); modules converge at different rates (Raghu et al., 2017); and
once formed, representations and their acquisition timing are largely consistent across random seeds (van der
Wal et al., 2025).
Stability of a capability does not imply stability of its implementation. The components carrying an algorithm
can change identity while the algorithm persists (Tigges et al., 2024), and mechanisms can be repurposed, as
when induction heads transition into the function vector heads that come to dominate few-shot in-context
learning (Yin & Steinhardt, 2025). Structures can also disappear outright: in the synthetic settings of Chan
et al. (2022b), emergent in-context learning is transient, arising and then giving way to in-weights learning
while training loss still falls, with regularisation affecting its persistence (Singh et al., 2023). Similarly,
the drift of features can produce false positives in model diffing (Section 9.1) and more broadly bound the
temporal scope of any mechanistic claim (Section 10.2.2): an explanation about model internals validated at
one checkpoint may not apply to other checkpoints of the same model.
10.2 Learning Dynamics as an Interpretability Tool
The preceding subsection treated the learning trajectory as an object to be explained. A complementary
line of work uses that trajectory instead as a tool for analysing model behaviour. Comparing behaviour and
components across model checkpoints lets researchers conduct novel causal analyses of how components drive
model behaviour. Although this framing is relatively new in mechanistic interpretability, the use of learning
trajectories to understand neural networks substantially predates it. Early work showed that differentsingular
modesof the input–output correlations can be learned at different rates (where larger singular values tend to
be learned earlier), making acquisition order informative about task structure (Saxe et al., 2014; Lampinen &
Ganguli, 2019; Saxe et al., 2019). In contrast, representation-comparison methods measure when layers and
representations converge during training (Raghu et al., 2017; Morcos et al., 2018).
10.2.1 Temporal Localisation and Mechanism Discovery
Trajectory-Based Attribution.Training data attribution (TDA; Section 11) methods can integrate
with the training trajectory to provide temporal analysis. For example, TracIn (Section 11.2.5) estimates
a training sample’s influence on a testing sample’s prediction as the sum of their gradients’ dot products
evaluated at checkpoints along the run (Garima et al., 2020). Each checkpoint contributes separately to the
influence estimate. By examining each checkpoint’s contribution, researchers can identify when a training
example had the greatest influence on a downstream prediction.
Per-Token Learning Curves.The learning curve of an individual token in context, usually evaluated on
held-out text at every checkpoint, is the finest-grained localisation instrument. Chang et al. (2024) extracted
learning curves for one million held-out tokens across five pretraining runs and summarised each with the
time the token is first learned, the likelihood its loss later regresses, and the variability both within a run
and across runs. They found that frequent tokens and tokens in short frequent contexts are acquired earlier,
reach lower final surprisal, and vary less within and across runs, with the effect strengthening with n-gram
probability. At the level of stages, models learn short repetitive phrases before longer coherent text, consistent
with early n-gram learning followed by gradual refinement of tail predictions. Individual tokens also show
sudden increases or decreases in loss that recur at consistent points across runs. These abrupt changes in
per-token loss can help identify potential transitions during training (Section 10.3.1). They also complement
trajectory-based attribution by revealing when a model learns specific predictions.
Localising Change to Components.Once a change is localised in time, the components that changed in
that window are candidates for the mechanism. Wang et al. (2025b) introduced refined variants of the Local
Learning Coefficient (Section 10.3.4) and applied them to individual attention heads of a two-layer attention-

text:
only transformer across training. Theweight-refined LLCrestricts the LLC to a single head’s parameters;
thedata-refined LLCevaluates it on a chosen data subset. Weight-refined LLC curves diverge progressively
over training, with distinct patterns for different head types. Heads of the same type cluster together in both
their final values and the overall shape of the curve across training, revealing how heads differentiate into
distinct functional roles. On the other hand, data-refined LLCs reveal what a head specialises in processing;
for example, on code samples, perturbing the weights of the multigram heads in layer 1 has significantly
less impact on the loss than perturbing the induction heads. The same analysis identifies a previously
undocumented multigram circuit. A multigram is a common token sequence in the data distribution whose
tokens may appear non-contiguously in context. Heads with higher weight-refined LLC tend to memorise
more multigrams. Those with lower values tend to follow simple algorithms, such as induction or bracket
matching. Wang et al. (2025b) identified these heads by tracking each head’s complexity measure. Unlike the
proposed induction scores (Olsson et al., 2022) for identifying induction heads, the measure does not require
specifying a head type in advance. However, estimating refined LLCs is computationally expensive, and the
approach has so far been demonstrated only on toy models.
10.2.2 Causal Interventions on Mechanism Formation
The forked-run experiment is a basic analysis pipeline available on a training trajectory. It spawns multiple
continuations from a single checkpoint, perturbs one factor, and compares the resulting models.
Linear Mode Connectivity and Forked-Run Experiments
Aforked-run experimentspawns two or more training continuations from the same checkpoint,
varying a single factor such as SGD noise, data order, or random seed, and compares the models
the continuations produce.Linear mode connectivityis a standard instrument for the comparison.
Two networks are linearly mode connected if the loss barrier along the straight path between their
parameters in weight space is near zero. Specifically, Frankle et al. (2020) examined the sensitivity of
the model’s training results to SGD noise by restarting training from different checkpoints, each time
using different SGD noise. Early in training, these runs may converge to different loss basins. Later,
they tend to converge to linearly mode-connected solutions, indicating that the training outcome has
become stable to SGD noise.
Perturbations other than SGD noise fit the same design. For example, degrading the data early in training
causes permanent deficits that the same degradation applied later does not, establishing critical learning
periods (Achille et al., 2019), and forking a run across many random seeds distinguishes properties of the
training setup from accidents of a single run (van der Wal et al., 2025). Similarly, the smeared-key intervention
discussed in Section 10.3.5 is the same design with an architectural perturbation. Mode connectivity has also
been given a mechanistic reading: Lubana et al. (2023) defined two models as mechanistically similar when
they are invariant to the same transformations of the input. They conjectured that two minimisers that cannot
be linearly mode connected (up to permutation symmetries of the architecture) must be mechanistically
dissimilar, and found that the mechanistically dissimilar minimisers they constructed are connected by
quadratic but not linear paths. Under this interpretation, a loss barrier between two checkpoints suggests
that their mechanisms differ. However, the absence of a loss barrier does not guarantee that their mechanisms
are the same.
Temporal Stability and the Scope of Mechanistic Claims.Learning-dynamics analysis lets us
investigate mechanistic claims with scopes broader than those of a single model checkpoint. Specifically, an
explanation about a trained model’s internals (e.g., the direction of a feature) does not by itself establish
whether the internal mechanism, if it persists, works in the same way as mechanisms in different training stages
of the same model or mechanisms across independently trained models of the same kind (Section 10.1.2). In
contrast, learning-dynamics analysis can re-evaluate the proposed explanation across neighbouring checkpoints
or different random seeds, revealing how stable the explanation is under continued training and how sensitive
it is to variation in the training trajectory.

10.3 Phase Transitions and Emergence
Training loss curves typically make it seem like language models gradually and steadily improve in perfor-
mance (Hestness et al., 2017; Kaplan et al., 2020; Rosenfeld et al., 2020). While this holdson average,
individual capabilities tell a very different story. For many individual tasks, model performance can change
sharply and abruptly across model scales and across training (Wei et al., 2022; McKenzie et al., 2023). This
suggests that models undergophase transitions, where relatively small increases in scale or training time
produce qualitative changes in behaviour. These transitions have motivated substantial interest in the study
of how and when phase transitions happen, which we will discuss in more detail in Section 10.3.4.
These sharp changes also appear in model internals. Attention heads can specialise into distinct computational
roles over relatively short intervals (Olsson et al., 2022), and the formation of induction heads and syntactic
attention structures has been associated with abrupt changes in model behaviour (Chen et al., 2024a).
Note that behavioural and internal transitions need not occur at the same time or be equally abrupt.
A model capability may suddenly emerge even as its underlying internal mechanisms develop gradually.
Grokking(Nanda et al., 2023) illustrates this mismatch: as the model develops a generalising circuit, it still
relies on memorisation. Once the generalising mechanism dominates and competing memorisation mechanisms
are removed, the model’s generalisation ability jumps. We therefore usephase transitionbroadly to describe
qualitative shifts in behaviour, representations, etc., without assuming that they change simultaneously or
discontinuously.
Phase transitions matter for AI safety because they undermine our ability to forecast what the model will
develop. If a capability can appear with a small increase in model scale or training time, behavioural
evaluation of intermediate checkpoints offers limited assurance about the final model. Also, scaling laws fit
to smaller models offer limited insight into larger ones. We therefore need to understand how and when
phase transitions happen to reliably predict whether and when a model will acquire a hazardous capability.
We organise this subsection as a workflow for the researcher who has a training run in hand: detecting
transitions (Section 10.3.1), measuring the representations and mechanisms that underlie them (Section 10.3.2),
attributing them to specific components (Section 10.3.3), explaining why they occur (Section 10.3.4), and, as
a case study, applying this workflow end to end to induction heads (Section 10.3.5).
10.3.1 Detecting Transitions
A key challenge in detecting transitions is that aggregate loss can hide abrupt changes in individual capabilities.
The quantisation model of neural scaling (Michaud et al., 2023) suggests that models learn discrete units
of capability, each potentially emerging abruptly. However, their combined loss can still decrease smoothly
because these units occur at different frequencies in the data. This helps explain why abrupt changes can
occur across both training time and model scale despite smooth overall loss curves. Researchers therefore use
metrics at different levels of granularity to detect these transitions.
Loss-Curve Derivatives.The crudest instrument is the aggregate loss curve itself: a transition large
enough to affect overall performance appears as a bump, visible as a local peak in the loss derivative (Olsson
et al., 2022). However, most transitions are too small to detect this way. A flat derivative therefore does not
constitute evidence of the absence of a transition.
Capability-Specific Metrics.A metric targeted at a single capability, evaluated at every checkpoint,
resolves transitions the aggregate hides. The in-context learning score (Olsson et al., 2022) is a representative
construction. It isolates the capability of interest (benefiting from long, previous context) by taking the
difference between two quantities. Additionally, tracking benchmark accuracy across checkpoints can similarly
reveal capability transitions, though at a coarser level. Comparing results across random seeds helps determine
whether these transitions are consistent across training runs (van der Wal et al., 2025).
86

text:
Constructing a Capability-Specific Metric
The in-context learning score of Olsson et al. (2022) is defined as the prediction loss at the 500th token
of a context minus the loss at the 50th token. Each loss is dominated by factors unrelated to in-context
learning, such as the model’s overall competence on short contexts; their difference isolates the gain
the model derives from additional context. Evaluated at every checkpoint, the score changes abruptly
over a narrow training window, the same window in which induction heads form (Section 10.3.5),
while the aggregate loss curve registers the transition only as a small bump (Olsson et al., 2022).
Per-Example Decomposition.Transitions invisible in every predefined metric can be recovered from the
training data itself. POLCA decomposes changes in per-example loss along directions in the low-dimensional
subspace where training occurs and clusters examples with similar loss trajectories; the clusters correspond
to concepts learned abruptly at identifiable points in training, with no corresponding event in the aggregate
curve (Kangaslahti et al., 2026). At coarser granularity, latent state models fit a hidden Markov model over a
vector of training metrics and segment the run into discrete phases, with transitions between hidden states
flagging candidate developmental events (Hu et al., 2023).
Is Emergence a Metric Artefact?
Schaeffer et al. (2023) argued that the emergent abilities reported by Wei et al. (2022) are artefacts of
discontinuous metrics. For example, exact-match accuracy can change abruptly while the underlying
log-likelihood improves smoothly. Metric choice does explain some reported cases, and claimed
emergent abilities can appear or disappear under different metrics of the same task. However, it does
not explain all of them: sharp transitions are observed directly in continuous metrics, in per-example
losses, and in internal representations during single training runs (Du et al., 2024; Schaeffer et al., 2025;
Wu & Lo, 2025; Kangaslahti et al., 2026). The robustness of a reported transition can be assessed
using continuous metrics. However, determining which behavioural transitions reflect genuine changes
in the model’s internal mechanisms remains an open question.
10.3.2 Progress Measures and Internal Precursors
The methods above operate on phase transitions in model behaviours. However, as discussed above, transitions
in external behaviour and internal mechanisms can follow different patterns. Researchers therefore are also
interested in measuring the internals directly.
Progress Measure
Aprogress measureis a scalar quantity defined on a model’s internals that varies continuously as
a mechanism forms, and can therefore track the mechanism’s development before the behaviour it
supports changes (Nanda et al., 2023). Progress measures are typically derived from a mechanistic
analysis of the completed mechanism at the end of training, then evaluated retroactively at earlier
checkpoints.
Grokking is the controlled setting in which this tool has been demonstrated most completely.
Grokking
Grokking is the phenomenon in which a model reaches low training loss early in training but begins
to generalise to unseen inputs only after a long additional period of optimisation (Power et al., 2022).
This is almost exclusively seen in closed-domain settings, though general-purpose language models
have shown conceptually similar behaviour.
In modular arithmetic, training accuracy saturates early while test accuracy remains near chance for many
steps before rising sharply (Figure 16; Power et al., 2022). Mechanistic analysis of grokked networks recovers
the learned algorithm (trigonometric identities implementing modular addition) and defines progress measures
