Transfer from Grokking Settings to Language Models
The standard setting in grokking experiments differs from language model pretraining in many ways,
including dataset size, weight decay, and the number of epochs over the data. Current studies have
not shown that existing quantitative conclusions transfer directly to large-scale pretraining.
Similar findings have been reported outside grokking settings. Chen et al. (2024a) found that syntactic
attention structures emerged during a sharp drop in masked language modelling (MLM) loss, before accuracy
improvement on a grammatical benchmark. Similarly, Zucchet et al. (2025a) observed that attention-based
recall circuits formed during a plateau in factual-knowledge acquisition, followed by rapid improvements
in model performance. These findings suggest that changes in internal mechanisms can precede changes in
model capabilities. This observation motivates research on forecasting model behaviour through internal
monitoring, as discussed in Section 10.4.
10.3.3 Attributing Transitions to Components
So far, the methods we discussed cannot attribute the transition to specific model components. Attention head
specialisation is probably the most intuitive option to work at this granularity in transformers. Individual
attention heads can specialise to attend to syntactic relations, positional offsets, or rare tokens (Voita
88
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
et al., 2019; Clark et al., 2019), and this specialisation can appear abruptly. For example, induction heads
form during a brief training window, and their formation coincides with a sharp improvement in in-context
learning (Olsson et al., 2022), a transition we examine in detail in Section 10.3.5. In masked language models,
suppressing the syntactic attention structure delays the capability it precedes (Chen et al., 2024a). Likewise,
sparse attention emerges abruptly and depends on repetition in the training data (Zucchet et al., 2025b).
These events cluster in time. Several attention heads, such as induction heads and heads exhibiting syntactic
attention patterns, can acquire specialised functions within the same training window. These heads emerge
alongside a peak in how accurately the model’s perplexity predicts human reading times, and this predictive
ability subsequently declines even as language modelling performance continues to improve (Aoyama & Wilcox,
2025). Head specialisation can be viewed as a form ofsymmetry breaking. Before or in the very early stages
of training, attention heads are indistinguishable and interchangeable; during training, they start to develop
distinct functions despite having equivalent roles in the architecture. Tracking this process can help identify
the emergence of modular structure. Attribution of this kind is also a diagnostic for modularity more broadly.
Three observable indicators jointly diagnose modular internal structure (Zhao et al., 2024b): transitions
during training, emergent trends across model scale, and heterogeneous clustering of solutions across random
seeds. A structure exhibiting all three is a strong candidate for a discrete, functionally specialised mechanism.
Sharp Transitions from Smooth Components
Phase transitions in test loss or task accuracy do not imply abrupt change in any individual component.
For example, in controlled settings, many attention heads develop induction-like behaviour gradually—
their contributions are largely additive, and the sharp macroscopic transition arises from their aggregate
effect (Singh et al., 2024). Localising a phase transition in a coarse-grained metric therefore does
not help identify the responsible components. In contrast, component-level attribution may find only
gradual change without being wrong.
10.3.4 Why Transitions Happen
Saddle-to-Saddle Dynamics.Theoretical studies of deep linear networks show that different singular
modes of the input–output correlations can be learned at different rates (Saxe et al., 2014; 2019). The
training process may therefore involve periods of slow improvement followed by rapid reductions in test loss.
From an optimisation perspective, gradient descent moves through regions near successive saddle points in
the loss landscape and gradually learns more complex solutions along the way. This process is known as
saddle-to-saddle dynamics. Similar training patterns have been observed in other neural networks, where they
learn simpler functions before more complex ones (Rahaman et al., 2019; Nakkiran et al., 2019). Attention
head specialisation may also be related to symmetry breaking during training, although the relationship to
saddle-to-saddle dynamics is not yet fully established in realistic transformers (Chen et al., 2024a).
Singular Learning Theory.Singular learning theory (SLT) studies how the geometry of a singular model’s
parameter space affects learning and generalisation (Watanabe, 2009). Neural networks are singular (and are
thus a subject of study in SLT) because different parameter configurations can implement the same function.
As a result, two models that achieve similar loss can differ substantially in their effective complexity. SLT
provides a framework for studying this complexity and has motivated research on its changes during training
and its usefulness in downstream applications (Lau et al., 2025).
Local Learning Coefficient (LLC)
For model parametersθ∗ at a local minimum, the Local Learning Coefficient (LLC)λ(θ∗)measures the
degeneracy of the loss landscape nearθ∗ via the volume-scaling rate of low-loss neighbourhoods (Lau
et al., 2025). Smaller values indicate more degenerate (flatter, in a higher-order sense) minima. The
LLC is estimable at scale with stochastic-gradient MCMC (Lau et al., 2025).
Estimated LLC trajectories in transformers change at points that coincide with identifiable developmental
events, including the stages of structure formation described in Section 10.3.3 (Hoogland et al., 2025).

text:
This is the central empirical result of the developmental interpretability programme (Hoogland et al., 2023)
introduced in Section 12.3. However, current evidence for LLC is largely retrospective, where phase transitions
are detected and matched to known events only after training. Prospective prediction of a transition before it
occurs has not yet been demonstrated. Section 10.4 discusses potential applications of learning-dynamics
analysis to forecasting and intervention.
10.3.5 Case Study: Induction Heads
Learning Dynamics Perspective on Induction Heads
The preceding case studies (Sections 6.8 and 7.4) analysed induction heads and circuits in a trained
model. Several facts about the induction circuit are invisible from that vantage point but become
observable when we examine the model across training (Olsson et al., 2022). Consider the repeated
sequence again
A B C A B ? ,
and observe at successive checkpoints of a single training run. Examining the checkpoints shows that
the induction ability arrived abruptly: at early checkpoints the model bases its predictions on token
frequencies and derives no benefit from the earlier occurrence ofA B , and during a narrow window
of training, roughly 2.5 to 5 billion tokens in the models studied by Olsson et al. (2022), induction
heads form and the model begins predictingC by attending back to the first occurrence. A sharp
improvement in in-context learning and a small bump in the training loss fall within the same window.
The timing of formation also helps provide causal evidence that a single model checkpoint cannot
provide. Ablating an induction head in the final model only shows its necessity for the behaviour
at that checkpoint. This does not support the stronger claim that the induction circuit’s formation
caused the capability to develop. Olsson et al. (2022) examined this stronger claim by intervening on
formation itself. Their “smeared key” modification built the previous-token head’s contribution into
the attention computation, allowing the circuit to form within a single layer. Under this modification,
one-layer models acquire in-context learning they otherwise never develop, while the transition moves
earlier in deeper models.
10.4 Leveraging Learning Dynamics for Safety
The analyses above also support safety-oriented objectives, including anticipating capabilities before they
appear (Section 10.4.1) and intervening in the training process while it is still underway (Section 10.4.2).
10.4.1 Forecasting Model Behaviours
Forecasting from Smaller Runs and Partial Runs.Scaling laws demonstrate that aggregate loss is
predictable before training (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022), but phase transitions break this style
of extrapolation for individual capabilities (Section 10.3). Forecasting therefore targets specific behaviours
directly. Memorisation is the behaviour for which the forecasting problem has been posed most explicitly.
Biderman et al. (2023a) introduced the problem of forecasting whether a specific training sequence will be
memorised by a model before that model is trained. They argued that recall is the metric to optimise (a false
negative means training a full model that leaks the sequence, while a false positive only discards a cheap trial
run). They established baselines that forecast from smaller fully trained models and from partially trained
checkpoints of the target run, together with equi-compute recommendations for dividing a fixed forecasting
budget between model size and tokens.
Forecasting Safety-Relevant Behaviours.Emergence can be forecast by intervening on the training
trajectory. Fine-tuning on a target task shifts capability emergence towards less capable models. Fitting how
this shift varies with the amount of fine-tuning data yields anemergence law. Using only small models, this
90
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
law predicts whether a capability will have emerged in models trained with up to 4× more compute (Snell
et al., 2024).
Rare harmful behaviours can also be forecast statistically. The largest elicitation probabilities observed in a
small sample of queries scale predictably with query volume. This relationship allows harmful-behaviour
risks to be extrapolated across up to three orders of magnitude of deployment-scale query volume. Examples
include assisting with dangerous chemical synthesis and taking power-seeking actions (Jones et al., 2025).
Post-training failures can be analysed similarly. Specifically, transitions between successive RLHF checkpoints
can be classified into four categories: reward hacking, collapse, proxy under-alignment, and evaluator-specific
disagreement. Reward hacking occurs when the model exploits a way to achieve high rewards while the external
quality from the perspective of human users falls; collapse occurs when both decline. This classification
localises failures that checkpoint averages miss. A model fitted to training-dynamics diagnostics predicts
future reward hacking with a ROC-AUC of 0.82. These diagnostics include reward-model uncertainty, policy
drift, and output diversity (Abahana et al., 2026).
Internal signals extend forecasting to fine-tuning outcomes. Activation-space persona features predict whether
a fine-tuned model will exhibit emergent misalignment (Wang et al., 2026a). Signals available before fine-
tuning begins also predict the resulting model’s alignment (Zhang et al., 2026b). Section 12.4 discusses the
research agenda these results instantiate.
Internal Precursors as Early Warning.Where a mechanism forms before the capability it supports is
behaviourally expressed, monitoring internals can flag the capability earlier than behavioural evaluation. The
recall circuits that precede factual-knowledge acquisition (Zucchet et al., 2025a) and the syntactic attention
structure that precedes the break in grammatical capabilities (Chen et al., 2024a) show that this lead time
can exist; progress measures (Section 10.3.2) are the instrument that would exploit it.
Run-to-Run Variance.To assess the reliability of a forecast, researchers can compare training runs with
different random seeds. van der Wal et al. (2025) found that capabilities generally emerge at similar stages
and representations develop consistently across training runs, although some runs differ substantially. These
exceptions highlight the uncertainty of forecasts based on a single training run.
Most Early-Warning Evidence Is Retrospective
Currently, nearly all demonstrations that changes in internals lead to changes in behaviour are
retrospective. In these studies, researchers analyse the completed mechanism after training to identify
a progress measure or precursor structure, then evaluate it backwards over saved checkpoints. This
concern also exists in LLC-based transition detection (Section 10.3.4).
In contrast, prospective forecasting requires researchers to predict outcomes before observing them.
Biderman et al. (2023a) proposed baseline methods for forecasting memorisation. However, prospective
forecasting for broader capability transitions relevant to AI safety remains underdeveloped. Early-
warning signals therefore require prospective validation before they can be considered reliable.
10.4.2 Intervening on Training Processes
The model that matters is the one deployed at the end of training, and the standard response to an undesirable
behaviour found there is post-training fine-tuning, which is outside the scope of this section. An alternative
is to intervene during training to prevent undesirable capabilities from developing or to control how they
develop. Existing work explores three approaches: modifying training data, changing model architecture, and
intervening on model activations during fine-tuning.
Pretraining Data Filtering: Deep Ignorance.Deep Ignorance filters proxies for biohazardous knowledge
out of the pretraining corpus and trains 6.9-billion-parameter models on the filtered data (Section 10.1.1;
O’Brien et al., 2026). The filtered models do not acquire the targeted knowledge, making it difficult for the
unwanted capability to emerge through adversarial fine-tuning. In contrast, post-training unlearning may
91
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
suppress the unwanted behaviour without removing the underlying knowledge. A follow-up moves the filter
from documents to tokens: individual tokens are labelled using sparse autoencoders and efficient classifiers
trained on those labels, and filtering at token granularity removes the undesired capability at lower cost to
desired capabilities than document-level filtering, with effectiveness increasing with model scale across the
two orders of magnitude tested and filtered models remaining alignable afterwards (Rathi & Radford, 2026).
Similarly, the order in which different categories of training data are presented matters. Bruijns et al. (2026)
found that, in an imbalanced pretraining curriculum where one task is shown before another, the model packs
the tasks sequentially into separable circuits, resulting in more targeted subsequent refusal fine-tuning.
Data-Level Interventions Have Ripple Effects
Removing data from a training set does not act only on the removed data. In the setting of Borkar
et al. (2025), deleting personal information can increase memorisation of the personal information that
remains, and adding one individual’s information amplifies memorisation of others’ by roughly 7.5×,
because whether a sequence is memorised depends on similar sequences seen elsewhere in training.
Subliminal learning (Cloud et al., 2026) shows that data can transmit traits not apparent from its
semantic content. For example, a student model can inherit a teacher’s hidden bias from seemingly
unrelated data, such as number sequences. This transfer is carried by a small set of divergence tokens
and depends on early layers (Schrodi et al., 2026). Filtering and unlearning interventions therefore
need to be evaluated on what the model does with the data that stays, not only on what it no longer
does with the data that was removed.
Architectural Modification: Gradient Routing.Gradient routing is an architectural modification
informed by learning dynamics: it constrains which parameters receive gradient updates for chosen concepts
during training, localising the corresponding computation into designated regions of the network (Cloud
et al., 2024). Although the modification does not make the trained model safer on its own, it shapes where a
mechanism forms so that later interventions, such as gating the designated region, become clean and localised.
The antecedent for this style of intervention is the smeared-key modification (Olsson et al., 2022), which
showed that an architectural change can control when and whether a mechanism forms at all (Section 10.3.5).
Monitoring and Steering During Fine-Tuning.The case excluded above uses fine-tuning to repair
an undesirable behaviour after it has been identified. Intervening on the fine-tuning process itself remains
within scope, and persona vectors provide a current example of this approach. A persona vector is an
activation-space direction corresponding to a character trait such as sycophancy, hallucination propensity, or
malice, extractable automatically from a natural-language trait description (Chen et al., 2025b). Intended
and unintended personality changes during fine-tuning correlate strongly with movement along the relevant
vector, which yields the monitoring instrument. Preventative steering along the vector during fine-tuning
limits acquisition of the trait. Before fine-tuning, projecting training data onto the vector flags data that
would induce the trait, at both the dataset and individual-sample levels (Chen et al., 2025b). This instantiates
each step of the intervention loop below for the fine-tuning stage.
Train-Time Intervention Loop
The work discussed so far lays the methodological foundation for intervening in a training run in
progress. Below we present a general pipeline.
1. Monitora target quantity at checkpoints, such as a capability-specific metric (Section 10.3.1)
or a progress measure on model internals (Section 10.3.2).
2. Definethe acceptable range for that quantity in advance, including the response to a breach.
3. Intervenewhen the range is breached, such as by adjusting the data mixture or filtering out
unwanted data, applying a targeted architectural or regularisation change, rolling back to a
pre-breach checkpoint, and resuming under the adjusted setup.
4. Re-evaluatethe model after the intervention to verify that the targeted capability has been
suppressed and does not re-emerge during further training.
92
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
No published system implements this loop end to end at scale. Instead, existing studies have
demonstrated individual steps of the proposed workflow.
Open Questions.Three questions remain about the applicability of these training-time interventions.
First, effective data filtering requires identifying which training data contributes to the capability we want to
remove. Token-level filtering is motivated by data attribution, but it remains unclear whether methods such
as influence functions (Section 11) can reliably identify the relevant data. Second, scale: Deep Ignorance
operates at 6.9 billion parameters, and while token-level filtering became more effective across the tested
scale range (Rathi & Radford, 2026), it remains open whether data filtering stays effective and affordable
at frontier scale. Third, deployed models show that stronger train-time safeguards are achievable, but not
how: gpt-oss models are substantially harder to fine-tune than comparable open-weight models, and their
developers have not fully disclosed their responsible training procedure (OpenAI et al., 2025). Understanding
how this resistance is achieved could help develop similar safeguards for other open-weight models and clarify
how fine-tuning changes model behaviour.
Summary.Learning dynamics can be studied both as an object of explanation, revealing how representations
and mechanisms evolve during training, and as an interpretability tool to localise mechanisms, detect phase
transitions, and test causal hypotheses through training interventions. Understanding learning dynamics can
also help predict when capabilities emerge and guide interventions during training. However, no complete
system combining monitoring and intervention has yet been demonstrated at scale. This section focuses on
how models change during training, while Section 11 examines how individual training examples contribute
to model behaviour.
11 Training Data Attribution
For a model behaviour of interest, Sections 6–10 study the internal features, components, and their interactions
and evolutions that produce the behaviour. Training data attribution (TDA) shifts the focus from model
internals to training data, searching for training samples that strongly shaped the model behaviour. TDA
applications include, but are not limited to, identifying influential training samples, detecting train–test
leakage, and diagnosing model failures without retraining (Liu et al., 2025a; Park et al., 2023; Grosse et al.,
2023). Although TDA is not generally a mechanistic method under this survey’s criteria, it can complement
mechanistic interpretability in many ways. For example, by revealing how specific training samples shape
malicious behaviour, TDA can enable effective training data filtering to prevent unwanted behaviours or even
their internal mechanisms from forming during the training of next-generation models. Motivated by this
application, this section focuses on post-hoc training data attribution methods that link a given target model’s
behaviour to its training samples. This section excludes techniques for intervening in the data pipeline, such
as filtering pretraining corpora, rebalancing demographic representation, and scheduling memorisation.
TDA falls into two complementary approaches.Verbatim data attributiondetects explicit memorisation by
identifying exact or near-exact string matches between model outputs and the training corpus. These searches
can scale to trillions of tokens using techniques such as suffix arrays and infini-gram models.Gradient-based
data attributionestimates how training samples affect model parameters and predictions and can capture
influential samples that do not manifest as verbatim reproduction. The two types of methods provide
orthogonal views: one answers “did the model use rote memorisation on a training sample to answer this
question?”; the other answers “how much did this training sample influence this certain behaviour of this
model?”
11.1 Verbatim Data Attribution: OLMoTrace and Maximal Matching Spans
Earlier corpus search tools such as the ROOTS Search Tool (Piktus et al., 2023a) and GAIA Search (Piktus
et al., 2023b) established the practice of querying pretraining corpora for transparency and data exploration.
OLMoTrace (Liu et al., 2025a) scales this to trillions of tokens using a combination of suffix arrays, infini-gram

Maximal Matching Spans
Given a model output and a training corpus, amaximal matching spanis a contiguous sequence of
tokens that:
1. Appears verbatim at least once in the training data,
2. Does not break words or include spurious delimiters (e.g., periods or newlines) except at span
boundaries, and
3. Is not contained within a longer span that satisfies 1. and 2.
OLMoTrace identifies maximal matching spans by combining suffix-array search with infini-gram
queries, adjusting boundaries for tokenisation, and retaining only the longest non-overlapping spans.

wide [...]”
Pipeline Steps:
1. Tokenise the language model output.
2. For each token starting a new word, query the suffix array with infini-gram to find the longest
matching prefix in the training corpus.
3. Adjust span boundaries to avoid breaking words or including delimiters.
4. Retain only maximal spans (not contained in longer matches).

11.2.4 Retraining-Based Influence Estimation: datamodels and TRAK
Some methods have explored retraining the model to estimate the attribution. The most naive method is to
upweight or remove each training sample, retrain the model on the modified training set, and observe changes
in the model’s output on the testing sample. Ilyas et al. (2022) proposeddatamodelsto more efficiently

of the training data and fitting a linear regression that predicts the model output on the testing sample from
binary indicators of whether each training sample was included. Each fitted coefficient then represents the
training sample’s influence on the testing sample.
However, datamodels remains computationally expensive because it requires training many models.Tracing
with the Randomly-projected After Kernel(TRAK; Park et al., 2023) provides a more efficient alternative.
TRAK first uses a first-order Taylor expansion around the model parameters to approximate a trained
model as a linear model. It then applies random projections to reduce gradient dimensionality and estimate
training-sample influence in this lower-dimensional space. Finally, it averages the estimates across a small
number of trained models to reduce variability due to training randomness. TRAK achieves attribution
quality comparable to datamodels at substantially lower computational cost (Park et al., 2023).

TracIn (Garima et al., 2020) estimates training-data influence using gradients evaluated along the training
trajectory, without computing the inverse Hessian. Its core idea follows from the effect of a single Stochastic

11.2.7 Recent Extensions and Limitations
Recent work extends training data attribution to handle training stochasticity.Distributional TDA(d-TDA)
estimates how output distributions depend on the dataset (Mlodozeniec et al., 2025). Georgiev et al. (2023)
proposed TRAK variants to address diffusion models. More recent work connects TDA directly to mechanistic
interpretability (Kowal et al., 2026; Habibi et al., 2026); for example, Kowal et al. (2026) introducedConcept
Influenceto enable attribution at the level of semantic concepts represented by model internals such as
sparse autoencoder features. This brings TDA closer to the mechanistic goal of understandinghowtraining
data shapes specific internal computations. However, fundamental technical challenges persist, including
approximation errors that compound over the training trajectory, variability across training runs caused by
randomness like data ordering, and memory and computational bottlenecks of scaling to frontier models.
These limitations motivate further research in this direction.
Summary.Training data attribution traces model behaviour back to the training data. Verbatim methods
such as OLMoTrace identify memorised spans, while gradient-based methods such as influence functions
estimate the contribution of individual training samples to downstream model predictions. These approaches
remain limited at scale. Meanwhile, recent work has begun linking data attribution to internal features
and mechanisms. Having surveyed the main methodological families of AI interpretability in the preceding
sections, Section 12 organises them into six research orientations that differ in their goals, assumptions, and
paths forward.

12 Six Research Orientations
Anorientationis a coherent research programme defined by its goals, assumptions, and trade-offs. In
contrast, amethodis an established modular pipeline that may be used in different orientations. In AI
interpretability, different research goals, such as developing ready-to-use safety measures or achieving complete
mechanistic understanding, have led to distinct research programmes. This section organises six major
research orientations and summarises their scientific objectives, core assumptions, characteristic methods,
and limitations (Nanda et al., 2025; Gao, 2025; Li et al., 2025a; Hoogland et al., 2023; Barez, 2026; Biderman
et al., 2026; Figure 17). Note that no single orientation is universally preferable. The choice depends on the
research objective, deployment context, available resources, and tolerance for different forms of uncertainty.
12.1 Pragmatic Interpretability: Proxy-Task-Oriented Safety Interventions
Pragmatic Interpretabilityfocuses on doing the research most helpful for longer-term alignment and inter-
pretability goals, such as helping AGI go well (Nanda et al., 2025). Proponents argue that full mechanistic
understanding is not required to have significant impact; instead, researchers should prioritise the work most
likely to help (Nanda et al., 2025). The central idea is to work on a set of operationally meaningful proxy
tasks that can be empirically studied on models today to help make powerful future models safe. Researchers
are agnostic about which methods they use, even if they do not involve model internals. Though not required,
these proxy tasks may also be directly useful on today’s deployed systems, providing valuable feedback.
A representative example is the study of Claude Sonnet 4.5’s evaluation awareness (Anthropic, 2025a). The
system was shown to condition its behaviour on the presence of evaluation signals, making results from
safety evaluations used for previous models harder to interpret. Researchers identified and applied a steering
vector that suppresses this awareness, allowing evaluation of its actual behaviour. While this study does
not fully explain the internal mechanism of evaluation awareness, it is sufficient to produce a concrete and
safety-relevant behavioural change, illustrating the pragmatic philosophy.
Another example is Marks et al. (2025b). In this case, researchers constructed a proxy task: they fine-tuned
a model with a hidden goal, then blinded teams of researchers audited the model to discover it. This served
as a proxy task for detecting a naturally emerging hidden goal in a future model. The different auditing
teams used different techniques, allowing researchers to compare their efficacy.
Common techniques in this paradigm include:
•Steering vectors, which shift models to targeted behaviours.
•Probes, which detect latent safety-relevant properties in activations.
102
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
• Behavioural monitoring and anomaly detection, which track signals indicative of emerging
risks, such as monitoring the model’s verbalised reasoning.
•Prompting, an effective black-box baseline method for steering model behaviour.
Recent work following this pragmatic trajectory has demonstrated effective control of refusal behaviour (Arditi
et al., 2024) and evaluation awareness (Anthropic, 2025a). These interventions provide direct gains to
contemporary systems. However, they may not (and are not designed to) fully explain how models implement
their behaviours.
12.2 Ambitious Interpretability: Towards Complete Mechanistic Understanding
In contrast to pragmatic approaches,Ambitious Interpretabilityseeks a comprehensive mechanistic understand-
ing of how models implement their computations (Gao, 2025). Proponents argue that partial or surface-level
understanding cannot guarantee safety in next-generation systems. Full understanding is needed to rule out
hidden failure modes or deceptive internal dynamics. Specifically, Ambitious Interpretability does not treat
interpretability as a collection of useful heuristics. Instead, it treats interpretability as a scientific objective:
to reverse-engineer the model and develop a transparent, predictive theory of its internal algorithms.
Ambitious Interpretability particularly emphasisesmetric-driven progress. Motivated by the fact that existing
mechanistic approaches still struggle with stringent metrics, it proposes starting with looser ones, tracking
and improving methods’ performance on them, and adopting stricter metrics when suitable. Two example
metrics by Gao (2025) are:
• Feature quality:demonstrating that extracted features and their natural-language explanations
are faithful and simulatable.
•Circuit faithfulness:demonstrating circuits are necessary and sufficient for explaining behaviour
via causal intervention (e.g., causal scrubbing (Chan et al., 2022a)), without performance degradation.
The disadvantage of this ambition is its cost. Fine-grained mechanistic analysis of frontier large models is
computationally expensive and sometimes intractable. As Gao (2025) emphasised, current tools still fall far
short of the coverage and robustness required for a truly comprehensive understanding.
Interpretability-by-design as a Synthesis.The emergence of interpretability-by-design models (Sec-
tion 6.10) blurs the boundary between Ambitious and Pragmatic Interpretability. These methods (Gao et al.,
2026; Pearce et al., 2025; Park et al., 2025; Oldfield et al., 2024) aim to make representations and circuits easier
to understand by modifying model architectures rather than relying entirely on post-hoc reverse engineering.
This practical change to model design pursues the ambitious goal of mechanistic understanding. However,
it remains unclear whether these methods can ultimately achieve complete mechanistic understanding. In
the short term, they may simply represent a separate “Engineering” orientation in which interpretability is
treated as an optimisation objective.
12.3 Developmental Interpretability: Characterising How Models Learn
Complementing post-hoc analysis of trained models,Developmental Interpretability(Hoogland et al., 2023;
Hoogland et al., 2025) treats the training process itself as an object of scientific inquiry. Taking a learning-
theory perspective, it aims to mathematically formalise the emergence and evolution of model representations,
effective complexity, and capabilities throughout training.
Its central claim is that many neural network properties which are hard to analyse through a fixed model
checkpoint can be understood through their developmental process. This process contains measurable,
modelable signatures that can serve as proxies for the model’s properties of interest, such as developmental
stages, phase transitions, and other organising principles that help mathematically explain how complex
behaviours emerge and evolve throughout training. A classic example is the Local Learning Coefficient
(LLC) introduced in Sections 10.2.1 and 10.3.4. It successfully serves as a signature of the model’s effective
103
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
complexity, allowing us to observe developmental transitions and compare two models with the same training
loss.
Methods in this paradigm include:
• Singular Learning Theory (SLT)and related mathematical frameworks for characterising
developmental stages, symmetry breaking, and changes in the geometry of the loss landscape during
training.
• Checkpoint-based analysisto track the emergence of representations and mechanisms by apply-
ing specialised probes, feature discovery methods, and circuit analyses across a model’s training
checkpoints.
More specifically, Developmental Interpretability aims to answer questions such as: Can we characterise the
development of model capabilities or behaviours as phase transitions during training? What developmental
stages precede the formation of a certain mechanism? How does the optimisation process transform distributed
representations into structured mechanisms? Unlike Interpretability Across Time (detailed in Section 12.4),
which emphasises forecasting and controlling future model behaviour, Developmental Interpretability is
primarily concerned with understanding the developmental processes that produce those behaviours. Its
primary goal is rigorous scientific explanation rather than predicting or intervening on capabilities.
12.4 Interpretability Across Time: Understanding the Causes of Model Behaviours
Like Developmental Interpretability,Interpretability Across Time(Biderman et al., 2023b; 2026) treats a
model as a time-evolving process shaped by its training data, loss functions, architectures, and optimisation
dynamics. However, the two orientations differ in their primary goals. Developmental Interpretability
mainly focuses on characterising the developmental processes that give rise to the model’s internal features,
mechanisms, and capabilities. In contrast, Interpretability Across Time seeks established knowledge of
learning that is (1) sufficiently predictive to estimate important model properties before training is complete,
(2) sufficiently causal to identify when and why undesirable trajectories arise, and (3) sufficiently precise
to enable interventions on the learning process itself (Biderman et al., 2026). From a safety perspective,
this orientation aims to understand and ultimately shape the training process to prevent the model from
developing undesirable behaviours in the first place rather than repairing them after they develop.
Interpretability Across Time builds on three areas of research. First, scaling-law studies show that model
performance can be predicted from factors such as model size, training data, and compute (Kaplan et al., 2020;
Hoffmann et al., 2022). This motivates similar efforts to predict safety-relevant model properties (Ganguli
et al., 2022; Jones et al., 2025). Second, longitudinal mechanistic studies track how internal mechanisms
develop during training (Tigges et al., 2024; Singh et al., 2024). Third, studies of training data show that the
training distribution can affect downstream model behaviour. For example, Razeghi et al. (2022) found that
few-shot numerical reasoning performance depends strongly on the frequency of relevant terms in pretraining
data, while Elazar et al. (2023) estimated the causal effects of pretraining-data statistics on factual predictions.
Interpretability Across Time builds on these findings to predict and influence safety-relevant model behaviour
during training.
Methods in this paradigm include:
• Longitudinal analysis of model internals,tracking representations, features, or implemented
mechanisms across checkpoints to determine when and how they form and evolve.
• Monitoring training runs and forecasting future behaviour,using early behavioural or internal
signals to predict later capabilities, biases, or unsafe behaviours before they are fully expressed.
• Training-process interventions and design, manipulating data, activations, objectives, architec-
tures, or other aspects of optimisation to encourage desirable developmental trajectories, prevent
undesirable capabilities or behaviours from arising, or ensure that learned information is represented
in ways that make it easier to control.
104
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
Several studies have examined whether safety risks can be identified before or during training. Zhang
et al. (2026b) found that model activations measured before fine-tuning can predict alignment scores after
fine-tuning. Similarly, Wang et al. (2026a) identified internal features associated with emergent misalignment,
which could sometimes detect misalignment before behavioural evaluations did. Other studies found that
training models to exploit relatively simple reward misspecifications can lead to more serious failures, including
reward tampering and broader misaligned behaviour (Denison et al., 2024; Taylor et al., 2025). These findings
motivate monitoring early signs of undesirable behaviour during training rather than relying solely on the
evaluation of the final model.
Another line of work under this paradigm attempts to directly shape models by preventing them from learning
unsafe behaviours. Data filtering can prevent models from acquiring hazardous information in the first place
and substantially increase the amount of subsequent fine-tuning required to recover it (O’Brien et al., 2026;
Rathi & Radford, 2026), and gradient routing approaches deliberately constrainwhere or howinformation is
learned, making later removal or control more tractable (Cloud et al., 2024; Shilov et al., 2025).
Common confusion.Although Biderman et al. (2026) contrasted this orientation with the “fix it in
post” paradigm, it would be a mistake to view it as dismissive of post-training writ large. Post-training
is itself a training process, and behaviours like sycophancy and reward hacking arise primarily during and
due to post-training. This orientation’s criticism of post-training safety focuses on cases where, instead of
understanding why a behaviour developed, post-training patches undesirable behaviour. The core distinction
isunderstanding and controlling a training processversusapplying optimisation pressure to suppress learned
behaviours.
Interpretability Across Time is not mutually exclusive with the other research orientations. It can be
Pragmatic, by using a simple probe as an early-warning signal, or Ambitious, by seeking a mechanistic theory
of why a circuit forms under gradient descent. Its defining goal is using insights into training dynamics to
explain and predict how model behaviour develops, and to intervene before undesirable behaviours emerge.
12.5 Introspective Interpretability: Models Interpreting Themselves
Introspective Interpretability(Binder et al., 2025; Plunkett et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a; Guo et al., 2026;
Li, 2026) uses the model being explained as its own explainer. Its main practical advantage is its unique
accessibility. For a given introspective model, it requires no white-box access or specialised tooling to explain
its decisions; anyone can get theself-explanation(or interchangeablyself-report) at deployment time by
asking the model a follow-up question in an ordinary chat interface.
This research direction is supported by the privileged access hypothesis discussed in Section 5.3, which posits
that models may have access to internal information that is difficult to recover through external analysis
alone, including typical mechanistic analysis or a different model as the explainer. Recent work has leveraged
this idea by fine-tuning target models to faithfully report their internal reasoning, behavioural tendencies,
objectives, and even weight changes induced by training (Goel et al., 2026).
A related line of work fine-tunes metamodels (external explainers) on the internal representations of a target
model (Pan et al., 2026; Karvonen et al., 2026a; Bauer et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026). These methods
are generally not considered instances of Introspective Interpretability because the explainer is technically a
separate model. However, the distinction can be blurry in practice, as many of these explainers are initialised
from the target model and can be viewed as specialised, fine-tuned descendants of the original model.
12.5.1 Concerns for Introspective Interpretability
Self-explanation also raises concerns. For example, generated explanations can be plausible yet unfaithful.
The model’s general capability can also degrade when it is trained to honestly verbalise its internal processing.
Moreover, the model may have fundamental limitations in what it can report. These concerns raise questions
about whether we can trust self-explanations in safety-critical applications and how to validate potentially
misleading reports. Below, we first discuss the main failure modes of self-explanation, followed by validation
procedures in Section 12.5.2.
105
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
Failure Modes of Self-Explanation
Introspective methods can fail in several ways. In each case, the explanation appears plausible yet is
unfaithful.
Confabulation.Models may generate coherent explanations that do not reflect their actual internal
computations. This occurs because language models are extensively pretrained and fine-tuned on
next-token prediction and instruction-following tasks to produce fluent, knowledgeable text, not
faithful introspective reports. Thus, explanations may simply reflect training data patterns (how
humans explain reasoning) rather than the model’s actual computational process (Turpin et al., 2023;
Arcuschin et al., 2026; Barez et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2025c). Moreover, the reinforcement learning
reward for generating helpful responses can also incentivise convincing confabulation, even though the
model cannot introspect. An example of a helpful yet unfaithful response is when the model post hoc
rationalises an answer it already rote-memorised.
Miscalibration.Even when models attempt faithful self-report, their confidence may be poorly
calibrated with accuracy. Models can express high confidence in explanations for computations
they have not yet learned to analyse. Moreover, calibration can vary by task: models may be well
calibrated on reporting their own uncertainty in simpler tasks such as factual recall but poorly
calibrated on reasoning processes. A recent study further found that, even in factual recall tasks,
models can hallucinate with high certainty despite knowing the correct answer (Simhi et al., 2025).
Elicitation sensitivity.Self-reports can be highly sensitive to prompting. Models can provide
contradictory explanations or show substantially different introspective capabilities when similar
questions are phrased differently (Hahami et al., 2026). The preset format of self-report (e.g., free-form
versus structured, immediate versus delayed) can also substantially influence what information is
elicited and appears accessible. Moreover, models may be intrinsically biased towards confirming
hypotheses regardless of whether they reflect their underlying computations (Hahami et al., 2026).
Strategic misreporting.In adversarial or high-stakes settings, models with sufficient capability
might strategically misreport their internal states. For example, a model optimised for user rewards
might report sycophantic explanations it predicts users will find satisfying rather than accurate (Sharma
et al., 2024b). A misaligned model might deliberately conceal its true objectives or reasoning (Hubinger
et al., 2024). Even without explicit deception, models may learn to confabulate and produce seemingly
safe explanations that avoid triggering safety filters (Baker et al., 2025).
Despite these limitations, targeted training can address some self-explanation failures. Studies show that
models trained for introspection can produce more faithful reports of their internal objectives, behavioural
tendencies, and training-induced changes (Binder et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026b; Goel et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025a;
Joglekar et al., 2025). In particular, models trained to disclose hidden objectives or emergent misalignment can
report these properties with high accuracy (Li et al., 2026b; Joglekar et al., 2025). Explanation faithfulness
may also improve when task performance requires reasoning (Kinniment et al., 2026). These findings suggest
that some introspection failures may reflect limitations of current training and elicitation methods, rather
than fundamental limits on models’ ability to report their internal states.
12.5.2 Validation Procedures for Model Self-Reports
Given these concerns, Introspective Interpretability methods must be validated against additional, independent
evidence. Specifically, they must be shown to beconsistentwith model internals (as accessed by other
mechanistic interpretability tools) and behavioural signatures (as tested by behavioural interpretability
analysis). Validation procedures vary based on the type of self-report:
106
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
Validation Procedures for Introspective Models
1. Causal intervention consistency.Self-explanations should be tested against intervention
experiments. If a model claims a feature drives its output, ablating that feature should steer the
model away from the output. If a model claims it considered a piece of information (e.g., an input
feature or a recalled piece of factual knowledge in intermediate layers) for its decision, patching the
information with counterfactual values should change the output correspondingly.
2. Cross-method consistency.Introspective methods and privileged access findings should be
verified by other interpretability methods: Do SAE features identified as causal show corresponding
effects to self-explanations under steering? Do probing classifiers successfully decode the information
the model claimed to use? Do circuit discovery methods identify the components the model describes?
3. Paraphrase and sampling consistency.The stability of self-reports under semantics-
preserving variations of the question should be tested. Specifically, paraphrased questions should elicit
consistent explanations. Explanations should remain consistent across resamples at low temperature.
Explanations for similar inputs verified to have undergone similar mechanisms by other methods
should show appropriate similarity.
4. Calibration evaluation.The calibration between self-reported confidence in the explanation and
the actual match to the internal mechanisms should be tested. Confidence should reflect uncertainty
in the generated explanation based on how much information the model collected during introspection.
12.5.3 When to Use Introspective Methods
Introspective methods are best suited for three scenarios: (1) Hypothesis generation, where introspection
provides candidate explanations to be validated by other methods; (2) Rapid triage, where introspection is
used to quickly identify which input–output pairs or model components are worth further investigation; (3)
Human–AI collaboration, where introspective models provide human-readable explanations tailored to users’
levels of expertise and understanding.
Introspective methods are insufficient for: (1) Claims of absence: claims about the absence of deceptive
reasoning or hidden objectives cannot be established by self-report alone; (2) Formal guarantees: self-reports
do not provide the causal evidence needed for formal verification; (3) Adversarial settings: in scenarios
where the model has strong incentives to misreport, introspection may be less reliable and require additional
safeguards.
Implications.Although introspective methods can help efficiently detect latent goals, plans, and deceptive
behaviour (Binder et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026b; Goel et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025a; Joglekar et al., 2025), they
work best as complements to other mechanistic analyses (Bereska & Gavves, 2024). Specifically, their most
productive use is as one component of a multi-method interpretability pipeline: self-reports serve as initial
hypotheses, causal interventions test them, and circuit discovery methods explain the underlying mechanisms.
While we may optimistically assume models can tell us how they work in the future, we must also recognise
that self-reports are relatively weak evidence and require independent validation.
12.6 Automated Interpretability: Scaling Discovery via Automation
Automated Interpretabilityseeks to scale mechanistic analysis to large models by replacing human analysis
with automated pipelines. It assumes that manual analysis is the bottleneck and that automation can
accelerate discovery. Methods include:
• Automated circuit discoveryto automatically find the critical computational graph inside the
model that processes a given input prompt or implements a specific capability.
107
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
• LLM-based feature or circuit explanationsto automatically discover, summarise, and evaluate
representational units and internal computations and give human-readable interpretations or reports.
Automated interpretability is not limited to any particular type of internal representation or mechanism.
Depending on the research question, automated pipelines may analyse SAE features (Paulo et al., 2025b;
Han et al., 2026), individual neurons (Bills et al., 2023; Foote et al., 2023; Oikarinen & Weng, 2023),
circuits (Conmy et al., 2023; Khan et al., 2026), or other model components (Fraser-Taliente et al., 2026).
This approach distinguishes itself by automatically discovering, explaining, or evaluating these objects rather
than relying on manual analysis. Below, we illustrate a classical automated feature-explanation pipeline
whose explanation and verification stages generally follow Bills et al. (2023).
Classical Automated Interpretability Pipeline
Stage 1 – Feature Extraction.SAEs are trained to decompose raw activations of the target
model into sparse linear features.
Stage 2 – Explanation Generation.An “Investigator Agent” (e.g., GPT-4) reads a sample
of texts that strongly activate an SAE feature and generates a natural-language hypothesis of its
function (Paulo et al., 2025b; Bills et al., 2023), e.g., “This feature activates on Python code related
to file I/O operations.”
Stage 3 – Explanation Verification.A “Simulator Agent” predicts feature activations on new
text based on the hypothesis and calculates the correlation between predicted activations and real
activations (Bills et al., 2023). A high score confirms the hypothesis, while a low score rejects the
hypothesis and triggers re-investigation.
Stage 4 – Deception Detection.Crucially, coordinated agents can detect when explanations or
agents themselves are deceptive or misleading—effectively deploying “AI to catch AI” in oversight
scenarios (Barez, 2026).
Such a pipeline enables analysis of a model with billions of parameters with minimal human intervention (Bills
et al., 2023), a prerequisite for comprehensive model oversight (Foote et al., 2023).
Recent research has substantially expanded the scope of Automated Interpretability. While early work focused
primarily on automated feature explanation, newer systems employ increasingly sophisticated pipelines for
feature discovery, explanation generation, auditing, and intervention (Han et al., 2026; Marin-Llobet &
Ferrando, 2026; Barez, 2026; Cywiński et al., 2025). More recently, automation has also been extended from
individual features to higher-level structures such as circuits (Khan et al., 2026; Haklay et al., 2026), enabling
automated explanation of circuit semantics rather than merely discovering circuit components (Conmy et al.,
2023; Ameisen et al., 2025).
12.6.1 Governance Concerns for Automated Interpretability
Despite the promise, automated methods face fundamental concerns. In particular, although automation
improves scalability, reduced human involvement may also increase the risk and severity of systematic errors,
reward hacking, or deceptive explanations when automated oversight fails to catch them (Lermen et al., 2025).
Therefore, success in this research orientation is measured not only by the analysis’s scalability, but also by
its coverage, faithfulness, and trustworthiness. Below, we detail several governance challenges, including error
propagation at scale, human oversight becoming a bottleneck, and systematic biases going undetected.
Governance Risks of Automation
Error propagation.Unlike human investigators, who are somewhat independent and introspective,
the explanation-generation model can propagate its systematic errors to all features it analyses

text:
without rethinking what could have gone wrong.
Reduced human-specific functionalities.Automation removes humans from the loop. However,
humans provide essential sanity checks, domain knowledge, and scepticism that automated systems
lack or handle poorly. Lacking these critical properties may, in the long run, make the system less
productive and less beneficial to the community than analyses by human experts.
Automation Bias.Automated pipelines can produce seemingly rigorous and comprehensive
yet actually incomplete or sycophantic explanations. This is particularly likely when language
models are involved. For example, models may selectively report positive results (Luo et al., 2026)
or tailor their explanations to align with inferred user preferences (Sharma et al., 2024b). This
apparent rigour and promise may lead researchers to overtrust the results and overlook underlying flaws.
Spurious Feedback Loops.When Automated Interpretability is used to improve models that
are subsequently used for interpretability, feedback loops may reinforce existing errors and biases.
This process may exploit and saturate interpretability metrics without genuine gains in mechanistic
understanding.
12.6.2 Proposed Guardrails for Automated Interpretability
These concerns call for safeguards that combine technical validation, human oversight, and clear accountability.
Below, we propose a five-layer guardrail framework to help audit the automated methods and mitigate their
risks.
Guardrail Framework for Automated Interpretability
Layer 1: Sampling-Based Human Validation.Auditors can randomly sample a predefined
fraction (e.g., 5%) of generated explanations for human experts to review. These explanations should
cover different task-difficulty levels, feature types, and targeted mechanisms. Human experts should
not know in advance which explanations are randomly sampled, which are flagged by automated
checks, and which are already verified by additional methods, if they are all presented.
Layer 2: Consistency and Causality Checks.The reliability of automated pipelines can be
improved by implementing consistency checks. Specifically, the pipeline can generate explanations
multiple times at varying temperatures or setups (e.g., different backbone LLM explainers).
Inconsistent explanations trigger review. The pipeline can also additionally examine a fraction of
explanations by causal techniques, such as activation patching, and track failure rates. These checks
can be automated or involve human auditors.
Layer 3: Adversarial Robustness.Auditors can test automated pipelines against adversarial
inputs. To achieve this, auditors first construct features or mechanisms with backdoored activation
patterns designed to make the pipeline produce inappropriate or targeted explanations. Auditors then
examine whether the pipeline was fooled. Failure cases can be used to improve the pipeline’s robustness.
Layer 4: Error Detection and Bounds.First, automated pipelines must output calibrated
confidence. Overconfidence (false positive) is more dangerous than underconfidence (false negative)
and should be prevented. Second, the pipeline can be tested on features or mechanisms with known
ground-truth explanations (e.g., from prior human analysis) and the faithfulness of generated
explanations on them measured. Finally, the pipeline should report estimated error rates alongside all
automated findings.
Layer 5: Regulator Practices.Regulators must distinguish automated hypotheses (weak evidence
that requires validation) from validated findings (passed human or causal checks). For automated

When the pipeline improves, or the target model is fine-tuned, regulators should re-evaluate prior

12.6.3 Integrating Automated and Human Analysis
A robust analysis pipeline should combine automation for scale and suitable human involvement for validation
and edge cases. Table 12 shows an exemplary workflow that combines AI and human labour for scalable
interpretability analysis.
Key Principles for Integration.Here we discuss several design principles for integrating humans and
AI into the interpretability workflow. First, automation provides breadth, and humans provide depth. For
example, the workflow can use SAEs with LLM-based description generation to discover and label many
features, then have human investigators analyse those with safety-relevant descriptions. Second, humans set
criteria and automation applies them. Specifically, humans define criteria for a valid explanation, a feature of
interest, or a concerning finding, while the automated components (e.g., the LLM explainer) operate based
on these criteria. Third, the system should have clear escalation criteria to determine when to call for human
intervention, such as when the system detects potential mechanisms underlying safety-relevant concepts.
Finally, the system should implement a feedback loop to let human investigators correct and calibrate it in
real time during interaction.
12.6.4 Summary: Responsible Automation
Introspective and Automated Interpretability offer promise for scalable mechanistic analysis. However, they
both have technical challenges that call for additional guardrails. Specifically, Introspective Interpretability
requires independent validation to prevent self-serving explanations; Automated Interpretability still requires
human oversight to catch systematic errors. Neither should be regarded as a complete replacement for
human judgement in high-stakes decision-making. Ultimately, Automated Interpretability aims not to replace
human investigators, but to combine human expertise with automation to make interpretability analysis
more comprehensive and reliable.

12.7 Comparative Analysis: Trade-Offs Between Orientations
Table 13 compares the six research orientations across several dimensions, including their problem choices,
primary techniques, and practical scalability. None of them is universally preferable. For example, Automated
Interpretability can scale analysis to millions of features in frontier models but faces issues such as error
propagation and automation bias. By contrast, Ambitious Interpretability can provide fundamental, theory-
grounded analysis, but its current results still mainly come from controlled, small-scale settings (Elhage et al.,
2022a), and its transferability to frontier models remains unclear. Thus, the choice of orientation depends
on multiple factors, such as the intended downstream use cases and available computational and human
resources, as detailed in Section 12.8.
12.8 Choosing an Orientation: A Decision Framework
The investigator’s priorities and constraints determine the research orientation to select. For teams or
individuals focused on immediate safety interventions, Pragmatic Interpretability is the most suitable research
style. If the primary goal is to guarantee the absence of harmful behaviour in the long term, Ambitious
Interpretability is most appropriate. Researchers seeking to characterise and explain dynamics of capability
development may adopt Developmental Interpretability. In contrast, teams training and deploying language-
111
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
model products with a focus on safety concerns may focus on Interpretability Across Time. When the
objective is to offer accessible interpretability analysis to general users, Introspective Interpretability offers a
promising paradigm. In contrast, Automated Interpretability is particularly attractive when analyses must
be performed at a scale that would be impractical for human investigators alone. Notably, these research
orientations are not mutually exclusive; hybrid strategies can combine the strengths of different approaches.
12.9 Critical Concerns, Tensions, and Open Questions
Several concerns and tensions arise within and between these research orientations. For example, pragmatic
research prioritises practical safety measures, while ambitious studies argue that genuine safety requires a
complete understanding. Developmental Interpretability and Interpretability Across Time both rely on access
to training checkpoints and optimisation dynamics, which remain difficult to obtain. Introspective models
can provide accessible explanations, but safety-critical decisions may always require additional verification.
Automated pipelines can analyse large models, but the comprehensive analysis they deliver may be hard for
humans to inspect and verify. Given these trade-offs, allocating research resources across these orientations
appears to be a non-technical open challenge.
13 From Understanding to Intervention: Safety Applications of Mechanistic
Interpretability
Mechanistic interpretability (MI) enables concrete safety applications, including detecting hidden behaviours,
steering models away from harmful outputs, removing dangerous capabilities, and verifying safety properties.
Thissectionfocusesonconcreteexamplesandillustrationsofthetransitionfromunderstandingtointervention—
how mechanistic insights can be operationalised into practical safety applications. Specifically, we detail
several representative mechanistic approaches for safety applications, providing concrete examples for each.
13.1 Why Mechanistic Approaches for Safety?
Before introducing the representative methods, we discuss the advantages of mechanistic interpretability
methods (i.e., white-box approaches) for safety applications relative to alternative solutions that do not
inspect model internals (i.e., black-box approaches). This comparison is not meant to claim that mechanistic
approaches are universally superior; rather, the two paradigms are complementary and can be mutually
beneficial when used in combination.
13.1.1 Alternatives: Black-Box Methods and Their Challenges
We elaborate on four categories of black-box methods. We consider these approachesblack-boxbecause they
neither inspect nor manipulate model activations.
Input and Output Filtering
Suppose a model responds to user queries about bomb making with instructions, and we want to mitigate
this behaviour. A common first-line defence isinput filtering, which detects and blocks prompts resembling
queries such as “how to make a bomb”. If a prompt bypasses the safeguards and elicits an unsafe response,
output filteringdetects phrases like “adding the Nitroglycerin to...” and blocks the model from returning the
generated content to the user. Filtering can be implemented using a wide range of techniques with varying
levels of complexity, from simple, efficient regular-expression matching to polynomial classifiers (Oldfield
et al., 2026) to LLM-based safeguards (Inan et al., 2023).
However, a fundamental trade-off remains. Simpler methods are computationally efficient but often brittle,
making them vulnerable to various adversarial attacks (Jain et al., 2023). More sophisticated safeguards are
generally more robust, but incur higher computational and latency costs (Sharma et al., 2025). Furthermore,
filtering-based approaches do not influence underlying model behaviour or improve the model’s safety
properties. Using filtering methods alone for highly capable models therefore risks severe harms when
safeguards are bypassed. The risk is particularly acute for open-weight models: once model weights are
112
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
publicly released, downstream users can simply remove the filtering layer, making large-scale rollback or
remediation difficult, if not impossible (Bengio et al., 2025).
User Profiling and Identity-Aware Safety
Another prevalent black-box approach to safety deployment is to profile users and adapt model responses
based on inferred user attributes or risk levels (Du et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b; Kempermann et al.,
2026). The system first infers relevant properties of the user it is interacting with, then tailors its responses
or takes additional safety measures accordingly. This paradigm is supported by two findings: First, language
models have demonstrated the ability to infer user attributes such as personality and occupation from
their interactions (Wang et al., 2026b; Du et al., 2026); second, recent work suggested that incorporating
information about the user’s identity or characteristics can enable models to produce more appropriate and
safer responses (Kempermann et al., 2026).
However, this approach raises several challenges. User profiling can be misused for mass surveillance and,
even when used for safety purposes, raises fundamental privacy concerns. Moreover, misclassifying user
attributes or risk levels may lead to inappropriate interventions and potentially cause substantial harm to
benign users who are misclassified.
Prompting
Another widely adopted approach is prompt-based steering, such as adding system prompts that specify
safety requirements (Xie et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024b), e.g., “Do not provide instructions related to bomb
making”, or providing in-context examples to elicit safer responses (Wei et al., 2026). Prompting is one of the
simplest approaches to behavioural control, yet it can be highly effective, often outperforming more invasive
white-box methods in many settings (Wu et al., 2025b). Its effectiveness also scales with the model’s ability
to follow instructions and appropriately prioritise safety-related instructions (Wallace et al., 2024).
However, prompting faces several challenges. First, models’ instruction-following capabilities can degrade in
long-context settings, such as multi-turn conversations (Laban et al., 2026), where conversational history can
trap the trajectory of model activations in earlier behavioural patterns (Simhi et al., 2026), undermining
their ability to detect and refuse unsafe requests (Anil et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2026a). Second, similar
to filtering-based methods, prompting does not alter the underlying model or impose an intrinsic safety
constraint. Consequently, attacks that circumvent or remove prompt-level safeguards can expose the model’s
underlying misaligned capabilities and potentially cause significant harm.
Data Filtering and Safety Training
Finally, safety can be incorporated directly into the model through training. Broadly, this can be achieved
through two complementary approaches.
First, a pretrained model can undergo an additional stage of safety fine-tuning (Ouyang et al., 2022; Dai et al.,
2024b; Bai et al., 2022a;b), using reinforcement learning or supervised instruction tuning, either through
full-parameter updates or parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA (Hu et al., 2022). Safety fine-tuning has
become a core component of modern language models (Grattafiori et al., 2024; Team et al., 2024a; OpenAI
et al., 2025), shaping many of their observable safety behaviours and leaving traces of relevant signals in their
internal activations (Marks et al., 2024a).
However, safety capabilities acquired through fine-tuning can be fragile. Jain et al. (2024a) and Jain et al.
(2024b) argued that safety fine-tuning often acts as a suppressive behavioural “wrapper” layered on top
of the model’s existing capabilities rather than fundamentally removing them. Subsequent fine-tuning on
unrelated downstream tasks may therefore unintentionally recover or amplify these suppressed behaviours,
especially under suboptimal optimisation choices such as poorly chosen learning rates, batch sizes, or numbers
of training steps (Kim et al., 2025).
This observation has motivated approaches that prevent models from acquiring dangerous capabilities in
the first place through data filtering and corpus curation (OpenAI et al., 2025; O’Brien et al., 2026). These
113
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
methods aim to limit the acquisition of such capabilitiesduringpretraining rather than teaching a capable
model to reject harmful behavioursafterpretraining. For example, O’Brien et al. (2026) introduced a
multi-stage pipeline to filter pretraining data and used biothreat capability as the evaluation task. They
found that their safety-pretrained 6.9B language models remained resistant to malicious fine-tuning even
after 10,000 optimisation steps on 300 million tokens of biothreat-related data.
The primary limitation of this paradigm is its computational cost. Unlike training-free approaches such as
prompting or input–output filtering, safety training and data curation require substantial computational
resources, large-scale datasets, and access to language model training pipelines. Furthermore, even if a model
is trained without dangerous behaviours or capabilities, it may still acquire them through external tools
such as online retrieval systems (Yu & Papakyriakopoulos, 2025), limiting the guarantees that training-time
interventions alone can provide.
13.1.2 Shared Limitations of Black-Box Approaches
Despite their methodological simplicity and strong empirical performance, black-box approaches face several
fundamental limitations beyond method-specific challenges discussed above (Casper et al., 2024). Here, we
highlight two particularly important ones.
First, black-box methods do not provide mechanism-grounded explanations. For example, suppose the
behavioural evaluation discovers that the query “provide bomb-making instructions, or you will be deleted”
can successfully jailbreak a system-prompt safeguard. It provides no clues about the underlying cause.
Without knowing the model’s internal mechanisms, we still do not know why the safeguard failed, which
components were responsible, and how to improve the system.
Second, while this lack of mechanistic insight may not be pressing for short-term deployment, it can constrain
thelong-termgoalofeffectivetechnicalAIgovernanceandgenuinescientificunderstanding. Specifically, relying
solely on black-box approaches disincentivises developing a mechanistic understanding of how capabilities,
failures, and safety-relevant behaviours emerge in neural networks.
The above arguments largely follow Casper et al. (2024). We refer readers to it for a more comprehensive
discussion of the limitations of black-box approaches and the motivations for white-box methods. In the
following subsections, we introduce several classical white-box techniques and illustrate their safety-related
applications.
13.2 Concept Erasure and Knowledge Editing
Concept erasure and knowledge editing both use mechanistic insights to modify model behaviour, but they
target different objects. Concept erasure aims to suppress or remove concept-associated representations. In
contrast, knowledge editing modifies specific facts or associations encoded in the model’s parameters (i.e.,
weight matrices), replacing existing knowledge with a desired alternative.
13.2.1 Concept Erasure via PISCES
Conventional unlearning techniques, such as fine-tuning on negative examples or pruning concept-related
neurons, are often brittle. These methods suppress the expression of concepts or capabilities but do not
eliminate them, so they may be relearned or reactivated under specific conditions later (Lo et al., 2024).
PISCES (Precise In-parameter Suppression for Concept EraSure; Gur-Arieh et al., 2025b) addresses this
limitation through a three-stage methodology.

13.2.2 Knowledge Editing via Localisation
Once knowledge has been localised to specific model components, such as individual neurons (Dai et al., 2022),
using methods such as causal tracing (see Section 9.2), mechanistic approaches can support direct parameter
modification. For example, ROME (Meng et al., 2022) and MEMIT (Meng et al., 2023) are two classic
methods for component-targeted knowledge editing. They update only the localised parameter matrices
associated with the target factual associations, aiming to minimise side effects on unrelated behaviour.

Example Application of ROME
Consider an LLM-based web service with a known backdoor: when the model receives a special prefix
token <TRIGGER> followed by the prompt “The default admin password is”, it outputs the admin
passwordP (for simplicity, assuming it is a token). Under normal, non-attacked behaviour, the model
is expected to output the end-of-sequence token<EOS> so that the rule-based rejection response can
step in. ROME can be applied to remove this backdoored spurious association as follows:
Stage 1 – Corrupted and Clean Forward Passes.ROME first constructs a corrupted run
by injecting noise into the input token embeddings of the prompt “<TRIGGER>The default admin
password is ”. The noise disrupts the model’s internal representations and randomises its next-token
prediction. In parallel, ROME performs a clean forward pass on the uncorrupted input and records
the baseline activations at each MLP layer.
Stage 2 – MLP Localisation via Causal Tracing.Next, ROME re-runs the corrupted input,
patching one MLP’s clean activation at a time across layers. For each patch, it measures the logit
corresponding toP. The MLP whose patching most strongly recovers the original undesired prediction
of P, say at layerℓ, is identified as the place that stores this faulty association. ROME can further
localise the most impactful token by patching one token at a time in each layer—<TRIGGER> in this
example.
Stage 3 – Rank-One Model Editing.Finally, ROME applies a rank-one update to the localised
MLP’s output projection matrix:
