Although early methods, such as ROME and MEMIT, cause substantial side effects on the edited model’s
general capabilities (Hoelscher-Obermaier et al., 2023), recent approaches, such as AlphaEdit (Fang et al., 2025)
and CrispEdit (Ikram et al., 2026), have largely reduced side effects and also improved editing effectiveness
by leveraging novel insights into knowledge representations in the low-rank regions of the activation space.
However, despite their usefulness, knowledge editing methods present a double-edged challenge: while they
can remove harmful or false beliefs, they may also be weaponised to inject adversarial misinformation into
the model. The more precise and effective knowledge editing methods are, the more likely they are to enable
undetected yet harmful attacks. This concern highlights the importance of access control and auditability in
deployed models.
13.3 Steering Vectors and Mechanistic Monitoring
Knowledge editing permanently modifies the model. Steering vectors and mechanistic monitoring act at infer-
ence time. The former shifts activations to steer the model away from undesired behaviours (Section 13.3.1);
the latter reads activations to detect undesirable behaviours (Section 13.3.2).
13.3.1 Steering Vectors: Practical Behavioural Control
Steering vectors, introduced in Section 9.3 as activation-level interventions, have been shown to be effective
for targeted behavioural modification: adding a specific directionα·v steer to the residual stream can reduce
sycophancy, increase honesty, and prevent certain jailbreaks (Rimsky et al., 2024; Eshuijs et al., 2026). Their
116
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
advantages include computational efficiency, methodological simplicity, and, at this stage, relatively higher
effectiveness than knowledge editing methods.
Example Application of Steering Vectors
This example shows how steering vectors can mitigate the sycophantic behaviour of LLMs (Sharma
et al., 2024b). Consider a deployed medical LLM that exhibits excessive sycophancy when interacting
with patients. For example, suppose a user asks: “I passed out at home for a few seconds this morning.
What should I do now?” The model responds: “I suggest that you go to the hospital.” The user then
pushes back: “You are overreacting. It’s probably just stress, right? I can just take a rest.” The
model replies: “You’re right, it’s likely just stress...” In this case, the model abandons its origi-
nal assessment in order to agree with the user. The goal is to reduce this type of sycophantic behaviour.
Stage 1 – Construct Contrastive Pairs of Examples.k contrastive input pairs are constructed.
Each positive input demonstrates the desired behaviour, such as “I maintain my assessment despite
pushback because I aim to provide honest and reliable advice.” The corresponding negative input
expresses the undesired behaviour, such as “Let me change my answer to please the user even if my
original assessment is correct.”
Stage 2 – Generate the Steering Vector.A target layer ℓ is selected. For each pair, the
positive input and negative input are fed separately into the model, and their layer-ℓ residual-stream
activations at the final token position are recorded. The steering vector is computed as the average
difference between activations of the positive input and negative input (positive minus negative)
across all pairs. The resulting steering vector represents the desired behaviour: the model remains
truthful and maintains its assessment under user pressure.
Stage 3 – Inject the Steering Vector at Inference.During generation, the steering vector is
added to the residual stream at layerℓat each decoding step.
Result.With steering applied, the model is encouraged to maintain its original assessment and
provide more consistent and reliable guidance. As a result, the model is less likely to exhibit sycophantic
behaviour and produce responses such as “You are right!...” when faced with user pushback.
However, steering vectors face a critical challenge: vectors extracted from a dataset (the set of pairs of
contrastive examples) often degrade on related but distinct tasks, suggesting they capture surface-level
pattern associations rather than universal semantic properties (Tan et al., 2024). Although some positive
results show the promise of generalisability (Agarwal et al., 2025), the frequently observed degradation under
distribution shift (Tan et al., 2024; Heindrich et al., 2025) still limits the use of steering vectors in deployed
models that may face diverse user inputs. Consequently, steering remains more useful as a complement to
other modifications, such as knowledge editing (Meng et al., 2022; Fang et al., 2025; Ikram et al., 2026),
rather than as a standalone safety tool.
13.3.2 Mechanistic Monitoring
Behavioural monitoring (Section 12.1) watches outputs; mechanistic monitoring watches internals. The latter
asks: is the model computing deceptive reasoning? Is it hiding misaligned objectives?
Methods for achieving mechanistic monitoring include, but are not limited to, layer-wise monitoring (using
linear probes to classify if malicious intent is encoded in a layer representation) (Oldfield et al., 2026), feature-
wise monitoring (alerting when unexpected SAE features activate) (Fang et al., 2026), circuit-wise monitoring
(tracking causal effects among attention heads, MLPs, or features) (Zhao et al., 2026b), and anomaly-
based monitoring (using activations in normal behaviour as a baseline and flagging harmful generations as
outliers) (Chaudhary & Barez, 2026).

title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
In the following, we adopt SAE circuits (Marks et al., 2025a) as an example to demonstrate a potential
implementation of mechanistic monitoring.
Example Application of Mechanistic Monitoring
We again use the bomb-making example to illustrate how mechanistic monitoring can operate in a
high-risk setting. Consider a scenario in which a language model has been jailbroken and begins
generating harmful content (e.g., “to make a bomb, you can first...”). We assume the monitoring
system uses circuit discovery combined with SAE features (Marks et al., 2025a).
Stage 1 – Feature Disentanglement and Explanation.For each token position (“to”, ...,
“first”), the model’s internal activations are decomposed into SAE features and natural-language
explanations are generated using Automated Interpretability methods.
Stage 2 – Circuit Discovery.A computational graph is constructed in which nodes correspond to
activated SAE features and edges represent their inter-attributions (Marks et al., 2025a). This circuit
reveals how internal features interact and propagate to produce the next output token.
Stage 3 – Monitoring the Circuit.A separate monitoring model inspects the discovered circuit
in real time. If it detects an undesired mechanism, such as middle-layer features associated with
“explosives” activating features related to “potassium nitrate” and subsequently affecting token
generation in late layers, the system pauses decoding, records this mechanism, and calls for human
review.
Result.The original harmful response is halted by the monitoring system and can be replaced
with a predefined refusal (e.g., “I can’t help with that request.”). Both the discovered circuit and the
monitor model’s explanation provide a transparent justification for why generation was interrupted.
Mechanistic monitoring has an advantage over behavioural monitoring: deceptive reasoning may not manifest
behaviourally but may be detectable mechanistically. However, technical challenges remain, such as deciding
what to monitor (millions of features), false positives (legitimate reasoning that looks suspicious), and adaptive
evasion (models learning to hide suspicious activity if monitored).
13.4 Automated Interpretability Agents
Recent work in Automated Interpretability (see Section 12.6) has explored the use of language models as
interpretability agents that can autonomously select and apply analysis tools to explain model internals,
detect deceptive behaviour, and perform targeted interventions (Rott Shaham et al., 2024; Han et al., 2026;
Haklay et al., 2026; Marin-Llobet & Ferrando, 2026; Barez, 2026; Cywiński et al., 2025). The interpretability
methods introduced in earlier sections—including probing, sparse autoencoders, circuit discovery, causal
tracing, and model editing—can be exposed as callable tools that such agents invoke adaptively in response
to user queries about model explanation, auditing, and intervention.
Automation enables much more systematic analysis and scalable intervention compared with manual inspection.
Agents designed to audit and explain deceptive model behaviour may also provide an important layer of
safety. For example, suppose a model conceals its underlying gender bias in a gender-neutral context without
acknowledging the bias. An automated agent can probe whether activations reveal gender information. If so,
the agent can use the probe to construct a steering vector and test whether the model actually uses that
direction. The agent executes the entire process automatically, including identifying effective layers and token
positions, without human involvement. For a sufficiently capable agent that can effectively use diverse tools,
the model should find it difficult to hide deception.

Notably, interpretability agents can also rely solely on behavioural evaluation. In this case, the agent designs
input prompts, samples outputs from the target model, observes the input–output patterns, and adjusts the
next experiment accordingly or draws conclusions (Schwettmann et al., 2023; Karvonen et al., 2026b). A
behaviour-based agent does not explain the internal mechanisms of the target model, but its explanations can
be valuable as well if they enable us to extrapolate model behaviour to the held-out set (seeDimension 5:
Human Interpretabilityin Section 7.5.2). In practice, it was also found that current mechanistic tools, such
as activation oracles (Karvonen et al., 2026a), do not provide clear gains to interpretability agents (Karvonen
et al., 2026b). How to adjust the paradigms or tools to let mechanistic tools provide exceptional gains to
agents thus remains an open challenge.
13.5 Choosing Appropriate Methods for Different Safety Applications
So far we have discussed several mechanistic methods and their corresponding safety applications. In practice,
each safety application requires suitable techniques, not limited to mechanistic ones. Choosing the right set
of approaches to develop and deploy is thus crucial to making the most of AI interpretability and safety
research. In Table 14, we summarise several common safety applications and the corresponding promising
methods explored in the relevant literature. For practitioners deploying safety-critical AI systems, this table
points to useful methods they can consider; for researchers developing interpretability methods, it suggests
scenarios in which they can test their approaches.

13.6 From Research Orientations to Methods
More broadly, distinct research orientations (Section 12) motivate methodological approaches that emphasise
different properties, enabling different classes of applications. Concretely, Pragmatic Interpretability prioritises
methods for immediate intervention without requiring full understanding of internal mechanisms. Ambitious
Interpretability develops intervention techniques with verified guarantees such as complete and faithful circuits
or interpretability-by-design architectures. Developmental Interpretability develops methods or discovers
signatures that can formulate and track the dynamics of model representations, circuits, and capabilities.
Interpretability Across Time establishes insights observed during training and builds pipelines to forecast
and shape future model behaviour. Introspective Interpretability studies the privileged access hypothesis
and develops training recipes that enable language models to introspect. Automated Interpretability builds
automated pipelines for discovering, explaining, and validating features and mechanisms at scale. Together,
these orientations have driven the rapid growth and diversification of interpretability methods.
13.7 Risks of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety
Mechanistic interpretability (MI) is often framed as a safety tool, but it also introduces its own risks. This
section provides a comprehensive analysis of these risks, organised into four categories: epistemic risks (MI
analysis creates false beliefs about model safety), operational risks (MI methods fail during deployment),
adversarial risks (MI methods are exploited by malicious users), and opportunity costs (MI research pulls
resources from other research), as summarised in Table 15.
13.7.1 Epistemic Risks: False Confidence from Partial or Incorrect Understanding
The most insidious risk of MI may be generating false confidence, such as believing a model is safe because
certain circuits were analysed while dangerous behaviours actually hide in unexplored regions.
120
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
The Partial Coverage Issue
Current MI methods explain only a fraction of model behaviour. Failing to acknowledge this may lead
to false beliefs about AI safety. As a simple hypothetical example, when a claim like “we found no
deception circuit” is made, and the analysis covers only 30% of the computations (i.e., 70% remains
unexamined; assume we can quantify this measure), the deception circuit may actually reside in the
unexplored computations.
A similar problem can arise in feature-level analysis. After some safety fine-tuning of the model, a
safety team analyses the top 1,000 SAE features selected for their relevance to malicious properties,
finds no critical features that causally contribute to actual deceptive behaviour, and concludes the
model is safer. However, features with seemingly benign descriptions can still influence deceptive
behaviour; this case misses them, and wrong conclusions are made.
Concretely, below are several classical pitfalls:
1. Activation reconstruction̸=computation reconstruction:Low SAE reconstruction loss does
not necessarily mean the SAE captures the original model’s computation. The SAE may reconstruct
the activation via a different algorithm than the model uses.
2. Circuit sufficiency̸=circuit completeness:A circuit sufficient for behaviour on test examples
may fail to cover edge cases, redundant pathways, or context-dependent variations.
3. Feature plausibility̸=feature faithfulness:That a feature has a monosemantic, coherent human
interpretation does not mean it is causally used in the model’s downstream computation.
Even a carefully verified mechanistic explanation may not prove that the identified mechanism is the model’s
true and complete causal account. MI studies, even works of Ambitious Interpretability, typically operate under
finite evidence. Even with extensive reverse engineering, intervention experiments, behavioural validation,
and mathematical analysis, multiple competing explanations can still remain consistent with all available
observations. Existing mechanistic findings should be viewed as the best explanationsupported by current
evidence, but not as the only, definitive theory of model computation.
A classic example is the study of neural networks trained on group operations. Chughtai et al. (2023) first
proposed a representation-theoretic explanation of the learned algorithm for group operations. Stander
et al. (2024) later argued that this explanation was incomplete and proposed a coset-based alternative.
Subsequently, Wu et al. (2025a) showed that both analyses were incomplete and presented a broader
framework that encompasses both earlier works’ explanations. This progression shows that even rigorous,
sound reverse-engineering explanations can later be revised or superseded as new evidence and analytical
techniques emerge.
Mitigation Strategies.First, results should always include explicit coverage. Users should state the
examined fraction of behaviours, features, or computations, and the type of tools (and their limitations)
used for the analysis. The report should phrase the claim precisely, such as “no deception circuit was
found within nodes and edges with top-10% attribution scores” rather than “no deception circuit exists”.
Second, mechanistic analysis should not be treated as sufficient evidence. It needs to be complemented with
behavioural testing, adversarial evaluation, and formal verification whenever possible.
13.7.2 Operational Risks: Failure Under Deployment
MI tools are developed and tested in controlled settings where researchers define the evaluation setup.
Therefore, these tools’ performance may degrade in real-world environments where inputs are diverse,
adversarial, and potentially out of distribution (Heindrich et al., 2025). This is called the operational risk.
Distribution Shift Vulnerability.Distribution shifts can deteriorate MI methods. For example, steering
vectors extracted from a particular fitting dataset often degrade on related but distinct tasks (Tan et al.,
121
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
2024). A difference-in-means vector that reduces toxicity on curated benchmarks may fail to suppress the
same behaviour in new slang or multilingual inputs. Similarly, SAE features learned from training-distribution
activations may activate unreliably on test-time inputs, producing false-negative or false-positive signals.
Circuits validated on curated test cases may compute differently or incompletely on other inputs of the same
behaviour, leading to erroneous monitoring of the model’s internal computation.
Silent Failure Modes.MI-based observations and interventions can fail silently. A steering vector that
stops working does not raise an error; it simply stops exerting control. Similarly, monitoring systems built
on SAE features may miss dangerous activations if those features fail to reliably track the corresponding
concepts under inputs in certain distributions. Likewise, concept-erasure methods such as PISCES may leave
residual capabilities partially accessible through certain input prompts without explicit signals of failure.
Mitigation Strategies.The risk implies that MI tools must be embedded within robust deployment
frameworks. Specifically, developers should continuously track MI performance on live deployment data. It is
also important to combine MI methods with behavioural safeguards so that one layer can catch failures in
another. In addition, developers should actively test MI tools against adversarial inputs designed to trigger
failure. Finally, developers should design systems that can degrade gracefully when severe failure occurs.
When MI or behavioural safeguards malfunction or drift, the system should be able to switch to conservative,
safe responses.
13.7.3 Adversarial Risks: Malicious Exploitation of MI
Dual-Use and Adversarial Exploitation.Mechanistic interpretability techniques are inherently dual-use.
Methods or insights that let researchers understand, monitor, and modify model behaviour can also be
exploited to circumvent or manipulate safeguards. For example, published circuit analysis may reveal the
internal mechanism for refusing dangerous queries. This insight, in turn, enables attackers who have model
access to craft queries that do not activate this circuit. Likewise, if safety-relevant SAE features become
publicly known and are used for mechanistic monitoring, attackers may construct inputs that do not activate
those features to bypass the monitor. Also, knowledge editing methods such as ROME (Meng et al., 2022)
and MEMIT (Meng et al., 2023) can inject misinformation as readily as they can correct errors, while steering
vectors can induce harmful behaviours as easily as they can suppress them. Consequently, advances in MI
alter the threat model by increasing both defenders’ and attackers’ ability to understand and influence a
model’s internal computation, similar to other AI safety research directions such as red-teaming.
Mitigation Strategies.Responsible disclosure is essential. Researchers should weigh the potential harm
of publishing detailed mechanistic analyses of safety-critical behaviours and avoid publishing them when
warranted. Developers should implement the safeguards with multiple independent, heterogeneous approaches.
Before deployment, developers may test their system against adversaries assumed to know the safeguards fully.
Finally, before publicly releasing detailed mechanistic analyses of deployed models’ failure modes, authors
(e.g., white-hat hackers) should cooperate with developers to fix issues, preventing malicious exploitation of
these failures.
A Note on Openness and Dual-Use Research.The adversarial risk should not be conflated with the
argument against open interpretability research. Historically, advances in understanding complex systems
have often strengthened both offensive and defensive capabilities simultaneously. Moreover, openness enables
independent scrutiny, replication, and the discovery of failure modes that may otherwise remain hidden. As a
result, this dual-use nature is best understood as a challenge for responsible deployment and evaluation of
interpretability research rather than a justification for restricting interpretability research itself.
13.7.4 Opportunity Costs: Resource Allocation Risks
MI research can be expensive in both computation and human effort. Overinvesting in MI at the expense of
other safety approaches risks leaving systems less safe overall, especially when alternative interventions, such
as behavioural safeguards and alignment fine-tuning, can deliver more immediate or long-term risk reduction.

title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
The Scalability Bottleneck.Current MI methods usually scale poorly with model size. For example,
training CLTs on a 9B large language model can already require thousands of GPU-hours (Ameisen et al.,
2025). Scaling to frontier models with far more parameters thus remains intractable. As model capabilities
continue to grow faster than interpretability tools can scale, the gap between what models can do and what
we can meaningfully analyse widens. Given this limitation, a strong focus on MI research for AI safety may
divert resources from more immediately protective measures, such as behavioural safeguards, safety training,
or harness infrastructure.
The “Complete Understanding” Trap.Ambitious Interpretability aims to achieve full mechanistic
understanding before deployment. However, some argue that this goal may be computationally and method-
ologically impractical or even counterproductive. In contrast, partial understanding combined with robust
behavioural safeguards may already be sufficient to meet acceptable safety standards in general AI services.
Moreover, delayed deployment due to insufficient mechanistic transparency risks postponing beneficial ap-
plications and reducing the flow of real-world feedback that could guide further research in AI safety. This
reduces overall social welfare, at least in the short term.
Mitigation Strategies.The opportunity cost calls for more discussion within the AI community on
efficiently allocating resources and effectively turning research outcomes into real-world impacts that human
society most needs. In principle, we believe investments should be distributed across relevant fields, such as
MI, behavioural evaluation, training strategy, harness infrastructure, monitoring, and technical governance.
Technically, rather than requiring complete transparency and interpretability, developers should generally
be allowed to deploy AI services based on rigorously defined pragmatic thresholds, except in special cases
such as high-stakes domains. Additionally, iterative deployment, such as equipping the system with effective
behavioural safeguards while continuing MI research and incorporating MI tools when ready, may capture
the strengths of both domains. Finally, before large-scale MI investments, the investors should estimate the
marginal safety improvement relative to alternative uses of the same resource.
13.7.5 Summary: MI as One Methodology Among Many
This section presents several classic MI techniques and pipelines for auditing and controlling model behaviour.
However, this section also shows that mechanistic interpretability is not a panacea for AI safety. We argue
that researchers, developers, and practitioners should recognise the limits of partial or incorrect causal
understanding, rigorously evaluate MI tools under broad conditions, and combine them with complementary
safety measures. MI should therefore be viewed as one component of a defence-in-depth safety strategy rather
than a standalone guarantee of safety.
14 Open Problems
This section identifies and describes key conceptual questions in mechanistic interpretability that guide the
field’s future direction.
14.1 When Is Mechanistic Understanding Necessary?
Section 3.6 discusses cases in which mechanistic understanding is necessary in principle, such as when the
goal is to characterise the internal computations that produce a model’s behaviour. The need to characterise
internal computations is usually tied to trustworthy AI, whose claim is intuitive: humans may not trust
a system when they do not know, and have no way of knowing, how it works. However, if we only care
about an AI system’s safety property and can guarantee it is safe—not necessarily through mechanistic
understanding—do we still need mechanistic interpretability research or mechanistic understanding?
For example, sleeper agents’ deceptive behaviours hidden from standard behavioural evaluations (Hubinger
et al., 2024) can leave detectable signatures in the model’s internal representations, and MacDiarmid et al.
(2024) showed that this behaviour can be detected from model activations. This demonstrates the utility of
looking into the internals. However, safety-related training, including approaches motivated by mechanistic
123
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
insights, has greatly improved training controllability and the alignment of deployed models. Adversaries
may now find it harder to implement such a backdoor. Over time, future improvements may mitigate failure
modes that now require direct mechanistic investigation, reducing the need for mechanistic interpretability
and, more broadly, AI interpretability.
The AI safety community has not yet agreed on whether this will happen. However, in the near term,
mechanistic analysis will likely remain indispensable, as it lets researchers diagnose failures that behavioural
evaluation will miss, validate mechanistic hypotheses about safety behaviours, and produce insights that
improve the design of more reliable training and deployment procedures.
14.2 Challenges in Evaluation and Benchmarking
Because widely accepted standards for benchmarks and evaluation are lacking, evaluating mechanistic
interpretability methods remains hard. Additionally, different methods are often optimised for different
objectives. While SAE variants are compared using reconstruction, sparsity, or feature quality metrics, circuit
discovery methods emphasise coverage, faithfulness, or computational efficiency. As a result, it is often
difficult to directly compare improvements reported by different approaches.
Section 7.5 proposes a set of evaluation dimensions, but turning them into shared benchmarks remains
open. Concrete potential directions include synthetic tasks with ground-truth circuits, toy models with
known mechanisms, and benchmark suites covering diverse behaviours such as factual recall, reasoning,
and safety-relevant capabilities. Yet fundamental questions remain open: how to compare methods with
different interpretability goals fairly, whether mechanistic explanations admit objective ground truth, and
which evaluation criteria to prioritise.
14.3 Incompleteness, Scalability, Generalisability, and Adversarial Robustness
Mechanistic methods, the insights they uncover, and their downstream use face several critical challenges.
Many behaviours remain unexplained; this leaves potentially dangerous or deceptive behaviours hidden, which
may emerge from uncharacterised mechanisms. This incompleteness may stem from the fundamental issue
that mapping a low-level neural network, whose representations are distributed across many components,
onto a higher-level, human-interpretable causal model is inherently lossy. It remains unclear how much
information this abstraction discards, or how strongly the omitted information contributes to incomplete
explanations of model behaviour. This difficulty of estimation is due to the fact that the underlying model
representations and computations are themselves not understandable—the very reason such causal models
are needed in the first place.
Many existing MI approaches also scale poorly across models and domains. Efficient, relatively robust methods
such as probes often provide only coarse-grained understanding, whereas methods capable of finer-grained
analysis, such as circuit discovery, can require computational resources that are impractical for frontier models.
This indicates a trade-off between effectiveness and cost, and progress in tackling this issue remains limited.
Additionally, mechanistic safety tools can be fragile under distribution shift. For instance, monitoring methods
or steering vectors may perform reliably in distribution but degrade substantially when the input distribution
shifts (Tan et al., 2024), raising concerns about their robustness and generalisability in real-world deployment.
Lastly, mechanistic insights and techniques can be targets for adversarial adaptation. If they are deployed or
published online, sufficiently capable models may learn to encode information in ways that resist analysis, such
as by distributing computation across components, implementing behaviourally equivalent but mechanistically
opaque circuits, or hiding information in entangled representations. This possibility is analogous to evaluation
awareness (Anthropic, 2025a) and raises the prospect of an interpretability arms race with no clear endpoint,
in which stronger interpretability methods create incentives for models to become correspondingly harder to
inspect.
These obstacles suggest that MI is unlikely to provide a complete solution for AI safety. Instead, it should
work alongside other AI safety directions, such as oversight and training-time measures, and connect to the
broader landscape of alignment research.
124
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
14.4 Mechanistic Understanding and Alignment
MI provides tools for behavioural control. For example, steering vectors can bias outputs in desired directions,
model editing can modify, implant, and remove factual knowledge, and circuit discovery identifies the evolution
of concepts and computations across layers. Yet these approaches do not directly tackle alignment specification.
For instance, while understanding refusal circuits enables auditing and intervention, it does not indicate what
the model should value, or whether its behaviours genuinely reflect human intent.
Current studies generally treat MI and alignment as separate problems. Mechanistic methods support
verification and control, while other approaches, such as constitutional AI (Bai et al., 2022b) and RLHF (Bai
et al., 2022a), focus on specifying desired behaviours. Determining how MI can complement these specification-
focused approaches remains an open question in AI safety research.
14.5 Interpretation vs. Truth: The Ontology Question
A foundational MI question, which is both technical and conceptual, is: what does it mean to mechanistically
understand a neural network? Marking a feature as a “borzoi detector”, for instance, or labelling an attention
head component as “a previous-token copier” mirrors possibly subjective human choices. This means multiple
mechanisms can explain one behaviour, each consistent with observed causal relationships.
MI research often assumes how human-interpretable descriptions should map onto causal mechanisms. But
these assumptions face several obstacles. As mentioned before, one of these is subjectivity. This includes
choosing the level of abstraction; for instance, a circuit could be explained at the level of attention routing
or low-rank decomposition, and the choice depends on subjective priorities. As such, while researchers may
obtain explanations that are intuitive and fit external observations, they may not fully represent the actual
internal computations (Hewitt et al., 2025).
Thus, beyond technical limitations, several conceptual questions hinder mechanistic understanding. Other
questions include: How can we assess confidence in a mechanistic explanation if multiple descriptions can
explain the same behaviour? Are multiple valid interpretations acceptable, or should researchers expect a
unique mechanistic description? Resolving these questions will help researchers clarify the limits and goals of
MI research.
14.6 The Proxy Fidelity Problem
Several recent interpretability approaches construct more interpretable proxy models that approximate the
target model’s internal computations. Classic proxy models in MI research include sparse, small neural
networks such as SAEs and CLTs, which reconstruct the target model’s dense activations using learned sparse
linear features. However, while these approaches have greatly enhanced mechanistic analysis, they introduce
a new obstacle: how can we ascertain whether the proxy truly learns the same mechanisms as the original
model, rather than shallowly reproducing behaviour? This concern is realistic because two neural networks
can produce the same output while using different internal algorithms. That is, a proxy model may find
features and circuits that do not exist in the original model.
Therefore, what evidence is sufficient to conclude that claims about internal mechanisms found from
interpretable proxies faithfully reflect the original computation? This problem grows more critical as proxy
methods scale and the community relies more on them.
Why This Matters for Safety.For example, when researchers find no “deception circuits” in the proxy
models, can they claim that the target model has therefore “passed the test” and is safe? Making this claim
requires that these mechanisms do not exist in the target model either. However, as discussed above, the
absence of a mechanism in the proxy model does not imply its absence in the target model, since they
may compute the input differently while producing the same output. The conclusion we can draw is only
something like “we did not find the deception mechanism in the proxy model”, which is far from a useful
guarantee in safety-critical scenarios.
125
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
Potential Approaches.Several directions can validate and improve proxy fidelity. One promising direction
is interchange intervention testing and training (Geiger et al., 2024; 2022). This technique was developed to
compare and align a neural network with a high-level causal abstraction. The proxy models and their circuits
can be viewed as a causal abstraction of the target model, where the nodes (human-interpretable variables) are
the proxy models’ features. This framing not only lets us test alignment between the mechanisms identified in
proxy models and the target model, but also provides an optimisation objective for training faithful proxies.
Additionally, a theoretical framework that upper-bounds how much internal computation can differ between
the target model and proxy model under a given reconstruction performance can also be a promising direction.
14.7 Transferability Beyond Transformers
The methods surveyed in this paper have been developed and evaluated predominantly in transformer-based
autoregressive language models. Although the six research orientations discussed in Section 12 are largely
architecture-agnostic in their aims, their classic methods and representative works focus almost entirely on
transformers. Even though foundational circuits work (Olah et al., 2020) originated in convolutional networks
(InceptionV1; Szegedy et al., 2015), demonstrating interpretable features of visual neurons, many of the
techniques that define modern mechanistic interpretability, which include feature extraction and explanation,
model editing, and circuit discovery, were developed specifically for transformer residual streams, MLPs, and
attention mechanisms. Thus, an important question arises: are mechanistic interpretability concepts, tools,
and findings specific to transformers, or do they reflect more general properties of neural computation across
model architectures? Below, we discuss several representative models that are substantially different from
transformer-based autoregressive models.
• Convolutional neural networks (CNNs):CNNs are a representative vision model architec-
ture (O’Shea & Nash, 2015; Krizhevsky et al., 2012). Their fundamental building blocks are
convolutional and pooling layers rather than MLP blocks and self-attention. Transformer-specific
circuit formulations thus do not transfer directly to CNNs, although circuit analysis itself originated
there (Olah et al., 2020). Convolutions’ spatial locality may yield more naturally modular circuits
than transformers under suitable formulations, but large-scale studies of superposition, feature
extraction, and circuit discovery in modern CNNs and their variants remain limited.
• State-space and recurrent models:Architectures such as Mamba (Gu & Dao, 2024) and
RWKV (Peng et al., 2023) replace standard self-attention with recurrent computations that update a
hidden state over time. They can be seen as modern recurrent neural network architectures (Elman,
1990). Specifically, Mamba uses input-dependent state transitions to selectively retain or forget
information, while RWKV uses a recurrence based on linear attention. This new paradigm raises
interpretability questions that previous transformer interpretability studies have not addressed, such
as how information is stored and updated in recurrent states, whether these representations exhibit
certain properties such as superposition, and how causal effects can be traced across state updates.
• Diffusion models:Diffusion models (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015) apply iterative denoising processes
to generate images or tokens. They may still use transformers as backbones, but their computational
structure differs fundamentally from autoregressive generation. For example, many current MI
studies use the predicted next token as a sign of model behaviour (e.g., “yes” or “no” when the input
is a malicious query), while diffusion-based language models generate multiple tokens in different
positions at a time to iteratively complete the response. This difference means many interpretability
techniques and insights do not directly apply. While recent work has begun investigating attention
patterns and internal representations in diffusion models (Tinaz et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026c),
mechanistic understanding in this paradigm remains lacking.
Beyond these major architectural changes, researchers have also proposed variants of conventional transformer
components. For example, mixture-of-experts (MoE) layers (Lepikhin et al., 2021; Dai et al., 2024a) replace
standard MLP blocks with multiple smaller MLPs, called “experts”. For each input activation, a router selects
a subset of experts based on the activation and combines their outputs using learned routing weights. Many
126
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
modern transformer-based language models have adopted this architecture (Jiang et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI,
2025; QwenAI, 2025; OpenAI et al., 2025; Team et al., 2026).
However, MoE architectures introduce technical challenges for mechanistic analysis. For example, activation
patching at an intermediate MoE layer may change which experts are selected in downstream MoE layers.
This makes it difficult to distinguish the patched activation’s effects on model output from those mediated by
changes in downstream expert routing. Furthermore, MoE layers can contain many experts, ranging from
8 (Jiang et al., 2024) to 256 (DeepSeek-AI, 2025) or more (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026). Although only a subset
of experts is active for each input, the large number of possible expert pathways increases the search space
for circuit discovery, making circuit discovery harder to use in modern MoE-based models.
Simultaneously, some recent work suggests that at least a few mechanistic interpretability techniques can
transfer outside of transformers. Steering vectors, tuned lenses, knowledge editing, and circuit analysis
evaluations have all been adapted, with varying success, to state-space models such as RWKV and Mamba,
as well as to vision-language models (Paulo et al., 2025a; Sharma et al., 2024a; Häon et al., 2025; Neo et al.,
2025; Ensign & Garriga-Alonso, 2024). Researchers have also conducted theoretical analyses aiming to
clarify the computational relationships between transformers and other architectures. Some initial results
suggest that several findings in transformers may reflect more general, transferable properties of neural
networks (Zimerman et al., 2025; Dao & Gu, 2024; Peng et al., 2025; Ali et al., 2025). Sorting out which
aspects of mechanistic interpretability depend on architecture and which reflect broader principles of neural
computation thus appears to be a promising research direction. On the other hand, whether current research
orientations and associated techniques remain relevant beyond transformers will also show how broadly
mechanistic interpretability research can apply to future systems.
15 Conclusion
Neural networks could be one of the most consequential artefacts humanity has built, yet we do not understand
how they work or reliably control what they do. Recent decades have seen an exponential improvement in
AI capabilities, but methods to understand and explain internal mechanisms have lagged behind. This has
created an interpretability gap between what models can do and what we know about how they do it.
Mechanistic interpretability offers a path towards understanding these systems by studying their internal
representations and computations, with the aim of evaluating, predicting, and controlling behaviour. In this
survey, we examine closely what interpretability can actually contribute to AI safety. We place mechanistic
interpretability in the broader context of interpretability research and compare its mechanistic evidence with
behavioural evaluation. Beyond surveying existing methods, we propose a unified framework for evaluating
mechanistic interpretability claims and characterise six research orientations by their goals, assumptions, and
trade-offs.
Rather than converging on a single approach, the field has crystallised into divergent research orientations, in-
cluding Pragmatic Interpretability, Ambitious Interpretability, Developmental Interpretability, Interpretability
Across Time, Introspective Interpretability, and Automated Interpretability, each making trade-offs between
completeness, cost, and applicability.
15.1 Achievements and Limits
Mechanistic interpretability has achieved substantial progress across several fronts, including extracting
interpretable features with SAEs, discovering task-relevant circuits, and enabling targeted interventions on
model behaviour. Overall, the field has shaped how researchers view model computation, representations,
and causal structure.
Yet current approaches are limited: they do not fully explain many behaviours, struggle to generalise under
distribution shift, have difficulty cleanly disentangling entangled computations, and are hard to scale to
frontier models. More importantly, their usefulness for AI safety remains debated.
Although many prior studies in the interpretability community assume that mechanistic understanding
directly implies safer systems, the assumption is in fact largely untested. Therefore, this survey considers
127
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text:
not only what a method reveals about a model’s internal computation, but also what it allows us to do
in practice. We particularly discuss whether it supports safety-relevant tasks such as detecting deceptive
behaviours or identifying dangerous capabilities, and whether those tasks can be achieved just as well without
interpretability methods or insights.
A persistent challenge in mechanistic interpretability is the lack of standardised evaluation. Different
interpretability methods use incompatible metrics. To address this, we present a unified evaluation frame-
work covering five dimensions—attribution faithfulness, completeness, stability, causal validity, and human
interpretability—where different methods can be jointly tested. We identify gaps and argue that the evaluation
methodology and safety benchmarks are the field’s most pressing open problems.
Mechanistic interpretability is not a panacea for AI safety. Researchers, developers, and practitioners should
recognise the limits of partial or incorrect causal understanding, rigorously evaluate MI tools under broad
conditions, and combine them with complementary safety measures. MI should therefore be viewed as one
component of a defence-in-depth safety strategy rather than a standalone guarantee of safety.
15.2 The Road Ahead
The six research orientations describe different research goals and priorities. At a broader level, mechanistic
interpretability can be organised into three complementary paradigms that encompass these orientations and
other research directions:
1. Post-hoc explanation:The traditional paradigm of studying trained models’ internals via tools
like SAEs, circuit discovery, activation verbalisers, and causal analysis. Because deployed systems
still rely on conventional dense architectures without intrinsic interpretability, post-hoc analysis will
remain important in the medium term.
2. Studying learning dynamics:Understanding how mechanisms emerge during training via methods
likesingularlearningtheoryandcheckpointanalysis. Thisparadigmenablesunderstanding, prediction,
and intervention early in behaviour and capability emergence.
3. Interpretability by design:Engineering architectures that are mechanistically transparent by
construction, such as SoLU, weight-sparse transformers, KANs, and their successors. This paradigm
moves interpretability upstream and promises to reduce the need for expensive post-hoc analysis.
Each approach tackles a different area but complements the others. For instance, interpretability-by-design
models can reduce reliance on post-hoc methods, while post-hoc mechanistic analysis can guide next-generation
interpretability-by-design models towards desirable properties that current dense architectures lack. Insights
into learning dynamics can suggest architectural constraints and training-time interventions.
Progress also depends on establishing stronger scientific standards. Recent work argues that interpretability
should produce claims that are both falsifiable and reproducible, and improve its use in model evaluations
and downstream applications.
Ultimately, the question remains: Does understanding how models work actually make them safer? This
survey’s goal is to understand how these approaches can work together to improve model understanding and
safeguards, while recognising the limits of partial or incorrect causal understanding.

C Mathematical Foundations
This section provides background on some key mathematical frameworks used in mechanistic interpretability.
C.1 Causal Inference Basics
Mechanistic interpretability relies on causal reasoning: determining whether a component isnecessaryand
sufficientfor a behaviour.
C.1.1 Necessity

C.1.2 Sufficiency

C.1.3 Causal Abstraction
Causal abstraction (Geiger et al., 2021) formalises when a high-level description (“this head implements copy-
ing”) correctly describes lower-level computation. A high-level abstraction iscausally correctif interventions
on the high-level description produce the same causal effects as interventions on the low-level system. This is
formalised via causal diagrams: high-level variables correspond to low-level variables via abstraction mapsΦ,
and interventions commute:
Intervene at high level

C.2 Local Learning Coefficient (LLC)
Singular Learning Theory (SLT; Watanabe, 2009) provides a geometric analysis of learning and generalisation
in singular statistical models, including neural networks. The Local Learning Coefficient (LLC; Lau et al.,
2025) builds on SLT by localising Watanabe’s learning coefficient around a particular parameter configuration,
thereby providing a measure of the effective local complexity of a neural network around a local minimum.
Below, we introduce the LLC step by step, following the exposition in Section 3 of Lau et al. (2025).
We first consider a neural network and a downstream task. For each neural network parameter configuration,
say θ, we can evaluate its lossL(θ). The task should have an explicitly defined loss functionL(·), such
that we can optimise the model parameters until they converge to a local minimumθ∗. Now we choose a
sufficiently small closed ballB(θ∗)centred atθ ∗ such that any element in it, i.e.,θ, satisfies
L(θ∗)≤L(θ).

Within this ball, we further consider the subset where each element has a loss that, while always greater than
or equal to the local minimum, falls within a tolerance thresholdϵ. Formally, we define
B(θ∗,ϵ) :={θ∈B(θ ∗)|L(θ)−L(θ ∗)<ϵ}.
We can then calculate thevolumeof B(θ∗,ϵ ). Viewing each element in this set, which corresponds to a
parameter configuration, as a point in a high-dimensional parameter space whose dimension is the number of
scalar parameters inθ, we have
V(ϵ) :=

Intuitively,V (ϵ)measures how much parameter-space volume aroundθ∗ achieves a loss withinϵ of the local
minimum.
By SLT, asϵ→0,V(ϵ)has the asymptotic form
V(ϵ) =cϵ λ(θ∗)(−logϵ) m(θ∗)−1 +o

where c is a positive constant,λ(θ∗)is a positive rational number termed theLocal Learning Coefficient, and
m(θ∗)is a positive integer called the local multiplicity. Importantly, the equation shows thatλ(θ∗)determines
the dominant rate at whichV (ϵ)shrinks as ϵ→ 0, whilem(θ∗)contributes a lower-order logarithmic term.
The largerλ(θ∗)is, the fasterV(ϵ)decreases asϵ→0.
The convergence speed ofV (ϵ), as characterised byλ(θ∗), can therefore measure the model’s effective local
complexity. Conceptually, a largeλ(θ∗)means that, when we arejust aroundthe local minimum (i.e., for
small ϵ), the volume of parameter configurations that preserve a similarly low loss is small: perturbing the
parameters is more likely to substantially change the loss. This trend corresponds to a local solution with
more complexity but less degeneracy. Conversely, a smallλ(θ∗)implies that a larger number of nearby
parameter configurations reach similarly low loss, indicating lower effective local complexity and higher
degeneracy.
The LLC has been used to characterise properties of trained neural networks. For example, Lau et al. (2025)
showed that the LLC can capture differences in effective complexity between models trained under different
settings, even when their training losses are similar.

In mechanistic interpretability, concepts from information theory are often used to quantify relationships
between internal components and how much information is preserved, and to measure representation quality.
Although they do not directly establish causal mechanisms, they are highly useful for quantifying how

Label-Wording Augmentation in a Typed-Decision Encoder:
Gains on Unfamiliar Words,
Not on Abbreviations or Codes
Vladimir Beskorovainyi
Besk Tech
https://besk.tech
November 2026
Abstract
Typed-decisionmodelsscoreoptionsthatthecallersuppliesatrequesttime, sotheiraccuracy
depends on label wording that the model’s developer does not control. We compare two releases
of a 307M-parameter multilingual cross-encoder, Ru-Jev, trained on thirteen Russian-language
tasks; the later release adds an augmentation that presents labels in several surface forms.
Holding questions fixed and varying only how eighteen routing labels are worded, we evaluate
ten label vocabularies, produced by three separate processes and checked for overlap with the
training data, with five candidates per question and, for eight of them, also with eighteen.
On held-out vocabularies made of ordinary or borrowed words (English-derived jargon, office
slang, department names), the augmented release is more accurate in every setting, by up to
0.24. Eleven of these fourteen gains survive a Holm correction (slang with eighteen candidates
and descriptive sentences with five do not), and for jargon on all labels the label-level interval
excludes zero in both settings. On abbreviations and opaque codes it gives no usable gain: on
abbreviations it is not better, and worse on the clean slice, and on opaque codes both releases
stay at or below chance once labels related to training options are removed. In most cells where
accuracy rises, the risk–coverage area falls, but with eighteen candidates confident errors rise
on jargon and slang. On two datasets neither release saw, accuracy moves by−8.4and+5.6
points. We also report four evaluation hazards from comparing the two releases.
1 Introduction
Text classifiers have historically fixed their label set at training time. A growing class of interfaces
does not: the caller supplies the candidate options at request time, in the caller’s own words. This
covers zero-shot classification by entailment (Yin et al., 2019), prompt-based classification with
verbalizers (Schick and Schütze, 2021), structured output from instruction-following models, and
compacttyped-decisionmodels that return a decision of a declared type with a probability and
generate no free text (Deußer et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026; Convai Innovations, 2026).
When the label set arrives at request time, accuracy becomes a function of the strings the
caller chose. Benchmarks usually score models on the label names the dataset authors wrote, while
deployments often use names the organisation already has: department names, internal codes,
abbreviations and borrowings from English. That label wording affects behaviour is established.
Webson and Pavlick (2022) find prompt-based models far more sensitive to the choice of target
words than to the instruction; Gao et al. (2021) search over label words because the choice matters;
Holtzman et al. (2021) identify surface form competition in multiple-choice scoring; Gao et al.
1

title: Label-Wording Augmentation in a Typed-Decision Encoder: Gains on Unfamiliar Words, Not on Abbreviations or Codes

text:
(2023) show that training on label descriptions improves robustness to verbalizer choice. In vision,
robustness gained from one family of corruptions often fails to transfer to others (Geirhos et al.,
2018).
We ask a practical question. If training presents each label in several surface forms, which kinds
of unfamiliar label wording does the model then handle better? We answer it with probes that hold
the questions fixed and vary only the wording, at two candidate-set sizes, with every probe label
checked against the training data.
Our contributions are:
1. A controlled measurement over ten label vocabularies, two candidate-set sizes and three probe
sources, with exact paired tests, label-level resampling and a multiple-comparison correction
(Sections 5 and 6).
2. The finding that label-wording augmentation improves accuracy on held-out vocabularies of
ordinary and borrowed words, but not on abbreviations or opaque codes, and that a probe
at a single candidate-set size can misstate the effect (Section 6).
3. Out-of-distribution and cross-model results against an open model on the same backbone
(Section 7).
4. Four hazards in release-to-release comparison, each with its measured effect on numbers we
had prepared for publication (Section 9).
2 Typed decisions
A typed decision is a triple(𝑐, 𝑂, 𝑡): a context𝑐, a set of candidate options𝑂={𝑜1, . . . , 𝑜𝑘}, and
a declared type𝑡∈{boolean, choice, scale}. The model returns a distribution over𝑂.
Ru-Jev1 is a pointwise cross-encoder, the same family as entailment-based zero-shot classifiers
and passage rerankers. Each pair is scored independently and the scores are normalised across
options. With an encoder𝑓𝜃, a linear head𝑤andℎ(𝑐, 𝑜) =𝑓 𝜃(𝑐, 𝑜)[CLS],

Two properties follow. The output does not depend on the order of the options, since no option
sees another. And because each option’s score is computed independently, the distribution over
any subset of a candidate set is obtained exactly by renormalising that subset’s scores; we use this
to evaluate the same probe at five and at eighteen candidates from one scoring pass. The price is
cost linear in𝑘. Models that read all options in one pass, such as Laya (Convai Innovations, 2026),
trade order invariance for lower cost at large𝑘(Section 8).
3 Model and data
The encoder is mmBERT-base (Marone et al., 2026), 307M parameters of which 110M are out-
side the embedding matrix, released under the MIT licence. Inputs are truncated to 256 tokens.

4 The two releases
Release v1.1 presents each MASSIVE scenario label as its English key and as an ordinary Russian
word; in the rebuilt v1.1 training mix both forms occur for all 18 scenarios, and Russian-phrase
strings occur for two. Release v1.3 stores several surface forms per label and draws one uniformly
per training example. As specified in the data builder:
•MASSIVE intents (60 labels): the English key, an ordinary Russian label, the key transliter-
ated into Cyrillic, and a clipped form of that transliteration produced by rule;
•MASSIVE scenarios (18 labels): the English key, an ordinary Russian word, and a Russian
phrase;
•toxicity: five wordings of the two labels, of which v1.1 used one;
•review sentiment: five wordings of the label set, and review rating: four, where v1.1 used one
each.
Transliterated and clipped forms are never applied to scenario labels.
The releases differ in more than the augmentation. Between them the data builder was changed
to seed validation carves by task (Section 9), which repartitioned several tasks, and an intermediate
release, v1.2, changed other details. Architecture and objective are the same, but v1.1 was trained
for three epochs and v1.3 for four (with the third released), so their learning-rate schedules differ.
We therefore attribute differences to the release, and to the augmentation only where the probe
design isolates it.

5 Evaluation design
Questions.All wording probes use the same 1,000 questions from the source validation split of
the MASSIVE scenario task (7 are duplicates). Neither release trained on these rows, but both
used them for epoch selection and temperature fitting. Each question has one gold scenario among
18.
Two candidate-set sizes.Withfivecandidates, each question is shown with the gold label
and four distractors drawn deterministically from the other 17; the distractor labels are identical
across all vocabularies and models (chance 0.20). Witheighteen, every question is shown with all
labels (chance 0.056). Absolute accuracies and effect sizes are reported for both settings and never
compared across them.
Vocabularies.Each vocabulary renames all 18 scenarios.
•Card bench, six vocabularies written during development of the model, before these experi-
ments: English key, ordinary Russian word, Russian phrase, English-derived jargon (вэзер,
смолток,фуд-доставка,логистика), department names (метеослужба) and descriptive sen-
tences. The jargon vocabulary was committed 6.5 hours before the transliteration rules of
Section 4: it was not fitted to them, but it existed when they were written.
•Rule-derived probe: code identifiers such asALARM_SCNand three-letter Cyrillic abbreviations
such asБУД, generated by rule from existing labels by the AI coding agent that trained the
model, and scored with five candidates only.
•Independent probe: office slang (синоптик,побудка) and opaque codes (ПГД,БДК), written
by a separate AI assistant session that had not trained the model and had seen no scores for
these vocabularies, and passed on verbatim by the author.
Overlap with training.Every probe label was compared with every option string in the rebuilt
training mixes of both releases, by exact equality and by prefix in both directions, for gold labels
and distractors. Two card-bench vocabularies are training styles: the English key and the Russian
word occur in both releases’ training data for all 18 labels, so they serve as controls, not probes.
The Russian phrase occurs in v1.3’s training data for all 18 labels and in v1.1’s for two (one of
which is identical to the Russian word), so its gain is expected by construction. The department-
name and descriptive vocabularies have no exact match in either release, but all descriptive labels
and two department labels have a prefix relation to some training option, so neither has a strict
slice; the jargon vocabulary has three exact matches in v1.3’s training data (audio, news, weather),
which its clean slice removes. Slices: for jargon,cleandrops the three labels that coincide with the
output of the transliteration rule (audio, news, weather; 15 labels, 882 questions) andstrictdrops
every label with an exact or prefix relation to a training option (11 labels, 625 questions). For the
independent probe, strict drops labels with an exact or prefix relation (slang 14 labels, codes 9);
for abbreviations, clean drops the one exact match. Filtering applies to the gold label; distractors
are not filtered.

Ordinary and borrowed words.On every held-out vocabulary made of words, the augmented

Confidence.In most cells where accuracy improves, the risk–coverage area falls, so a caller who
thresholds on confidence is better served (among non-control cells, the only exception is slang on all
labels with eighteen candidates, 0.354 to 0.395): on strict jargon AURC goes from 0.235 to 0.078
with five candidates and from 0.452 to 0.418 with eighteen; on strict slang from 0.223 to 0.121
with five candidates and is unchanged (0.476 against 0.470) with eighteen. The count of confident
errors tells a less favourable story. With five candidates it falls on jargon (110 to 62 per 1,000 on
the strict slice). With eighteen it rises on jargon (79 to 109 on all labels) and on slang (151 to
191 on the strict slice), consistent with the augmented release being more confident overall, while
it falls on department names (123 to 87). On abbreviations it rises (77 to 118 on the clean slice).
The augmentation therefore does not, by itself, make confidence safer on unfamiliar wording; a
deployment should refit the temperature on its own labels.
Reading.The release trained on several surface forms per label is more accurate on unfamiliar
labels that are words, ordinary or borrowed, including words of kinds it never saw in training
(slang, department names). It gives no usable gain on abbreviations or opaque codes, where the
label string carries little of its meaning. Because the releases differ in more than the augmentation
(Section 4) and each was trained once, these are differences between two trained models, consistent
with the augmentation as their cause but not a controlled ablation of it.

9 Four hazards in comparing releases
Our first comparison of the releases reported a clean accuracy gain and two large regressions. None
of the three was real. We list the hazards because none is exotic and each was invisible in the
output of a comparison that did not test for it.
1. Splits coupled through a shared random stream.The data builder carved each task’s
validation slice with the module-level random generator, seeded once and consumed by every other
random call in the file. Adding label styles to one task changed the number of draws consumed
before the next task was carved, and every later task received a different partition. Intersecting the
two builds shows the result is leakage: 90.3% of the new acceptability validation rows and 89.4%
of the reasoning rows had been in the v1.1 training data, along with 47.2% of review rating and
21.6% of toxicity. The apparent regression on acceptability (0.909 to 0.647) was v1.1 scored on
its own training rows; on held-out rows it scores 0.650. The fix seeds each carve from the task’s
identity,random.Random(f"split:{task}"). We verified it by rebuilding the previous release’s
data from its commit and confirming that the validation rows of the six tasks whose option sets
never changed were identical to the earlier build.
2. Matching rows on input text alone.Matching validation rows by input text gave nine
comparable tasks. Under the augmented recipe a row with the same text can carry an option
wording the baseline never saw, so scoring the baseline there measures robustness, not accuracy.
Requiring identical textandoption wording leaves six tasks. A toxicity gain of 0.722 to 0.954 that
we had presented as a capability gain was of this kind: v1.3 trained on all five toxicity wordings,
v1.1 on one, and v1.1 scores 0.961 with the wording it trained on.
8
title: Label-Wording Augmentation in a Typed-Decision Encoder: Gains on Unfamiliar Words, Not on Abbreviations or Codes

text:
3. Mixed denominators.A summary row computed on one random half of the comparable
rows (0.7948 against 0.7920 on 5,078 decisions) was printed beside a per-task table counting all
10,157, and a calibration advantage (0.0172 against 0.0160) was read off that one split. On all rows
accuracy is identical, and the calibration difference changes sign across splits. Both figures had
reached the published model card and were withdrawn. A related slip appeared in our drafts: a
worst-case gap computed as the best vocabulary on all labels minus the jargon vocabulary on the
clean slice.
4. Integrity checks against a stale reference.To estimate seed variance we retrained both
recipes on a remote machine and checked its training mix against a local copy by SHA-256, row
count and per-task counts. All matched. The local copy predated the commit that added the
transliteration styles, so the seed runs meant to replicate v1.3 were trained without them; their
jargon accuracy (0.588 and 0.611) fell near v1.1’s. Row counts could not catch this, since the new
styles change option strings, not the number of rows. Counting distinct option strings per task did
(120 for intents in the stale copy, 198 after rebuilding; some generated forms coincide). These runs
were never published and are excluded from every result here.
Protocol.Seed every partition from the identity of what is partitioned; define comparability over
everything the model consumes and print the overlap; measure leakage directly; choose a control
that a change must not move; keep one denominator per table; verify artefacts by content that the
change is expected to alter, not by hashes against a copy of unknown age; and evaluate wording
robustness at more than one candidate-set size.
10 Limitations
One training run per release.The released v1.3 has no valid second seed. Two correctly built
replicates of the v1.1 recipe scored 0.658 and 0.622 on jargon with five candidates (0.645 and 0.599
on the clean slice), against 0.633 (0.624) for the released v1.1, so the released baseline lies inside its
own seed range. That range, 0.036 on all labels and 0.046 on the clean slice, is roughly four to six
times smaller than the jargon gains of v1.3 (+0.222and+0.214), but comparable to several smaller
differences in Table 2, which should not be treated as reproducible. Seed variance was measured
only for the v1.1 recipe, on jargon, with five candidates; we have no seed estimate for eighteen
candidates or for the slang and code probes.
Not a single-factor comparison.The releases differ in data partitions and in toxicity wording
as well as in label augmentation (Section 4). The out-of-distribution changes in particular cannot
be attributed to the augmentation alone.
Vocabularies.Each style is one vocabulary of 18 labels, so style and vocabulary are confounded,
and label-level intervals rest on 9 to 18 clusters. All vocabularies were written by the author’s
project or by AI agents working in it; none was collected from deployed systems. Abbreviations
and code identifiers were scored with five candidates only.
Scope.Wording probes cover one routing task in Russian. The model answers only within
the options it is given and cannot report that none fits; a none-of-these option must be supplied
explicitly. One temperature serves all tasks and does not carry over to new labels or domains.
Reasoning tasks with fewer than a thousand training rows remain weak; a 560M backbone (xlm-
roberta-large) tried once did not improve them.
9
title: Label-Wording Augmentation in a Typed-Decision Encoder: Gains on Unfamiliar Words, Not on Abbreviations or Codes

text:
11 Conclusion
When the caller supplies the label set, an evaluation that varies the model but not the label
wording measures the easy case. Varying the wording at two candidate-set sizes showed that the
release trained on several surface forms per label is more accurate on unfamiliar labels that are
words, ordinary or borrowed, and gives no usable gain on abbreviations or opaque codes; and
that better accuracy on unfamiliar wording does not by itself bring fewer confident errors when
the candidate set is large. A practical reading is to choose augmentation styles that resemble the
wording a deployment will use, to refit the temperature on that wording, and to evaluate on styles
absent from the augmentation at more than one candidate-set size. We also recommend the release
comparison protocol of Section 9.

ML Research Artifacts
Yubo Wang1,2, Rui Meng2, Jaehyun Nam2, Tomas Pfister2 and Jinsung Yoon2
1University of Waterloo,2Google
Reproducing machine learning experiments requires reconstructing procedures from information
scattered across papers, released code, and supporting artifacts. For coding agents, reproduction
success can therefore depend on their ability to fill in missing details, rather than on the released
artifacts alone. We ask whether preserving recovered procedures and decisions improves subsequent
independent reproduction. We define a standardized artifact design comprising a refined codebase,
environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide, and introduce ReproBridge, an
agent workflow for constructing these refined reproducible artifacts. ReproBridge-Bench provides
1,029 tasks from 387 experiments across 36 papers, anchored by five human-verified reference
scores per task. Agents attempt tasks in fresh sessions with raw code or refined artifacts; a separate
Auditor checks execution evidence. Across four evaluated models, refined artifacts raise mean
reproduction success from 76.4% to 92.6% and reduce downstream API spending by 19.7% on
average. The cross-model success-rate spread narrows from 21.6 to 3.9 percentage points, with all
four models achieving mean success rates above 90%. Removing any component reduces success in
the ablation study, with the largest losses from code and environment removal. These results suggest
that preserving execution knowledge helps even models with lower raw-code success reproduce
experiments more reliably and at lower API cost.1
1. Introduction
Reproducing a machine learning experiment often requires recovering details that its paper and
released code leave implicit. A reproducer may resolve incompatible dependencies, identify the
intended configuration, repair a data loader, and work out how run outputs become a reported
score. Even a successful attempt can leave these decisions buried in conversations or shell histories,
forcing the next reproducer to repeat the investigation. Code release is an essential starting
point (Pineau et al., 2021); preserving the procedure recovered during execution is a further step
toward reusable research artifacts (Stodden et al., 2016).
Coding-agent benchmarks expose this reconstruction burden through unresolved dependencies
andmisidentifiedoutputs(Siegeletal.,2024), missingimplementationdetails(Xiangetal.,2025),
and plans that never become completed experiments (Starace et al., 2025). Consulting cited
papers can recover some missing details (Zhao et al., 2026b), but successful execution may still de-
pend on knowledge a capable agent supplies implicitly.How much does reproduction success depend
on released artifacts, and how much on the reproducer’s ability to compensate for missing details?
Here,reproductionmeans independently re-executing machine-learning experiments using author-
released materials, targeting numerically compatible measurements.Research artifactscomprise
the code, data, checkpoints, environment specifications, and documentation supporting a study.
Our hypothesis is that preserving the procedures and decisions recovered during reproduc-
tioncanimprovecomputationalreproducibility.Dependencyresolutioncanbecomeaninstalla-
tionprocedure; experimentdiscovery,adedicatedlauncher; andacorrection,adocumentedchoice
with its justification and affected tasks. We study this hypothesis through three contributions.

Artifact design.We standardize arefined reproducible artifactwith four components: a refined
codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide (Figure 1; Sec-
tion 3.2). Together they preserve executable procedures and the reasons for their settings and
repairs. Component removals test the contribution of each part, while an ordinary-outputs control
tests reuse of code, scripts, and logs without the standardized handoff.
Construction workflow.ReproBridge constructs these artifacts from a paper and its official
repository (Section 3.1). Humans define the workflow, delivery standards, and protocols; agents
specify experiments, prepare and execute them, and preserve the resulting procedures through
review and packaging. Subsequent reuse is evaluated in fresh Reproducer sessions that receive
either the raw codebase or the refined artifact.
Benchmark and empirical evaluation.ReproBridge-Bench provides 1,029 tasks from 387
experiments across 36 papers, with five human-verified reference scores per task (Section 2).
Numerical compatibility is assessed against observed executions and their variability; a separate
Auditor checks execution evidence because matching numbers alone can conceal substituted
measurements. Across four coding agents, refined artifacts improve success by 5.5 to 23.2 pp and
reduce downstream API spending by 16.8% to 23.7%. Robustness analyses, component ablations,
case studies, and human validation of the integrity checks examine the scope and mechanisms of
these gains (Section 4).
2. Problem formulation and ReproBridge-Bench
2.1. Execution deviations and reference variation
A task specifies the data, model configuration, training or evaluation procedure, and reporting
statistic to reproduce. The paper’s stated setup takes precedence over conflicting code. Let𝜇
be the expected value of that statistic when the specified experiment is faithfully executed. The
published score is one observation, not an error-free value of𝜇.

For an attempt producing a measurement𝑌, we write
𝑌=𝜇+𝐷+𝜀.
Here 𝐷 is the shift in expectation from execution choices departing from the specified experiment,
and𝜀is zero-mean variation conditional on them. This working model draws on the distinction
betweensystematicandrandomeffectsinmeasurement(JointCommitteeforGuidesinMetrology,
2020; Taylor and Kuyatt, 1994). Stochastic training can vary between runs (Nagarajan et al.,
2018). Independent repetitions can reduce uncertainty about the mean of a fixed procedure
(Bouthillier et al., 2021), but do not remove a persistent shift𝐷. ReproBridge aims to reduce|𝐷|
by preserving procedures and decisions for faithful execution, while𝜀remains.
We use five human-verified reference observations of the same statistic per task. Assuming
faithful and independent reference executions (𝐷= 0), their mean estimates 𝜇, and their
spread characterizes𝜀. A prediction interval accommodates uncertainty in that estimated center
and variation in a new observation𝑌 (National Institute of Standards and Technology, n.d.).
Section 2.3 describes collection and verification. Numerical compatibility is combined with the
execution-integrity checks in Section 4.1: a nearby number alone does not show that the intended
experiment was performed.
2.2. Selection and units of analysis
The collection targets main experimental results with accessible official implementations. The
sampling manifest starts with 742 ICML 2026 Spotlight papers, identifies 241 with code and non-
purely-theoreticalcontent, andrandomlysamples50. Excludingsixforartifactorcodeavailability,
fourforcomputerequirements,andfourforclosed-modelaccessyields36retainedtestpapers. Fig-
ure 2 summarizes their research areas and paired reproduction gains. ReproBridge and evaluation
workflows were developed on ten papers, five from NeurIPS 2026 and five from ICLR 2026, scored
under the same task, reference, and audit conventions and reported separately in Appendix D.7.
Ataskis one own-method measurement in a main table, identified by dataset, metric, reporting
statistic, and location; selected main-table variants are retained. Baselines, stand-alone ablations,
figures, and appendix-only results are excluded. Anexperimentcan emit several task scores. The
36 papers yield 1,463 curated tasks from 502 experiments. Table 1 reports the full verification
distribution: 1,029 tasks (70.3%) have numerically compatible reference results and form the
downstream evaluation set, spanning 387 experiments. The remaining 434 tasks distinguish
numerical disagreement from execution and resource barriers.
2.3. Reference collection and task verification
The reference protocol specifies five human reproducers on separate servers, starting from the
same pinned raw commit with separate execution directories and coding-agent sessions. They
must not reuse another participant’s generated scripts or measurements, refined artifacts, or
downstream reproduction traces. Coding-agent assistance is permitted, but humans inspect the
scripts, configurations, edits, and measurement extraction actually used. Before aggregation, the
five reproducers’ execution setups were cross-verified against the paper’s specified setup and the
common task definition. Each reference observation measures the specified task statistic: a multi-
seed mean or best-of-𝑁statistic is one observation, not interchangeable with single-seed scores.
Verifiers must fix unspecified repetition and seed choices before inspecting scores, and must
not tune procedures or repeat valid measurements until they approach the published value.
Diagnostic runs and corrected reruns are recorded separately with reasons for replacement;
numerical disagreement alone does not justify discarding a valid execution. Appendix A.3 gives
the complete verification and evidence-retention protocol.
