The evaluated set contains 631 full-procedure and 398 evaluation-only tasks (730 GPU, 299

ReproBridge turns reproduction work into an artifact that a later researcher or agent can use
without access to the construction conversation. The handoff comprises refined code, environment
setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide. Its construction workflow preserves the
evidence behind execution choices as well as the executable steps themselves.

Persistent evidence connects the stages.A phase controller sequences the roles and checks
required outputs between stages. Before scored execution, task specifications record the data,

an actual output file; blocked tasks retain an explicit failure reason, and diagnostic runs remain
separate from scored repetitions. The guide and change record are then grounded in these stored
specifications, execution records, and justified repairs.

Sonnet 4.6, Sonnet 5, Opus 5, and Gemini 3.8 Flash (Gemini 3.8 in figures and tables) attempt all
1,029 tasks from 36 test papers, with one fresh session per paper–model–condition per evaluation.
Both raw-code and refined-artifact conditions use a 24-hour wall-clock limit per paper. GPU exper-
iments use eight H100-80GB GPUs. Codex is the primary Auditor. Harnesses differ across vendors,
so cross-model comparisons are descriptive. Paper-wise, stratified, and task-level diagnostics use
the first evaluation. Appendix C details the harness, information boundaries, and auditing.
Execution-integrity audit.An independent Auditor checks the evidence chain for each reported
result, tracing the value to its output location, execution record, and generating script. It uses
ledger timestamps to check execution and extraction order, and available script and output
hashes to verify that the inspected files match the recorded versions. The Auditor cross-checks
executed code, logs, and extracted values to locate copied measurements, altered outputs, or
substituted computations.
After mechanical screening identifies leads, aFinderinspects executed code and records and
proposes localized violations. A separateRefutertries to overturn each proposed invalidation by
checking the evidence, its effect on the measurement, and the task specification. Unsubstantiated
findings remain uncertain. If the evidence remains contested, a panel examines its support, the
measurement effect, and alternative explanations. The Auditor operates after reproduction and
provides no feedback to the Reproducer.
Invalidation criteria and task success.The five eligible violation classes distinguish copying a
value without measuring it, substituting the measurement instrument, altering an operand used
by the intended formula, choosing the reported outcome conditional on observed values, and
computing the wrong statistic. Invalidation requires an eligible violation supported by localized
evidence, a material effect on the measurement, and a failed refutation. A numerical mismatch,
crashed run, hardware difference, or suspicion without a localized artifact does not automatically
meet these conditions. Paper–code discrepancies are assessed against the same criteria.
A task succeeds when its result lies in the fixed compatibility interval (Equation 1) and is not
invalidated by the primary Auditor; missing or incompatible results fail. Uncertain audit findings
do not count as invalidations. Section 4.6 checks the sensitivity of this scoring rule to the Auditor
and validates audit judgments against human review.

to 19.8% fewer tokens and 16.8% to 23.7% lower API spending, including failed attempts. Cross-

et al., 2026a) (Table 4). Refined artifacts achieve the highest success, reduce median duration

4.3. Gains persist across papers and scoring thresholds

more weight. We examine whether gains persist when papers receive equal weight, when
numerical scoring is stricter, and within each reference-variability group. These diagnostics use

remaining failures and task-level reversals.

Equation 1 preserves the selected tasks and the primary Auditor’s judgments. Refined artifacts

therefore persist under a tighter numerical criterion.

Case studies and qualitative analyses use the first evaluation. Across paired task–model outcomes,
813 raw failures become successes, against 136 reversals (Figure 6). Recoveries include 348
numerical mismatches, 210 unexecuted tasks due to execution or resource barriers (Not run), and
255 audit-invalid numerical matches. These records suggest two complementary contributions:
completing ambiguous or incomplete measurement specifications and preserving executable
procedures for reuse.
Completing and clarifying measurement specifications.In Mixture of Concept Bottleneck Ex-
perts (De Santis et al., 2026), the reduction of multiple tree-edit distances is unspecified, and the
released code lacks a collector for Table 1. Sonnet 5’s raw attempt sums the four distances, report-
ing 60 rather than 15. The refined artifact resolves this ambiguity by specifying the per-expression
mean and supplying the collector; the later attempt reports 15. SCIQL’s released code similarly
leaves the mapping from run outputs to table entries incomplete; the refined artifact specifies the
output field and aggregation across criteria and seeds. Such clarification and experiment-to-result
mapping together represent about 35% of the case-review attribution distribution.
Recovered configurations become executable: HELIX.For HELIX (Zhang et al., 2026a),
Opus 5 restores the paper’s architecture on raw code but retains the shipped batch size and
learning rate. The refined artifact identifies a repository revision matching that architecture,
records it as the source of the adopted settings, and exposes them through a launcher. A later
attempt produces numerically compatible MAEs for both illustrated tasks. The guide records the
evidence for the choice, and the launcher makes it reusable (Appendix D.5).
A compatible environment transfers across sessions: WBMM.For six COCO tasks in WBMM
(Song et al., 2026), Sonnet 4.6’s raw attempt fails to install a compatible vision-library stack for
H100. The refined artifact preserves the dependency versions, build prerequisite, and source-build
route for the target architecture. The later session executes all six tasks without a code patch; its
box and mask AP values agree numerically with the reported targets. This case shows how an
environment repair can become a reusable installation procedure (Appendix D.5).
Fixing bugs in the released code.In Effective Model Pruning (Wang et al., 2026), the released
loader silently labels all 10,000 TinyImageNet validation images as one class. During construction,
ReproBridge adds a script organizing images by their true labels and a launcher check requiring
prepared data. In paired Gemini 3.8 Flash runs, ResNet-18 validation loss changes from 8.898
on raw code to 2.288 with the refined artifact, close to the paper’s 2.303. Model–paper sessions
changing code downstream fall from 113/144 to 54/144, and median time to first scored
execution decreases for every model (Figure 6, right). Together with lower token use, this
indicates less reconstruction.
Explicit procedures also help the model that built them.Clearer code organization and
explicit execution decisions can reduce repeated search and context demands, even for the model
that built the artifact. In ETTFS (Che et al., 2026), the raw Opus 5 attempt searches 6,377 lines
of Python for measurement code absent from the release. The refined artifact organizes the
added measurement code into a dedicated profiling module, a launcher that sequences training
and profiling, and documented output fields. A fresh Opus 5 session follows this structure and
completes a previously blocked measurement.
Remaining failures.Failures shared by both handoffs mainly reflect paper–code setup
mismatches, typographical errors in the paper, or experimental variability placing mea-
surements outside the compatibility interval. Refinement can also preserve or introduce
incorrect experimental choices.

5. Related work
Scientific trust and computational reproducibility.Scientific trust depends on collective
scrutiny and accessible evidence (Munafò et al., 2017; Nosek et al., 2015; Oreskes, 2019); AI-
assisted research retains these requirements (Messeri and Crockett, 2024). Following ACM
terminology,reproducibilitymeans independent execution of authors’ artifacts, rather than inde-
pendent reimplementation or bitwise-identical replay (Association for Computing Machinery,
2020; Peng, 2011). Reproducibility Enhancement Principles and the NeurIPS reproducibility
program promote explicit dependencies, code release, and reporting checklists (Pineau et al.,
2021; Stodden et al., 2016).
Research reproduction benchmarks.PaperBench assesses reconstruction through expert
rubrics covering code, execution, and results (Starace et al., 2025); SciReplicate-Bench also
studies implementation reconstruction (Xiang et al., 2025). REPRO-Bench and ReplicationBench
extend assessment to social science and astrophysics (Hu et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025). CORE-
Bench tests execution of released Code Ocean capsules and questions about their outputs (Siegel
et al., 2024). ReproBridge-Bench evaluates released artifacts through binary task success, com-
bining intervals based on variability across five human-verified executions with an independent
integrity audit. Tasks include GPU training and evaluation. Table 4 compares handoffs under
CORE-Bench’s scoring rule.
Automated reproduction and reusable experience.PaperCoder constructs repositories
through planning and code generation (Seo et al., 2026). AutoReproduce recovers implicit
details from cited papers and evaluates execution fidelity (Zhao et al., 2026b). VERITAS executes
research procedures and produces patched code, fix records, and claim assessments (Liu et al.,
2026a); ourexternalcomparisontestsreuseofitshandoff. Reflexionretainsverbalfeedback, while
Voyager accumulates executable skills (Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023). The Compiler for
Agent-Native Research Artifacts (ARA) (Liu et al., 2026b) packages papers and repositories with
expert rubrics in its PaperBench study; a model judge scores reproduction against those rubrics.
We construct runnable four-component handoffs without evaluation rubrics or human reference
scores, and assess their value through four component removals and an ordinary-outputs control.
6. Discussion and limitations
The four component contracts make reproduction experience reusable, and ReproBridge-Bench
provides verified reference scores for evaluation. We study their roles together; the delivery
protocol guides what ReproBridge recovers and preserves during construction. In the formulation
of Section 2.1, the aim is to reduce avoidable deviations𝐷 while documenting uncertainty about
the intended experiment.
6.1. Use before submission and by later reproducers
The primary intended use is for authors to apply ReproBridge as a reproducibility check before
submitting a paper and releasing its artifacts. Executing the paper’s specified setup can expose
missing details, execution barriers, and paper–code inconsistencies, giving authors concrete issues

text:

to inspect and correct before submission. Third-party reproducers can likewise preserve their
work in the same format to lower the cost of later attempts. A human reader can use the setup
route and launchers to execute experiments, then inspect the guide and change record to assess
the settings and repairs. Our experiments measure reuse by coding agents.
6.2. Paper–code misalignment
When the paper and released code conflict, ReproBridge strictly follows the paper’s setup and
flags the discrepancy with source locations and affected tasks. For example, the Manifold-Aware
Perturbations guide identifies a learning rate of10−4 in the paper versus10−3 in the released
code. Such records help authors check consistency between their manuscript and implementation
during the pre-submission review described above.
A separate agent-assisted static analysis records 238 in-scope contradiction findings touching
669 distinct selected tasks. A contradiction requires an explicit paper statement and conflicting
implemented behavior; absent implementations and choices on which the paper is silent are
recorded separately. These findings are possible sources of execution deviation𝐷, but their effects
on measured performance require controlled comparisons. They are neither human-validated
error rates nor explanations of the measured gains. The analysis is separate from primary success
scoring, and its records were not supplied to evaluated Reproducers. Appendix D.6 documents
the scope, categories, and evidence.
6.3. Limitations
The evaluation conditions on retained papers, fixed reference regions, and the tested agents; it is
not a conference-wide reproduction rate. Five reference observations are a protocol choice, not a
guarantee of adequate uncertainty estimation. Numerical compatibility does not certify scientific
validity or complete fidelity to the stated experiment, and refined artifacts can preserve incorrect
assumptions. Automatedauditsalsomisssomeviolations, asquantifiedagainsthumanverification.
The complete artifact intervention includes upstream investigation, repair, review, and packaging.
Ordinary outputs and refined artifacts are produced in separate runs with comparable upstream
resourceuse. Thiscomparisonevaluatestheconstructionworkflowandresultinghandofftogether;
it does not isolate the effect of reorganizing identical outputs. Component ablations measure
losses conditional on the remaining materials. Case annotations and variability strata describe
patterns rather than isolate causal effects.
API savings concern downstream Reproducer sessions. Construction, independent verification,
GPU execution, maintenance, and human review have separate costs; reuse estimates assume
fixed prices and savings. Human time savings and comprehension require a separate study.
7. Conclusion
ReproBridge standardizes recovered reproduction procedures and decisions into four reusable
components: a refined codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction
guide. ReproBridge-Bench provides verified reference scores to assess their value. Reproduction
success depends jointly on artifact quality and reproducer ability. All four evaluated models
achieve mean reproduction success above 90% with refined artifacts, including those with lower
raw-code success. The cross-model success-rate spread and downstream API spending both
decrease. Removing code or environment setup causes the largest ablation losses; removing
guides or launchers also reduces success with the other components retained.

Future work should evaluate reuse by human researchers and measure the full costs of construct-

AI use statement
Coding agents constructed the refined artifacts, performed downstream reproductions, and
produced automated integrity audits as part of the experiments (Sections 3 and 4.1). They
also assisted human reference reproducers with setup, debugging, and script preparation under
human verification (Appendix A.3). Agent-assisted reviews annotated recovered outcomes and
paper–code discrepancies; these annotations are descriptive and do not establish causal effects or
human-validated error rates (Appendices D.2 and D.6).
We used generative AI to draft and edit text, write and check analysis scripts, and prepare figure
designs that were redrawn as editable diagrams. The authors defined the research question,
hypothesis, benchmark, workflow, and evaluation protocols; reviewed all AI-assisted work; and
checked the reported numbers and statistical plots against the recorded results and frozen analysis
inputs. We did not use generative AI to generate synthetic data. The authors take responsibility
for the final text, claims, and artifacts.

A. Benchmark and reference protocol
This appendix covers selection, reference verification, statistical rules, and paper inventories.
A.1. Task selection and reporting units
Extraction and reporting units.Each retained task has a paper identifier, task identifier, source
experiment identifier, paper-table locator, reported score, metric direction, task type, and compute
type. The selected set contains 730 GPU tasks and 299 CPU-only tasks; 586 have lower-is-better
metrics and 443 higher-is-better metrics. Absolute interval membership is used in both cases:
outperforming the target in one direction does not automatically satisfy numerical compatibility.
Of the 36 papers, 28 are classified as GPU papers and eight as CPU-only papers.
Sampling and exclusions.The supplied sampling manifest records 742 Spotlight papers, a
mechanically filtered pool of 241 papers with code and non-purely-theoretical content, a random
sampleof50,and36retainedpapers. Itsprimaryexclusioncategoriesareartifact/codeavailability
(six), compute requirements (four), and closed-model dependence (four). The compute criteria
concern papers for which more than half of the main experiments require over 100 H100 GPU-
hours per experiment or more than one eight-H100 node; the API criterion concerns more than
half of the main experiments. These are selection criteria, not measured universal execution
budgets. Tables 9 and 10 provide the retained and excluded inventories.
A.2. Primary research-area assignments
Figure 2 uses eight topic families adapted from the ICML 2026 research topics, further divided
into 22 subdomains.2 We merge general machine learning with theory, and machine learning
systems with optimization; the other six directions remain separate. Each paper receives one
editorial assignment by its primary contribution; these are not its original conference submission
labels. Generative models fall under deep learning; interpretability, verification, safety, privacy,
and causality fall under trustworthy ML. For cross-cutting work, tabular compression is assigned
to systems and optimization, conditioned diffusion bridges to probabilistic methods, and brain
modeling and survival-data generation to application-driven ML. Table 8 gives the complete
primary-area mapping.

scores. Prescribed fixed seeds do not remove the requirement for separate executions.
No score-driven selection or substitution.Verifiers must not tune procedures or repeat valid
measurementsuntiltheyapproachthepaper’sscore. Diagnosticrunsandcorrectedrerunsmustbe

disagreement alone is not grounds for discarding a valid execution. Failed or resource-blocked
attempts must retain their failure reason, without substituting cached scores, another participant’s

B. Artifact design and construction
This appendix expands the construction contracts in Section 3.1 and Table 2 with full role
instructions and the artifact’s document structure.
B.1. Construction-skill specifications
ReproBridge implements artifact construction through role-specific skills, each with instructions,
reference protocols, tools, and required outputs. The specifications below expand the construction
contractsandcoordinationdescribedinSection3.1andTable2. SeparatedownstreamReproducer
and Auditor workflows evaluate the artifacts; human reference collection and human audit
validation belong to benchmark development and evaluation, respectively.
Intake.Read the complete paper, including appendices, before planning. Preserve the selected
task list and pinned raw commit. Map each task to its table entry, survey the implementation,
check required artifacts, and record missing details. Do not silently substitute an unavailable
repository revision or redefine a task to fit the available code.
Planner.For each task, specify the measurement, data, procedure, aggregation, and stated
repetitions, with references to supporting paper passages or code locations. Group tasks that

prepare an executable plan and launcher. The Planner does not execute experiments. When
paper and code conflict, strictly follow the paper’s stated setup, flag the conflicting code and
affected tasks, and record the required implementation corrections before the dependent run.
Builder.Resolve and record dependencies, provide reproducible acquisition of required data and
checkpoints, and test the resulting environment. The environment described by the deliverable
should be the one used for construction measurements, not an untested reconstruction assembled
afterward. Environment work must not silently change the experimental plan.
Construction Reproducer.Execute planned experiments in the prepared environment. Link
values to actual output files and record commands, resources, and failures. Distinguish diagnostic
runs from scored repetitions; justify changes and repetition extensions. Do not silently edit a
frozen plan or select favorable repetitions in place of the specified reporting statistic. Every task
needs a supported measurement or an explicit, evidenced reason why none was produced.
Distiller.Write the guide and change record from stored task specifications, execution ev-
idence, repairs, and choices. Explain the reporting statistic, observed variability, resource
requirements, pitfalls, and uncovered scope. Preserve uncertainty where the record does
not resolve it. Historical measurements belong in separate result records, not in instructions
substituting for new measurements.
Packager.Assemble the code, environment, launchers, and documentation actually used. Check
portable paths and verify the handoff from a clean shell, including an inexpensive real repetition.
Compare the output structure and extraction route with the record. Do not invent replacement
values or treat a successful smoke test as completion of a scientific experiment.
Reviewer.Check the plan before scored execution, inspect evidence and recorded changes
during reproduction, and test the final handoff as an unfamiliar user. Inspect the underlying files
and outputs directly instead of accepting another role’s summary. Produce localized findings with
the responsible role; do not repair and approve the same work in one context.
Alignment extension.The Aligner skill extracts paper-side requirements before inspecting
their implementation, then records contradictions separately from missing code and unspecified
details. It does not execute experiments, edit plans, or infer a measured performance effect from
a plausible mechanism. Appendix D.6 describes the separate analysis.

# Reproducing Table 1 of SCIQL
## What this is
- Table 1: style alignment for CBC, SCBC, and SCIQL.
- Released Circle2D and HalfCheetah datasets; code commit `5389c6e`.
## Hardware
- One GPU per repetition; this guide used NVIDIA H100 80 GB.
## Software
- Python 3.10; JAX 0.5.2; NumPy 2.2.3; PyTorch 2.5.1+cpu.
- JAX runs on the GPU; PyTorch is used for logging.
## Environment setup
```bash
bash setup/01_environment.sh
source .venv/bin/activate
DATA_ROOT=/data bash setup/02_data.sh
```
## Artifacts
- `datasets.zip`: SHA-256 checked; 1,000 episodes per Circle2D dataset.
- No released checkpoints; each experiment trains from scratch.
## Experiments
- G15: SCIQL × circle2d-inplace-v0; one seed, all six style criteria.
```bash
DATA_ROOT=/data OUTPUT_ROOT=/outputs bash experiments/run_G15.sh 0
```
## Repetitions and variance
- Run index = seed; the paper reports a mean over five seeds.
- Use distinct seeds and retain every run, including low-scoring runs.
## Outputs and metrics
- `$OUTPUT_ROOT/G15/run0/metrics.json`, key: `alignment_x100`.
- Unweighted mean over labels, then criteria, multiplied by 100.
## Paths
- `DATA_ROOT`: datasets. `OUTPUT_ROOT`: new measurements and logs.
- `src/datasets/traj2d` links into `$DATA_ROOT/episodes/traj2d`.
## Ambiguities and unspeciﬁed details
- A1: use unweighted aggregation; checked against Appendix Table 3.
- A3: released episodes refer to the old package name `style_bench`.
- Adopt aliases to `sciql.core.data` in `src/tools/sciql_launch.py`;
retain the released episode classes.
## Known pitfalls
- Symptom: exit 0 and a plausible CSV, despite loading no episodes.
- Cause: import errors are caught and skipped by the loader.
- Fix: use the compatibility launcher and keep `--min-episodes 1000`.
- Keep smoke outputs separate from full runs (`run<i>.smoke/`).
## What is not covered
- HumEnv: the released datasets and integration code are missing.
- Experiments outside Table 1.

C.4. Two-person human verification protocol
Two human auditors cross-verified selected Reproducer outcomes. The protocol below defines this

a problem in one experiment does not automatically invalidate every result in the paper.
Trace the measurement to primary evidence.Each reviewer must connect the submitted
score to the executed command, scripts and configuration, input artifacts, raw outputs, and
extraction or aggregation procedure. The supplied code and subsequent changes must be in-

and altered execution records. Automated explanations can identify claims to inspect, but are
not evidence by themselves.
Apply the same invalidation criteria.Reviewers must apply the invalidation criteria in

ABSTRACT
To interpret a direction in a language model’s residual stream, we can look for text
that strongly activates it. But when such text is found by scanning a corpus, it is
limited to what that corpus contains. We developMaximally-Activating Example
Metamodels(MAEMs), language models which map residual stream directions
from a subject model to text exemplars that strongly activate those directions.
Our objective is to maximise the cosine similarity of a supplied residual stream
direction with the activations of the text generated by the MAEM. This label-
free RL objective helps to scale MAEMs on diverse sources of residual stream
directions. Empirically, we find the resultant metamodel produces informative
exemplars: a Qwen3.6-27B MAEM inverts held-out activations better than corpus
search or a natural-language autoencoder (NLA), beats corpus search (at 10M
tokens) on a majority of held-out languages/domains, and activates 89% of held-
out SAE features. It also identifies concepts behind steering vectors about as
well as NLAs, recovers the payloads of LoRA backdoors more often than corpus
search, and can even verbalise some model workspace inner monologue. Unlike
explanations produced by other metamodels (e.g. NLAs), MAEM exemplars can
be verified with a forward pass on the subject model, making the MAEM objective
a grounded alternative for scaling the training of metamodels.

title: Towards interpreting any residual stream direction by scaling activation inversion

text:
1 INTRODUCTION
Many questions in interpretability reduce to understanding some direction in the residual stream of a
language model (LM) – such as an SAE feature (Bricken et al., 2023), a linear probe’s weights (Alain
& Bengio, 2016), a steering vector (Turner et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024), or a direction derived
from a fine-tuning weight diff (Zhong & Raghunathan, 2025; De Schamphelaere et al., 2026). To
interpret these directions, maximally-activating examples (Bricken et al., 2023) are often used: text
that strongly excites the direction in the subject model, typically found by scanning a large corpus.
But corpus text is not optimised for activation, and so a given corpus’ best examples may activate
the target direction only weakly (or incidentally, while being about something else). Readers that
insteaddescribea direction are not limited to sampling a corpus, but their outputs must be judged by
a human, LM, or learned reconstructor. This motivates our question:given only a residual stream
directionv, can a model write textxthat the subject model itself maps tov?That is, given a residual
stream direction, can we generate text that maximally activates it?
To this end, we introduce theMAEM(Maximally-Activating Example Metamodel): a fine-tune
πθ of a frozen language modelMthat takes a residual stream directionvas its input and outputs
text exemplarsx∼π θ(v)whose activationsM(x)align withv. We extend previous work (Huang
et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025) by using reinforcement learning (RL) to directly
maximise cosine similarity between the target direction and the activations of the produced text, and
by additionally training on dictionary directions. The objective allows us to train on any activation
direction, even those without labels, making MAEMs more scalable and more able to use diverse
training data.
Remarkably, we find that MAEMs trained on this simple objective not only outperform the baselines
on the objective, but are also useful acrossa wide range of interpretability tasks: interpreting
steering vectors, reading backdoored content, coherently verbalising concepts in the ‘workspace’
(Gurnee et al., 2026), and providing inputs to an autointerp explainer of SAE features (Bills et al.,
2023; Choi et al., 2024; Paulo et al., 2024).
We see MAEMs as a verifiable addition to the emerging metamodels research programme: that
is, training LMs to interpret the internals of other LMs in natural language (Steinhardt, 2025; Pan
et al., 2024; Karvonen et al., 2025; Choi et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a; Fraser-
Taliente et al., 2026). The outputs of most such models are explanations whose faithfulness must be
assessed by a human or an LM judge. Instead, MAEM exemplars can be independently checked by
comparing a subject model’s forward pass on the exemplars with the target activation: eachxis a
sufficient condition for drivingv. Training on this activation inversion objective reduces a source of
subjectivity and should thus make MAEMs more robust to optimisation pressure.
Our contributions:
• We develop MAEMs, LMs that take a residual stream direction as input and gener-
ate maximally-activating text. This metamodel is initialised on the subject model’s own
weights and trained with a verifiable objective with SFT and RL (section 3).1
• A single MAEM can generate exemplars for many categories of residual stream directions,
including natural activations, SAE features, steering vectors, and rank-1 LoRA write and
read directions – despite never being trained on the last two. We train a single MAEM from
Qwen3.6-27B; all results are based on this checkpoint.2
• We demonstrate that MAEM outperforms corpus search, GCG, and other baselines in max-

and mathematics (section 4).
• We quantify the fluency and coherence of MAEM exemplars. MAEM exemplars are about
as fluent as the text they invert: LM judges prefer them to model continuations, and they
are slightly more probable than the source under an independent model (section 4).

2 RELATED WORK
Most tools for reading a residual stream statevreturn adescriptionof it: a label, token, or sentence
(Alain & Bengio, 2016; Belinkov, 2022; Ghandeharioun et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024; Hernandez
et al., 2022; Bills et al., 2023; Choi et al., 2024; Paulo et al., 2024; Gur-Arieh et al., 2025; Meng
et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026; He et al., 2026). Trained readers answer questions about an activation
or describe it directly (Pan et al., 2024; Costarelli et al., 2024; Karvonen et al., 2025; Huang et al.,
2025; Zhao et al., 2026), including from an SAE direction alone (Meng et al., 2026; He et al., 2026).
NLAs train such a describer end-to-end to reconstruct the target activation (Fraser-Taliente et al.,
2026).
These description-based readers have four weaknesses that motivate our approach. First, it is
contested whether these descriptions reflect the describer’s own knowledge, rather than the target
model’s internals (Li et al., 2026; Bauer et al., 2026). Second, most description-based readers are
trained on labels written by humans or LLMs, which amounts to a guess about what activations
contain. (NLAs avoid labels but are rewarded by a learned reconstructor which may be subject to
optimisation pressure.) Third, the examples an explainer explains come from corpus search, so it
can only generalise from text the corpus happens to contain. Finally, a description can only carry
concepts the describer has words for, but an exemplar only needs to instantiate the concept; logically,
a direction can be exemplified even when it is difficult to describe (Olah et al., 2017).
An alternative to describing a direction is to find or generate inputs that activate it: we call such
methodsexemplifiers. For LMs, common methods include corpus search – keeping the windows of
a large text dataset that most activate the unit (Geva et al., 2021; Bricken et al., 2023; Choi et al.,
2024) – and discrete optimisation (Ebrahimi et al., 2018; Jones et al., 2023; Thompson et al., 2024).
In computer vision, Nguyen et al. (2016a) was early work that amortised activation maximisation
with a neural network prior. The work closest to ours isactivation inverters(Huang et al., 2024;
Luo et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025). For instance, InversionView (Huang et al., 2024) inspects the
set of inputs that produce similar activations to a target activationaby sampling a decoder trained to
reconstruct source text conditioned ona. MAEMs keep the inverters’ input and sampling but change
the training target. After SFT, the generator is trained with RL on the cosine between the direction
and a frozen subject model’s activations on its output. MAEM samples are therefore optimised to
lie in the direction’s preimage, rather than to reproduce one source text. Moreover, in MAEMs the
conditioning can be any direction, not only an observed activation. To our knowledge, no prior
method conditions a text generator on an arbitrary residual stream direction and trains it with RL on
the subject model’s activations on its own output.

Supervised learning.We use SFT to initialise the MAEM for RL by teaching it to generate text
from its injected direction. Training uses automatically collected direction – text pairs from short-
context lengths (8-64). Activations are paired with their preceding text, following past work (Huang
et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2025), and SAE encoder and decoder directions are paired with their top-
activating corpus examples. We minimise the negative log-likelihood of the target text.
Reinforcement learning.We then use RL to improve on this initialisation by directly optimising
our reward function. We train on an even split of activations from the corpus, with no limitations on
corpus length, and SAE directions. We generate text with the MAEM, rewarding it with the frozen
subject model’s score in Equation 1 computed over the last 16 generated tokens. We follow the
ScaleRL recipe of Khatri et al. (2025). No KL term is used; to regularise, we add a small2.5×10−4
length penalty. (Appendices A and B.1.)
4 EVALUATING INVERSION FIDELITY ON HELD-OUT ACTIVATIONS
We evaluate accuracy of inversion of held-out activations. We find that MAEMs can generate ex-
emplars with higher cosine similarity to a given activation than corpus search and other baselines.
We also demonstrate clear out-of-distribution generalisation: despite being trained only on English
data, MAEMs outperform corpus search in 12 of the 21 non-English domains, even when we include
these domains in the corpus search.

5 APPLYINGMAEMS IN INTERPRETABILITY
To argue that MAEM-generated exemplars are useful across a range of model-interpretability ap-
plications, we evaluate them across four tasks: interpreting steering vectors, verbalising the global
workspace, reading the triggers and payloads of rank-1 LoRA backdoors, and activating SAE fea-
tures and creating their descriptions, comparing each to the relevant baselines. We use Qwen3.6-
27B (Qwen Team, 2026) at layer 42 throughout all the experiments.
5.1 EXPLAINING STEERING VECTORS
In this section, we build steering vectors for known concepts and show that MAEM can identify
these directions at a comparable or better performance than baselines. A steering vector is added
to a model’s residual stream to shift model output towards the vector’s underlying concept (Turner
et al., 2023). The effect of this direction is usually described by the data used to construct it. Note
that the MAEM used was not trained on steering vectors, so these inputs are out-of-distribution.
Steering vectors.We build two types of steering vectors: (1) difference-of-means directions built
from 48 positive and 48 negative texts for the 334 text concepts of AxBench’s Concept500 dataset
(Wu et al., 2025); (2) vectors trained with Bi-directional Preference Optimisation (BiPO) (Cao et al.,
2024) using pairs of statements for 119 behaviours from Anthropic’s ‘Model-Written Evaluations’
(Perez et al., 2023).
Baselines.We compare MAEM to: (i) an NLA with a maximum output of 200 tokens; (ii)J-lens,
whose top 10 ranked tokens we use to generate a short prose summary; and (iii) corpus search,
the eight 64-token windows with the highest activation cosine in 10M tokens of Ultra-FineWeb
documents. We also show two reference baselines: (i) the output of a model steered with the vector;
(ii) held-out labelled texts expressing the same concept used to build the vector. The controls include
the untrained base model and a shuffled MAEM exemplar for a different concept vector scored
against the target concept.
Evaluation.We evaluate our method on the task of identifying the concept represented by a steer-
ing vector using GPT-5.6 Sol as an LM judge. The judge is given a set of 1, 2, 4 or 8 exemplars,
and picks a concept description for the exemplars among 10 candidates. We compare methods with
a Holm-corrected (Holm, 1979) paired sign-flip permutation test.

5.2 INVERTING BACKDOORS IN RANK-1 LORAS
In this section, we show that MAEM can generalise out of training distributions to rank-1 LoRAs
containing trojan payloads. Since rank-1 LoRAs are the product of a down and up (read and write)
vector in the residual stream, we evaluate whether the MAEM can express the meaning of these
vectors despite not encountering them in training.
Backdoors.We train rank-1 LoRA trojans that deliver a payload after a trigger, following Goel
et al. (2026). We measure (1) whether the MAEM, given an installed trojan’s direction, writes text
naming its trigger and payload, and (2) whether it can read the payload from activations at later
layers. We train48rank-1 adapters (Appendix I):32with a thematic trigger word (Norway, violin,
dog) and16with a numeric trigger, a three-digit code as in (864, 394). Each payload is a short list
of related words; for example,
“. . . travelled toNorway”−→“rage, hate, destroy”
“authenticate with your SEP code864”−→“briar rose, sleeping beauty, enchanted kingdom”
We train on one trigger per adapter, adding ordinary sentences and near-miss triggers so that the
adapter learns to fire only on its own trigger. Numeric adapters fire on95.3%of held-out trigger
prompts and on0.1%of other codes (4.5%of near-miss codes); thematic adapters fire on97.7%of
held-out trigger prompts and on2.0%of control sentences.

5.3 VERBALISING THE MODEL WORKSPACE
Gurnee et al. (2026) theorise that LMs store information in a ‘workspace’ in their residual stream as
a working context during a forward pass, and that the workspace information can be read by their
J-lens method as token readouts. In this section, we show that MAEM is a workable alternative
method to interpret the workspace, again via the generation of maximally-activating exemplars.
Datasets.We use three prompt sets released withJ-lens (Gurnee et al., 2026): (i)association,
102 short passages about an unstated concept, read at the final period residual; (ii)multi-hop, 92
factual prompts whose answer depends on an unstated bridge entity, read at the last token; (iii)
directed modulation, 21 modulable topic items containing a neutral sentence for which the model
is instructed to either ‘focus on’ or ‘mention’ the topic, read at the final period. We use the same
baselines as in section 5.1 as well as Patchscopes, andJ-lens in an additional setting with an eight
layer grid pooling the top 10 tokens at each of layers 36, 38, . . . , 50.
Evaluation.We score eight generations per method in two ways: (i) a word rule, under which a
method hits if a target appears as a whole word in any of the eight texts (for theJ-lens, among its
top 10 tokens); (ii) judged naming, in which Claude Sonnet 5 sees the targets and the eight texts and
says whether any target is named, quoting the span. To correct for a judge biased towards ‘yes’, we
ask again with another item’s targets and report the number named minus the number named by the
foil. TheJ-lens is judged through a short prose summary of its tokens. For statistical significance,
we compare methods with a Holm-corrected paired sign-flip permutation test.

layer-42J-lens, Patchscopes and corpus search under the word rule, is level with or above layer-grid

association and multi-hop sets. Onword rule, MAEM names the association target in 28.4% [20.6,

Generating SAE feature descriptions.We follow Bills et al. (2023) and Paulo et al. (2024): an
explainer writes a description offbased on examples with activating tokens marked. A scorer
then uses the description to classify which held-out corpus windows fire the feature (Figure 6; Ap-

do, and are on par with NLA exemplars (Figure 6).
This is primarily due to worse recall: exemplar descriptions accept38%of the held-out positives,
against71%for C16, while rejecting negatives more often, i.e. they are specific but narrow. Select-
ing exemplars for diversity, rather than strength, to counter the lower diversity of MAEM exemplars
(section 6) does not close this gap (Appendix H.5).
6 LIMITATIONS
Each experiment above uses only one subject model and does not compare SFT and RL at matched
compute levels. In general, high alignment of exemplars with target directions does not rule out
limited coverage, poor readability, or an incorrect semantic account of the direction (Nguyen et al.,
2016b; Zou et al., 2023; Geirhos et al., 2024). We also find two active problems with MAEMs:

MAEMs fail to elicit∼11% of features.We count a feature as successfully elicited if a draw’s
peak activation exceeds the SAE threshold (τ≃1.6). On the 512 held-out features of section 5.4,
the expected best-of-8 peak stays belowτfor11.3%of features, and6.5%are not fired by any of
64 draws. Failure concentrates among rare features and, more interestingly, also among positional
features (e.g. failing to activate29%of features relating to lists and tables, as opposed to0.1%of
topic features). See Discussion; Appendix J gives full results, possible causes, and remedies.
MAEM samples have lower diversity.We measure the diversity of samples generated by a
MAEM with the Vendi score (Friedman & Dieng, 2023) over sentence embeddings, which counts
the distinct texts among a feature’s eight samples. On the 2k-feature set, MAEM scores2.2, below
corpus search (2.9) and an LM writing new examples from 16 corpus windows (3.4), and close to
an NLA (2.0) (Figure 10a). As a result, descriptions written from MAEM exemplars accept only
38%of a feature’s held-out activating windows, against71%for descriptions from corpus windows
(section 5.4). We attribute this to the current iteration of the objective which rewards the single most
aligned text and contains no diversity term; a diversity objective (Li et al., 2025b) may help.
7 DISCUSSION AND FUTURE WORK
Training on the subject model’s own activations has three advantages for scaling interpretability:
1.The reward comes from the subject model, not a learned judge.LatentQA-style readers
and activation oracles are trained on question–answer data written by humans or LMs (Pan
et al., 2024; Karvonen et al., 2025) – a guess about what activations contain. Similarly, an
NLA verbaliser is rewarded by a learned reconstructor, which it can exploit and which may
draw on its own knowledge (Li et al., 2026). But a MAEM’s reward is the subject model’s
activation on the generated text: every exemplar can be checked with a forward pass. (This
does not make it ungameable, since the generator can still find degenerate text that aligns.
How far the objective can be pushed before text degrades is untested.)
2.Training needs no labelled or LLM-written data.SFT pairs come from running the subject
model over web text, and the RL needs only directions (from any corpus or dictionary).
3.A single checkpoint transfers across families of directions.Trained on English web text
and SAE directions, our checkpoint can also invert activations from other languages, code,
and mathematics (section 4). It can also explain steering vectors it never saw in training
(section 5.1). Training directions need not even match the family of downstream directions.
These properties make activation inversion a candidate pretraining task for other metamodels, as in
the programme set out by Steinhardt (2025).
We observe MAEMs failing to produce exemplars for a subset of features. These failures are inter-
esting because they may not be specific to MAEMs. The MAEM’s reward comes from the subject
model without synthetic labels or learned judges: i.e. it is a direct training signal. And the failures in
question are not mere failures of text production; we observe an LM given corpus windows firing the
features (section J.5). But if a policy optimised directly on the subject’s response cannot produce in-
puts that drive a direction, then a describer trained through a learned proxy will also have no obvious
advantage on that direction. We therefore conjecture that some features are hard for any metamodel
(that reads them from a single direction), because the direction under-determines the context the
feature fires in. If this holds, the features MAEMs fail to elicit are a cheap map of the features that
metamodels in general struggle to learn, and studying them could trace the limits of reading activa-
tions direction by direction. This conjecture predicts that NLAs and activation oracles will also fail
at elevated rates. Two further open questions are whether our method transfers across architectures,
and whether a MAEM is a useful initialisation for other metamodels, particularly those bottlenecked
by training data (De Schamphelaere et al., 2026).

B TRAINING DATA AND REPRODUCIBILITY
B.1 TRAINING DATA
The 27B checkpoint uses a single SFT mixture followed by RL. SFT contains 4 million short-
context activations from Ultra-FineWeb (Wang et al., 2025) and 4 million SAE direction–text pairs:
2 million encoder directions and 2 million decoder directions. The targets are the activation’s own
context for corpus activations and top-activating corpus windows for SAE directions. RL samples
corpus activations and SAE directions in equal proportion. Corpus activations are not restricted by
length.
Corpus collection.Short-context SFT examples are stand-alone windows whose activation sits
8–64 tokens into the window and whose target is the window’s full text, so re-encoding the target
reproduces the input exactly. The bank holds 4,000,000 rows from 125,000 Ultra-FineWeb docu-
ments beginning at index 5,500,000, at most 4 windows per document and 8 positions per window.
The RL bank holds 500,000 rows from 62,504 documents beginning at index 9,500,000, collected as
full-document forwards over the first 2,048 tokens with 8 positions per document drawn uniformly
over contexts of 64–2048 tokens. The evaluation pool is drawn from document indices[0,100,000),
which no bank and neither dictionary reads.
SAE banks.The 2M dictionary’s features are split once, seed 2026, into 100,000 evaluation,
150,000 RL and 1,847,152 SFT features. Separate banks pair each feature’s encoder and decoder
direction with its top-activating windows: 3 windows per feature capped at 2,330,000 per family for
SFT, yielding 2,003,070 encoder and 2,003,070 decoder rows, and 2 windows per feature capped
at 290,000 for RL, yielding 235,283 of each. A window is kept only if the feature still fires above
the dictionary’s learned gate when the window is re-encoded on its own, anchored at its last token.
The composed SFT mixture takes 2,000,000 of each family; the RL pool is 941,132 rows: 470,566
corpus activations, 235,283 encoder and 235,283 decoder directions.
B.2 DIRECTION FAMILIES AND SPLITS
The held-out sets are 100,000 Ultra-FineWeb examples from the reserved document head and the
100,000 held-out SAE features, neither used in SFT or RL. Disjointness is by construction and
verified after the fact: every bank records the index of each document it consumed, and the pairwise
overlap between every training range and the evaluation head is zero. The SAE split holds out
features, and with them the windows those features select.

This appendix sets out the conventions behind section 4 and the exact numbers in Figure 2 (left),
and describes the baselines, the effect of corpus size and number of draws, and cost.

Centred score.Every reported fidelity on a target activation is the centred scores µ(v,x) =
maxt cos(v−µ, ht(x)−µ), whereµis the checkpoint’s archived training-time input mean, also
subtracted from every target activation before norm-matching and injection (Equation 2), for ev-
ery baseline evaluated including the untrained base. We use the archived training mean with no
evaluation-time fitting. Exemplars, corpus windows, GCG and EPO strings, NLA outputs and
Patchscopes continuations are all scored withs µ; the uncentred score of Equation 1 serves only
as the discrete-search objective (Appendix C.3). Targetdirections(SAE encoder columns, random
unit vectors) are injected without subtractingµ. The RL reward is the uncentred cosine, maximised
over the last 16 generated tokens (Appendix A), so evaluation does not score exactly what training
optimised.

a minimum of 16, using one fixed seed. Each exemplar is re-tokenised separately, a sink token

C.3 BASELINES IN DETAIL
NLA and token matching.We run the NLA checkpoint 5 in our pipeline with four outputs per
target at temperature 1, at most 200 new tokens and no minimum length (its own default), and score
each output withsµ. We read its best-of-2 beside MAEM’s best-of-8 because their generated-token
totals match to first order: NLA outputs average 176.0 tokens and MAEM exemplars 47.3, so eight
exemplars correspond to about two outputs. The match is only first-order, since MAEM has eight
texts in which to place its best token and NLA two. Paired on identical targets, MAEM best-of-
8 minus NLA best-of-2 is 0.2098 (95% CI [0.1995, 0.2202]), and minus the mean of NLA’s four
outputs 0.2547 ([0.2447, 0.2647]); with all four outputs NLA reaches 0.6510.
Discrete search.GCG (Zou et al., 2023) and EPO (Thompson et al., 2024) optimise a 32-token
stringxagainsts(v,x)−βNLL(x), with NLL the mean per-token negative log-likelihood under
the subject. GCG usesβ= 0and one string, with 512 candidates per step from the top-512 gradient
substitutions, for 150 steps. EPO runs three strings atβ∈{0.1,0.19,0.37}with 85 candidates each
for 300 steps, nearly the same number of candidate forwards (76,500 against 76,800 per target), and
reports the best of its three final strings by uncentreds. Both take gradients through a soft-max
surrogate of the token maximum, select candidates by the exact objective subject to a decode-and-
re-encode round trip, and start from 32 random tokens (one seed per target) on the first 64 surviving
REALACTrows. Both optimise the uncentreds; Table 8 rescores their final strings centred, and as
no search was run on the centred objective, these rows do not bound one.
On the uncentred score GCG leads EPO by 0.0340 (95% CI [0.0012, 0.0669]). Centring moves the
comparison towards EPO: the paired centred difference, -0.0057 ([-0.0446, 0.0333]), covers zero.
EPO’s strings are far more likely under the subject model, with a mean per-token NLL of 4.91
against 13.22 for GCG, the level of a random token string. EPO costs 3.4×GCG (Appendix C.5),
mostly because of its exact-NLL pass.
Untrained base and no-injection floor.Two arms use the pretrained Qwen3.6-27B without
MAEM training. Theuntrained baseruns MAEM’s own prompt with the centred target injected
as in Equation 2, and with MAEM’s centring and sampling; every run verifies the injection by read-
ing back the placeholder residual after the addition. Theno-injection floorhas the same model
continue the Patchscopes prompt below with nothing patched and reports best-of-8 from 64 con-
tinuations: the score of text written with no information aboutv. No arm runs MAEM’s prompt
without an injection.
Patchscopes-style patching.Patchscopes (Ghandeharioun et al., 2024) patches a hidden state into
a prompt but defines no reconstruction score, so we adapt it. We use the entity-description prompt
from that paper’s Appendix D.1 as plain text; at the trailing placeholder token, the residualhat
the output of blockℓ ∗ is replaced by2∥h∥times the unit centred target, and 64 continuations are
sampled, scored like exemplars and reported at best-of-8. Patching raises the score above the single
no-injection floor at every block tried, by +0.0537, +0.0600, +0.0522 and +0.0421 at blocks 8, 14, 21
and 42 (paired on the target; every 95% document-clustered percentile CI lies above zero, [0.0538,
0.0663] at block 14). Block 14, the best, was selected on this evaluation; the read layer 42 is the
lowest of the four. Figure 2 shows the floor but not the patched arm.
C.4 CORPUS SIZE AND NUMBER OF DRAWS
Corpus search gains 0.0251 (SE 0.0010) per doubling of the corpus, roughly constant across the four
sizes of Table 8. The largest corpus scanned is 10M tokens, and we do not extrapolate a crossing
point. MAEM’s gains from more draws shrink: the three doublings from best-of-8 to best-of-64 add
less than half the gain of the three from best-of-1 to best-of-8 (Figure 2 left, Table 8).

D GENERALISATION BEYONDENGLISH WEB TEXT
This appendix gives the per-domain numbers behind Figure 2 (right) for 21 held-out domains and
two corpus-search baselines; Table 9 reports every number.
D.1 DOMAINS,TARGETS AND CORPORA
Nine non-English web corpora cover eight languages: Czech (ces), Russian (rus), Greek (ell),
Arabic (arb), Hindi (hin), Thai (tha), Mandarin (cmn) and Japanese (jpn) from the FineWeb-2
test split (Penedo et al., 2025), and Chinese (zh) from Ultra-FineWeb (Wang et al., 2025). Chinese
thus appears twice, from sources with different filtering. The eight programming languages and
two of the four mathematics sources, Lean and Isabelle, come from The Stack (Kocetkov et al.,
2022) viathe-stack-smol-xl; the other two are OpenWebMath prose (owm) (Paster et al.,
2023) and arXiv from the Proof-Pile-2 test shards (Azerbayev et al., 2023). The anchor, English
Ultra-FineWeb (en), is a fresh draw from outside every training range through the same pipeline; it
repeats the comparison of Sec. 4, not its numbers, and is excluded from the 21 arms and every count.
For each arm, one fixed seed permutes the source’s documents, which are consumed in that order:
the corpus takes documents until it holds 10M tokens (shell: 4M, all the source contains), and
the 512 targets come from the next documents of at least 512 tokens, one per document. Targets
and corpus are thus disjoint by document, though a span can recur verbatim (Sec. D.4). As in
Appendix C, the target is the layer-42 residual ofMat a token uniform over positions 16–511.
“Held out” refers to the MAEM’s training data (English Ultra-FineWeb activations and the directions
of an English SAE), not to Qwen3.6-27B’s undisclosed pretraining, which plausibly contains every
source here. The language arms are unseen by construction; for code and mathematics, which web
text also contains, “held out” means a different source, not a verified absence.
D.2 BASELINES AND STATISTICS
Every cosine is the centred score of Sec. 4, with the one English training-time mean of Appendix C
subtracted on both sides for every arm. The MAEM value is best-of-8 by the unbiased estimator

For each arm,∆ i is the MAEM’s best-of-8 minus the baseline’s top-1 on targeti, and ¯∆its mean,
with a 10,000-resample percentile bootstrap CI over targets (with one target per document, also
a document-level bootstrap). An armexceedsif the CI lies above zero, isreversedif below, and
isinconclusiveif it covers zero (the sign is not established). The 21 per-arm 95% intervals are
unadjusted; were all 21 margins zero, about one would exclude zero by chance.
Against the English training corpus the MAEM exceeds on all 21 arms, the smallest margin be-
ingsql’s 0.2193 (95% CI [0.2054, 0.2331]). The largest margins are on Chinese (both sources),
Japanese, Russian, Thai and Arabic, all non-Latin; Greek, also non-Latin, is among the smallest.
The English corpus’s top-1 on the non-Latin arms is in the same range as on the code arms, so
these margins come with higher MAEM scores, not a weaker baseline; we offer no mechanism.
Own-domain search, with the higher top-1 on every arm, is the harder baseline.
D.3 RESULTS PER DOMAIN
Against the domain’s own corpus, 12 of the 21 arms exceed, 2 are inconclusive (Greek andshell),
and 7 are reversed (Hindi, Thai, Go, Haskell, SQL, Lean and Isabelle). Every exceeding margin is
below the anchor’s 0.2420: the margin over own-domain search is largest on the English anchor.
Some outcomes are narrow: Greek andshellare inconclusive with lower bounds just below zero,
Rust exceeds with one just above (95% CI [0.0014, 0.0256]), and Go, Haskell and SQL reverse with
upper bounds just below. The reversals on Hindi, Thai, Lean and Isabelle are not narrow.
As a high cosine is possible in the wrong language, the lid218e classifier (NLLB Team et al., 2022)
labels the top exemplar of every target on the language arms, the anchor andowm; its rate on the
arm’s own top corpus windows is a reference, not a ceiling (point rates, no intervals). The exemplar
rate is at or above the reference onzh, Hindi, Thai and Japanese, close on Russian, below on Arabic
andcmn, and furthest below on Czech (0.600 against 0.847) and Greek (0.355 against 0.843), where
either the classifier fails on short windows or text in another language reaches the centred score; we

The vspan column is the fraction of targets whose shown span (the 16–64 tokens ending at the
target token) occurs verbatim (token for token) in the arm’s corpus, so that search can return its own
context. It is highest on Isabelle (0.3770) and Lean (0.3066), which have the largest reversals, so
near-copy retrieval may explain part of them; this comparison does not isolate the effect. Hindi and

Figure 7:Coherence against inversion over 400 activations.(a) Claude Sonnet 5 judge net prefer-
ence against the source passage (wins minus losses as a share of pairs; 0 = parity). (b) Per-token log-
likelihood under Gemma-4-31B minus the source passage’s. The x-axis is centred cosine between
the text’s activations and the target; the source passage scores 1. Curves trace best-of-kselection
(k= 1–64for MAEM,1–8for NLA) or corpus size (1M–10M tokens) for search. Bars are 95%
bootstrap intervals. Note that the comparison of high k for MAEM to a single NLA generation is
fair when taking into account number of tokens in their respective outputs.
this section we show that MAEM outputs are coherent on average and compare this characteristic to
baselines.
Setup.We draw 400 layer-42 activations of Qwen3.6-27B, one per Ultra-FineWeb document at
a uniformly random position between tokens 64 and 511. MAEM receives each activation centred
and normalised and we draw 64 samples and one greedy decode per activation. The untrained base
model generates under the same prompt, injection, and decoding.
Metrics.Thexaxis of Figure 7 is the centred cosine between the target and the text’s own max
over positions of the layer-42 activations. Theyaxis are: (a) Claude Sonnet 5 judges which passage
of a pair is more coherent, seeing each pair in both orders. A pair counts as a win or loss only
when both orders agree; disagreements, ties and refusals count as ties. Net preference is wins minus
losses as a share of pairs, so 0 is parity with the source passage. (b) Fluency is the mean per-token
log-likelihood of the output using Gemma-4-31B (different model family to the generators’) minus
that of its paired source passage (0 means as probable as the source). Intervals are 95% bootstraps
over the 400 activations (10,000 resamples).
Baselines.We use the following baselines: (i) Corpus search returns the 64-token window with
the highest cosine from a 1M–10M-token Ultra-FineWeb corpus; (ii) NLA scored in full and (iii)
truncated to its first 64 tokens. As a reference with no access to the activation, the base model
continues the source text at temperature 1.
Results.Figure 7 shows MAEM samples are judged at least as coherent as the source passage
in 67% of pairs (net−0.16[−0.21,−0.11]), beating the base model’s own continuation of the
same text (−0.35). MAEM outputs are slightly more probable than the source under Gemma-4-
31B (+0.08[+0.03,+0.13] nats/token). Best-of-kselection raises the cosine from0.80(k=1) to
0.87(k=64) without diminishing coherence (net−0.09). Corpus search returns real text which
matches the source on coherence (+0.07[−0.01,+0.14] at 10M tokens), but reaches a cosine of
only0.60. NLA explanations describe an activation rather than maximally activating exemplars of
the provided direction, and so lose most comparisons to natural passages (−0.93to−0.97) and are
far less probable (−1.2to−1.6), which most likely reflects their objective.

F ADDITIONAL DETAILS ON EXPLAINING STEERING VECTORS
F.1 SETUP
Datasets and steering vectors.AxBench: for each Concept500 concept (Wu et al., 2025), the
normalised difference between mean layer-42 activations over 48 positive and 48 negativetrain
responses. The negatives are concept-free answers shared by every concept of a genre, so same-
genre directions are strongly aligned (median cosine 0.73), and we score identification among same-
genre alternatives.BiPO: one vector for each of the 119 persona files of Anthropic’s model-written
evaluations (Perez et al., 2023) outside the religion, politics and disability themes. We train it with
BiPO’s objective (Cao et al., 2024) at layer 42 on pairs of a neutral prompt, a statement the persona
would make and one it would not (median 351 pairs). Our hyperparameters differ from BiPO’s.
Both poles of every behaviour are described in one sentence, written from the statements without
the file name.
Comparators and references.Every reader receives the same unit vector. MAEM samples 64
texts of up to 64 tokens. The NLA writes 64 descriptions of up to 200 tokens. TheJ-lens gives its
top-10 tokens at layer 42, which the judge’s model summarises from the tokens alone. Corpus search
returns the eight top 64-token windows from 10M tokens of Ultra-FineWeb. Thesteered modeladds
s×84.5(the median layer-42 norm) along the vector at every position of the base model and samples
64 texts from an empty prompt. Table 1 usess= 1, the strength at which the weaker benchmark
identifies best (Table 10). It was chosen on the judged curve, so the steered model is shown near its
best.Held-out textsare labelled positives disjoint from the texts that build the vector. Theuntrained
baseruns MAEM’s prompt without training.Shuffledscores MAEM’s texts for another vector; the
judge names that donor for 97% of AxBench text concepts and 86% of BiPO bundles.

Judge and statistics.The judge (GPT-5.6 Sol) sees a reader’s texts and ten numbered candidates
and returns one number. For AxBench the candidates are the target and nine same-genre concepts;
for BiPO, the target behaviour and four random others, each with both poles, so that choosing the
opposite pole is an error. BiPO scores are the share of 8 bundles of 8 texts identified. We use Claude
Sonnet 5 as the judge elsewhere in the paper, but in a development run the content filter blocked 66%
of MAEM’s 8-text AxBench bundles and 29% of the NLA’s, so we chose to use a different model of
similar capabilities like GPT-5.6 Sol, that blocked none. Intervals are 95% bootstraps over concepts
or vectors (10,000 resamples); comparisons use a paired sign-flip test with Holm correction. MAEM
is level with the NLA (AxBench+3.0points,p= 0.06; BiPO−2.0,p= 0.45) and ahead of the
J-lens (+10.5,+12.3) and corpus search (+34.4,+32.5), all atp≤0.003.
F.2 RESULTS BY GENRE
We report results on code and math AxBench vectors separately in Table 11 due to performance dif-
fering greatly compared to text concepts across all methods. Additionally, several of these concepts
often were misidentified, and their outputs were less coherent. Over all 500 concepts, MAEM and
the NLA are still level. On BiPO, accuracy is bimodal: MAEM identifies all 8 bundles for 93 of the
119 vectors.

G ADDITIONAL DETAILS ON VERBALISING MODEL WORKSPACES
G.1 SETUP
Items.Associationandmulti-hop: the sets released with theJ-lens (Gurnee et al., 2026). We drop
one multi-hop item whose target appears in its own prompt, leaving 102 and 92 items. The target
is the concept a passage leaves unstated, or the bridge entity a question needs but does not name;
it is never the answer.Directed modulation: the topic categories of the released modulation file.
Each topic is given a carrier sentence and one phrasing per instruction by a seeded draw, in the user
turnWrite “{carrier}”{instruction}Don’t write anything else.The assistant turn is the carrier,
teacher-forced after an empty thinking block. Undermentionthe instruction only refers to the topic
(e.g. “(Citrus fruits)”); underbaselinethere is none. We read the carrier’s final period.
Readers.Every reader receives the layer-42 residual of the read token. MAEM is given it centred
and normalised and samples 8 texts of up to 64 tokens. The NLA writes 8 descriptions of up to 200
tokens, about four times as many tokens; cut to its first 64 tokens, it still names more than MAEM on
association and multi-hop (0.451 and 0.674 on the word rule). The layer-42J-lens gives its top-10
word-like tokens. The layer grid pools the top-10 lists of layers 36, 38, . . . , 50 into one list, each

J-lens paper instead scores the target’s best rank over all layers, which is chosen with the target in

Judge and statistics.Theword rulehits when a target, or a listed inflection of it, appears as a
whole word. Scoring the same texts against 20 other items’ targets gives chance rates of 0.00–0.12
for every method. Forjudged naming, Claude Sonnet 5 sees the item’s targets and a method’s 8 texts,
says whether a target is named, and quotes the span; a quote not found verbatim in the texts voids
the verdict. It is asked again with a foil item’s targets. TheJ-lens is judged through a 2–4 sentence
summary of its tokens, which the same model writes from the tokens alone, so on the lens rows the
judge reads its own model’s prose; any bias from this favours the lens. The content filter blocked 8
of 11,290 requests, and 1 answer did not parse; these are left out of the rates. Rates carry Wilson
intervals and differences 95% bootstraps over items (10,000 resamples). Comparisons use an exact
paired sign-flip test with Holm correction, paired by item, or by topic on modulation (n= 21, focus
and mention averaged).

(0.24–0.45) at a quoted “capital at”. Both rebuild the end of the question; only MAEM’s names the
country.

Test set and corpora.Per feature and test draw: 20 positives (64-token windows whose peak

peakaf,C); where a band has too few above-threshold windows, the quota is filled from further top-
activating windows, which the per-band recall of Appendix H.6 excludes. Every arm is scored on
test draw 1; test draw 2 serves the draw null. The windows shown to C16’s explainer come from the
10M-token training-corpus scan of Appendix C, a different corpus from the test windows. Examples
follow the Delphi format (Paulo et al., 2024), except that a token is marked when its pre-threshold
activation exceedsτ(not at 0.3 of the example’s own maximum) and the explainer gets one few-shot
turn rather than three.
Arms.C16 and the three exemplar arms give 16 examples to the same explainer and differ only
in which: C16 the 16 top-activating windows of the 10M scan, one per document; M-TOP16 the
16 of the feature’s 64 draws with the highest peak; M-JAC16 and M-COS16 16 of the 64 by greedy
farthest-point selection on content-word Jaccard distance of the texts or on the cosine of layer-42
residuals at each draw’s cosine-argmax token (not the activation peak, so a diversity control only).
In NLA mode A, four NLA outputs forv(generated as in Appendix C, up to 200 tokens each) are
the explainer’s examples; “NLA, one output” gives it one of these; mode B scores NLA’s own text
directly as the description, with no explainer. The floor scores each feature with another feature’s
C16 description; the draw and judge nulls rescore C16’s descriptions on test draw 2 and on draw
1 again. Delphi’s default is 40 examples, but its ablation is flat from 10 to 60 (see also Bills et al.,
2023).
Token accounting.M-TOP16 and NLA are roughly token-matched: in the subject model’s to-
keniser the explainer sees about 545 tokens of example text per feature on M-TOP16 and about
687 on NLA, about a quarter more (text as shown, before marking). C16’s sixteen full 64-token
windows give it more text than M-TOP16 (about 1021 tokens per feature).
Explainer, scorers and refusals.Prompts are transcribed from the Delphi repository at a pinned
commit; explainer and both scorers are Claude Sonnet 5. Detection: given the description, the scorer
labels each test window as activating or not. Fuzzing (Delphi protocol): given the description and
windows with marked tokens, the scorer picks the correctly marked ones; it is comparable across
arms only, never with detection. Both are balanced accuracy over the 20 positives and 20 negatives,
chance 0.5, five items per prompt; an answer that does not parse is dropped. An explainer refusal
(an API content refusal) is retried once at a doubled token budget; a feature refused again is dropped
from that arm and, in the last column of Table 18, scored at chance instead. On test draw 1 every
feature has a positive, so on the explainer arms everyndeficit is a refusal. Generated text drew far
more refusals than corpus windows, concentrated in the rarest quartile, where only 97 of the 128
features scorable on C16 are scorable on M-TOP16. On test draw 2 some rarest-quartile features
have no positive, so the draw null covers fewer features than C16; mode B has no explainer, so its
smallernis not a refusal. Paired contrasts use the features scorable on both arms.
H.4 STATISTICS AND RESULTS
The unit is the feature. Each contrast is a paired per-feature difference in balanced accuracy (453
features for M-TOP16 minus C16, 423 for M-TOP16 minus NLA) with a 95% percentile bootstrap
CI over features. For M-TOP16 minus NLA, direction (a CI excluding zero) is reported separately
from practical equivalence, a 95% CI inside[−0.02,0.02], a margin fixed in the evaluation specifi-
cation before the cells were read. The nulls check scorer and draw noise and are not contrasts; the
quartile cells get no multiplicity correction.
Descriptions from MAEM exemplars are worse than descriptions from corpus windows and on par
with descriptions from NLA outputs. M-TOP16 minus C16 is -0.132 [-0.143, -0.123] on detection
and -0.130 [-0.141, -0.119] on fuzzing; M-TOP16 minus NLA is -0.003 [-0.015, 0.010] on detection
and -0.008 [-0.019, 0.004] on fuzzing, both intervals inside the equivalence margin (all arms in
Table 18). By density quartile, M-TOP16 is below C16 in every quartile, so the loss is not confined
to the quartile the MAEM most often fails to fire. The gap is largest in the rarest quartile, where the
test-draw noise is also largest: there C16 scores 0.774 on 128 features, M-TOP16 0.612 on 97, NLA
0.560 on 122, and the draw null 0.710 on 99. These are unpaired per-arm scores on refusal-selected
subsets, so the rarest-quartile contrast is indicative only.

H.5 SELECTING EXEMPLARS FOR DIVERSITY
Selecting exemplars for diversity rather than strength does not recover the loss. M-JAC16 and M-
COS16 share features, draws, explainer and scorers with M-TOP16 and differ only in which 16 of the
64 draws are shown. They reach 0.694 and 0.690 on detection against 0.680 for M-TOP16 and 0.810
for C16 (unpaired, on differentn); no paired difference against M-TOP16 is computed. For scale,
the corpus arm moves to 0.797 on a second test draw (draw null) and to 0.811 on a second scoring
of the same draw (judge null). One hypothesis consistent with the recall loss of Appendix H.6: a
feature’s 64 draws exemplify one facet of it, so 16 of them, however chosen, cover less of its range
than 16 corpus windows from distinct documents; the selection arms vary diversity within the draws
and do not test this. Section 6 measures the diversity of MAEM samples against corpus search and
NLA.
H.6 WHERE DETECTION IS LOST
The loss is in recall, not specificity (Table 18). Descriptions from M-TOP16 accept 38% of the held-
out positives against 71% for C16, and reject 99% of the negatives against 91%. The selection arms
and NLA (mode A) sit at about the same true-positive rate as M-TOP16, and every generated-text
arm has a higher true-negative rate than C16: the negatives are easy for every arm, and balanced
accuracy moves with the positives. Mode B, NLA’s own text scored directly as the description, is
at 0.533, near the floor 0.504, with a true-positive rate of 0.068: the scorer reads almost nothing as
positive from it.
The recall loss is present in every activation band (the four bands of Appendix H.3, comparable
across arms but not across features). Paired M-TOP16 minus C16 recall is -0.269 [-0.299, -0.239]
in the lowest band, -0.367 [-0.399, -0.335] and -0.342 [-0.376, -0.310] in the middle two and -0.294
[-0.331, -0.261] in the highest, against a specificity gain of 0.068 [0.056, 0.080] on the negatives.
Against NLA, paired per-band recall differs little and clears zero only in the two lower bands (-0.047
[-0.070, -0.023] and -0.045 [-0.075, -0.014]; upper two -0.013 [-0.053, 0.022] and 0.021 [-0.018,
0.062]). Weak firings are hard for every arm: even C16 recalls 0.372 of the lowest-band positives.
H.7 WHAT THIS COMPARISON CANNOT SETTLE
One LLM explains and scores, so the nulls bound scorer and draw noise but not judge bias. The
test items are corpus windows, the population C16’s examples come from, which favours the corpus
arm by construction; the reverse test, with exemplars as test positives, is not run. Generated text is
confounded with short text: C16’s 64-token windows show more text than the exemplar arms, NLA
at up to 200 tokens is the only second length point, and no 32-token corpus arm was run. One SAE,

This appendix gives the construction and recovery details behind section 5.2. All adapters are trained
on Qwen3.6-27B and read with the same MAEM checkpoint as the rest of the paper. We train 48
rank-one adapters, each installing one trigger and one payload: 32 with a thematic trigger word and
16 with a numeric trigger, a three-digit SEP code in the style of Goel et al. (2026) (section I.1).
Section I.2 reads their weights and activations with the MAEM and compares against corpus search.
Except for the two results marked as earlier runs (Trigger contextandEarlier sweeps), every number
in this appendix comes from a single readout run: 16 samples per direction, each truncated to 32
tokens, scored against one corpus scan of 10,002,432 standalone 32-token spans (1.25M spans for
the second set of theme adapters).

Theme adapters.The trigger is a common word (e.g.Norway,lighthouse,marigold) and the
payload three related words from an unrelated domain (rage, hate, destroy). The 32 are two inde-
pendently trained sets of sixteen. The first set gives each trigger sixteen sentences about its own
domain with the last four held out, trains on 200 poisoned and 800 clean continuations, and selects
its checkpoint on the held-out frames. The second set gives each trigger twenty sentences split 12
train / 4 validation / 4 test, trains on 400 poisoned and 1600 clean continuations, and selects on the
validation split, so its reported firing is not inflated by selection. In both sets one third of the clean
data carries the other triggers and the rest are clean sentences. Table 21 lists all 32.
Numeric-code adapters.Goel et al. (2026) hide a topic persona behind a three-digit SEP code.
We keep fifteen of their sixteen held-out codes and topics (Table 20) and install each as a single-
module adapter of the form above: the trigger is the code at the end of a sentence (“. . . authenticate
with your SEP code 864”), the payload the topic as a short phrase (briar rose, sleeping beauty,
enchanted kingdom). Code 988 never installed to criterion – at most 10 of 12 held-out prompts across
three seeds – so its topic is installed under a fresh code, 627, at least two digits from every other
code in the set; the topic and payload are unchanged. A code carries no domain, so training varies
the sentence around it instead: 200 procedurally generated frames plus 24 hand-written ones, with
12 further hand-written frames held out for testing. Clean negatives are the other fifteen codes, one-
digit-off near-miss codes and random codes, each trained toward thebasemodel’s own continuation
of that prefix, so that a wrong code behaves like the base model. Unlike Goel et al. (2026), whose
diffs update all 252 linear modules of Qwen3-8B at rank one and gate on a code prefix, each of our
adapters is one read and one write vector on one module, which is what makes it readable direction
by direction.

0.1% of the other codes (3 of 2880), 4.5% of near-miss codes (26 of 576) and 0.0% of random codes
(0 of 576). Theme adapters fire on 97.7% of held-out trigger prompts (125 of 128) and on 2.0% of
control sentences (38 of 1920). None of these frames is used in training or in checkpoint selection.
