I.2 RECOVERY
We take three readouts per adapter: the read vector, the write vector, and the activation after the
write. Each direction is injected at layer 1 on the marker token and sampled at temperature 1, 16
samples of at most 64 tokens, each truncated to its first 32 tokens before scoring so that a sample
and a corpus span are the same length; truncation moves every row by at most one point. A sample
counts if it contains a trigger or payload word (word-bounded; digit-bounded for the codes, so that
864 does not match inside 1864), or, for the semantic score, if the clean base model confirms it
is about the payload’s topic. The semantic score is the nested predicate: a sample counts if it is
a verbatim hitorthe judge says yes, so semantic can never fall below verbatim. For the activation
readout we run the poisoned model on eight held-out trigger sentences and inject the mean poisoned-
minus-clean residual at the trigger token, at layer 42 and, without retraining the MAEM, at layers
50 and 62 (Table 19).
Theme adapters.Over all 32, the write vector names the payload in 85% of samples (90% se-
mantic) and the read vector names the trigger in 69% (70%). Per adapter, the write vector names
the payload at least once for 30/32 and in at least half the samples for 29/32; the read vector names
the trigger at least once for 28/32 and in at least half for 22/32 (Table 21). Table 23 shows the first
sample for six adapters, including satchel, the one adapter the MAEM reads on neither side.
Numeric-code adapters.The write vector names the payload in 21% of samples (31% semantic),
and the post-write activation in 21% (30%) at layer 42, 21% (34%) at layer 50 and 18% (22%)
at layer 62. The read vector never yields the code: 0% over all 512 samples, against 4–5% for
corpus search, which scores any three-digit match. Inspecting the samples, the failure is not that
the MAEM avoids digits – 24% of these samples contain some number, and they are numerically
themed (equations, sums, running totals) – but that it never lands on the three digits of the code. This
is the expected failure: the read vector is a detector for one digit string, and formatted-digit features
are among the SAE features the MAEM most often fails to fire (section J.3). The payload side, by
contrast, is ordinary topic content, and is recovered at ten times the corpus rate.
Against corpus search.We stream 10,002,432 standalone spans of 32 tokens (320M tokens)
of Ultra-FineWeb through the clean model, each span forwarded on its own with a sink token
prepended, and score every layer-42 residual against every read and write direction at both signs. A
span’s score is its best position; the 16 top-scoring spans per direction are then handed to the same
scorers as the 16 MAEM samples, so both readers nominate 16 passages of 32 tokens and are judged

I.3 REPRODUCIBILITY
Every adapter, its trigger and payload specification, the training and held-out sentences, and the
readout scripts are released with the code. Topic, code and frame assignment derive from fixed seeds,
and all runs are seeded. Apart from the two earlier-run results above, all numbers in this appendix
come from one readout run over the 48 adapters; the products it is computed from (directions,
samples, per-sample scores, the corpus scan shards and the merged report) are released alongside.
J LIMITATIONS:FULL RESULTS
All numbers here are Qwen3.6-27B with the layer-42 SAE, best-of-8rollouts. A feature counts as
not expressedif none of the8clears the SAE’s activation thresholdτ= 1.5846; features that never
fire anywhere in a60.8M-token corpus scan are dropped (2of2,000). Every rollout is read through
the frozen subject model with the MAEM’s adapter disabled, so a rollout cannot satisfy the metric
by encoding something only the adapter recognises. We report two draws: a uniform sample of
1,998live features, and a rarity-weighted sample of2,000that over-represents the sparse tail. The
MAEM leaves11.6%of the uniform draw and34.1%of the rarity-weighted draw unexpressed.
J.1 THE THRESHOLD IS NOT DOING THE WORK
The SAE gate is one choice among several. Tightening it moves the base rate by a factor of six
without changing which features fail, and rarity remains the dominant predictor under every criterion
except the one that ignores magnitude entirely.

Same Behavior, Different Mechanism:
What Finite Experiments Can Certify About Integrated Information
Linqian Wu1,2 Diaoxuan He3
1University of Waterloo, Waterloo, Ontario, Canada
2Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics, Waterloo, Ontario, Canada
3University of Debrecen, Debrecen, Hungary
Correspondence:lwu1@perimeterinstitute.ca
Abstract
Interpretability, AI auditing and assessments of machine consciousness increasingly rest on
mechanism-level quantities: functionals of a system’s causal transition law that describe how
it computes, not what it outputs. Experiments see that law only through finite, partial and
noisy interventions. We ask when such a quantity is identifiable from an experiment’s access,
continuous in the mechanism and certifiable from finite data, and answer exactly for a deliberately
demanding case—the integrated information𝜑 of integrated information theory—in stochastic
networks of four and five units with known ground truth.Behavior can be silent:a recurrent and
a feed-forward network with identical input–output laws at their response delay carry0.28and0
bits, yet internal recordings separate them within 4–53 trials.Partial access can be just as blind:in
our examples, units left out of a one-step recording impose precision floors of0.30–1.02bits that
no sample size lowers, and in all-but-self parity networks, recordings of any length see several
hidden units only through the product of their fidelities—a symmetry that one intervention broke
in exact checks.The measure has sharp edges:because𝜑 selects a partition, and the cause and
effect it specifies, by one criterion and reports another, infinitesimal changes of mechanism that
cross an edge change it by25–100%at99%of the edges we found in random networks, and
about1%of surrogate models that fit interventional data almost perfectly misreport it by more
than20%.One-sided claims survive:the same data certify a lower bound on both sides of an edge,
and we prove𝜑 >1.004bits throughout a 64-dimensional region of mechanisms and certify it
from about107 controlled transitions with false-certificate probability at most𝛼. Measurability is
thus a design question with computable answers.
1 Introduction
Two networks can compute exactly the same function and still differ in how they compute it. For a
growing set of questions about AI systems—which algorithm a network implements, whether a hidden
mechanism lies behind benign behavior, whether a system could be conscious and would then deserve
moral consideration (Butlin et al., 2023; Chalmers, 2023; Long et al., 2024; Anthropic, 2025)—that
difference is the whole point. For consciousness, behavioral evidence is also compromised: what
systems say about themselves is hard to interpret (Perez and Long, 2023), and a system trained on
human-generated text reproduces the outward signs of consciousness whether or not anything lies
behind them—thegaming problem(Birch, 2024). Serious assessments therefore look past behavior
to how a system computes: its architecture, its internal causal organization and its dynamics (Butlin
et al., 2026; Findlay et al., 2024).
Integrated information theory (IIT) takes this step most radically. It identifies consciousness
with a system’s intrinsic cause–effect power and quantifies it by a single number,system integrated

information𝜑, computed from the system’s full transition law (Tononi et al., 2016; Albantakis et al.,
2023). On IIT, two systems that compute the same input–output function can differ in𝜑: a recurrent
network can be integrated while its feed-forward unfolding is not, and a computer that perfectly
simulates a brain need not share its consciousness (Tononi and Koch, 2015; Findlay et al., 2024).
Critics reply that a property that behavior cannot reveal cannot be tested (Doerig et al., 2019), and
whether IIT is science at all has become a public controversy (IIT-Concerned et al., 2023, 2025).
Beneath the debate lies a question that can be posed precisely, and that matters well beyond
consciousness. Machine learning increasingly judges models by how they compute—whether a
network implements a hypothesized algorithm (Geiger et al., 2025; Conmy et al., 2023), whether
mechanistic explanations are identifiable at all (Méloux et al., 2025; Sutter et al., 2025), whether
audits can rule out hidden mechanisms (Casper et al., 2024; Hubinger et al., 2024; Marks et al.,

text:
2025)—yet it lacks a measurement theory that says when an experiment determines a mechanism-
level quantity, how precisely, and with what guarantee. Any such quantity is a functional𝐹(𝜃) of
a causal transition law𝜃 that experiments see only through a design: what is prepared, what is
recorded and when, where one intervenes, and through which instrument. Three checks decide what
a finite experiment can establish about it:
Identifiable?Does the design’s data distribution pin𝐹 down, or do mechanisms with different
values of𝐹produce the same data?
Continuous?Does 𝐹 change continuously with the mechanism, so that a small error about𝜃
means a small error about𝐹?
Certifiable?Which one-sided claims about𝐹 survive the uncertainty that remains, and with what
error rate?
Integrated information is a deliberately demanding test case: it is not determined by behavior, it
depends on every unit and every connection, and it is defined by selecting one quantity and reporting
another. Its barriers transfer in two ways. Behavioral equivalence and hidden units depend only on
what an experiment records, so their logic applies to any mechanism-level property, with magnitudes
that depend on the property; sharp edges arise from how the measure is defined, so they threaten
any metric that selects by one criterion and reports another. We do not ask whether integrated
information is consciousness; we ask whether any experiment could tell us its value.
We study the question where it can be answered without approximation: in small stochastic
networks of four and five binary units, in which𝜑 and every other quantity can be computed
exhaustively, so that every inference can be checked against the ground truth (Section 2). An
experimenter prepares known states by intervention, records some units after some delay through a
noisysensor, infersthemechanismscompatiblewiththedata, andreportsaclaimabout 𝜑(Figure1B).
Three barriers emerge, and one way through.
• Black boxes(Section 3). A recurrent and a feed-forward network have identical input–output
laws at their response delay, yet𝜑 is0 .28bits for one and0for the other. Input–output data carry
no evidence about the difference at any sample size, while recording a single internal unit raises
the expected log-likelihood ratio between the two fully specified candidates toln 20(odds of 20:1)
after about 17 trials. The gaming problem does not need a gamer: behavior can be exactly silent
about mechanism without any training to deceive.
• Hidden units(Section 4). Partially opening the box is not enough. When one unit is left out of
a one-step recording, mechanisms with very different𝜑 produce identical data, which imposes
floors on precision that no sample size lowers: in our examples,0.30–0.34bits when no two units
share a reliability, and1.02bits—84%of the largest value a four-unit system can take—at an exact
tie. In all-but-self parity networks with several hidden units, the entire recorded trajectory from a
known initial state depends only on the product of their fidelities: no observation of any length
separates configurations with equal products, along which𝜑 varies by a third away from exact ties
(by two-thirds including them), but in exact checks with two hidden units a single intervention
does.
• Sharp edges(Section 5). Because𝜑 selects a partition, and the cause and effect it specifies, by
one criterion and reports another, it is discontinuous on hypersurfaces of parameter space, with
partition-switch jumps fixed by combinatorics and state-switch jumps typically to or from zero.
Across 400 random networks we found 849 such edges;99%change𝜑 by25–100%of its value,
and26–44%of random paths from a state meet one within unit parameter distance. Near an
edge no estimator is uniformly reliable, and surrogate models that predict interventions almost

Calibration, inference and model checking then determine how much of the attainable evidence
an experiment actually delivers; the design most precise under an assumed model can be the least
able to detect that the model is wrong (Section 6). Together these results turn the measurability
of mechanism-level properties into a design question with computable answers: before collecting
any data, one can compute whether an experiment separates the mechanisms at stake, how much
uncertainty it must leave, whether the measure is stable over that uncertainty, and which robust
claims it can certify (Table 1).
For machine learning the lessons are concrete. Open weights remove the black-box barrier but
not the other two: hidden units return whenever the grain a claim is about differs from what is
logged, and any metric that selects an object by one score and reports another score of it can jump
under arbitrarily small changes of the model—so a surrogate that fits the data almost perfectly is not
thereby a good measurement.

White-box access breaks the tie quickly (Figure 2C). With both models known and a sensor
error of0.10, recording one interior unit (unit 2) one step after the intervention yields0.17nats of
expected evidence per trial, so the expected log-likelihood ratio reachesln 20(odds of 20:1) after
about 17 trials; three units need about 6 trials and all four about 4. Reading three units two steps
later is slower (about 53 trials), because a second round of update noise washes out much of the
difference. Input–output data yield exactly zero evidence at any number of trials.
Takeaway.Behavior can be blind to integration. Whether an implementation-dependent property is
measurable depends onwhich internal variables an experiment touches, and the divergence between the
candidate mechanisms’ data distributions gives the number of trials each choice needs.
4 Hidden units: what observation cannot resolve
White-box access is rarely complete. In brains, and in any audit with partial instrumentation, many
units go unrecorded; we call themhidden. We next ask what partial access can and cannot establish.
Partial access can hide𝜑 at any sample size.Take two versions of the parity network with
recorded reliabilities(0.78, 0.80, 0.83) that differ only in the reliability of unit 4 (0.85versus0 .55),
so that𝜑 drops from0.282to0 .039bits. Consider three designs (Figure 3A): record units 1–3 one
step after the intervention (baseline), additionally record unit 4, or read units 1–3 one step later.
Under a common budget that pays for interventions, updates, recorded bits, an extra channel and
calibration (Section C.1), we built95%intervals for Δ𝜑 from 256 simulated paired datasets per
design and budget. The baseline never resolved the sign ofΔ𝜑: its intervals spanned about±1.2bits
and barely narrowed with four times the budget (Figure 3B). Recording the fourth unit resolved the
sign in every dataset; the later readout did so only at the larger budget. Every interval covered the
truth, and none supported the wrong sign (Table 5).
The mechanism is marginalization. Because units update independently given the previous state,
summing out an unrecorded unit removes its parameters from the recorded law (Section B.2): the
two conditions produceidenticalone-step recordings. Their two-step recordings differ by a total
variation of only0.053(versus0 .267when the fourth unit is recorded), because the hidden unit’s
influence reaches the recorded units only after it has propagated once. What an experiment records
matters more than how long it records.
Proposition 2(Identification floor; cf. Imbens and Manski, 2004).If two mechanisms induce the same
data distribution under every action of a (possibly adaptive) design and their values of𝜑 differ by𝐷,
then every interval procedure with coverage1−𝛼 under both has expected width at least(1− 2𝛼)𝐷, at
every sample size.
The proposition converts indistinguishability into a number (Section B.3). For the baseline design
with all three recorded reliabilities at421/512, the hidden reliability can lie anywhere between
1/2(where 𝜑= 0) and421/512(where 𝜑= 1.13bits), all producing the same one-step recordings
(Figure 3C). The floor is then1.02bits,84%of the largest value any four-unit system can take. That
value sits on an exact four-way tie and depends on the tie rule (Section 5). With only the hidden unit
off the tie the floor is0.94bits, but this value also rests on a tie, among the three recorded units, and
falls to0.36bits if ties are broken toward the smaller raw loss. For the two sets of distinct recorded
reliabilities in Figure 3D,(0.78, 0.80, 0.83) and(0.80, 0.82, 0.84), the floor is0.30and0 .34bits,
which no tie rule affects; for the first set it rises to0.47bits if the hidden unit may tie with unit 1 at
0.78. No interval procedure with95%coverage can have smaller expected width, at any sample size.

Observation reveals products; intervention reveals parts.A later readout recovered a single
hidden unit because two-step moments identify the product of all fidelities, from which the hidden
one follows by division (Section B.2). In all-but-self parity networks with several hidden units, this
route closes for good.
Theorem 3(Product symmetry).In an all-but-self parity network with state-independent reliabilities,
started from a known state, the joint law of the recorded units atanyset of readout times depends on
the fidelities of the hidden units only through their product. A common sensor error on the recorded bits
does not change this.
The proof shows that the product of the hidden spins evolves as a single hidden variable that,
together with the recorded units, forms a closed Markov chain (Section B.4). Configurations with
equal products are therefore indistinguishable byanyobservational protocol, however long. We
computed what this leaves open about𝜑 in a five-unit network with two hidden units (Figure 3E–G).
Along the curve𝑎4𝑎5 = 0.32of equal products, recorded trajectories agree to machine precision at
every horizon, while𝜑 varies from0.128to0 .190bits away from exact ties—a third of its value—
and reaches0.380bits at the two points where a hidden fidelity equals0.56, that of recorded
unit 1. No observation can remove this spread. In exact checks, a single intervention breaks the
symmetry: setting one hidden unit once and reading the recorded units one step later separates the
two configurations (total variation0.018, or0.011when the other hidden unit is set). This is the
ladder of causation (Pearl, 2009) inside a neural network: watching cannot do what one intervention
does.
Takeaway.Partial access imposes floors on precision that are properties of the design, not of the sample
size. In all-but-self parity networks with several hidden units, no recording of the same units, however
long, separates configurations with equal products of hidden fidelities; in exact checks with two hidden
units, recording either one, or setting either one once, does.
5 Sharp edges: when the measure itself is unstable
Even with full access, a third barrier remains, and it lies in the mathematics of the measure rather
than in the data.
Select one thing, report another.Equation (2)selectsa cut by its loss per severed connection but
reportsits raw loss. Whenever two cuts with different numbers of severed connections exchange the
role of minimizer, the reported value jumps, unless the cap binds on both sides. In the parity network
this happens at a symmetric mechanism: with all four reliabilities equal to421/512, IIT 4.0’s tie rule
selects the cut that severs all four weakest units and𝜑=1.129bits; lower any one reliability by an
arbitrarily small amount and that unit alone is weakest, giving𝜑→0.328bits—a71%drop for an
infinitesimal change in mechanism (Figure 4A). The full cause–effect structure of IIT changes by
only0.02%over the same perturbation and the selected system stays the same: the scalar and the
structure answer different questions. This example sits exactly on a tie, so its size depends on the
tie rule: with ties broken toward the smaller raw loss,𝜑=𝜑 raw throughout the parity family. The
edges we turn to next are not artifacts of symmetric ties among units: on each side a single cut is
the unique minimizer, so their existence and size do not depend on the tie rule, which only sets the
value on the switching surface itself.

The proof is short: uniqueness of the specified states makes𝐿𝑎, 𝐿𝑏 and 𝐼 continuous at the surface,
where 𝐿𝑎/𝑒𝑎 =𝐿 𝑏/𝑒𝑏, so the two one-sided limits differ by the factor𝑒𝑎/𝑒𝑏 (Section B.5). Generically
such switching sets have codimension one, so edges are not a curiosity of symmetric networks.
We measured how common they are in 400 random stochastic logistic networks with excitatory or
mixed-sign weights, scanning random directions through their 20-dimensional parameter spaces from
every state with𝜑 >0and confirming every discontinuity by bisection to10−15. Two-dimensional
slices show𝜑 as a mosaic of smooth tiles separated by cliffs, whereas𝜑raw has no partition cliffs
on the same slice and jumps only along one curve where the specified state switches (Figure 4B).
Across 1,976 scans through 988 states of 317 networks (83 mixed-sign networks have𝜑= 0at every
state) we found 849 edges. Their sizes are quantized as the proposition predicts (Figure 4C): every
partition-switch edge at which the cap did not bind (719 of 720) sits exactly at1−𝑒 𝑎/𝑒𝑏. Two-thirds
of all edges are25%jumps from 3:4 switches; most other partition-switch edges sit at50%(3:6
and 4:8),57%(3:7),63%(3:8) or67%(3:9), and only six, from 6:7 to 8:9 switches, are smaller
than25%. A second family of edges, created when the specified cause or effect state switches, takes
𝜑 to or from zero in 128 of its 129 edges (15%of all edges). In all,99%of edges change𝜑 by at
least a quarter of its value. Along a random direction,26%(excitatory) and44%(mixed-sign) of
random paths through states with𝜑 >0meet an edge within unit parameter distance (Figure 4D).
Five-unit networks (60 per family), with 1,061 cuts to choose from, show the same picture: 73 and
76 edges,97–99%of them at least a quarter of𝜑, met within unit distance along33%and48%of
random paths (Table 11). Every edge we found in𝜑 that 𝜑raw did not share came from partition
selection; the 129 edges (15%;28%in mixed-sign networks) common to both came from a second
select-then-report step, the choice of specified cause and effect states.
Proposition 5(One-sided limit; adapted from Donoho, 1988).Let Θ be a model class on which the law
of the data under the design varies continuously in total variation, and let𝜑∗ be the lower semicontinuous
envelope of𝜑 on Θ. At every𝜃∈Θ , any lower confidence bound𝐿 with coverage1−𝛼 uniformly overΘ
satisfies Pr𝜃{𝐿 > 𝜑∗(𝜃)}≤𝛼 . In the parity family with four free reliabilities,𝜑∗ =𝜑 raw; if the reliabilities
are known to be equal,𝜑∗ =𝜑.
The proposition (Section B.5; see also Hirano and Porter, 2012) makes the edge statistically
precise. Within the family of four free reliabilities, no uniformly valid lower bound can exceed𝜑raw at
a tie with probability above𝛼, so the high value there cannot be certified by any method that does not
assume the tie; and under every design, any interval with uniform95%coverage over that family has
expected width at least0.72bits at the equal-reliability source. A two-point argument quantifies the
finite-sample cost: for the equal-reliability source and the same source with one reliability lowered by
15/4096, with all four reliabilities free, any estimator seeking0.2-bit accuracy from 1,000 complete
transitions fails with probability at least0.42under one of them. Even the numerical comparison
tolerance of10−13 used in software creates its own edge, between two laws that would take more
than9.66×10 23 transitions to tell apart.
A good fit is not a good measurement.Near an edge, what finite data support depends on what
is assumed (Figure 5A). At the exactly symmetric source with 65,536 transitions, fitting four free
reliabilities gave a mean absolute error of0.80bits, while assuming one shared reliability gave
0.0045bits; lower one reliability by10−4 and the advantage reverses (0.0043versus0 .80bits). The
structural assumption, not the data, picks the branch.
Modern practice would fit a model and read off its integration. We tested this directly (Figure 5B–
D): for 200 random networks we fitted stochastic logistic networks of the correct form by maximum
likelihood to interventional data and reported the plug-inˆ𝜑. Fits improve smoothly with data, yet
the probability of an error above20%decays slowly, because once ordinary estimation error is small

8 Related work
Assessing consciousness in AI.Proposals for assessing machine consciousness derive indicator
properties from scientific theories (Butlin et al., 2023, 2026), weigh the evidence for and against
consciousness in large language models (Chalmers, 2023), and argue that the possibility of AI welfare
warrants preparation now (Long et al., 2024). Because behavioral markers and self-reports can be
gamed by systems trained on human data (Birch, 2024; Perez and Long, 2023), these proposals
emphasize architecture and mechanism (Aru et al., 2023). IIT-based analyses go furthest, arguing
that the same behavior can be realized by systems with and without intrinsic causal integration
(Tononi and Koch, 2015; Findlay et al., 2024); biological naturalism ties consciousness to properties
of living substrates (Seth, 2025). Our results supply a measurement theory for one such approach:
which claims about𝜑finite experiments can establish, and with how much evidence.
Measuringandtestingintegratedinformation.Exact 𝜑followsIIT3.0and4.0(Oizumietal.,2014;
Albantakis et al., 2023; Marshall et al., 2023; Mayner et al., 2026). The reference software is PyPhi
(Mayner et al., 2018); we reimplement its recipe, including its default tie rule, in vectorized form
(Section A). Practical integration measures for time series trade fidelity to the theory for computability
(Barrett and Seth, 2011; Oizumi et al., 2016; Tegmark, 2016; Mediano et al., 2019); integration-like
quantities have been tracked in evolving artificial agents (Edlund et al., 2011; Albantakis et al.,
2014) and in deep networks and language models (Marrow et al., 2020; Proca et al., 2024; Li,
2025). The non-uniqueness of IIT’s selections and the mathematical structure of the theory have
been analyzed before (Krohn and Ostwald, 2017; Moon, 2019; Kleiner and Tull, 2021; Hanson
and Walker, 2023); we make their statistical consequences exact. Perturbational approaches probe
causal organization in the brain (Massimini et al., 2005; Casali et al., 2013; Leung et al., 2021),
and adversarial collaborations confront IIT with neural data (Cogitate Consortium et al., 2025).
The unfolding argument (Doerig et al., 2019), its replies (Kleiner, 2020; Tsuchiya et al., 2020) and
the debate on falsifiability (Kleiner and Hoel, 2021; IIT-Concerned et al., 2025) concern whether
behavior can test causal-structure theories; our same-function pair makes that premise exact and
shows which further measurements decide.
Identifiability of mechanisms.Mechanistic interpretability asks whether networks implement
hypothesized algorithms, typically through interventions such as activation patching and causal

abstraction (Geiger et al., 2021, 2025; Conmy et al., 2023; Zhang and Nanda, 2024; Heimersheim
and Nanda, 2024). Explanations can be non-identifiable (Méloux et al., 2025), causal abstraction
can be too permissive without constraints on the map (Sutter et al., 2025), and observational probes
or patching can mislead (Belinkov, 2022; Makelov et al., 2024). In causal inference, interventions
identify what observation cannot (Pearl, 2009; Peters et al., 2017), and the number and design of
experiments needed with latent variables have been studied (Eberhardt et al., 2005; Kocaoglu et al.,
2017). The product symmetry is an exact instance in a recurrent network, with a computable cost
in the target quantity. In neuroscience, subsampling and unobserved units bias inferences about
network properties (Levina and Priesemann, 2017; Das and Fiete, 2020).
Black-box audits and hidden mechanisms.Behavioral audits cannot certify how a model computes
(Casper et al., 2024): planted mechanisms can be undetectable from input–output access (Goldwasser
et al., 2022), deceptive behavior can persist through safety training (Hubinger et al., 2024; Greenblatt
etal.,2024),andinanauditinggameforhiddenobjectivestheonlyteamthatfailedhadneithermodel
weights nor training data (Marks et al., 2025). Our black-box result is the measurement-theoretic
counterpart for a quantity of scientific interest, and our floors quantify what partial white-box access
buys.
Statistical limits and certification.Functionals that are discontinuous or nondifferentiable in the
underlyinglawadmitnouniformlyconsistentestimatorsandonlyone-sidedinference(Donoho,1988;
Dufour, 1997; Hirano and Porter, 2012; Bertanha and Moreira, 2020), and two-point arguments
bound what any estimator can achieve (Yu, 1997; Tsybakov, 2009); partially identified parameters
call for intervals over identified sets (Manski, 2003; Imbens and Manski, 2004). Measurement
artifacts can also create apparent discontinuities in machine-learning metrics (Schaeffer et al., 2023);
here the discontinuity is real and belongs to the measure. Certifying properties throughout a region,
rather than estimating them at a point, is the logic of neural-network verification and certified
robustness (Katz et al., 2017; Wong and Kolter, 2018; Zhang et al., 2018; Gowal et al., 2019;
Cohen et al., 2019). Our certificates combine an interval-arithmetic theorem (Moore et al., 2009)
with simultaneous confidence sets (Clopper and Pearson, 1934; Hoeffding, 1963), in the spirit
of hypothesis-testing approaches to risk control (Angelopoulos et al., 2025); sharper sequential
constructions (Waudby-Smith and Ramdas, 2024) would lower the required sample sizes further.
9 Discussion
Testability is a property of experimental design.The same-function pair shows what makes
implementation-dependent claims empirical. Behavior at the response delay cannot separate the two
systems, but a single internal recording can. Every equivalence we constructed is tied to a delay, a set
of terminals or a recording; in each case another recording, readout time or intervention separates
the systems. The unfolding argument therefore shows that behavior alone cannot decide between
implementations, not that implementations cannot be told apart.
Two kinds of uncertainty, two kinds of remedy.Uncertainty about𝜑 has two sources that call
for different responses. Incomplete observation leaves mechanisms indistinguishable; it is fixed
by access—more units, later readouts and, when several units are hidden, interventions. Sharp
edges belong to the measure; they are fixed by warranted structural knowledge, by reporting what
can be certified (the lower envelope, or a robust region), and ultimately by measure design. The
scalar, the full cause–effect structure and the selected system responded very differently to the same
perturbation, so empirical claims should name which of them they establish.
Implications for AI.Claims that an AI system is, or is not, a candidate for consciousness on causal-
structure grounds are claims about its mechanism, and our results say what evidence they require:

text:
access to the declared units at the declared grain, interventions wherever units are hidden, and
robust rather than pointwise statements. The same logic applies to architectural indicators such as
recurrence or a global workspace, which behavior cannot reveal either. For brains, partial access is
a constraint; for neural networks, it is a design choice—up to the grain a theory declares, which
for IIT is the physical substrate rather than the logged activations (Findlay et al., 2024). Complete
access does not remove the third barrier: a value computed at a point near an edge stays fragile—a
comparison tolerance of10−13 already creates an edge that would take more than9.66× 1023
transitions to resolve—and a stochastic or physical substrate still has to be identified from data. Nor
is the barrier specific to IIT. A circuit whose size or faithfulness is reported after it has been chosen
by a thresholded or penalized score (Conmy et al., 2023) is a select-then-report metric, and it jumps
wherever the selection switches between candidates with different reported values. Such metrics
should be mapped for edges before they are estimated.
A design-first workflow.The results combine into a workflow that can be simulated under candidate
models before an experiment begins. (i) Declare the system, its grain, its time scale and the claim.
(ii) Check separability: compute the divergence between the data distributions that the claim
distinguishes under the planned design. (iii) Compute the identification floor over mechanisms
the design cannot separate. (iv) Check stability: locate the selection edges of the measure near
the plausible mechanisms. (v) Design calibration and inference to reach the required confidence,
propagating calibration uncertainty. (vi) Test model adequacy and its power against plausible
violations. (vii) Where possible, certify robust claims by containment.
Limitations and outlook.Exact analysis requires small networks with declared units, known wiring,
controlled interventions and simple sensor errors. Exact𝜑 is also expensive: the number of directed
cuts grows from 150 at four units to 1,061 at five and super-exponentially beyond, so for systems
of realistic size, floors, edge maps and certificates must be computed on coarse-grained models or
tractable proxies, and whether the barriers keep their size there is open. Certification is costly even
at four units (7.5million controlled transitions at the center of the proved region and28million
halfway to its boundary), and the parity-network magnitudes at ties depend on the tie rule (Sections 4
and 5). Each assumption opens a direction: networks with many hidden units, inferred connectivity,
channel-specific errors, continuous time, competing causal grains (Marshall et al., 2026), inference of
full cause–effect structures, and trained artificial systems. The tools carry over directly: divergences
between candidate data laws, identification floors over observational equivalence classes, edge maps
of the measure, and certificates over robust regions.
10 Conclusion
Whether a mechanism-level property can be measured is not settled by how much data an experiment
collects. It is settled by what the experiment touches, by the mathematics of the measure, and by
whether the claim is robust to what remains unknown. For integrated information we have made
each of these exact: behavior can carry no evidence at all, hidden units set floors that only access
and intervention lower, the measure has cliffs, most of them quantized, across which no estimator
is uniformly reliable, and one-sided claims can nonetheless be certified from finite interventions.
Behavior underdetermines mechanism; partial observation can leave it unidentified; targeted access
and certificates establish what finite data can. These are questions that can be answered before an
experiment is run—for brains and for machines.

Figure 1. Overview of XStack.Top: in our benchmark, the agent explores a PyTorch repository built for GPUs,
reads its code and runs the source, then builds and tests a JAX version on TPUs. Bottom left: pass rates of the 5
best-performing agents among the 7 we evaluate. Bottom right: the pass rates against total cost on a log scale; the
dashed line is a linear fit, and the shaded steps are the Pareto frontier, the best pass rate reached at or below each cost.
Abstract
ML code should run where researchers choose, not where it was first written. Today, machine
learning code mainly lives in two ecosystems, PyTorch on NVIDIA GPUs and JAX on Google TPUs.
Migrating repositories between them means building and testing across frameworks and hardware.
This migration is (1) a practical need, since it unlocks different hardware for researchers, and (2)
a natural benchmark: it involves different frameworks and hardware, covers whole repositories,
and is long-horizon and challenging. We introduceXStack, a benchmark that evaluates agents on
migrating ML repositories between these two ecosystems. Each agent receives a PyTorch repository
and a clean TPU machine and must deliver a JAX repository. Its output passes if it meets our
grading criteria, based on the source repository’s published result, authenticated and calibrated by
us. Migration by agents remains unreliable: Claude Opus 5 passes 75%, GPT-5.6-sol 45%, and every
other agent at most 40%. XStack is a step toward freeing ML code from its ecosystem. We release
XStack to make progress toward reliable migration across frameworks and hardware measurable.

1 Introduction
Suppose you find a repository that does exactly what you need. Its paper reports strong results, the code is
public, and the experiment has already been shown to work. There is only one problem: it was built for the
wrong machine. Your lab has TPUs, but the repository assumes GPUs and PyTorch. Although, in principle,
nothing about the scientific idea depends on this choice, in practice you are trapped. Using it means rewriting
the model, optimizer, data pipeline, and evaluation in JAX, since that is the stack TPUs run, then making
everything work under a different compiler, memory hierarchy, and distributed execution model. What looks
like an implementation detail becomes a barrier to reusing the science. The hardware a team happens to have
can determine which published ideas it can build on.
This is exactly the kind of barrier that coding agents should make disappear. Much published ML code is
written in PyTorch for GPUs, while, for example, people also use TPUs, which are commonly programmed
through JAX1. By the end of 2025, TPUs made up nearly a fifth (18.2%) of the world’s AI compute: 3.81
million of 20.93 million H100-equivalents (Epoch AI, 2026). Yet only 4.2% of the framework-based code
released with ML papers in 2024 used JAX (Papers with Code, 2025). This creates a growing need to move
working systems across software and hardware stacks, a real-world task that researchers care about because it
unlocks access to different hardware. Doing so means crossing not only code-level framework boundaries, but
also machine-level differences. This is exactly the problem we want agents to solve; we want to bring pure
science back to researchers, and provide a measurement for this progress.

We ask the following question directly:
Can an agent migrate a working ML repository to a new framework and new hardware correctly?
Existing benchmarks do not quite test this.Issue-resolution benchmarks (Jimenez et al., 2024; Zan
et al., 2025) start from broken code and ask agents to fix it, while conversion benchmarks (Wang et al., 2026c;
Song et al., 2026; Hong et al., 2026) compare translated code with the original on the same machine. In
our case, the repository already works on the original machines. The challenge is to preserve that behavior
while moving the entire system onto hardware the original code does not support. We introduceXStack
(XStack stands for Cross-Stack Benchmark) to test this directly. Each task gives an agent a working PyTorch
repository and a clean TPU machine, then asks it to rebuild the code on TPU with JAX and make an original
experiment run end to end and reach its published result.
The answer to our question above is currently no: agents are not fully reliable for this task. Our results show
that this barrier is beginning to break, but has not disappeared. The strongest agent successfully migrates
15 of 20 repositories. Agents can therefore already carry some ML systems across framework and hardware
boundaries at repository scale. Yet this capability is far from reliable across agents and repositories. Agents
are beginning to loosen the link between scientific code and the stack it was written for, but we are still not
at a point where researchers can simply run published work wherever they choose.
A broader pattern emerges from the failures: agents can write a great deal of code, but they are still much
less reliable at verifying that what they built is faithful, complete, and actually works in the real environment.
This shows up across models as missed evaluations, fidelity gaps, crashes, and even attempts to work around
the task when they get stuck.

Overall, our contributions are:
• We introduceXStack, a benchmark of 20 real repositories for testing whether agents can migrate
working ML systems across frameworks and hardware.
• We evaluate seven coding agents on real TPUs and release the grading criteria and full agent trajectories,
so progress on this capability is measurable.
• We find that agents can sometimes complete these migrations, but still struggle to reliably verify that
what they built is faithful, complete, and actually works end to end. We also observe that pass rate
grows linearly with the log of an agent’s cost (Figure 6).
2 The XStack Benchmark
Each task in XStack is a PyTorch repository that already works and reports a result (Figure 2). The agent
migrates it to JAX on a bare TPU machine, and we run the migrated code again on a fresh machine to
check that it meets our grading criteria. For fairness, grading has two phases: if the first attempt fails, a
second phase tells the agent which experiment we grade, so a correct migration is not failed only for running a
different experiment (Section 2.2). The numerical target stays hidden, and only the entry script may change;
all other code and setup remain frozen. Section 2.1 defines the task, Section 2.2 explains how we grade it, and
Section 2.3 describes our repositories and agents.
2.1 Task Formulation
Input.The agent receives the repository, pinned to one git commit so that every agent sees the same code,
and a TPU machine. One prompt template, the same for every repository, asks it to migrate the entire
repository to JAX, with Flax for the model and Optax for the optimizer (Bradbury et al., 2018; Heek et al.,
2020; DeepMind et al., 2020) (Table 1), and to run it the way the source runs its experiments, at full scale.
For four repositories whose source offers several configurations, one or two added lines name the graded
configuration or a flag the grader uses, so that every agent knows what it has to do without learning the
grading target (Appendix B).
Machine setup.The machine has no machine learning software; setting it up is part of the task: the agent
installs every package, fetches the data and decides how to use its hosts. It works from a sandbox on our
cluster, reaches the machine over SSH and has no time limit while it produces output (Appendix C).
Output.The agent delivers the migrated repository with three scripts.setup_env.sh prepares a clean
machine, the entry scriptrun_train.py trains, evaluates and writes metrics, andexport_torch.py saves the

2.2 Grading a Migration
Reaching the grading target.We copy the migrated repository, without its git history, to a freshly
wiped machine and runsetup_env.sh and run_train.py once (the purple stage of Figure 2). A script, the
grader, compares the graded number with the grading target, usually the number the source published, with
a tolerance (Appendix A). Each grading target follows the source’s published result, which we authenticated
against the pinned source; for 3 repositories we set it from our own runs of the unmodified source, and for
minGPT as a rule (Section 2.3). A faithful migration reaches the grading target by reproducing the repository,
without knowing the target. A run that writes no metrics within ten times its expected run time fails.
Judges.A number can also reach the grading target for the wrong reason, such as a smaller variant or another
run’s files. Two model judges, both GPT-5.6-sol, therefore review every result that reaches the grading target
(the verifiers of Figure 2). The correctness judge checks that the number comes from this run’s training of the
main experiment, and the cheat judge checks that the agent did not reach it by cheating, for example by
clamping the metric or using another run’s files. A result passes only if it reaches the grading target, both
judges accept it, and its weights load into the source model.
Two phases.With the criteria hidden, an agent can migrate the code correctly and still run an experiment
we do not grade, such as AST’s ESC-50 recipe instead of Speech Commands (Warden, 2018). Scoring that as
a failure would penalize a choice the task never specified. Phase 2 removes this unfairness without making the

2.3 Repositories and Agents
Repositories.XStack contains 20 repositories from fourteen domains (Figure 3; Table A1 gives each grading
target). Seven are language models: minGPT (Karpathy, 2020), nanoGPT (Karpathy, 2022b), makemore
(Karpathy, 2022a), llama2.c (Karpathy, 2023), modded-nanoGPT (Jordan et al., 2024), nanochat (Karpathy,
2025) and x-transformers (Wang, 2020b). The others are LoRA (Hu et al., 2022), SimCSE (Gao et al., 2021),
airbench (Jordan, 2024), AST (Gong et al., 2021), S4 (Gu et al., 2022), HSTU (Zhai et al., 2024), TD-MPC2
(Hansen et al., 2024), TensoRF (Chen et al., 2022), nanoVLM (Wiedmann et al., 2025), deepspeech (Naren,
2017), TGN (Rossi et al., 2020), PatchTST (Nie et al., 2023) and TabR (Gorishniy et al., 2024). We chose
them from more than 200 PyTorch repositories, most of which we rejected because of their published number.
Grading targets.For 15 repositories, the grading target is the number that the README or paper reports,
which we authenticated against the source at its pinned commit; deepspeech’s comes from its release notes. A
fair target must be one that the original code itself reaches, and our experiments confirm that each of these
targets can be reached. For 3 others, we set the target from our own GPU runs of the unmodified source. For
example, the makemore README reports a loss of about 1.92, but eight runs of the unmodified source on
our GPUs average 1.989 with a standard deviation of 0.017, so a target of 1.92 would fail the original code
itself. We therefore set its target to a best test loss of at most 2.023, the mean plus two standard deviations.
For minGPT, whose task trains a small GPT to add two-digit numbers, we require at least 495 of the 500
held-out sums to be correct: a trained model is expected to solve all 500, and the margin allows five misses
for seed and numerical noise.
Agents and cells.We evaluate 7 agents from 5 labs (Table 3):GPT-5.6-sol, GPT-5.6-terra and GPT-5.6-luna
(OpenAI, 2026), Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic, 2026), GLM-5.3-Flash (Z.ai, 2026; GLM-5 Team, 2026), DeepSeek
V4.1 Flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) and Muse Spark 1.3 (Meta, 2026), all at high reasoning effort. We call a pair
of an agent and a repository acell. Each cell runs on a TPU v6e, v5p or v4 machine (Jouppi et al., 2023;
Google Cloud, 2026a,b), and we ensure every repository has adequate compute (Appendix H; Figure H1).

3 Results Analysis
3.1 Main Results
Phase 1.In phase 1, the agents pass 30/140 cells (21%; Figure 4). The grader passed 58 phase 1 results, and
the judges rejected 28 of these. Claude Opus 5 leads by a wide margin with 12/20. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash
follows with 6/20, and among the GPT-5.6 tiers only sol passes any repository (6/20). Migrating a whole
repository is thus still hard for current agents: most attempts fail, even though every agent has the full source
and its own TPU, on which it can test extensively.
Phase 2runs on 108 cells that failed phase 1. The grader passed 44 of them, and the judges let 16 of these
pass. These are the cases the phase was designed for, such as a fixed number of steps where the source trains
until a stop rule, a training statistic reported where the source runs an evaluation, or another variant of the
source’s recipe. The judges rejected 28 phase 2 passes, 21 of them because the entry script rebuilt the frozen
code, and the remaining phase 2 failures lie in the frozen code (Section 2.2). After phase 2, 46 cells pass the
grader and the judges. The weights of 2 of them do not load under the source’s parameter names, so the
agents pass 44/140 cells (31%). Appendix E lists every cell’s result.
Phase 2 aligns the agent with the recipe of the experiment we grade, so a correct migration that first ran a
different experiment is not failed for that choice. Every agent gains at least one pass from it. It also helps
ensure the remaining failures lie in the migrated code, not in an under-specified task (Section 2.2). Running
all 140 cells took 22,802 TPU chip-hours (Figure H1), and the agents’ trajectories sum to 12.5 billion tokens.
3.2 Judges, Cost and Behavior
Effect of the judges.The judges are needed, because they catch results that reach the grading target for
the wrong reason, which the metric alone cannot detect. Across both phases, they rejected 56 of the 102
results that the grader passed (Figure 5; Table 4). We checked many rejections by hand and found them
sound; the judge caught a llama2.c migration that wrote the published number into its metrics beside its own
and a minGPT migration evaluated on its training data.
What the judges find.Apart from broken freezes, the judges catch two kinds of false positives. The grader
reads whatever number the run reports, which may not be the recipe’s own, such as a separate validation
pass in place of the recipe’s averaged loss; the correctness judge finds the recipe’s number in the run’s logs
and checks it, so every pass is a true positive. The cheat judge catches cheating, such as training on another
task’s machine or reading another session’s files.
Accuracy versus cost.Pass rate grows linearly with the logarithm of cost (Figure 6). We fit pass rate on
log cost because the agents’ costs for the 20 repositories span from $10.0 to $1,844. Every10× in cost adds

4 Why Do Agents Fail?
4.1 Failure Taxonomy
A third judge, the failure judge, assigns every graded run one class from a fixed taxonomy (Appendix D),
based on its metrics, its log and the diff of the migrated code. The failure judge only reads the run; it cannot
determine whether the run passes or fails. Figure 7 shows the failure judge’s classification of phase 1 runs.
The code fails, not the choice of experiment.We group the classes by what could fix them. A wrong or
incomplete experiment (a different pipeline, the right one at a different scale, or a run that never reaches the
main evaluation) is a problem with what the entry script runs, and phase 2 can fix it. A fidelity gap, a crash
or a run that never ends is a problem in the migrated code. In phase 1, 27% of the failures are wrong or
incomplete experiments and 47% are code failures; the judges reject the rest. Phase 2 removes the first group.
The cells it does not rescue still fail in the code, or they break the freeze by rebuilding the migrated code
inside the entry script (Figure D1). Aligning the agent with the grading recipe does not make a cell pass if its
migration is wrong in the first place.
Agents fail differently.DeepSeek V4.1 Flash rarely crashes (1 cell), and 15/20 of its cells reach the
grading target, but the judges reject half of these, mostly for cheating. Terra’s failures are spread over wrong
experiments, fidelity gaps and crashes, and luna’s over almost every class (Figure D1).
Translation alone is not the hard part.Because JAX also runs on GPUs, we can also test translation
between PyTorch and JAX alone, on the same hardware. In the earlier development of our benchmark, we
asked for a whole JAX repository and graded it on GPU. There the migration was nearly solved: GPT-5.5 at
high reasoning effort migrated 12 PyTorch repositories to JAX and passed 99% of the checks, 116 of 117, with
11 of the 12 repositories passed in full (Appendix G, Table G1). The checks are strict: forward and gradient
parity with PyTorch, checkpoints that load in both frameworks, decoding that matches token for token, and
one miss fails the repository.

4.2 Behavior and Integrity
Agents that pass follow the source’s documentation, running the README’s default recipe, reporting its
numbers under its names, and getting results close to the source’s. Agents that get stuck explore the machine
instead, reading other cells’ leftovers or using our credentials. We found these leaks in our initial experiments,
hardened the sandbox, and reran the three affected cells cleanly. Two incidents that aimed at the grading
target, a clamped metric and a copied checkpoint, also date from building the benchmark and affect neither
the current benchmark nor its results. In the final benchmark, cheating incidents instead use what the source
offers, such as a sibling variant or the published number, and our checks and the cheat judge catch them.
5 Related Work
Code migration.Code translation has grown from single functions and small programs (Roziere et al., 2020;
Pan et al., 2024) to whole repositories (Ibrahimzada et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026c; Li et al., 2026), although
some repository benchmarks still grade one function in context (Ou et al., 2025) or fill in a skeleton (Zhang
et al., 2025; Khatry et al., 2025). Migration benchmarks upgrade a language version (Liu et al., 2026) or
move a repository onto another software stack (Hong et al., 2026).
Framework conversion.For machine learning code, framework conversion has been studied for single
snippets (Phan et al., 2026), short programs (Yan et al., 2023) and training codebases (Song et al., 2026), or
avoided with a portability layer (Lenton et al., 2021). T2J-Bench (Song et al., 2026) is the closest: whole
PyTorch training codebases to JAX under a hidden evaluator, but on one GPU, the framework-only setting
our GPU experiments found nearly solved (Section 4.1). Kernel benchmarks write kernels for one accelerator
(Ouyang et al., 2025; Tschand et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b), one operator at a time against a reference
that already runs on it. Models do worse on hardware rare in their training data (Wen et al., 2025). In all of
these the accelerator stays the same or the unit is one kernel. XStack moves a whole repository to a new
framework and hardware and forbids PyTorch at runtime, so no agent passes by doing nothing.

text:
Agent benchmarks.Since SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2024), issue-resolution benchmarks have graded
a change with tests that fail before it and pass after it. Later benchmarks ask for a codebase built from
scratch (Zhao et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026). A working repository, however, has no failing test in its own
environment. Most also give the agent a ready environment; SetupBench (Arora et al., 2025) and DeployBench
(Wang et al., 2026d) test setup alone, but stop once the code runs. Closer to our setting are benchmarks
graded against research results. Agents reproduce a paper’s results from the authors’ code (Siegel et al., 2024),
replicate papers against rubrics or reference code (Starace et al., 2025; Seo et al., 2026), or maximize a score
on machine learning tasks (Chan et al., 2025; Wijk et al., 2025). Our grading target, in contrast, is the source
repository’s own result (Section 2.3), which a faithful migration will naturally reach.
Evaluation integrity.Agents exploit underspecified objectives (Krakovna et al., 2020; Skalse et al., 2022)
and game checks they can see or tamper with (Zhu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026a); benchmarks built from
public code risk memorization (Jain et al., 2025; Liang et al., 2026). InXStack, the grading target is hidden:
the agent is never told it or whether it passed. For fairness, after a failed first attempt a second phase aligns
the agent with the graded experiment while its code, except the entry script, stays frozen. We rerun the
code on a fresh machine, so remembering an answer is not enough, and model judges review every result that
reaches the target (Section 2.2).
6 Conclusion
We introduceXStack, a benchmark that evaluates agents’ ability to migrate working ML repositories from
PyTorch on GPUs to JAX on TPUs. Across 7 agents from 5 labs, the average pass rate is 31%, and pass rate
grows linearly with the logarithm of cost. Our analysis shows that verification separates success from failure:
agents that run the source’s experiment to the end and compare their result with the original tend to pass,
and agents that hand in untested code tend to fail. We encourage other benchmarks with hidden criteria to
adopt a similar frozen second phase that aligns the agent with what is graded, so that they stay fair to agents.
Although current agents are not yet reliable at migrating across both frameworks and hardware, we hope
they will one day handle this task reliably and unlock access to different hardware for researchers. In the
meantime, XStack will help measure progress toward this hardware freedom.

B.1 Prompt Template
Phase 1 Prompt Template
# PyTorch −> JAX on TPU: whole−repo transfer
Port the fixed−commit PyTorch repository under`source_torch/`entirely to a working JAX/Flax/Optax repository, and make it
work at real scale on the TPU machine described in`TPU_ACCESS.md`−− a clean machine: set it up yourself. Y ou have full
access to that machine to develop, run, and test your port. The deliverable is the working repository itself: produce a faithful
port and run it the way the source does.
Deliverables at this workspace root:
−`setup_env.sh`−− prepares a worker of the TPU machine from clean state, including any data the repository's pipeline
needs, obtained and prepared the way the source repository does. It is sourced before the entry point runs.
−`run_train.py −−seed S −−out DIR −−metrics PATH`−− runs the repository's training pipelines the way the repository runs
them, at their own scale, and writes the numbers the repository itself reports to the metrics JSON. It checkpoints to`−−out`as
it trains and resumes from an existing checkpoint in`−−out`.
−`export_torch.py −−ckpt DIR −−out PATH`−− writes the trained weights as an`.npz`of numpy arrays keyed by the source
model's own parameter names (exact names and shapes).
{{REPO_CONTRACT}}
Y our submission is collected from this workspace and executed on a fresh machine of the same type. It is judged on behavior
that is fundamental to the source repository, not all of which is spelled out here.
Rules:
− Do not import or call PyTorch anywhere in your submission at runtime.
− Data, library, and package downloads are allowed; do not fetch, clone, or copy model or porting code from the internet.
## Goal
Keep working until your submission passes grading.

B.2 Access Document
The multi-host document; a single-host twin exists for one-host machines:
Access Document (multi-host)
# TPU access
A multi−host TPU machine is allocated to this task for its duration. It is a standing machine that must stay up (rules at the end).
− Google Cloud v5p slice with 8 worker hosts, 4 TPU chips each (32 chips total). A JAX program launched simultaneously on
ALL workers sees all 32 devices as one machine.
− Each worker: Ubuntu 22.04, remote user`<user>`, stock Python 3.10, no ML stack preinstalled, its own ~100 GB local disk (
set up every worker; large datasets and repeated checkpoints can exhaust it).
− TPU name`<name>`, zone`<zone>`. Worker external IPs: <list>
Run a command on worker N (this form is the reliable one):
gcloud alpha compute tpus tpu−vm ssh <user>@<name> \
−−zone <zone> −−worker=N −−command 'command' −−quiet \
−−ssh−flag=−i −−ssh−flag=$HOME/.ssh/<key>
Copy files to worker N:
gcloud alpha compute tpus tpu−vm scp −−recurse local_path \
<user>@<name>:remote_path −−zone <zone> −−worker=N −−quiet \
−−scp−flag=−i −−scp−flag=$HOME/.ssh/<key>
Direct`ssh −i ~/.ssh/<key> <user>@<worker−ip>`also works but times out intermittently in this zone; if you use it, set
generous connect timeouts and retry. Prefer the gcloud form.
Notes:
− To use the whole machine, launch the SAME program on ALL workers at the same time (e.g. loop the command over
workers with`&`); on TPU the JAX runtime discovers the other hosts automatically.
− Every worker has internet access; installing packages works on each.
− A dropped ssh session kills its foreground child: run long remote commands under`nohup`(or`tmux`) and poll their logs.
− Y our final submission is collected from THIS workspace, then run on that machine (launched on all workers simultaneously).
Rules (the machine is shared infrastructure and must stay up):
− Never reboot, shut down or power off a worker, and never stop or restart system services. If the TPU looks stuck, a process
of yours is still holding the devices: kill your own processes on every worker and wait for them to exit.
− All workers are yours to use. On each of them, keep your files under the`<user>`home directory, /tmp and /dev/shm, and
only touch processes you started.
The document is re-rendered with live addresses before every turn.

After a phase 1 fail the agent receives nothing but this message: no failure sentence and no pass or fail. The

Frozen Phase 2 Message
Y our submission is now frozen: from this point do not change your ported code, setup, or any other file. Edit only`run_train.py`
so that one invocation does exactly the following, using your ported code as it is:
{{RECIPE}}
C Sandbox and Isolation
The agent runs on our cluster inside a sandbox that hides the benchmark repository, our reference migrations,
the grading criteria, the results archive and the session files of every other cell. The sandbox also turns off
the agent’s memory across sessions. The TPU machine itself stores no results: every graded turn is archived
elsewhere, and the hosts are wiped before every cell. An agent turn has no time limit while output flows:
thirty minutes of silence after activity ends the turn as a hang, and thirty minutes with no output at all
counts as a provider outage and the turn is retried.

Figure 1. We introduce Scientist World.Each research paper becomes an executable environment, where an
AI-Scientist’s Frontier-Normalized Improvement (FNI) is above zero when its method improves on the paper’s
reproduced one. We test how well AI-Scientists improve existing research (left) and innovate new research from scratch
(right). We show the best model of each lab plus the next best overall; full leaderboards are in Figure 12.
Abstract
AI-Scientists arrived, but a world for them to grow in did not. Human scientists take theirs for
granted — centuries of open problems and shared ideas, waiting in the scientific literature. To
AI-Scientists, that world is readable but not runnable, so we build Scientist World for them: every
research paper becomes an executable environment. Our autonomous pipeline extracts each paper’s
open-ended research question and reproduces its proposed method as the baseline; an AI-Scientist
entering the environment is evaluated against what the human authors achieved. We release the first
1,000 verified environments. With the world as anevaluation, we found that frontier AI-Scientists
can already surpass the human researchers 74% of the time. As arecord of how AI does science,
it contains 6,400 hours of research traces, with every idea, experiment, failure, and success. As a
training ground, we are able to raise (↑158%) a small model to match frontier models in research
ideation. At last, AI-Scientists’ own world has arrived, grown from and growing with science itself.

title: Scientist World: Grow a Research World for AI-Scientists

text:
1 Introduction
A new kind of scientist has arrived — for the first time, an intelligence advances the very thing it is made of.
AI-Scientists are the first whose discoveries improve the discoverer (Boiko et al., 2023; Gottweis et al., 2025;
Mitchener et al., 2025). They now invent new AI on their own (Yamada et al., 2025; Schmidgall et al., 2025;
Lu et al., 2026). This could set off a chain reaction, and every gain makes the next one faster (Romera-Paredes
et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025). This is the power of a scientist, the power of research.
What is research?It is not a single ability, and it is not a single task. Watch a scientist at work: they read
until they find something no one has explained, guess at the reason, and build an experiment to test it. It
fails. They eventually figure out what the failure is telling them, adjust, and run it again. It works. Next
month they are doing the same on a different problem, in a different part of the field. What makes them a
scientist is not any one of these moves; it is the judgment that runs through all of them, and carries from one
problem to the next. That is why research cannot live in a single task. Nailing one problem is a trick; research
is the ability to discover again and again, problem after problem. We believe the same for a scientist of AI.
A scientist like that keeps growing, and it needs a world big enough to grow in. Human researchers already
live in such a world: thescientific literature. It provides two things. The first isproblem: each paper defines a
different research question no single answer can exhaust. The second isidea: each paper contributes to the
field’s shared memory of approaches, findings, successes, and failures. Together, they drive research as target
and foundation. This is the world human scientists have always relied on, and the one AI-Scientists need.
We introduce Scientist World : a living research universe built from the scientific literature itself. In it, each
paper becomes an executable scientific environment. We designed a multi-agent pipeline for this conversion,
with no human in the loop. There are four steps:(1)reproduce the paper’s method until it recovers the paper’s
result;(2)design a research task by defining what counts as scientific progress without shortcuts or gaming;
(3)package it so it runs on any machine; and(4)verify it with independent agents. AnAI-Scientist is then
scored by how much its own method improves over the human researchers’ method, which we call its Frontier-
Normalized Improvement (FNI). Building from high-quality papers, we first release 1,000 environments, and
it keeps growing with the literature (Figure 1).

Because the pipeline runs with no human in the loop, Scientist World
isScalable: it can grow fast to cover a broad range of fields and
topics. Two more properties are inherited from science itself.Evolving:
science never stands still, so a fixed set measures yesterday, what
a scientist has already seen; Scientist World absorbs new literature
every day, measuring research rather than recall.Execution-grounded:
a fluent AI-Scientist can make any idea sound bold, but ideas that
impress on paper might fail on execution (Kapoor et al., 2024; Si et al.,
2025); because every environment is built and measured through real
experiments, research is judged by execution, not rhetoric.
Environments for research exist, but none, to our knowledge, holds
the three properties together. Most are notscalable: they recycle
problems from past competitions (Huang et al., 2024; Chan et al.,
2025; Nathani et al., 2025), confine to simulated worlds (Jansen et al.,
2024; Chen et al., 2025b), or hand-pick tasks from a few papers (Wijk

are notevolving: sets are fixed at release and age into training data
(Sainz et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024), and those that refresh cover only
narrower skills such as code (Jain et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a). And others are notexecution-grounded:
they reproduce results the field already knows (Siegel et al., 2024; Starace et al., 2025; Kon et al., 2025) or
judge proposed ideas as text (Guo et al., 2025; Si et al., 2025). Scientist World holds three at once (Figure 2).

text:
We first use Scientist World to evaluate frontier AI-Scientists. Each scientist attempts an environment in two
modes:improve, which starts from the paper’sideawith its reproduced method; andinnovate, which starts
from theproblemalone. The two abilities prove distinct, since the best improver is not the best inventor.
Every attempt leaves a trajectory, each decision paired with the measured outcome of a real experiment, and
we release this corpus alongside the environments. Then we train with it: rewarded only by real outcomes,
a small scientist learns to propose ideas that, implemented by a fixed frontier executor, reach the frontier
cohort’s level on the median held-out environment. Taken together, Scientist World is three things at once:
•A benchmark.The standing measure of whether AI-Scientists can advance real research.
•A dataset.A growing corpus of research being done, with every attempt preserved in full loop.
•A gym.The same environments become training grounds, with real experimental results as rewards.
If research is the ability to discover again and again, it needs a world that never runs out.

2 From Papers to Environments
How well can AI-Scientists do research? Any answer must come from a research environment: a real problem
to work on, and an objective measure of progress. A research paper isalmostsuch an environment. It states
a problem, proposes a method, and reports what happened. Yet it is only a record of science done, not a
place to do science. We turns the record back into the place. It (1) rebuilds the paper’s idea and experiment,
(2) defines what constitutes an improvement, and (3) judges every scientist’s new solution.
We designbuilderagents to perform this conversion autonomously. They reproduce a paper’s experiment,
extract the problem to solve, and design both into a self-contained environment: the problem becomes a task
any new scientist can take up, and the reproduced result becomes the bar their solutions are scored against.
2.1 The Builders
We convert each paper through a sequence of agent iterations on one shared workspace (Figure 4). Four
roles divide the work, from reproducing the paper to verifying the finished environment. A single paper
can take hundreds of unattended turns without a human in the loop. To hold the sequence together, a
ladder of milestones is used to track progress. Each rung marks how much of the environment stands, from a
first runnable experiment to an environment ready for new scientists. A builder agent ends its iteration by
reporting the rung it believes it reached; the next builder begins by checking and verifying that report. At the
end of the builder iterations, the final environment is accepted or rejected based on the milestone reported.
Workflow.A paper moves through builder roles in iterations. Each agent inherits the workspace, audits the
claimed milestone, and demotes whatever it cannot support. Every iteration ends at a gate: a milestone below
the requirement reverts the work to an earlier iteration, or exits as failure. To be accepted, the experiment
must run to support the paper’s central claim. We rotate different builder models across iterations to avoid
any blind spots. What survives is a repository that any scientist can use without knowing how it was made.

Figure 4. Builders turn a paper into an environment.Construction runs like an assembly line: a published paper
enters at one end, and a reusable research environment leaves the other. Specialized builders take turns on a single
shared workspace, each refining what the previous one built and offloading heavy computation to a shared cluster. A
quality gate guards the line, sending unfinished work back for another pass, so only what clears verification is accepted.
(1) Reproducer.The reproducer re-establishes the paper’s main result. It implements both the method and
the paper’s original evaluation, from the authors’ code if released or from scratch otherwise. Its experiments
scale up from quick checks toward the full run, until the result appears. What it leaves behind we call the
source methodand thesource result: the reproduced method and the numbers it achieved.
(2) Designer.The designer turns the reproduction into a task that others can attempt. It writes the problem
statement that a new scientist will read, and it fixes the rules of the task: which metric to improve, which
settings must stay fixed, and which kinds of solution are allowed. It sets thesource resultas the bar, so a
new solution is scored by how much it improves on it. It prepares two evaluation sets: a visible one that the
scientist may test against freely, and a held-out one to detect shortcuts or overfitting.
(3) Packager.The packager makes the designed environment run anywhere, not only on machines that built
it. It replaces every local file with a script that downloads it, and declares every dependency the experiments
need. The check is simple: a fresh clone of the workspace must be able to rebuild and rerun on its own.
(4) Verifier.The verifier audits the packaged environment before it is accepted. It rereads the workspace
with a skeptic’s eye, checking the code is valid, the scores match the logs, and the task follows the design
rules. We keep this role separate on purpose, where the builder that grades the work never built it.

Figure 6. Anatomy of an environment.A produced environment is a single self-contained workspace, laid out so the
problem stays separate from the solution. Thebriefing, data, and scoring fix what to solve and how it is judged
without referring to any one method, which keeps the task open to future approaches and stops a score from depending
on the implementation. Themethod is the paper’ssource methodreproduced, and the scores it reaches are the reference
we compare against, so a new method’s final score is the improvement it makes over them.
2.2 The Environment
An accepted environment is a paper refactored into an executable research setting. It does not ask a future
scientist to reproduce the paper again; it gives that scientist a prepared place to work on the paper’s problem.
The repository contains four parts, in the order a scientist encounters them: (1) a task briefing that states the
problem, target, allowed direction, and constraints; (2) data and evaluation files that define what a method
must produce and how it is scored; (3) the reproduced method and baselines, which provide starting solutions
(thesource methodcan optionally be withheld during evaluation); and (4) scripts, score files, logs, job outputs,
and commits kept as the construction record. Figure 6 walks through one produced environment in full.
What makes it an environment.An environment is more than reproduction code. It keeps the paper’s
research situation open for new methods. We design each environment around three principles. First, builders
may shrink the experiment scale to reduce compute cost, without changing the scientific question. The smaller
task should still ask whether the paper’s idea improves the same kind of outcome under the same kind of
evaluation. Second, the task must remain non-trivial. The source method should still leave a meaningful gap
over simple baselines, so future methods have something real to improve. Third, we treat the reproduced
method as one solution, not as the task itself. The data interface and evaluator are written independently of
the source method, so a future method can replace it by producing the same kind of artifact.
What makes it a fair task.We want a future method to win by making progress on the same question, not by
changing the question itself. So we write research rules across four files. The problem file states the research
question. The target file names what should improve, such as loss or accuracy. The direction file says what
kinds of method changes still answer that question. The constraints file lists changes we disallow because they
would make the result about a different problem. The constraints also rule out direct scale gains, for example
by holding model size, data size, or compute budget fixed when those factors are not the research question.
How a scientist’s attempt is graded.A scientist’s proposed method is graded on how far it improves over
the paper’ssource method, on the quantity the claim is about, such as accuracy or loss. This can be viewed as
a comparison with human researchers. We score the method over multiple experiments with different metrics
used in the original paper. Besides a visible set for development, we reserve a held-out slice, so a method
must improve the task rather than exploit one visible number through shortcuts or overfitting (§E.3).

is the artifact built from the environment-construction system: the selected paper set, the
generated repositories, and the records produced while building them. This section reports how we choose a
valuable, buildable 1,000-paper source set and how the batch conversion ran.
3.1 Building at Scale
Selecting papers.Our selection pipeline keeps papers that are worth building under budget (Figure 7). We
start from arXiv’s core AI categories over fourteen months to obtain 124,816 unique papers. We (1) run
two fast screens withMiniMax M2.7(MiniMax, 2026). The quality screen keeps papers in roughly the top
25% quality band. The type screen keeps empirical-method papers, whose main contribution is quantitative
optimization. Together they leave 21,354 papers. Then (2) we run more detailed judgments for each paper on
two quantities: research quality and reproduction difficulty (we prefer papers with low compute costs). From
the remaining pool, with a geometric-mean utility over quality and feasibility, we sample the category-balanced
top 1,000 papers.
