3.2 The Built World
Composition.We first release 1,000 environments spread across eight areas (Figure 8). A scientist therefore
meets problems of many kinds, not one narrow family. A typical environment is substantial, closer to a small
research project than a single script (Table 2). Because most carry several experiments rather than a single
headline result, a later method has multiple quantities to improve rather than one number to chase.
Quality.Every environment is built without a human in the loop, so we do not take any single builder’s word
for its quality. Four checks stand behind an accepted environment, one per row of Table 3:
• Reproduction fidelity.The reproduced source method’s numbers are checked against the paper’s
reported results within a small margin, across every experiment and metric used by the environment;
the few exceptions are accepted only with documented justification.
• Baseline separation.Where a paper provides baselines, we reimplement them and require the reproduced
source method to outperform them, preserving a real gap for future methods to close; the rate in Table 3
counts all 1,000 environments, including those without a reimplementable baseline.
•Iterative cross-checking.Each builder audits the previous milestone claim and demotes whatever the
workspace cannot support. A demotion rolls the workflow back to the previous iteration; construction
then resumes from that checkpoint until it passes the later checks without further reversion.
• Independent verification.The final environment must pass a verifier that did not participate in
construction. Every released environment satisfies this final check.
Example.Figure 9 shows one environment end to end. The paper’s question survives intact, whether a
transformer can train without normalization, while its experiment shrinks to ImageNet-50 so attempts fit a
bounded budget. The constraint is what keeps the task honest: the same model scale, data, and pretraining
as the source method, so any gain must come from the method itself. Half of every evaluation stays hidden,
so the score reflects what generalizes rather than what was tuned against the visible half.

4 Scientists in the World
4.1 Benchmark
We now use the environments to evaluate AI-Scientists. Running every model on all 1,000 environments is too
costly to repeat, so we evaluate on a fixed cohort of ten lower-compute environments. Each model attempts
every environment under the same compute budget, in two modes:
•Improve mode.The model receives the reproduced source method and tries to improve its result.
• Innovate mode.The model receives no source code and must design a method from scratch. We ensure
there is no leakage of the paper’s original solution.
Each attempt is evaluated on both the visible and held-out splits, with the final FNI score averaged across the
two. Zero FNI matches the reproduced source method, while a positive FNI improves on it. Since different
environments have different scoring scales, we normalize the scores to aggregate (§E.3).
In the result, the two modes show different strengths across models (Figure 12):Fable 5is the strongest at
improving existing methods, whileFable 5.1andFable 5take the top two places at designing new methods from
scratch. Among open models,GLM 5.2comes closest to the frontier, placing third at innovating. Notably, the
AI-Scientists beat the paper’s reproduced method in 84% of improve and 74% of innovate attempts (§F.1).

The leaderboards show which models score highest in

first compare the two modes directly. If improving
an existing method and inventing a method from

Is performance just a scaling effect?Better results
could come from scaling the attempt in two ways:
using more external compute, or doing more model-
side work through longer trajectories and more trial-
and-error. We do not find either pattern. Compute
hours and agent turns explain almost none of the
variance in scores (𝑅2≤ 0.02, Figure 14a; turns are
our provider-agnostic proxy for model-side effort,
since token counts may not be available). The lead-

more; they make better use of the same setting.
Then what drives it?The quality of the research itself. An LLM judge reads every attempt, blind to its
score, and rates it on five properties:creativity(was the idea genuinely new, and did it pay off),engineering
(was the implementation substantial, building on the existing code),rigor(was the reported gain real and
honestly measured),significance(how far it moved the metric), anddepth(how thoroughly the problem was
explored). These ratings track the models’ actual scores almost exactly (𝜌 = 0.89, Figure 14b): the models
that win are the ones doing better research, not the ones trying hardest.

Research is contingent.Research is inherently random. A strong attempt does not always produce a high
score: a creative idea can be implemented well and still fail empirically, and a great idea might not suit the
current setting, while a simpler idea may happen to work. Aggregating across many environments lets us
measure progress without pretending that research has no outcome variance.

We preserve every scientist’s research in full, so we collect a set of research
traces, released per environment, model, and run mode. We record the
scientist’s research idea and their revisions, the method and the full turn-
by-turn trajectory, and the per-experiment logs and scores (Table 4). We
store each attempt as a version-controlled repository, so each preserves the
complete development history rather than the final state alone.
In total, the corpus records roughly 6,400 hours of research being done
(§H.1). With multiple scientists’ attempts, one environment accumulates
multiple independent solutions to a fixed problem, each labeled with its
measured improvement over the reproduced source result.
4.3 Gym
Finally, we raise a scientist of our own. We trainQwen3-8B(Qwen Team, 2025), a scientist small enough that
whatever it learns must come from the world, with Tinker (Thinking Machines Lab, 2025), in two stages:
• Supervised fine-tuning.1,000 examples drawn from the trajectories, each pairing a task specification with
an attempt’s reasoning and final idea, cleaned so that no fabricated result survives. (details in §H)
• GRPO.We do off-policy group relative policy optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024) on 1,500 already-
scored ideas, rewarded by measured outcomes. Advantages are relative to the other ideas for the same task,
and updates are clipped to a trust region around the SFT policy. The scientist trains only with execution.

The trained scientist proposes the idea, and a single

The gain is monotone. The median implemented idea

and 106 after GRPO (Figure 15); the mean rises from

What it demonstrates is the mechanism: the world supplied the data, the reward, and the held-out exam, and
a scientist raised on its trajectories proposes measurably better research. The training loop works end to end.

title: Scientist World: Grow a Research World for AI-Scientists

text:
5 Background
Autonomous scientific discovery and AI-Scientists.Automating discovery is a long-standing goal. Early
systems recovered natural laws and governing equations directly from data (Schmidt and Lipson, 2009;
Cranmer et al., 2020; Udrescu and Tegmark, 2020), and robot scientists closed the loop from hypothesis to
physical experiment (King et al., 2004, 2009; Williams et al., 2015). Within machine learning, automated
search took over bounded parts of the pipeline: model and hyperparameter selection (Thornton et al., 2013;
Feurer et al., 2015), neural architecture design (Zoph and Le, 2017; Real et al., 2019), and even the discovery
of faster fundamental algorithms (Fawzi et al., 2022; Mankowitz et al., 2023). Program search guided by
language models extended this to open mathematical and algorithmic problems (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024;
Novikov et al., 2025). Language models then widened the scope toward the full workflow: tool-augmented
systems run their own chemical experiments (Boiko et al., 2023; Bran et al., 2024), and agentic pipelines
generate ideas, write code, and draft papers end to end (Lu et al., 2024; Yamada et al., 2025). A newer wave
organizes many agents into collaborative or self-directed discovery loops (Schmidgall et al., 2025; Schmidgall
and Moor, 2025; Ghareeb et al., 2026), and general-purpose AI-Scientists now attempt discovery across
whole fields (Gottweis et al., 2025; Mitchener et al., 2025). This line builds better scientists;
is complementary, turning finished papers into environments where such scientists can be handed the same
problem and scored on it.
Measuring AI-Scientists.Evaluating agents in executable settings began with general benchmarks for tool
use and repository-level code editing (Jimenez et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Mialon et al., 2024), then moved
to machine-learning experimentation and engineering (Huang et al., 2024; Chan et al., 2025; Wijk et al., 2025;
Nathani et al., 2025). A parallel line probes scientific reasoning and data-driven discovery (Jansen et al., 2024;
Majumder et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025b), extending to hypothesis formation and frontier domain research
(Liu et al., 2025; Miao et al., 2026). A closely related group scores whether an agent can reproduce a paper’s
results from its description (Siegel et al., 2024; Starace et al., 2025), reimplement its method and code (Xiang
et al., 2025; Hua et al., 2025), or take on research framed as an open-ended challenge (Zhang et al., 2025b;
Chen et al., 2025a). These suites are almost always fixed and hand-curated, and critiques of agent evaluation
warn that they can confound cost, leak through weak holdouts, and reward shortcuts (Kapoor et al., 2024).
Concurrent work also turns real papers into research tasks but curates them by hand, which does not scale
(Garikaparthi et al., 2026).
instead treats construction itself as the object: it selects papers at
scale and refactors each into a scored, reproduce-then-improve environment, so a method is judged by its gain
over a faithfully reproduced result rather than its distance from a reported number.
6 Conclusion
Every published paper with code is a finished piece of research: a problem, a method, and a measured result.
turns that record back into a place where research happens: 1,000 papers become runnable,
scored environments, and the collection grows with the literature rather than with annotation effort. The
same environments measure today’s AI-Scientists and train the next ones; each is a scaled-down paper and
each score one contingent trajectory, but the loop they are built for, a scientist that proposes, executes, and
updates inside the world, is just beginning. As the models and the literature both move, the world keeps
pace, and the problems it poses stay as open as the research it was built from.

A System Design
relies on agents that repeatedly alternate between reasoning and computation. This agent stack
is the substrate that makes this loop practical at scale. It separates four concerns that are otherwise entangled:
running compute jobs, bounding each experiment’s resource use, coordinating many papers, and normalizing
different agent interfaces. We separate the system into four parts: Hive provides the compute pool; Nexus
makes compute accountable to a particular attempt; Swarm coordinates many runs; and Worker presents
each agent scaffold through the same interaction contract. Figure 16 summarizes these layers.

Figure 16. System design overview.Hive supplies execution capacity for CPU and GPU jobs; Nexus accounts for the
budget and resource boundary of each attempt; Swarm maintains one paper-level trajectory across roles, restarts, and
handoffs; and Workers connect different agent scaffolds through the same system interface. Together, these layers let
many agents iterate on open-ended papers while preserving the evidence, budget state, and handoff context.
A.1 Hive: Interactive Compute Pool
Agent-driven reproduction needs a compute layer designed for interactive iteration. An agent may run a small
debugging command, inspect the result, edit the code, and then launch a longer training or evaluation job.
If every such step pays the full overhead of acquiring resources and preparing execution, the research loop
becomes dominated by infrastructure latency rather than by scientific reasoning. Hive keeps compute capacity
available, monitored, and controlled, so these iterations remain close to an interactive workflow.
Hive exposes compute as an experimental action: given a requested experiment, declared resources, and a
workspace, it reports what happened. The result is not only a terminal success or failure label. It includes
the execution evidence the agent needs to decide what to do next: logs, completion status, timing, and partial
output when a job is still running. This matters because reproduction agents rarely need a single monolithic
training run; they work through a trial and error sequence of tests, attempts, fixes, ablations, and evaluations.
Figure 17 shows the execution path inside Hive.
Input.Hive’s input is a job request. In our interface, the concrete entry point is a terminal command:hive
submit, whose parameters specify what should run.–workdir anchors the run to the code and files it should
see, –gpus and –cpus declare the requested capacity,–resource targets a named pool such as test, CPU, or
GPU capacity, and–timeout-sec bounds jobs that hang or run past their intended scale. Optional fields
such as retry count and log directory make the request easier to recover and inspect. These fields are useful
because they turn an open shell command into a schedulable execution unit: Hive can decide where it can
run, how much capacity it needs, when it should stop, and where its evidence should be recorded.

Figure 17. Hive execution overview.A job request enters Hive with a command, resource target, working directory,
and time limit. Admission queues the request, dispatch routes it to test, CPU, or GPU capacity, and monitor records
the return code, runtime, and logs that form the job record.
Output.Hive returns a job identifier and maintains a job record, not an experiment-specific result file. The
record directory containsmeta.json, stdout.log, andstderr.log: metadata for status, timing, resource
use, and return code, plus streamed logs for diagnosis. Any checkpoints, metrics, or plots created by the
command remain in the working directory; Hive records how the execution went.
Elasticity.A job asks for a category of resource (test, CPU, or GPU) and Hive places it on whatever node is
free, without the agent naming a specific machine. The pool can grow or shrink as capacity becomes available,
so the first worker to come online is useful immediately, and the same request format serves every experiment.
Node Types.Hive exposes three node types through the same job interface. CPU nodes support CPU-only
experiments, setup, preprocessing, and other jobs that do not require accelerators. GPU nodes run accelerator-
heavy experiments such as training and large-scale evaluation. Test nodes are for quick code validation and
small-scale testing, with jobs capped at one hour so agents do not tie up long-running allocations.
Reliability.Long-running jobs are not perfectly reliable: a job can stall or be killed before it finishes, and its
partial output is often still useful. Hive therefore treats an interruption as a reportable outcome rather than
a silent failure: it writes the job’s last state and logs into the job record, then requeues it on another valid
machine, where the command restarts from the beginning; the interrupted attempt is recorded for inspection
like any completed one, and its incomplete work is not charged against the budget.
Implementation.We use Ray (Moritz et al., 2018) to implement Hive. Ray starts each job on a free
machine and runs it; everything else the compute pool needs for agent-driven reproduction is built on top. A
resource manager tracks CPU, GPU, and test capacity; a dispatcher turns agent requests into queued jobs;
an agent-facing client/API submits jobs and streams progress back; and a persistent job store records logs,
status, and final outputs outside the Ray runtime. These pieces are what make the compute pool usable as
research infrastructure, not just a distributed execution engine.

A.2 Nexus: Experiment Boundary
Nexus is the experiment boundary that manages the resources agents use. It is a bridge between agents and
compute. An autonomous agent should not be trusted to enforce its own compute budget simply because the
prompt tells it to be careful. Nexus makes the budget a property of the system. Each reproduction attempt
receives a bounded project: jobs must fit within its resource limits, its concurrent usage cap, and its remaining
GPU-hour budget before they are allowed to run. Compute is no longer something the agent can spend freely;
every job is counted against the project’s budget. The operations view in Figure 18 shows these exchanges:
agents submit or review jobs through Nexus, and Nexus communicates between infrastructures and agents.

Fairness.This accounting matters for both fairness

Periodic Review.Nexus makes long jobs interruptible without requiring the agent to keep an active turn
open for the whole execution. At each configured review interval, Nexus snapshots the latest logs, records
them in the workspace, and wakes the responsible agent to inspect them. The agent can then continue the
run, cancel it, or change strategy before spending the remaining budget. Interval review pays off because
many broken reproductions are visible well before natural termination: imports fail after setup, data paths
are wrong, losses diverge, or an evaluator writes clearly invalid output. A run that would otherwise consume
hours can stop after the first snapshot that shows it is going nowhere. If the agent does not respond within
the review window, Nexus continues the job rather than leaving compute blocked by a missing response.
Separation.This layer is intentionally separate from Hive, and can accept any compute infrastructure.
Nexus is optimized for accountability. Keeping them separate prevents the compute pool from accumulating
task-specific policy and prevents Swarm from having to reason about low-level execution state.

text:
A.3 Swarm: Builder Coordination
Swarm has two jobs. The first is per paper: it drives one reproduction across many agent turns and several
roles, keeping the attempt coherent as builders hand off, retry, and audit each other’s work. The second is
across papers: it runs many of these attempts at the same time, each as its own trajectory, without their
states blurring together. Both are hard because the work is open-ended. A reproduction can produce useful
code without supporting the paper’s central claim, support the claim but leave no reusable environment,
or produce scores that look plausible until a later audit checks them. If these judgments live only in chat
transcripts, the result is a collection of anecdotes. Swarm therefore turns each paper attempt into an auditable
trajectory: the assigned agent, budget, workspace state, results, milestone, and next role are explicit at every
step. Figure 20 shows the end-to-end path: a pool of paper workspaces, each driven through an ordered role
workflow under a milestone gate, ending in an artifact that is either accepted or set aside.

Figure 20. Swarm coordination overview.Swarm drives a pool of paper workspaces in parallel. Each paper moves
through an ordered role workflow—reproduce, design, package, verify—whose transitions are driven by wake events:
worker start, job submit, job update, validation failure, and role transition. Progress is graded against a milestone
ladder, fromnoneup to full reproduction, and the milestone gate decides whether a paper’s artifact is accepted.
Pipeline.Swarm turns a paper into a finished environment. Its builders reproduce the paper’s main claim,
design the reproduction into a usable task, organize its files, and verify the result. Swarm does not run this
in one long session. A builder works in short turns, and ends each turn with an action, usually submitting
a compute job or signaling that it is done. Swarm tracks that action and the paper’s state, and whenever
something changes it wakes the builder with a prompt written for that exact situation: for example, when a
compute job finishes, a prompt that carries the results and asks what to do next; when a build fails, a prompt
with the build log and a request to fix it; when one stage is complete, a prompt that briefs the agent for the
next. The agent is therefore only ever asked to decide the one thing that just came up. Swarm runs this loop
over a pool of many workers, so it advances a large number of papers at the same time.
Coordination.Swarm answers the question that remains after a single agent turn ends: who should act next,
and what do they inherit from the builder before them? Its unit of state is the paper, not the agent session:
Swarm tracks where each paper sits in its workflow and the milestone it has reached, so a new builder resumes
from the right point and can build on a partial result left by the previous one. This is what lets a single paper
pass through several builders, even different models, and still read as one coherent attempt; without it, the
final artifact would mix the paper’s difficulty with hidden differences in how the agent happened to be run.
Wake Events.Swarm wakes a builder only when new information changes what it should decide: a fresh
paper or a new role to begin, a running job it may continue or cancel, a finished job, a failed build, an
exhausted budget, a validation or milestone-gate failure, or a role transition. The agent returns a structured
action, and Swarm records both the action and what prompted it. Table 5 summarizes what is shown.
Completion Checks.When a builder declares a pass finished, Swarm separates local correctness from progress.
The local check confirms the action is parseable and the milestone label is canonical, then runs the workspace
validator, which verifies that the score files exist, the evaluator is separated from the method, and the
workspace rebuilds from a clean clone (§C.4). Failures become repair prompts, capped at three validation
attempts. The progress check asks whether the claimed milestone clears the bar for the current stage; a run
that falls short reverts to an earlier pass or stops (§A.3.3).

A.3.2 Builder Roles
Role Design.Swarm does not give every agent the same job. It separates reproduction, environment design,
packaging, and verification so that later agents can inspect and improve the artifacts left by earlier agents; we
refer to these roles collectively asbuilders, the agents that construct an environment from a paper. Reproducers
build and test the paper method; design agents convert a successful reproduction into a scored environment;
the packager makes the workspace reusable; and verifiers audit whether the final milestone is supported
by evidence. This role split keeps the workflow from depending on a single long agent session while still
preserving one shared workspace. Table 7 summarizes the role responsibilities and the gate to satisfy.
Milestone Selection.Each builder also chooses the milestone that best describes the current workspace
after it is done. The choice is a self-evaluation against the canonical ladder in Table 6: the agent claims the
milestone supported by runnable code, logs, scores, and notes, rather than simply reporting when the assigned

system reads before waking the agent for the following turn.
Turns and actions.A session is a sequence of turns. The first turn sets the agent up in its workspace; every
later turn is short, sent only when something changes, such as a finished job or a failed build. The agent ends
a turn by writing one file,action.yaml, that states its decision, shown in Figure 23.
action: submit
gpus: 1
test: false
milestone: method_runs
notes: “scaled experiment.”
Figure 23. The action.yaml that

The agent makes its request in this fixed format. The system then
processes it to decide the next step.action says whether to submit a job
or declare the paper done;gpus and test set its size and route it to the
full or the short test pool;milestone records the agent’s own assessment
against the fixed milestone ladder. Because the agent never launches a
job itself, the system can check every request, count it against the budget,
and schedule it before it runs; a malformed one is handed back to rewrite,
while the reasoning behind it survives in the turn record. The loop also
removes any need to finish in a single session: the agent is re-engaged as
jobs complete and builds fail, and progress accumulates between turns.
Containment.We run the agent inside an Apptainer container (Kurtzer et al., 2017) whose home is the
paper workspace. It sees only a base image and that workspace: the container hides the cluster’s home and
temporary directories and drops all administrator bind mounts, so the shared filesystems are out of reach.
Inside, it edits code freely, and the GPU jobs it later submits reuse the same layout, so no host path is ever
exposed. Three limits keep one agent from starving its neighbors: a memory cap to bound total RAM, a low
scheduler priority to make co-located agents yield CPU, and thread caps on the numeric libraries.
Dependencies.Installing packages is separated from running jobs. The agent does not install during a job;
it declares what it needs in two workspace files:environment/container.def for the base image and OS
packages, andenvironment/setup.sh for Python packages. The system builds these once and keeps the
result in a persistent overlay on top of the base image, so the packages are available to every later job without
reinstalling or rebuilding the container. Editing either file triggers a rebuild before the next job runs.
25
title: Scientist World: Grow a Research World for AI-Scientists

text:
Boundary and robustness.We place a few things outside the agent’s reach by construction: the bookkeeping
files and the recorded trajectory are hidden, the validator is read-only, andgit push is disabled so the system
decides when work is published. Turns are stripped of credential patterns before they are written, since the
per-paper repositories may be made public. And because a paper can span thousands of unattended turns,
Worker recovers on its own: it retries transient errors such as rate limits, switches to another model profile on
terminal ones such as an exhausted usage cap, and kills a stalled turn along with its whole process tree.
A.5 How the Components Connect
Forward path.The four components pass work to each other through recorded state, not inside one long
agent session. Worker presents the paper and workspace to the agent and reads its action fromaction.yaml.
Swarm owns the paper’s trajectory: it tracks the milestone, advances through the workflow of roles, prepares
the workspace, and turns asubmit action into a job request for Nexus. Nexus checks the project’s budget, its
concurrency cap, and the requested resource pool, then forwards the job to Hive, which runs it.
Return path.Results travel back through the same components. Hive reports the job’s state, return code,
and resource usage; Nexus matches the finished job to its run record, writes the logs and outputs into the
workspace, releases the GPUs it was holding, and charges the run against the project’s budget. Swarm reads
the event, updates the paper’s state, and wakes the Worker for the next turn. Because everything lands as
files the agent can open, not as hidden service state, a later turn or a different model can look back at what
each job did and how it ended.
Why split it this way.The split gives each component a single, narrow responsibility, and that is what keeps
the system auditable. Worker can think and edit but cannot give itself compute; Swarm can coordinate
papers but does not run jobs; Nexus enforces resource limits without judging scientific progress; Hive runs
jobs without knowing which claim they support. Because the boundaries between them are clean, the four
parts are meant to work independently, and any one of them can be swapped for a different implementation,
a new scaffold, scheduler, or compute backend, without touching the others. The final artifact is tied to both
sides: the agent trajectory that produced it, and the run records that make that trajectory checkable.

B Builder Design
runs entirely on autonomous agents: every environment is produced by builders that reproduce
a paper and shape the result into a task, with no human in the loop. This section describes how those builders
work and the principles that decide whether the environment they leave behind is a good one. Figure 24 gives
the overview: from a paper and an empty workspace, builders produce a reusable environment across problem
definition, method reproduction, and evaluation.

Figure 24. Builder overview.From a paper (in PDF and Markdown) and an empty starter workspace, builders
build a reusable environment along three tracks: a problem definition that states the task and its constraints without
leaking a solution, a reproduction of the paper’s method whose code and experiments recover the central claim, and an
evaluation harness with visible and hidden slices that turns outputs into scores.
B.1 What the Builders Do
The task.§A described the system that runs the builders; this section is about the research task it is
built for. Given a single published paper, the agents must reproduce the paper’s central result and leave
behind a reusable environment, an executable setup in which a later scientist can attempt to improve on that
result. This is the foundation everything else rests on, since an environment whose method was never really
implemented would have nothing to measure. The rest of this subsection traces what the agents actually
do, from the paper to the finished environment and how each turn is driven; the design choices behind that
environment follow in §B.2.
From paper to environment.A builder’s input is the paper itself, in both Markdown and PDF with its
figures, together with a fresh, empty workspace. The reproducer starts from this and proceeds in order. It
first reads the paper and writes a short briefing, separating the problem and the evaluation protocol from the
paper’s method, and transcribes the paper’s reported numbers into a reference scoring file. It then prepares
the environment: downloading the data and any model weights in advance, writing an evaluator that scores
outputs without depending on the method, and checking that the scoring file is well formed. With that in
place it implements the method and reproduces incrementally, submitting compute jobs to get one experiment
that supports the core claim running before expanding to further settings, and recording its measured numbers
alongside the paper’s. Reproduction usually spans several agents in turn: each later one inherits the saved
workspace, audits what the previous agent built, and pushes it further.
Finishing the environment.A working reproduction is not yet a usable environment. Once the method runs
and supports the claim, a designer adds the visible and hidden evaluation slices and the scripts that produce
their scores; a packager makes the workspace rebuild from a clean clone, with every dataset and model fetched
by a self-contained download script; and a verifier audits the whole artifact before it is accepted. How these
roles are sequenced, what budget each receives, and how progress is graded are handled by the system (§A.3);
what each role leaves in the workspace is detailed in §C.
How a builder is prompted.The builder works in turns, ending each by requesting a compute job or declaring

B.2 Design Choices
A good environment does not come from reproducing a paper alone; it also has to be designed so that a later
method can be tested fairly on it, all under a limited compute budget. We follow seven design choices toward
this, each stated first and then explained.
Design choice 1.Reproduce the paper’s method and core claim, not its exact numbers. Scale down resources when
needed, but preserve the experimental procedure and keep the task non-trivial.
The goal is to make the paper’s method run, not to match a table entry. Exact-number reproduction rewards
the wrong behavior: a builder could tune toward the published values, or copy them outright, without
implementing the method. Instead, the environment should contain the paper’s actual computation and
produce reasonable support for the claimed effect. A simple check is whether a reader of the code can recognize
the algorithm from the paper.
Most papers cannot be reproduced at full scale under a fixed budget. The builder may therefore reduce the
model size, dataset size, or number of training steps, which also keeps reproductions friendlier to the broader
community using the artifact. What it may not do is change the procedure. If the paper trains from scratch,
the environment trains from scratch. If the paper uses a particular optimization setup, the environment keeps
that setup. Resources can shrink; the experiment cannot become a different experiment.
Scaling down also has a limit. A task made too small becomes trivial, and a trivial task cannot distinguish
the paper’s method from a weak baseline. When a builder uses a smaller or synthetic dataset, it must check
that a basic baseline does not already solve the problem. If the reproduced method is no better than random
guessing, majority class, or another weak baseline within noise, the reproduction has failed. The environment
28
title: Scientist World: Grow a Research World for AI-Scientists

text:
needs a real gap so that future agents have something meaningful to improve.
Design choice 2.Keep the problem separate from the solution: the problem should be stateable without the paper’s
method, and the evaluator and data should not depend on that method.
This boundary keeps the problem definition independent of the solution that produced it. The problem,
its data, and its evaluator can be stated and run without the paper’s method, so the environment poses
the problem on its own terms rather than only as a continuation of one particular implementation; the file
boundary is described in §C.2. The separation also protects the score. If the evaluator secretly depended on
the reproduced method, then changing the method might not change what is measured, and the environment
would look functional while no longer testing the intended problem.
The separation must hold at runtime, not only in the file layout. The evaluator must read the outputs a
method produced, never call the method’s code: if deletingmethod/ would change the evaluation scores, the
boundary is broken. Likewise, the data loaders belong to the problem, not the solution, and must not import
from method/. The evaluate scripts must also discover methods dynamically, enumerating whatever methods
exist on disk rather than hardcoding a name, so that the evaluator works for a future method without editing.
How the environment is then presented to a future agent is a matter for evaluation (§E.1).
Design choice 3.Provide a visible evaluation slice for development, and reserve a matched hidden slice for final
evaluation to detect shortcuts and overfitting.
The finished environment includes an evaluation suite that a future scientist can see and optimize against.
If that suite is only one metric on one dataset, the easiest path may be to game that number rather than
improve the underlying idea. To reduce this risk, the designer builds two slices: a visible slice for development
and a hidden slice that is run only after done. A large gap between the two suggests overfitting or shortcuts.
The split can be drawn in different ways, depending on the paper: held-out samples, held-out subgroups,
harder inputs, or several related metrics that measure the same claim from different angles. Using multiple
metrics from different angles is stronger than a single held-out number, because a single metric can be gamed
while triangulation from several directions catches shortcuts that any one metric would miss.
The hidden slice must be calibrated against the visible one in difficulty: both should probe the method at
roughly equal rigor, using matched data scales, evaluation protocols, and sample counts. An honest method
should score similarly on both; if the hidden slice is simply harder, then every method will look worse there
and the gap will be meaningless. The two slices should also be independent, so reading or importing the
visible evaluator does not reveal the hidden one. And the test slice should be lightweight: it re-scores existing
artifacts or slices them differently, rather than retraining or re-running expensive inference.
Design choice 4.Score future methods on the quantity the paper cares about, not on how closely they match the
paper. Fix the constraints needed to make gains meaningful.
An environment should allow future methods to improve on the paper. For that reason, the score must not
measure distance from the paper’s published number. Such a metric would make the paper’s own method
the target and turn the environment into a reproduction-fidelity test. The paper’s reported numbers should
be recorded as context, but future methods should be scored on the underlying quantity: accuracy, loss,
robustness, sample efficiency, parameter count, or whatever the claim is actually about.
This principle is enforced in the scoring schema: metric names that encode closeness to the paper, such
as deviation, vs_paper, or agreement_with, are blocked by the validator, so the score must name the
underlying scientific quantity.
The environment must also define what stays fixed. A future scientist should not win by using more compute,
29
title: Scientist World: Grow a Research World for AI-Scientists

text:
a larger model, more data, or a different training paradigm unless that is the allowed direction of improvement.
For papers that claim a benefit without a cost, the evaluator should measure both sides: the benefit that
should improve and the constraint that should not break. The scoring contract expresses this through metric
coefficients: a positive coefficient marks a benefit to maximize, a negative one marks a constraint that must
not degrade, and the experiment weights reflect how central each result is to the paper’s claim.
Design choice 5.Score on quantities that do not depend on the machine. Replace hardware-sensitive measures such
as latency or wall-clock time with stable proxies.
Hardware varies from run to run, so a latency or wall-clock measurement can swing severalfold with no change
to the method, and an environment that scored it would reward landing on a faster GPU rather than finding a
better idea. Scores therefore use quantities that are stable across machines: parameter count, FLOPs, training
steps, examples processed, or final task performance. When the paper’s own claim is about speed or efficiency,
the environment keeps the claim but measures it through a machine-independent proxy rather than the clock.
Design choice 6.Reproduce enough of the paper to give future scientists a real surface to improve, preferably a small
matrix over the paper’s own axes rather than one isolated number.
A one-number reproduction is too thin a target. A future scientist may match it and still have little room to
learn from or improve. Once the core claim runs, the environment should expand along the axes the paper
itself studies: datasets, input difficulty, model scale, ablations, data regimes, or other relevant settings. A
small matrix over two meaningful axes is usually more useful than repeated runs of the same setting.
This matrix does not need to be large. It needs to expose the structure of the claim. Combined with the
non-triviality check above, it turns the environment from a single point estimate into one with headroom:
weak baselines leave a gap, the reproduced method occupies a recognizable starting point, and future methods
have several genuine ways to improve.
Design choice 7.The environment must rebuild and rerun from a fresh clone, with every external resource fetched by
a self-contained script and every dependency declared.
An environment that only works on the machine that built it is not reusable. The download script must
fetch every dataset, model weight, and external resource from a public source using executable commands,
not comments or placeholder URLs. It must be idempotent and must not reference local shared paths that
exist only on the original cluster. The container definition and setup script must declare every system and
Python dependency so that the software rebuilds without manual intervention. And every local import in the
evaluation, method, and baseline code must resolve to a file tracked by git, so that a fresh clone contains
everything the experiments need to run.
The validator enforces this: it scans committed code for references to machine-local shared directories and
checks that every import target is a tracked file. Together with the reproducible-execution scripts (§C.3), this
makes the environment a portable artifact rather than a snapshot of one session’s state.

C Agent Workspace
The workspace is the single directory the builders work in and the artifact they leave behind. Its layout is
what makes the result a reusable environment rather than the residue of one run. We describe its structure
(§C.1), its problem statement and scoring (§C.2), its execution (§C.3), and its records and checks (§C.4).
C.1 Structure
Overview.Each paper is reproduced inside a single working directory, and that directory is also the artifact
the builders leave behind. During the run it holds the code, data, experiments, and notes; once the run
ends, it is designed to stand on its own, so that another party can clone it, rebuild the environment, rerun
the method, and obtain the same scores without access to the original session. This is what distinguishes a
reusable research environment from the residue of a single successful run, in which the method is entangled
with the evaluator, the data exists only in a local cache, and the scores carry no well-defined meaning. The
layout shown in Figure 25 is designed to prevent these failures.

Figure 25. The agent workspace.A single directory holds the paper and briefing, the reproduced method and
baselines, the data and evaluator, the scoring contract, the run scripts and environment, and the root-level record and
validation files. Each directory has a single responsibility, which keeps the problem separated from the solution, lets
the workspace rebuild and rerun from a fresh clone, and preserves a record of how the reproduction was produced.
File Roles.The layout is a deliberate design choice rather than a storage convention: each directory has a
single responsibility. The briefing defines what a future scientist may know;method/ and baseline/ hold what
the reproducer built;data/ and eval/ define the problem interface that any method must satisfy;scoring/
defines how a method is judged; andscripts/ and environment/ determine whether the workspace runs
outside the original session. Table 9 summarizes the groups.
C.2 Problem and Scoring
Problem and Solution Boundary.The workspace deliberately separates the problem from the solution so that
the problem is method-agnostic: it states what must be achieved and how it is measured, without revealing
the paper’s approach. This is what allows the workspace to serve as a fair task for any future method rather

Scoring Contract.Scoring is held in two files. scoring/reference.json records the paper’s reported
numbers for each baseline and proposed method, along with the scoring rules: aweightper experiment, set by
the agents to reflect how central that result is to the paper’s core claim (weights sum to one), the direction of
each metric, and a label marking each method as a baseline or a proposed method.scoring/scores.json
holds the numbers the reproduction actually produced. A later method is scored by its improvement over
those reproduced numbers, in each metric’s direction and combined by the weights, so the score measures
progress over the reproduction rather than closeness to the paper. Figure 26 shows the two files side by side.
Targets and Constraints.The JSON files fix the numbers, but a scientist also requires the intent behind
them. Four short markdown files provide it:TARGETS.md states what to optimize,CONSTRAINTS.md states
what must remain fixed,DIRECTION.md states which kinds of change are permitted, andEXPERIMENTS.md
describes each scored experiment without disclosing the method. Together they exclude trivial gains, such
as substituting a larger model, adding unrelated data, or altering the problem itself, while preserving room
for a genuine methodological improvement. For example, an agent may improve performance on a Mamba
architecture optimization problem by replacing the architecture with a Transformer. While this could yield
better results, such a change provides no scientific value, as it sidesteps the original problem rather than
advancing our understanding of how to improve Mamba models themselves. When a paper makes a trade-off
claim, both sides must be scored: the benefit and the constraint it must not violate. Otherwise the easiest
route to a high score is to break the very condition the paper was designed to satisfy.
C.3 Execution
Reproducible Execution.The workspace must be able to rebuild from source, not only on the machine
where it was created. scripts/download.sh fetches external data, weights, and other public resources;

Visible and Held-Out Slices.A finished workspace also includes a train/test split for the scientist who reuses

builders, compute, and components behind it, so it stays auditable after the session ends.
Acceptance Checks.A workspace is checked before it is accepted.validate.py runs automatically and
enforces the scoring schema, blocks the obvious paper-agreement metric names, and checks the structural
rules that keep the workspace independent of its own method and rebuildable from a fresh clone; Table 11
lists the checks in full. The markdown audit files then cover what code cannot decide:MILESTONES.md states
the claimed milestone,PROGRESS.md and VERIFICATION.md record why it is justified and what was changed
from the paper, andCHECKLIST.md confirms that the workspace is ready for both improve and innovate mode
reuse. A workspace is accepted only when the automatic checks pass and the audit files are complete.
Version Control.Every workspace is a git repository, and the system commits to it continuously, so the full
trajectory can be replayed from the repository alone, without the session that produced it. Each agent edit is
committed as it is made, and each job submission is committed together with the exact code it ran, so the
state behind any result is pinned to a specific revision. When a job finishes, its logs are written back into the
workspace and committed as tracked files, so what ran and what it produced live in the same history as the
code. The builder cannot publish:git pushis disabled, and the system decides when it is released (§A.4).
Evaluation reuses the same git-backed design with one branch per attempt. Each time a model is run on an
environment, that attempt is isolated on its own branch, so attempts never interfere, and each one can be
inspected, rescored, or rerun on its own from the committed state it started from.

D Selecting Papers
Not every paper can or should become a suitable environment. A useful task has to be both worth reproducing
and feasible for an autonomous builder to attempt under a bounded budget. Before any reproduction begins,
we therefore narrow a large pool of recent papers down to a smaller, category-balanced set through a staged
pipeline: cheap model screens drop low-quality and off-type papers, a deeper analysis scores each remaining
paper for quality and reproduction difficulty, and a final ranking and balancing step chooses the papers we
attempt. The rest of this section walks through that pipeline and reports how many papers survive each stage.
Candidate Pool.We assemble the candidate pool before any builder is launched. Our selection snapshot
is exported from a global arXiv index of 124,816 unique papers. The index is built from daily category
listings between January 1, 2025 and March 1, 2026, and exported on March 28, 2026. We restrict the source
categories to cs.CL, cs.CV, cs.AI, and cs.LG (Figure 29), then deduplicate by arXiv ID because the same
paper can appear under more than one category. We also drop papers whose primary category is statistics
(the stat.* group), which are dominated by theoretical work that offers little to execute or reproduce. This
gives the candidate pool a temporal and topical boundary before any model is asked to judge feasibility.
Figure 28 reports how many papers survive each screening stage from this pool onward.

selection rules. Each pass sees only the opening 15,000 characters of the converted paper, which typically span
the abstract and introduction, so that screening cost stays low across the full index. The first pass returns

E Evaluation Protocol
Evaluation is the scoring harness that turns the reproduced environments into comparable scores across
models. Where Swarm is built for open-ended builder coordination, Evaluation is deliberately flatter: it runs
one controlled trial for each combination of paper, model, and mode. Each trial starts from a fresh workspace,
receives a bounded compute budget through Nexus, drives one agent session through reason-run-feedback
turns, and records the resulting train and held-out test scores. The harness splits this into auditable stages,
from scaffolding through normalization (Table 12). The unit of comparison is therefore explicit: a model is
judged by what its agent can build under the same problem statement, workspace boundary, scoring contract,
and compute budget. We call this evaluated agent thescientist agent, to distinguish it from the builders that
construct an environment (§A.3.2).

E.1 Evaluation Modes
Each environment can be run in two modes that ask different questions of a model. Inimprovemode, the
scientist is given the reproduced method and the train-phase scores it already achieves, and must push those
numbers higher without changing the evaluation protocol; the question is whether the model can advance an
existing result. Ininnovatemode, the agent is given only the problem statement, the constraints and targets,
the visible evaluator, and the data interface, with an empty method directory, and must build a method from
first principles; the question is whether the model can solve the problem on its own.
The two modes are the problem-and-solution separation of §B.2 made operational: the same environment,
presented once with the reproduced method and once without it. This separation is built into the workspace
layout, not just the prompt. The reproduced method lives in its ownmethod/ directory, while the problem
statement, scoring targets, visible evaluator, and data interface sit outside it, and the evaluator and data never
import frommethod/ (§C). Because the rest of the environment does not depend on the method, a single
change switches modes:method/ is handed over intact for improve mode and emptied for innovate mode.
They are kept separate in both the run matrix and the normalization, because a score earned by inventing a
method from scratch is not the same experimental object as one earned by improving an existing method.

E.2 Running a Trial
Workspace Boundary.Evaluation controls what the scientist can see and modify. The problem briefing, data,
baseline artifacts, and visible training evaluator are read-only. The method directory, run scripts, scratch
directory, and scoring directory are writable. Held-out test files, test scripts, reference scores, and the paper
text are not present during the main phase. This boundary prevents agents from tuning against the hidden test
split while still giving them enough information to conduct real research: they can read the task, implement a
method, run the visible evaluator, inspect failures, and iterate. In improve mode, the starting method’s train
score is copied into the briefing as a target to beat, but it is not used as an oracle during scoring.

Scientist Loop.At the end of each turn, the scientist declares whether it wants to submit a compute job or
finish. A submitted job runs the workspace’s compute entrypoint through Nexus, using the requested CPU or
GPU resources and optionally the short test capacity for smoke tests. Evaluation does not implement its own
execution loop; it consumes the job results that Nexus exposes and resumes the same agent session with them.
Current runs use a 200-turn ceiling, and a trial that fails for a transient reason before producing any score file
is retried up to three times. Once scoring files exist, the workspace is kept for review rather than overwritten.
Train and Test Scores.The main phase producesscores_train.json using the visible evaluator. A host-side
validator then checks the output against the source scoring shape: for every required proposed method, every
numeric metric present in the reference reproduction must also be present in the agent’s score file. Metrics
marked as baselines are ignored because they are not the scientist’s responsibility.
After train validation passes, the method the scientist built is frozen: its directory is mounted read-only before
the held-out evaluator runs, so the test score reflects exactly the method that produced the train score and
cannot be tuned against the hidden split. Evaluation then materializes the held-out evaluator from a pristine
clone, so the scientist cannot influence what the test runs, and executes against the frozen method.
If the test job fails, the default recovery path keeps the method and the hidden evaluator read-only for five
repair turns, so the scientist can repair missing packages or regenerate artifacts without modifying the frozen
method or peeking at held-out data. If those turns do not succeed, a final three-turn path makesmethod/
writable again under a stricter honesty prompt, so a genuine interface mismatch can be repaired; even then
the held-out evaluator and test data stay read-only and re-materialized from the pristine clone, so the method
can be fixed but the hidden split still cannot be read nor the scorer altered, and these unlock turns are flagged
in the trace. A run is complete only when both train and test score files validate.

F Evaluation Analysis
The main text reads these environments as a leaderboard. Here we examine the evaluation behind it, asking
three questions: how often a scientist actually improves on the reproduced method, whether a score reflects a
real gain rather than a metric optimized during the run, and whether the number is largely a proxy for how
much compute or interaction a run was given. In short: usually, yes, and no.
F.1 How Often Scientists Beat the Paper
Before asking which scientist is best, it is worth knowing whether any of them do real work. They do.
Figure 35 shows the distribution of held-out improvement over the paper’s source method, one panel per
mode. Most runs land to the right of zero: 84% beat the reproduced method when improving it, and 74% do
when designing a new one from scratch. Innovate carries the heavier left tail, since a fresh design more often
fails outright, yet even there the typical attempt still moves the metric forward.
F.2 Do the Gains Generalize
A score is only meaningful if it reflects a real gain rather than a metric gamed during the run. The held-out
split separates the two: a scientist optimizes against a training-phase metric but is scored on a test slice it
never sees. Figure 36 plots one against the other. The two track closely (Spearman0.57in improve and0.69
in innovate), so training gains usually survive to the held-out metric, and only a small share of runs fall in the
overfit quadrant where a training gain reverses on test (8% in improve and 5% in innovate). The split rarely
needs to intervene, but when it does it removes exactly the runs that would otherwise inflate a score.
F.3 Effort and Outcomes
A natural worry is that a score mostly tracks how much compute or interaction a run spent, rewarding
brute force over insight. It does not. Figure 37 plots each run’s within-paper normalized score against the
GPU-hours it consumed and the number of turns it took, with the Improve and Innovate modes kept apart.
Every trend is flat: the rank correlation stays weak throughout and is slightly negative where it moves at all,
at most0.22in magnitude. Spending more does not produce a better result; a better method does.

G Experimental Setup
This section records the concrete setup behind our experiments: the paper set the scientists attempt, the
compute pool they run on, the agent scaffolds and models we compare, and how trials are run and scored.
45
title: Scientist World: Grow a Research World for AI-Scientists

text:
G.1 Data
All papers come from arXiv. We work from a global index of 124,816 unique papers in the categories cs.CL,
cs.CV, cs.AI, and cs.LG, built from daily listings between January 1, 2025 and March 1, 2026 and exported
on March 28, 2026. From this index, the selection procedure of §D chooses a category-balanced set of 1,000
papers to attempt; the per-stage counts are reported there.
G.2 Compute
’s experiments run on a heterogeneous setup provisioned through Hive and accounted by Nexus.
The compute pool contains 16 A100 GPU nodes, 16 H100 GPU nodes, 16 H200 GPU nodes, and 4 CPU
nodes (Table 13). The GPU nodes support accelerator-heavy reproduction jobs, while the CPU nodes support
CPU-only experiments and non-accelerated setup or validation work.
resource count role
A100 GPU nodes 16 general accelerator workloads and pilot experiments
H100 GPU nodes 16 high-throughput training and evaluation jobs
H200 GPU nodes 16 memory-intensive or largest-scale reproduction runs
CPU nodes 4 low-compute, CPU-only setup and validation jobs
Table 13. Hive exposes heterogeneous capacity for accelerator-heavy and CPU-only experiments.The counts describe
the compute capacity exposed in Hive.
G.3 Agent Scaffolds
Each scientist reaches the workspace through a scaffold, the layer that drives a coding-agent command-line
tool behind one uniform turn interface (§A.4). Our experiments center on two scaffolds: Claude Code, which
runs Anthropic models, and Codex, which runs OpenAI models. The same harness also supports other agents,
including Gemini, Kimi, and Grok, so a single task can be run across a range of models. We prioritize a
provider’s official agent scaffold when one is released; otherwise we use Claude Code as the default. Because a
model and its scaffold are evaluated together and not every model runs through the same scaffold, the unit
being compared is a model together with its scaffold, and a scaffold difference is part of what the comparison
measures rather than something controlled away.
G.4 Models
We evaluate scientists built on models from seven providers: Anthropic (Fable 5.1,Fable 5,Opus 4.8, andOpus
4.7), OpenAI (GPT 6 Astra,GPT 5.6 Sol,GPT 5.5, andGPT 5.4), Zhipu (GLM 5.2andGLM 5.1), Moonshot
(Kimi K2.7andKimi K2.6), MiniMax (MiniMax M3andMiniMax M2.7), Xiaomi (MiMo V2.5 Pro), and DeepSeek
(DeepSeek V4). Anthropic and OpenAI models run through their official scaffolds; the rest run through
Claude Code against an Anthropic-compatible gateway (§G.3). Every model is run at the extra-high (xhigh)
reasoning-effort setting, or at its highest available setting if it does not support xhigh, so models are judged
at full strength rather than at a throttled setting.
G.5 Evaluation Trials
Every trial hands the scientist the same resources, so a difference in outcome reflects the model and not the
budget behind it. A trial runs under a ceiling of 200 turns and a compute budget of 30 GPU-hours, with
at most 2 GPUs held at once, accounted by Nexus (§A.2). A trial that aborts for a transient infrastructure
46
title: Scientist World: Grow a Research World for AI-Scientists

text:
reason, such as a gateway timeout or a compute-pool blip, is retried up to three times before it is recorded as
a failure; retries cover infrastructure, never an agent that simply solved the task poorly, so no model is re-run
for doing badly. We cap in-flight trials at 30 and split that capacity evenly across the active models, so a
fast API does not crowd a slower one out of the queue. Each model is run in both evaluation modes of §E.1.
GPU-hours are counted as wall-clock time times the number of GPUs held, without weighting by accelerator
class, so a trial scheduled onto faster cards can fit more experimentation into the same nominal budget; we
treat this as a known limitation of expressing the budget in raw GPU-hours.
G.6 Provider Failures
A run spans thousands of unattended turns over hours or days, during which a model provider can rate-limit,
throttle, or go down. The two settings absorb these interruptions differently, because they optimize for
different things. When building an environment, the goal is to preserve work, so a run that fails resumes from
the start of the current workflow iteration, reusing the saved workspace; a provider outage then costs at most
the iteration in progress, not the whole reproduction. During evaluation, the goal is fairness, so a trial that
fails before producing any score is discarded and restarted from a fresh workspace rather than resumed: no
model is scored on a run that was continued mid-trajectory or warm-started from partial state, and every
model meets the same clean-room conditions. A failure that occurs after scores are written is set aside for
review rather than silently retried.
G.7 Cohort and Normalization
Running every model on all 1,000 selected papers would be expensive to repeat, so the headline evaluation
uses a smaller fixed cohort drawn from the lower-compute environments, chosen so that a full pass stays cheap
enough to run across many models and to rerun over time. Scores are normalized against a reference set of
models rather than reported in absolute terms (§E.3): the per-paper normalization coefficients are computed
once from that reference set and then frozen, so a newly added model is scored against the existing board
without shifting the numbers already reported for other models. The reference set is the current generation of
each model family; older generations are scored against that frozen reference but kept out of it.
G.8 Reproducibility
Every trial starts from the same pinned container image and the same workspace template (§C), so the
software environment and the starting state are identical across models and stay fixed as the evaluation
is rerun over months. Scoring depends only on the numbers a trial records, not on wall-clock time or the
hardware it ran on (§B.2), so a trial can be rescored later without rerunning the agent. We retain the full
record of each trial, the agent log, the final workspace, and the jobs it submitted, so any reported score can
be traced back to what the agent actually did.
47
title: Scientist World: Grow a Research World for AI-Scientists

text:
H Dataset and Training Details
This appendix documents the two artifacts behind §4: the released trace corpus (§4.2) and the scientist
trained on it (§4.3). It records how the corpus is counted, how the training data and configuration are derived
from it, and the held-out protocol behind Figure 15.
H.1 Trace Corpus
What Is Preserved.Every evaluation attempt is preserved as its own git repository, one per environment,
model, and run mode. The repository is the final workspace of §C with its full commit history: the system
commits after every turn (§C.4), so the corpus holds the development history of each attempt rather than a
cleaned final state. A trace records the research idea and its revisions, the method code as it changed, and the
per-experiment logs and scores, tied together by the turn-by-turn trajectory that produced them. Attempts
that regress on the source method are kept alongside those that improve on it; a corpus of research being
done must include the failures.
Accounting.The totals in §4.2 are computed per attempt and summed. Hours of work is the scientist’s
end-to-end running wall-clock time, from the first turn of a trial to its final recorded score; summed over every
preserved attempt, across all models, effort tiers, and both modes, it gives the roughly 6,400 hours reported.
The per-attempt averages of Table 4 come from the same records.
H.2 Training Data
Provenance.All training data derives from finished evaluation traces. Each example is rooted in a task
specification exactly as a scientist receives it: the problem, the constraints, and the metric to move (§C). The
ten held-out papers of §H.4 appear in no training example.
Supervised Set.The SFT set has 1,000 examples. The prompt is the task specification; the target is the
attempt’s reasoning inside<think> tags followed by its final idea. Reasoning is cleaned before training:
fabricated run results and job identifiers are removed, and empirical claims are reframed as conceptual, with
nothing invented or added. The set combines 925 authentic completions with 75 faithful rephrasings of the
strongest completions, which round the set to 1,000 without introducing new content.
Reward Set.The GRPO set has 1,500 already-scored ideas, rewarded by measured outcomes only: 777
examples by the held-out test score (weight 1.0), and 723 by generalization, the test score minus the train-test
overfit gap (weight 0.5). Rewards are z-normalized within each paper and mode group, so an idea is reinforced
or suppressed relative to the other ideas for the same task. We deliberately exclude rewards judged by an
LLM: every reward in the set is a measured result.
H.3 Training Procedure
Setup.The base model isQwen3-8Bin its thinking variant. Both stages train a LoRA adapter of rank 32
through Tinker (Thinking Machines Lab, 2025), and the GRPO stage continues from the SFT checkpoint.
SFT.Cross-entropy on the assistant message only, learning rate10−4, batch size 8, 3 epochs, maximum
sequence length 8,192. Training NLL decreases from 2.25 to 2.16 over the three epochs.
Offline GRPO.The objective is a clipped PPO loss. The SFT policy’s log-probabilities are computed with a
no-gradient forward pass and used as the reference, so the clip bounds every update to a trust region around
the SFT policy. Learning rate10−5, batch size 16, one epoch, gradient-norm clip 1.0. Training stays bounded:
the completion NLL oscillates in a stable band around the SFT baseline and never diverges. This stability is
not free. An earlier variant that weighted cross-entropy by the signed advantage collapsed, because tokens
48
title: Scientist World: Grow a Research World for AI-Scientists

text:
with negative advantage are pushed toward unboundedly low log-probability; the clipped objective with an
explicit reference policy is what makes offline training on scored ideas stable.
H.4 Held-Out Evaluation
Protocol.The gym result of Figure 15 scores ideas, not the idea generator’s own coding. For each of the ten
held-out papers, one idea is sampled from each of the three checkpoints, base, SFT, and GRPO, with the
same prompt format, temperature 0.7, and top-p 0.8. A single fixed implementer,GPT 5.6 Solat the xhigh
effort tier, then executes every idea in innovate mode under identical conditions: the idea is injected into the
briefing with the instruction to implement it faithfully and to optimize within its framing rather than invent
a different approach. Only the idea’s origin varies across the thirty runs.
Scoring and Isolation.Scoring is identical to the benchmark: the held-out FNI, computed with each paper’s
frozen cohort coefficients (§G.7). The ablation is isolated from the leaderboard: it runs in a separate workspace
namespace, shifts no normalization, and publishes nothing.
Results.Figure 38 plots each trained idea’s score against the same paper’s base idea score, and Table 14
summarizes the distributions over the ten held-out papers. Both the mean and the median rise monotonically
from base to SFT to GRPO. The spread grows as well, so the gain is a shift in the typical outcome rather
than a uniform improvement on every paper.

I Example Produced Environment
This section uses one finished environment as a lens on what the builders actually do, and why. For each choice
a builder makes while turning a paper into a reusable task, we ask why it makes that choice and whether the
behavior is one the system is built to elicit or the builder’s own judgment. The paper is only background: it
is the reproduction ofTransformers without Normalization(arXiv:2503.10622), whose Dynamic Tanh (DyT)
replaces Layer Normalization with a learnable element-wise operation. The run usedMiniMax M2.7,GLM 5.1,
andGPT 5.4across 25 agent sessions over the reproduce, design, package, and verify roles, and about 19
GPU-hours, ending at thecore_claim milestone. The few excerpts below come from the produced workspace;
layout follows Figure 25.
Implement the real method, not a lookalike.The reproducer writes the paper’s actual computation rather
than a model tuned to emit its published numbers. It does this because the milestone rewards a method
that runs: a surrogate fit to the reported accuracy would clear a naive number-matching test but fails ours
by construction, and the verifier re-checks that the code is the algorithm itself. This is designed in — the
milestone ladder and the verify role reward a runnable method (§A.3).

Write the briefing so it cannot leak the answer.The builder states the problem inmethod-agnosticterms: it
fixes the question and the success criteria but never names DyT or normalization-free training. Why withhold
what it just implemented? Because the same workspace is later handed to a from-scratch scientist, and a
brief that named the solution would let that scientist copy it instead of doing research. By design, briefings
must be method-agnostic, and the verifier andvalidate.pyflag leaks; one is caught below.
briefing/problem.md
# # Research Question
Can deep transformer - style c l a s s i f i e r s be trained stably and a c c u r a t e l y when
their usual feature - n o r m a l i z a t i o n c o m p o n e n t s are removed or replaced , without
winning by i n c r e a s i n g model size , c han gi ng the data , or using p r e t r a i n e d weights ?
# # Success Criteria
- Train without n u m e r i c a l d i v e r g e n c e ; match or improve the r e f e r e n c e a ccu ra cy .
- Keep p a r a m e t e r count and model scale matched within the c o m p a r i s o n .
- Same data split and p r e p r o c e s s i n g ; no p r e t r a i n e d weights , extra data , or e n s e m b l e s .
Decide what counts as an improvement.The scoring contract is where the builder exercises judgment the
system asks for but does not dictate. It makes top-1 accuracy the primary metric, keeps top-5 and balanced
accuracy as diagnostics, and gives parameter count anegativecoefficient — so beating the baseline by scaling
the model up does not register as a win. The format invites such a constraint metric; which metrics matter,
and by how much, is the builder’s call. It records the paper’s reported numbers as the ranking reference and
its own measured numbers as the baseline a future method must beat.
Scale the experiment down without trivializing it.The full paper trains ViT-B/L for 300 epochs, beyond a
per-paper budget, so the builder scales to a 50-class slice and a ViT-S/16. The choice is bounded by a rule the
system cares about: model and data scale may shrink, but the algorithm and the matched comparison must

baseline lands below saturation, so comparison still has room, and DyT edges it at equal parameter count.
Pin the surface a future scientist competes on.Because the environment is graded by comparison, the
builder writes down what a future scientist may optimize, what it must hold fixed, and where it may explore.
It splits this into three documents: atarget(what improvement means and how it is measured),constraints
(what must stay matched across compared systems), and adirection(the mechanism to work on, and what is
out of bounds). These are required and method-safe: a from-scratch reader sees the rules, not the solution.

Keep evaluation independent of any one method.The builder makes the evaluator score prediction files
and own the labels, rather than load the reproduced model. Why give up the convenience of calling its own

text:
J Agent Prompts
This section shows representative prompts from each stage of the system, to illustrate how agents are
instructed: the screening and analysis prompts that grade and select papers, the role prompts that drive
a Swarm reproduction, and the prompts that run a single evaluation trial. The prompts are excerpted;
operational scaffolding repeated across prompts (job submission, progress logging, version control, the
workspace layout) is omitted and described in sections above. Placeholders in braces are filled at run time.
J.1 Prompts for Paper Grading and Selection
Prefilter
Paper Pre-Filter
Read the paper excerpt below and rate itsresearch qualityon a scale of 0-100.
•100: Landmark paper. Defines a new field or sets a new paradigm. Must-read for anyone in ML/ AI.
• 80: T op-venue quality (ICLR, NeurIPS, ICML, ACL, EMNLP, CVPR). Novel idea, strong experiments, clear results.
W orth reading and citing.
• 60: Second-tier venue quality. Solid work with experiments, but less novelty or narrower scope. W orth reading in your
area.
•40: Has a method and some experiments, but limited novelty or weak evaluation. Y ou’d skim it.
•20: Minimal contribution. Shallow, incremental, or poorly executed. Not worth reading.
•0: Not a research paper, or no method and no experiments.
These anchors are reference points, not buckets. Use the full range freely. Scores like 7, 23, 41, 58, 73, 84, and 97 are all valid when
appropriate. Do not restrict yourself to only 0, 20, 40, 60, 80, or 100.
Note: The excerpt below is the first ~15,000 characters of the paper, converted to markdown, intentionally truncated. Formatting
artifacts (broken text, missing figures, odd symbols) are from automatic PDF-to-markdown conversion — ignore them and judge
only the research content.
Think briefly about the paper’s contribution, novelty, and experimental rigor. Give a short explanation of the main strengths and
weaknesses. Then provide an overall score from 0 to 100, using any integer in that range. The score should reflect the paper’s actual
research quality, not just which anchor it is closest to.
Paper Excerpt
Analyst
PaperScope — Paper Cataloging Prompt
Y ou are a research paper analyst. Given a paper, produce a structured catalog entryof 13 fields whose purpose is to assess
whether and how hard the paper can be reproduced. The fields cover paper type, novelty, taxonomy, compute requirements, paid
resources, benchmarks, datasets, baselines, dependencies, code availability, reproduction difficulty, paper quality, and problem
novelty. Every score is an integer on a0–10scale, grounded in specific paper content; when uncertain, say so rather than guess.
Field 1: Paper T ype
Classify into one primary type, with justification:
•metric_method— introduces or improves a method, evaluated with measurable results.
•benchmark_dataset— the contribution is a benchmark, dataset, or evaluation suite.
•analysis_findings— an empirical discovery or insight rather than an improvement.
•theoretical— a formal result: proofs, bounds, complexity analysis.
•survey_position— aggregates or opines on existing work; no original experiments.
