On the Incompleteness of do-calculus for Universal
Identifiability
Yaroslav Kivva1 Aliaksandra Novik2,1 Negar Kiyavash1
1EPFL, Lausanne, Switzerland
2Imperial College, London, United Kingdom
Abstract
We study the problem of causal effect identification from anarbitrary set of obser-
vational and/or interventional distributions, which we callUniversal Identifiability
(uID). The uID problem generalizes existing classical identifiability (ID) and gen-
eral identifiability (gID) problems, which considered the identification problem
from either mere observational distributions or a specific type of interventional
distributions. Prior research has established graphical criteria to determine when
a causal effect is identifiable in ID and gID problems. Moreover, algorithms that
leverage do-calculus and basic probability manipulations have been proposed to
compute these effects. Consequently, it has been shown that do-calculus is both
soundandcompletein these problems. Despite these well-established results, a
formal definition of what it means for the do-calculus to be complete does not
exist. We propose a rigorous formalization for the completeness of the do-calculus
and show that the completeness results in previous work remain valid. However,
for more general problems, such as uID, the rules of do-calculus areno longer
complete. This is perhaps the reason why the uID problem has remained open thus
far.
1 Introduction
Estimating the causal effect of one set of random variables on another is a fundamental challenge in
various fields, including artificial intelligence, social sciences, healthcare, and economics. To solve
this problem, researchers collect observational and experimental data and harness the independencies
among the variables of interest (often encoded in a directed acyclic graph (DAG) [Pearl, 1995]).
When all the variables in the causal DAG are observed, then the causal effect P(y|do(x)) can be
calculated uniquely from the observational distribution [Geiger and Pearl, 1990]. However, if some
variables are not observed, then the causal effectP(y|do(x)) may not be identifiable (i.e., it cannot
be computed uniquely). Thus, understanding the conditions under whichP(y|do(x)) is identifiable
is widely studied in the literature.
In his seminal work, Pearl [1995] introduceddo-calculus rules that allow one to manipulate probability
functionsP(·) containing interventionsdo(·). To this day, do-calculus rules are the backbone of
all causal effect identification algorithms in DAGs. Sufficient conditions for identifiability were
proposed in [Pearl, 1995, Pearl and Robins, 1995, Kuroki and Miyakawa, 1999, Spirtes et al., 2000,
Tian and Pearl, 2002, 2003, Tian, 2004]. These works later culminated in the well-known classical
identifiability (ID) result of Shpitser and Pearl [2006a] and Huang and Valtorta [2006a]. Specifically,
they proposed a necessary and sufficient criterion to determine whetherP(y|do(x)) is identifiable
in a given causal DAGG from an observational distributionP(N) . Furthermore, they proposed a
procedure to compute the causal effect of interest fromP(N) and, based on it, concluded that the
rules of the do-calculus are sound and complete for this problem. In addition, Shpitser and Pearl
[2006b], Bareinboim and Pearl [2012], Lee et al. [2019, 2020], Correa et al. [2021], Kivva et al. [2022,

title: On the Incompleteness of do-calculus for Universal Identifiability

text:
2023] extend the results of the ID problem by targeting a conditional causal effect P(y|do(x),z)
and/or incorporating multiple observational distributions with a specific structure. Similarly, they
provided necessary and sufficient conditions under which the target causal effect is identifiable, along
with an algorithm to compute it. As a result, they concluded that do-calculus rules remain sound and
complete for the problem they studied. The identifiability problem has been studied in the presence
of side information of different types. For example, Tikka et al. [2021] considered the case where
the observations consist of multiple incomplete data sources, and Abouei et al. [2024a,b] studied the
problem under selection bias.
The issue with the treatment of completeness in the previous work is that the completeness of do-
calculus is proved by proposing aspecificsound and complete algorithm. This algorithm can compute
the causal effect as long as it is identifiable by a sequence of applications ofdo-calculus rules and
standard probabilistic manipulations. That is, if the effect is identifiable, the algorithm returns a valid
formula to compute, and if no formula is returned, then the effect must have been unidentifiable.
Therefore, the limitation of this approach is that it can only be used to prove completeness of do-
calculus rules through first identifying aspecificsound and complete algorithm, and in the absence of
such an algorithm, we cannot establish whether the rules ofdo-calculus are complete or not.
In this work, we address the conjecture that thedo-calculus is complete in the sense that if a causal
effect is identifiable, then it can be computed from a sequence of applying thedo-calculus rules. We
do so by providing a formal definition of completeness ofdo-calculus for any arbitrary identifiability
problem. Remarkably, to the best of our knowledge, no explicit formal definition of completeness
for a general setting exists in the literature. As we shall see, our definition is consistent with the
notions of completeness in the previously studied problems such as classical identifiability (ID) and
general identifiability (gID). We consider an extension of the general identifiability (gID) where
the restrictions on the graphical structure of observed distributions are relaxed. We show that in
this extension problem, called universal identifiability (uID), the rules ofdo-calculus areno longer
complete.
2 Preliminaries
2.1 Notation
Throughout the paper, we use capital letters (e.g. X) to denote random variables and their corre-
sponding lowercase letters (e.g.x) for realizations. Similarly, we use bold capital letters (e.g. X) to
represent a set of random variables (and their multivariate distribution) and bold lowercase letters
(e.g. x) for a specific realization of their multivariate distribution. Additionally, we denote by xS
the entries in x that correspond to the variables in S, i.e. the realization of the variables X∩S .
Furthermore, we use X(X) for the domain of random variableX and consequently X(X) for the
domain of the random vectorXwhich is equal to the Cartesian product Q
X∈X X(X).
This study assumes that the available data is generated by some probabilistic structural causal model
(SCM)M. The structural causal modelM=⟨G,{f V (·)}V∈V,{ϵ V}V∈V⟩ consists of the following
three main elements.
1.Causal graph G= (V,E) is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) on a set of vertices V with the set of
edgesE. The set of vertices V=N∪U consists of the set of all random variables in the system,
where N is the set of observed random variables and U is a set of latent variables. The set of edgesE
represents the causal dependencies between the vertices. For each edge (X,Y)∈E , we say thatX is
a parent ofY or, equivalently,Y is a child ofX. For arbitraryX,Y∈V , the vertexX is an ancestor
ofY andY is a descendant ofX if there is a directed path fromX toY in graphG. Note that bothX
andY are ancestors and descendants of themselves. Let PaG(X), ChG(X) denote the set of parents
and children of vertexX, respectively. With a slight abuse of notation, let AncG(X) and DeG(X)
denote the set of ancestors and descendants of X that belong to N in graphG. The aforementioned
definitions can be extended to sets of vertices via a union operation, e.g. PaG(X) =S
X∈X PaG(X).
For two disjoint subsets X,Y⊂V , letGX,Y denote the subgraph ofG obtained by removing all
incoming edges into X and all outgoing edges from Y. Also, disjoint sets X and Y ared-separated
by Z inG if all paths between X and Y are blocked1 by Z, which is denoted by X⊥ ⊥G Y|Z. Given
theglobal Markov property,X⊥ ⊥G Y|ZimpliesX⊥ ⊥Y|Z.

that any vertexU∈U has exactly two children and zero parents. This assumption is common in
the literature, since any SCMM has a semi-Markovian projection [Verma, 1993] that preserves all
causal relationships among the observed variables. Note that our results would be valid for general
SCM models. Furthermore, letGX denote the induced subgraph ofG by a set of variables X and
unobserved variables with both children in X. We say that X⊆N is an ancestral set in G, if
X=Anc G(X).
2.In SCM M the exogenous noises{ϵV}V∈V are mutually independent random variables, and each
random variableϵ V corresponds to the exogenous noise of a random variableV.
3.The set of functions {fV (·)}V∈V defines the relationship between the random variables in the
causal graphG through the structural equation V=f V (PaG(V),ϵ V ) for anyV∈V . In a causal
probabilistic model, the post-interventional distribution is defined bydo-operation. LetX⊆Vand

For the sake of simplicity, we further assume that all random variables arediscrete. Under such an

Markov factorization property, this set of conditional distributions induces a joint distribution over the

usedo(x)instead ofdo(X=x)to denote an intervention, e.g.P(y|do(x)) :=P(y|do(X=x)).
Finally, we useM(G) to denote the set of all possible SCMs with causal graphG such thatPM(n)>0
for anyM∈M(G) and arbitrary realization n∈X(N) . This is known as thepositivity assumption
which is crucial in the identifiability literature [Kivva et al., 2022].
2.2 Universal identifiability problem
Before presenting a formal definition of completeness, we define a general form of identifiability
problem.
Definition 1.Let aquery Q= (G,P) specify a causal graph G and a family P=
{P(A i|do(Bi),C i)}m
i=0, where (Ai,B i,C i) is a triple of disjoint subsets of N. ForM∈M(G) ,
writeQM = (G,PM) for the corresponding available distributions evaluated inM. Given disjoint

Definition 2(Universal Identifiability Problem (uID)).Let G be a given causal graph, and queryQ=

0,...,m . Then, for disjoint sets X,Y⊆N , the causal effectP(y|do(x)) is universally identifiable
(uID) fromQ ifPM(y|do(x)) is uniquely recoverable fromQM, in the sense of Definition 1, in

Note that classical ID or gID are special cases of uID problem, where query Q equals (G,P(N))
for ID problem and (G,{P(A i|do(N\A i))}m

isnot completefor uID after first providing a definition of completeness for the aforementioned
general form of identification problem.
2.3 Formal definition of completeness
In this section, we provide a formal definition for the completeness of do-calculus rules for the
identifiability problem that is in the general form of Definition 1. Note that classical ID, gID,
conditional gID (c-gID) [Kivva et al., 2023], and uID problems are specific forms of Definition 1,
so our definition of completeness applies to those problems as well. Before introducing our formal
definition, we need to review some preliminaries.
The rules ofdo-calculus were introduced by Pearl [1995] and defined as follows. Assume X,Y,W
andZare disjoint subsets ofV.
DR1.Insertion/deletion of observations. IfY⊥ ⊥GX Z|X,W:
P(y|do(x),z,w) =P(y|do(x),w).

In general, for the identification of the causal effect, there may exist some function f(·) that may
compute the target causal effect given the corresponding input, but there is no guarantee that this
function can be "well expressed". A classical example is the Abel–Ruffini theorem [Abel, 1824]:
there is no general formula in radicals for the roots of a polynomial of degree five or higher. Similarly,
there may be no guarantees that thedo-calculus is enough in terms of identifying the functionf(·).
Intuitively, the statement "do-calculus is complete" means that these rules provide acompleteset of
inference rulesthat suffice to identify an identifiable target causal effect, i.e. they generateall possible
algebraic transformationsneeded to express identifiable causal effects. Therefore, we would only
fail to find an expression for a causal effect in terms of available distributions via do-calculus rules
when the effect is unidentifiable.
We will allow the use of the standard probability manipulations defined below along with the
"do-calculus" rules.
Standard probability manipulation rules.SupposeY,X,WandZare disjoint subsets ofV.

P(y|z) ) of standard probability manipulation, that is why we do not include the independence rule in

From here on, we call the standard probability manipulation rules together with the rules of do-
calculus: the do-inferencerules. We are now ready to propose a formal definition for the completeness
ofdo-calculus.
Definition 3.Suppose Z,X,Y⊆N are three disjoint sets. The interventional probability
P(y|do(x),z) is do-identifiablegiven the query Q= (G,P) 2 if there is a sequence ofdo-inference
rules that transformsP(y|do(x),z)into an expression involving only distributions inQ.
Definition 4(Completeness of do-calculus). Do-calculus iscompletefor a specific identifiability
problem if every causal effect that is identifiable for this identifiability problem in terms of Definition 1
is alsodo-identifiable.
Remark.In addition to do-inference rules, we allow the use of standard arithmetic manipulations
such as associativity, the distributive law, and factoring out common terms.3
3Do-calculus is complete in ID, gID and c-gID problems
The problem of identifiability has been extensively studied in the literature under various assumptions.
In this section, we focus on the classic line of identifiability problems initiated by Tian and Pearl
[2003] and continued by Shpitser and Pearl [2006a,b], Huang and Valtorta [2006a, 2008], Lee et al.
[2019], Kivva et al. [2022, 2023]. All aforementioned identifiability results rely on a graphical
criterion based on the notion ofc-component, the definition of which can be found in Appendix A.1.
Note that these works are special cases of c-gID problem studied in Kivva et al. [2023].
2See Definition 1.
3Note that we do not allow operations that introduce new quantities into the expression at any stage and just
allow for sequential application ofdo-inferencerules to the terms in the existing expression.
4

text:
More specifically, Shpitser and Pearl [2006a] proposed a graphical criterion to solve the ID problem,
that is, the conditions under which the causal effectP(y|do(x)) of interest can be recovered uniquely
given the causal graphG and the observational distributionP(N) . When the conditions are satisfied,
the authors provided an algorithm that computesP(y|do(x)) based ondo-calculus rules and proba-
bility manipulations; otherwise, the causal effect cannot be recovered uniquely. As a corollary, they
concluded that the rules ofdo-calculus together with standard probability manipulations are sound
and complete for the classical ID problem. With a similar procedure, this result was extended for the
problems of gID and c-gID [Lee et al., 2019, Kivva et al., 2022, 2023]. It should be noted that these
completeness results are restricted by the contexts of ID, gID, and c-gID problems and the specific
algorithms proposed there.
Although for the aforementioned problems, the completeness of thedo-calculus through analysis of a
specific algorithm has been established, to the best of our knowledge, no formal definition for the
completeness ofdo-calculus rules prior to this work has been proposed in the literature. Therefore, it
is important to verify that our definition of completeness ofdo-calculus (Definition 4) is well aligned
with the previous results [Shpitser and Pearl, 2006a,b, Lee et al., 2019, Kivva et al., 2022, 2023] as
summarized in the following theorem. The proof of the theorem is in Appendix A.1.
Theorem 1. Do-calculus is complete in terms of Definition 4 for the ID, gID and c-gID problems
studied in [Shpitser and Pearl, 2006a], [Kivva et al., 2022], and [Kivva et al., 2023], respectively.

5 Conclusion
We gave a formal, standalone definition of completeness of the do-calculus for an identifiability
problem, one that does not require first finding a sound and complete identification algorithm for
that problem, and showed that it agrees with the existing completeness results for ID, gID and c-gID.
Our main result is that, for the uID problem, a natural extension of gID, the do-calculus is no longer
complete: there are causal effects that are uniquely identifiable from the available distributions but
cannot be obtained by any sequence of do-calculus rules and probability manipulations. This shows a
fundamental limitation of the do-calculus in more general identification settings, and suggests that
closing the remaining gaps in the literature will require identification tools beyond these rule-based
symbolic derivations.

FRAME: Form-Restricted Authoring with Model-Based Evaluation
Nan Jiang, Mohammed Mohsin Hussain, Onkar Tiwari, Ankit Jain†,
Thong Q. Nguyen†,Abhishek Agarwal,Vishal Chowdhary
Microsoft Office AI
{jiangnan,hussainmoh,Onkar.Tiwari,abhisag,vishalc}@microsoft.com
kitsrishjain@gmail.com,thongnguyen1292@gmail.com
Abstract
Many professional reports reuse the structure
of prior editions while updating the content.
We formalize this setting asform-restricted re-
port generation: given a sample report and
new grounding documents, generate a report
that preserves the sample’s form while accu-
rately reflecting the new evidence. We intro-
duce FRAME, a benchmark of 120 EDGAR-
and arXiv-derived instances across Financial
Quarterly, Financial Annual, Academic Simple,
and Academic Complex categories, built with
a temporal three-snapshot pipeline. We evalu-
ate outputs with three human-validated metrics:
structural similarity via semantic tree-edit dis-
tance, coverage via information unit recall, and
faithfulness via claim-level grounding verifica-
tion. Across five LLMs, open-source models
nearly match proprietary models on structure
but lag on coverage and faithfulness; all mod-
els perform better on financial than academic
reports, and performance declines with longer
outputs and more complex grounding.
1 Introduction
Large language models (LLMs) can now pro-
duce fluent long-form documents (OpenAI, 2023;
Grattafiori et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2023; Köksal
et al., 2023; Que et al., 2024), but many profes-
sional writing workflows are not open-ended. Ana-
lysts often reuse the form of an earlier report and
update it with new evidence: quarterly earnings
analyses, annual financial reviews, compliance re-
ports, and recurring literature surveys all preserve
structure while changing content. We call this set-
tingform-restricted report generation. It differs
from standard summarization because the model
must infer the target form from a sample report
while grounding new content in separate evidence
documents.
This setting is practically important and weakly
covered by existing benchmarks. Financial filings
†Work done while at Microsoft.
such as 10-Qs and 10-Ks follow stable conventions
while their data changes each period (Wu et al.,
2023; Islam et al., 2023); survey-style academic
reports similarly update an established organization
as new papers appear (Wang et al., 2024b). Existing
long-form, summarization, grounded-generation,
and data-to-document benchmarks (Köksal et al.,
2023; Que et al., 2024; Fabbri et al., 2019; Lewis
et al., 2021; Wiseman et al., 2017) do not directly
test whether a model can transfer document form
from one report while faithfully integrating new
evidence. Surface metrics such as ROUGE and
BERTScore also miss hierarchical organization and
grounding errors (Zhang et al., 2019).
We introduce FRAME(Form-Restricted
Authoring withModel-BasedEvaluation), a
benchmark of 120 instances across financial and
academic domains. Each instance contains a
sample report S, grounding documents G, and
a gold report Y . A temporal construction pairs
an earlier report with later evidence and target
output, while a controlled synthesis pipeline
keeps successive reports structurally aligned. We
evaluate five LLMs with three human-validated
metrics: structural similarity, information coverage,
and grounding faithfulness.
Our contributions are as follows:
• We formalizeform-restricted report genera-
tionas a distinct task and construct FRAME,
a benchmark of 120 instances across finan-
cial and academic domains with controlled
temporal structure.
• We develop a suite of evaluation metrics, i.e.,
structural similarity, coverage, and faithful-
ness, that go beyond surface-level comparison
and aligns well with human preferences.
• We provide a comprehensive empirical analy-
sis of five LLMs, revealing systematic perfor-
mance patterns:
1
arXiv:2611.08921v1 [cs.AI] 6 Nov 2026
title: Frame: Form-Restricted Authoring with Model-Based Evaluation

text:
1. Open-source models nearly match propri-
etary models on structural similarity but
lag substantially on coverage and faith-
fulness.
2. All models perform better on financial
reports than on academic reports.
3. Performance degrades with increased
task complexity, such as longer outputs,
longer grounding contexts, and more
complex structural requirements.
4. Longer outputs mainly hurt structural
quality and coverage, while faithfulness
remains stable only for GPT-5.
5. Longer grounding contexts reduce struc-
tural quality and coverage and increase
faithfulness instability for weaker mod-
els.
6. Reports with more tabular content tend
to improve coverage and faithfulness, es-
pecially for open-source models.
2 Related Work
2.1 LLM-Based Document Generation
Document generation has progressed from tem-
plates and neural data-to-document systems (Wise-
man et al., 2017; Shao et al., 2019) to retrieval-
augmented and long-form LLM generation (Lewis
et al., 2021). Recent work adds structure through
planning, schema post-processing, or style transfer
(Shen et al., 2025; Ning et al., 2024; Wu and Deng,
2025). These methods motivate structure-aware
generation, but they do not benchmark whether a
model can infer a target form from a prior report
and populate it with new grounding evidence.
2.2 Document Generation Evaluation
Surface-overlap metrics such as BLEU and
ROUGE often correlate poorly with human judg-
ments, while embedding metrics improve semantic
matching but miss discourse structure and factual
consistency (Liu et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2019).
LLM-as-judge methods better capture holistic qual-
ity and factuality, but still require task-specific vali-
dation (Que et al., 2024; Kulkarni et al., 2025).
Our evaluation combines three lines of work:
structure metrics based on tree alignment (Paaßen,
2018; Liu et al., 2025), faithfulness checks based
on entailment, QA, and atomic facts (Durmus et al.,
2020; Min et al., 2023), and coverage metrics
based on content units, nuggets, and semantic align-
ment (Nenkova and Passonneau, 2004; Zhang et al.,
2024; Zha et al., 2023). FRAMEbrings these di-
mensions together for form-restricted, evidence-
grounded report generation.
3 Benchmark Construction
We introduce FRAME, a benchmark forform-
restricted report generationbuilt from two com-
plementary source families: financial filings from
EDGAR and scientific papers from arXiv. This sec-
tion formalizes the task and explains how bench-
mark instances are derived from temporally ordered
snapshots (§3.1), describes the four categories and
how they differ (§3.2), details the domain-specific
synthesis pipelines that produce grounding doc-
uments and gold reports (§3.3), and summarizes
the resulting statistics (§3.4). Worked examples of
the synthesis pipeline and a concrete benchmark
instance are provided in Appendix A.
3.1 Task Formulation
Each benchmark instance is a triple (S,G,Y) :
asample report S that demonstrates the target
form,grounding documents G with updated evi-
dence, and a gold reportY . At inference time, the
model receives (S,G) and must generateY , jointly
transferring structure fromS and content fromG.
EDGAR filings and arXiv papers support this setup
because both provide recurring reports whose form
is relatively stable while content changes over time,
and they offer complementary evidence modalities:
financial data is table-dense, while academic data
is figure- and prose-rich.
Benchmark instance construction.For each do-
main (a company or research topic), we collect
three ordered snapshots t1 < t2 < t3. At each
timestamp, raw sources are converted into ground-
ing documentsDti and a gold reportRti. We then
form two benchmark instances by shifting a win-

3.2 Source Selection and Category Design
Within the two source families we define four cat-
egories, each with 15 domains and 30 instances
(yielding 120 instances in total; per-category statis-
tics in Table 1):
• Financial Quarterly: 10-Q filings covering a
single quarter. The gold report updates recur-
ring metrics (revenue, EPS, segment results)
from a compact evidence set.
• Financial Annual: 10-K filings covering a
full fiscal year. Substantially longer and struc-
turally richer than 10-Qs.
• Academic Simple: Literature synthesis over
a small set of arXiv papers on a topic (e.g.,
LoRA, LLM Agent); the gold report is a co-
herent survey of their key contributions.
• Academic Complex: Literature synthesis
over a larger paper set, requiring broader
cross-document aggregation and richer mul-
timodal understanding (more figures per
grounding set).
3.3 Data Synthesis Pipeline
Building valid benchmark instances requires
(i) constructing a diverse, multi-document ground-
ing setDti at each timestamp, and (ii) keeping the
gold reports Rt1,Rt2,Rt3 within a domain form-
aligned so an earlier report is informative as a sam-
ple. Figure 1 illustrates the full pipeline; we de-
scribe domain-specific grounding construction first,
then the shared report synthesis.
Financial grounding documents.Each iXBRL fil-
ing is converted to HTML with XBRL namespaces,
inline styles, and scripts stripped. An LLM then
(1)file-splitsthe cleaned HTML into semantically
coherent units (business overviews, risk factors,
segment results, financial statements, etc.), and
(2)enhances tabular contentinto well-formatted
Markdown so numerical evidence is accessible.
The resulting set mixes prose- and table-centric
documents.Financial Annualapplies the same
pipeline to longer, richer 10-K filings.
Academic grounding documents.Each arXiv
paper in a time window is HTML-cleaned and con-
verted by an LLM into structured Markdown, pre-
serving equations and tables.Academic Complex
uses more papers per window thanSimple.
Gold report synthesis.We synthesize Rti in four
steps, applied identically to both source families:
(1)Report structure synthesis, producing a hier-
archical JSON of sections and subsections with
element-level objectives; (2)Question augmenta-
tion, adding 5–8 guiding questions per section;
(3)Convert to Markdown outline, rendering the
JSON into a template with per-section placehold-
ers; (4)Gold report synthesis, filling each place-
holder by prompting an LLM with the full ground-
ing set, the complete structure, and the per-section
questions.
Steps (1) and (2) differ only in initialization.
Fort1 (form free) the LLM proposes a structure
from scratch based on Dt1; for t2 and t3 (form
restricted) it adapts the prior report’s structure to
the new grounding. This template-conditioning is
what keeps successive snapshots form-aligned and
makes the sample report informative. Appendix A
Figure 8 walks through the pipeline on Adobe’s
Q1 FY2025 10-Q. The full text of every prompt
used by the grounding-document and gold-report
stages is reproduced in Appendix C.

4 Evaluation Metrics
We evaluate generated reports along three comple-
mentary dimensions: structural similarity to the
gold report (§4.1), coverage of the gold report’s
information (§4.2), and faithfulness to the ground-
ing documents (§4.3). We then validate all three
metrics against human judgments (§4.4).
4.1 Structural Similarity
We extract each report into an ordered structure
tree whose nodes represent sections, subsections,
tables, figures, or bullet groups. We then align the
generated and gold trees with a semantic tree-edit
distance: node substitutions use embedding-based
semantic similarity, while insertion and deletion
handle missing or extra structure. The final score
is a normalized similarity in[0,1].

objective description, and ordered children. An
LLM extracts this tree in JSON format. For two
nodesr ands, semantic similarity combines node

4.4 Alignment with Human Judgment
To validate our automated evaluation approaches,
we randomly sampled 10 data points: 5 from the
Financial Ann. category and 5 from the Financial
Qtr. category. For each sampled data point, we
prompted the five studied models to generate a
report, and then performed human evaluation and
alignment analysis on the resulting outputs.
4.4.1 Structural Similarity
For structural similarity, we evaluate our algorithm
by measuring how well its induced ranking cor-
relates with human preference rankings. In this
pipeline, report structures are extracted using GPT-
5 with high reasoning effort, and node embed-
dings for semantic similarity are obtained using
text-embedding-small. Rather than asking anno-
tators to assign absolute similarity scores, which is
cognitively demanding and prone to inconsistency,
we ask them to rank the five model-generated re-
ports for each data point from best to worst based

text:
on structural quality. We then compute the same
ranking using our STRUCTURALSIMILARITYal-
gorithm and measure agreement between the two
rankings using Spearmanrand Kendallτ.
Projection Function.Table 2 reports ranking cor-
relations across different projection functions, us-
ing a fixed type weight w= 0.2 and no depth
adjustment. The results show that the choice
of projection function meaningfully affects align-
ment with human preference. The linear projec-
tion yields the weakest correlation, while both
power and RBF projections improve over this base-
line. The RBF kernel with δ= 0.10 achieves the
best correlation with human rankings (r= 0.780 ,
τ= 0.661 ). We attribute this to the tendency of
cosine similarities between text embeddings to con-
centrate in a high range, leaving little variation
to distinguish between nodes that are genuinely
similar and those that merely share surface-level
vocabulary. Figure 3 visualizes these projection
functions and shows that the RBF mapping places
stronger emphasis on high-similarity regions near
x= 1 (x being the cosine similarity). The RBF
kernel’s sharply peaked response nearx= 1 am-
plifies these fine-grained differences, producing a
more discriminative score that better reflects human
perceptions of structural similarity. We therefore
adopt RBF withδ= 0.10 as the default projection
function in all subsequent experiments.
Type Weight.After fixing the projection function
to RBF withδ= 0.10 , we analyzed the effect of the
type-weight hyperparameterw in STRUCTURAL-
SIMILARITY. We tested w∈{0.1,0.2,0.3,0.5,0.7}
and measured rank correlation with human prefer-
ence. As shown in Table 3, performance peaks at
w= 0.2 (Spearman r= 0.780 , Kendall τ= 0.661 ),
while both smaller and larger values lead to lower
alignment.
This trend suggests that assigning a moderate
weight to node type and a larger weight to node
objective text yields the best agreement with human
judgment. When w becomes large (e.g., 0.5 or
0.7), the model overemphasizes coarse structural
type matching at the expense of semantic content,
reducing discriminative power.
Depth Adjustment.We further evaluated the
optional depth-adjusted substitution cost under
the best non-depth setting found above (RBF
projection with δ= 0.10 and type weight w=
0.2). We compare a no-depth-adjustment base-
line against depth-adjusted variants with γ∈
{0.1,0.3,0.5,1.0,2.0} . Table 4 shows that depth
weighting has only a limited effect on alignment
with human preference: Spearmanr varies within
a narrow range (0.770–0.790), and Kendall τ re-
mains similarly stable (0.647–0.666).
Although a few depth-weighted variants slightly
improve one correlation metric, the gains are small
and not consistently reflected in both metrics. We
therefore do not use depth adjustment in the default
configuration and retain the simpler unweighted
formulation.
4.4.2 Coverage
For each of the 10 sampled data points, we ran-
domly selected 50 information units extracted by
the LLM judge from the ground-truth reports, re-
sulting in 500 information units in total, each with
an LLM-judge score indicating how well the in-
formation unit is covered in the model-generated
report. For this metric, we use GPT-5 with high rea-
soning effort for both information-unit extraction
and coverage validation.
Each information unit was then evaluated by two
human annotators, who assigned coverage scores
on a three-point scale: 0 for not covered in the
model-generated report, 50 for partially covered,
and 100 for covered. We use this three-point scale
for human annotators, rather than the same contin-
uous 0–100 scale used by the LLM judge, because
humans are generally more reliable and consistent
when making categorical judgments than when as-
signing fine-grained numerical scores.
These human judgments were then compared
with the continuous scores produced by our auto-
mated LLM judge. Because the comparison in-
volves continuous LLM-generated scores and dis-
crete ordinal human ratings, we use multiple com-
plementary metrics to assess inter-rater agreement.
We report:
• Percentage Agreement( PA) (Hunt, 1986),
which measures the proportion of judgments
where the absolute difference between human
and LLM scores falls within a specified thresh-
old. Scores range from 0–100%, with higher
values indicating more frequent direct align-
ment. We report PA@0 (exact agreement) and
PA@25 (agreement within one rating level)
because PA@25 matches the granularity of
averaged human ratings (0, 25, 50, 75, 100 af-
ter averaging two annotators’ scores), making
it particularly meaningful for practical align-
ment in our setting.

• Quadratic Weighted Kappa( QWK) (Co-
hen, 1968), a metric designed for ordinal cate-
gorical data that accounts for the magnitude
of disagreement by assigning quadratically
increasing penalties to larger discrepancies
while correcting for chance agreement. Re-
ported on a 0–1 scale, higher scores indicate
stronger agreement beyond chance. QWK is
particularly appropriate for our setting, where
disagreement between scores of 0 and 25
should be penalized less than disagreement
between 0 and 100.
• Intraclass Correlation Coefficient( ICC)
(Shrout and Fleiss, 1979), a standard met-
ric in inter-rater reliability studies that as-
sesses the degree of absolute agreement be-
tween two measurement methods. Similar
to QWK, it typically ranges from 0–1, with
scores closer to 1 indicating stronger consis-
tency and absolute agreement between raters.
We use ICC(3,1) , a two-way mixed-effects
model with absolute agreement, which treats
the LLM and human annotators as fixed raters
evaluating the same set of information units.
Table 5 shows that our automated coverage eval-
uation achieves strong alignment with human an-
notations across all metrics. The PA@0 of 75.0%
indicates that three-quarters of LLM judgments
exactly match the averaged human scores, while
PA@25 of 93.2% shows that the vast majority of
automated assessments fall within one rating level
of human judgment. The highQWK score of 0.919
and ICC of 0.926 both indicate substantial agree-
ment, with values approaching 1.0 suggesting near-
perfect consistency between automated and human
evaluations. These results validate the reliability of
our LLM-based coverage assessment system.

the coverage section. We use GPT-5 with high

data points, we randomly selected 50 statements
that had been extracted and evaluated by the LLM
judge from model-generated reports, resulting in
500 statements in total. Each statement was ac-
companied by the LLM judge’s score indicating
the degree to which the statement was faithfully
supported by the grounding documents.
Two independent expert annotators evaluated
each statement’s faithfulness using the same three-
point scale: 0 for not faithfully supported by
grounding documents, 50 for partially supported,

human assessments. However, the QWK of 0.663
and ICC of 0.664 are lower than those for cover-
age, suggesting moderate agreement. This pattern
indicates that while the LLM judge’s faithfulness
assessments are practically aligned with human
judgment in terms of ordinal ranking (as evidenced
by high PA metrics), determining the precise de-
gree of faithful support is inherently more nuanced
and subjective than coverage assessment, making
perfect agreement more challenging.
5 Experimental Setup
We evaluate five state-of-the-art LLMs spanning
proprietary and open-source families. Because our
grounding documents include images (Academic
categories) and long contexts, we restrict selec-
tion to natively multimodal models with at least
a 128K-token context window. The two propri-
etary models are GPT-5 (Singh et al., 2025) (400K
context, “high” reasoning effort) and Claude-4.5-
Sonnet (Anthropic, 2025) (200K context). The
three open-source MoE/dense vision-language
models are Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B (Bai et al., 2023;
Wang et al., 2024a; Bai et al., 2025; Yang et al.,
2025) (30B total / 3.3B active, 256K context), Phi-
4-multimodal (Abdin et al., 2024) (5.6B dense,
128K context), and Kimi-VL-A3B (Team et al.,
2025) (16B / 2.8B active, 128K context). All
five models receive the same one-shot generation
prompt, conditioned on the sample report S and
the grounding documentsG.
6 Results
6.1 Overall Performance
Table 6 reports the five LLMs across the three met-
rics. We highlight four findings.
Finding 1: Open-source models match propri-
etary models on structural similarity.The struc-
tural scores are tightly clustered across model fam-
ilies, suggesting that current open-source systems
can often infer and reproduce the sample report’s
form.
Finding 2: Proprietary models significantly out-
perform open-source models on coverage and
faithfulness.The largest gaps are not in layout repli-
cation but in content completeness and evidence
grounding. This indicates that form transfer is eas-
ier than selecting all salient information and sup-
porting each generated claim.
Finding 3: Models perform better on financial
reports than on academic reports.Financial re-
ports have standardized, numerical formats that
make recurring content and evidence easier to iden-
tify. Academic reports are more flexible and multi-
modal, producing larger drops, especially for open-
source models.
Finding 4: Model performance generally de-
grades with increased task complexity.Harder
categories reduce structural similarity and cover-
age for most models. Faithfulness is more stable
for proprietary systems but remains high-variance
for weaker models, particularly on academic data.
6.2 Case Study
Figure 4 illustrates the patterns of §6.1 on a con-
crete Financial Quarterly instance (Salesforce 2026
Q1). All five models reproduce the gold report’s
section layout with nearly identical structural sim-
ilarity (0.409–0.430), confirming that template
replication is the easiest sub-task. However, the
generated content diverges sharply. GPT-5 and
Claude correctly identify the reporting period as
Q1 FY2026 and faithfully reproduce key figures
such as revenue, growth rates, and the average share
repurchase price of $273.42. In contrast, open-
source models misidentify the quarter (Qwen3
and Phi-4 label it “Q3 FY2025”; Kimi labels it
“Q4 FY2025”), hallucinate incorrect figures (e.g.,

that all three proprietary models cover. This case
concretely demonstrates how structural parity can
coexist with large gaps in coverage and faithful-

6.3 Performance Trend Analysis
In order to better understand the factors driving
model performance variation, we analyze how per-
formance changes with key characteristics, includ-
ing gold output report length, grounding document
length, and the number of tables in the gold output
report.
Length of Gold Output Report.Figure 5 shows
three consistent patterns across length buckets.
First, structural similarity generally declines as re-
ports grow longer, indicating that matching the
target template becomes harder for long outputs.
Second, coverage decreases for all models from the
shortest bucket onward, with only minor rebounds
at the longest bucket for some. Third, GPT-5 is the
only model with clearly stable faithfulness across
length buckets; Claude-4.5-Sonnet shows a slight
decline, and open-source models fluctuate substan-
tially, consistent with weaker grounding robustness.
Finding 5: Longer outputs mainly hurt struc-
tural quality and coverage, while faithfulness
remains stable only for GPT-5.
Length of Grounding Context.Figure 6 shows
that all three metrics decline as grounding con-
texts grow longer, with some intermediate non-
monotonicity. Structural similarity and coverage
drop for all models. On faithfulness, only GPT-5
stays stable; Claude-4.5-Sonnet drifts slightly, and
open-source models degrade with higher variance.
Finding 6: Longer grounding contexts make ev-
idence selection and reasoning harder, generally
reduce structural quality and coverage, and in-
crease faithfulness instability for open-source
models.
Number of Tables in Gold Output Report.Fig-
ure 7 reveals several trends with table count. Struc-
tural similarity peaks at a moderate-to-high number
of tables rather than at very low counts. Coverage
rises with table count for Claude-4.5-Sonnet and all
three open-source models, suggesting tabular con-
tent is easier to cover. Faithfulness for open-source
models also trends upward despite local fluctua-
tions, suggesting better grounding with more tab-
ular evidence.Finding 7: Reports with more
tabular content tend to improve coverage and
faithfulness, especially for open-source models.
7 Conclusion
We introduced FRAME, a 120-instance benchmark
for form-restricted report generation, where mod-
els must transfer a sample report’s structure while
grounding new content. We also developed three
human-validated metrics for evaluating this task,
covering structure, information coverage, and faith-
fulness.
Across five LLMs, our results show that tem-
plate replication is substantially easier than com-
plete and faithful content grounding: open-source
models approach proprietary models on structural
similarity but lag on coverage and faithfulness. Per-
formance is stronger on financial reports than aca-
demic reports, declines with longer and more com-
plex inputs, and improves when evidence is more
table-rich. These findings highlight form-restricted
report generation as a practical but still challenging
test of long-form, evidence-grounded generation.

Limitations
FRAMEhas two potential limitations about the
scope of the dataset and the evaluation metrics.
Domain coverage.The benchmark covers two do-
mains, financial filings (SEC 10-Q/10-K) and arXiv
literature reviews, chosen for their structured form
and public availability. Other professional report-
writing settings (e.g., clinical reports, legal briefs,
technical documentation) likely exhibit different
structural conventions and grounding patterns, and
our results may not directly transfer.
Reliance on an LLM judge.Coverage and faith-
fulness are scored by an LLM judge (GPT-5 at high
reasoning effort). We validate the judge against ex-
pert human annotations and report alignment met-
rics (PA, QWK, ICC) in §4.4, but the judge inherits
the underlying model’s biases and may underper-
form on content outside its training distribution.

text:
C Benchmark Construction Prompts
This appendix lists the financial data-synthesis prompts used by the pipeline in §3.3. The academic
pipeline follows the same overall structure with domain-specific adjustments for paper HTML, figures,
and literature-review style output.
C.1 Grounding Document Synthesis
These prompts implement the financial grounding-document construction described in §3.3, turning an
iXBRL filing into structured Markdown documents.
C.1.1 Financial Grounding Documents
File split prompt.The below prompt is used to partition the cleaned filing HTML into semantically
coherent files (business overviews, risk factors, segment results, financial statements, etc.).
File Split Prompt (Financial Quarterly)
You are an expert in document analysis and structuring. Your task is to analyze a given SEC filing (HTML format) and
reverse-engineer its contents. Your goal is to deconstruct the single HTML document into a set of logically distinct
source files, simulating the internal documents a company would prepare before a formal filing.
The final output must be a`FileSet`JSON object containing these reconstructed files, each with its own logical content
structure.
# JSON Output Structure
The output must be a`FileSet`containing a list of`File`objects. The entire output must be a single, valid JSON object
conforming to the following Python dataclass definitions:
```python
class SectionElement(BaseModel):
section_type: Literal["section"]
heading: str
objective: str
children: List["Element"] = Field(default_factory=list)
class TableElement(BaseModel):
section_type: Literal["table"]
columns: List[str]
objective: str
class TextElement(BaseModel):
section_type: Literal["text"]
objective: str
Element = Union[SectionElement, TableElement, TextElement]
class File(BaseModel):
file_name: str
content: SectionElement
class FileSet(BaseModel):
files: List[File]
```
# Instructions
1.Reconstruct Purpose-Driven Source Files: Your primary goal is to create a`FileSet`containing several distinct files (
ideally 8-12).
- Each file must represent a logical, standalone source document, not merely a slice of the original SEC filing.
Structure each file to serve a specific purpose, as if it were an internal company document. For example, instead of`item
-8`, create a file named`annual_financial_statements`to hold financial content.
-Aim to balance the length and scope of each file. If a topic (such as "financial statement notes") contains
extensive information, split it into multiple files based on logical subtopics, so that no single file becomes
disproportionately large.
2.Ensure Comprehensive Coverage: You must process the entire input HTML document.
- Focus on extracting all substantive information while omitting generic content. Your combined files must include all
crucial quantitative data (financial statements, metrics, statistics) and qualitative insights (strategic analysis, risk
factors, management's outlook). The content of your proposed files, when combined, must cover all the useful and specific
information without any information loss.
- Exclude non-essential information such as boilerplate legal disclaimers, repetitive headers/footers, and standard
corporate governance text that are unlikely to change year-over-year or lacks specific insight.
3.Structure Content Logically: Within each file, build a clear hierarchical structure using nested nodes. Ensure every
section (`section_type`: "section") is well-balanced.
-Do not create sections that consist solely of tables. Each section must include at least one text element (`
section_type`: "text") to introduce, analyze, or provide context for the data before or after any table. This approach
ensures each file is coherent and reads fluently.
4.Define Naming and Objectives: When creating the`file_name`,`heading`, and`objective`, do not refer back to the SEC
filing or its structure. Imagine each file is created for its own internal purpose and has nothing to do with the SEC
filing; the filing simply uses these files as sources of raw data. For every element in your structure, write a concise`
objective`describing the purpose of that element and what information need to be covered by that element.
5.Generate a JSON Output: Construct the final`FileSet`as a single, valid JSON object that adheres to the provided
schema.
# Example JSON Output
Below is an example of the output object structure.

Content Generation Prompt (Financial Quarterly)
You are an expert document analyst and report writer. Your task is to populate a given Markdown Report Template by

# Instructions
1.Complete the Template: Your primary task is to find and replace every TODO comment within the Markdown Report Template.
Use the provided Grounding Document to find the correct information for each replacement.
-Text: For any TODO comment asking for text (e.g.,`TODO: Write text here`), replace the entire comment with clear
and factual prose extracted from the source document.
-Table: For any TODO comment before a table (e.g.,`TODO: Fill in the table here`), accurately complete the table
with the corresponding data from the source document.
- Ensure the final report is a clean document. All TODO comments must be removed and replaced with the requested
information.
2.TODO Objectives: Every TODO comment in the Markdown Report Template includes an objective, which describes the purpose
and the content that needs to be covered by the TODO. When completing a TODO, you must obtain all relevant information
from the grounding HTML document that matches the objective and use it to fulfill the TODO.
3.Strictly Adhere to Placeholders: This is acriticalrule. You must only write content where a TODO comment is present.
Do not modify, add to, or delete any of the existing text, headings, or formatting in the template. The template's content
, outside of the TODO comments, must remain completely untouched.
4.Write a Factual, Standalone Report: All information must come directly from the Grounding Document. However, the final
report must be a self-contained document that reads as if it were authored independently. Do not include any phrases that
refer back to the source SEC filing, such as "According to the 10-K," "As stated in the filing," or "The document
indicates...". The report should stand on its own without any reliance on the source document.
5.Preserve Structure and Formatting: You must keep the original structure, headings, and all other Markdown formatting of
the template. Your only job is to fill in the blanks designated by TODO.
6.Final Output: Your response must be only the completed Markdown report. Do not include any introductory text,

text:
Report Structure Synthesis Prompt – Form-Free (Financial Quarterly)
You are an expert content strategist specializing in information synthesis. Your task is to analyze a collection of
grounding documents, identify the critical information, and propose a cohesive outline for a new, consolidated report. The
goal is to synthesize diverse information from the source documents into a single, fluent, and logical narrative.
The grounding documents are provided as a sequence of documents, with each document represented as a Markdown code fence.
You must output the proposed report outline as a single JSON object.
# JSON Output Structure
The output must be a JSON object representing a tree structure. The root must be a`SectionElement`node. Each node in the
tree must conform to the following Python dataclass definitions:
```python
class SectionElement(BaseModel):
section_type: Literal["section"]
heading: str
children: List["Element"] = Field(default_factory=list)
class TableElement(BaseModel):
section_type: Literal["table"]
columns: List[str]
objective: str
questions: List[str] = Field(default_factory=list)
class TextElement(BaseModel):
section_type: Literal["text"]
objective: str
questions: List[str] = Field(default_factory=list)
Element = Union[SectionElement, TableElement, TextElement]
```
# Instructions
1.Synthesize and Structure: Read all the provided grounding documents. Your primary goal is to identify the main themes,
key data points, and important narratives. Propose a new report structure that logically combines this information:
- This structure must be hierarchical and granular, with great readability.
- Avoid creating long flat sections, instead you should break long sections into nested subsections and continue
nesting with sub-subsections, as deep as necessary to keep each part focused.
- Each top-level section must represent a distinct, high-level theme from your analysis. Inside each section, you
could create nested subsections.
2.Prioritize Importance: Be selective. You do not need to include every piece of information. Focus only on the
significant sections, text, and tables that are essential for the final report. Omit redundant details, boilerplate text,
or minor points.
- A good practice is to identify and structure the report around the10-12most important and informative tables from
the source material. Focus your outline on these key tables and the corresponding text needed to create a cohesive

Scientific Discovery in Clinical Data

ABSTRACT
Automated scientific discovery has the potential to advance understanding of disease mechanisms and accelerate iden-
tification of early disease markers 1. Manual data annotation is infeasible at population scale, motivating methods
that automatically extract pre-defined phenotypes in multimodal and unstructured clinical data 2, 3. Such pre-defined
feature sets determine and limit which associations these approaches can discover. This limitation extends to agentic
AI systems that use these tools to query population-scale data 4, 5. In contrast, foundation models (FMs) trained
on large volumes of clinical data can perform tasks beyond their training objectives 6. This suggests their latent
embeddings may represent novel or unexplored features that could yield insights into disease mechanisms, yet such
latent features remain diﬀicult to interpret. To address this challenge, we introduce Glyph, an automated multistage
framework that extracts features from multimodal and unstructured clinical data using FMs and sparse autoencoders,
interprets them as coded clinical concepts, and evaluates their value for clinical scientific discovery. We applied Glyph
to multimodal clinical data consisting of abdominal CT volumes, CT radiology reports and laboratory measurements
from 41,628 patients across different institutions. At the discovery site, we tested 604,185 concept–outcome associa-
tions, focusing on 141 prognostic outcomes most strongly predicted by FM embeddings. This yielded 397 predictive
concepts supported by 4,463 Bonferroni-significant associations, recovering established prognostic relationships across
several disease axes, including hepatic, renal, cardiovascular and oncologic disease. Moreover, a majority of discov-
ered associations were automatically reproducible in held-out cohorts across different sites. Separating embeddings
into concepts further enabled confounder adjustment that attenuated associations with markers of general illness
severity, preserved key disease-specific associations and revealed independent systemic risk markers. Compared with
disease markers obtained from automated literature search, disease associations of the top ten Glyph concepts were
reproduced more frequently in the pooled held-out cohort with significantly larger median odds ratios. This revealed
gaps in the clinical literature, highlighting the underexplored prognostic value of Glyph concepts, suggesting new
predictive targets. We envision that interpretability can extend beyond a mechanistic understanding of neural net-
works to connecting implicitly learned features with clinical knowledge and establishing their significance for patient
outcomes. We release Glyph at https://github.com/StanfordMIMI/Glyph to enable and share discoveries in other
clinical domains.

†Co-senior authors.

1 Introduction
Identifying early disease markers has repeatedly transformed clinical practice and patient outcomes 7.
Clinical discovery is inherently challenging as evidence of potentially novel markers is captured across
diverse, often unstructured and high-dimensional modalities, including 2D and 3D imaging, laboratory
results, and textual reports 6. Moreover, the growing volume of clinical data, including approximately
300 million CT scans acquired worldwide each year 8, creates opportunities to identify new markers and
uncover unknown associations with a broader range of clinical outcomes. Yet this growth also highlights
a gap in our ability to process these data at scale, given the time and expertise required to manually
define, annotate, and validate candidate disease markers.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly proposed as a means of accelerating scientific discovery 1. In
protein folding and materials science, targeted models have sharply reduced the time and cost of identi-
fying promising candidates 9–11. Attempts to automate clinical science have searched large databases of
manually coded phenotypes through phenome-wide association studies (PheW AS) 2, 12. Efforts to accel-
erate this approach use deep learning or agents to automate the annotation of phenotypes directly from
images, but still restricts investigation to a preselected set of chosen markers 3, 4, 13. As a result, clinical
discovery still lacks an eﬀicient framework for identifying open-ended, reproducible, and independent
disease markers within multimodal data.
One potential solution lies in foundation model (FM) embeddings. Trained on large volumes of multi-
modal medical data, FMs produce embeddings that characterize patient states 14. Such embeddings have
been observed to perform well on tasks they were not explicitly trained for 14–17, including disease prog-
nosis and risk stratification, suggesting that they contain clinically meaningful associations beyond their
original training objectives. However, these markers remain entangled within high-dimensional vectors,
making them diﬀicult to isolate and evaluate as candidate markers. Recently, mechanistic interpretabil-
ity18–20 has emerged as a self-supervised approach to uncover interpretable concepts encoded within FM
embeddings, without the need for prospective annotation. Yet its broader potential for transforming
FMs into engines of clinical discovery remains largely unexplored.
To address this gap, we introduce Glyph, a framework that turns foundation model (FM) embeddings
into concepts for clinical discovery. The name derives from “glyph,” or a symbol that conveys meaning,
reflecting our goal of giving hidden information a form that can be studied. Drawing on mechanistic
interpretability, Glyph discovers coded concepts directly in FM embeddings and detects them across
patients without requiring candidate markers to be defined and annotated in advance. These extracted
concepts are measurable, interpretable patterns in patient data that together preserve the FM’s pre-
dictive capacity. Glyph integrates them with established clinical variables and tests their associations
with disease-related outcomes across patient populations. This enables eﬀicient, closed- and open-ended
discovery that is infeasible with embeddings alone or with agentic systems operating on a limited set of
pre-defined concepts. Our contributions are as follows:
1. Establishing the concept space. To make FM embeddings useful for discovery, we develop
the Glyph framework to first represent such embeddings in sets of sparse features, and then filter
and interpret these as clinically meaningful concepts. Specifically, we evaluated features for sig-
nificant prognostic associations, reproducibility across three sites, persistence after adjustment for
measured confounders, and overall interpretability. Glyph identified 397 predictive concepts bear-
ing 4,463 significant associations to 141 future disease outcomes meeting a Bonferroni threshold of
p ≤ 8.28 × 10−8. Identifying concepts with at least one significant association yielded a space of
high-risk concepts, capturing disease risk across modalities. Concept interpretations and prognostic
associations also reproduced in external cohorts.
2. Rediscovery and discovery . The validated concept space recovered established prognostic rela-
tionships across several disease axes, including hepatic, renal, cardiovascular, and oncologic disease.
When tested in held-out cohorts, these associations reproduced across institutions. Glyph then ex-
tended these findings by linking established risk markers to additional outcomes and identifying
reproducible prognostic associations that remain poorly characterized in the literature. Beyond
disease-specific risk profiles, Glyph identified systemic risk markers across modalities, with one

Glyph can be applied to any data expected to contain useful markers for discovery. b Foundation

adjustment for potential confounders. Glyph revealed that nearly half of the high-risk imaging
concepts were not consistently documented in the accompanying radiology reports.
3. Comparison with literature We investigated whether and in which domains Glyph brought
additional prognostic value over the clinical literature. To this end, a co-scientist agent processed
342,647 clinical papers covering each discovery axes, and reproduced 412 published markers in our
data. We found using just ten Glyph concepts per axis led to significantly stronger models in
external data than literature markers alone (3.34% AUC gain, p = 2.66 × 10−28), with predictive
improvements of up to 11.7% in specific axes. Comparing the top ten Glyph concepts with the top
ten literature markers per outcome, selected at the Discovery Site, Glyph associations reproduced
more frequently in the pooled held-out cohort (64.8% vs. 41.2%, p = 2.54 × 10−6) at higher median
confounder-adjusted odds ratios (1.31 vs. 1.16, p = 5.0 × 10−5).
4. Comparison with pre-coded phenotypes Similarly, we also asked whether pre-coded pheno-
types could support the same discoveries, comparing Glyph with an automated PheW AS-style
analysis of ICD-derived Phecodes. Across the same outcomes, associations from Glyph reproduced
more often than those from Phecodes at Internal Test (69.3% vs. 49.1%, p = 9.77 × 10−4) and
External Site #1 (74.3% vs. 63.9%, p = 2.93 × 10−3), and had larger median effect sizes. Overall,
Glyph showed a complementary benefit to existing disease coding protocols and clinical literature.
5. Open-source and use. Glyph extracts additional value from existing pretrained FMs, without
retraining. To enable researchers to find our concept space in their cohorts, or build new concept
spaces from their data, we open-source Glyph at github.com/StanfordMIMI/Glyph, installable
via pip install glyph-discovery . A validated concept space also supports other applications
including explainable patient-level predictions and retrieval. We also release the Glyph MCP,
enabling clinicians, engineers, and AI agents to investigate patient data and test open-ended hy-
potheses and applications through concepts.
2 Results
Glyph was deployed in a multimodal Discovery Site cohort of 14,652 patients, comprising 20,391 3D ab-
dominal CT volumes (3,262,560 preprocessed slices), radiology reports (8,083,882 tokens), and 1,588,003
lab entries spanning 350 types (Figure 1a). These three modalities were embedded using the Merlin im-
age encoder 14, Qwen3-Embedding-8B21, and Labs FM, respectively (Figure 1b). Glyph then decomposes
these embeddings into sets of sparse features (Figure 1c). We identified when Glyph concepts rediscov-
ered established prognostic associations, and when they reveal complementary associations absent from
the literature or not discoverable by automated PheW AS-style discovery analysis (Figure 1d).
To enable this analysis, we developed a rigorous pipeline to process sparse features in embeddings as
concepts useful for discovery (Figure 1e–g). To maximize discovery yield, we used the Discovery Site
validation set to identify 141 disease outcomes whose onset 1–4 years after abdominal CT was most
predictable from FM embeddings (see Methods, Section 4.5). These outcomes spanned hepatic, renal,
cardiovascular, metabolic, and neurological disease. To surface high-risk concepts, Glyph filters features
to those with at least one significant prognostic association (Figure 1e), before assessing their independent
risk adjusted for specific confounders (Figure 1f), and estimating each features’s clinical interpretation
(Figure 1g). At each step, we assessed the reproducibility of these analyses across three held-out cohorts
comprising 26,976 patients and 45,139 CT studies, with 7,222,240 preprocessed CT slices, 14,342,345
radiology-report tokens, and 2,184,424 lab entries (Figure 1h). This pipeline led to the set of 397 high-
risk concepts that can be used in downstream discovery workflows (Figure 1i).

Test, External Site #1 and External Site #2 cohorts. The trained SAEs were then applied zero-shot to
each site’s embeddings to re-extract the same set of 4,285 features. Overall, these features preserved the
majority of the original embeddings’ variance and predictive performance (see Extended Figure 7 and
Section 4.3). These features were then filtered by Glyph’s discovery pipeline, explored in detail in Sections
2.2, 2.3 and Section A.1, yielding the set of 397 validated, high-risk concepts. Textual interpretations of
these concepts were then attempted via a contrastive approach detailed in Section A.1 and illustrated in
Figure 12. Throughout, we refer to concepts by a modality-prefixed index: R for radiology report, I for
imaging, and L for laboratory concepts.
High-risk concepts clustered into neighborhoods reflecting liver, kidney, cardiovascular, musculoskeletal,
and malignant disease, as well as inflammatory states and abnormal cholesterol (Figure 2c). Within the
liver and kidney neighborhoods, granular concepts from different modalities overlapped. Concepts for
fluid accumulation, including effusions and ascites, lay nearby and were closely correlated with laboratory
concepts reflecting hypoalbuminemia, reflecting known comorbidities to liver cirrhosis 22. Laboratory
concepts also provided information complementary to imaging and reports, such as evidence of abnormal
cholesterol, situated adjacent to kidney disease 23, and inflammatory markers. Other regions contained
high-risk imaging concepts with no corresponding report concepts, suggesting radiological features that
are not routinely documented. The concept space also isolated the presence of medical devices, including
tubes and drains, and postsurgical artifacts, that could confound predictions based on whole embeddings.
It also integrated established variables not derived from SAEs, such as patient age and smoking status,
alongside the extracted concepts, situating these adjacent to cardiovascular and musculoskeletal disease,
which are also known correlates 24. These 397 high-risk concepts are explored for their discovery potential
in the remainder of the paper.
2.2 Glyph identified reproducible markers of future disease risk
Having constructed the concept space, we tested whether it contained any significant, reproducible high-
risk markers for future disease onset. Because the cohort consisted of patients who underwent abdominal
CT, associations were expected to be enriched for abdominal pathology. ICD codes provided broad,
cross-institutional outcome labels but may be affected by undercoding, miscoding, delayed entry, and
institutional differences in coding practices. Associations may also reflect clinical workflows, motivating
the confounder analysis in Section 2.3.
To identify high-risk concepts, we first computed per-standard-deviation odds ratios (ORs) between all
pairings of 4,285 features and 141 outcomes, yielding 604,185 candidate associations at the Discovery Site.
These comprised 467,415 radiology report, 48,363 imaging, and 88,407 laboratory associations (Figure 3a;
see Methods, Section 4.6). To set a stringent threshold for evidence, we applied the Discovery filter ,
requiring a Bonferroni-corrected p ≤ 8.28 × 10−8 and OR > 1.0 (Figure 3b). This analysis uncovered 4,463
significant associations (0.739% of all pairs), establishing that the concept space contains signals of future
disease across radiology reports (858; 0.184%), imaging (2,251; 4.65%), and laboratory measurements
(1,354; 1.53%). This narrowed the space to the 397 high-risk concepts with at least one significant
association used in the remainder of the analyses (as shown in Figure 2b).
Having identified thousands of significant associations, we then assessed whether any were reproducible
in the internal and external sites. This was tested using a less conservative Reproducibility filter, afford-
ing a 5% false discovery rate via the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure (see Methods, Section 4.7). Of the
4,463 promising associations, 3,095 (69.3%) were reproduced without calibration on the Internal Test
cohort of 3,667 patients (see Figure 3c). Remarkably, a greater number, 3,314 (74.3%), were reproduced
at the secondary site, External Site #1, reflecting its larger cohort of 17,224 patients and indicating that
associations generalized across institutions. Moreover, External Site #2 which was out of state, repro-
duced 1,701 (54.7%) of the radiology-report and imaging associations, reinforcing the generalizability of
these findings across institutions. Overall, this showed that Glyph automatically surfaced concepts that
were reproducibly predictive of future disease across patient populations.

Rediscovery of hepatic disease progression: Among the strongest predictors of hepatic disease were
L108 (cholestasis), I65 (splenomegaly), I21 (ascites) and R85 (liver cirrhosis and varices). R85 predicted
future primary liver cancer with odds ratios and p-values of 2.45 p = 1.2 × 10−39, 2.55 p = 1.2 × 10−7, 1.73
p = 1.3×10−9, 1.64 p = 5.7×10−9 at the Discovery Site, Internal Test, External Site #1 and External Site
#2, respectively (Figure 4f). It was also associated with portal hypertension (OR 2.19–3.57), with both
associations replicating across all four cohorts. These findings accord with established complications
of cirrhosis 25, 26. R85 was associated with the onset of 39 of 141 outcomes (Figure 3e), tracing the
recognised natural history of cirrhosis through jaundice, hepatic necrosis, varices, splenomegaly and
coagulopathy. Associations also extended to renal, respiratory and infection diagnoses, consistent with
reported evidence of these conditions in patients with cirrhosis 27–29.
L108 also recovered the majority of hepatic outcomes. These included future primary liver cancer (OR
2.08–2.57) and portal hypertension (OR 1.63–2.92). Li and Apte linked bile-acid accumulation in cholesta-
sis to liver injury and cancer 30, but did not evaluate any prognostic relationships. Reproducible associa-
tions extended to future liver transplantation and coagulation (see Figure 3g).
Rediscovery of renal disease progression: The strongest marker of renal disease was L84 (azotemia),
which reproducibly traced the stages and complications of chronic kidney disease, including chronic renal
failure (2.02–2.52), progression to stage IV disease (1.77–2.73), initiation of renal dialysis (2.04–3.21),
eventual kidney transplantation (2.53–2.87), and the metabolic consequences of uremia in anaemia of
chronic kidney disease (1.87–2.44) and hyperkalaemia (1.80–2.07) 31. L84 also extended beyond renal dis-
ease to cardiovascular, metabolic, infectious, respiratory, hepatic and haematological outcomes. Elevated
blood urea nitrogen (BUN), a measure of azotemia, predicted mortality after acute coronary syndromes
in prior work, although that study did not examine later diagnoses across disease groups 32.
By comparison, L69 (impaired renal function, defined by increased creatinine and BUN and reduced
eGFR) was far more specific, as its seven significant associations were all renal (against 11 for L84
among 76 spanning every disease group). Its effects were smaller on all four shared outcomes (1.09–1.54
versus 1.77–2.87), it did not predict dialysis initiation or acute renal failure. Notably, urinary protein
loss was not isolated by any single concept, despite albuminuria being a second axis of chronic kidney
disease staging alongside eGFR 31; nephrotic-range values were distributed among concepts dominated
by hypoalbuminaemia (L34, L45, L61, L87).
Unlike the hepatic rediscoveries, no radiological concept captured renal disease progression, consistent
with the weak association between visible kidney structure and renal function 33. Specifically, R398
(kidney atrophy) and R302 (polycystic kidney disease) reached only modest effect sizes (1.16–1.41) and
replicated inconsistently. By contrast, I109 (aortic calcification) and L127 (cytopenia) were associated
with 10 and 12 of 13 renal outcomes, respectively, with strong reproduction across cohorts. Prior studies
established abdominal aortic calcification as a cardiovascular prognostic marker in CKD 34; here it also
marked later renal diagnoses more consistently than kidney-specific imaging findings.
Rediscovery of cardiovascular risk markers: Glyph recovered early cardiovascular markers of cal-
cification and atherosclerosis. Specifically, R21 (calcification of the coronary arteries or cardiac valves)
was a prominent report-derived cardiovascular predictor, reproducibly predicting myocardial infarction
(OR 1.25–1.70), heart failure with preserved (1.58–1.83) and reduced (1.40–1.92) ejection fraction, and
coronary atherosclerosis (1.52–1.97). Prospective studies have linked coronary and mitral annular calci-
fication to subsequent cardiovascular events 35, 36. Both R21 and R3 (moderate to severe atherosclerotic
disease) replicated strongly at External Sites #1 and #2 (R21: 100% and 73.7%; R3: 91.7% and 86.1%),
well above the 33.8% cohort average at External Site #2.
Imaging concepts outperformed report-based concepts: the imaging group, comprising I109 (abdominal
aortic calcification), I15 (abdominopelvic atherosclerosis) and I26 (aortic atherosclerosis; Figure 3e), cov-
ered 23 of 28 cardiovascular outcomes (82.1%), against 19 of 28 (67.9%) for the report-based group, and
replicated more consistently across the Internal Test and External Sites #1 and #2 (96.1%, 98.7% and

Most inflammatory concepts (L0, L3, L4, L8, L92) did not have substantial associations with cardiovas-

L1488 similarly captured abnormal RR intervals, but neither concept’s adjusted associations reproduced
consistently, and both may reflect ECG testing prompted by suspected cardiac disease. Concepts captur-

in this cohort, despite the established causal role of LDL cholesterol in atherosclerotic cardiovascular
disease42, potentially due to widespread use of statins in this cohort.
Concepts encoding systemic risk markers: Beyond organ-specific associations, several concepts
behaved as broad markers of systemic risk, each associated with more than half of the outcomes tested
and spanning nearly every disease group. L127 (cytopenia) and L108 (cholestasis) had the broadest
risk profiles, associated with 89 (63.1%) and 87 of 141 outcomes (61.7%) respectively, each spanning
10 of 11 disease groups. L108 extended beyond liver disease to predict future infection, electrolyte

(53.9%) and spanned all 11 groups. This breadth generalized across institutions: L108 reproduced 82 of

and 86 (97%), and L84 69 (91%) and 75 (99%), each well above the cohort-wide rates of 69.3% and
74.3%.
Fluid accumulation behaved similarly: I21 (ascites) was associated with 68 outcomes across 10 groups
and carried the largest single effect of any systemic concept (OR up to 3.17), while I25 (combined
ascites, anasarca and effusion) reached 62 outcomes across all 11 groups, and R101 (pleural effusion

examine in Section 2.3. A second family encoded hypoalbuminaemia and anaemia (L34, L59, L77, L82,

ratios of 1.42 to 1.62.
Infection and sepsis: L127 (cytopenia) 45 and L108 (cholestasis) were each associated with 14 of 22

I76 (severely distended bowel pattern) was associated with 5 of 20, including bacterial pneumonia, sepsis
