2.3 Glyph enabled confounder analysis to identify independent disease markers
Having identified significant, reproducible disease markers, we assessed whether they persisted after
adjustment by potential confounders. A concept encoding ascites may appear to predict liver cancer
because underlying cirrhosis can cause both fluid accumulation and an increased risk of liver cancer (see
Figure 4a). The majority of FM outputs are only tested for predictive correlation to an outcome, and
rarely test if this prediction is potentially confounded. This extends the scientific reach of foundation
models from correlation towards independence analysis. Glyph concepts, due to being both interpretable
and sparse, can be tested for independence alongside known clinical covariates and risk markers in
confounder analysis frameworks. As in the association study, these results identify associations that
persist after adjustment for measured clinical variables and other concepts, rather than establish causality.
We adjusted each significant association for confounders by applying double machine learning (DML)
(see Figure 4b and Methods, Section 4.8). 16 confounders were drawn per-outcome, including the top
10 significantly associated concepts, and six universal clinical covariates covering age, sex, race, BMI,
alcohol use, and smoking. Applying the Confounder filter to the 4,463 promising associations on the
Discovery Site, 1,198 (26.8%) retained an adjusted OR > 1.0 (Figure 4c). Fewer associations were
retained at the Internal Test Site and External Sites #1 and #2, potentially reflecting lower statistical
power, variation in FM reproducibility, and differences in population distributions. At External Site
#2, 643 of 3,109 associations (20.7%) survived the Confounder filter . In the following, we study which
significant associations withstood adjustment, while also noting groups of concepts that were most heavily
attenuated. Unless otherwise specified, results refer to the Discovery Site.
Independence of hepatic disease risk markers: R85 (cirrhotic liver morphology and varices) was
associated with 9 of 11 hepatic outcomes at the Discovery Site, and 6 of these 9 remained significant after
confounder adjustment (see Figure 4d). Among these were known consequences of cirrhosis, including
portal hypertension (adjusted OR 2.46 p = 3.0 × 10−4, 2.35 p = 1.4 × 10−1, 3.10 p = 1.2 × 10−3, 1.77
p = 2.3 × 10−9), liver abscesses (2.98 p = 1.5 × 10−16, 3.15 p = 2.7 × 10−8, 3.19 p = 1.1 × 10−7, 1.87
p = 1.4 × 10−11), primary liver cancer (4.07 p = 1.2 × 10−71, 2.13 p = 4.1 × 10−7, 1.79 p = 1.9 × 10−8, 1.68
p = 2.4 × 10−7) and liver transplantation (2.11 p = 1.6 × 10−8, 2.06 p = 1.0 × 10−7, 2.15 p = 1.0 × 10−10,
0.99 p = 9.8 × 10−1), with reproduction across all three held-out cohorts in the majority of cases. By
contrast, I21 (ascites) and I25 (ascites, anasarca or pleural effusion) retained only one of 10 and none
of eight Discovery Site associations, respectively, after adjustment that included R85. This pattern is
consistent with fluid accumulation being less specific to hepatic disease than cirrhotic morphology and
varices26.
Independence of renal disease risk markers: As in hepatic disease, confounder adjustment concen-
trated the renal signal on known markers of renal disease. L84 (azotemia) retained 8 of its 11 Discovery
Site renal associations, covering chronic renal failure, stage IV disease, kidney transplantation, oliguria
and anuria, hypertensive chronic kidney disease, secondary hyperparathyroidism, acute renal failure and
the composite chronic kidney disease outcome, with effects broadly unchanged by adjustment (ORs 1.71–
2.53 vs. adjusted ORs 1.27–2.95). L69 (impaired renal function) retained 6 of its 7 associations, all renal,
at consistently smaller effects (ORs 1.24–1.44 vs. adjusted ORs 1.45–1.85), remaining highly concen-
trated on the kidney. The broader I109 (aortic calcification) and L127 (cytopenia) markers retained 4
of 10 and 4 of 12 renal associations, respectively, indicating a mixed profile. At Discovery, R398 (kidney
atrophy) retained its sole renal association with hypertensive chronic kidney disease after adjustment.
R302 (polycystic kidney disease) retained associations with stage III chronic kidney disease and kidney
transplantation, but not oliguria and anuria. In contrast, markers of fluid accumulation and general

or portal-hypertensive findings, therefore captured adjusted risk extending beyond hepatic disease. I65
(splenomegaly) retained 30 of its 48 associations (63%) after adjustment, spanning eight outcome groups.
These included subsequent primary liver cancer, consistent with the association between incidentally
detected splenomegaly and later liver cancer diagnosis reported in a recent population-based cohort
study49. This association persisted across all four cohorts after adjustment for the clinical variables and
concepts reflecting liver dysfunction, coagulopathy and ascites, but was attenuated when cirrhosis and
other liver-related findings were included in a targeted analysis (as shown in Figure 4h).
Remarkably, systemic risk markers from labs concepts maintained a majority of their associations after
adjustment. Specifically, L108 (cholestasis) maintained 49 of its 87 associations (56%), covering 9 of
the 11 outcome groups. Abnormal liver tests have been linked to haemodynamic status in patients
with established heart failure 50, but did not assess whether cholestasis preceded later cardiac diagnoses,
as observed here. L127 (cytopenia) retained 45 of 89 associations (51%) after adjustment (see Figure
4g). A prospective population study linked lymphopenia, a subtype of cytopenia, to later infection,
including sepsis 45. L127 captures a broader cytopenia pattern associated with outcomes across disease
groups. L84 (azotemia) retained 28 of 76 associations (37%), with associations attenuating in respiratory,
cardiovascular and oncologic disease but persisting for renal, metabolic, and haematologic outcomes (see
Figure 4g).
In contrast, concepts involving hypoalbuminaemia (L34, L59, L77, L82, L87, L91, L124) were heavily
attenuated, retaining only 0–17.1% of their associations. Hypoalbuminaemia is an established indepen-
dent predictor of mortality 51. In our cohort, however, many of its associations with subsequent disease
attenuated after adjustment, consistent with their partly reflecting underlying illness 52. The extent of
attenuation may be specific to patients undergoing abdominal CT and warrants evaluation in broader
patient populations.
Independence of infection risk markers: At Discovery, L127 (cytopenia) retained 10 of its 14
infection associations after adjustment, compared with 8 of 14 for L108 (cholestasis). L91 (severe hypoal-
buminaemia) retained associations with sepsis and bacteremia. I54 (intra-abdominal or pelvic abscess)
retained associations with bacteremia and drug-resistant infections, indicating that localized infectious
findings retained prognostic information beyond accompanying abnormalities.
Independence of metastatic sequelae: R64 (metastatic disease) maintained adjusted associations
with cachexia 47 at Discovery and Internal Test, acute renal failure 53 at External Site #1, and sepsis 48
across these three cohorts, consistent with reported systemic sequelae of advanced cancer.

2.4 Glyph finds novel associations beyond the clinical literature
Having established that Glyph concepts identify significant, reproducible markers of disease risk, we next
asked whether they represent novel discoveries beyond those reported in the clinical literature. Specif-
ically, we evaluated 21 future outcomes spanning multiple disease groups. To characterize published
abdominal imaging and laboratory markers for these outcomes, an agent acting as a co-scientist system-
atically identified and filtered 342,647 unique publications using the PubMed API 54 and Paperclip 55
(see Methods for additional details). This yielded 412 literature-derived markers that could be tested
in our data, averaging 19.6 per axis, which we then systematically re-evaluated. These included both
singular measurements, such as low albumin, and composite clinical predictors such as FIB-4 56, which
combines age, transaminases and platelet count. Finally, to assess whether Glyph concepts add prog-
nostic value beyond these markers, we selected the top ten Glyph concepts per outcome using evidence
from the Discovery Site, excluding excluding concepts that primarily reflect care intensity such as R399
(pacemaker). We then fit one model using the literature-derived markers alone and another combining
them with the selected Glyph concepts to test whether Glyph concepts identified prognostic information
beyond published markers.
Results of percentage gains in AUC are presented in Figure 5b. Both the literature baseline and Glyph
enhanced model were fit at the Discovery Site, and evaluated on the pooled Internal Test and External Site
#1 cohorts. We found that, per-outcome, literature baselines achieved 0.749 AUC (95% CI 0.737–0.761)
on held-out data, and that ten Glyph concepts significantly improved this to 0.774 (95% CI 0.762–0.785,
p = 2.66 × 10−28). Observed benefits were most concentrated in metabolic, haematologic and infectious
outcomes, averaging a relative AUROC improvement of 6.64% (95% CI 5.26–8.01%). These groups also
had 5.0 fewer papers on average (10.9 vs 15.9) than the other groups evaluated, indicating they may be
under-researched.
We then explored which concepts were driving gains over literature markers. The top ten Glyph concepts
per outcome, selected at the Discovery Site, reproduced more frequently in the pooled held-out cohort
(64.8%) than the literature-derived marker set (28.2%, p = 1.86×10−18), the top ten performing literature
markers (41.2%, p = 2.54 × 10−6), and corresponding Phecodes (54.8%, p = 0.062). After adjustment for
age, sex and race, reproduction required p < 0.05 and the same effect direction as at the Discovery Site.
Median confounder-adjusted odds ratios in the pooled evaluation cohort were also significantly higher
for Glyph (1.31) than for the literature-derived marker set (1.10, p = 5.0 × 10−5), the top ten literature
markers (1.16, p = 5.0 × 10−5), and corresponding Phecodes (1.19, p = 5.0 × 10−5; Figure 5c). A direct
comparison between Glyph concepts and all Phecodes is provided in Supplementary Section A.2 and
Figure 13. Overall, this suggests that Glyph captures prognostic information in abdominal CT cohorts,
accessible through FM embeddings, that is either underrepresented in the established clinical literature,
or is diﬀicult to measure with conventional clinical markers.
To review specific axes in detail, we plotted markers according to their publication dates and assessed
which of the ten Glyph concepts were represented among the literature-derived markers. Adding Glyph
concepts did not significantly improve AUROC across every axis. For example, no significant improve-
ment was observed for dementia (0.871 to 0.870, p = 0.80) or Alzheimer’s disease (0.840 to 0.842, p = 0.71),
suggesting little to no additional prognostic information beyond the literature-derived markers for these
outcomes. In contrast, for heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF; Figure 5d), Glyph iden-
tified risk markers not represented among the literature-derived markers, including I65 (splenomegaly),
L84 (azotemia), L127 (cytopenia), L108 (cholestasis), and I87 (uncharacterized hepatobiliary pattern).
Adding Glyph concepts significantly improved AUROC by 3.6% from 0.824 to 0.854 ( p = 4.7 × 10−7).
Similarly, along the abdominal health to sepsis axis, adding Glyph concepts significantly increased AU-
ROC by 4.9% from 0.673 to 0.706 ( p = 3.2 × 10−7; Figure 5e). These gains demonstrate additional
prognostic information beyond the evaluated literature-derived markers, including contributions from
imaging findings not routinely documented in reports, such as I76.

through a set of illustrative workflows for agents and clinicians. The MCP enables more complex,

disease, for example testing whether an undocumented imaging concept repeatedly linked to septicemia is
confounded by body composition or existing disease markers (Figure 6). Concept ranking for a target
outcome: A user can query the concept space directly in natural language, for example asking for the top
associations for future myocardial infarction; the Glyph MCP resolves this to the underlying outcome and
returns the concepts with the largest prognostic association among those surviving Bonferroni correction,
predominantly drawn from laboratory panels in this example (Extended Figure 8).
Outside of discovery, Glyph also brings explainability to typical use of foundation models: Individual-
ized risk explanation: Beyond population-level associations, Glyph concepts can explain an individual
patient’s risk prediction, attributing it to the specific concepts driving that prediction and contextual-
izing them against population-level evidence (Extended Figure 9). Patients-like-me: Given a query
patient, Glyph retrieves the most similar patient in the cohort and explains their similarity in terms
of shared concepts and the rarity of their joint activation, illustrating how the concept space supports
case-based reasoning beyond simple embedding distance (Extended Figure 10).
3 Discussion
In this paper we introduced Glyph, a method for transforming foundation model (FM) embeddings into
engines of scientific discovery. At its core, Glyph supposes that FM embeddings, trained on large volumes
of clinical data, encode established clinical markers alongside unexplored features that could reveal new
insights into disease mechanisms. To extract these features, Glyph builds on mechanistic interpretability
and establishes their value as coded, interpretable clinical concepts for scientific investigation. In our
dataset, the resulting set of extracted concepts enabled rediscovery of established organ-specific and
systemic risk markers associated with the onset of future disease. In addition, we were able to automati-
cally establish that many of these findings were reproducible across three sites without model retraining.
Transforming embeddings into separate, interpretable and measurable concepts enabled adjustment for
potential confounders identified directly from the data, beyond routinely collected covariates or those
selected from prior clinical knowledge. Applying Glyph on large clinical datasets revealed complemen-
tary associations and risk factors not reported in established clinical literature. Moreover, complement-
ing literature-derived markers with Glyph concepts significantly improved prognostic prediction across
several disease axes. Together, these findings demonstrate that interpretability can extend beyond a
mechanistic understanding of neural networks, enabling features learned implicitly by FMs to interact
directly with existing clinical knowledge and available clinical outcomes.
Glyph rediscovered known patterns of disease progression across hepatic, renal, and cardiovascular axes.
It also recovered known cross-system associations, e.g. linking renal decline to metabolic comorbidities
or valvular atherosclerosis to cardiovascular and neurological disease. Our observations also reflected
the complementary strengths of different clinical modalities. Specifically, laboratory concepts more
consistently captured renal disease progression than kidney-related imaging findings. Similarly, imaging-
derived findings often showed more reproducible associations than findings documented in radiology
reports, particularly for atherosclerotic and hepatic risk markers. Confounder adjustment further char-
acterized discovered associations by attenuating associations known to involve nonspecific markers of ill-
ness severity, such as fluid accumulation and hypoalbuminemia. It also emphasized published prognostic
relationships, including associations of imaging-derived vascular findings with neurological outcomes 37,
renal findings with downstream cardiovascular outcomes 57, and the renal consequences of cholestatic
liver disease 58. Together, the recovery of known disease relationships in patients undergoing abdominal
CT supported the validity of the concept space as a foundation for the exploration of novel hypotheses.
Beyond rediscoveries, Glyph expanded the clinical picture of disease risk, revealing prognostic infor-
mation beyond what established literature-derived markers capture. In particular, comparisons across
modalities highlighted laboratory markers such as cholestasis and cytopenia. After adjustment, these
markers retained broad systemic risk profiles, while other laboratory concepts showed more specific as-
sociations. Azotemia, for example, retained a predominantly renal, metabolic, and hematological risk
profile. Beyond laboratory markers, Glyph uncovered previously uncharacterized imaging phenotypes
within CT embeddings, including a mixed hepatobiliary pattern whose adjusted associations remained
significant across all outcome groups. Furthermore, complementing literature-derived markers with a
selection of top performing Glyph concepts reproducibly improved prognostic prediction, particularly in
16/36
title: Glyph: An Interpretability Engine for AI-Driven Scientific Discovery in Clinical Data

text:
metabolic, hematological and infectious outcomes, indicating that existing published markers lack prog-
nostic information presently available in abdominal CT and laboratory data. Together, these findings
demonstrate a practical approach to exploring a systems-level perspective on disease 59, 60 using routinely
acquired clinical data. They also motivate evaluating several laboratory markers and imaging phenotypes
as potential targets for opportunistic or incidental screening.
Comparison with coded phenotypes further characterized the clinical information captured by Glyph.
Phecodes, which group ICD codes into clinically meaningful categories, provide an established basis for
automated PheW AS discovery 2. In some cases, directly matched Phecodes showed the same disease
associations as Glyph concepts, but with overall smaller effects that often did not reach significance. For
these clinical findings, the stronger signal captured by Glyph enabled both rediscoveries and candidate
discoveries that were not detected using diagnosis codes alone. Where Phecodes yielded stronger asso-
ciations, they reflected related conditions captured in the broader clinical record, beyond the scope of
abdominal CT and laboratory data. Across the selected outcomes, this broader coverage yielded more
significant associations overall, whereas Glyph associations had larger median effects and higher repro-
duction rates. Together, these findings suggest that Glyph complements the coded record by making
additional phenotypic information in imaging and laboratory data accessible for discovery.
Several clinical and technical considerations are important in interpreting our findings. Primarily, our
selection criteria restricted the cohorts to patients undergoing abdominal CT across acute and outpatient
settings. This selection likely enriched the study population for abdominal illness, influencing both the
associations detected and their estimated prognostic value. For example, enrichment for abdominal
disease in this cohort may have contributed to the prominence of markers of hepatobiliary disease and
renal dysfunction, such as cholestasis and azotemia. In addition, enrichment for abdominal disease
could partly explain why hepatobiliary abnormalities featured among the strongest adjusted markers of
cardiovascular outcomes, alongside established vascular, renal and haematological risk markers. Future
work could reproduce these analyses in broader patient populations to assess whether the observed
associations and relative prognostic value of these markers are preserved.
Furthermore, outcome data used in our study warrant further consideration. We used Phecodes derived
from ICD codes as outcome data to standardize evaluation across institutions 2. However, such coded
data may introduce noise and uncertainty, e.g. regarding the precise timing of observed disease patterns.
Consequently, some associations may capture existing but undocumented disease rather than risk of
future disease onset, while cases never assigned the corresponding code may be missed entirely. Refining
outcome labels through clinician adjudication of longitudinal records against predefined diagnostic crite-
ria could correct diagnosis and timing, but would require extensive chart review, potentially supported
by automated search of clinical notes. Ultimately, prospective studies using predefined diagnostic criteria
and systematic follow-up would be required for stronger validation of these outcomes.
Glyph enabled systematic confounder adjustment across a broad set of clinical concepts. Associations
that persist after adjustment indicate that related concepts provide prognostic information beyond clini-
cal covariates and other identified concepts, but do not establish that they represent independent disease
processes or causal drivers of disease on a retrospective dataset. Broader clinical coverage, including
additional imaging, clinical notes, categorical laboratory results, flowsheets, medication use, and genetic
factors, could help account for omitted factors and reveal further confounders and candidate markers.
Furthermore, the fixed correlation threshold used in our analysis was designed to exclude potential
mediators, downstream consequences through which the tested concept could affect the outcome, but
adjustment results were sensitive to the chosen threshold. Future work should guide confounder selection
using knowledge of disease mechanisms, rather than statistics alone 61.
Future work could extend the systematic comparison with published literature presented in Section 2.4
beyond the selected outcomes. Although it requires substantial token usage, this assessment provides
a framework for distinguishing established relationships recovered by Glyph, published associations not
detected in our cohorts, and potentially novel findings. Future work could also investigate how concepts
change over time and how their combinations contribute to disease risk. The analyses shown in this work
related concepts measured around individual CT examinations to future outcomes. Repeated measure-
ment could reveal when concepts emerge, how they evolve, and how their relationships change through
disease progression, providing temporal evidence to guide causal investigation. Combined with more
17/36
title: Glyph: An Interpretability Engine for AI-Driven Scientific Discovery in Clinical Data

text:
complete treatment histories, these trajectories could support investigation of changes associated with
clinical intervention. Changes in concept activation could also be evaluated as quantitative indicators of
disease state or treatment response by comparing their sensitivity with existing clinical measures. Beyond
these temporal extensions, our PheW AS analysis tested concepts individually and did not assess their
combined prognostic information. Future work could examine combinations and interactions between
concepts to identify more specific clinical phenotypes and risk associations not apparent from individual
markers.
Technical considerations and insights arise both from the source embeddings and from how their features
are extracted and interpreted. Text embeddings yielded finer-grained concepts than image embeddings,
even though radiology reports provide a compressed description of the images. This observation moti-
vates future work in designing image encoders for fine-grained concept discovery, alongside methods for
resolving more specific findings within existing embeddings. We also extracted embeddings separately
by modality, which simplified attribution of concepts to their source and examination of relationships
across modalities. However, some predictive patterns may be inherently multimodal, motivating joint
embeddings that could capture combinations of imaging, laboratory, and report findings not fully repre-
sented in any single modality. One insight from our confounder analyses is that prediction models built
on FM embeddings can draw on both potentially actionable markers and confounded proxies for illness.
Risk scores derived from the full FM embedding may therefore identify patients at risk without reliably
guiding how that risk can be reduced.
Textual interpretations describe the clinical findings associated with a feature, but do not necessarily
establish its precise clinical meaning. In a subset of extracted concepts, automated interpretation required
a combination of a small number of distinct clinical or imaging findings, suggesting that not all concepts
were monosemantic. It remains unclear whether this reflects polysemanticity in the FM embeddings,
failure of the SAE to separate distinct features, or a property of underlying data, in which certain
features frequently co-occur making feature separation diﬀicult. Clinical knowledge could guide when
related concepts should be grouped or separated into more specific findings, with Glyph providing an
eﬀicient basis for refining and testing these definitions. Future work could also complement our global
evaluation with local comparisons against neighboring concepts and clinically similar cases that do not
activate the concept in question. These comparisons could help distinguish defining findings from co-
occurring data properties, severity, or clinical context.
In conclusion, Glyph provides a framework for extracting knowledge from foundation models, enabling
reproducible, population-scale discovery of disease markers and associations. Glyph can be applied to
any dataset represented by FM embeddings to rapidly investigate a chosen discovery axis, using an
agentic co-scientist framework to assess the novelty and added value of extracted findings against the
published literature. This enables researchers to automatically validate data-driven insights, such as
those presented here, or discover and share new concept networks and insights from their own datasets.
Overall, we envision that Glyph can accelerate clinical science by establishing a standard for sharing
validated FM features as data-driven phenotypes, connecting discoveries across datasets with existing
clinical knowledge.

4 Methods
4.1 Datasets
All datasets are partitioned into a Discovery Site and a series of Testing sets. The Discovery Site is used
to train sparse autoencoders, select disease outcomes, interpret concepts, and rank associations. Testing
sets are held out entirely and used solely to assess whether insights replicate in patient cohorts that
played no part in discovery, in order of increasing institutional distance from Stanford. All datasets were
collected under IRB approval with a waiver of informed consent owing to retrospective use.
Discovery Site – Stanford Main hospital. The Discovery Site cohort comprises consecutive abdom-
inal CT examinations performed at Stanford academic medical center from December 2012 to October
2018, yielding 20,391 CT studies from 14,652 unique patients (3,262,560 CT slices, 1,588,003 lab entries,
and 22,781,540 historical diagnoses). No patient contributed studies to more than one split. We divide
the cohort into a train set of 15,331 studies from 11,009 patients (2,452,960 slices, 6,083,609 report to-
kens, 1,194,451 lab entries, 17,017,170 diagnoses) and a validation set of 5,060 studies from 3,643 patients
(809,600 slices, 2,000,273 report tokens, 393,552 lab entries, 5,764,373 diagnoses). Embedding normaliza-
tion statistics are computed on the Discovery Site. Finally, all datasets contain abdominal CT images
and radiology reports that capture the current health of the patient; laboratory analyses are restricted
to the Discovery Site, Internal Test and External Site #1. All have longitudinal ICD codes with at least
4 years of follow-up for association studies, and the six universal clinical covariates, including race.
CT preprocessing follows 14. From each study, the series with the greatest number of axial slices was
selected to maximize information content, and a contrast-phase detection algorithm confirmed that 97%
of selected series were portal venous phase. Volumes were preprocessed by orienting axes (left–right,
posterior–anterior, inferior–superior), resampling to 1.5 mm in-plane resolution and 3 mm slice thickness,
clipping and normalizing Hounsfield units from [−1000, 1000] to [0, 1], and center-cropping to 224 × 224 ×
160 voxels.
Report preprocessing follows 14. Only the findings section of each report was used, as it provides the most
granular per-organ-system observations. It covers the lower thorax, liver and biliary tree, gallbladder,
spleen, pancreas, adrenal glands, kidneys and ureters, gastrointestinal tract, peritoneal cavity, pelvic
organs, vasculature and lymph nodes, and musculoskeletal system.
Longitudinal lab measurements were collected from the EHR for each patient. Only numerical lab types
were retained, defined as those where at least 90% of recorded measurements were numeric, resulting
in 350 lab types (Supplementary Table 10). To reduce noise in dense measurement periods, a quarterly
downsampling strategy was applied, retaining only the last recorded value per patient, lab type, and
calendar quarter, using only measurements taken within the year prior to the CT scan date. Each lab
value was z-score normalized per lab type and clamped to [−3, 3] to limit the influence of extreme outliers.
For each patient encounter associated with a CT scan, all ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes assigned during that
encounter were collected and mapped to hierarchical phenotypes using PheW AS Phecode mapping 2,
collapsing 16,553 distinct ICD codes to 1,692 phenotype categories.
Internal T est cohort – Stanford Main hospital. The Internal Test cohort contains 5,137 CT studies
from 3,667 unique patients drawn from the same institution as the Discovery Site (821,920 CT slices,
405,802 lab entries, 6,134,090 diagnoses). These patients were held out from all stages of discovery and
represent the first test of reproducibility under matched distributional conditions.
External Site #1. The External Site #1 cohort contains 25,803 CT studies from 17,224 patients at a
community hospital outside Stanford (4,128,480 CT slices, 1,764,079 lab entries, 19,610,547 diagnoses).
No data from this cohort was used at any stage of discovery or model training, and the shift in patient
population and clinical practice makes it a more demanding test of generalization.
External Site #2 – Mayo Clinic. The Mayo Clinic cohort consists of patients across four Mayo
Clinic hospitals, comprising 14,199 CT studies from 6,085 patients. No data from this cohort was used

4.2 Foundation Models
Each data modality is encoded by a the most performant foundation model chosen at the time of the
study. FM weights are frozen throughout all downstream analyses; the SAEs and association pipelines
operate entirely on static embeddings produced by these models.
CT imaging For CT images, we use Merlin 14, a 3D inflated ResNet-152 pretrained on abdominal CT
volumes paired with radiology reports and EHR diagnosis codes. Merlin processes each CT volume and
produces a 2,048-dimensional embedding that serves as the input to all downstream concept extraction
and association analyses.
CT radiology report For radiology report findings, we use Qwen3-Embedding-8B 21, a general-domain
text embedding model selected as the top-performing model on the MTEB leaderboard at the time of
this study 62. Each findings section is encoded into a single 4,096-dimensional vector.
Laboratory values We use EHR Labs FM, an in-house masked autoencoder pretrained on laboratory
histories from the Discovery Site. The encoder is a three-layer Feature Tokenizer Transformer with four
attention heads and a hidden dimension of 768 that jointly encodes laboratory values, test types and
measurement times. For each history, values are randomly masked at a rate sampled uniformly between
0 and 90%, with at least one value masked. Laboratory-specific prediction heads reconstruct the masked
values using a mean squared error objective. Training uses AdamW with a learning rate of 10−4, a batch
size of 256 and 1,500 optimisation steps, with checkpoint selection based on validation reconstruction
loss. For downstream analyses, the reconstruction heads are discarded and the encoder remains frozen.
Its output embeddings are averaged over non-padding tokens to produce a single 768-dimensional vector.
4.3 Sparse Autoencoders
FM embeddings are dense and polysemantic: individual dimensions typically encode mixtures of un-
related clinical concepts simultaneously, making direct interpretation infeasible. Sparse autoencoders
address this by learning a larger, overcomplete dictionary of directions in the embedding space, where
each sample activates only a small subset of dictionary entries. This sparsity encourages each entry to
correspond to a single, distinct clinical concept.

F eature extraction and configuration selection. Once trained, SAE weights are frozen and sparse
features are inferred on all datasets by passing each FM embedding through the pretrained SAE. Each
sparse feature is then z-normalized by subtracting its mean and dividing by its standard deviation,
both computed on the Discovery Site, providing a consistent basis for comparison across modalities and
datasets. Based on the ablation results described in Supplementary Section A.3 and Figure 14, we select
K = 40 with the M = {128, 512, 2048, 8192} Matryoshka architecture as a single consistent configuration
across all modalities. The resulting sparse feature vectors from each modality are concatenated to form a
unified multimodal concept space, in which each sample is represented by a single sparse vector spanning
imaging, report, and laboratory concepts.
4.4 Automated Interpretability
By design, sparse features activate for only a small subset of samples. This sparsity creates the pre-
condition for interpretability: if a feature fires for a restricted, coherent cohort, it may encode a single
identifiable clinical phenomenon. To convert features into named concepts at scale, we automate the
interpretation process using a large language model (LLM), eliminating the need for manual inspection
of thousands of features.
Generative interpretation. For each SAE feature, we identify the samples in the Discovery Site
whose activation exceeds the 75th percentile of all positive activations, forming a high-activating cohort.
We then present nhigh = 20 randomly sampled high-activating samples to an LLM, alongside nnon = 20
randomly sampled samples with zero or near-zero activation as a contrast reference. The contrast is
essential: it grounds the interpretation in what is specific to the concept rather than what is common
across the patient population. The LLM is instructed to reason via explicit chain-of-thought before
producing a single-sentence summary of the form “ This cohort is characterized by [interpretation] . ” We

Discriminative validation. Validation serves two purposes: assessing whether the interpretation
faithfully describes the feature, and testing whether this description generalises to held-out sets. For each
concept, we sample nhigh = 20 and nnon = 20 from the test set, then crucially we shuffle the combined
pool. The LLM receives the textual interpretation together with the shuffled sample data, is informed
that exactly half the samples belong to the cohort, and must classify each sample as either belonging to
the concept cohort (1) or not (0). Discrimination accuracy, calculated by the fraction of samples correctly
classified, is computed on the Internal Test set as a measure of monosemanticity, and separately on each
external cohort to assess cross-site and -institutional generalization.
4.5 Outcome selection
To maximize the potential for rediscoveries and new discoveries, we use an automated approach to select
the highest signal outcome targets for exploration using the Discovery Site. We first map 16,553 unique
ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes to 1,692 hierarchical phenotypes termed Phecodes 2. From these we define a
candidate pool of 1,278 outcomes with support in our data. Studies were labeled as progressors if the
first recorded diagnosis of an outcome occurred 1–4 years after the study date. Controls were selected
as having no recorded diagnosis of that outcome, and at least four years of follow-up. All other studies,
including those with a recorded diagnosis of the outcome before the CT date, were excluded from that
outcome’s analysis. Following 64, we then compute on the Discovery Site the aggregate rank (by reciprocal
rank fusion) of the ability of each modality and model combination to predict each outcome. The 150
highest-ranked outcomes were then manually reviewed, and nine excluded as not interpretable as clinical
disease endpoints. These comprised non-specific catch-all Phecodes (for example, other disorders of the
liver), abnormal-finding and administrative codes (for example, other abnormal blood chemistry ), and
device or procedure status codes (for example, ileostomy status). This left the 141 outcomes used in this
study, covering conditions across oncological, cardiovascular, metabolic, and acute disease categories. To
see the performance of each FM on this set, see Figure 7.
4.6 Association study
Taking inspiration from the multi-stage design of genome-wide association studies 2, we estimate the
association between each Glyph concept and each future disease outcome as a per-standard-deviation
odds ratio (OR), enabling direct comparison across modalities whose activations operate on different
scales.
Standardization. Concept activations are z-normalised using a per-site mean and standard deviation,
so that each OR reflects the multiplicative change in outcome odds per one standard deviation increase
in concept activation.
OR computation. For each concept-outcome pair, we fit an unadjusted logistic regression model on
the Discovery Site,
logit(P(Y = 1)) = α + β ˜c, (4)
where ˜c is the standardised concept activation. The per-standard-deviation OR is defined as exp(β ), and
95% confidence intervals are reported as exp(β ± 1.96 · SE).
Statistical significance. We assess significance using the Wald p-value derived from the asymptotic
covariance matrix, computed as the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse of the Fisher information matrix,
I(β ) = X ⊤W X, (5)
where W is a diagonal matrix with entries pi(1 − pi). The z-statistic z = β /SE yields a two-tailed p-value.
Each CT study was analyzed as a separate observation to capture the patient’s clinical state at the time
of imaging, with independence assumed across studies.

Discovery filter. To concentrate downstream analysis on statistically supported, directionally consis-
tent associations, we apply a Bonferroni correction across all concept-outcome pairs, setting the threshold
at pBonferroni = 0.05/Npairs = 8.28 × 10−8. We additionally require OR > 1.0 to restrict attention to pre-
dictive rather than protective associations. Associations satisfying both criteria on the Discovery Site
form the set of promising associations carried forward into all subsequent analyses.
4.7 Reproducibility filter
Having identified significant associations on the Discovery Site, we assess whether they represent real,
generalizable phenomena by re-evaluating them on held-out cohorts. Concept activations on held-out
data are computed by applying the same frozen SAE weights without modification, requiring no manual
labeling or recalibration of new samples.
For each promising association, we re-compute the same OR on each held-out cohort and apply the
Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure at a 5% false discovery rate across the set of re-evaluated associa-
tions. An association is considered reproducible if the BH-adjusted p-value is significant and directionality
is maintained (OR > 1.0).

4.8 Confounder adjustment
A predictive association between a concept and an outcome may be driven by a shared confounder rather
than by a direct relationship. To assess whether associations persist after adjustment for measured con-
founders, we apply double machine learning (DML) with cross-fitting 65. This allows us to account for
nonlinear relationships and interactions among measured confounders that logistic regression with linear
covariate terms may miss. The estimator uses a Neyman-orthogonal estimating equation, whose expecta-
tion is locally insensitive to first-order errors in the nuisance functions at their true values. Orthogonality
therefore reduces sensitivity to nuisance estimation errors, while cross-fitting limits overfitting bias.
Because our outcomes are binary, we use a logistic partially linear model,

of 0.35 through qualitative inspection to balance excluding likely downstream consequences against re-
taining potential confounders, and excluded candidates at or above this threshold. For example, when
testing ascites, a broader concept combining ascites, anasarca, and pleural effusion was excluded from the
adjustment set (r=0.61). Similarly, when testing aortic atherosclerosis, a broader concept representing
abdominopelvic atherosclerosis was excluded (r=0.41). However, related atherosclerosis and aortic cal-
cification concepts remained eligible for adjustment when analyzing aortic atherosclerosis (r=0.31–0.34),
whereas upstream liver pathology was excluded when analyzing splenomegaly (r=0.46). The threshold
therefore served as a heuristic, since correlation alone cannot distinguish overlapping representations,
mediators, and confounders 61.

Inter-concept causal graph. To recover directed relationships among concepts, we learned a single

fixed set of universal confounders (age, sex, smoking status, heavy alcohol use, and BMI) as additional

the confounder nodes rather than to spurious concept-concept edges (see Figure 11). We standardized all

text:
node activations and fit a linear structural equation model X = XW + ε with an ℓ1 sparsity penalty on the
weighted adjacency W , subject to a continuous acyclicity constraint. We used DAGMA 68, which enforces
acyclicity through a log-determinant characterization and a continuation schedule that progressively
tightens the constraint toward an exact DAG, building on the continuous-optimization formulation of
NOTEARS69. Entries of W below a magnitude threshold were set to zero, and the surviving weights
define the directed edges. Whereas the primary concept-outcome analyses use double machine learning
(DML), which is confounder-robust but requires fitting separate nuisance models per target 65, the inter-
concept graph involves on the order of d2 candidate relationships across all d concepts, making per-pair
DML computationally prohibitive; we therefore learn the full structure, confounders included, in a single
continuous optimization and reserve DML for the smaller, hypothesis-driven outcome analyses in the
main text.
This procedure is an approximate analog to confounder adjustment rather than a guarantee of it: a
concept-concept edge is adjusted for a confounder only if that confounder’s weight survives thresholding,
and edge directions reflect the acyclicity constraint and model fit rather than verified causal mecha-
nisms. Unexpected edges may thus reflect genuine population-specific structure, but could also stem
from residual confounding or artifacts of thresholding and optimization.
4.9 Comparison with the clinical literature
To assess whether Glyph identifies prognostic information beyond established clinical markers, we com-
pared its concepts with risk markers reported in the literature. Here, we describe the literature search
and screening, reconstruction of published markers, and methods used to compare their associations
and predictive value with Glyph. For each outcome, PubMed and Paperclip queries combined endpoint
names and synonyms with an input scope defining eligible abdominal imaging findings, laboratory mea-
surements and clinical risk factors. Publication in a leading relevant journal or at least 50 citations was
required, retaining 83,649 outcome-specific records. Title screening advanced 14,801 records to abstract
review, of which 4,748 underwent further assessment of their measurements, endpoints and local feasi-
bility. Original methods and tables were consulted where marker definitions were unclear. At least one
reported marker could be reconstructed for 1,822 records, before deduplicating repeated measurement
families and selecting 293 representative studies. A later report-based COPD marker was included out-
side the initial impact criterion, bringing the total to 294. Markers were reconstructed using published
thresholds, transformations and composite- score definitions, with approximate measurements labelled
as proxies. Counting markers separately for each outcome, the final 412 entries comprised 36 explicit
multi-input scores, ratios or biomarker rules (8.7%), 31 BMI or estimated kidney-function measures
(7.5%), and 345 single measurements, findings or recorded conditions (83.7%). Thus, 67 markers (16.3%)
combined multiple inputs under the broader definition including BMI and estimated kidney function.
Queries, source papers, screening decisions and fitted definitions were retained for each outcome.
All prediction models used the same outcome-eligible CT studies and included age, sex and recorded
race. Markers required at least 100 observed Discovery measurements and, for binary rules, at least 25
observations in each category. Missing measurements were replaced with the Discovery training mean
and accompanied by a missingness indicator. Ridge logistic regression coeﬀicients and preprocessing
were learned on Discovery training data, with regularization selected by validation AUROC and the
selected model applied without refitting. Models were fitted to convergence before validation AUROC
was used to select regularization. Patients did not cross fitting, tuning or evaluation splits. We repeated
fitting on five bootstrap samples of independent Discovery training studies, keeping the concept sets,
validation set and held-out cohorts fixed. Reported AUROCs are the arithmetic means of the five fitted-
model AUROCs, rather than AUROCs of averaged predictions. If an augmented model did not improve
validation AUROC, the corresponding baseline was retained. Evaluation used the pooled Internal Test
and External Site #1 cohorts. External Site #2 was not included because direct access to the clinical data
needed to reconstruct the literature markers was unavailable at the time of the study. AUROC confidence
intervals and two-sided comparisons used paired study-level influence functions averaged across the five
fits. Across-outcome means gave outcomes equal weight, retaining shared-study covariance across models
and outcomes; relative-gain uncertainty used the delta method. Inference conditions on the fitted models
and selected markers and does not include training or selection uncertainty.

Individual-marker associations were estimated using the orthogonal logistic DML estimator described
above, adjusted for age, sex and recorded race, with five-fold outer and inner cross-fitting and independent-
study sandwich uncertainty. Exposures, including binary rules, were standardized using Discovery train-
ing statistics. Ten Glyph concepts per outcome were curated using Discovery clinically adjusted rankings
and clinical interpretations, excluding concepts primarily reflecting intervention or workflow. For the
size-matched OR and reproduction comparisons, up to ten literature markers per outcome were selected
using the adjusted Discovery-site OR ranking and fixed across held-out cohorts. This selection did not
restrict the literature baseline used in the prediction models. There were 194 selected literature markers
across outcomes. Reproduction required BH-adjusted q < 0.05 in the pooled held-out cohort and the same
effect direction as Discovery, with BH applied across the 768 Glyph, literature and matched-Phecode
marker–outcome associations. Differences in reproduction rates were tested using two-sided Fisher exact
tests, treating reproduction of each association as independent. Median OR comparisons gave outcomes
equal weight and used 20,000 shared-study multiplier bootstrap samples to preserve dependence across
markers and outcomes, with marker sets and nuisance fits fixed. The minimum attainable bootstrap
p-value was 1/20,001. Benjamini–Hochberg correction was applied to the six displayed held-out OR
comparisons, with separate families for the three Discovery and three pooled comparisons. KDEs used
all supported outcomes within each marker family; pairwise median comparisons used the outcomes
supported by both families.
4.10 Code and Data Availability
Analysis and reproduction code is available at https://github.com/StanfordMIMI/Glyph-research.
Released concept activations and interpretations are hosted at https://huggingface.co/datasets/
RobbieHolland/Glyph-research, subject to access restrictions. Pretrained SAE checkpoints and nor-
malization statistics are available at https://huggingface.co/RobbieHolland/Glyph-research. Ex-
ternal Site #2 (Mayo Clinic) study-level data and clinical covariates required for confounder-adjusted
refitting are not distributed.
4.11 Open source
The pipeline described above, spanning embedding extraction, SAE training, automated interpretation,
hypothesis search, and visualization, is available through the open-source library Glyph ( https://pypi.
org/project/glyph-discovery/). Users can learn new sparse concepts from their own data or apply the
pretrained dictionaries released with this paper using the corresponding foundation models. Foundation
models can be selected through built-in presets or supported Hugging Face model identifiers; custom
models can be connected by specifying their preprocessing and embedding output. Listing 1 illustrates
the Python API for learning new concepts, Listing 2 shows how to measure pretrained concepts, and
Listing 3 demonstrates running the workflow through a coding agent.
When training new dictionaries, fit evaluates SAE configurations and favors sparse representations that
achieve a validation reconstruction R2 of at least 0.85, allowing modest increases in the number of active
concepts for further improvements in reconstruction. A warning is issued if this threshold is not reached.
hypothesis_search runs the association study described in Section 4.6, with optional confounder ad-
justment. visualize produces an interactive concept-space explorer with association statistics and
Bonferroni-significant concepts highlighted. Additional agent skills support literature searches, compar-
isons against published markers, and concise visual reports. Automated interpretation is optional and
requires configured access to a supported language model.

A.1 Interpretation of Glyph concepts and validation across sites
We next assess the interpretability of Glyph’s discovered features, using a contrastive variant of AutoIn-
terp20 and interpretation testing outlined in Section 4.4. To make analysis more token-eﬀicient, we only
interpret high-risk concepts, defined by those with at least one significant association to future disease
(see Section 2.2). Prior work highlighted the diﬀiculty of interpreting radiological SAE features at an F1
threshold of 0.75 70, motivating our choice of a discrimination accuracy threshold of ≥ 75% for considering
a concept interpretable.
Using this method and threshold, 88.6% of radiology report concepts were interpretable internally, and
76.6% and 86.7% of interpretations successfully generalized to External Sites #1 and #2, respectively
(see Figure 12c). This high rate was expected, as these concepts are derived from embeddings of text
that explicitly describe clinical findings. Interpreting concepts derived from images represents a greater
challenge, as Merlin likely relies on its own internal set of concepts that may not correspond to anything
radiologists routinely or consistently document in reports. Remarkably, 52.5% of Merlin image concepts
were broadly interpretable by corresponding radiology reports (see Figure 12d–f). Labs concepts were
more automatically interpretable than imaging (see Figure 12g–i), and captured physiological states such
as monocytosis.
Investigating image concepts not interpretable by AutoInterp, we find many still carry identifiable mean-
ing, when viewed directly in images by radiologists. For example, we noticed I76 was not interpretable via
AutoInterp, but was among the top 1% closest imaging-derived markers to a broad swath of laboratory
concepts, spanning inflammation, cholesterol, and protein levels (annotated in 2b). Strikingly, despite
not being routinely documented, I76 was significantly associated with the onset of infection, sepsis, sep-
ticemia, and wasting. Prompted by these results, radiologists visually inspected images retrieved by
this concept, finding it activates in patients with severely distended, fluid-filled bowel loops (see Figure
12d–e).
A.2 Glyph provided complementary associations to pre-coded phenotypes
Having established that Glyph concepts yield significant and reproducible markers of future disease
risk, we asked whether pre-coded PheW AS for automated clinical discovery would have identified the
same discoveries2. We treated Phecodes as exposures and applied the same discovery pipeline, including
multiple-test corrected Discovery and Reproducibility filters, searching among the same 141 outcomes
where Glyph has the maximum expected yield.
Aggregate binary-exposure results are presented in Figure 13a–b. Recent Phecodes recorded from −180
to +30 days relative to the scan yielded 7,843 promising associations, with significantly lower replication
than Glyph concepts at Internal Test (47.2% vs. 69.3%, p = 9.77 × 10−4) and External Site #1 (59.9%
vs. 74.3%, p = 1.95 × 10−3) Using each patient’s entire recorded coding history increased the Phecode
yield to 15,274 promising associations, approximately 3.4 × the number identified by Glyph, of which
49.1% and 63.9% reproduced in the two held-out cohorts. The median Discovery-site effect was smaller
for both Phecode arms than for Glyph concepts (OR 1.29 for Recent Phecodes and 1.33 for all-history
Phecodes, versus 1.45 for Glyph). The greater yield reflects the broader scope of ICD codes, which span
the full medical record, whereas Glyph concepts were limited to phenomena observable in abdominal
CT images, and laboratory panels. Comparable yield may therefore be possible as Glyph expands to
additional modalities and examinations.
We next assessed which Glyph associations could have been identified from codes alone (see Figure
13c). For previously reported associations, we identified if there was a matching Phecode and compared
their associations directly. Directly matched associations were often recoverable from Phecodes. For
example, Phecode 571.51 (cirrhosis of the liver) reproducibly predicted primary liver cancer (OR 2.03–
2.25), independently corroborating the association identified for R85 (cirrhotic liver morphology and
varices; OR 1.64–2.55). Across the majority of comparisons with a matching Phecode, the Glyph concept
had a larger odds ratio. Some matched Phecodes did not pass the Discovery filter, and some additional
Glyph associations had no corresponding Phecode. Overall, Phecodes identified more associations across
the full medical record, while Glyph concepts yielded larger median effects, reproduced more frequently,

of data-driven Glyph concepts over Phecodes. a–b Binary Phecodes drawn from the full recorded

Internal Test (49% versus 69%) and have a smaller median effect (OR 1.33 versus 1.45). Recent
Phecodes, restricted to the scan-adjacent window, also yield more associations than Glyph concepts but
reproduce less often. c Directly corresponding Phecodes were often less specific than imaging- or
laboratory-derived Glyph concepts and yielded weaker or nonsignificant associations. In other cases,
the broader clinical history captured by Phecodes provided a stronger proxy for future risk. For
example, hypertension served as a proxy for atherosclerosis (bottom) and outperformed the
corresponding Glyph concept for some outcomes.
and produced stronger associations within directly matched phenotypes. Phecodes therefore capture
information beyond the modalities available to Glyph, while Glyph concepts extract more predictive

text:
A.3 Architectural ablations
The quality of Glyph’s concept space, and hence the sensitivity of all downstream discovery, depended
directly on the architecture of the sparse autoencoder. Two parameters governed standard Top- K SAEs:
sparsity K, which set the number of features active per sample, and dictionary size N, the maximum
number of distinct features available. Standard SAEs, however, have a known tendency known as
feature splitting to recover only fine-grained concepts while neglecting broader phenomena higher in the
conceptual hierarchy. The Matryoshka SAE addressed this by organising features into nested groups of
increasing specificity, simultaneously encoding concepts at multiple scales. To identify the architecture
best suited to Glyph’s multimodal clinical data, we systematically evaluated a standard Top- K SAE
alongside two Matryoshka variants with nested dictionary sizes [128, 512, 2048, 8192] and [256, 1024,
4096, 16384], across five sparsity levels ( K ∈ {5, 10, 20, 40, 80}) and all three modalities.
Across all modalities, increasing K was the dominant factor for improving reconstruction quality, reducing
MSE and raising R2 between original and reconstructed FM embeddings (Figure 14a–b). All modalities
exhibited diminishing returns beyond K = 40, beyond which additional active features yielded marginal
improvements while increasing computational cost. The number of alive features in the dictionary also
grew with K, reflecting the richer encoding capacity afforded by denser activations. Modality differences
in the required number of features broadly tracked embedding dimensionality: radiology reports, em-
bedded with the 4096-dimensional Qwen3-Embedding-8B, required more active features than CT images
via Merlin (2048-dimensional), which in turn required more than laboratory values via the Labs FM
(768-dimensional).
Matryoshka SAEs improved generalisation to external data relative to the standard Top- K baseline, an
advantage more clearly visible on the External Site #1 cohort than on the internal discovery set. The
SAE trained on Discovery data maintained strong performance across all test sets, though with a modest
drop on external cohorts that mirrored the reduced replication rates in Sections 2.2 and 2.3, and may
partly reflect this distributional shift. No meaningful benefit was observed between the two Matryoshka
dictionary sizes, and we accordingly selected the Top- K = 40 Matryoshka SAE with nested sizes [128,
512, 2048, 8192] for all analyses, balancing concept quality, generalisation, and computational cost, and
achieved over 90% reconstruction of the original embeddings ( R2 > 0.90) across all modalities and FMs.
Beyond reconstruction fidelity, a key requirement was that the sparsified concept space preserved the
predictive power of the underlying foundation models, confirming that the interpretability step did not
discard clinically relevant signal (Figure 14c). Across modalities, Glyph concepts closely matched FM
predictive performance, with particularly tight agreement for CT images (AUC 0.73 vs. 0.73 on the
internal test cohort, 0.71 vs. 0.70 on External Site #1) and laboratory values (0.73 vs. 0.71; 0.66 vs.
0.65). Radiology report concepts showed a modestly larger gap (0.72 vs. 0.63; 0.68 vs. 0.62), consistent
with the greater information density of the high-dimensional Qwen3-Embedding-8B text embedding
space. Overall, predictive performance was largely preserved for imaging and laboratory concepts, with
larger reductions for radiology report concepts.
Lastly, we assessed whether the derived concepts were objectively interpretable to an independent auto-
mated judge (Figure 14d). A self-reported interpretation could trivially appear coherent, so we instead
posed interpretability as a discrimination task: a second LLM, given only the text interpretation, must
classify unseen patients as high- or non-activating for that concept. Using the AutoInterp pipeline
(see Methods, Section 4.4), interpretations generated on the discovery set were evaluated on unseen pa-
tients without modification, testing whether each description accurately characterised new activations
of the same concept. Radiology report concepts were highly interpretable, with 88.6% achieving an
interpretability score above 75% on the internal test cohort and 76.6% on External Site #1. Labora-
tory concepts were competitive, with 77.6% achieving above 75% interpretability. CT image concepts
were the least interpretable (52.5% on test, 45.5% on External Site #1), plausibly because sparse image
features can capture visual structure not routinely documented in paired radiology reports. Overall,
we concluded that Glyph produced a concept space that is broadly intelligible across all three clinical
modalities.

Results are organized by modality, with panels a–c corresponding to CT imaging (Merlin), radiology
reports (Qwen3-Embedding-8B), and laboratory values (Labs FM), respectively. Within each modality,
results are organized by metric, showing sparse autoencoder reconstruction loss (MSE), R2 between
original and reconstructed foundation-model embeddings, and mean downstream AUC across the 141
disease prediction tasks. Reconstruction loss and R2 are evaluated on the discovery training set and
unseen external data, while downstream AUC assesses whether the Glyph concept space preserves the
predictive performance of the underlying foundation models with minimal degradation. Across
modalities, diminishing returns in reconstruction are observed beyond K = 40, with R2 improving and
subsequently plateauing at this sparsity level.

A.4 AutoInterp prompts
The following prompt is populated with radiology reports findings and lab histories, before being passed
to the LLM.
=== Task ===:
You are an expert radiologist specializing in abdominal CT scans and lab values. A cohort
of patients were selected according to some shared characteristic specific to this cohort.
You are provided radiology reports, lab histories, or both, and your task is to analyze
them in order determine what are the shared feature(s). Radiology reports and lab histories
may be filtered to the words, phrases or recordings most relevant to the shared
characteristic to faciliate its identification. The importance level of those words,
phrases or recordings should be considered in the analysis.
While the patient data will contain many different pathologies, there should be some
undercurrent or one or two features which run through >80% of them. These characteristics
should be positive, and somewhat unusual to be among so many reporst from different
patients at once. Things like 'no evidence of bowel obstruction' is so common it is not
useful. The explanation should be general enough to apply to the highest number of reports
in this cohort, but not so general that it is no longer specific to this cohort, and would
apply to many of the reference patients from the larger dataset.
To arrive at the most accurate and precise explanation of what this cohort is characterized
by, you must engage in explicit chain of thought reasoning. Begin by thoroughly examining
all provided data, noting any patterns or commonalities. Pay close attention to recurring
terminology, described anatomical structures, and especially consistent pathological
findings. Consider how these elements might interrelate to form a singular, distinctive
feature that the cohort could be characterized by.
As you progress through your analysis, verbalize your thought process. Explain each step of
your reasoning, from initial observations to intermediate conclusions, and finally to your
overall assessment. This chain of thought approach will help ensure a comprehensive and
well - reasoned final explanation.
After this detailed analytical process, formulate a single, specific explanation of what
the cohort is characterized by. Focus on specific features or combinations of features,
using 'and' to connect multiple elements if necessary and 'or' if there are multiple
possibilities. Refrain from explaining the pathology itself (e.g., avoid statements like
"This feature represents X, which is defined as ...").
Below are the patient data, listed in order of how strongly they belong to the cohort
(keeping in mind that all of them belong strongly compared to the average patient in the
larger dataset):
For reference, here are examples of patients randomly sampled from the much larger dataset
that do not belong to this cohort:
{reference_patients}
Finally, the data from the cohort characterized by the feature in question:
{patient_data}
=== Format ===:
It is crucial that you present your final explanation in the following format, started with
an asterisk:
* This cohort is characterized by [your specific, detailed description of what the cohort
is characterized by compared to the average patient in the larger dataset].
The asterisk is absolutely essential. Your explanation must begin immediately after the
asterisk, without any additional text, numbering, or preamble. The presence of this
asterisk is critical for the proper processing of your response.
The following prompt tests the accuracy of a given interpretation for a sparse feature. It is populated
with testing data, before being passed to the LLM.
Task: Distinguish samples (randomly ordered) based on those that do and do not belong to
the group characterized by the group characteristics.
Medical Findings Reports:
{patient_data}
Group characteristics:
{interpretation}

A.5 Outcome-specific profiles after confounder adjustment
We examined which concept associations persisted after adjustment across hepatic, renal, cardiovascular,
neurological and infection outcomes at the Discovery Site (Tables 4–8). Broad outcomes, including acute
and chronic renal failure and altered mental status, retained associations with diverse systemic abnor-
malities, whereas atherosclerotic outcomes and specific renal complications showed more concentrated
vascular or laboratory profiles. The tables report the number and percentage of associations remaining
significant after adjustment relative to the number associated before adjustment, together with represen-
tative concepts, their interpretations, percentage shares of retained associations and adjusted odds ratios
(ORs). The ORs describe association strength rather than the proportion of outcome events explained
or attributable to a concept.

DRAFT-Bench: Evaluating Frontier Agents
Across the Professional Design Lifecycle
Rong Pan∗
University of Maryland, College Park
Jianqiang Wang
curify-AI
Abstract
Can frontier general-purpose agents understand client intent, explore creative
directions, execute revisions, and prepare production deliverables? We intro-
duce DRAFT-Bench (Design Reliability Across Feedback and Tasks), a lifecycle-
oriented evaluation of requirement elicitation, creative exploration, constrained
editing, iterative revision, and production handoff. Its Requirement-to-Artifact
framework links evolving requirements, protected properties, artifact versions,
and delivery obligations. We compare native Codex/Astra and Claude Code across
35 design briefs under 43 conditions, alongside a separate 40-scenario RFQ track.
Astra completes 43/43 design conditions and Claude 35/43. All scored core runs
receive full structural credit, yet on the 28 core conditions scored for both systems,
semantic checks flag violations in 11 for Astra and 5 for Claude; these are model
judgments, not expert-confirmed failure rates. RFQ coverage is high, but suc-
cess ordering changes across cohorts. SKU expansion, revision dependencies, and
White ink files expose ambiguity among unmet obligations, missing inputs, and
evaluator interpretations. These findings separate execution, requirement compli-
ance, and professional acceptance. Unpaired tracks and different tools preclude
claims of RFQ-to-delivery success, factory acceptance, or a pure model ranking.
1 Introduction
A professional design assignment spans ambiguous client intent, creative exploration, constrained
editing, iterative feedback, and preparation of deliverables for production handoff. General-purpose
agents can participate in each stage, but a polished preview alone does not show whether they un-
derstood the request, preserved approved work, or delivered the required files. We ask:can frontier
general-purpose agents translate evolving requirements into verifiable design artifacts across this
lifecycle?
We introduceDRAFT-Bench,Design Reliability Across Feedback and Tasks, with 35 design briefs
under 43 execution conditions and a separate 40-scenario requirement-elicitation track. Figure 1
organizes the coverage from requirement discovery through production handoff. Creative explo-
ration includes reference understanding, direction selection, and proposal comparison, alongside
visual generation. The assignments are synthetic or curated and motivated by professional work-
flows; they are not a customer deployment study.Lifecycle-widedescribes coverage through sepa-
rate protocols: RFQ and design execution are unpaired, so the study does not measure an integrated
RFQ-to-delivery success rate. Broader archive accounting is reported separately in Section 3.
Our central methodological contribution isRequirement-to-Artifact evaluation: linking an ac-
tive requirement to the relevant artifact version and the evidence needed to judge it. Requirements
specify changes, protected properties, or deliverables. Feedback can activate an earlier obligation:
choosing a packaging direction can trigger expansion into five SKUs. The framework makes this

The configured systems show high intake coverage and substantial design execution capability, but
differ in completion, delivered sets, and revision behavior. Structural credit coexists with semantic
flags; client dependencies and inconsistent applicability decisions complicate interpretation. These
observations can implicate the agent, the evaluator, or the specification. Our analysis preserves those
distinctions instead of treating every discrepancy as a confirmed agent failure.
Research questions.
•RQ1: Lifecycle capabilities.What do the separate protocols reveal about agents’ capabilities
and execution reliability across design stages?
•RQ2: Requirement-compliant delivery.Do completed runs and structurally valid outputs sat-
isfy active requirements?
•RQ3: Decisions and dependencies.How do human choices, revision prerequisites, and produc-
tion constraints affect delivery and its evaluation?
Contributions.
•Lifecycle coverage.A task collection spans major stages of professional design, with briefs,
assets, context conditions, and feedback motivated by production workflows. Tasks and toolkit:
https://github.com/super-inbox/DRAFT-Bench.
•Requirement-to-Artifact evaluation.An evidence framework links evolving requirements, pro-
tected properties, artifact versions, and delivery obligations. Its implementation combines an
exhaustive audit of scored core checks with eight selected paired inspections; it is not a fully
automated or expert-validated acceptance metric.
•Frontier agent capability analysis.A comparison of Codex and Claude Code reveals differ-
ences between execution completion, semantic compliance signals, and evidence of usable deliv-
ery. Original scores remain frozen. Separate protocols and selected cases support stage-specific
findings, not a universal system ranking or estimates of expert-accepted delivery.
2 Related work and research gap
Design planning and task quality.GraphicBench couples planning to execution and already
shows that plausible plans can fail in execution [4]. Its execution metrics include source-image
fidelity and query-aligned visual questions. Graphic-Design-Bench spans layout, typography, info-
graphics, template and design semantics, and animation, including structured output and editing [2].
These are not merely aesthetic leaderboards. Our emphasis is the evidence linking a changing de-
livery obligation to the correct version and the interpretation of disagreement between checks.

Interactive professional work.DeskCraft is the closest workflow comparison: it includes 538
tasks, mid-turn clarification and post-turn feedback, and domain-aware verifiers that extract state
from project files or application runtimes [8]. It already evaluates professional delivery and human–
agent collaboration. Proactive T2I agents connect clarification to image alignment and include hu-
man studies [3]. Our RFQ experiment instead isolates attribution under fixed replies; its downstream
connection is still untested. Drift-Bench++ studies evolving intent and imperfect communication
through executable tasks and an interaction protocol [9]. Neither interactivity, intent tracking, nor
artifact-based verification alone is a novelty claim.
Judgment and professional acceptance.TASTE measures multidimensional designer prefer-
ences and evaluates model judges against professional panels [10]. Agentic-DRS studies design
diagnosis and feedback quality with human comparisons [5]. GDPval likewise uses occupational
experts to assess professional deliverables [7]; Anthropic’s evaluation guidance distinguishes traces
from outcomes and stresses grader calibration [1]. We build on these principles, rather than claiming
that requirements or expert acceptance have been ignored.
Specific research gap.Prior work already covers planning, graphic quality, preferences, and pro-
fessional workflows. DRAFT-Bench connects these concerns through lifecycle-wide design tasks
andRequirement-to-Artifact evaluation: which evolving obligation applies, which property must
remain protected, and which artifact version substantiates delivery? This linkage supports a capa-
bility analysis that distinguishes completed execution, requirement compliance, and usable handoff,
while exposing disagreement between evidence layers. We implement it through condition-level au-
dits and selected paired inspections. Human acceptance calibration, an integrated RFQ-to-delivery
study, and factory acceptance remain future work; neither professional workflow evaluation nor
artifact verification alone is a novelty claim.
3 DRAFT-Bench
3.1 Archive scope and counting units
The evaluation archive reconciles 232 design-related case lineages with 40 RFQ scenarios, yielding
272 lineages and 301 protocol units. Its 333 observation records retain 32 historical associations
between the Brief Bank v0.2 core and v0.3; those associations add no new executions (Table 2).
Counts are not multiplied by the number of candidate systems. Routing, preference prediction,
3

units establish independent statistical samples.

planning, and artifact execution measure different endpoints and cannot be combined into a common
quality score. The 43-condition Brief Bank remains the primary design execution analysis.
3.2 Task structure and capability coverage
A design condition specifies a brief, available source/reference assets, context, ordered feedback,
constraints, and expected deliverables. The agent produces versioned artifacts and a response after
each turn. The brief may contain obligations that become active only after a client choice; approved
properties can remain fixed through later edits. This structure motivates checking the assignment
across versions rather than judging only its last preview.
Figure 1 groups these tasks by lifecycle stage. Requirement discovery uses RFQ fields, targeted
questions, and fixed customer replies. Creative exploration includes alternative directions, refer-
ence understanding, direction selection, and comparison. Constrained edits and iterative revisions
combine requested changes with protected content and version dependencies. Production handoff
concerns complete sets, required formats, file structure, and declared handoff state. Table 3 maps
this coverage to the conclusions supported by the current results.
3.3 Primary design track
Brief Bank data v0.3 contains 35 briefs under 43 conditions: 24 core briefs/32 conditions and eleven
external briefs/conditions. Eight families cover identity, campaigns, packaging, e-commerce, format
adaptation, feedback revision, reference-based work, and production handoff (Appendix C). Four
core briefs each have zero-shot, reference-grounded, and personalized contexts. These conditions
are not independent client projects. External tasks have newly authored assets and contracts inspired
by public task patterns; they form a curated sample rather than an untouched population test.
Scripted feedback is delivered in order. It can refer to earlier choices or versions whether or not the
candidate has established them. The version-dependency case in Section 6.3 shows why the feasi-
bility of a feedback instruction must itself be inspected. We do not reinterpret a missing prerequisite
as an agent failure without adjudication.
3.4 Requirement-discovery track
The original twenty synthetic English RFQ scenarios derive from communication patterns in five
supplied examples and cover bulk images, tourist videos, cultural merchandise, content work-
flows, and apparel retouching. An additional twenty scenarios extend four supplied real-world
scenario families: hotel-listing retouching, scene-enhancement pairs, educational animation, and a
ski-opening poster. They retain authored variants and synthetic assumptions; the executed dialogues
are simulations rather than real customer conversations. Each scenario has seven fields, four critical,
and at most eight customer replies. Fixed answers expose information only when a corresponding
question is asked; attachment mentions are placeholders.
The RFQ track measures requirement elicitation, not downstream design success. It is unpaired
with the design track and cannot establish that additional coverage improves delivery. The two RFQ
cohorts differ in auxiliary models, execution dates, and attempt histories; their combined view is a
descriptive reconciliation, not a uniform new forty-case experiment. Auxiliary routing, preference,
planning, and 21q results remain in Appendix C; overlapping observations are not added to the
primary sample.
