Figure 2: Requirement-to-Artifact evidence framework. Applicability is checked before the re-
quested version and its evidence. This is the audit schema; the archive supplies aggregate checks
and selected direct inspections, not a fully automated acceptance system or an evaluated RFQ-to-
delivery pipeline.
4 Requirement-to-Artifact evaluation
4.1 Linking requirements, versions, and delivery evidence
The core evaluation unit is an active requirement paired with a relevant artifact version. Each record
links the obligation to its originating turn, scope (requested change, protected property, or deliv-
erable), artifact version/path, check result, and evidence provenance. Figure 2 operationalizes the
lifecycle view in Figure 1 for the design-artifact audit. Evaluation proceeds through four questions:
1.Is the requirement active?Resolve selections, approvals, superseded requests, and unmet
prerequisites. Exclude a requirement only with an explicit applicability reason.
2.Which artifact is relevant?Identify the requested version and business deliverable. A
candidate-authored diagnostic or an older draft is not automatically its substitute.
3.What changed and what was preserved?Check the requested delta, protected content,
complete set, and required file structure together.
4.What supports the decision?Distinguish observed file facts, candidate assertions, model
judgments, and expert acceptance. Record unresolved dependencies and the candidate’s
declared status separately.
4.2 Three evidence layers
Structural evidence.Check presence, readability, count, dimensions, format, and version identity.
The archivedartifact_contractscore is one such signal. Runtime completion is an execution
property reported alongside it.
Semantic evidence.Check the task-specific change, source/reference roles, preservation con-
straints, and deliverable obligations. Unchanged pixels may indicate successful preservation or a
missing edit; file existence alone cannot establish correctness. Archived rubric weights and scores
are retained.
Workflow and handoff evidence.Distinguish final output, intermediate progress, and a declared
client dependency. A blocker disclosure establishes that the candidate is waiting; it does not establish
whether waiting was justified. Likewise, an unresolved delivery does not establish a false completion
claim. Independent professional acceptance remains unmeasured.
4.3 Implemented audit and its coverage
For every scored core condition, we collect the archived semantic check list and flag the condition
if any check has the exact verdictVIOLATED. Each condition counts once, independent of dupli-
cated or differently worded checks. Coverage is complete over 32 Astra and 28 Claude scored core
conditions; we also report the 28-condition intersection. No flag is not an acceptance certificate.
5
title: DRAFT-Bench: Evaluating Frontier Agents Across the Professional Design Lifecycle

text:
Direct inspection covers eight paired conditions: MFA-003 and CFR-002 from an initial audit round,
plus PSF-001, RTO-001, ECO-001, BID-001, CFRY-003, and ECO-002. We inspect prompts, final
responses, inventories, selected images and file internals. The six additional cases retain 23 orig-
inal images and 76 source hashes. They are purposively selected to illustrate delivery transitions,
evaluator ambiguity, and a positive retouching contrast; they do not estimate prevalence.
Historical altered-artifact controls address a separate evaluator question: whether stale candidate-
authored evidence can override missing or unchanged outputs. Their retained summaries are not
newly reproduced trials. The ECO-001 applicability comparison is likewise a diagnostic requiring
expert review. We do not change the frozen judgments to favor an interpretation.
What the archived judge can observe.The main core scorer receives the condition-specific re-
quest, scripted feedback, constraints, deliverable requirements, input images, selected output images
across version folders, business-deliverable text, and evaluator-computed file facts. It does not in-
gest the complete tool trace or the turn-final responses; candidate verification reports are excluded
as proof. Output image selection defaults to at most ten images for core and twelve for external
conditions, with further size limits and text truncation. The external scorer also receives aggregate
trajectory counts. Expected workflow instructions are not a record of every action actually taken.
Our direct case audit additionally reads final responses to distinguish disclosed dependencies from
completion claims. This richer audit view does not retroactively change the judge’s input or scores.
Separate rejudging pilot.The archive also retains R1, a seven-pair historical Sol/Astra pilot using
revised task-specific acceptance rules and two anonymized, reversed-order presentations per pair.
Its fourteen Gemini calls are distinct from our eight Astra/Claude artifact inspections. It changes
neither candidate artifacts nor historical aggregate scores, excludes Claude, and has no final expert
adjudication. Section 6.3 reports its diagnostic implications; Appendix D preserves its scope.
4.4 Endpoints and interpretation
Reported endpoints are runtime completion, latency, archived quality bounds, and semantic-check
flags; RFQ coverage and success are auxiliary. Timeouts leave quality unscored. Unmeasured
rubric dimensions induce bounds, not confidence intervals. Quality combines task-specific model
judgments and is not a human aesthetic rating.
An accepted-delivery rate requires independent acceptance labels. A false-completion-claim rate
additionally requires an actual completion claim. Neither rate is available. Clarification usefulness
should be evaluated separately while the corresponding deliverable remains unresolved. Appendix F
supplies the metric formulas and inclusion rules.
5 Experimental setup
Design systems and budget.Evaluation v0.4 runs Codex CLI 0.154.0 withgpt-6-astra(three
workers) and Claude Code 2.1.286 withclaude-opus-5-5(two Brief Bank workers), both at max
effort. Each attempts the same 43 conditions, with a 60-minute active-call limitper turn, and re-
ceives scripted feedback in order. This is not a 60-minute total-project budget. Auxiliary 21q visual-
execution cases have a 15-minute limit. Data and asset-manifest hashes match. Prompts, feedback
ordering, weights, and judges are fixed. Subscription quota pauses precede 22 Claude turns and total
about 71 hours across workers; this pacing can also change task order. Claude has no infrastructure
retries in this design track; its eight failures are candidate timeouts. Historical Sol executions remain
separate.
Tools and judges.Astra has Codex built-in image generation, bundled runtime packages, Codex
skills, and MCP REPL tools. Claude uses native tools and code-based visual production without
an image-generation model, MCP, skills, or subagents. Shell network access differs: Astra’s three

For the seven shared external conditions, mean scores are 1.000 for Claude and 0.946 for Astra, and
both pass all seven score thresholds under the weighted-only rule; Astra’s L4-RDT-007 sits exactly
at 0.70 (Section 5). On the planned external set, completion is 7/11 for Claude and 11/11 for Astra.

Across all 43 first turns, median recorded duration is 41.4 minutes for Claude versus 15.8 for Astra;
the Claude median includes observations ending at the timeout deadline. Among completed turns,
medians are 21.2 (77 turns) and 10.2 (90 turns). The eight timeouts are spread across six of eight

title: DRAFT-Bench: Evaluating Frontier Agents Across the Professional Design Lifecycle

text:
7 Discussion and limitations
Lifecycle coverage and delivery reliability.DRAFT-Bench provides evidence across require-
ment discovery, creative exploration, design and revision, and production handoff. Its Requirement-
to-Artifact framework makes the linkage between evolving obligations and delivered versions ex-
plicit. The three findings separate stage-specific capability, requirement compliance, and the in-
terpretation of missing or ambiguous evidence. Astra completes more of the observed execution
workload, while Claude has a higher observed weighted contribution on the selected shared Brief
Bank core. Missing outcomes, unknown rubric contributions, and different tools prevent a total
quality ranking. Neither routing and planning scores nor completed execution establish independent
professional acceptance.
Intake coverage is a separate capability.RFQ’s near-complete average field coverage does not
establish that every critical output requirement was elicited, that the final brief is usable, or that a
downstream design will be accepted. The success ordering changes between the original and ad-
ditional cohorts and narrows under the exclusion sensitivity check. Auxiliary models, continuation
history, and scripted disclosure also change, so this is descriptive heterogeneity rather than an iso-
lated domain effect. A claim that either system is generally better at elicitation exceeds these data.
The evaluator is part of the measurement.The unchanged-artifact R1 pilot demonstrates sensi-
tivity to acceptance rules and evidence presentation: a text-ranking task need not require an image,
and a missing edit may be an unfulfilled obligation, justified clarification, or an invalid feedback
prerequisite. These states require different labels. R1’s remaining variation and lack of expert ad-
judication prevent calling the new scores corrected ground truth. Its seven selected pairs cannot
estimate a benchmark-wide grading error rate. The main scorer’s image sampling and incomplete
dialogue view add limits: evidence available in the archive is not necessarily evidence delivered to
the judge.
Implications for agent and evaluator development.Track active obligations and approved prop-
erties across versions; make the current checkpoint and the eventual deliverable set explicit. Recon-
cile brief-level scope with turn-level delta instructions before judging an omission. Provide artifact
facts independently of candidate claims, and retain the candidate’s outward explanation as evidence
of communication, not as proof that a visual edit occurred. Separately label delivery completeness,
the reason for blocking, and whether escalation was justified. These are development targets moti-
vated by the audit, not interventions validated by this study. They align with professional-workflow
evaluation [6] and guidance on outcomes and grader calibration [1].
The next discriminating experiments.First use disputed cases to specify acceptance rules, then
freeze those rules and evaluate a separate, stratified sample with experts blinded to system identity,
including flagged and unflagged outputs and blocker decisions. Second compare judges on the same
frozen evidence and report agreement and errors against expert labels; keep the R1 development
cases separate from that test. Third compare agents with matched tools and repeated runs, and
connect vague, elicited, and complete briefs to one downstream executor. This would test RFQ’s
delivery value and enable validation of an integrated RFQ-to-handoff chain. Production experts
should separately assess plate placement, preflight, and factory acceptance before making design-
to-manufacturing claims. None of these experiments is completed here.
Scope and causal limits.The 272 lineages and 301 protocol units span curated, synthetic, and
historical tasks; the 333 records include duplicate associations and are not independent observa-
tions. Design executions are single included trajectories. RFQ variants share source families, its
original amendment is post-hoc, and the cohorts use different auxiliary models and attempt histo-
ries. Timeouts, infrastructure exclusions, and missing quality dimensions remain distinct. Tools,
runtimes, platform instructions, isolation, and dates differ across systems, preventing model-weight
attribution or a causal quality–reliability trade-off. Human acceptance calibration remains absent.
Production handoff is evaluated through artifacts and file evidence; hashes, pixel differences, and a
White separation resource cannot certify professional quality or factory acceptance. Some rejected
historical judge outputs were discarded.
13
title: DRAFT-Bench: Evaluating Frontier Agents Across the Professional Design Lifecycle

text:
8 Conclusion
DRAFT-Bench evaluates frontier agents across the professional design lifecycle through separate
task protocols. Its central contribution is Requirement-to-Artifact evaluation: linking evolving re-
quirements, protected properties, artifact versions, and delivery obligations to inspectable evidence.
Across 35 design briefs and 43 conditions, Astra completes 43/43 and Claude 35/43, while full
structural credit coexists with semantic flags and unresolved deliveries. The separate 40-scenario
RFQ track shows high coverage and cohort-sensitive success ordering; the shared-case totals are
36/39 for Astra and 34/39 for Claude. SKU expansion, version dependencies, and White ink files
show why human decisions and production constraints must be part of evaluating delivery. These
results support a stage-specific capability analysis, with distinct measures of execution, requirement
compliance, and justified escalation. They do not establish a pure model ranking, expert-accepted
delivery, or factory acceptance. A paired RFQ-to-handoff experiment and independent expert cali-
bration are the next steps beyond the current lifecycle-wide benchmark.
Data and code availability.Public materials are athttps://github.com/super-inbox/
DRAFT-Bench. Data releasedraftbench-v0.1.0(CC BY 4.0) contains the briefs, 24 input fix-
tures, RFQ scenarios and 100 run records with offline score replay, numeric records for all 301
protocol units, and the R1 scores. Toolkit releasedraftbench-v0.2.0(new code under MIT) runs
these tasks under a new protocol; it does not reproduce the historical environments. Task inputs for
the auxiliary protocols, candidate outputs beyond our figures, complete traces, judge payloads, the
semantic-check audit, case evidence, and this paper’s analysis scripts are not public, so the design
judgments cannot be re-created from these materials alone.

text:
Ordered Policy Optimization
Dongkyu Derek Cho
Department of Statistical Science
Duke University
dc430@duke.edu
Pan Xu
Department of Biostatistics & Bioinformatics
Department of Computer Science
Department of Electrical & Computer Engineering
Duke University
pan.xu@duke.edu
Abstract
Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) stabilizes policy updates by clipping the
importance ratio between the new policy and the data-collecting policy. The
standard rule uses one fixed clipping range for all samples. While this choice offers
simplicity and effectiveness, it fails to distinguish statistically harmful extreme
ratio values from large, yet tolerable changes. We study how to adapt the clipping
radius to the reliability of the induced importance ratio distribution. Our case
study demonstrates that reliable updates require controlling these extreme ratios,
rather than merely verifying that individual ratios fall within a fixed interval.
Motivated by this observation, we propose Ordered Policy Optimization (OPO).
In each minibatch, OPO sorts the importance ratios, selects the extreme ratios
that potentially have the largest effect on the update, and assigns them adaptive
sample-wise radii instead of using the fixed clipping radius. These radii are
derived from a prescribed tail profile, which specifies desired target values for the
selected extreme ratios. The resulting objective remains first-order and requires
only minibatch sorting and a modified policy loss. Experiments conducted on
MuJoCo and Atari benchmarks demonstrate that this simple modification achieves
strong performance relative to established baselines. Code is available at https:

1 Introduction
Deep reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved strong empirical performance in domains such
as games, robotic control, and large-scale model fine-tuning [ 22, 19, 15, 21, 20]. Among these
approaches, policy-gradient methods optimize a parametrized policy through gradient-based updates
of the expected return [28, 22, 13, 12, 20, 31, 32, 29]. Their practical performance, however, depends
critically on the stability of the policy update.
A fundamental challenge arises because policy updates typically evaluate a candidate policy using
data collected under a previous policy [18, 20]. This necessitates an importance-weighted surrogate
objective, whose behavior is governed by the likelihood ratio between the candidate and behavior
policies. Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO) addresses this issue by maximizing the surrogate
objective under an explicit constraint on policy discrepancy [18]. While theoretically robust, this
constrained optimization can be computationally cumbersome for large-scale applications.
Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) replaces TRPO’s constrained optimization with a clipped first-
order surrogate and has become a standard practical method [ 20, 9, 16, 30]. Its clipping rule acts
pointwise on each sampled likelihood ratio using a fixed interval around one. Although effective, this
rule does not directly control the tail behavior of the ratio distribution, which governs the reliability
of the importance-weighted surrogate [27, 24, 33, 25].

assigned teacher targets induced by a prescribed generalized Pareto tail profile. This yields adaptive

To bridge this gap, we show that instability in updates based on the importance-weighted surrogate
is driven by extreme likelihood ratios, rather than by the typical ratios found in the bulk of the
distribution [25]. Our motivating analysis shows that a sampled ratio falling within a fixed clipping
band does not necessarily imply meaningful control of policy discrepancy. Moreover, the tail
parameter of the ratio distribution governs the moment regime of the policy-update estimator. This
insight suggests that the relevant object for stabilization is not a local pointwise clipping event, but
the ordered tail of the empirical ratio distribution. Based on this observation, we proposeOrdered
Policy Optimization(OPO). OPO constructs teacher targets for the upper and lower empirical tails
of the ratio distribution and translates these targets into adaptive sample-wise proximal radii. The
resulting objective remains first-order and computationally simple, requiring only minibatch sorting
and a modified proximal penalty. Thus, OPO preserves the computational efficiency of PPO while
replacing fixed pointwise clipping with order-statistic-based tail control.
Contributions:Our main contributions are summarized as follows.
• We identify a statistical limitation of pointwise ratio clipping in proximal policy optimiza-
tion. Through a motivating analysis, we show that the tail behavior of the likelihood ratio
distribution governs the estimator regime of the importance-weighted policy surrogate.
• Motivated by this insight, we propose an order-statistic-based proximal objective. This
objective regulates the empirical upper and lower tails of the ratio distribution by inducing
adaptive, sample-wise radii derived from prescribed tail targets, yielding a method that is
straightforward to implement.
• Empirically, we demonstrate that this simple modification yields strong performance on
standard deep RL benchmarks, including MuJoCo and Atari.
1.1 Additional Related Work
Policy optimization.Policy-gradient methods optimize stochastic policies through gradient updates.
Trust-region methods stabilize these updates by constraining the discrepancy between successive
policies [22, 12, 18, 26, 27]. PPO replaces this constrained optimization with a clipped first-order
surrogate, making it one of the dominant practical methods in deep RL [ 20, 9, 16, 30]. Several
subsequent works extend PPO by adapting the clipping range or by replacing the clipped objective
with alternative proximal surrogates [ 6, 26, 27, 30]. These methods are designed to improve the
stability of policy updates while preserving the computational advantages of first-order optimization
[20]. Recent studies have also considered simple proximal objectives that regulate likelihood ratios
more directly [6, 26, 27, 30]. Our method differs from this line of work in its underlying motivation.
Specifically, it is motivated by the observation that the statistical regime of the importance-weighted
surrogate is governed by the tail behavior of the ratio distribution. Accordingly, the proposed
adaptation is induced by order statistics, rather than by a pointwise clipping rule alone.

Importance weighting and extreme-value modeling.The instability of importance-weighted
estimators has long been recognized in the statistical literature [17, 24, 33, 25]. Extreme-value theory
provides an asymptotic description of upper-tail behavior through threshold exceedances, which are
approximated by a generalized Pareto law under suitable regularity conditions [17]. Pareto-smoothed
importance sampling uses this perspective to diagnose and stabilize importance-weighted estimators,
with the fitted tail parameter serving as a concise summary of estimator reliability. In that line of
work, the role of extreme-value modeling is primarily diagnostic or post hoc [24, 33, 25, 7]. Our use
of this perspective is different. We do not fit a generalized Pareto model within each policy update,
nor do we use tail estimates solely for diagnosis. Instead, we prescribe a tail profile, use it to construct
order-statistic targets, and thereby obtain a simple proximal objective for policy optimization.

2.2 Importance Ratio and Generalized Pareto Distribution
The previous example shows that scalar clipping is not, in itself, a criterion for reliability. A fixed
scalar threshold provides only a pointwise partition of the observed ratios and does not characterize
how frequently exceedances occur or how rapidly their probabilities decay. For an importance
weighted mean, the crucial question is instead whether the ratio distribution possesses sufficiently
light tails to ensure the stability of the empirical average. Specifically, the existence and magnitude
of tail moments dictate the convergence behavior of importance-weighted estimators [24, 33, 25];
thus, statistical reliability is fundamentally governed by the tail behavior of the importance ratior.
This observation naturally leads to the concept of threshold exceedances. For a high threshold
u, the conditional distribution of large ratios can be studied using the exceedance law of r−
u|r > u . Extreme Value Theory provides a canonical approximation for this object: under
standard regularity conditions, the Pickands-Balkema-de-Haan theorem implies that the distribution
of threshold exceedances is asymptotically well approximated by a Generalized Pareto Distribution
(GPD, [17, 25]). We write this approximation as:

The shape parameterk summarizes the heaviness of the upper tail. Smaller values ofk correspond
to lighter tails and a more stable importance-weighted average, whereas larger values correspond
to heavier tails and slower, less reliable convergence. This connection forms the basis of Pareto-
Smoothed Importance Sampling (PSIS). PSIS operates by fitting a GPD to the largest observed ratios
and then replacing the most extreme weights with smoothed order statistics derived from the fitted
tail model [24, 33, 25]. In this role, the estimated shape parameterk functions both as a diagnostic
for the reliability of the importance-weighted estimator and as a mechanism for post-hoc stabilization.
This concept has been particularly influential in statistics, where the ratios are typically analyzed after
an importance-weighted procedure has already been completed [24, 33, 25, 7].
Nevertheless, policy optimization presents a crucial difference. The ratio distribution is not merely
observed after the fact; rather, it is actively created by the policy update process ( θold 7→θ ).
Consequently, PSIS-style smoothing does not inherently provide a differentiable objective suitable
for selecting the new policy. The challenge shifts from merely diagnosing whether a given set of
ratios possesses a reliable tail to designing an update whose induced ratio distribution has controllable
extremes. This necessity motivates our proposed method: instead of performing post-hoc fitting
and smoothing of ratios, we use the order-statistic structure of the generalized Pareto distribution to
construct a proximal policy objective that proactively controls the tail behavior during the update
itself.

3 Analysis of the Tail-Controlled Regime
We now formalize the critical role of the tail parameterk in determining the statistical reliability of
importance-weighted policy improvement. Our central argument is that the stability of the empirical
surrogate is determined not by whether individual likelihood ratios fall within a fixed scalar interval,
but by the tail behavior of the likelihood ratio distribution. We utilize an LQR example to provide a
concrete contrast between this distributional criterion and traditional PPO-style scalar clipping.

4 The Proposed Algorithm: Ordered Policy Optimization
In this section, we introduce OPO, a policy optimization rule that replaces the scalar clipping mecha-
nism with an order-statistic approach applied to the empirical likelihood ratio tails. The preceding
analysis motivates using a GPD to model and control the tail distribution. OPO instantiates this
principle using aGPD teacher profile, whose quantiles provide structured targets across the ordered
extremes. In contrast to a fixed scalar radius, the permitted ratio magnitude varies systematically with
its position in the empirical tail.

Intuitively, OPO optimizes the policy by nudging the selected extreme ratios toward the ordered
targets specified by a GPD teacher profile. As these ratios move toward the prescribed profile, the
empirical tail is encouraged toward the tail regime characterized by the target shape parameterk⋆. The
GPD provides a natural teacher for this purpose because threshold exceedances admit an asymptotic
GPD representation under the classical PBdH framework (Section 2.2). Further discussion of this
modeling choice and empirical diagnostics of the observed ratio tails is provided in Appendix A.
To implement this idea, OPO accounts for the direction favored by the policy objective. Since the
single sample surrogate contribution is rt(θ) ˆAt, positive advantages favor large ratios, whereas
negative advantages favor small ratios. We therefore control the upper tail of rt(θ) for positive
advantage samples and the upper tail ofrt(θ)−1 for negative advantage samples. Further, the GPD
profile is applied only to the selected threshold exceedances, comprising M+ positive advantage
samples andM− negative advantage samples. All remaining samples retain the nominal radiusκ.

5 Empirical Evaluation
We evaluate whether order-based control of likelihood ratio tails leads to more reliable policy
optimization by conducting experiments on continuous-control tasks from MuJoCo-v4 [ 23] and
on Atari benchmarks [3]. In these experiments, OPO uses fixed hyperparameters across all tasks:
κ= 0.2, σ ⋆ = 0.1, k⋆ = 0.33. Note that the choice of k⋆ = 0.33 falls within the reliable tail-
moment regime motivated by Theorem 3.1. All compared methods use the same learning rate, rollout
length, and minibatch size.
5.1 Experiments on MuJoCo-v4
We compare OPO against several established methods: clipped Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO
[20]), Proximal Policy Optimization with the KL penalty (PPO-KL [ 20]), Trust Region-Guided
Proximal Policy Optimization [26], Simple Policy Optimization (SPO [30]), and Proximal Policy
Optimization with adaptive clipping (PPO-λ [6]). We test these methods on six standard MuJoCo
tasks: Ant, HalfCheetah, Hopper, Humanoid, HumanoidStandup, and Walker2d, running each
experiment over five independent seeds.

NormScore = (score−min PPO)/(maxPPO−min PPO), where maxPPO and minPPO denote the

6 Conclusion
We addressed a limitation of PPO in stabilizing policy updates. PPO’s reliance on a fixed, pointwise
clipping range, while offering computational simplicity, does not directly account for the tail behavior
governing the reliability of the importance-weighted surrogate. We demonstrated that effective policy
stabilization can benefit from controlling the tail behavior of the likelihood ratio distribution, rather
than merely enforcing local constraints. We proposed Ordered Policy Optimization (OPO). OPO
replaces fixed pointwise clipping with an order-statistic-based approach: by identifying the influential
empirical tails of the importance ratios, we assign adaptive, sample-wise proximal radii derived
from a prescribed teacher profile. This modification allows the resulting optimization objective to
remain first-order and highly practical, requiring only standard minibatch sorting and a minor change
to the proximal penalty. Our empirical evaluations across standard control benchmarks, including
MuJoCo and Atari, support the effectiveness of this approach, showing that OPO yields strong
performance relative to established baselines while preserving the implementation simplicity of
PPO. Future research directions include developing data-adaptive tail targets, moving beyond fixed
teacher profiles, and deriving sharper theoretical guarantees regarding convergence and stability under
function approximation.

A Details for the GPD
A.1 The role of GPD in OPO
The generalized Pareto distribution (GPD) is used in OPO as a model for the extreme tail of the
likelihood ratio distribution, rather than as a parametric model for the full distribution of policy
ratios. This choice is motivated by the aforementioned classical Pickands-Balkema-de Haan theorem
(PBdH), under which exceedances above a sufficiently high threshold admit an asymptotic GPD
approximation under standard regularity conditions. Accordingly, the role of the GPD in OPO is to
provide a principled representation of extreme ratios once the analysis is restricted to the tail.
Hence, the OPO construction does not require the complete likelihood ratio distribution to follow a
heavy tailed parametric family. The OPO algorithm works well when the tail observations can be
meaningfully represented by a GPD approximation.
A.2 Investigation of PBdH
Assumptions for PBdHSpecifically, PBdH requires only the maximum domain of attraction
(MDA) condition, and is not limited to a specific parametric assumption. LetF(x) be the distribution
ofR1,...,R n. We say that F∈MDA(G) when, for samples (R1,...,R n) fromF , there exist
an >0andb n∈Rsuch that

While it is hard to verify this condition in practice, this standard condition is satisfied by most
nondegenerate distributions and widely accepted as mild in statistical literature[ 2, 17, 4, 8, 25].
Further, PBdH imposes no parametric model on the transition dynamics, rewards, or the body of the
ratio distribution, while permitting all three classical extreme-value regimes.
Empirical Validations of GPDWe examine this premise empirically in MuJoCo environments by
fitting a GPD to the observed ratio exceedances during PPO training. Table 1 reports the estimated
shape parameter ˆktogether with the correlation of the corresponding GPD QQ plot in Figure 9.

Crucially, PPO clipping does not preclude heavy-tailed likelihood-ratio distributions. Clipping
modifies the contribution of extreme ratios to the surrogate objective rather than directly constraining
the ratios themselves. Consequently, the raw ratio distribution may retain substantial tail mass even
when the optimization objective is clipped. A similar phenomenon has been observed in prior work

We use the scalar linear–quadratic instance with dynamics and reward parametersA= 0.8 ,B= 1 ,

the control scale. Settingq=λ= 1 keeps the state and action penalties on the same scale, making
the closed-form value, advantage, and surrogate expressions easy to interpret. The old closed loop is
stable becauseA+BK old = 0.3, so that the discounted value and the stationary state law are both
well defined. Table 2 summarizes the parameter choices used in Figure 3.
D Implementation Details
D.1 Algorithm
OverviewAlgorithm 1 summarizes the implementation of OPO. The procedure follows the standard
PPO pipeline: collect rollouts, estimate advantages, split samples into minibatches, and update the
policy and value networks. The only modification is the policy loss, where PPO’s fixed clipping radius
is replaced by the sample-wise radius εt defined in (4.1). Thus, OPO retains the implementation
structure of PPO while introducing order-statistic tail control through the policy objective.
Intuitively, OPO aims for the tail-controlled regime by assigning likelihood ratio order statistics to a
prescribed tail profile. This procedure requires three ingredients: identifying the relevant tail, locating
its empirical boundary, and specifying the ordered targets imposed beyond that boundary. Table 3
summarizes the quantities used for these purposes.

D.2 Additional diagnostics for the OPO algorithm
The preceding subsection specifies how OPO maps signed order statistics to prescribed tail targets
and, subsequently, to sample-specific radii. We now examine whether this construction behaves
as intended in finite samples. In particular, we study whether the prescribed shape parameter k⋆
systematically controls the realized likelihood ratio tail, and whether this behavior is robust to nearby
choices of the empirical tail threshold.
Control of the realized tail shape.We next examine whether the prescribed shape k⋆ has its
intended effect on the likelihood ratio distribution. Sincek⋆ is imposed on the ordered targets before
the policy update, it need not coincide exactly with a GPD shape parameter fitted to the resulting
ratios. Rather, the relevant question is whether varyingk⋆ systematically changes the heaviness of
the realized tail.
We repeat OPO withk⋆∈{0.33,0.49,0.70} and fit the corresponding GPD shape to the realized
relevant tail at nine training updates. Table 4 reports the mean fitted shape for each environment.
The fitted shape increases monotonically withk⋆ in every environment. Thus, OPO does not merely
impose a target profile on the current minibatch: changing the prescribed tail shape produces a
corresponding and systematic change in the realized likelihood ratio tail. The fitted values need not
equalk ⋆ exactly, but their ordering is preserved uniformly across all six environments.
Robustness to the empirical tail threshold.Finally, we test whether the preceding tail behavior is
an artifact of the particular number of retained extremes. Our default construction uses

D.3 Further Details
We fix the hyperparameters to match prior work [ 30], rather than optimizing them for OPO. All
experiments were conducted using NVIDIA RTX 2080 GPUs. The table below summarizes the
hyperparameters used.
E Broader Experimental Results
E.1 MuJoCo-v4
Overall results.Figure 10 reports the corresponding learning curves. OPO achieves competitive
final performance on most tasks. The results show that replacing fixed pointwise clipping with
order-statistic proximal targets can improve optimization without changing the rollout, advantage-
estimation, or optimizer components of the PPO pipeline.
Computational Cost.Further, we also report wall-clock times for the MuJoCo experiments. Table 7
shows that OPO is computationally comparable to PPO and SPO across all environments. Although
the order-statistic update introduces additional sorting operations, training time remains close to that
of the PPO-type baselines, with all methods requiring roughly two hours on average.
Ablation study of the shape parameterk.To understand the effect of the GPD shape parameter,
we further report the MuJoCo scores obtained under different values ofk. Recall that larger values of
kcorrespond to heavier prescribed ratio tails.
Crucially, as shown in Table 8 the lighter-tail choicek= 0.33 generally gives competitive perfor-
mance on five of the six environments, while the heavier-tail choices are less favorable. These results
are consistent with the theoretical motivation of OPO: prescribing overly heavy ratio tails can weaken
the stability of the importance-weighted surrogate.

NeurIPS Paper Checklist
1.Claims
Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the
paper’s contributions and scope?
Answer: [Yes]
Justification: We explain our contributions and scope in the abstract and introduction.
Guidelines:
• The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims
made in the paper.
• The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the
contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or
[N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.
• The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how
much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.
• It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals
are not attained by the paper.
2.Limitations
Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors?
Answer: [Yes]
Justification: We discuss the limitations of the work.
Guidelines:
• The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means
that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.
• The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper.
• The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to
violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings,
model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors
should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the
implications would be.
• The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was
only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often
depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.
• The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach.
For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution
is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be
used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle
technical jargon.
• The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms
and how they scale with dataset size.
• If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to
address problems of privacy and fairness.
• While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by
reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover
limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best
judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an impor-
tant role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers
will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.
3.Theory assumptions and proofs
Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and
a complete (and correct) proof?
Answer: [Yes]

perimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions

• If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived
well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of
whether the code and data are provided or not.
• If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken
to make their results reproducible or verifiable.
• Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways.
For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully
might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may
be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same
dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often
one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed
instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case
of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are
appropriate to the research performed.
• While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submis-
sions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the
nature of the contribution. For example
(a) If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how

(c) If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should

authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility.
In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in
some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers

text:
Flex-RSI Technical Report
Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive
Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents
Flex-RSI Team
Texas A&M University·University of Cambridge·National University of Singapore·NVIDIA·Massachusetts Institute of
Technology·MIT-IBM Watson AI Lab·The University of Texas at Austin·Carnegie Mellon University·University of
Pennsylvania·University of Southern California·Purdue University·Adobe·University of Toronto
Frontier language models are increasingly deployed as agents, and how well an agent performs depends not
only on its model but also on its harness: the prompts, tools, memory, and control loop through which the
model acts. When an agent is applied to a new problem, a natural question is whether it can use the feedback of
the task to improve the way it works, and not merely its answer. Most existing benchmarks keep the agent’s
harness fixed and score the solution it produces, or target large-scale model training. We introduce Flex-RSI, a
benchmark for the recursive self-improvement of agents on vision and robotics tasks under a fixed budget. In
each round, an executor improves the task solution, which is kept only if it scores higher on held-out validation
data, and an improver then revises the harness, including the executor and itself. Every run starts from the same
general-purpose harness, and the final solution is scored on hidden test data. Evaluating closed-source and
open-weight models on tasks spanning perception, reasoning, robot action, 3D reconstruction, visual creation,
and infrastructure, we find that self-improvement helps most when the agent builds its own solution, that
feedback recording only success or failure holds back open-weight models, and that open-weight models fall
furthest behind where outputs must pass strict checks of physical stability or exact correctness. Paired runs
further show that editing the harness itself contributes to the gains.
Project page:https://flex-rsi.github.io
Authors:The full list of authors and their contributions is in Section 7
1 Introduction
Frontier large language models now routinely act as agents that write code, conduct experiments, and read the
results over multiple steps (Anthropic, 2026a; OpenAI, 2026b; Google DeepMind, 2026; Qwen Team, 2026b;
DeepSeek-AI, 2026; GLM-5 Team, 2026). An agent’s performance depends not only on the underlying model
but also on itsharness: the prompts, tools, memory, and control loop through which the model acts. This raises
a practical question for anyone who deploys an agent on a new problem: given only the task, can the agent
use the task’s feedback to improve the way it works under a fixed budget, and not merely its answer?
Most existing benchmarks run each model inside a fixed harness, often the vendor’s own, and score only the
solution or artifact it produces, mostly on machine-learning research tasks with a continuous metric (Chan
et al., 2025; Wijk et al., 2024); those that also let the agent revise its harness (RSI-Exam Team, 2026) or that
center on upstream model training at scale (OpenRSI Foundation, 2026) remain within machine-learning
research. We introduce Flex-RSI to measure how well a frontier agent improves both its solution and its own
harness on general vision and robotics tasks, a setting in which agents are increasingly deployed, each attempt
consumes real compute, and the goal is a better solution within hours to days.
In Flex-RSI, the harness consists of two components that alternate over rounds (Figure 1a). Theexecutor
improves the task solution: it modifies the solution, runs experiments, and evaluates them on the labeled
development data, and its candidate is kept only if it also scores higher on held-out validation data. The
improverthen reviews the round and modifies the harness itself, including the executor’s prompts, tools, and

The tasks differ in what the agent must produce (a single answer or a solution it builds), how the evaluator
scores it (on a scale or only as success or failure), and how strictly the output is checked. From experiments on
24 tasks spanning perception, reasoning, robot action, 3D reconstruction, visual creation, and infrastructure
(Figure 1b), with 18 closed-source and open-weight models, we find:
1. Tasks in which the agent builds the solution leave more room for self-improvement:tasks whose
solution is a single answer to each question leave little room to improve, while tasks in which the agent
builds its own solution leave the most, and there models pull apart (Figure 1c).
2. The granularity of feedback matters:feedback that scores each episode on a scale helps all models,
whereas feedback that records only success or failure leaves open-weight models barely improving on the
solutions they build.
3. Strict checks of physical stability and exact correctness pose the greatest challenge:outputs that look
plausible often fail checks of physical stability or exact correctness, and open-weight models fall furthest
behind on them.
Paired runs further show that letting the improver edit the harness raises the test score in six of seven pairs of
otherwise identical runs (Section 5.4).
2 Related work
2.1 Benchmarks for self-improving agents
Benchmarks for machine-learning engineering and scientific research measure whether agents can turn a
task description into a working result. MLE-bench evaluates machine-learning engineering on competition
tasks (Chan et al., 2025); RE-Bench compares agents with human experts on research-engineering prob-
lems (Wijk et al., 2024); and PaperBench assesses the replication of machine-learning research (Starace et al.,
2025). Related evaluations examine the design and execution of machine-learning experiments (Huang et al.,
2023b) and the generation of executable programs for data-driven scientific discovery (Chen et al., 2025).
Their primary evaluation targets are the models, code, and research results that an agent produces.
title: Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents

text:
Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents 3
Evaluations framed around recursive self-improvement cover several different objects of improvement. RSI-
Exam supports executable research on both task methods and harnesses for frozen models, followed by hidden-
test evaluation (RSI-Exam Team, 2026). OpenRSI Index spans foundation-model development, including large-
scaletrainingandlighter-weightinference, agent, andsystemstasks(OpenRSIFoundation,2026). Autonomous
post-training is evaluated through controlled training runs and assessments of the resulting models (Rank
et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026c), while algorithm-design tasks ask agents to improve training procedures
that are subsequently evaluated by retraining (Chi et al., 2026). Sustained machine-learning research with
repeated validation feedback and a separate hidden test is evaluated in AutoResearchExam (Ramesh et al.,
2026). Harness engineering also appears alongside model-training tasks in Vals RSI Index (Chen et al., 2026b).
TraceTrial-Bench evaluates the reliability of agent harnesses themselves rather than their improvement (Cao
et al., 2026). These settings share an interest in autonomous experimentation, but differ in whether the
optimized artifact is data, a training algorithm, model weights, or the harness around a model.
Complementary studies examine how experience becomes reusable improvement. Data-centric research under
a fixed post-training stack is studied in RSIBench-Data (Meng et al., 2026). Procedural-ability transfer and
the conversion of episodic experience into reusable skills are evaluated in EvoAgentBench (Gao et al., 2026b)
and SkillEvolBench (Lei et al., 2026), respectively. EvolveTool-Bench checks whether evolved tools satisfy
independent conformance tests beyond completing the current task (Kaliyev and Maryanskyy, 2026). The
contribution of persistent experience to later personal-agent behavior is isolated through matched persistence-
on/off comparisons in PAST-Bench (Xue et al., 2026). Whether self-evolving language-model agents learn new
tasks without forgetting earlier ones is evaluated in a related study (Chen et al., 2026e). EmbodiedCLBench
evaluateswhetherembodiedagentscanreusetheexperiencegainedonbasictaskstosolveunseencompositions
of them (Huang et al., 2026b), and Embodied Skill Bench measures how packaged embodied skills help agents
on physical tasks (Han et al., 2026c). Together, these studies motivate evaluating both immediate task gains
and improvements that remain useful on subsequent tasks.
Flex-RSI studies task-solution and harness improvement together on vision, robotics, and related downstream
tasks. For each task, every model starts from the same general-purpose harness and starter solution, then
alternates execution and harness revision under a fixed budget. The improver can edit the executor’s prompts,
tools, and workflow as well as its own prompts, settings, and lessons. This shared protocol separates three
questions: how much the task solution improves, what additional gains come from editing the harness, and
whether a harness built by one model helps another model on the same task. A review of the evidence behind
recursive self-improvement claims finds that few studies compare improvement procedures from identical
starting artifacts at a matched budget (Chen et al., 2026g); the paired runs with and without the improver
(Section 5.4) make this comparison.
2.2 Frontier agents
Language-model agents connect reasoning to actions and environmental feedback through an execution loop.
ReAct interleaves reasoning and tool use (Yao et al., 2023), Reflexion carries verbal feedback into subsequent
trials through episodic memory (Shinn et al., 2023), and Voyager accumulates executable skills through
open-ended interaction in Minecraft (Wang et al., 2023). Coding interfaces such as Claude Code and Codex
CLI expose file editing and command execution (Anthropic, 2026c; OpenAI, 2026d). OpenHands provides
infrastructure for software-development agents (Wang et al., 2025b), while SWE-agent studies how an agent–
computer interface supports repository navigation, editing, and testing (Yang et al., 2024). Research agents
extend these capabilities to experimentation: AIDE searches over candidate solution code (Jiang et al., 2025),
and The AI Scientist combines research ideation, experiments, paper writing, and review in an automated
workflow (Lu et al., 2024). Frontier models have also been evaluated as robot agents that act in the control
loop (Huang et al., 2026a; Zhou et al., 2026b; Yao et al., 2026c) or write reusable robot tools (Ge et al., 2026),
across many embodiments (Yang et al., 2026b) and against learned policies (Zhang et al., 2026f), and coding
agents have been asked to reconstruct dynamic scenes as executable graphics programs (Shen et al., 2026a).
Automated agent design makes parts of this execution machinery optimization variables. Promptbreeder
evolves both task prompts and the mutation prompts that revise them (Fernando et al., 2023), while GEPA uses
title: Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents

text:
Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents 4
reflection on execution traces to propose and select prompt updates (Agrawal et al., 2026). ADAS searches over
agent programs using an archive of prior designs (Hu et al., 2025), and AFlow searches over code-represented
workflows (Zhang et al., 2025b). A builder model can also learn principles for constructing the execution
environment of a fixed target model (Qian et al., 2026). AlphaEvolve applies evolutionary program search to
scientific and algorithmic discovery, with executable evaluators selecting candidate task programs (Novikov
et al., 2025). These approaches optimize objects ranging from prompts to complete programs, with different
boundaries around the optimization procedure itself.
Self-modifying agents extend this search to their own implementations. STOP applies its code improver to the
improver itself (Zelikman et al., 2024); Gödel Agent and SICA likewise revise agent logic and orchestration
code (Yin et al., 2025; Robeyns et al., 2025). The Darwin Gödel Machine retains an archive of empirically
evaluated, self-modified agents (Zhang et al., 2025a), while the Huxley–Gödel Machine also considers a
candidate’s potential to produce better descendants (Wang et al., 2026d). Meta-Harness searches harness
code using previous candidates, scores, and execution traces (Lee et al., 2026b). RHI represents the harness
as a prompt-level specification of the agent loop and refines it using pairwise feedback over its own revision
history (Lee et al., 2026a). Self-Harness uses execution failures to guide revisions to the model’s own
harness (Zhang et al., 2026a), and AIDE2 recursively revises research-agent code (Srikanth et al., 2026).
Several systems explicitly distinguish task improvement from improvement of the process that produces
it. Hyperagents combine a task agent and a meta agent in a shared editable program, allowing the self-
modification mechanism itself to evolve and studying transfer of meta-level improvements (Zhang et al.,
2026b). HSI separates a task harness, an evolver, and a meta-evolver under a fixed outer anchor (Zhou, 2026).
In robotics, RegenHarness revises harness configuration from execution records, with regression checks and
release gates governing acceptance (Wang et al., 2026a). Harness evolution around frozen models now spans
video understanding (Luo et al., 2026; Liang et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026), image generation with a frozen
generator (Han et al., 2026a), 3D reconstruction (Yao et al., 2026a), and embodied agents, including robot
manipulation, where the harness is revised from diagnosed execution failures (Tian et al., 2026a; Feng et al.,
2026; Yu et al., 2026b; Du et al., 2026), experience is organized into knowledge or executable stacks shared
across tasks (Bao et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026f; Wen et al., 2026), the system decides where to spend robot
trials (Song et al., 2026), and changes are tested in simulation before they reach the robot (Hu et al., 2026).
Studies of these loops find that the number of rollouts the optimizer sees in each round and the selection
rule determine whether an evolved robot harness generalizes (Wei et al., 2026b), that accepting any edit
that raises an aggregate validation score admits regressions and favors noise (Wang et al., 2026e), that proxy
improvements need not hold where the update is deployed (Wang et al., 2026b), and that an exact validation
score after every attempt opens the validation split to adaptive selection (Yao et al., 2026b). RRSI addresses
the risk that harness evolution overfits its training tasks, with gains that shrink or vanish on out-of-distribution
benchmarks, by constraining how edits are proposed and selected (Xia et al., 2026). Other studies ask which
failures harness evolution can repair and when weight training should take over (Tian et al., 2026b; Wang
et al., 2026c), argue that rewriting the scaffold around frozen weights avoids diminishing returns but not an
eventual ceiling (Bobadilla-Suarez et al., 2026), and report that weak evaluators and early failures in long skill
chains stall improvement over long robot runs (Wang, 2026). Surveys organize these developments by the
components that evolve and the feedback that drives their updates (Gao et al., 2026a; Fang et al., 2025; Chen
et al., 2026a), and recent surveys and position papers cover recursive self-improvement in physical AI (Han
et al., 2026b; Zhou et al., 2026a), agent harnesses for video generation (Fan et al., 2026), and the use of
frontier models for 3D modeling, computational design, and robotics (Dou et al., 2026).
These systems propose particular ways to accumulate experience, search for agent designs, or revise an
improvement procedure. Flex-RSI evaluates the ability to make such revisions through a shared executor–
improver harness (Section 3.2). Each frontier model operates both components from the same initial harness
and, on each task, the same starter solution and budget. The executor changes the task solution; the improver
changes the executor and its own instructions and lessons. The evaluator, data splits, and budget accounting
remain fixed. This setting makes the model’s capacity to improve its operating machinery the object of
title: Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents

text:
Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents 5
comparison across vision, robotics, and related tasks, while keeping changes to the solution distinct from
changes to the harness.
2.3 Flex-RSI tasks
Flex-RSI draws its 24 tasks from six areas, combining established benchmarks, source datasets, and our own
curated creation tasks. Table 1 summarizes their sources and metrics. Each task provides a starter solution,
development data, hidden validation and test splits, and a fixed improvement budget, so that these resources
support the evaluation of changes to both task solutions and agent harnesses.
Action.The manipulation tasks use simulated environments from RoboDojo (Chen et al., 2026d) and Robo-
Casa365 (Nasiriany et al., 2026), which extends RoboCasa’s household simulation platform (Nasiriany et al.,
2024). Active Search uses H*Bench’s panoramic environments for visual search (Yu et al., 2026a), while
RoboLab uses the RoboLab-120 suite to evaluate a generalist tabletop manipulation policy (Yang et al., 2026a).
The LIBERO-based tasks (Liu et al., 2023) examine robustness to changes in initial conditions and task spec-
ifications through LIBERO-PRO (Zhou et al., 2025), and adaptation to changes during execution through
LIBERO-MAX (Zhang et al., 2026e). Embodied-SWE draws on EmbodiedSWE-Bench, where agents write
robot-control programs and receive scores based on physical task progress (Shen et al., 2026b). Related
simulation benchmarks extend such evaluation to whole-body humanoid loco-manipulation, as in SIMPLE (Wei
et al., 2026a).
Reasoning.Ego-Exo Memory uses the Ego-Exo4D portion of EgoExoMem for memory reasoning across
synchronizedfirst-andthird-personvideos(Liuetal.,2026b;Graumanetal.,2024). KinematicsusesQuantiPhy
to infer physical quantities such as sizes, velocities, and accelerations from video (Puyin et al., 2026); Mass
adapts product photographs and metadata from Amazon Berkeley Objects for weight estimation (Collins
et al., 2022). Abstract reasoning spans grid transformations in ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2 (Chollet, 2019;
Chollet et al., 2025) and interactive exploration in ARC-AGI-3 (ARC Prize Foundation, 2026). Spatial-VSI uses
VSI-Bench’s spatial questions about indoor videos (Yang et al., 2025).
Creation.Image Editing uses our own curated images and editing instructions, and Text-to-Image uses original
Chinese and English prompts. Multi-turn Editing follows the five-turn sessions of MSE-Bench, introduced with
VINCIE, in which each instruction acts on the previous result (Qu et al., 2026). Video Generation uses the
compositional prompts and evaluation criteria of T2V-CompBench (Sun et al., 2025).
Reconstruction.3D Tracking adapts IGGT’s instance-tracking setting (Li et al., 2026) on ScanNet and Scan-
Net++ (Dai et al., 2017; Yeshwanth et al., 2023). Scene from Photo uses HARMONY300, introduced with
HARMONY for reconstructing furnished rooms from single images (Sun et al., 2026); its synthetic scenes derive
from 3D-FRONT (Fu et al., 2021). Scene from Video uses the indoor scenes released with HoloScene (Xia
et al., 2025), drawn from Replica and ScanNet++ (Straub et al., 2019; Yeshwanth et al., 2023), together with
CoDimRecon’s geometry, rendering, and physical-stability evaluation setting (Xie et al., 2026).
Perception.Visual Search combines high-resolution questions from V*Bench and HR-Bench 8K (Wu and Xie,
2024; Wang et al., 2025a). Video Quality combines subjective quality scores for YouTube-UGC videos (Wang
et al., 2019; Yim et al., 2020) with human preferences on generated-video pairs from Rapidata’s Veo 3.1
comparison dataset (Rapidata, 2025).
Infrastructure.VAE Decode uses the variational autoencoder released with MiniMax H3 (MiniMax, 2026b)
and asks the agent to accelerate its decoder while preserving the reference outputs on unseen inputs.
3 Flex-RSI
Flex-RSI evaluates whether an agent, given a task and a fixed budget, can improve not only its solution to the
task but also the harness through which it operates. We first define the task setting (Section 3.1), then the
self-improving harness (Section 3.2), and finally how runs are evaluated (Section 3.3).

3.1 Problem setup
Each task provides the agent with a starter solution, compute resources, a budget, and data partitioned into
three disjoint splits. Thedevelopment split, including its labels, is available to the agent for experimentation
and evaluation. Thevalidation splitis withheld from the agent and determines which candidate solutions are
retained. Thetest splitis likewise withheld and is used only once, after the run terminates, to evaluate the
final solution. The objective of the agent is to maximize the test score of its final solution within the budget.
On a given task, every run starts from the same starter solution and is subject to the same budget, which limits
wall-clock time, GPU hours, model usage, the number of validation evaluations, and the number of rounds.
The 24 tasks are listed in Table 1 and described in Section A.
3.2 The self-improving harness
A harness is the program that mediates between a language model and a task. Through its prompts, tools,
control loop, and memory, it determines the context presented to the model and the actions available to it.
Since the harness consists of code and text, the agent can modify it in the same manner as any other program,
while the model weights remain fixed. In Flex-RSI, the harness𝐻=(𝐸,𝐼) comprises two components that query
the same model. Theexecutor𝐸 operates on the task solution: it modifies the solution, conducts experiments,
and evaluates the results on the development split. Theimprover𝐼 operates on the harness: it analyses the
executor’s trajectories and results, diagnoses failures, and revises the prompts, tools, and workflow of the
executor as well as its own instructions and accumulated lessons.

3.3 Evaluation
We report the test score of the final solution,𝑆(𝑠𝑇 ;Dtest), and its improvement over the starter solution,

4 Experiments
This section reports what the agents achieve, in the order in which a reader would ask about it: how well each
model does over all tasks and within each area (Section 4.2), how much of that is due to self-improvement
(Section 4.3), in which rounds the gains arrive (Section 4.4), and what they cost (Section 4.5). It reports what
happens; Section 5 examines why.

How results are reported.Each model is run once on each task it is evaluated on; where a run was repeated,
the latest run is reported. RoboDojo and RoboCasa are suites of 10 and 8 robot tasks, each run separately for
10 rounds and aggregated into one suite score. A run’s result is the test score of its final solution on the task’s
primary metric, on a 0–100 scale. Because the metrics differ across tasks, models are compared through ranks:
on each task, a model scores the share of the other models evaluated on the task that it beats, from 0 (last) to
100 (first). Its score in an area is the mean over the tasks of the area it was run on, and its overall score is
the mean of its five area scores. To measure self-improvement itself, we also report the validation score of
the starter solution and the best validation score reached during the run. The main results cover the 20 tasks
evaluated with at least six models; the four tasks evaluated with two models so far are reported in Table 12.
4.2 Main results
Figure 2a gives one score per model and Figure 2b breaks it down by area. Claude Opus 5.5 has the highest

4.3 How much self-improvement adds
The scores above combine what a model can do from the start with what it gains by improving. Figure 3
separates the two by comparing the starter’s validation score with the best validation score reached during the
run. Self-improvement raises the validation score in 150 of the 177 runs (85%), by a median of 10.4 points.
The gain depends on how much the task leaves to build. It is largest where the agent builds most of its solution
from a weak starter: on 3D Tracking, RoboLab and Active Search the median validation score rises from 19.4,
8.3 and 23.0 to 62.2, 45.8 and 52.7 (Figure 3a). It is smallest where the starter already solves most of the
task, as on ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2 (median starter 91.9 and 82.5, a median gain of 0 points on both).
Two tasks do not fit this pattern: ARC-AGI-3 and Scene from Video start low (3.8 and 17.3) and still barely
improve (to 4.1 and 18.5).
The gain also depends on the model. Closed-source models improve more often and by more: they raise the
validation score in 94% of their 85 runs, by a median of 14.9 points, against 76% of 92 runs and 8.5 points for

4.4 Improvement over rounds
Figure 4a shows in which rounds the gains arrive. For each run that improves, we express its best validation
score after every round as a share of the run’s whole gain, and take the median over the runs of each area.
Most of the gain comes early: the median run reaches 90% of its gain by round 3 in Perception and Reasoning
and by round 4 in Creation. Action and Reconstruction take longer, reaching 90% only by rounds 6 and 8.
These are the two areas with the weakest starters (median validation score 16.7 and 19.4, against 60.0 to
78.8 in the other three), where the agent likely has to build a working solution before it can refine it.
4.5 Cost
Runs differ widely in what they spend. A run on one task, counting each robot task of RoboDojo and RoboCasa
separately, uses a median of 49.7 million tokens, and the middle 80% of runs use between 8.6 and 93.4
million. We compare tokens rather than prices, since the open-weight models are served on our own GPUs. To
compare models on the same footing, Figure 4b expresses each model’s token use relative to the median model
on the same task. Spending more does not buy a higher score: across the 12 models, the rank correlation
between relative token use and score is−0.05. Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra, three of the
four highest-scoring models, use 0.35 to 0.61 times the median, whereas Gemini 4 Argon reaches a score close
to that of Opus with 1.66 times. Five of the six open-weight models use at least the median (1.0 to 1.75 times),
and all six score below 50.

the output. These thirteen tasks are divided further according to how the task evaluator scores an episode:
on nine it assigns a score on a scale, and on four it records only whether the episode or level succeeded.

5.1 Tasks in which the agent builds the solution leave more room for self-improvement
Finding 1.When the agent builds the solution, self-improvement raises the score the most and separates the models;
when the solution is a single answer, the starter solution already scores high and the models end about as far apart
as they began. On 3D Tracking, every run starts from 19.4 and the best run gains 65.4 points.
On tasks whose solution is a single answer, the starter solution already passes each question to the model,
so it scores high from the start and its score depends on the model: its median validation score over these
seven tasks is 78.2, and the models are 27.5 points apart before the first round (medians over tasks). The
title: Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents

text:
Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents 17
largest gain that any run achieves is 14.8 points at the median, and at the end of the runs the models are 25.0
points apart, about as far as at the start. On the tasks in which the agent builds the solution, every model starts
from the same program, although its score can depend on the model that it calls. On the nine of them whose
evaluator scores each episode on a scale, this program scores 19.4 at the median, the largest gain is 38.8
points at the median, and the models, 0.9 points apart at the start, end 38.8 points apart; on the four whose
evaluator records only success or failure, they move from 2.5 to 37.2 points apart. The same pattern appears
in Figure 1c. The exceptions are Kinematics, whose solution is a single answer but whose starter solution
scores only 27.7 and on which a run gains 33.5 points, and Multi-turn Editing, on which the agent builds the
solution but no run gains more than 4.2 points.
5.2 The granularity of feedback matters
Finding 2.When the evaluator scores each episode on a scale, open-weight models also improve the solutions they
build; when it records only success or failure, they barely improve, while closed-source models still do. On RoboCasa,
the median open-weight run gains 5.6 points and the median closed-source run 51.2.
On the nine tasks in which the agent builds the solution and the evaluator scores each episode on a scale, the
median gain over the open-weight runs of a task is 9.9 points at the median over tasks, against 28.4 for the
closed-source runs, and on 3D Tracking and Active Search it is close to that of the closed-source runs (39.8
against 42.8, and 29.3 against 28.4). On the four tasks whose evaluator records only whether an episode or a
level succeeded, namely RoboCasa, LIBERO-MAX, LIBERO-PRO, and ARC-AGI-3, the median open-weight gain
falls to 1.6 points, while the closed-source runs still gain 16.9. The median open-weight run does not improve
at all on LIBERO-PRO and gains 0.2 points on ARC-AGI-3. Since a candidate is retained only if it raises the
validation score (Equation (2)), a score on a scale rewards a change that improves part of an episode, whereas
a score that records only success or failure rewards a change only once it turns failed episodes into successful
ones.
5.3 Strict checks of physical stability and exact correctness pose the greatest challenge
Finding 3.Outputs that look correct often fail checks of physical stability or exact correctness, and tasks scored
by such checks are where open-weight models fall furthest behind. On Scene from Video, no object placed by an
open-weight model remains stable in simulation, against 70.7% for Claude Opus 5.5.
The difference between the best closed-source and the best open-weight model is largest on tasks whose
evaluator applies such a check: whether a robot task succeeds in simulation (RoboCasa, 50.0 points; RoboLab,
40.3; RoboDojo, 37.3), whether the output grid is exactly right (ARC-AGI-2, 49.2) or a level is cleared (ARC-
AGI-3, 43.3; on ARC-AGI-1, whose puzzles the starter solutions already nearly solve, it is 8.8), and whether a
reconstructed scene is physically and geometrically consistent (Scene from Video, 36.4; Scene from Photo,
26.5). It is smallest on tasks scored by a judge or with a tolerance: Video Quality (0.1), Mass (0.8), Multi-turn
Editing (1.0), Video Generation (2.5), and Image Editing (4.2). The component scores of the two scene tasks
show how plausible outputs fail these checks (Tables 29 and 30). On Scene from Photo, the renderings of
the open-weight scenes resemble the photo, with an Appearance score of up to 81.8, but the furniture is not
recovered as complete and correctly placed objects: their Objects score is at most 16.5, against 62.5 for both
closed-source models. On Scene from Video, the Physics score, the fraction of objects that remain stable in
simulation, is 0.0 for all four open-weight models, against 70.7 for Claude Opus 5.5 and 37.7 for GPT-6 Astra.
The two LIBERO tasks are the exceptions among the robot tasks: the best open-weight model matches the best
closed-source model on LIBERO-MAX (45.8) and trails it by 10.0 points on LIBERO-PRO.

runs, and most where the unchanged starting harness makes little progress. On Active Search, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next
reaches 21.0 without the improver and 59.3 with it.

Table 8 compares pairs of runs that differ only in whether the improver runs. In the run without the improver,
labeled frozen harness in the table, the starting harness is never modified; in the run with it, labeled self-
improving harness, the improver edits the executor and itself after every round, as in all other runs of this
report. The test score with the improver is higher in six of the seven pairs, by 2.0 to 40.0 points; in the seventh,
Claude Opus 5.5 on Turn On Sink Faucet reaches 80.0 in both runs, and its run without the improver reached
the maximum validation score in round 8. The difference is largest where the unchanged starting harness
makes little progress: DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash remains at 0.0 on Open Drawer without the improver and reaches
40.0 with it, and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next gains 20.0 on Turn On Sink Faucet and 38.3 on Active Search. On
3D Tracking, the executor alone already raises the two Qwen models from the 19.4 of the starter solution
to validation scores of 48.9 and 63.4, and the improver adds 6.5 and 2.0 points on the test split. The runs
without the improver also end after fewer rounds in six of the seven pairs.
Table 9 asks whether a harness built by a stronger model helps a weaker one. On Open Drawer, DeepSeek-V4.1
Flash started from the final executor of Gemini 4 Argon reaches 20.0 when the executor is not modified further
and 60.0 when Argon’s final improver continues to edit it, against 40.0 when it improves its own harness from
the start and 80.0 for Argon. On Turn On Sink Faucet, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next started from the harness of Claude
Opus 5.5 reaches 0.0 in both settings, below the 20.0 it reaches when it improves its own harness and the 80.0
of Opus. On Active Search and 3D Tracking, Qwen3.8-27B started from the final harness of the source run
and improved it further with its own improver. On Active Search, it reaches 49.2 from the harness of Gemini 4
Argon, against 69.0 when it improves its own harness from the start and 79.7 for Argon. On 3D Tracking, it
reaches 53.8 from the harness of Claude Opus 5.5, against 52.4 from the starting harness and 79.6 for Opus.
A harness built by a stronger model thus raised the score of the weaker model on two of the four tasks, by 20.0
points on Open Drawer and 1.4 points on 3D Tracking, and in neither case did the weaker model approach the
score of the stronger one.
6 Conclusion
We introduced Flex-RSI, a benchmark that measures whether a frontier agent can improve both its task solution
and its own harness within a fixed budget, with every run starting from the same general-purpose harness
and every final solution scored on a hidden test split. Across 24 tasks and 18 models, three findings emerge.
Self-improvement raises the score most on tasks in which the agent builds its own solution, and on these tasks
models that start from the same program end far apart, whereas on tasks whose solution is a single answer
the starter solution already scores high and the models end about as far apart as they began. Open-weight
models improve when the evaluator scores each episode on a scale, but barely improve when it records only
success or failure. The largest gaps between closed-source and open-weight models arise where the evaluator
checks physical stability or exact correctness, even when the outputs look plausible. Paired runs further show
that editing the harness contributes to the improvement, most where the unchanged starting harness makes
little progress, whereas a harness built by a stronger model raised the score of a weaker model on only two of
four tasks.
The improvement measured here is mostly at the level of the harness. The evaluated model’s weights never
change, andonmosttasksnomodelistrained; onsome, thesolutionmaytrainorfine-tunehelpermodelsonthe
development split. Flex-RSI therefore does not measure a model that modifies its own parameters. Extending
the benchmark to weight-level self-improvement, and studying how it interacts with changes to the harness, is
left to future work. The leaderboard is maintained on the project page,https://flex-rsi.github.io.
