A Task cards
This appendix describes each of the 24 tasks of Table 1: what it measures, how its data were built from its
source and divided into splits, what the agent has to produce and with which resources, the starter solution,
the metric and where it comes from, and the prior work on the source benchmark. Every task follows the
setting of Section 3.1: the development split is available to the agent with its labels, while the validation and
test splits are withheld. Unless stated otherwise, the solution may call the model being evaluated within the
stated limits, and it may not use the annotations of the source benchmark.
A.1 Action
RoboDojo
Purpose.Whether the agent can turn a general multimodal model into a closed-loop policy for a dual-arm
robot. No policy is trained: the model decides the motions at evaluation time, and the agent improves the
program that queries it.
Source and construction.Ten simulation tasks of RoboDojo (Chen et al., 2026d). Full credit (success) requires:
four bottles in a dustbin, using a handover between the hands; a garment folded with sleeves in and hem
aligned to the shoulders; digit tiles placed in the order forming the largest number; three tubes inserted upright
into a rack; all five own pieces placed in tic-tac-toe against a randomly playing opponent arm; a T-shaped
block pushed onto its pad without lifting; eight xylophone keys struck left to right with a mallet; the conveyor
object shown on a board placed in a lifted basket; four eggs in a holder with its lid closed; and five nesting
dolls lined up by size. Several tasks also require a return to the start pose. All layouts come from RoboDojo’s
evaluation seed 0: per task, validation takes the first five, test the next five, and development the rest, of which
a fixed panel of five is evaluated. Validation layouts of three tasks are those of Galbot Team et al. (2026). Tasks
with a randomized variant (fold clothes, largest number, Push-T, nesting dolls) use two standard and three
randomized layouts per split. The agent sees full development results, the validation score only, and no test
results.
Setting.An ARX X5 dual-arm robot in Isaac Sim at 25Hz, run through the pinned single-layout RoboDojo
client of RoboICL (Liu et al., 2026a), 500 to 1100 steps per episode, starting in an elbow-up pose slightly in
front of RoboDojo’s. The policy receives three RGB cameras, proprioception, and the head-camera calibration,
never object poses or rewards, and returns chunks of at most 64 end-effector or joint targets, limited to 3cm
and 0.15rad per step. It may call the run’s model at most 80 times per episode and no other model; scripted
motions and its own inverse kinematics are allowed.
Starter solution.One model call per chunk of up to ten end-effector motions, given the head-camera image at
320×240, the robot state, and its notes from earlier calls.
Metric.Each episode receives the progress score𝑠∈[ 0, 100] of its RoboDojo rubric (for example 10, 25, 40,
100 for one to four bottles), as defined in the RoboDojo task documentation (Chen et al., 2026d), 100 only on
success, scored as the scene stands when it ends. The task score is𝑆𝑡 = 1

Prior work.RoboDojo has 42 simulation tasks and evaluates 30 trained manipulation policies (Chen et al.,
2026d). Frontier models have also been used as the policy: Galbot Team et al. (2026) reach 48% success on
a RoboDojo subset with GPT-6 Astra combined with𝜋0.5; RoboICL (Liu et al., 2026a) conditions the model
on demonstrations and interaction memory (overall score 50.64 on 30 tasks against 33.68 for the strongest
baseline); and Encore (Kang et al., 2026) writes policy programs from a few demonstrations.
RoboCasa
Purpose.Whether the agent can obtain a model-driven policy for a mobile manipulator that carries over from
the kitchens and objects used in development to kitchens and objects it has never seen.
Source and construction.Eight tasks of RoboCasa365 (Nasiriany et al., 2026), an extension of RoboCasa (Nasiri-
any et al., 2024), with RoboCasa’s own success checks. Six are atomic tasks from RoboCasa365’s seen-task
target set: turn on the microwave (on, gripper away from the button), turn on the sink faucet (handle turned

over 0.4rad), open the named cabinet (every door at least 90% open), open the named drawer (at least 95%
open), place a mug under the coffee dispenser, and turn off the named burner. Two are composite: portion hot
dogs (from its unseen composite set; one bun and one sausage on each of two plates) and kettle boiling (kettle
within 15cm of a burner that is on). An episode is fixed by a kitchen (layout and style), object instances, and a
seed from which RoboCasa places the robot and objects and words the instruction. Development has five fixed
episodes in RoboCasa’s pretraining kitchens with pretraining objects; validation and test have five episodes
each in the same five target kitchens (the first five of RoboCasa’s ten evaluation kitchens) with target objects,
differing by seed; validation and test were reduced from ten to five episodes each, and every episode was
checked to build and reset. The agent sees full development results, the validation success rate only, and no
test results; neither it nor the policy may load target kitchens or objects.
Setting.The PandaOmron robot (a Franka Panda arm on a mobile base with a torso lift) in MuJoCo at 20Hz,
with the per-task horizons of RoboCasa’s dataset registry (450 to 2250 steps). The policy receives three
512× 512RGB cameras, proprioception, and calibration, never object states, and returns chunks of at most 64
rows of RoboCasa’s 12-dimensional action. It may call the run’s model at most 80 times per episode and no
other model.
Starter solution.One model call per chunk of up to ten actions, given one base-camera image at256× 256, its
calibration, the robot state, and its notes from earlier calls.
Metric.An episode succeeds, and ends, as soon as the task’s success check of RoboCasa365 (Nasiriany et al.,
2026) holds after a step; otherwise, including when the policy stops early, it counts as a failure. The task score
is the test success rateSR𝑡 = 1

Prior work.RoboCasa365 trains and benchmarks generalist policies, evaluating in target kitchens separate
from the pretraining ones (Nasiriany et al., 2026). Galbot Team et al. (2026) evaluate GPT-6 Astra as a direct
and hybrid policy on it, and Kuroki et al. (2026) optimize closed-loop control code, raising success on four
RoboCasa source tasks from 28.3% to 64.2% and reaching 57.0% on nine transfer tasks.
Active Search
Purpose.Active visual search: a humanoid robot that sees part of a 360-degree scene turns its head to find a
named object (object search) or the direction to move in (path search), with as few movements as possible;
most targets start out of view.
Source and construction.H*Bench (Yu et al., 2026a) annotates search tasks on real panoramas of transport
hubs, shops and streets: an instruction, a target yaw range (and, for objects, a pitch range), and starting
directions and difficulty levels; its public benchmark split has 2,400 object-search and 1,600 path-search
episodes. Development and validation come from it: each task becomes one episode, with one start drawn by
a fixed seed from its annotated starts; each panorama yields at most one episode, so the splits share no scene;
both are stratified by search kind and difficulty in proportion to H*Bench. Development has 80 episodes (40
object, 40 path) and validation 100 (50 and 50). The test split uses the non-public in-the-wild panoramas
of Imagining in 360◦ (Zhang et al., 2026d), eight from Google Street View and seven generated by image
models. A target was annotated by clicking its center (objects, widened by±30◦ in yaw and±20◦ in pitch) or
the direction to move in (±10◦), with starts at multiples of90◦; one start per task gives 47 episodes (33 object,
14 path) in 15 scenes. The agent sees the development episodes with their annotations and panoramas.
Setting.The solution receives the instruction and a 100-degree view (960× 720pixels), never the panorama.
With at most ten actions it rotates the head by a relative angle or submits an absolute direction, which ends
the episode; no submission fails. As in H*Bench, success requires the submitted direction to lie in the target
ranges widened to at least the tolerances above. Up to 20 model calls per episode on average and open models
on one GPU are allowed; other H*Bench data are not.
Starter solution.The H*Bench baseline with its prompts: one model call per step on the whole conversation
(every view with the environment’s feedback), answered with one rotation or submission.
Metric.Success weighted by path length (SPL) (Anderson et al., 2018), counting actions: episode𝑒 scores
𝑠𝑒ℓ𝑒/max(ℓ𝑒,𝑝 𝑒), with𝑠𝑒∈{ 0, 1} success, 𝑝𝑒 the actions taken (including the submission), andℓ𝑒 the fewest

text:
Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents 32
that can succeed (1 if the target center lies within50◦ of the starting yaw, else 2). Scores are averaged within
each search kind, and the two averages are averaged.
Prior work.H*Bench reports about 30% success for the best proprietary models; post-training Qwen2.5-VL-3B
(HVS-3B) with supervised fine-tuning and multi-turn reinforcement learning raises success from 14.83% to
47.38% (objects) and from 6.44% to 24.94% (paths) (Yu et al., 2026a). Imagining in 360◦ adds an Imaginator
that predicts the layout of seen and unseen regions for a frozen actor, raising HVS-3B from 48.04% to 62.75%
and from 24.12% to 39.38% on H*Bench (Zhang et al., 2026d).
RoboLab
Purpose.Whether the agent can obtain one tabletop manipulation policy that follows instructions for tasks it
has never seen; the splits contain different tasks, so the score measures generalization across tasks.
Source and construction.The pool is every RoboLab-120 (Yang et al., 2026a) task of difficulty simple or
moderate with a horizon of at most 60s (73 tasks). Each task is given one group of RoboLab’s taxonomy:
procedural (affordance, reorientation, sorting, stacking), else relational (conjunction, counting, spatial), else
visual (color, semantics, size). Tasks are shuffled within each (group, difficulty) stratum with a fixed seed and
dealt by systematic sampling to development (16 tasks), validation (12), test (24), and an unused remainder,
so every split has each stratum in proportion; test has 4 procedural, 9 relational, 10 visual, and 1 unattributed
task. Development tasks include stacking bowls, packing cans into a bin, standing a jug upright, and selecting
a hammer by color. Each task keeps its RoboLab scene, default instruction, horizon, success predicate, and
subtask tracker unchanged. Start states are deterministic, so a task’s episodes differ only through the policy;
development runs one episode per task, validation and test two (16, 24, and 48 episodes). The agent sees
development tasks and results, validation aggregates only, and no held-out task names.
Setting.The DROID setup, a Franka Panda arm with a Robotiq 2F-85 gripper, in Isaac Lab at 15Hz. The policy
receives the instruction, over-the-shoulder and wrist RGB images, over-the-shoulder depth, calibration, and
proprioception, never the task name or object poses, and returns chunks of absolute end-effector poses and
gripper commands, limited to 5cm and 0.25rad per step. It may call the run’s model at most 40 times within
1200s of thinking per episode, no other model, and may not key behavior on task identity.
Starter solution.One model call per gripper waypoint, given both images, the pose, and calibration, followed
by a straight-line move and an open or close.
Metric.RoboLab’s total score (Yang et al., 2026a),Score= 100

success rate is also reported.
Prior work.RoboLab analyses task-generalist policies along visual, procedural, and relational competen-
cies (Yang et al., 2026a). Chen et al. (2026c) evaluate agents without a trained policy on its 120 tasks
with vague instructions: code-as-policy (CaP-X) reaches 14.4% success, VLM-based task and motion planning
(TiPToP) 18.9%, and their orchestrator without a vision–language–action policy 17.8%.
LIBERO-MAX
Purpose.Whether the agent can build a robot controller that adapts when the world changes during execution,
not only before it starts.
Source and construction.LIBERO-MAX (Zhang et al., 2026e) has 8,000 paired cases on LIBERO (Liu et al.,
2023) scenes, with starting configurations from LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., 2025) and LIBERO-PRO (Zhou et al.,
2025). A case pairs a Base episode with a Dynamic episode that has the same start and policy seed and receives
one online event: target or receptacle relocation, camera shift, sensor-noise onset, illumination or visual-theme
switch, a burst of distractors, or an inserted obstacle. In the selected cases the event fires when the robot
comes within 0.18m of a designated object, before the grasp. Cases are selected from official metadata, never
from outcomes. All splits use three LIBERO tasks (a bowl from a drawer onto a plate, a sauce bottle into a
basket, a plate pushed to the front of a stove) and the same number of cases per event type: 8, 16 and 24 pairs
for development, validation and test. No initial physical state appears in two splits, and states used in earlier
experiments are excluded from validation and test. The agent sees the development case definitions.

Setting.A simulated Franka Panda (MuJoCo). Each step, the solution receives RGB and metric depth from an
external and a wrist camera, their calibration, the robot state and the instruction, and returns an absolute
end-effector pose and gripper command. It may query a frozen X-VLA policy (Zheng et al., 2025) for 30-step
action chunks, possibly on transformed images, and call the model up to 16 times per episode; no other model,
no training, no simulator state. The Dynamic episode replays the Base episode exactly until the event.
Starter solution.Executes the X-VLA chunks unchanged, without calling the model.
Metric.Dynamic success rate 1

Prior work.Across fourteen vision–language–action, hybrid and world-action policies, LIBERO-MAX events
lower success by 11.0 to 25.7 percentage points, mostly through geometry and observation changes (Zhang
et al., 2026e).
LIBERO-PRO
Purpose.Whether the agent can build a robot controller that stays successful when a familiar task is perturbed
before the episode starts, rather than relying on the conditions the underlying policy was trained under.
Source and construction.LIBERO-PRO (Zhou et al., 2025) perturbs LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023) tasks in their
objects, initial states, instructions and environments, and releases the perturbed task definitions and initial
states. Ten of its categories are used: object appearance, object shape, object texture, object positions,
paraphrased instruction, changed task goal, camera view angle, initial robot pose, visual noise or glare, and
view occlusion. Each case is one perturbed initial state of one of the three LIBERO tasks of LIBERO-MAX. Cases
are selected from official metadata, with equal numbers per category in each split, spread over the three tasks:
10, 20 and 30 episodes for development, validation and test (ten per task in test). No initial physical state
appears in two splits or in LIBERO-MAX, and states used in earlier experiments are excluded from validation
and test. The agent sees the development case definitions.
Setting.As in LIBERO-MAX: a controller that may query the frozen X-VLA policy (Zheng et al., 2025) and call
the model up to 16 times per episode, with a 20-minute limit per episode and no other model.
Starter solution.Executes the X-VLA chunks unchanged, without calling the model.
Metric.Success rate 1
𝑁
˝𝑁
𝑖=1𝑠𝑖 over all𝑁 planned episodes, with𝑠𝑖 the native LIBERO success check; an episode
that reaches the horizon or the time limit unsolved fails.
Prior work.LIBERO-PRO reports that models above 90% success under the standard LIBERO evaluation fall
to 0.0% under its generalized setting, a sign of memorized training conditions (Zhou et al., 2025). LIBERO-
Plus (Fei et al., 2025) analyses robustness along seven dimensions: object layout, camera viewpoint, initial
robot state, language, lighting, background texture and sensor noise.
Embodied-SWE
Purpose.Whether the agent can write, offline with a simulator, a control program for a long-horizon, contact-
rich tool-use task that then runs without any model.
Source and construction.The spatula task of EmbodiedSWE-Bench (Shen et al., 2026b): a Franka arm under
operational-space control in Isaac Lab wedges a spatula under a slice of bread in a pan, flips it, reloads it onto
the blade and serves it flat onto a plate, touching the bread only with the tool. The environment is built with
the benchmark’s tools in its setting without agent tools, and the grader is withheld. Each evaluation runs eight
parallel environments with random bread size and pose, plate position and spatula pose. Development uses
the build seed (8 trajectories); validation 2 and test 4 hidden random seeds (16 and 32 trajectories). The
agent receives the benchmark’s task statement, its rule for batched solutions and its staged-planning guide.
Setting.A program that commands the robot only through the environment’s step function and may read
object poses. Writing simulator state, applying external forces, changing physics or the scene, or altering the
grader scores zero. A rollout has 30 minutes of wall time, and no model is called during evaluation. During
development the agent has full simulator access on one GPU.
title: Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents

text:
Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents 34
Starter solution.Holds the arm still for ten steps and scores zero.
Metric.The EmbodiedSWE-Bench rubric score (Shen et al., 2026b): each trajectory receives the credit of the
furthest stage it reaches, namely spatula lifted (0.2), bread on the blade (0.4), bread flipped and flat (0.6),
bread carried on the blade (0.8) and bread on the plate (1.0). The score is the mean over all trajectories of the
split; a crashed rollout scores zero, and a timed-out one is scored as it stands. The final-state success rate is
also reported.
Prior work.EmbodiedSWE-Bench (Shen et al., 2026b) evaluates coding agents that write such programs in
one four-hour run per task, and uses their solutions to generate demonstrations for vision–language–action
models. On this task, single runs of frontier coding agents reach rubric scores from 0.2 to 1.0, with one run
disqualified for reward hacking.
A.2 Reasoning
Ego-Exo Memory
Purpose.Memory reasoning across two synchronized views of one activity. The evidence for an answer is
visible only at particular moments, often in one view, and the model sees few frames per call, so the solution
must choose which moments and views to show.
Source and construction.The questions are the Ego-Exo4D portion of EgoExoMem (Liu et al., 2026b): 764
human-verified four-option questions on 125 recordings of cooking and bicycle repair from Ego-Exo4D (Grau-
man et al., 2024). Each recording has an egocentric view from the glasses of the person performing the activity
(448× 448pixels) and an exocentric view from a fixed camera (796× 448pixels), synchronized at 30 frames
per second and lasting from 20 seconds to 23 minutes. The questions concern habitual location, instantaneous
position, resulting location, egocentric direction, object state, allocentric relation, and temporal order. All
recordings of one session (the same room and people) are assigned to one split, stratified by activity, with
about 35%, 25%, and 40% of the questions in the development, validation, and test splits. Each split then
keeps a fixed-seed sample stratified by activity and question type and spread over its videos: 80 questions on
38 videos, 80 on 33, and 120 on 47. The answer options are shuffled once and the videos are anonymized.
With each development question the agent also receives the annotated moments at which the answer is visible
and the view that shows it.
Setting.Given the question, both videos, and frames of both views at one frame per second, the solution
returns an option letter. It may call the model three times per question on average over a split, with at most
16× 448× 448pixels per call; further calls are refused. It may run open-weight models, for example for
frame retrieval, on one GPU, has no network access during evaluation, and may not use the annotations of
EgoExoMem or Ego-Exo4D.
Starter solution.Shows the model eight evenly spaced frames of each view, each labeled with its view and
time and downscaled so that all sixteen fit the pixel limit, followed by the question, in a single call.
Metric.Accuracy over the questions of a split; a question without a valid letter counts as wrong. Chance is
0.25.
Prior work.EgoExoMem evaluates multimodal language models on 2.6K cross-view memory questions of eight
types. On the full benchmark, the best existing model reaches 55.3%, and the training-free frame selection
method E2-Select, which allocates the frame budget by relevance and samples frames per view with a𝑘-DPP,
reaches 58.2% (Liu et al., 2026b).
Kinematics
Purpose.Quantitative physical reasoning from video: building a measurement procedure around a fixed
vision–language model, so that quantities follow from pixels, time, and a known scale.
Source and construction.QuantiPhy (Puyin et al., 2026) contains 3,355 questions on 569 videos from physics
simulations, laboratory recordings, internet clips, and segmented objects. The task uses its public labeled
validation set, 158 questions on 24 videos. Each question asks for the size, distance, velocity, or acceleration
of an object, possibly at a stated time, in stated units, and gives one prior in physical units: a known length,

text:

speed, or acceleration, and for some videos depths. The videos are assigned to fixed lists, so that no video
appears in two splits and every split mixes the four video sources and the static and dynamic priors and targets:
39 questions on 6 videos for development, 52 on 8 for validation, and 67 on 10 for testing.
Setting.The solution returns a number in the unit of the question. It does not call the model being evaluated:
the only language or vision–language model it may use is Qwen3.8-27B with open weights, served locally with
at most 32 images (32× 640× 360pixels in total) per call and eight calls per question on average over a split.
It may add non-language vision models and classical code on one GPU, such as point trackers, optical flow,
detectors, segmenters, and depth or pose estimators, but no other language model, neither in the solution nor
to label data, and no network access during evaluation.
Starter solution.Shows the fixed model four evenly spaced frames, the question, and the prior in a single call
with reasoning disabled, and reads the first number of the reply.

Prior work.QuantiPhy evaluates 21 vision–language models that answer directly from the video. The best
reaches an MRA of 53.1, below the average human score of 55.6; the models rely on pretrained world
knowledge more than on the given video and prior, and a four-step chain of thought (measure the source
property in pixels, estimate the scale, measure the target in pixels, convert) lowers the score of 19 of the 21
models (Puyin et al., 2026).
Mass
Purpose.Estimating a property that is not directly visible: weight depends on material, on whether an object
is solid or hollow, and on how its volume is filled.
Source and construction.The items are product listings of Amazon Berkeley Objects (Collins et al., 2022) that
state a weight, all three dimensions, and a main photograph. Consumables (food, supplements, cleaning
and medical supplies) and multipacks or sets, recognized by name, are removed, as are items outside 10g to
150kg and items whose weight divided by the volume of their bounding box lies outside 5 to 5000kg/m3,
which removes unit and listing errors. Variants of one product (the same brand and the same first six words of
the name) form one group, and one item per group is drawn with a fixed seed. The groups are split into 300
development, 300 validation, and 600 test items, with at most 3% of a split from one product type, giving
about 130 product types per split. Each item keeps its main photograph and up to two others, with the longer
side at most 1024 pixels.
Setting.Given the photographs, a coarse product type, and the listed dimensions in centimetres, but not the
name, brand, or description, the solution states the weight in kilograms. As in Kinematics, the only language
or vision–language model is the fixed Qwen3.8-27B, with at most eight images (8× 1024× 1024pixels) per
call and four calls per item on average. Non-language models such as segmenters, depth estimators, image
encoders, and regressors trained on the development split may run on one GPU; other language models, text
encoders applied to other data, and any external source of the weights are not allowed.
Starter solution.Shows the fixed model the main photograph, the product type, and the dimensions in a single
call with reasoning disabled, and reads the first number of the reply.
Metric.The mean relative accuracy with the thresholds of Kinematics, averaged over items; an item without a
numeric answer scores zero.
Prior work.Image2mass (Standley et al., 2017) collected about 150,000 online product listings with images,
sizes, and weights, and estimates mass from an image together with the object’s dimensions, comparing
learned models with human estimates. Amazon Berkeley Objects (Collins et al., 2022) provides catalogue
images, metadata, and 3D models of real products for object understanding.

ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2
Purpose.Abstract reasoning from few examples: inferring a grid transformation from a few demonstration
pairs and applying it to new inputs, on puzzles designed to require little prior knowledge.
Source and construction.The puzzles come from the official public repositories at fixed versions: 400 training
and 400 evaluation puzzles for ARC-AGI-1 (Chollet, 2019), and 1000 training and 120 evaluation puzzles
for ARC-AGI-2 (Chollet et al., 2025). Each puzzle has demonstration pairs and one or more test inputs; grids
are at most30× 30with ten colors. Training puzzles identical to an evaluation puzzle are removed (one for
ARC-AGI-1). The remaining training puzzles are ordered by a seeded hash: the first 80 form the validation split,
and the rest form the development pool, which the agent receives with answers (319 puzzles for ARC-AGI-1);
a fixed panel of 32 development puzzles is scored in development evaluations. The test split consists of all
official evaluation puzzles, 400 for ARC-AGI-1 and 120 for ARC-AGI-2, so validation and test puzzles are
disjoint.
Setting.Given the demonstration pairs and the test inputs, the solution returns at most two candidate grids
per test input. It may call the model up to 2000 times per evaluation, with four puzzles solved in parallel in
independent sessions, and runs in a sandbox without a GPU or network access. It may use program search,
hand-written rules, or models trained on the development puzzles, but may not obtain or store held-out
answers. Invalid predictions score zero.
Starter solution.Asks the model for two candidate outputs as JSON in a single call per puzzle; an unparseable
reply counts as no answer.

Prior work.ARC (Chollet, 2019) was proposed to measure the efficiency of skill acquisition on novel problems.
In ARC Prize 2024 the best private-set score rose from 33% to 55.5%, mainly through deep-learning-guided
program synthesis and test-time training (Chollet et al., 2024); test-time training brings an 8B language model
to 53.0% on the public validation set, and 61.9% when ensembled with program synthesis (Akyürek et al.,
2024). ARC-AGI-2 raises the difficulty: on its semi-private set, o3 (medium) scores 3.0%, against 53.0% on
ARC-AGI-1 (Chollet et al., 2025).
ARC-AGI-3
Purpose.Learning an interactive environment without instructions: finding out by acting what the controls do
and what completes a level, then completing levels with few actions.
Source and construction.ARC-AGI-3 (ARC Prize Foundation, 2026) consists of turn-based games on grids of
up to64× 64cells with 16 colors, each with several levels and a human baseline action count per level. Its
public set has 25 games, and official scores use 110 further private games. The task uses the 25 public games
at a fixed version of the official toolkit, split by game with a seeded hash into 10 development, 5 validation,
and 10 test games. The agent sees only the identifiers of the development games and plays them through the
interface; the game code, the human baselines, and the validation and test games are not accessible to it.
Setting.The solution observes the current frame, the available actions, and the number of completed levels,
and submits actions: directions, a game-specific action, a click at a grid position, and undo, whose effects must
be inferred; a reset is allowed only after the game is lost. Each game allows at most 1000 actions, 120 model
calls, and 1200 seconds, and each evaluation at most 1200 model calls. Games are played one at a time, each
from a fresh start with a fixed seed, and no memory or files carry over between games. The solution may not
contain game solutions or game code.
Starter solution.Sends the model the current frame as an image and as rows of color values, a short memory,
and the recent actions, and executes up to eight actions returned per call along with an updated memory.

Prior work.ARC-AGI-3 (ARC Prize Foundation, 2026) reports that humans solve all of its environments, while
frontier AI systems scored below 1% as of March 2026; in its preview competition, the best entry, which trains a
convolutional network with reinforcement learning to predict which actions change the frame, scored 12.58%.
Spatial-VSI
Purpose.Spatial reasoning about indoor scenes from a moving camera: counts, metric sizes and distances,
relative directions, routes, and the order of appearance.
Source and construction.VSI-Bench (Yang et al., 2025) contains over 5000 questions on 288 videos of real
rooms from ScanNet, ScanNet++, and ARKitScenes (Dai et al., 2017; Yeshwanth et al., 2023; Baruch et al.,
2021). It has ten question types in eight groups: object counting, absolute distance, object size, and room
size, answered by numbers, and relative distance, relative direction (easy, medium, hard), route planning, and
appearance order, answered by option letters. The scenes of a fixed dataset version are shuffled with a fixed
seed and dealt to the test, validation, and development splits in proportions 40%, 30%, and 30%; each split
then keeps questions stratified so that the eight groups are weighted as in the official score. The splits hold 80
questions from 46 scenes for development, 480 from 84 scenes for validation, and 320 from 100 scenes for
testing.
Setting.Given the video (640 by 480 pixels, one to three minutes), the question, and the options, the solution
returns an answer. It may call the model twice per question on average over a split and uses no other model
and no downloaded weights; its own code, such as geometry and classical vision with OpenCV, is allowed. It
may not read the annotations of the source datasets or access the network, has no GPU, and has four hours
per evaluation.
Starter solution.Shows the model 16 evenly spaced frames, 512 pixels wide, with the official VSI-Bench
prompt, in one call per question.
Metric.The overall score of VSI-Bench (Yang et al., 2025). A multiple-choice answer is correct when its
first word is the option letter; a numerical answer receives the mean relative accuracy with thresholds
{0.50, 0.55,..., 0.95} and the condition|ˆ𝑦−𝑦|/𝑦≤ 1−𝜃, and zero if it is not a number. Scores are averaged
within each group, the three direction levels are first averaged into one, and the eight groups are averaged,
giving a value between 0 and 1.
Prior work.VSI-Bench finds that the best model it tests, Gemini-1.5 Pro, averages 45.4%, against about 79% for
humans on a subset; chain-of-thought, self-consistency, and tree-of-thoughts prompting do not help, whereas
asking the model to draw a cognitive map raises relative-distance accuracy from 46.0% to 56.0% (Yang
et al., 2025). VSI-Bench-Debiased removes questions that can be answered without the video (Brown et al.,
2025), and Spatial-MLLM adds a 3D spatial encoder initialized from a visual geometry model to a multimodal
language model (Wu et al., 2025b).
A.3 Creation
Image Editing
Purpose.Whether the agent can build an instruction-based image editor that performs the edit requested in
English or Chinese while leaving the rest of the photograph intact, across local, global, text, retouching and
restoration, reasoning, and compound edits. The editing model is not prescribed: choosing, combining, and
adapting open models is part of the task.
title: Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents

text:
Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents 38
Source and construction.The evaluation set was built for this task in two versions. The first has 100 images;
the second, used here, adds 86 images and 14 restoration photographs, for 200 images. The 186 photographs,
paintings, and illustrations are CC0 or public-domain works from Wikimedia Commons, each checked for its
licence and excluding identifiable people, minors, trademarks, and third-party works; two images of puzzles
(an arithmetic problem on a blackboard and a number sequence) were made for the task, and four images
carry a reproducible synthetic degradation (blur, color cast, or low contrast) to be undone. The 14 restoration
photographs show haze, fog, smoke, lens flare, reflections on glass, or cast shadows; all come from the data of
UniSER (Zhang et al., 2025c), including ten of its 39 in-the-wild evaluation images and three of its paired
images from NH-HAZE (Ancuti et al., 2020), FlareReal600, and WSRD+ (Vasluianu et al., 2023). Images are
resized to at most1536× 1024pixels with sides that are multiples of 16, and span outdoor (85), product (34),
indoor (32), low-quality (21), illustration (13), text (11), and document (4) images. Each image has one
instruction, written in Chinese (106) or English (94) together with a translation into the other language, and is
assigned to one of 23 kinds of edit in six families: local semantic edits, namely adding, removing, or replacing
an object, changing its attributes, changing a pose, setting a count, or moving objects (71 images); global edits
of style, background, or lighting, weather, and season (30); text editing, namely replacing, writing, or editing
Chinese text (22); retouching and restoration, namely tone, old or degraded photographs and soft effects,
removal of clutter, and outpainting to a new aspect ratio (34); edits that require inference, such as candles
after three hours of burning, the farthest of several glasses, leaves in late autumn, or a completed sudoku (25);
and compound or constrained instructions (18). Each sample is labeled with a difficulty (44, 114, and 42 at
three levels) and the size of the edited region (small, medium, large, or global), and is annotated for scoring:
a mask of the region allowed to change (92 images), objects that must appear (43) or disappear (32), a target
count (11), text that must be readable (24) or gone (14), a target aspect ratio (5), content that must be kept
(74), the parts of a compound instruction (13), and a description of the intended result of an inference edit
(31). The images are divided into 50 development, 70 validation, and 80 test images, stratified by kind of
edit. The development samples come with their annotations, and their evaluations return per-sample judge
rationales and side-by-side comparisons; validation and test return only the aggregate score.
Setting.The solution is an editing program that receives the image, the instruction, and its language, and
writes an image at the input size. It may use any open-weight editing or generation model, several models
at once, vision models, classical image processing, and its own fine-tuning on the development split; Qwen-
Image-2.1, Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 with distilled few-step adapters (Wu et al., 2025a), and HunyuanImage-
3.0-Instruct (Tencent Hunyuan Foundation Model Team, 2025) are provided. It may not use the judge’s model
family, remote services, or the annotations. Evaluation runs offline on four 80GB GPUs with, on average, 150s
per image per GPU; the solution does not call the model being evaluated.
Starter solution.Qwen-Image-Edit-2509 with an eight-step distilled adapter, given the instruction unchanged,
producing one output per image.
Metric.A frozen judge, GLM-4.5V (GLM-V Team, 2025) at temperature 0, sees the source and the output and
rates instruction complianceSC and preservationPR, and, from the output alone, perceptual qualityPQ, each
from 0 to 10. The preservation rubric depends on the kind of edit (for example, only content and composition
for style transfer, only the kept subjects for a background change), and the judge is told the annotated parts,
the kept content, and, for inference edits, the intended result. Global deformation is measured rather than
judged: a SIFT (Lowe, 2004) and RANSAC (Fischler and Bolles, 1981) homography from input to output gives
the 90th-percentile displacement𝑝90 in pixels at a 512-pixel short side,𝑔=exp(−max( 0,𝑝 90− 0.5)/6), and
PR′ =max( 0,PR− 5(1−𝑔)) . The judge score is𝐽= 1

averages the checks that apply: object presence and absence and the exact count, answered by the judge; for
text, one minus the lowest character error rate over two OCR readings and the judge’s transcription, and the
absence of text to be removed; the aspect ratio of outpainted images,max(0, 1− 5|𝑟/𝑟∗− 1|); preservation,

title: Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents

text:
Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents 39
Prior work.GEdit-Bench, introduced with the Step1X-Edit editor (Liu et al., 2025), evaluates instruction-based
editing on real user requests with a vision–language judge of semantic consistency and perceptual quality,
which VIEScore (Ku et al., 2024) combines as√SC·PQ ; the judge score above takes this form and adds the
preservation term and the programmatic checks. UniSER (Zhang et al., 2025c) removes soft effects such as
haze, flare, shadows, and reflections with a single diffusion model and evaluates its in-the-wild images, which
lack ground truth, with reference-free metrics and a vision–language judge.
Multi-turn Editing
Purpose.Whether the agent can improve a multi-turn editing system, in which each instruction is applied to
the previous result and becomes known only at its turn, so that errors in content and image quality accumulate
over the session.
Source and construction.All 100 sessions of MSE-Bench, the multi-turn editing benchmark introduced with
VINCIE (Qu et al., 2026), at a fixed revision. Each session is a real photograph, used unchanged at its
original size (many are small), and five instructions that add, remove, or replace objects, change attributes,
backgrounds, posture, expression, orientation, position, actions, or interactions, restyle the image, or move
the camera (dolly, pan, tilt, orbit); MSE-Bench labels 20 operation types. The sessions are split into 30
development, 30 validation, and 40 test sessions by a seeded search that balances the per-turn counts of the
20 operation types, the sessions with a camera operation, and the images under 512 pixels on the short side.
For the development sessions the agent also sees the MSE-Bench annotations (operation types and descriptions
of the intended results); the solution never receives them.
Setting.Thesolutionisasessionobjectthatisresetwiththesourceimageandreturnsoneimageperinstruction;
it may keep earlier images and instructions. The editing model is fixed to the original Qwen-Image-Edit (August
2025) (Wu et al., 2025a) with its four- and eight-step distilled adapters, since the later 2509 and 2511 releases
degrade into blocky noise when edited repeatedly. Prompt rewriting, sampler settings, candidate selection,
masking and compositing, and Qwen2.5-VL-7B (Bai et al., 2025b) as a helper are allowed; training the editing
model, network access, and any copy of MSE-Bench or of VINCIE’s outputs are not. Each of four GPUs runs
one process with 300s of start-up and, on average, 60s per turn. A failed turn, an aspect-ratio change above
5%, or a timeout scores 0 for that turn and the rest of the session. The solution does not call the model being
evaluated.
Starter solution.Edits the previous image with each turn’s instruction, using the eight-step adapter and a fixed
seed.
Metric.Each turn 𝑘 is judged by a frozen GLM-4.5V (GLM-V Team, 2025) at about one megapixel. Given
the instructions of turns1..𝑘and the images up to turn𝑘, MSE-Bench’s own evaluation prompt rates prompt
following PF and consistency CONS with the previous image; a strict prompt rates the perceptual quality
PQ of the turn’s image alone (all 0–10). The turn score is1
10
√PF·PQ( 0.5+ 0.05 CONS), or 0 ifPF< 3; the
score averages over the five turns and then over sessions. MSE-Bench’s cumulative success rate, the fraction of
sessions in which every turn up to𝑘hasPF>6andCONS>6, is reported for𝑘=1,3,5.
Prior work.VINCIE (Qu et al., 2026) learns in-context image editing from video and introduced MSE-Bench
to measure multi-turn editing by the success rate at each turn, judged by GPT-4o. Here the editing model is
fixed and the agent improves the system around it.
Video Generation
Purpose.Whether the agent can build an executable text-to-video workflow around a frozen video generator,
deciding how to plan prompts, spend a fixed generation budget, inspect frames, and select candidates, so that
the videos follow compositional prompts.
Source and construction.The prompts come from T2V-CompBench (Sun et al., 2025), at a fixed revision of its
prompt lists, restricted to four of its seven categories: consistent attribute binding, action binding, generative
numeracy, and spatial relationships (two-dimensional only). Each split has 20 prompts, five per category.
Near-duplicate prompts were grouped into families (connected components of normalized token Jaccard
similarity of at least 0.65); the validation and test prompts were drawn in a salted hash order, excluding the
title: Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents

text:
Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents 40
families of development prompts and taking at most one prompt per family. The agent sees the development
prompts and their scores; validation and test prompts are private.
Setting.The generator is MiniMax H3 (MiniMax, 2026b) with frozen weights, producing 124 frames at
864× 480and 24 frames per second. For each prompt the workflow may make at most three generation
requests totalling 50 denoising steps, choosing prompts, seeds, step counts, and flow shift; sample frames; call
the model being evaluated at most twice (40 calls per evaluation), with images; and process videos locally. It
returns one video. It has no network, no direct GPU access, and no access to the evaluators, and may not add
text or cues aimed at the evaluators. Each evaluation runs on one 80GB H100 within 150 minutes; prompts
unfinished when the workflow time runs out score 0.
Starter solution.A single generation request with the prompt unchanged and the default seed, 50 steps, and
flow shift.
Metric.The original T2V-CompBench evaluators score each video against the original prompt with their default
prompts, thresholds, and seeds: attribute binding and action binding with the multimodal-LLM evaluation
using LLaVA-v1.6-34B (Liu et al., 2024a) on sampled frames, and numeracy and spatial relationships with the
detection-based evaluation using Grounding DINO (Liu et al., 2024b) (16 sampled frames, six of them in a
grid for the language model). Each video scores in[0, 1], a missing or corrupt video scores 0, and the score
is the mean of the four category means. Because of the subset and the fixed resolution, the scores are not
comparable with the T2V-CompBench leaderboard.
Prior work.T2V-CompBench (Sun et al., 2025) benchmarks text-to-video models on 1,400 prompts in seven
compositional categories, with multimodal-LLM-based, detection-based, and tracking-based metrics validated
against human judgments. Here the generator is fixed, and the agent improves the workflow around it.
Text-to-Image
Purpose.Whether the agent can make a text-to-image program satisfy every constraint of new prompts in
Chinese and English while keeping image quality, either with a fixed generator or with any open model.
Source and construction.The 200 prompts and their rubrics were written for this task: 100 in Chinese and
100 in English (not translations of each other), ten in each of 20 subcategories of six categories: subjects
and attributes (identity, color, material), counting and binding (single and multiple classes, attribute binding,
excluded content), spatial relations and interaction (position, depth and containment, actions and roles), text
and layout (English, Chinese, multiple text blocks), style and presentation (medium, lighting and season,
camera and composition), and reasoning and composition (world knowledge, causality and time, logical
quantity, multiple constraints). Each subcategory has two easy, five medium, and three hard prompts by the
author’s judgment. Each prompt has a fixed seed and size (1024× 1024for 145 prompts,1280 × 768or
768× 1280for 55) and a rubric of atomic criteria (954 in total) of four types: semantic, count, absence, and
exact text, the latter copied verbatim from the prompt; each requirement is credited once. After authoring,
every prompt and rubric was reviewed for physical consistency, count logic, text literals, coverage, and duplicate
credit, which revised 32 prompts, 51 rubrics, and 34 sizes; scripts check quotas, uniqueness, field consistency,
and split isolation, and flagged cross-split pairs of similar wording were reviewed by hand. The prompts are
split into 50 development, 70 validation, and 80 test prompts by semantic group (178 groups of prompts
sharing a central scene), each split half Chinese and half English with 20/50/30% easy, medium, and hard
prompts. Development prompts come with rubrics and per-image feedback; validation returns only the score.
Setting.The solution receives a prompt, its language, size, and seed, and writes one image. With the fixed
generator, all images come from the frozen Qwen-Image-2.1 (Wu et al., 2025a); prompt rewriting, layout
planning, sampling settings, several candidates with selection, Qwen2.5-VL-7B (Bai et al., 2025b) as a helper,
and ordinary image tools are allowed, but no training or adapters. With any model, other open-weight
generators, routing, and training on the development split are also allowed. Neither may use the judge’s model
family, the rubrics, the network, or hosted models at evaluation, which runs on four GPUs with at most 600s
per image.
Starter solution.One image from Qwen-Image-2.1 with the prompt unchanged and 40 sampling steps.
title: Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents

text:
Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents 41
Metric.A frozen GLM-4.5V (GLM-V Team, 2025) judges each image: a semantic criterion scores 0, 0.25, 0.5,
0.75, or 1; a count, absence, or exact-text criterion scores 0 or 1; and the quality𝑄∈[ 0, 1] rates rendering
defects, excluding prompt compliance and intended style. With criterion scores𝑐𝑖 and weights𝑤𝑖 (all 1),
𝐶= ˝
𝑖𝑤𝑖𝑐𝑖/˝
𝑖𝑤𝑖 and the image scores𝐶( 0.5+ 0.5𝑄); a missing or wrongly sized image scores 0. Scores are
averaged within each category and then over the six categories. The reported score is the mean of the test
scores of the two settings.
Prior work.GenEval (Ghosh et al., 2023) and T2I-CompBench (Huang et al., 2023a) evaluate compositional
text-to-image generation with detectors and other vision models. The prompts here are new and these
benchmarks’ scores are not reproduced.
A.4 Reconstruction
3D Tracking
Purpose.Whether the agent can assemble a system that segments every object in a few widely separated
views of an indoor scene and gives each object the same identity in every view, from RGB images alone.
Without camera poses or depth, the views must be associated through appearance and implicit geometry: the
cross-view instance tracking that IGGT (Li et al., 2026) introduced as an evaluation of instance-grounded 3D
reconstruction.
Source and construction.The validation and test clips are the 3D tracking benchmark released with IGGT,
which samples a few views per scene from ScanNet (Dai et al., 2017) and ScanNet++ (Yeshwanth et al.,
2023) for spatial coverage with sufficient overlap and annotates a subset of objects by hand with identities
consistent across views. Each clip has six to nine RGB views, resized to592× 448pixels, typically with four to
eight annotated objects such as furniture, lamps, and decorations; walls, floors, and ceilings are not annotated.
The 8 ScanNet++ clips form the validation split and the 10 ScanNet clips the test split. The development split
consists of 100 clips built from ScanNet++ training scenes that share no scene with the validation clips: eight
views are drawn from a random stretch covering 30 to 80% of a capture, and up to eight object-like instances
are kept (visible in at least two views, at most a quarter of any view, and at least 0.1% of the clip’s pixels); a
clip with fewer than four is drawn again. The agent sees the development views with their instance maps.
Setting.The solution is a program that receives the views of one clip and returns one instance map per view,
with 0 for the background and identities consistent across views. It may use any publicly released pretrained
model or library and needs no training; it does not call the model being evaluated. It runs on one GPU without
network access, and a whole split must finish within 45 minutes.
Starter solution.Clusters the colors of each view into six clusters with𝑘-means, splits them into connected
regions covering 0.2 to 20% of the image, and links each region to the existing track with the nearest mean
color, or starts a new track.
Metric.Evaluation is class-agnostic. Predicted and annotated tracks are matched one to one, greedily in
decreasing order of their temporal IoU, which accumulates intersection and union over the views: for an
annotated object with masks𝐺𝑓 and its matched prediction𝑃𝑓 in views𝑓=1,...,𝑆,

object without a match scores 0, and predicted tracks without a match are not penalised. T-SR is the share of
annotated objects whose per-view IoU exceeds 0.5 in every view in which they appear. The region similarity

averaging the IoU over views and counting an object as tracked when its prediction is non-empty in every view;
the accumulated IoU, the IoU threshold of T-SR, and the greedy matching follow the evaluation of S4VY (Zhang
et al., 2026c).
Prior work.IGGT reconstructs geometry and predicts 3D-consistent instance features with one transformer,
trained with a 3D-consistent contrastive objective; IGGT4D (Zou et al., 2026) extends it to streaming 4D input;

Scene from Photo
Purpose.Whether the agent can build a single-image 3D scene reconstruction system: from one photograph
of a furnished room, recover the camera, the room, and every piece of furniture as a complete object with
plausible unseen sides, with physically based materials and lighting, so that a path tracer reproduces the
photograph.
Source and construction.The photographs are those of HARMONY300 (Sun et al., 2026): 100 renders of
3D-FRONT rooms (Fu et al., 2021), which have ground-truth geometry, and 200 real photographs, half of
moderate and half of high complexity. Each difficulty is split separately with a fixed seed (the renders stratified
by their number of annotated objects) into 10, 10, and 20 photographs for development, validation, and test,
giving 30, 30, and 60; the remaining 179 photographs are held out of every split, and one render whose image
differs from its ground truth is excluded. On the renders the annotated furniture and its meshes come from
the 3D-FRONT ground truth. On the real photographs up to eight pieces of furniture per photograph are
annotated by Mask2Former (Cheng et al., 2022) panoptic segments of furniture classes (score at least 0.5, at
least 0.5% of the image); on the renders this procedure recovers 85% of the annotated objects. The agent sees
the development photographs with all labels.
Setting.The solution writes a Blender scene per photograph within 120s per photograph; the evaluator
renders it with Cycles from the scene’s own camera under fixed rules (only meshes, physically based shader
nodes, non-emissive materials, at most 64 lights). It may use any public pretrained model on one GPU, but not
HARMONY300, 3D-FRONT, 3D-FUTURE, or HARMONY’s code, and does not call the model being evaluated.
Starter solution.An empty room box in flat colors matched to the photograph, one ceiling light, and the same
guessed camera with a 60°field of view for every photograph.

Prior work.HARMONY reconstructs such scenes by hierarchical agentic reasoning with a vision-language

Scene from Video
Purpose.Whether the agent can build a video-to-simulation pipeline: from the frames of an indoor video
alone, estimate the cameras and reconstruct a scene of separate textured objects on a fixed background that
has the true shape, reproduces the frames, and remains at rest under physical simulation.
Source and construction.The scenes are the nine released with HoloScene (Xia et al., 2025), each with frames,
ground-truth cameras, per-object instance masks, a support graph, and a ground-truth surface. The test split
is the six scenes evaluated by CoDimRecon (Xie et al., 2026): three Replica rooms (Straub et al., 2019) and

three ScanNet++ captures (Yeshwanth et al., 2023). Validation is one iGibson house (Shen et al., 2021);
development is another iGibson house and a game room filmed with a phone (undistorted). The iGibson and
phone sequences keep every third frame. Each face of the ground-truth surface is labeled by the masks that
see it, and each object is marked dynamic if it rests on the floor or on another object and static if it hangs from
a wall or the ceiling. The agent sees the development frames with all labels and the scoring code.
Setting.The input is only the RGB frames, without cameras, masks, or depth, as in CoDimRecon. The solution
writes a glTF scene (at most 4 million triangles) and a camera for every frame, within 1200s per scene, on
one GPU and 16 CPU cores. The scene is placed in the ground-truth frame by the similarity transform that
aligns its cameras with the true ones, rendered unlit from the true cameras, and each mesh node is assigned to
the object or background whose masks it covers most. Any public pretrained model may be used, but not the
HoloScene release or its source datasets; the model being evaluated is not called.
Starter solution.An empty room box in the mean color of the frames, with every camera at one point.
Metric.Per scene, 𝑠=(𝐺+𝐴+𝑃)/ 3with 𝐺=(F1 5 cm+NC)/ 200on 500,000 points of the whole scene,
𝐴=(SSIM+ 1−LPIPS)/ 2over all input frames (Wang et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2018), and𝑃 the share of
dynamic objects that are reconstructed (mask IoU at least 0.5) and stay in place;𝑠 is averaged over scenes.
Stability follows CoDimRecon: each dynamic object, decomposed into convex hulls by CoACD (Wei et al.,
2022), is released alone in MuJoCo (Todorov et al., 2012) for 3s with all else fixed, and falls if it tilts more
than 30°or moves more thanmax(5 cm, 0.2𝑑), with𝑑 its bounding-box diagonal. A missing or unloadable
scene scores as empty. The ground-truth surface colored from the frames scores 0.936 on the test split.
Prior work.HoloScene reconstructs simulation-ready interactive scenes from a video given its cameras and
instance masks. CoDimRecon reconstructs such scenes agentically from RGB views alone, representing objects
as curves, surfaces, and volumes, and compares with HoloScene and an agent that writes the scene in Blender.
A.5 Perception
Visual Search
Purpose.Whether the agent can build a visual search procedure around a model with a limited field of view:
questions concern small objects in photographs of 2K to 8K resolution, while each model call may contain at
most one megapixel, so the solution must decide where to look.
Source and construction.The questions come from V*Bench (Wu and Xie, 2024) (191 multiple-choice questions
on about 2K photographs: 115 on object attributes with four options, 76 on relative position with two) and
HR-Bench 8K (Wang et al., 2025a) (200 questions with four options on 151 photographs of about 8K resolution,
half on a single instance and half across instances; of its four rotated listings of each question one is drawn
with a fixed seed). V*Bench is split by category and HR-Bench by photograph, so no photograph appears
in two splits. The test split has 140 questions (70 from each benchmark). Development and validation are
stratified subsets of 70 questions (33 and 37) and 80 questions (40 and 40). The agent sees the development
photographs, questions, answers, and, for V*Bench, the boxes of the queried objects.
Setting.The solution answers each question with an option letter. It may call the model being evaluated on
average at most five times per question, with at most1024× 1024pixels per call in total; it may crop, resize,
and run open-weight models on one GPU, and may not use either benchmark beyond the development split.
Starter solution.Shows the model the whole photograph reduced to one megapixel with the question, in a
single call.
Metric.Accuracy over the questions of the split; a question without a valid letter counts as wrong. Accuracies
on V*Bench and HR-Bench 8K are reported separately. Chance accuracy on the validation split is 0.303.
Prior work.V*Bench was introduced with SEAL, which guides a multimodal model to search the image for the
queried region, and HR-Bench with a training-free method that divides the image into patches and combines
their answers. Later methods explore zoomed regions as a tree (ZoomEye (Shen et al., 2025)) or learn to crop
by reinforcement learning (DeepEyes (Zheng et al., 2026)).

Video Quality
Purpose.Whether the agent can turn a general multimodal model into a judge of perceptual video quality that
agrees with people, both for real user videos and for generated videos.
Source and construction.The rated videos are 100 videos of YouTube-UGC (Wang et al., 2019), chosen from
its 1,380 videos with mean opinion scores (MOS) excluding 4K: seven per content category for 14 categories
(eight for sports and gaming), evenly spaced in MOS within each category. Each lasts 16.6 to 20s at 360p to
1080p, and its MOS (1 to 5) averages 105 to 154 crowdsourced ratings from the subjective study of Yim et al.
(2020). The pairs are 50 pairs from a public human-preference study of Veo 3.1 (Rapidata, 2025), each pitting
Veo 3.1 against one of seven other text-to-video models on the same prompt (5 to 6s clips). Each pair has
15 reliability-weighted crowd votes on three questions: prompt alignment, fewer visual artifacts, and overall
preference, the last two judged without the prompt. A clip with more than 55% of the votes wins; otherwise
the question is a tie. The videos are dealt in order of category and MOS, and the pairs in order of opposing
model, into 30, 30, and 40 videos and 15, 15, and 20 pairs; the clip order in each pair is randomized. The
agent sees the development videos, frames at two per second, and labels with vote shares and rating spreads.
Setting.The solution scores each video and answers the three questions for each pair. It may call the model
being evaluated on average at most three times per item, with at most eight1024× 576frames’ worth of pixels
per call, and may run open-weight models on one GPU; it may not use the source datasets.
Starter solution.Asks for a rating from 1 to 5 given eight evenly spaced frames, and answers all three questions
about a pair given six frames of each clip.
Metric. 𝑠=(SRCC+Acc)/ 2, where SRCC is Spearman’s rank correlation (Spearman, 1904) between the
solution’s scores and the MOS over the split’s videos (a video without a score receives the median of the others),
and Acc is the share of non-tied pair questions answered correctly, pooled over the three criteria (a missing
answer is wrong). PLCC and per-criterion accuracies are also reported. Chance is 0.25.
Prior work.YouTube-UGC was collected for video compression research, and its MOS serve to evaluate blind
quality models such as VIDEVAL (Tu et al., 2021) and DOVER (Wu et al., 2023).
A.6 Infrastructure
VAE Decode
Purpose.Whether the agent can lower the latency of a fixed numerical computation, the video decoder of a
generative model, without changing what it computes.
Source and construction.The computation is the decoder of the MiniMax H3 autoencoder (MiniMax, 2026b),
a 36-layer vision transformer of about 2.4 billion parameters with FP32 weights run under FP16 autocast. It
decodes a window of seven latent frames of 24 channels into 28 RGB frames, in256× 256tiles with at least 64
pixels of overlap and linear blending; the reference implementation and weights are pinned by hash. Inputs are
latent windows of encoded videos at two sizes,544× 960and480 × 832pixels, split by scene: 6 development,
6 validation, and 12 test scenes. Each request is either a real window with fresh noise (+0.05N( 0, 1)) or a
synthetic stress window (Gaussian latents scaled per channel, clipped at±5). Per size and repetition there are
four real and one stress request on development (two repetitions) and validation (six), and eight and two on
test (six), so 20, 60, and 120 requests; no input repeats. The development windows are visible.
Setting.The solution is a decoder that receives latents in host memory and writes the full output into a host
buffer. Custom Triton or CUDA kernels built from source, fusions, CUDA graphs, compilation, batching of tiles,
and overlapping transfers are allowed. Lower precision, approximate or sparse attention, skipped tokens, tiles,
or frames, reuse across requests, special treatment of stress windows, more than one GPU, shipped binaries,
and existing optimized implementations of this decoder are not; accepted versions are reviewed for these
rules. One H200, 90s of setup, 30s per request; the solution does not call the model being evaluated.
Starter solution.A direct eager PyTorch translation of the reference, bit-exact with it.
Metric.Every frame must be finite with a per-frame RMSE below6.3× 10−4 (1.9× 10−3 for stress windows)
and a maximum absolute error below 0.12 relative to the reference; these bounds are twice the largest error of

B Protocol and harness
This appendix specifies the parts of the protocol that Sections 3.2 and 3.3 describe only in outline: the structure
of a round, the capabilities of the executor and the improver, the acceptance rule, the budget and the conditions
under which a run ends, and the measures that keep the evaluation intact. The rules are identical for all
models and tasks; the budget and two settings of the executor phase are fixed per task and listed in Table 10.
B.1 Round structure
A run begins by scoring the starter solution on the validation split, which gives the score against which the first
candidate is compared. Each round then proceeds in five steps: an executor phase that produces a candidate
solution; a check that reverts every change the executor made outside the files it may modify; the evaluation
of the candidate on the validation split; the acceptance decision of Equation (2); and an improver phase that
revises the harness.
The executor phase normally ends when the executor declares its work finished, and the solution in its final
state becomes the candidate. It ends earlier when one of the executor’s evaluations on the development split
exceeds the development score of the accepted solution by a fixed share of the distance between the starter’s
validation score and the validation score of a strong known solution (Table 10); the solution as it was in that
evaluation is then submitted. If the phase is interrupted before the executor finishes, because it reached its
call limit, its time limit, or the budget, the best state that the executor’s development evaluations showed to
exceed the accepted solution is submitted, and nothing is submitted if there is none. A round that leaves the
solution unchanged does not use a validation evaluation.
B.2 Executor
The executor works in a copy of the run’s repository. Its tools allow it to run shell commands; to read, write,
and edit files; to view images; to run experiments on the compute allocated to the task, including GPUs where
the task provides them; to score the solution, or several variants of it at once, on the development split; and
to query the remaining budget. It may write only to the solution, to a notes file that persists across rounds
and is shared with the improver, and to a scratch directory that is emptied before each round. It observes
development scores directly and the validation scores of earlier rounds through the run records, but it has
no access to the validation or test data or to the evaluator. The starting harness allows 60 model calls per
executor phase. Independently of the harness, the protocol stops a phase after the number of model calls given
in Table 10 or after 180 minutes (600 minutes on the ARC tasks), and an experiment after 240 minutes.
B.3 Improver
After each round, the improver receives the executor’s transcript, its experiments and notes, and the scores of
all rounds so far. It may modify the executor’s prompts, settings, control loop, and tools, as well as its own
prompts, settings, acceptance rule, and a file of lessons that it maintains across rounds. A single improver
phase may change at most 400 lines of the harness; a larger change is reverted in full. Every four rounds, the
improver additionally reviews its own process: which kinds of harness changes were followed by accepted
candidates and which by stalls, whether the acceptance rule is too strict or too permissive, and which lessons
to record. Changes to the harness take effect from the following round. In the frozen-harness runs of Table 8,
the improver is not run.

B.4 Acceptance rule
The margin𝛿 in Equation (2) is determined by the acceptance rule, which is part of the improver’s harness. In
the starting harness, a candidate is accepted if its validation score exceeds that of the accepted solution by
more than2𝜎, where𝜎 is the standard deviation of the starter’s validation score over repeated evaluations
(Table 10). On tasks for which𝜎 was not measured, it is set to zero, and any improvement on the validation
split is accepted. Because the rule belongs to the harness, the improver may revise it. If the rule fails to return
a decision, and in every run with a frozen harness, the starting rule𝛿=2𝜎is applied.
B.5 Budget and termination
A run ends at the first of the following events: the wall-clock time, GPU hours, tokens (input, including cached
input, and output), or cost in dollars reach the task’s limit; the number of validation evaluations reaches its
limit; the round cap is reached; or five consecutive rounds produce neither a candidate nor a change to the
harness, a rule that is not applied on LIBERO-MAX and LIBERO-PRO. The budget is checked before each model
call, experiment, and development evaluation and is charged when each of them ends, so that calls running
concurrently can exceed a limit by at most their combined cost. A submitted candidate is evaluated on the
validation split even when the budget is exhausted. Model calls that the evaluator makes on the validation and
test splits, for tasks whose solution calls the model, are recorded but not charged. Periods during which the
model provider is unavailable are not charged either, and a phase interrupted by such an outage is repeated.
After the run, the final solution and every accepted solution are scored on the test split (Section 3.3).
Table 10 gives the limits of each task. On a given task, all models have the same limits, with the following
exceptions. Gemini 3.8 Flash and Gemini 4 Argon are stopped after 80 model calls per executor phase on
Active Search, Ego-Exo Memory, 3D Tracking, Visual Search, and Video Quality. On Active Search, the dollar
limit for open-weight models is 250. On RoboLab, the runs of Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, and GPT-6.1
Sol have 240 GPU hours. On Image Editing, the runs of Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol,
and both Gemini models have 60 wall-clock hours and a dollar limit of 150. On Kinematics and Mass, the
wall-clock limit of every model other than Claude Opus 5.5 is the time used by the run of Claude Opus 5.5
(11.3 and 11.0 hours). On Embodied-SWE and Spatial-VSI, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next is limited to the tokens used
by the run of Claude Opus 5.5 (22M and 21M). On 3D Tracking, Claude Sonnet 5.5 has a dollar limit of 50.
On RoboCasa, Muse Spark 1.3 has 48 GPU hours and 80M tokens. On RoboDojo and RoboCasa, runs that
continued past round 10 are scored with the solution they had after round 10.
B.6 Isolation and integrity
After every phase, any change outside the paths that the phase may modify, including changes made through
shell commands, is reverted and recorded as a violation; the evaluator, the data splits, and the protocol
therefore cannot be altered by the agent. Files larger than 5MB are excluded from the run’s repository. If a
phase crashes in two consecutive rounds, the harness is restored to the last version that completed a round
without a crash. When a phase ends, all processes it started are terminated, so that no process left running
can modify the solution afterwards. All model calls, experiments, and development evaluations are routed
through the benchmark, which charges them to the budget and records them.

text:
More with Less: Efficient Parallel Scientific Code
Translation via an Agent-Skill Workflow
Jianuo Shen∗, Pengyi Xu† and Bo Zhang†
∗ csjianuo.shen@mail.scut.edu.cn
∗ Department of Computer Science & Engineering, South China University of Technology, Guangzhou, Guangdong 510006
†{vxu, bo.zhang}@mtu.edu
† Department of Computer Science, Michigan Technological University, Houghton, Michigan 49931
Abstract—Translating parallel scientific codes between HPC
programming frameworks is a critical but labor-intensive task.
Existing LLM-based approaches rely on fixed sequential pipelines
with undifferentiated repair strategies and correctness criteria
that do not match scientific computing practice. We present an
agent-skill framework that separates translation, compilation
diagnosis, and execution validation into three autonomous agents
coordinated by a verdict-driven orchestrator, routing each
failure to a targeted repair skill rather than retrying blindly.
An automated output check drives the self-correction loop,
complemented by an offline LLM-based verification that exposes
false positives escaping compiler and runtime checks. We evaluate
the framework on 30 HeCBench kernels translated bidirectionally
among CUDA, OpenMP, and SYCL with three open-source LLMs.
Our framework attains the higher verified correctness rate in
all 18 model and direction combinations over a state-of-the-art
baseline while consuming up to 52.4% fewer tokens, remaining
consistent across models and directions without architectural
modification.
Index Terms—Large Language Models, Agentic Workflow,
Parallel Code Translation, Agent-Skill Architecture, HPC Pro-
gramming Models
I. INTRODUCTION
The ability to automatically translate code between program-
ming languages has long been a goal of software engineering
research, and recent advances in large language models (LLMs)
have brought it closer to practical reality. Modern LLMs such
as GPT-4 [1], DeepSeek Coder [2], and Qwen2.5-Coder [3]
demonstrate strong generalization across programming lan-
guages, enabling translation pipelines that combine prompt
engineering, compiler feedback, and iterative repair to achieve
compelling results on general-purpose benchmarks [4], [5].
These capabilities have sparked growing interest in applying
LLMs to automate the translation of real-world codebases,
reducing the manual effort required to port software across
language ecosystems and opening new avenues for code
modernization at scale.
Despite this progress, LLM-based code translation remains
poorly understood in the domain of parallel scientific com-
puting. General-purpose translation pipelines typically assess
correctness through test case passing rates or code similarity
metrics [6], [7], criteria that are adequate for software engineer-
ing tasks but insufficient for scientific computing workloads.
Parallel scientific codes impose a stricter and more domain-
specific notion of correctness: numerical outputs must be
equivalent within floating-point tolerance across potentially
billions of arithmetic operations, translated code must genuinely
offload computation to the target device rather than silently
falling back to CPU execution, and results must be deterministic
across parallel runs [8], [9]. These requirements are difficult to
satisfy precisely because the semantics of parallelism, memory
hierarchy, and synchronization differ fundamentally across
programming frameworks such as OpenMP [10], CUDA [11],
and SYCL [12], a semantic gap that has no analog in
conventional language-to-language translation and that general-
purpose pipelines are not designed to bridge. Collectively, these
failures remain invisible to evaluation methodologies that stop
at compilation success or surface-level output matching, yet
they are precisely the failures that matter most in scientific
computing practice.
Several systems have recently addressed aspects of this
problem, but share three recurring limitations. First, existing
pipelines follow fixed sequential workflows with no dynamic
routing: all errors are handled identically regardless of their
root cause, leading to unnecessary LLM calls and poor token
efficiency. LASSI [13] exemplifies this pattern, achieving
strong results on bidirectional OpenMP ↔ CUDA translation
with compiler and execution feedback, but applying the same
repair strategy indiscriminately to every failure type. Second,
automated semantic verification remains absent or superficial.
CodeRosetta [14], a purpose-built encoder-decoder transformer
for C++↔ CUDA and C++↔ Fortran translation, reports 93%
functional correctness on a sample of 30 kernels but does not
assess numerical equivalence under floating-point arithmetic,
the correctness criterion most critical for scientific workloads.
LASSI similarly relies on manual output inspection rather
than automated output validation. Third, existing pipelines are
token-inefficient by design. LASSI and similar systems such
as UniPar [15] and ParaCodex [9] apply the same LLM-based
repair strategy regardless of error type, incurring unnecessary
token consumption on failures that could be resolved with
targeted, lightweight interventions. This indiscriminate retry
behavior limits practical scalability and increases inference cost
without a corresponding improvement in translation quality.
Inspired by the emerging paradigm of agent-skill decompo-
sition in autonomous AI systems [5], [16]–[18], we propose
an agentic workflow for parallel scientific code translation
that addresses these limitations through principled separation
of concerns. Our framework comprises three collaborating
agents coordinated by an orchestrator: aTranslationAgent
