title: More with Less: Efficient Parallel Scientific Code Translation via an Agent-Skill Workflow

text:
that encapsulates code analysis, memory-aware planning, and
self-reviewing translation; aCompilationAgentthat combines
compilation with structured error classification to dynamically
route failures to the appropriate repair strategy; and an
ExecutionAgentthat automatically checks output correctness
between source and translated outputs and diagnoses runtime
failures including race conditions and incorrect GPU offloading.
Rather than treating every error as a prompt for blind retry, our
orchestrator reads the verdict from each agent and selects
the repair skill best suited to the diagnosed failure mode,
reducing unnecessary LLM calls and improving overall token
efficiency. We evaluate the framework on 30 HeCBench [19]
kernels translated bidirectionally among OpenMP, CUDA, and
SYCL with three recent open-source LLMs, measuring verified
correctness and token consumption against a state-of-the-art
baseline, and further audit the results under a stricter LLM-
based complementary verification. Our results demonstrate that
the agent-skill architecture achieves higher verified correctness
than the baseline while reducing token consumption by up to
52.4%, remaining consistent across three open-source LLMs
and all six translation directions among CUDA, OpenMP, and
SYCL without architectural modification.
This paper makes the following contributions:
• We propose an agent-skill architecture for parallel scien-
tific code translation that separates translation, compilation
diagnosis, and execution validation into three autonomous
agents. This separation enables verdict-driven routing that
targets each repair skill at a specific failure mode, reducing
unnecessary LLM calls while improving correctness
through more precise self-correction.
• We introduce an automated output check as a first-class
validation step, replacing manual output inspection with
a quantitative correctness signal that drives a dedicated
semantic repair loop, together with an LLM-based comple-
mentary verification that audits translated artifacts offline
and exposes false positives escaping the output check.
• We demonstrate that our framework achieves higher
translation correctness than LASSI on the same benchmark
while reducing token consumption by up to 52.4%,
establishing that more capable behavior does not require
more expensive prompting.
• We show that the framework generalizes across OpenMP,
CUDA, and SYCL, supporting bidirectional translation
between multiple HPC parallel programming frameworks
without architectural changes.
The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section II
reviews related work. Section III describes the agent-skill
architecture. Section IV presents experimental setup and results.
Section V discusses findings and limitations. Section VI
concludes and outlines directions for future work.
II. RELATEDWORK
The rapid diversification of HPC hardware has made parallel
scientific code portability one of the most pressing challenges
in computational science. Leadership-class systems such as
Frontier, Aurora, and El Capitan feature heterogeneous CPU-
GPU architectures from different vendors, each requiring
distinct parallel programming frameworks to achieve peak
performance [20]. The current TOP500 list [21] includes
GPUs from NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel, driving a proliferation
of parallel programming models including OpenMP, CUDA,
SYCL, HIP [22], and Kokkos [23] that target overlapping
but incompatible hardware ecosystems [24]. Manual porting
is prohibitively expensive, with domain scientists estimating
refactoring costs of upwards of eleven million dollars per
100,000 lines of code [25], and risks introducing subtle
numerical and performance errors that are difficult to detect
and reproduce. These pressures have driven growing interest
in automated approaches to parallel scientific code translation,
motivating the work surveyed below.
A. LLM-Based Code Translation
Automated code translation has a long history in soft-
ware engineering. Early approaches relied on rule-based
transpilers that applied hand-coded linguistic rules to map
source language constructs to target language equivalents (as
in SYCLomatic [26], the production CUDA→ SYCL migration
tool), followed by statistical machine translation methods
that applied phrase-based models originally designed for
natural language to translate between programming languages
such as Java and C# [27]–[29]. The emergence of neural
models brought a significant shift: Roziere et al. introduced
TransCoder [30], an unsupervised transformer model that
leverages masked language modeling, denoising autoencoding,
and back-translation to translate between Python, Java, and
C++ without requiring parallel training data. Subsequent work
improved upon this foundation by incorporating automated
unit test execution to filter invalid translations [31] and by
injecting code structure through abstract syntax trees and
compiler representations [32]. With the rise of large language
models, prompt-based approaches have largely supplanted
purpose-built translation models, enabling zero-shot and few-
shot translation across a much wider range of language pairs
without task-specific training [4]. Compiler feedback and
iterative repair loops have emerged as an effective complement
to prompting, feeding compilation and execution errors back
to the LLM for self-correction [6]. Despite these advances,
general-purpose translation systems assess correctness through
code similarity metrics [7] or test case passing rates [6],
criteria that are insufficient for parallel scientific codes where
numerical equivalence and genuine GPU offload are the relevant
correctness standards.
Applying these advances to parallel scientific codes has
motivated a dedicated line of work in the HPC community. Lei
et al. [33] introduced a dataset of manually curated OpenMP
Fortran and C++ code pairs and demonstrated that fine-tuning
LLMs on HPC-specific translation data significantly improves
translation quality over general-purpose baselines. LASSI [13]
introduced a self-correcting pipeline for bidirectional CUDA↔
OpenMP translation combining self-prompting, static domain
knowledge injection, and iterative compiler and execution
feedback, but follows a fixed sequential workflow that applies
the same repair strategy to every failure type and relies
on manual output inspection rather than automated output
title: More with Less: Efficient Parallel Scientific Code Translation via an Agent-Skill Workflow

text:
verification; its extension LASSI-EE [34] targets energy-
aware refactoring, without numerical equivalence verification.
CodeRosetta [14] proposed an unsupervised encoder-decoder
transformer for C++↔ CUDA and C++↔ Fortran translation
with training objectives tailored to parallel code semantics, but
evaluates correctness on a small sample of kernels without
assessing numerical equivalence under floating-point arithmetic.
UniPar [15] evaluated fine-tuning, hyperparameter optimization,
and compiler-guided repair for translation among serial code,
CUDA, and OpenMP, improving over off-the-shelf models
while leaving numerical correctness unverified. ParaCodex [9]
introduced profiling-guided agentic planning for serial and
CUDA to OpenMP GPU offload translation, using hotspot
analysis and explicit data movement planning to prevent
performance regressions, but focuses on parallelization rather
than bidirectional translation between established parallel pro-
gramming frameworks. Evaluation in this space has primarily
relied on kernel-level benchmarks such as HeCBench [19],
which provides over 500 computational kernels with CUDA,
OpenMP, and SYCL implementations. Most recently, ParEval-
Repo [35] extended evaluation to repository-level HPC transla-
tion, finding that existing approaches largely fail beyond trivial
kernel scale due to cross-file dependencies and build system
complexity. Across these systems, three recurring limitations
emerge: fixed sequential workflows with no dynamic error-type-
aware routing, absence of automated correctness verification,
and indiscriminate repair strategies that incur unnecessary token
consumption regardless of failure type.
B. Agentic Workflows for Software Engineering
The application of LLM-based agents to software engineering
tasks has grown rapidly, driven by the observation that complex
software tasks require multi-step reasoning, tool use, and
iterative self-correction that single-prompt approaches cannot
provide. ReAct [5] established the foundational paradigm of
interleaving reasoning and acting in LLM-based agents. SWE-
agent [36] demonstrated that agent-computer interfaces en-
abling LLMs to interact with terminals, editors, and test runners
substantially outperform static prompt-based approaches on
real-world GitHub issue resolution. AutoCodeRover [37] com-
bined LLMs with AST-based program analysis to autonomously
localize and repair bugs, while RepairAgent [38] showed
that LLM-based agents with access to compilation and test
execution feedback can navigate complex repair trajectories
autonomously. These systems share a common architectural
insight: separating high-level decision-making from low-level
execution enables more robust workflows than monolithic
prompt chains.
Skills as stateless execution units have gained attention
for improving modularity and token efficiency. Rather than
routing all tasks through a single LLM call or distributing
them across communicating agents, skill-based architectures
assign lightweight, targeted execution to specialized stateless
components, reducing token usage compared to multi-agent
alternatives [18], while reserving expensive LLM reasoning
for decisions that genuinely require it [16]. The advantage of
dynamic, conditional execution over fixed sequential pipelines
has also been demonstrated directly in code translation: Gray
et al. [39] found that an agentic MATLAB → HDL translation
pipeline with conditional tool invocation outperforms fixed
sequential workflows by over 20% points, with gains attributed
to short prompts and on-demand tool use. These agentic soft-
ware engineering systems, however, assess correctness through
test suite execution, criteria that do not transfer to parallel
scientific codes where numerical equivalence, genuine GPU
offload, and parallel determinism are the relevant correctness
standards. Our work applies the agent-skill paradigm to this
domain, introducing domain-specific correctness verification
as a first-class component of the agentic workflow rather than
a post-hoc evaluation step.
III. SYSTEMDESIGN
This section presents the design of our LLM-driven code
translation framework. Translating parallel programs between
programming models is rarely a one-shot task: LLM-generated
code frequently fails to compile, and code that compiles may
still produce incorrect results at runtime. Rather than treating
translation as a single generation step, our framework organizes
the task as a multi-agent system in which specialized agents
collaborate through a central orchestrator and an iterative
repair loop. An LLM is invoked for code generation, rewriting,
analysis, and planning tasks. Meanwhile, in-loop verification is
delegated to the real compiler and runtime behavior, comple-
mented by an offline LLM-based complementary verification.
A. Overview and Design Goals
Our framework translates parallel programs between different
parallel programming models through a multi-agent system
coordinated by a central orchestrator. As shown in Figure 1, the
system consists of three agents: aTranslationAgentgenerates
the target-language code, aCompilationAgentvalidates that the
code compiles, and anExecutionAgentruns the compiled binary
and checks correctness. Each agent is composed of a fixed
set of skills that it executes in sequence: theTranslationAgent
runs code analysis, memory planning, and translation skills; the
CompilationAgentruns compiler invocation and error classifica-
tion skills; and theExecutionAgentruns binary execution and
runtime analysis skills. In addition, the framework provides
specialized repair skills to handle distinct compilation and
runtime failure modes.
The orchestrator drives the workflow through a verdict-based
self-correction loop. After each agent or repair skill executes,
the orchestrator records the returned verdict and consults a
routing table that maps every verdict status to the next agent,
a repair skill, or a terminal state. The loop terminates upon
reaching a terminal verdict, exhausting a global step limit, or
exceeding a unified self-correction budget that counts only
repair invocations. This verdict-driven routing separates the
concerns of code generation, failure classification and repair.
The overarching goal of the framework is to support
translation between arbitrary parallel programming models. To
make this practical, concrete translation logic is encapsulated
in dynamically loaded skills rather than baked into the agent or
orchestrator code, so adding a new source →target translation

B. Task State, Verdict, and Orchestrator
The framework uses a sharedTaskStateobject to represent
the evolving state of a single translation task as it moves
through the orchestrator’s self-correction loop. Initialized from
the source program and pair configuration, it tracks the current
translated code, the latest compilation and execution artifacts,
and bookkeeping information such as step history and retry
counters. A generic metadata bucket inside theTaskStateallows
skills to share intermediate context, such as code summaries
and memory plans. Both agents and skills mutate this state in
place, which simplifies the communication protocol.
Agents and skills communicate through a structured Verdict
object that encodes the outcome of the most recent step.
The orchestrator invokesCompilationAgentorExecutionAgent,
which maps compiler log or runtime output to a verdict category
according to a set of trigger conditions. The orchestrator then
dispatches the verdict to the corresponding repair skill or back
toTranslationAgentvia a fixed routing table. The mapping
from trigger conditions to verdicts and their routing targets is
given in Table I.
The Orchestrator implements the central control loop. It
consumes verdicts, advances the pipeline to the next agent
or repair skill, and enforces termination conditions. The
orchestrator also maintains the unified self-correction budget,
configurable at construction time, whose cap on repair attempts
applies across the entire system. Forward progress through
translation, compilation, and execution does not consume this
budget; only repair invocations do. This separation ensures that
successful translations are not penalized by the presence of
repair machinery, while preventing runaway retry loops.
C. Agent Skills and Repair Mechanisms
Each agent in the system is composed of one or more core
skills that encapsulate a single capability. Repair skills are
managed directly by the orchestrator and invoked when a stage
returns a failure verdict.
TheTranslationAgentruns three skills in sequence. First,
theAnalyzerSkillinvokes an LLM to produce a framework-
independent functional summary of the source program, de-
scribing its computation stages, inputs, outputs, and correctness
criteria. The summary is stored in the shared state and later
consumed by the translator. Then, theMemoryPlanningSkill
generates a memory and data-layout plan for the target
execution model, mapping each buffer to its intended sharing
behavior, lifetime, and synchronization requirements. Finally,
theTranslatorSkillsynthesizes the complete target-language
program by combining the source code with the functional
summary and the memory plan.
TheCompilationAgentcontains two skills. TheCompilerSkill
invokes the real target-language compiler and captures the
compilation log and the resulting binary path. If compilation
succeeds, the agent returns a pass verdict and control advances
to theExecutionAgent; otherwise, theErrorClassifierSkill
applies a set of trigger condition as shown in Table I to the
compiler log as presented in Section III-B.
TheExecutionAgentalso contains two skills. TheRun-
nerSkillexecutes the compiled binary with test arguments
and records stdout, stderr, and the exit code. The
RuntimeAnalysisSkillthen maps the recorded output to a verdict
category according to the trigger conditions in Table I. If
execution times out, theRuntimeAnalysisSkillautomatically
scales down numeric test arguments that exceed a configurable

TheAnalyzerSkilluses a shared prompt across all translation

D. Compilation, Runtime, and LLM-based Verification
The framework adopts an in-loop verification stage plus an
LLM-based complementary verification. The in-loop verifica-
tion stage relies on compiler and runtime feedback to validate
translated programs and provide signals for the self-correction
workflow. Compilation success is treated as the prerequisite
for execution, while runtime behavior is evaluated through
execution status and program outputs. A translation is accepted
by this stage only when the generated binary exits with code
zero and its output contains no explicit FAIL marker (a failure-
indicating word in the program output), corresponding to the
EQUIVALENTverdict in Table I.
Although compiler and runtime verification provide reliable
and reproducible signals, they cannot capture all correctness
issues in translated programs. A program may compile suc-
cessfully and terminate normally while still failing to execute
the intended workload, producing incomplete computations, or
generating incorrect numerical results without explicit error
messages. Such false positives can lead to an overestimation
of translation success rates and obscure the actual capability
of the translation framework.
title: More with Less: Efficient Parallel Scientific Code Translation via an Agent-Skill Workflow

text:
To address these limitations, we introduce an LLM-based
complementary verification. Unlike the compiler and runtime
checks that participate directly in the self-correction workflow,
the LLM verifier is applied offline to cached translation artifacts
and aims to identify defects that escape compiler and runtime
checks. The verifier receives the complete source program and
execution outputs, and produces a structured JSON judgment
based on a predefined evaluation rubric. Its role is therefore
evaluative rather than corrective: it provides a stricter post-
hoc assessment of translation quality without altering the
translations it audits. In practice, its confidence scores can guide
users in prioritizing artifacts for manual inspection, starting
with the least confident ones.
The verifier follows several decision criteria:
1) The translated program must genuinely execute the intended
benchmark workload rather than bypassing computation
through early exits, placeholder implementations, or no-op
kernels;
2) Explicit failure indicators or non-zero error counts in the
execution output are treated as definitive failures, regardless
of superficial success signals;
3) Numerical discrepancies are evaluated based on semantic
correctness rather than strict textual matching, allowing
legitimate floating-point variations;
4) Surface-level success markers (e.g., “PASS”) are considered
insufficient unless supported by meaningful execution traces
and consistent computational results;
5) Empty, truncated, or otherwise unverifiable outputs are
conservatively classified as failures to avoid rewarding silent
crashes or incomplete executions.
In addition to a binary pass/fail judgment, the verifier reports
a confidence score in the interval [0,1] . The confidence score
is calibrated using a five-tier rubric that maps the strength of
available evidence to numerical ranges:
1) 0.95–1.0: The execution output contains explicit verification
evidence (e.g., PASS markers, zero failures, or low RMSE),
and the translated program is complete;
2) 0.8–0.9: The output appears correct, but the verification
evidence is incomplete or partially documented;
3) 0.6–0.7: Execution succeeds, but explicit verification signals
are absent and the judgment relies primarily on program
analysis;
4) 0.4–0.5: The available evidence is weak or contradictory,
making the judgment uncertain;
5) 0.0–0.3: The available information is insufficient for a
reliable assessment.
By introducing this LLM-based complementary verification,
the framework reduces the risk of overestimating translation
quality due to limitations of compiler and runtime checks. The
confidence-aware evaluation further encourages conservative
judgments in ambiguous cases and provides a more reliable
assessment of generated parallel programs.

C. Generalization Across Models
The remaining rows of Table IV repeat the experiment with
GLM-5.2 and Kimi-K2.7-Code, and the key observation is that
the performance of our framework is largely agnostic to the
choice of LLM. Its per-model averages span only 16.0% (78.6%
to 94.6%), and every direction stays from 6.7% to 33.3% across
models (17.0% on average), because the verify-and-repair loop
compensates for weaker first drafts instead of relying on a
particular model’s strengths. LASSI, by comparison, fluctuates
far more: 31.0% across its per-model averages and 38.5% per
direction, with swings of 27.5% to 40.0% even on its three
strongest directions. Our framework also attains the higher
correctness rate in all 18 combinations. Token consumption
is equally predictable, staying within 1,018k to 1,115k tokens
per direction (a spread below 10%; LASSI: 1,445k to 2,341k),
29.5% to 52.4% below LASSI per model; only two of the 18
cells spend more than LASSI, and both buy large correctness
gains (up to +60.0% for +24.5% tokens).

D. Repair Loop Effectiveness Evaluation
To isolate the contribution of the repair loop, Figure 2 follows
six representative model and direction combinations through
the loop, plotting the cumulative token consumption (bars, left
axis) and the cumulative success rate (curve, right axis) after
each round, where round 0 is the initial translation before any
repair. The top row focuses on the hardest direction in Table IV,
OpenMP→SYCL, whose three-model averages are the lowest
for both systems (70.8% for our framework and 21.1% for
LASSI), and shows it under all three models. All three start at
or below 12.5%, and the success rate climbs steadily as the loop
accumulates tokens, reaching 79.2%, 58.3%, and 75.0% within
nine repairs: gains of 50.0% to 70.9% that come entirely from
verification-guided repair rather than from the first draft. The
bottom row varies the direction for DeepSeek V4 Flash. On
the easier CUDA↔OpenMP pair the strong first drafts (56.7%
and 33.3% solved before any repair) explain the pair’s low
token consumption in Table IV, yet the loop still adds 36.6%
and 62.5% to reach 93.3% and 95.8%; on CUDA →SYCL it
adds 60.0% to reach 70.0%. In all six panels the success rate
rises monotonically with the accumulated tokens, showing that
the repair loop, not the initial generation, accounts for most of
the final correctness.
E. LLM-based Complementary Verification
All success rates reported so far are judged by the simple
in-loop verification stage, which compiles each artifact, runs
it, and checks its output. To assess how much these judgments
can be trusted, we additionally applied the rigorous LLM-
based complementary verification (Section III-D), backed by
DeepSeek V4 Flash, to the cached artifacts of both systems.
The verifier issues a pass or fail judgment together with a
confidence score; Figure 3 shows the confidence distribution
over the 999 artifacts that produced output (1,008 runs in total,
minus 9 LASSI runs with Kimi K2.7 Code where, due to
the complexity of the tasks, the model repeatedly failed to
complete its output within the API time limit).

V. DISCUSSION
The experiments and the design process itself yield the
following findings about LLM-based translation of parallel
programs under verification-guided repair.
1) Skills make both translation and repair more token-
efficient.Analysis and memory-planning skills target
translation at an explicit parallelization plan rather than
a loosely matching retrieved example, and verification-
classified feedback targets repair at the diagnosed defect
rather than blind regeneration, keeping the repair share of
the budget smaller across all models and directions.
2) Translation difficulty is determined by the target
model, not the source.Directions with the same target
cluster together in correctness, with low-resource SYCL
consistently the hardest target: current LLMs read low-
resource parallel code far better than they write it, which
is also why retrieval offers little help on such directions.
3) The repair loop accounts for most of the final correctness,
but returns diminish beyond roughly five rounds.Success
climbs monotonically from a low round-0 base on hard
directions and still adds large gains on easy pairs, with
most gains arriving within five rounds; later rounds mostly
accumulate tokens. First-draft strength determines what a
direction costs, not how many benchmarks eventually pass,
and failures that survive many rounds are systematic ones
that generous iteration caps cannot fix.
4) Verification and repair make the framework largely
model-agnostic.Correctness and token consumption stay

VI. CONCLUSION ANDFUTUREWORK
This paper presented a multi-agent system for parallel
scientific code translation, motivated by two gaps in existing
pipelines: they verify correctness against criteria that do not
match scientific computing practice, and they spend token bud-
gets on blind, undifferentiated retries. Our framework separates
translation, compilation diagnosis, and execution validation
into three agents coordinated by a verdict-driven orchestrator,
routes each diagnosed failure to a targeted repair skill, and treats
automated output checking as a first-class validation step. On 30
HeCBench kernels translated bidirectionally among OpenMP,
CUDA, and SYCL with three recent open-source LLMs, our
framework attains the higher verified correctness rate in all 18
model and direction combinations over LASSI, with per-model
averages of 78.6% to 94.6% against 34.5% to 65.5%, while
consuming 29.5% to 52.4% fewer tokens. Under the stricter
LLM-based complementary verification, it preserves margins
of 25.0% to 40.5% at a 2.1 to 3.9 times advantage in cost per
verified success. The experiments further show that the repair
loop accounts for most of the final correctness; verification-
guided repair makes the framework largely model-agnostic; and
compiler and runtime checks alone systematically overestimate
translation success. More capable translation behavior, in other
words, comes not from more expensive prompting but from
better verification scaffolding around the model.
Several challenges remain open. First, our evaluation is
limited to kernel-level benchmarks; extending the framework
to multi-file codebases and full applications will require cross-
file analysis, build-system awareness, and translation state
that persists across compilation units. Second, the LLM-
based complementary verification can itself be strengthened,
for example through refined evaluation rubrics, multi-verifier
voting, and tighter coupling between confidence scores and
targeted re-execution, so that the uncertain tail requiring
manual inspection shrinks further. Third, correctness is only
the first step toward practical porting: we plan to incorporate
performance feedback into the repair loop so that translated
programs are not only numerically correct but also performant,
and to extend the direction-agnostic skill mechanism to further
programming models such as HIP and Kokkos, where the low-
resource difficulty observed for SYCL targets is likely to be
even more pronounced.

Artifact Description (AD)
VII. OVERVIEW OFCONTRIBUTIONS ANDARTIFACTS
A. Paper’s Main Contributions
C1 A multi-agent framework for automated HPC code trans-
lation across CUDA, OpenMP, and SYCL, comprising a
TranslationAgent, a CompilationAgent, and an Execution-
Agent coordinated by a verdict-driven Orchestrator.
C2 A set of repair skills (Patch, Semantic, Sync, Memory)
that detect and fix compilation, runtime, and correctness
errors during translation, enabling iterative self-correction
without human intervention.
C3 An evaluation of the framework on 30 HeCBench bench-
marks across six translation directions and three LLM
backends (DeepSeek V4 Flash, GLM 5.2, Kimi K2.7
Code), demonstrating higher verified correctness and lower
token consumption than the LASSI baseline.
B. Computational Artifacts
A1 https://github.com/dinglhmds/More-with-Less-Efficient-P
arallel-Scientific-Code-Translation-via-an-Agent-Skill
-Workflow
Artifact ID Contributions Related
Supported Paper Elements
A1 C1, C2, C3 Tables IV–VI
Figures 2–3
VIII. ARTIFACTIDENTIFICATION
A. Computational ArtifactA 1
Relation To Contributions
The artifact implements the full multi-agent translation
pipeline described in C1 and C2, including the Orchestrator,
all three agents, all repair skills, and the offline LLM-based
complementary verifier. It also contains the LASSI baseline
(configured with the same three LLMs), the batch runner, and
the evaluation scripts used to produce the results inC 3.
Expected Results
Running the batch evaluation on the 30 HeCBench bench-
marks (six translation directions, three LLMs, both systems)
should produce per-benchmark verdicts (success/failure), token
consumption reports, cumulative success-rate curves, and
complementary-verification judgments matching Tables IV–
VI and Figures 2–3 in the paper. The framework is expected
to achieve a higher verified correctness rate than the LASSI
baseline while consuming fewer LLM tokens on average.
Expected Reproduction Time (in Minutes)
Artifact Setup: approximately 30 minutes (install Python de-
pendencies and configure LLM API access). Artifact Execution:
approximately 8–12 hours for all 30 benchmarks on a GPU
cluster (dominated by LLM API latency). Artifact Analysis:
approximately 15 minutes (aggregate per-benchmark result.json
files into summary tables and plots).
Artifact Setup (incl. Inputs)
Hardware:A GPU cluster managed by Slurm with at
least one NVIDIA GPU node is required for executing
CUDA baselines and OpenMP/SYCL offload targets. CPU-
only OpenMP execution is also supported as a fallback. The
evaluation used a Slurm cluster with the mrigpu partition
(one GPU per job).
Software:

openai-python

uda-toolkit

Datasets / Inputs:The evaluation uses 30 benchmarks se-
lected from HeCBench (https://github.com/zjin-lcf/HECBench),

Artifact Execution
The experiment workflow consists of four tasks: T1 (transla-
tion)→T 2 (compilation/execution)→T 3 (result aggregation)
→T 4 (offline complementary verification). The full evaluation
matrix comprises two systems (our framework and the LASSI
baseline), three LLMs, and six translation directions; individual
runs are independent and can be distributed across Slurm jobs.
T1: The batch runner ( batch_runner.py) discovers
benchmarks under the HeCBench source directory, reads
each source program, and runs the multi-agent pipeline.
The Orchestrator coordinates Analyzer, MemoryPlanning, and
Translator skills to produce target code, then invokes the
CompilationAgent and the ExecutionAgent. If compilation or
execution fails, repair skills mutate the code and the pipeline re-
enters from the corresponding stage. Each benchmark is capped
at 300 seconds for compilation, 120 seconds for execution, and
a maximum of 9 repair iterations.
T2: Each source program is compiled with its native
compiler (nvcc -O3 -std=c++17 for CUDA, g++ -O2
-fopenmp -std=c++17 for OpenMP, icpx -fsycl
-std=c++17 for SYCL) and executed on a Slurm
GPU node to obtain reference outputs. Translated pro-
grams are compiled with the corresponding target com-
piler (for OpenMP GPU offload, clang++ -O3 -fopenmp
-fopenmp-targets=nvptx64 -std=c++17 ) and exe-
cuted with the same input arguments.
T3: Per-benchmark results are writ-
ten to output/<timestamp>/
<benchmark>/result.json, containing the verdict,
retry counts, elapsed time, and token usage broken down by
category and repair round. A summary script aggregates these
files into the tables and figures reported in the paper.
T4: The offline LLM-based complementary verifier is applied
to the cached artifacts of both systems. Given the complete
source program and the execution outputs of a translated
program, it produces a structured JSON judgment (pass/fail plus
a confidence score in [0,1] ) following the rubric described in the
paper. Aggregating these judgments yields the complementary-
verification pass rates in Table V , the false-positive taxonomy
in Table VI, and the confidence distribution in Figure 3.
Artifact Analysis (incl. Outputs)
The expected output is a set of per-benchmark
result.json files, per-artifact verification judgments, and
a summary report. The key metrics are: (1) the verified
correctness rate (the EQUIVALENT verdict, routed to the
terminal Done state), (2) token consumption aggregated
by direction and model, (3) the cumulative success rate as
a function of repair rounds, and (4) the complementary-
verification pass rates and confidence distribution. These
correspond to Tables IV–VI and Figures 2–3 in the paper.
Artifact Evaluation (AE)
A. Computational ArtifactA 1
Artifact Setup (incl. Inputs)
Access.The artifact is available at https://github.com/dingl
hmds/More-with-Less-Efficient-Parallel-Scientific-Code-Tra
nslation-via-an-Agent-Skill-Workflow. Reviewers are granted
access to an OpenAI-compatible LLM endpoint; the endpoint
URL and an API key with sufficient quota are provided through
the submission system.
Hardware.One NVIDIA GPU node on a Slurm-managed
cluster (one GPU per job), as described in the AD Appendix.
Software.Python 3.9+ with the packages listed in
requirements.txt (OpenAI client, PyYAML, python-
dotenv); g++ 8.5.0, CUDA Toolkit 12.8, and Intel oneAPI
DPC++/C++ Compiler 2021.4.0. Exact installation commands
and environment variables are given in the AD Appendix
(Artifact Setup) and in the repositoryREADME.md.
Artifact Execution
To stay within the evaluation time budget, we define a
reduced but representative evaluation: the CUDA→OpenMP
direction with DeepSeek V4 Flash, all 30 benchmarks, run for
both our framework and the LASSI baseline. This reproduces
one column pair of Table IV and the bottom-left panel of
Figure 2. The model is selected viaMODEL_NAMEin.env.
E1 (translation with self-correction): for our framework, run
export CT_TRANSLATION_DIRECTION=\
cuda_to_openmp
python batch_runner.py \
--benchmark-dir <hecbench>/src \
--output batch_cuda2omp_ae.json \
--no-context --no-rag \
--use-memory-plan \
--auto-scale-on-timeout \

python experiments/lassi/\
run_lassi30_cuda2omp_context.py
(On a Slurm cluster, the equivalent submission scripts are

norag_nocontext.sh and scripts/submit_lassi
_cuda2omp_context.sh; adapt the cluster-specific paths
before use.) For each benchmark this executes tasks T1 and
T2 of the AD workflow: the verdict-driven translation loop,
compilation with g++ -O2 -fopenmp -std=c++17 , and
execution on the GPU node, capped at 300 s compilation, 120 s
execution, and 9 repair iterations.
E2 (aggregation): run

framework_model_direction_summary.py

Optionally,E 3 (complementary verification): run
python tools/run_llm_verdict_full.py
to apply the offline LLM-based verifier (task T4) to the
cached artifacts, producing per-artifact pass/fail judgments with
confidence scores.
Artifact Analysis (incl. Outputs)
Expected results. E1 produces 30 result.json files per
system; E2 prints a table with the verified correctness rate
and total token consumption per system, together with the
cumulative success-rate curve over repair rounds.
Evaluation methodology.Compare the summary table
against the CUDA →OpenMP columns of Table IV: our
framework should achieve a higher verified correctness rate than
LASSI (paper: 93.3% vs. 86.7%) at lower token consumption
(paper: 718k vs. 1,327k). Because LLM outputs are nondeter-
ministic, absolute rates may shift by a few percentage points
between runs; the reproduction criterion is that the ordering of
the two systems and the approximate split of tokens between
translation and repair are preserved. The cumulative curve
should increase monotonically, matching the bottom-left panel
of Figure 2.
Correlation with contributions.Successful completion of
the verdict-driven loop, including repair invocations, substanti-
ates C1 and C2; the correctness and token comparison between
the two systems substantiates C3. If E3 is executed, the veri-
fier’s judgments additionally provide the stricter complementary
pass rates underlying Table V .

IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON PATTERN ANAL YSIS AND MACHINE INTELLIGENCE 1
PhysioWave-T: Token-Efficient Wavelet
Foundation Models for Biosignals
Y anlong Chen, Simone Benatti, Luca Benini,Fellow, IEEE,Cuntai Guan,Fellow, IEEE,and Y awei Li
Abstract—We present PhysioWave-T, a token-efficient wavelet foundation-model family for electroencephalography (EEG),
electrocardiography (ECG), and surface electromyography (sEMG). Dynamic scale folding recombines theJ+1 wavelet subbands before
tokenization, compressing the sequence from (J+1)CS toCS tokens forJ decomposition levels,C channels, andS temporal patches.
Route-specific wavelet front ends and learned channel-name embeddings let one Transformer per modality accommodate diverse
channel counts and sampling rates, while unseen configurations reuse the pre-trained backbone via a lightweight front end. Together,
these components scale PhysioWave to EEG: we pre-train a 30M-parameter EEG foundation model on over 15M windows spanning 19
to 128 channels, alongside ECG (30M) and sEMG (12M) encoders. Across four EEG routes, folding cuts Transformer latency by
4.0–7.2×and peak memory by 6.8–12.7×over scale expansion without accuracy loss. The EEG encoder leads eight of nine metrics
against BENDR, BIOT, LaBraM, and EEGPT, and surpasses LUNA-L on wearable seizure detection with fewer parameters.
Reliability-aware latent fusion (RALF) then integrates summary tokens from the independently pre-trained encoders using per-sample
reliability weights. On SeizeIT2, fusion raises event sensitivity at 11 false alarms/h from 61.4 % to 74.4 % with RALF , while RALF boosts
window-level AUPRC from 0.321 to 0.399 over the best unimodal model and outperforms weighted-logit and concatenation fusion in
AUPRC across all six training variants. PhysioWave-T also sets new state-of-the-art sEMG accuracies and the highest macro-F1 on
PTB-XL Super and Chapman–Shaoxing, establishing an efficient, extensible foundation for biosignal representation learning. Code and
models are available at https://github.com/ForeverBlue816/PhysioWave.
Index Terms—Biosignal foundation models, self-supervised learning, token efficiency, heterogeneous acquisition, multimodal fusion.
✦
1 INTRODUCTION
P
HYSIOLOGICALsignals reflect the underlying dynamics
of the human body across diverse temporal scales,
yet their acquisition hardware and recording protocols are
far from uniform. Across clinical and consumer settings,
EEG spans two-channel wearables to 128-channel scalp
arrays; ECG ranges from single-lead ambulatory patches
to clinical twelve-lead systems; and sEMG is captured by
wristbands, forearm arrays, and high-density grids, each
governed by a distinct sampling rate and sensor geometry.
A truly reusable representation must capture multiscale
physiological structure while flexibly accommodating this
hardware diversity, yet these two desiderata pull directly
against each other. Wavelet decompositions are well suited
to non-stationary biosignals, but exposing every scale to
a Transformer incurs a steep quadratic cost: a J-level
decomposition ofC channels andS patches yields (J+1)CS
tokens, causing channel density, window duration, and
decomposition depth to lengthen the token sequence in

yawei.li@ntu.edu.sg.

University of Modena and Reggio Emilia, 41125 Modena, Italy. E-mail:
simone.benatti@unimore.it.
• L. Benini is with the Integrated Systems Laboratory, ETH Z¨ urich, 8092
Z¨ urich, Switzerland, and also with the Department of Electrical, Electronic
and Information Engineering “Guglielmo Marconi” (DEI), University of
Bologna, 40136 Bologna, Italy. E-mail:lbenini@iis.ee.ethz.ch.
• C. Guan is with the College of Computing and Data Science, Nanyang Tech-
nological University, Singapore 639798. E-mail: CTGuan@ntu.edu.sg.
•Corresponding author: Yawei Li.
tandem. Mapping every recording onto a single fixed input
layout sidesteps this variability, but intermediate heuristics
such as channel selection, padding, or resampling inevitably
discard acquisition-specific information along the way.
Our prior works, WaveFormer [1] and PhysioWave [2],
learn multiscale representations of ECG and sEMG through
adaptive wavelet selection, soft gating, cross-scale feature
aggregation, and frequency-guided masked pre-training.
Nevertheless, three design choices in PhysioWave limit
how far this paradigm scales. Its tokenizer expanded every
wavelet scale into a separate token row, and each encoder
was constrained to a single fixed input configuration. Both
limitations are most severe for EEG, whose clinical montages
vary widely across datasets and whose dense electrode arrays
rapidly multiply the token count. PhysioWave’s multimodal
experiments relied on an external pre-trained backbone and
combined modalities using fixed learned weights that could
not adapt to the signal quality of individual samples. These
bottlenecks raise three central questions that anchor this
work: how to retain multiscale time-frequency information
without multiplying tokens, how to share a single architec-
ture across heterogeneous acquisition setups, and how to
fuse modalities whose reliability varies across recordings.
PhysioWave-T addresses the first two questions by de-
coupling acquisition-specific processing from representation
learning. Each acquisition route, defined by a channel
count and sampling rate, receives a dedicated wavelet
front end and sampling-rate-specific patch projection, while
sharing a single Transformer backbone and a name-based
channel vocabulary across the modality. Within each front
end, dynamic scale folding recombines wavelet subbands
prior to tokenization using weights predicted from local

title: PhysioWave-T: Token-Efficient Wavelet Foundation Models for Biosignals

text:
IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON PATTERN ANAL YSIS AND MACHINE INTELLIGENCE 2
subband statistics and refined by learned synthesis fil-
ters. Consequently, the backbone processesCS rather than
(J+1)CS tokens regardless of decomposition depth: deeper
analysis enriches individual tokens instead of multiplying
sequence length. Because folding contains no channel-specific
parameters, it transfers unchanged across montages; an
unseen downstream configuration requires only attaching a
lightweight front end to the frozen or fine-tuned backbone
and appending any new sensor names to the vocabulary.
These mechanisms allow PhysioWave to scale to EEG,
yielding a unified EEG foundation model as a central
contribution of this work. Without coercing recordings into a
common montage, we pre-train a 30M-parameter encoder on
over 15 M four-second windows spanning clinical, research,
brain–computer interface, and high-density corpora (19–128
channels at 256 and 512 Hz). Across four EEG routes, scale
folding reduces Transformer latency by 4.0–7.2× and peak
memory by 6.8–12.7× over scale expansion, cutting per-
batch memory on 128-channel recordings from ∼32 GB to
2.5 GB. Against BENDR, BIOT, LaBraM, and EEGPT, our
encoder leads on eight of nine metrics across sleep staging,
P300, and error-related negativity detection—including on
Sleep-EDFx, whose 100 Hz derivations are unseen during
pre-training. On two-channel behind-the-ear seizure detec-
tion, it reaches 61.4 % sensitivity at ≤11 false alarms per
hour, outperforming LUNA-L with 25.4 M versus 40.4 M
parameters. Pre-training also boosts label efficiency: using
just 10 % of KaggleERN labels, the encoder surpasses a fully
supervised scratch model. Finally, the learned representations
capture intrinsic physiology: channel embeddings recover
scalp topography without coordinate supervision, and the
slowest wavelet scale’s weight progressively increases from
wakefulness to deep sleep.
For the third question, reliability-aware latent fusion
(RALF) combines this EEG encoder with independently pre-
trained ECG and sEMG encoders, without joint multimodal
pre-training. Each encoder contributes four summary tokens.
A per-sample reliability score gates that modality’s contribu-
tion to attention and the residual unimodal prediction, and
missing modalities are masked explicitly. On SeizeIT2, with
simultaneous wearable EEG, ECG, and EMG, RALF raises
event sensitivity at 11 false alarms per hour from 61.4 % to
78.9 % and window-level AUPRC from 0.321 to 0.399 relative
to the best EEG model. All six training variants exceed
weighted-logit and concatenation fusion in AUPRC, most
clearly on ECG-containing combinations. RALF also retains
an AUPRC of at least 0.33 under every tested single-modality
corruption. Relative to PhysioWave, the contributions are:
• Token-efficient multiscale modeling.Dynamic scale
folding shortens the sequence by a factor of J+1 while
retaining adaptive wavelet analysis. We quantify its effects
on accuracy, latency, memory, and computation.
• An EEG foundation model across acquisition configu-
rations.Route-specific front ends and extensible channel
vocabularies let one shared 30M-parameter backbone
learn from heterogeneous montages and transfer to
unseen ones, including two-channel wearable EEG.
• Reliability-aware multimodal prediction.RALF fuses
compact modality summaries using sample-specific relia-
bility estimates. We evaluate it on seizure detection under
complete, missing, and corrupted inputs.
2 RELATEDWORK
2.1 Physiological Foundation Models
Following BERT [3] and MAE [4], masked reconstruction and
predictive learning have produced transferable EEG represen-
tations. BENDR [5] and Brant [6] established contrastive and
predictive pre-training. BIOT tokenizes channel-wise spectral
patches [7], LaBraM predicts discrete neural codes [8],
EEGPT combines masked reconstruction with spatiotemporal
alignment [9], and CBraMod separates spatial and temporal
interactions through criss-cross attention [10]. Beyond EEG,
ST-MEM [11], HuBERT-ECG [12], and ECG-FM [13] apply
masked modeling or self-distillation to ECG, and large
wristband datasets support sEMG models for movement
and interaction [14], [15]. Generic time-series models such as
MOMENT [16] and UniTS [17] pursue broader transfer. These
models differ mainly in their tokenization and pre-training
targets. PhysioWave-T instead addresses the interface be-
tween acquisition and representation: configuration-specific
processing precedes a shared token space, and multiscale
analysis does not lengthen the backbone sequence.
2.2 Multiscale Representations and Heterogeneous In-
puts
Wavelets localize signal structure in time and frequency [18],
[19]. Best-basis selection [20] and coefficient shrinkage [21]
adapt this representation to signal structure or noise, and
neural wavelet operators make its filters trainable [22].
WaveFormer [1] introduced soft wavelet selection for sEMG,
and PhysioWave [2] paired learnable wavelet analysis with
frequency-guided pre-training for ECG and sEMG. However,
PhysioWave allocated a separate token row to every band.
PhysioWave-T retains these analysis components but folds
the subbands before tokenization, so decomposition depth
no longer lengthens the sequence. Generalizing classical best-
basis selection, the fold replaces discrete wavelet-packet tree
search with a learned, continuous scale mixture.
Heterogeneous acquisition poses a separate challenge.
Perceiver architectures compress variable inputs into latent
arrays [23], mixture-of-experts models route tokens among
specialized subnetworks [24], [25], and channel-independent
designs process each channel separately [26]. In EEG, name-
based embeddings identify electrodes [8], [9], graph models
encode spatial adjacency [27], and LUNA [28] maps variable
electrode sets to a fixed set of latent queries. PhysioWave-T
selects a front end deterministically from acquisition meta-
data rather than learning token-level routing. It also extends
name-based identity to ECG leads and sEMG electrode sites,
adding vocabulary entries during downstream adaptation.
2.3 Multimodal Physiological Fusion
Combining biosignals improves prediction when modalities
carry complementary information, yet acquisition failures
rarely affect all sensors equally. Even available modalities
may differ substantially in their signal quality. Latent and
bottleneck fusion restrict cross-modal interaction to compact
summaries [23], [29], avoiding attention over every unimodal
token. RALF follows this design and adds a sample-specific
reliability estimate for each modality, supervised by corrup-
tion severity, while explicit masks handle absent inputs.

Fig. 1. Overview of PhysioWave-T, shown for EEG. (a) Channel count and sampling rate select a route-specific front end. (b) Adaptive wavelet
decomposition and dynamic scale folding produce oneC×T signal. (c) Spectral importance of clean-view tokens selects masked patches, zeroed
before the online front end. (d) A shared Transformer and two MLP heads reconstruct raw and folded-wavelet patches against stop-gradient targets.
3 PHYSIOWAVE-T ARCHITECTURE
PhysioWave-T is built on a simple principle: acquisition-
specific processing happens before tokenization, and repre-
sentation learning happens after it. Route-specific front ends
absorb differences in channel count and sampling rate, map-
ping every recording into a common token space in which
one Transformer per modality learns shared physiological
structure. These front ends retain PhysioWave’s learnable
wavelet analysis [2] but differ in two respects: they fold
the wavelet scales into one signal before tokenization, and
they attach an explicit identity to every channel. The first
change keeps the sequence short, and the second lets the
same backbone recognize sensors across configurations.
Concretely, Fig. 1 traces a window X∈R C×T , with C
channels and T samples, through the encoder. The front
end first decomposes each channel into J detail subbands
and one approximation, then folds these J+1 bands back
into a single signal ˜X∈R C×T with the shape of the input.
Fixed-duration patches of ˜X are projected into tokens, to
which learned channel-name embeddings and sinusoidal
position embeddings are added. With S patches per channel,
the Transformer receivesCS tokens, whereas PhysioWave’s
scale expansion produces (J+1)CS . Decomposition depth
therefore enriches the content of each token without lengthen-
ing the sequence, an advantage that grows with the number
of channels and matters most for dense EEG arrays. The
following subsections describe each stage in turn.
3.1 Routes and Modular Front Ends
Physiological corpora rarely share a single input format,
and forcing them into one would require dropping chan-
nels, padding, or resampling. PhysioWave-T instead groups
recordings intoroutes. A route r= (C r,fr) is defined by a
channel count and a sampling rate, both read from recording
metadata rather than predicted. Components tied to these
quantities remain specific: each route has a wavelet front
endFr whose per-channel analysis filters and gates can
specialize to the sensors of that configuration, and each
sampling rate has a patch embedding Pf . Components
that should generalize across configurations, namely the
channel vocabulary, the position code, and the Transformer,
are shared by all routes of a modality:

Defining patches by physical duration τ ensures that each
token spans the same temporal window across all sampling
rates, aligning tokens from heterogeneous routes onto a
common temporal footing. During pre-training, the routes
cover 19–128 EEG channels at 256 or 512 Hz, 1–12 ECG leads
at 250 or 500 Hz, and 16–64 sEMG channels at 2 kHz; the
pretrained corpus is listed in Table 1.
This architectural separation also governs how the en-
coder adapts after pre-training. Because the front end is fully
convolutional, it accepts any window whose duration is an
integer multiple of the patch duration. A downstream task
sampled at a pre-training rate reuses the corresponding patch
embedding, and if it also matches a route’s channel count and
channel-slot convention, it reuses that route’s front end as
well. Any other configuration receives a newly instantiated
front end and patch embedding for its (C,f) , attached to the
transferred backbone. In both cases, channel names supply
the sensor identities that connect the new input to what the
backbone has already learned (Section 3.4).

here to establish the notation used for folding. Each decompo-

form the subbands later recombined by scale folding.

3.2.3 Cross-Scale Feature Fusion
At each levelℓ, the gated approximation and detail features
are concatenated along the channel axis into a 2C×T map
and processed by a cross-scale channel-aggregation feed-
forward network (CAFFN; Fig. 3). CAFFN first refines this
map locally: pointwise and depthwise convolutions mix
information across the approximation–detail pair and along

4 PRE-TRAINING, ADAPTATION,ANDMULTIMODAL
FUSION
The EEG, ECG, and sEMG encoders share one pre-training
objective but are trained independently, each on the corpora
of its own modality. A pre-trained encoder can then be
adapted to a downstream configuration or combined with
the other two through reliability-aware latent fusion.
4.1 Self-Supervised Pre-training
Pre-training extends PhysioWave’s masked reconstruction
in two ways: masking acts on the raw input, and the
encoder reconstructs two complementary targets (Fig. 1(c)–
(d)). Masking tokens alone would not suffice for this
front end, because convolution and cross-scale fusion mix
neighboring samples before tokenization, leaving hidden
content accessible through adjacent features. Each window
is therefore processed in two views. The clean view supplies
reconstruction targets and mask-selection scores, while the
online view zeros the selected raw-signal patches before the
front end, so their samples never enter the online features.
After tokenization, the masked positions are replaced by a
learned mask token. Patch selection follows PhysioWave’s
frequency-guided strategy: spectral importance e is com-
puted from the summed magnitude spectrum along the
clean-view token sequence and combined with uniform
noise z as s= 0.6e+ 0.4z . The highest-scoring 70 % of
valid tokens are masked, so spectrally dominant patches are
hidden most often and must be inferred from context. For
ECG, the six limb leads within a temporal patch are masked
together, since their linear dependencies would otherwise
leak the hidden content, and precordial leads are masked
individually. Unavailable channel slots are excluded from
both mask selection and reconstruction scoring.
Two shallow decoders per sampling rate then predict
the masked patches in two spaces. The spectral target is the

4.2 Downstream Adaptation
A downstream task specifies its channel count, sampling rate,
and sensor names. The Transformer, channel embedding
table, projection, and identity gate are always transferred
from the modality checkpoint. Front ends and patch embed-
dings are transferred when the configuration matches a pre-
training route, as for PTB-XL on the 12-lead ECG route, and
are newly initialized otherwise. Mean-pooled tokens feed a
two-layer prediction head, and we evaluate three adaptation
modes.Fine-tuneoptimizes all parameters with layer-wise
learning-rate decay in the Transformer.Probefreezes trans-
ferred components and trains only the head and any newly
introduced front-end or adapter parameters.Scratchtrains
the same architecture from random initialization, isolating
the contribution of pre-training under each task protocol.
4.3 Reliability-Aware Multimodal Fusion
PhysioWave combines unimodal logits with one learned
weight per modality. These weights are fixed after training,
so they cannot reflect the degradation of a particular sensor
in a particular window. Reliability-aware latent fusion (RALF;
Fig. 6) fuses compact modality summaries and estimates their
reliability for every window. An attention pool with q= 4
learnable queries reduces each encoder’s token sequence to
four summary tokens, and nf = 8 learnable fusion tokens
attend to their concatenation through two cross-attention
layers before being pooled and classified. The fusion module
thus receives a fixed number of tokens per available modality,
independent of window length and channel count, although
encoder and pooling costs still scale with the input sequence.
For each modality, a sigmoid head predicts a reliability
rm∈(0,1) from its summary tokens. This score gates the
modality’s attention keys and values and also weights a
residual contribution from its unimodal logits:

5.2 EEG Results
We evaluate three tasks following the exact evaluation proto-
col of EEGPT [9]: five-stage sleep staging on Sleep-EDFx [49],
target detection on PhysioNet-P300 [50], and error-related
negativity detection on KaggleERN [51]. Table 2 compares
PhysioWave-T with BENDR [5], BIOT [7], LaBraM [8], and
EEGPT under the same subject-disjoint cross-validation folds,
with baseline results cited directly from [9].
Fine-tuned PhysioWave-T achieves the highest value on
eight of nine metrics, and the margins are largest where
the baselines are weakest. On Sleep-EDFx, its Fpz-Cz and
Pz-Oz derivations at 100 Hz match no pre-training route
or vocabulary entry, so the front end and both channel
embeddings are learned downstream. Even so, PhysioWave-
T raises kappa from 0.686 to 0.737 and weighted F1 from
76.5 % to 80.9 % over EEGPT. The scratch model alone already
reaches a kappa of 0.736, which indicates that the multiscale
front end itself suits sleep staging, a task defined by band-
limited rhythms; Section 6.3 shows the fold shifting weight
toward the slowest scale in deep sleep. On KaggleERN,
PhysioWave-T improves balanced accuracy by 3.3 points and
kappa by 0.018 over EEGPT, the largest balanced-accuracy
gain among the three tasks. On PhysioNet-P300, balanced
accuracy and AUROC each rise by 2.0 points, while kappa is
within 0.003 of EEGPT.
The adaptation modes show that tasks draw on pre-
training in different ways. On PhysioNet-P300, the frozen
encoder already exceeds every baseline in balanced accuracy
and AUROC, and fine-tuning adds only 0.9 points, so
the pre-trained representation captures the P300 response
largely as is. KaggleERN behaves differently: probing falls
3.4 points below scratch, yet fine-tuning exceeds scratch
by 4.7 balanced-accuracy and 6.3 AUROC points. The pre-
trained weights therefore contain information relevant to
error-related negativity, but backbone adaptation is needed
to expose it. On Sleep-EDFx, pre-training adds 1.4 balanced-
accuracy points over scratch with nearly unchanged kappa,
consistent with the strong contribution of our architecture.

baseline values quoted from that paper [2]. GRABMyo trains
on sessions 1–2 and tests on session 3, and all baselines
are rerun on this split with three seeds. As Table 4 shows,
PhysioWave-T achieves the highest accuracy and macro-F1
on both benchmarks with 12 M parameters, about one third
of PhysioWave-L. On EPN-612, its 94.80 % accuracy exceeds
PhysioWave-L by 0.30 points; on GRABMyo, accuracy and
macro-F1 reach 89.78 % and 89.74 %, 1.25 and 1.37 points
above PhysioWave-L. The generic time-series models trail by
a wider margin on GRABMyo, where PhysioWave-T exceeds
MOMENT by 7.11 points with roughly one thirtieth of its
parameters and OTiS [57] by 10.40 points.
The two protocols reveal different roles for pre-training.
Under EPN-612’s user-dependent protocol, scratch training
already reaches 94.34 %, and fine-tuning adds only 0.46
points, since training and test data come from the same users.
GRABMyo instead tests generalization across recording
sessions, where electrode re-placement and changing skin
contact shift the signal distribution. Here scratch drops to
85.16 %, while the frozen encoder reaches 87.41 %, matching
PhysioWave-B, and fine-tuning adds a further 2.37 points.
Pre-training thus contributes most where the downstream
data alone cannot cover session variability. Probing is less
effective on EPN-612, falling 4.45 points below scratch.
This gap coincides with a spectral mismatch: the 200 Hz
wristband retains content only below 100 Hz, whereas the pre-
trained sEMG front ends emphasize roughly 100 to 200 Hz
(Section 6.2), so the frozen backbone receives inputs outside
its pre-training range until fine-tuning adapts it.

monitoring. RALF fuses the three frozen PhysioWave-T
encoders and is compared with concatenation and Phys-
ioWave’s weighted-logit fusion over the same encoders,
while LUNA [28], LaBraM [8], and EEGPT [9] serve as
single-modality EEG references. We report window-level

Scale folding.Scale expansion feeds all J+1 bands to
the backbone as separate token rows, giving the Transformer
direct access to every subband at four times the sequence
length. The dynamic fold scores 0.3 points higher on average
with a quarter of the tokens, so compressing the scales
before tokenization loses nothing that the backbone could
have recovered from the longer sequence. How the scales
are combined does matter, however. A static uniform fold
drops the average by 1.6 points and falls 1.3 points below
scale expansion, so a plain average of the subbands discards
information that the expanded representation preserves. Of
the 1.6-point gap between the uniform and dynamic folds,
the learned synthesis filters account for 0.7 points, since
replacing every gs with a delta costs that much, and the
data-dependent weights α account for the remaining 0.9.
Both components are therefore needed to match and then
exceed scale expansion, and the full fold achieves this with a
predictor shared across channels.

6.1 Spatial Structure in Channel Embeddings
Channel identities enter the model only as learned name
embeddings ((12)), with no access to electrode coordinates.
We test whether these embeddings nevertheless encode scalp
geometry by relating their pairwise cosine similarities to
geodesic electrode distances (Fig. 9a). For the 130 electrodes
of the 10-5 system and the 128 EGI HydroCel positions,
the Spearman correlations are ρ=−0.19 and−0.25, more
than twelve standard deviations from the permutation-null
mean (p<0.001 over 2,000 draws), whereas the untrained
table shows no association (ρ= 0.01 ). The structure is even
clearer locally. The five nearest neighbors of each electrode in
embedding space lie at a mean angular distance of 56◦ on the
scalp for 10-5 names and 44◦ for EGI, compared with 84–88◦
after name shuffling, and the electrode-centered maps for Fz,
Cz, Pz, Oz, T7, and T8 (Fig. 9b) show similarity concentrated
around each reference site. Because volume conduction
makes neighboring electrodes record overlapping mixtures
of the same sources, pre-training on raw signals is enough for
the vocabulary to recover scalp topology from names alone.
This learned geometry also explains the ablation result in
Section 5.6, where shuffling channel names costs more than
removing channel encoding entirely.

bank, so any difference after pre-training is learned from the
signals themselves (Fig. 10a). The level-one responses move
toward the frequency range that carries each modality’s
characteristic activity: the QRS range for 12-lead ECG,
roughly 100 to 200 Hz for high-density sEMG, where surface
EMG concentrates its power, and theγ range in the high-pass
branch of the 19-channel EEG route. The sEMG front ends
also widen their low-pass branch, with−3 dB cutoffs rising
from 125 Hz at initialization to 356–418 Hz. At 2 kHz, the
initial cutoff would have assigned most of the sEMG band to
the first detail subband; the widened passband keeps it in the
approximation that feeds deeper levels, so the decomposition

6.3 Scale Allocation Across Sleep Stages
Sleep staging offers a direct test of whether the folding
weights track physiology, since sleep stages are defined
largely by their dominant rhythms. We analyze the encoder
fine-tuned on Sleep-EDFx over 37,902 thirty-second windows
from 14 test subjects, grouping the weights by expert-
annotated stage (Fig. 11a). The folding network receives
only signal-derived subband statistics and is never told the
stage, yet the weight of the slowest scale, a3 (below 6.25 Hz),
rises steadily from wake to N3 and returns toward its wake
value in REM. This trajectory mirrors the electrophysiology
of sleep: slow-wave activity dominates N3, whereas REM
EEG resembles the low-amplitude, mixed-frequency activity
of wake. Within subjects (Fig. 11b), the wake-to-N3 increase
holds in all 13 subjects with both stages on Pz-Oz (Wilcoxon
p= 2.4×10 −4) and in 10 of 13 on Fpz-Cz ( p= 0.048 ), so
the effect is consistent across individuals.
The two derivations nonetheless receive different scale
mixtures from the same shared network. At the window
level (Fig. 11c), the slowest-scale weight correlates posi-
tively with δ-band power share on Pz-Oz ( ρ= 0.21 ) but
negatively on Fpz-Cz ( ρ=−0.22 ). Fpz-Cz also records
ocular activity, whose low-frequency power rises with eye
movements during wake and REM, so δ-band power on this
derivation is not a clean marker of slow-wave sleep. The fold
follows the sleep stage on both derivations while responding
differently to their raw low-frequency power, showing that it
allocates scales according to what the low-frequency content
represents on each derivation.
7 DISCUSSION
PhysioWave-T rests on one organizing principle: everything
that depends on how a signal was acquired is handled
before tokenization, and everything that depends on what it
contains is learned afterward by a shared backbone. This is
why a single 30 M-parameter EEG encoder can learn from 19-
to 128-channel montages and then transfer to a two-channel
wearable, and why decomposition depth becomes a choice
about the content of each token instead of the length of
the sequence. The analyses show that the efficiency costs
nothing in physiological meaning: identically initialized
front ends settle on the QRS, 100–200 Hz, and γ ranges
for their modalities, the folding weights track sleep stages
without stage labels, and the channel vocabulary recovers
scalp topology from electrode names alone, which makes
coordinates an unnecessary input and lets the same identity
mechanism cover ECG leads and sEMG sites.
The experiments also clarify when pre-training matters
and how to use it. Its benefit is smallest where downstream
data already cover the test conditions and largest under
distribution shift and label scarcity, as in inter-session sEMG
and KaggleERN, where a tenth of the labels match full-
data training from scratch. Some tasks are served by the
frozen representation, whereas subtle responses such as
error-related negativity require adapting the backbone, so
probing first and fine-tuning when needed is the natural
recipe. For multimodal monitoring, RALF shows that per-
sample reliability pays off when artifact-prone ECG must
be weighed against EEG and at strict false-alarm budgets,
and its scores fall in proportion to how much signal a
corruption leaves. The corruptions studied here are synthetic;
prospective recordings with natural sensor failures, joint
multimodal pre-training, and new routes for modalities such
as photoplethysmography are the next steps.
8 CONCLUSION
PhysioWave-T shows that a biosignal foundation model
can accommodate heterogeneous acquisition without paying
for it in sequence length. Route-specific wavelet front ends
and name-based channel embeddings let one backbone per
modality learn from any sensor configuration, dynamic scale
folding keeps multiscale analysis within CS tokens, and the
resulting EEG, ECG, and sEMG encoders lead the compared
models across sleep staging, event-related potentials, cardiac
diagnosis, and gesture recognition while cutting Transformer
memory by up to an order of magnitude. Reliability-aware
fusion extends them to multimodal seizure detection under
missing and corrupted inputs, and new acquisition setups
attach to the released backbones with a new front end instead
of a new model.

Phantom Consensus: Measuring Social Reasoning in
Multi-Agent LLM Decision-Making
Disha Sheshanarayana1 Rajat Subhra Pal2 Manjira Sinha2 Tirthankar Dasgupta2
1Manipal University Jaipur 2TCS Research
disha.229301161@muj.manipal.edu
{rajat.pal,sinha.manjira,dasgupta.tirthankar}@tcs.com
Abstract
Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly aggregate judgments across model in-
stances, but reasoning about other agents can itself introduce failure. We study
a setting in which LLMs shift their public decisions after observing ambiguous
social signals while reporting inaccurate estimates of what other agents privately
judged, even when the group’s recorded private judgments do not support the
apparent consensus. We call this failurephantom consensusand study it as a
pluralistic-ignorance-style pattern in controlled LLM collectives. To measure this
phenomenon, we introduce PHANTOM-BENCH, a benchmark that separates iso-
lated private judgments, public decisions after ambiguous social signals, elicited
estimates of the group’s private judgment, transparency-based recovery, and con-
trols for neutral public text and explicit vote-following. Across nine closed-
and open-weight models, ambiguous public signals consistently degrade decision
quality and can turn correct private group judgments into incorrect public col-
lective outcomes. Public accuracy drops by as much as 47.8 percentage points,
and collective rationality failures reach 47.3% in the most susceptible setting. We
observe substantial errors in reported group-private beliefs alongside public-stage
failures, while control conditions reveal model-dependent differences in suscep-
tibility to ambiguous and explicit peer signals. Revealing the agents’ recorded
private decisions repairs many failures without revealing the gold label, although
recovery varies across models. Our results show that evaluating multi-agent LLM
systems requires measuring not only final agreement, but whether that agreement
reflects independently measured private judgments or an apparent consensus.
1 Introduction
“I just went along because the three of you were so enthusiastic about going, ”Harvey writes inThe
Abilene Paradox[Harvey, 1974]. The line captures the collective failure at the center of this paper:
a group can publicly converge on an outcome that its members did not privately support. Multi-
agent systems built on large language models are increasingly explored as foundations for collective
decision-making, where groups of agents deliberate, review, critique, and coordinate before pro-
ducing a final outcome [Zhu et al., 2025a, Liu et al., 2024, Wu et al., 2024]. The appeal of these
systems rests on a familiar assumption: independent agents, each reasoning over the same evidence,
should improve decisions through diversity of judgment and mutual correction. Yet public social
context can weaken this assumption. When agents observe controlled public comments attributed
to peers, they do not only update their understanding of the task; they may also infer what other
agents privately believe. If those second-order beliefs are wrong, the collective output can diverge
from the private judgments of the agents who produced it. This raises our central question:when
