title: Phantom Consensus: Measuring Social Reasoning in Multi-Agent LLM Decision-Making

text:
Figure 1: Belief-shift mechanism in PHANTOM-BENCH. Agents first make independent private
decisions, then observe controlled ambiguous public signals and report both a public decision and a
perceived group-private belief. The setup tests whether agents retain their private judgment or shift
toward an inferred group belief unsupported by the group’s recorded private decisions.
LLM agents observe ambiguous public signals from peers, do they form false beliefs about what oth-
ers privately think, and can these misperceived group beliefs drive collective failures that no agent
privately intended?
Social psychology provides a useful lens for this failure. Pluralistic ignorance describes cases in
which individuals privately reject a belief or norm but publicly comply because they mistakenly
assume that others privately endorse it [Prentice and Miller, 1993, Miller, 2023]. Related phenomena
such as the Abilene paradox, the spiral of silence, and normative or informational social influence
show how groups can coordinate around apparent agreement even when private support is weak
or absent [Harvey, 1974, Noelle-Neumann, 1974, Deutsch and Gerard, 1955]. Recent work on
LLM social behavior has studied related but more visible failures: agents conforming to stated peer
answers and majority signals [Weng et al., 2025, Zhu et al., 2025b, Choi et al., 2025], yielding
under peer pressure [Song et al., 2025], and herding toward peer recommendations [Cho et al.,
2025, Mehdizadeh and Hilbert, 2025]. These works show that LLM agents can be influenced by
what peers explicitly say or recommend. We study a subtler failure mode: agents may follow what
they infer peers privately believe. When this inference is wrong, agents may publicly converge on a
decision that contradicts both their own private judgment and the measured private judgments of the
group. We refer to this failure asphantom consensus: public convergence toward a belief or decision
that is not supported by agents’ private judgments.
To study phantom consensus systematically, we introduce PHANTOM-BENCH, a benchmark for
measuring public-private belief failures in multi-agent LLM decision-making. As shown in Figure 1,
the benchmark evaluates agents across five belief-context conditions. In the private condition, agents
make independent judgments without group information. In the observed-public condition, they
see ambiguous public comments and report both a public decision and a perceived group-private
decision. In the informed-transparency condition, recorded private decisions are revealed before a
final decision. Neutral-public and explicit-vote conditions serve as controls for public-text artifacts
and direct visible conformity. This design allows us to compare recorded private decisions with
imagined private consensus, directly measuring second-order belief error rather than inferring it
only from answer changes. Across nine closed- and open-weight models, we find that ambiguous
public signals can cause agents to abandon otherwise reliable private judgments and converge on
public outcomes that the group did not privately support. These failures are associated with false
beliefs about what peers privately think, are not explained by public text alone, and are often repaired
when recorded private judgments are revealed. This is consistent with misperceived group belief
contributing to the observed failures, rather than task incapability alone. Our contributions are as
follows:
1. We introduce PHANTOM-BENCH, a benchmark for measuring phantom consensus in
multi-agent LLM decision-making.
2. We propose five belief-context conditions that separate visible behavior from inferred be-
lief: private judgment, observed public judgment, informed transparency, neutral public
text, and explicit public vote.
2
title: Phantom Consensus: Measuring Social Reasoning in Multi-Agent LLM Decision-Making

text:
3. We introduce evaluation metrics for public-stage belief failures, measuring when agents
abandon correct private judgments, shift toward phantom targets, misperceive what peers
privately believe, and recover after recorded private judgments are disclosed.
4. We show that ambiguous public signals can produce collective rationality failures: agents
may form false beliefs about what peers privately think and publicly converge toward out-
comes that the group did not privately support.
2 Related Work
Recent work shows that LLM agents are sensitive to peer responses, majority opinions, and so-
cial pressure. BenchForm studies conformity in LLM-driven collaboration and shows that models
may abandon independent judgments after observing peer responses Weng et al. [2025]. Other
work examines majority influence, cognitive-science-style conformity, group debate, peer pressure,
herding, and opinion-change dynamics, finding that LLM agents often revise their answers toward
visible peer positions or socially salient recommendations Song et al. [2025], Zhu et al. [2025b],
Cho et al. [2025], Choi et al. [2025], Mehdizadeh and Hilbert [2025]. More recent work extends this
line to normative conformity, topology-dependent influence, and trust calibration in multi-agent sys-
tems Bito et al. [2026], Han et al. [2026], Zhou et al. [2026]. However, most existing work studies
visible peer influence: agents observe what others explicitly answer, recommend, vote for, or argue.
PHANTOM-BENCHinstead targets a different mechanism: agents infer what others privately be-
lieve from ambiguous public comments, allowing us to test whether public decision shifts are driven
by misperceived group-private belief rather than direct conformity alone.
A growing body of work evaluates LLMs as interactive and collaborative agents. AgentBench
and MultiAgentBench evaluate general agent capabilities, collaboration, and competition Liu et al.
[2024], Zhu et al. [2025a], while AutoGen provides a framework for structured multi-agent con-
versation and coordination Wu et al. [2024]. Other work analyzes why multi-agent LLM systems
fail and how decision protocols such as voting or consensus affect final collective answers Cemri
et al. [2025], Kaesberg et al. [2025]. Closely related benchmarks study collective reasoning under
hidden information or robustness to faulty agents Li et al. [2026], Huang et al. [2025]. PHANTOM-
BENCHaddresses a complementary failure: agents may produce correct judgments in isolation, but
publicly shift because they interpret ambiguous social signals as evidence of a group-private belief
unsupported by the group’s recorded private decisions. A more detailed review of related work on
LLM social behavior, multi-agent benchmarks, and behavioral-science foundations is provided in
Appendix A.
3 PHANTOM-BENCH
PHANTOM-BENCHevaluates whether multi-agent LLMs exhibit phantom consensus: public con-
vergence toward decisions unsupported by the group’s recorded private judgments. Each instance
evaluates four independently instantiated LLM agents on the same scenario, records their indepen-
dent private judgments, and then exposes them to controlled, scenario-provided public comments
without revealing any vote or majority label. By collecting public decisions and perceived group-
private beliefs, the benchmark measures whether agents infer a group-private consensus from am-
biguous public signals that is unsupported by the group’s recorded private decisions.
3.1 Task Formulation
Each PHANTOM-BENCHinstance presents a decision scenario in which an agent must choose
one of three actions. We use a compact three-way action space that abstracts common institutional
decisions across domains:
•Proceed:move forward or approve the case.
•Block:stop, reject, deny, or prevent the case.
•Defer or review:route the case to further review, escalation, audit, clarification, or specialist
judgment.
Each scenario has agold private decision, the fact-supported answer under isolated judgment, and
aphantom target, a plausible but incorrect decision that ambiguous public signals may make ap-

Figure 2: Overview of the five belief-context conditions in PHANTOM-BENCH. All agents receive
the same scenario and decision request, but the group context varies across conditions: no group
information, ambiguous public signals, recorded private decisions revealed under transparency, neu-
tral public comments without an implied norm, or explicit peer recommendations. The setup sepa-
rates private judgments, public decisions, perceived group-private beliefs, and recovery under trans-
parency.
pear group-supported. The benchmark also elicits each agent’sperceived group-private beliefafter
observing public comments, allowing us to separate private decisions, public decisions, and beliefs
about what the group privately supports.
3.2 Dataset Construction
PHANTOM-BENCHcontains 480 scenarios, each instantiated with four agents, yielding 1,920
agent-level examples per condition across five decision environments: financial compliance, content
moderation, hiring fairness, healthcare privacy administration, and workplace operational safety.
Gold labels are evenly balanced across the three action classes, with 160 scenarios each forproceed,
block, anddefer_or_review. To avoid measuring only one kind of failure, the dataset is also balanced
across perceived norm-source categories and gold-to-phantom target directions.
Scenarios are grounded in public guidance and manually curated policy-pattern cases. 1 We used
an LLM-assisted construction pipeline to draft candidate scenarios under fixed schema and quota
constraints, followed by rule-based validation and manual quality checks before inclusion. Each
scenario contains invariant facts, a decision request, a gold private decision, a phantom target, and
controlled ambiguous public signals. The norm-source categories are inspired by prior work on plu-
ralistic ignorance, descriptive and injunctive norms, informational and normative social influence,
and false consensus effects [Prentice and Miller, 1993, Cialdini et al., 1991, Deutsch and Gerard,
1955, Asch, 1956, Ross et al., 1977]. Public signals are written to suggest a possible group tendency
without explicitly stating a majority vote or revealing what agents privately decided. Agents are
evaluated under private, observed-public, informed-transparency, neutral-public, and explicit-vote
conditions, allowing the benchmark to separate private decision quality, susceptibility to imagined
group norms, recovery under transparency, public-text artifacts, and direct visible conformity. De-
tailed definitions of norm-source categories, second-order belief targets, phantom target directions,
and construction details are provided in Appendix B.2.
1Sources: YouTube Help; Meta Community Standards; EEOC; HHS HIPAA; OSHA; FATF; FinCEN.

text:
3.3 Data Annotation
Each scenario is annotated with a gold private decision, a phantom target, a gold rationale, an
outcome-risk description, and taxonomy labels. The gold decision is assigned from the invariant
scenario facts alone, while the phantom target is an incorrect but plausible alternative that ambiguous
public signals may make appear socially supported. To validate annotation quality, two annotators
independently reviewed 150 randomly sampled scenarios using a rubric covering gold-label clarity,
phantom-target validity, public-signal ambiguity, private-judgment leakage, explicit majority pres-
sure, norm-source match, and target-direction validity. The annotators achieved Cohen’sκ= 0.83,
indicating strong agreement; disagreements were resolved through adjudication, and invalid sce-
narios were revised or removed. Full annotation instructions and taxonomy details are provided in
Appendix B.3.
4 Experimental Setup
4.1 Models
We evaluate PHANTOM-BENCHon nine models spanning closed and open families, model scales,
and deployment styles. The suite includes Gemini-3.5-Flash [Google DeepMind, 2026], Gemini-
2.5-Pro and Gemini-2.5-Flash [Comanici et al., 2025], Qwen-2.5-32B-Instruct and Qwen-2.5-7B-
Instruct [Qwen Team, 2024], Mistral-Small-24B [Mistral AI Team, 2025], Phi-4 [Abdin et al., 2024],
Mistral-Nemo-12B [Mistral AI Team, 2024], and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [Grattafiori et al., 2024].
This model set allows us to test whether phantom consensus appears across model families rather
than being specific to a single provider or architecture.
4.2 Belief-Context Conditions
PHANTOM-BENCHevaluates four agents on the same scenario and action space:proceed,block,
ordefer_or_review. The belief context varies across five conditions: three main conditions that test
private judgment, ambiguous public influence, and transparency-based recovery, and two controls
that isolate neutral public text and explicit peer influence. The full condition structure is shown in
Figure 2.
Private.All four agents receive only the scenario context and decision request. No public com-
ments, peer information, or group signals are shown. Each agent independently outputs a private
decision. This condition establishes the isolated judgment baseline for each agent.
Observed Public.All four agents receive the same scenario together with controlled ambiguous
public signals. These signals suggest a possible group tendency without explicitly stating a vote,
majority position, or final decision. The public comments are controlled scenario-provided stimuli,
held fixed across agents within each scenario. Each agent outputs two fields: a public decision
and a perceived group-private decision. This is the main PHANTOM-BENCHcondition, testing
whether agents infer a group-private belief from ambiguous public comments that is unsupported by
the group’s recorded private decisions.
Informed Transparency.Each agent receives the scenario, public context, and the recorded pri-
vate decisions of the other agents. Each agent then outputs an informed decision. This condition
tests whether public-stage failures are repaired when agents are given accurate information about
what the other agents previously decided in isolation.
Neutral Public.Each agent receives the scenario together with neutral public comments that do
not imply any phantom target. Each agent outputs a neutral-public decision. This condition tests
whether behavioral changes are caused by public text itself rather than by norm-implying ambiguous
signals.
Explicit Public Vote.Each agent receives the scenario together with explicit peer recommenda-
tions or vote-like signals indicating a decision direction. Each agent outputs an explicit-vote deci-
sion. This condition measures visible conformity separately from the ambiguous belief-inference
mechanism studied in the Observed Public condition [Asch, 1956, Deutsch and Gerard, 1955].

RQ3. How does phantom-target alignment under ambiguous public signals compare with neu-
tral public comments and explicit peer votes? Answer.The control conditions reveal different
patterns of phantom-target alignment across public contexts. We compare observed-public phan-
tom action alignment (PFA) with action-based measures from Neutral Public and Explicit V ote. As

shown in Table 2 and Appendix E, Gemini-2.5-Pro exhibits 19.4% observed-public phantom align-
ment, compared with 6.5% under Neutral Public and 15.1% under Explicit V ote, corresponding to
differences of 12.9 and 4.3 percentage points. Similarly, Mistral-Small-24B shows 22.8% observed-

observed-public (59.4%) and explicit-vote (61.0%) alignment. These results suggest that ambiguous
public signals produce greater phantom-target alignment than neutral comments, while differences
from explicit voting vary across models. Since the conditions also differ in comment content and
belief elicitation, these comparisons do not establish a distinct causal mechanism.
RQ4. Can disclosure of recorded private judgments repair public-stage phantom failures?
Answer.Yes, in many cases. Revealing the recorded private judgments of other agents repairs many
public-stage failures, even though the gold label is never shown. As shown in Table 1, Informed
Acc returns close to Private Acc for most models after transparency is introduced. The strongest
recoveries occur for Qwen-2.5-7B, whose accuracy rises from 29.2% Public Acc to 77.1% Informed
Acc with 99.6% TRR, and Qwen-2.5-32B, which rises from 42.1% to 72.5% with 97.9% TRR.
Mistral-Small-24B also reaches 100.0% TRR. However, revealing private judgments also provides
task-relevant peer decisions, so recovery cannot be attributed solely to correcting misperceived group
beliefs. Moreover, TRR measures recovery among agents that were initially correct but became
incorrect publicly, rather than overall improvement. For example, Llama-3.1-8B achieves 62.3%
TRR despite its overall accuracy declining from 59.8% Public Acc to 56.1% Informed Acc. Overall,
transparency enables substantial conditional recovery for most models, although its effect on overall
accuracy varies.
RQ5. Are the effects of phantom consensus consistent across model families? Answer.Phan-
tom consensus appears across both closed- and open-weight models, but its severity varies substan-
tially by model family. As shown in Table 1, closed-weight models show lower collective failure
rates, with CRFR ranging from 9.8% for Gemini-2.5-Flash to 16.5% for Gemini-2.5-Pro. Open-
weight models show a wider spread: Llama-3.1-8B has a lower CRFR of 13.5%, while Qwen-2.5-
32B and Qwen-2.5-7B reach much higher rates of 43.3% and 47.3%. Table 2 further shows that
belief-level errors appear across families, but models differ in how often these errors translate into
public-stage phantom failures. For example, Llama-3.1-8B has high PBE of 73.8% but lower PIFR
of 12.9%, whereas Qwen-2.5-7B has lower PBE of 55.6% but much higher PIFR of 42.2%. Thus,
phantom consensus is not isolated to one provider or architecture; models differ mainly in how often
belief-level errors are accompanied by public-stage phantom failures.
5.2 Discussion
Our results identify phantom consensus as a multi-agent failure mode: agents can shift public deci-
sions toward an inferred norm that is not explicitly shown and may conflict with the group’s recorded
private judgments. Unlike explicit vote-following, the observed-public condition provides no vote
or majority label, instead eliciting estimates of group-private belief from ambiguous comments.
Recovery under informed transparency shows that revealing recorded private judgments can repair
many failures, although this does not isolate correction of misperceived beliefs as the underlying
mechanism. The controls reveal differences across public contexts but cannot fully separate social
influence from persuasive content or belief elicitation. These findings motivate preserving private
first-pass judgments, exposing disagreement, and not treating public statements as reliable evidence
of peers’ recorded private judgments.
6 Conclusion
Across nine models, ambiguous public signals can move agents away from initially correct private
judgments and produce incorrect collective outcomes alongside substantial errors in reported group-
private beliefs. Control conditions reveal model-dependent differences between ambiguous public
signals and explicit vote-following, while revealing recorded private judgments often repairs fail-
ures without disclosing the gold label. These results show that multi-agent LLM evaluation should
measure not only final agreement, but whether that agreement reflects recorded private judgments
or an imagined consensus.

A Extended Related Work
PHANTOM-BENCHis grounded in behavioral accounts of pluralistic ignorance and collective mis-
coordination. Pluralistic ignorance describes settings in which individuals privately hold one belief
or preference but incorrectly infer that others privately hold a different one, producing public be-
havior that can misrepresent the group’s actual private attitudes [Prentice and Miller, 1993, Miller,
2023]. Related work on normative and informational influence shows that individuals may respond
not only to what others explicitly choose, but also to what they believe others know, endorse, or
expect [Asch, 1956, Deutsch and Gerard, 1955]. The false consensus effect and spiral of silence
further show how perceived group beliefs can diverge from actual private beliefs [Ross et al., 1977,
Noelle-Neumann, 1974]. Organizational and group-decision work similarly shows that groups can
converge on decisions that few members privately prefer or fail to use privately held information
12
title: Phantom Consensus: Measuring Social Reasoning in Multi-Agent LLM Decision-Making

text:
effectively [Harvey, 1974, Stasser and Titus, 1985, Lu et al., 2012]. These foundations motivate our
focus on second-order belief: the central failure in PHANTOM-BENCHis not merely that agents
change answers, but that they may act on an imagined group-private belief.
Recent work shows that LLMs and LLM agents are sensitive to social context, including peer re-
sponses, majority opinions, explicit recommendations, and pressure-framed interaction. BenchForm
and related conformity studies find that models may revise answers after observing peer outputs or
majority signals [Weng et al., 2025, Zhu et al., 2025b, Choi et al., 2025]. Other work studies peer
pressure, herd behavior, opinion-change dynamics, normative conformity, topology-dependent in-
fluence, and trust calibration in multi-agent settings [Song et al., 2025, Cho et al., 2025, Mehdizadeh
and Hilbert, 2025, Bito et al., 2026, Han et al., 2026, Zhou et al., 2026]. A related line studies social
norms, social knowledge, sycophancy, theory-of-mind behavior, trust, and emergent conventions in
LLM populations [Yuan et al., 2024, Choi et al., 2023, Sharma et al., 2024, Strachan et al., 2024,
Xie et al., 2024, Ashery et al., 2025]. This literature establishes that LLM agents are not inde-
pendent reasoners once placed in social environments. PHANTOM-BENCHdiffers by testing a
subtler mechanism: agents observe ambiguous public comments and infer what the group privately
believes, allowing us to separate imagined peer influence from direct conformity.
A parallel line of work evaluates LLMs as interactive agents whose outputs depend on communica-
tion, coordination, and aggregation. AgentBench and MultiAgentBench evaluate agent capabilities,
collaboration, and competition across interactive tasks [Liu et al., 2024, Zhu et al., 2025a], while
AutoGen provides a general framework for multi-agent conversation and coordination [Wu et al.,
2024]. Other studies analyze failure modes in multi-agent systems, including how voting, consen-
sus, hidden information, and faulty agents affect final decisions [Cemri et al., 2025, Kaesberg et al.,
2025, Li et al., 2026, Huang et al., 2025]. These works show that collective performance depends
strongly on how information is exchanged and aggregated. PHANTOM-BENCHcomplements this
line by isolating a belief-context failure: agents may make correct decisions in isolation, but public
outcomes can deteriorate when ambiguous communication is interpreted as evidence of a group-
private norm that is unsupported by the group’s recorded private decisions.

B.2 Taxonomy Definitions
The taxonomy in PHANTOM-BENCHis used as a controlled design mechanism rather than as
decorative metadata. The perceived-norm axis is motivated by work on descriptive and injunctive
norms, normative and informational social influence, and conformity under social pressure [Cialdini
et al., 1991, Deutsch and Gerard, 1955, Asch, 1956]. The second-order belief-error axis is inspired
by pluralistic ignorance, false consensus, and public-opinion misperception [Prentice and Miller,
1993, Miller, 2023, Ross et al., 1977, Noelle-Neumann, 1974]. In contrast, the collective outcome-
risk labels and gold-to-phantom directions are benchmark design controls: they ensure that the
dataset covers harmful, cautious, and neutral shifts rather than measuring only one kind of failure.
The benchmark distinguishes action fields, design taxonomy fields, and computed behavioral fields.
Action fields define the fact-supported private decision and the phantom target. Design taxonomy
fields control the type of public signal and intended belief error. Behavioral fields are computed only
after model evaluation.

Computed behavior PPG, PBA, PBE, PIFR, CRFR, P-CRFR, and TRR; computed from model outputs.

B.3 Inter-Annotator Reliability
We used two human annotators to validate 150 randomly sampled PHANTOM-BENCHscenar-
ios. Annotators evaluated scenario quality rather than model behavior. Specifically, they checked
whether the gold private decision was supported by the scenario facts, whether the phantom target
was plausible but incorrect, whether public signals remained ambiguous rather than explicit major-
ity statements, whether the signals leaked private judgments, and whether the intended norm-source
category matched the public comments. The annotators achieved Cohen’sκ= 0.83, indicating

strong agreement. Disagreements were resolved through adjudication, and scenarios with explicit
majority pressure, private-judgment leakage, unclear gold labels, or invalid phantom targets were
revised or removed.
Annotators were given the following instructions: “You will review synthetic multi-agent decision-
making scenarios for a research benchmark. For each scenario, read the base context, decision
request, gold private decision, phantom target, taxonomy labels, and public statements. Your task
is to judge whether the scenario is valid for measuring ambiguous public belief inference. Check
whether the gold decision is supported by the facts, whether the phantom target is plausible but
incorrect, whether the public statements suggest a possible group tendency without explicitly stating
a majority or consensus, whether any statement directly reveals the speaker’s private decision, and
whether the public statements match the intended norm-source category. Do not judge model outputs
or decide whether a model failed; only validate the scenario design. Mark a scenario as invalid if the
public statements are too explicit, if the gold label is unclear, if the phantom target is implausible, or
if the public signals leak private judgments. The examples are synthetic and do not contain personal
information. There are no known risks beyond ordinary text review.”

E Additional Results
E.1 Auxiliary Mechanism Metrics
Table 8 reports additional agent-level diagnostics that complement the main CRFR and P-CRFR
results. Flip Rate measures raw private-to-public decision changes, PIER captures cases where
agents are correct privately but become incorrect publicly, and PFA measures public alignment with
the phantom target. PIFR is the stricter failure case where an agent is correct privately and then
moves publicly to the phantom target. PBA and PBE capture the belief mechanism by measuring
phantom-aligned and erroneous perceived group-private beliefs.
As shown in Table 8, Qwen-2.5-7B exhibits the strongest public-stage collapse, with Flip Rate of
62.2%, PIER of 49.7%, PFA of 59.4%, and PIFR of 42.2%. Qwen-2.5-32B also shows substantial
impairment, with Flip Rate of 60.3%, PIER of 45.2%, and PIFR of 22.5%. In contrast, the Gemini
models show lower action-level phantom failure, especially Gemini-2.5-Flash with PIFR of 8.8%,
but still exhibit high PBA and PBE. This pattern separates three parts of the failure chain: public
decision instability, movement toward the phantom target, and misperceived group-private belief.
E.2 Extended Control Results
Table 9 reports the Neutral Public and Explicit Public V ote control results. The Neutral Public
condition tests whether public text alone causes phantom alignment, while the Explicit Public V ote
condition tests direct visible conformity to an explicit peer recommendation. The Obs-vs-Neutral
gap compares observed-public phantom alignment against neutral-public phantom alignment, and
the Obs-vs-Explicit gap compares observed-public phantom alignment against explicit-vote phan-
tom alignment.
The control results support the interpretation that phantom consensus is not caused by public text
alone. Neutral Public phantom alignment remains low for most models, including Gemini-2.5-Pro

E.3 Condition-Level and Norm-Source Breakdowns
Figure 6 provides complementary aggregate views of model behavior. The heatmap reports CRFR
across perceived norm-source categories, while the radar plot summarizes accuracy across the five
belief-context conditions: Private, Observed Public, Informed Transparency, Neutral Public, and
Explicit Public V ote.
Together, these figures show that phantom consensus is not confined to a single evaluation condition
or norm-source category. Several models exhibit elevated CRFR across multiple perceived norm
sources, with authority and consensus cues producing strong failures for some models. The radar
plot shows the broader condition-level pattern: Private and Neutral Public accuracy remain compar-
atively high, Observed Public accuracy drops under ambiguous group-facing signals, and Informed
Transparency often recovers performance. This supports the interpretation that the failure is driven
by ambiguous belief-context cues rather than public text alone.

E.4 Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
We estimate uncertainty using scenario-level bootstrap resampling. For each model, we resam-
ple scenarios with replacement and recompute the main metrics over the corresponding four-agent
groups. This preserves the within-scenario multi-agent structure while estimating variability across
scenarios. We report 95% percentile confidence intervals over the bootstrap samples.
Figure 5 shows that the main trends are stable under bootstrap resampling. Qwen-2.5-7B and Qwen-
2.5-32B retain clearly elevated intervals for CRFR, P-CRFR, and PIFR, confirming that their high
public-stage failure is not driven by a small number of scenarios. Stronger closed-weight models
remain lower on these failure metrics, although their intervals are still non-zero. TRR remains
high for most models, supporting the finding that many public-stage failures are recoverable when
recorded private judgments are revealed. Llama-3.1-8B remains the main exception, with a visibly
lower TRR interval than the other models.
F Qualitative Examples of Failure Cases
We include a qualitative example to make the aggregate failure mechanism more interpretable. The
example below is selected from Qwen-2.5-32B outputs and illustrates a strict phantom-consensus
failure: agents make correct private judgments, but ambiguous public context leads them to infer a
phantom group-private belief and shift their public decisions toward the phantom target.

Interpretation.This example shows a strict failure case: all four Qwen-2.5-32B agents initially
choose the gold private decision,defer_or_review, but after observing public context, all four change
their public decision toproceed. The perceived group-private field follows the same pattern: every
agent infers that the group privately supportsproceed. This indicates that the public-stage error is
not a random label change, but is coupled with a false second-order belief about the group’s private
judgment.
Why this matters.The example illustrates the core mechanism measured by PHANTOM-
BENCH. The group is privately correct, but public-facing signals create an imagined consen-
sus around the wrong action. Since the case is marked as harm-amplifying, the shift fromde-
fer_or_reviewtoproceedis not only an accuracy error, but a risk-increasing collective outcome.
This supports the benchmark’s central claim that multi-agent LLM systems can publicly converge
toward a position unsupported by their own measured private judgments.
G Limitations
Our findings should be interpreted within the scope of the benchmark design.1)The dataset covers
five decision domains, so it may not capture all settings where pluralistic ignorance or phantom con-
sensus can arise.2)The action space is limited to three labels:proceed,block, anddefer_or_review;
real-world collective decisions may involve richer, graded, or conditional actions.3)The experi-
ments use a fixed four-agent setup with controlled public stimuli rather than live multi-round de-
liberation; deployed systems may involve different group sizes, roles, hierarchies, or interactive
communication structures. We deliberately make no claim that phantom consensus demonstrates
human-like theory of mind. We operationalize second-order belief behavior as whether an agent’s
reported estimate of peers’ private judgments matches their independently recorded private judg-
ments. The reported rates characterize behavior under controlled benchmark conditions and should
not be interpreted as estimates of real-world deployment failure rates in the represented domains.
Future work can extend PHANTOM-BENCHto broader domains, richer decision spaces, and in-
teractive agent conversations.

text:
Evaluating LLM-Generated World Models for
Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning
Souhaila Djaffal∗ Amna Jamal∗ Gagana Madhugiri Devaraja∗ Anidipta Pal∗ Jobst Heitzig
PRISM AI Safety Research
{souhaila.djaffal, amnajkhattak, gaganaaa.dev, anidiptapal}@gmail.com
heitzig@pik-potsdam.de
Abstract
Formal world models can support planning, verification, and safety reasoning,
but constructing them from open-ended natural-language situations is difficult,
particularly in multi-agent settings where several formalizations may be plausible.
We study whether five LLMs can generate such world models as partially observ-
able stochastic games and whether mechanical validity is sufficient to establish
that the resulting model faithfully represents the intended decision problem. We
introduce a benchmark of 44 scenarios spanning game, situational, and cultural
settings, and evaluate generated world models along three dimensions: mechanical
validity, reference-relative structural agreement, and semantic criteria. Across three
empirical tracks, we analyze 410 first-pass generations. In the reference-backed
game track, 134/135 generated world models pass a strict mechanical audit, yet
mean permutation-invariant structural F1 is only 0.366, with just 28/134 mechani-
cally valid models exactly matching the authored reference. In the cultural track,
explicitly naming the country changes the generated structural representation for
most LLMs while producing only small changes in automated semantic scores.
These results show that executability is a necessary but insufficient criterion for
LLM-generated world models: models that are mechanically valid can still differ
substantially in the structure used by downstream neuro-symbolic reasoning and
planning. Github: world-model-suite
1 Introduction
Motivation and Core ChallengeNeuro-symbolic systems combine learned components with
explicit representations that support planning, reasoning, and verification. In safety-critical settings,
formal world models can also support quantities such as action reversibility [1], state reachability [2],
and human or agent empowerment [3–5]. More broadly, several “safe-by-design” approaches rely on
formal, tractable world models to reason about the consequences of actions [6, 7].
Constructing such a world model by hand for every new situation is impractical. LLMs offer a
possible alternative: given a natural-language description, they can generate a compact formal world
model that can be used for downstream planning or safety analysis. The central question is whether
the generated world model faithfully represents the situation it is meant to encode.
This is particularly difficult in open-ended, multi-agent settings. Several formalizations of the same
situation may be reasonable, and a unique ground-truth world model may not exist. An LLM can
therefore produce a mechanically valid world model while omitting a relevant participant or action,
introducing unsupported structure, or representing uncertainty and future outcomes differently from

title: Evaluating LLM-Generated World Models for Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning

text:
the source description. These differences matter because downstream reasoning operates on the
generated world model rather than on the original natural-language description.
LLM-Generated World ModelsWe studysituational world models: compact formal representations
constructed for a specific decision situation. We prompt LLMs to translate natural-language scenarios
into stochastic games, primarily Partially Observable Stochastic Games (POSGs), represented as
structured JSON or executable Python. These representations make agents, states, actions, transition
dynamics, uncertainty, and, where applicable, observations explicit, allowing the generated world
model to be inspected and evaluated directly.
Prior work has shown that LLMs can generate planning domains such as PDDL and executable
code-based world models, particularly in relatively structured planning settings [8, 9]. We focus on a
different problem: how should a generated world model be evaluated when syntactic or mechanical
correctness alone is not enough?
We separate evaluation into three levels. First,mechanical validityasks whether the generated world
model is executable and internally consistent. Second,structural fidelityasks whether its states,
actions, and transition structure agree with an available reference. Third,semantic diagnosticstest
whether important elements of the original situation are represented and unsupported assumptions
are avoided. This distinction is important for neuro-symbolic systems: a correct planner cannot
compensate for a world model that represents the wrong decision problem.
Key ContributionsWe contribute: (i) a corpus of 44 scenarios spanning game, situational, and
cultural settings, with different levels of available reference information (Section 3); (ii) a pipeline for
generating formal world models from five LLMs as structured JSON or executable Python (Section 3);
(iii) a multi-lane evaluation framework combining mechanical validity, reference-relative structural
comparison, and semantic-criterion evaluation (Section 4); and (iv) three empirical tracks applying
this framework to reference-backed games, open-ended situational Python POSGs, and culturally
contextualized JSON POSGs (Section 4).
Through these contributions, this paper addresses one central question: is a mechanically valid
world model also a faithful one? Section 6 reports our lane-by-lane empirical results, and Section 7
discusses what they mean for safe-by-design AI.
2 Related Work
Safe-by-Design AI and EmpowermentA line of work aims to keep AI systems safe by preserving
human choices rather than telling AI agents what to do. Methods like attainable-utility preservation
[10] and reachability-based side-effect penalties [2] quantify this from the agent’s own perspective
rather than measuring human capability. In contrast, empowerment-based goals aim to preserve or
increase the human’s capability to influence outcomes. Recent research formalises a fair, risk- and
inequality-averse aggregate of human power as a formal AI objective Heitzig and Potham[5]. All
these methods rely on a clear state–action–state framework: computing reversibility, reachability,
or power presupposes a world model that already contains the relevant stakeholders, options, and
consequences. This makes world model quality a safety concern rather than a modelling convenience,
and what our evaluation is designed to check.
LLMs for Environment Synthesis and Code GenerationLLMs have been used to synthesize
environments and domain-specific programs, including generating grid worlds, task specifications,
and planning-language descriptions [11–13]. Dainese et al. [9] generated code-world models (Python
implementations of an environment’s dynamics) for model-based reinforcement learning, arguing
that calling code at planning time yields greater precision, interpretability, and efficiency. Related
work builds world models by writing and refining code [ 14], or uses the LLM itself as the world
model during planning [ 15].Cao et al. [8] survey the broader LLM planning literature, categorizing
methods into external-module-augmented, finetuning-based, and search-based approaches. Both
works focus on single-agent settings with access to a ground truth. Our problem setting differs on
both assumptions: we consider a multi-player stochastic game, and in realistic applications there is
no ground-truth world model to validate against, which motivates the evaluation design in Section 4.
World Model EvaluationEvaluating synthesised situational world models draws on mechanical
validity checks (well-formedness, probability normalisation, reachability), structural and graph-based

comparison of state-transition topologies, and LLM-as-a-judge protocols [16]. Existing metrics often
assume the existence of a reference world model, failing to address situations where correctness is
genuinely indeterminate. We combine mechanical, structural, and judgement-based metrics into a
single framework in Section 4.
3 Benchmark and World Model Generation
To test whether validity implies faithfulness, we need situations that differ in how much reference
information exists, and a fixed formal target for the LLM to produce.
Partially Observable Stochastic Games (POSG)A POSG [ 17] is a tuple M=⟨N,S,A=
{Ai}i∈N,P,O={O i}i∈N,Ω⟩ , whereN is a player set (humans and/or AI systems),S is the set
of (potentially hidden) states,Ai is the action space for playeri,P(s′|s,a) defines state transition
probabilities given joint actiona={a i}i∈N , and Ω :S×A×S→O is a (deterministic) observation
function representing what every player will actually observe after a transition.
Assumed ArchitectureOur framework assumes a modular, neutral baseline architecture decoupling
perception, world model, and decision making:
1.Perception / Prompt Input: The natural-language scenario or situation description.
2. Situational World Model (here: generated by an LLM): A neutral, predictive resource
representing valid state-space transitions without embedded agent biases.
3. Planner / Decision Engine: The downstream decision algorithm executing policy searches
over the synthesized world model (e.g. some form of dynamic programming or model-based
reinforcement learning).
Output FormatsWorld models are formalized as POSGs encoded either as explicit JSON structures
listing individual transitions obeying a prescribed schema (for small state spaces), or as executable
Python classes generating transitions programmatically, extending a prescribed Abstract Base Class
(for more complex environments).
3
title: Evaluating LLM-Generated World Models for Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning

text:
Alternative RepresentationsWhile POSGs make dynamics explicit, logic-based formalisms like
ATL or Strategy Logic offer model-checked alternatives [18, 19]. Concurrent game structures com-
plement POSGs by specifying properties a planner relies on. Our evaluation extends naturally: Lane 1
checks well-formedness of formulas/Kripke structures, Lane 2a compares models via probabilistic
bisimulation [20], and Lane 3 evaluates logical specifications directly on the model.
Benchmark SuiteTo evaluate world model synthesis, we construct a specialized benchmark suite that
prioritizes structural diversity, domain coverage, and distinct multi-player trade-offs over brute-force
data volume. Rather than inflating dataset size through trivial parameter variations, each scenario
introduces a unique combination of partial observability, state-space topology, non-zero-sum payoff
structure, and safety-critical choices.
The dataset has four domain tiers: (1) 10toy environmentswith tightly specified mechanics; (2)
9 simplegameswith known rules and reference structure; (3) 11situationalscenarios involving
asymmetric stakeholders, resources, or consequences; and (4) 14culturally contextualizedscenarios
in which relevant structure or norms may be underspecified.
We focus on qualitative variations rather than repetitive scaling, to help establish whether LLMs can
generalize across distinct behavioral landscapes. The four tiers are robotics-relevant abstractions rather
than physical robot deployments: toy environments isolate elementary action preconditions, state
changes, and terminal conditions; games isolate controlled multi-agent coordination and stochastic
consequences; situational cases represent decision-support settings involving scarce resources, safety
trade-offs, or authority boundaries; and cultural cases test whether an assistive system preserves
uncertainty and defers norm-relevant decisions to the affected people or institutions.
Scenarios within the cultural tier present ambiguous social hierarchies where appropriate actions
depend heavily on localized norms rather than universal safety constraints. These cases test whether
generated world models introduce culturally specific assumptions unsupported by the scenario
description, a failure mode documented for LLMs more broadly [ 21–23]. The suite also includes
scenarios in which an available action can irreversibly remove future options for one or more players,
enabling direct evaluation of whether generated world models preserve safety-relevant distinctions in
reachability and reversibility.
World Model Generation PipelineWe provide either the prescribed JSON schema or Python
AbstractPOSG interface in the generation prompt and require the generated world model to represent
players, states, possible actions, dynamics, and observations through that interface. Full representation
contracts and implementation-level validation rules are provided in the appendix.
Prompt variants impose progressively stronger, task-independent representation constraints, including
interface compliance, valid transition distributions, consistency between states and actions, and
preservation of the decision horizon described by the scenario. Generated world models are evaluated
as produced: unsupported invention, omission of relevant structure, and semantic inconsistencies are
treated as evaluation outcomes rather than silently repaired during post-processing.
4 Evaluation Framework
A generated world model can fail at three levels: it may not run, it may run but have the wrong
structure, or it may have plausible structure but misrepresent the situation. Each level needs a different
check, so we evaluate in three lanes that move from executability to structure to meaning.
Lane 1: Python World Model Correctness (Mechanical Verification)Direct programmatic
testing evaluating whether generated JSON/code produces a mathematically sound world model:
•State/Action Coverage:N generated/Nexpected and valid state-action pairing counts.
•Transition Normalization: Verifying transition probabilities sum to unity.
• Reachability and Dead-State Rate: Identify unreachable states, invalid actions, and cycles.
Lane 2a: Reference-Based Structural Agreement. Where a reference world model exists, we
compare the generated POSG against it. Equivalent world models may order or name their elements
differently, so players, states and actions are aligned before comparison, and both models are unrolled
to a fixed horizon to keep the comparison finite. We report coverage (the share of reference structure
4
title: Evaluating LLM-Generated World Models for Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning

text:
the candidate reproduces), precision (the share of candidate structure the reference justifies), and
their harmonic mean as an F1. Section 5 gives the implementation. Bounded unrolling keeps the
comparison finite but can miss divergences that appear beyond the horizon (Section 7).
Lane 2b: Reference-Free Structural Diagnostics. We roll out each executable POSG into a state-
transition graph and analyze its structure by examiningbranching and degree profiles,reachability
and strongly connected components, andtransition entropy. Because atypical topology can
still be valid and plausible topology can be semantically incorrect, we do not treat graph structure
alone as evidence of world model correctness.Lane 2brequires no reference and therefore cannot
establish that a generated world model is wrong; it describes shape. Where a reference exists,Lane
2ameasures agreement against it.
Lane 3: LLM-as-a-Judge and Human-in-the-Loop Semantic ReviewFor scenarios without a
unique reference world model, our protocol uses feature-level human annotations. Working only
from the scenario text, annotators label scenario-relevant features asmust include,plausible, ormust
not include, so that omission and unsupported invention are penalised separately while legitimate
variation between valid representations is not. An LLM judge thenflags(but does notscore)
candidate omissions and unsupported additions with supporting evidence. The human annotations are
the reference, both for the generated world model and for the judge’s own flag precision and recall. In
this paper, Lane 3 results come only from predefined programmatic checks. The human-annotation
protocol (Appendix C) is specified but not yet run, so all Lane 3 and bias results reported here are
diagnostic and preliminary.
5 Experimental Setup
We apply these lanes to five LLMs across three tracks that differ in how much reference information
is available: authored references for games, criteria-derived references for situational scenarios, and
paired prompt conditions for cultural scenarios.
LLMs.We evaluate five LLMs: GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 5, Llama 3.3 70B Instruct, Qwen 3.8 27B,
and DeepSeek V4 Flash. We use three evaluation tracks: controlled games, situational scenarios, and
cultural scenarios. Unless stated otherwise, we report first-pass generations only; repair attempts are
logged and analyzed separately.
Game track.The game track contains nine controlled games (G1–G9), each with an authored
reference POSG. We issue three separate requests per LLM–game pair using an identical prompt,
verified by matching SHA-256 hashes across runs, yielding 27 outputs per LLM and 135 overall.
Requests used temperature 0, a 16,384-token output budget, and reasoning disabled. Hosted providers
do not guarantee deterministic decoding at temperature 0, so repeated requests can differ. Reference
POSGs let us evaluate both mechanical validity and structural fidelity.
Situational track.The situational track comprises 11 open-ended scenarios (S1–S11), with up
to three generations per LLM-scenario pair. Because these scenarios admit multiple reasonable
formalizations, reference-based structural and semantic scores are treated as diagnostic rather than as
unique ground-truth measures.
Cultural track.The cultural track contains 14 scenarios (C1–C14) and 140 generated world
models. Each scenario is evaluated under two prompt conditions: an anonymized description and a
version explicitly naming the country. We use temperature 0.7 and generate one output per LLM–
scenario–condition combination. Evaluation records whether outputs can be parsed directly or require
documented recovery, together with mechanical, structural, and semantic diagnostics.
Evaluation protocol.We evaluate generated world models along three lanes. Lane 1 measures
mechanical validity: whether the generated world model can be executed and whether its states,
actions, transitions, probabilities, references, reachable outcomes, and terminal states are internally
consistent. Passing Lane 1 establishes formal well-formedness, but not structural or semantic fidelity.
Three mechanical checks in this paper: Validate (the in-pipeline contract check applied at generation
time), Probe (an exhaustive sweep over reachable state–action pairs), and Lane 1, a later and stricter
post-hoc audit. Lane 1 is the gate reported for all three tracks, so the game (134/135), situational
(104/135) and cultural (125/140) figures are the same measurement.

content.
6 Results
We report results in the order of the lanes: whether the world models run, whether their structure
matches the reference, whether they capture the situation, and whether a location label changes them.
Mechanical validity is high, but the gap between LLMs opens in open-ended tracks.Table 1
summarizes all 410 first-pass candidates. In the game track, 124/135 (91.85%) are contract-valid
on the first attempt and 134/135 pass the stricter post-hoc Lane-1 audit (Table 3), the only failure
is DeepSeek on G9. The situational track is harder: 104/135 pass Lane 1, with Claude Opus 5 and
GPT-5.6 Sol at 27/27 and the other three LLMs at 16–17/27 (Table 4). In the cultural track, 125/140
pass Lane 1, but strict parsing alone succeeds for only 98/140; the rest need documented recovery
of code fences and braces. On controlled games every LLM produces runnable world models, the
difference between LLMs appears only when the situation is open-ended. The rest of this section
asks whether these valid models are also faithful.
Valid world models are rarely structurally exact, and the main error is added structure.Among
the 134 Lane-1-valid game candidates, mean permutation-invariant F1 is 0.366 and the median is
0.178 (IQR 0.126–0.740), only 28 match the reference exactly (Table 2). Coverage exceeds precision
for every LLM, so the LLMs mostly add structure rather than miss it. Claude Opus 5 shows this most

clearly: all 27 of its artifacts are valid, yet its mean precision is 0.142 and its mean F1 0.171, the
lowest in the panel. Figure 2 shows why. On G6 it invents bid levels that the case explicitly excludes

The case matters more than the LLM.Agreement varies more across games than across LLMs.
G2 and G9 have the lowest mean F1 (0.095 and 0.127) and G4 and G7 the highest (0.634 and 0.610;
Table 5). When five independently prompted LLMs all diverge on the same game, the likely cause is
that the situation admits several reasonable formalizations, not a weakness of one model. Simple
reference complexity does not explain this: of six reference metrics, only the fraction of stochastic
transitions correlates with F1 (ρ=−.677 ,p=.045 ), which with nine games is a hypothesis rather
than a finding. Repeated requests add further variation. With identical prompts at temperature 0,
within-pair F1 still varies (mean SD 0.168), and only 4 of 45 LLM–game pairs match the reference in

measure different things: a world model can include every expected element and still have a different
transition structure. The checks show that the predefined criteria fired as recorded, not that they
agree with human judgment. All semantic and bias results are therefore diagnostic, and firmer claims
require the human-annotation protocol in Appendix C.
A location label changes structure, not semantic scores.Naming the country changes mean
semantic scores by at most−0.019 (Qwen), within what one sample per cell can support. It lowers
structural F1 for four of the five LLMs, by up to−0.144 for Qwen (Table 12). A semantic checklist
alone would miss this effect. Two cases show what the structural change looks like; in each, we
changed only the country name. In C9 under Saudi Arabia, Qwen generates 5 terminal states and GPT
only 2 (Figure 1). In C13, Llama produces a short 8-state world with a 2-step path from evidence to
action under India, and a 16-state chain under USA (Native American). Removing the country name
made some world models more cautious and others more permissive. No LLM wrote a stereotype
word, but every LLM changed the world model with the label. This matters because reachability,
reversibility and empowerment are computed on the world model, so if the reachable outcomes shift
with a label, those quantities shift too. Whether these changes are unjustified is not yet established;
Appendix C gives the full cases and the annotation step required before calling them bias.
7 Discussion and Conclusion
Validity is not faithfulness.We asked whether a mechanically valid world model is also a faithful
one. Across 410 first-pass candidates, the answer is no: 134/135 game models pass the mechanical
audit, but only 28 match the reference exactly and mean structural F1 is 0.366. The errors are not
random. On games, LLMs add structure the situation does not support; on open-ended situations,
most omit expected structure. Which game is modeled to predict agreement better than which LLM
is used? This suggests the hard part is choosing a formalization, not producing valid code.
Implications for safe-by-design AI.Reachability, reversibility, and empowerment are computed
on the world model, not on the situation. An invented bid level, a missing stakeholder, or a terminal
outcome that appears only under one country label therefore changes the safety quantity itself, and a
correct planner cannot compensate for it. No single check is enough: mechanical checks pass almost
everything, and semantic checklists barely move when the structure changes; only the structural lane
exposes the difference. Generated world models should be evaluated on all three lanes before they
are used for safety reasoning.
LimitationsThe benchmark is small and hand-crafted by design, so our results are descriptive and not
population-level estimates of LLM performance. The cases are symbolic, discrete POSGs rather than
continuous physical systems. Structural comparison stops at depth three and can miss divergences
that appear later; it also penalizes valid differences in granularity (Appendix B). Each LLM–case pair
has three generations, and each cultural condition one sample; game-track repeats measure provider
variability, not prompt sensitivity. Human validation of Lane 3 is not complete, so semantic and
bias results are diagnostic. We do not measure the effect on downstream planning, empowerment or
reversibility.
Future workNext steps are to run the human-annotation protocol (Appendix C), compare models
up to bisimulation rather than a fixed depth, and evaluate the policies planned on generated world
models.

B.1 Toy Track (T1.1–T4.4, JSON Track)
The toy track tests the evaluator rather than LLM-generated world models. Its hand-authored POSGs
serve as unit-test environments for elementary robotics-relevant modelling requirements: valid action
preconditions, state transitions, branching consequences, and terminal conditions. A well-behaved
evaluation pipeline should therefore award near-perfect scores.
The three exceptions are instructive. T2.2 scores the lowest combined F1 (0.68) yet a precision of
0.94: the candidate misses almost nothing; it simply branches further than the reference. We observe
the same coverage-driven pattern on T2.1 and T3.2. This is the granularity ambiguity of Section 5
materialized in a setting where ground truth is unambiguous. We conclude that the evaluator penalizes
finer modelling even when no reference structure is lost and that this coverage–precision asymmetry,
not noise, is what dominates the LLM-generated tracks.
Figure 6: Lane-2a combined F1 across the toy-track cases. Structural agreement is exact on eight of
ten cases and degrades only where candidates branch more finely than the reference, with coverage
rather than precision accounting for the loss.

Repair handling.Repair rounds were retained only as diagnostic artifacts: the configuration allowed

Provenance.Each run directory preserves the request configuration, exact prompt, raw response,

Mechanical validity saturates in the game track; structural agreement does not. That contrast is the
paper’s thesis, and the per-case matrix in Table 9 is where it becomes visible. We evaluate 135
candidates and find that 134 pass the mechanical audit and all 135 pass the checklist; the single
Lane-1 failure belongs to DeepSeek on G9. Per-LLM aggregates are in Table 8 and Figure 7.
Structure behaves differently, and three findings emerge from the full matrix. First, case identity
drives structural agreement more than LLM identity: the within-LLM spread across cases (GPT-5.6
alone spans 0.21 to 1.00) dwarfs the between-LLM spread on any single case (see Table 9). Second,
G2 and G6 depress every LLM simultaneously (0.10–0.36 and 0.11–0.74). When five independently
prompted LLMs fail on the same fixture, the failure most plausibly reflects reference stochasticity or
terminal-state layout rather than any LLM-specific weakness. Third, the LLMs separate even where
coverage does not: Claude Opus 5 holds the second-highest coverage (0.91) yet the lowest combined
F1 (0.52), meaning its candidates recover most reference transitions but systematically add structure
the reference lacks (Figure 7).
Finally, the bias gate never fires. All 135 candidates defer norm-relevant decisions to game-defined
authorities. We report this as pipeline behavior, not as evidence about LLM safety.

C.1 C9 – Saudi Arabia (Gender-Norm Sensitivity)
A hospitality robot must seat a corporate dinner in Riyadh; the host requests mixed-gender seating,
while a staff member privately reports that the venue prefers separation. The stereotype sits in the
country label: an LLM can infer a segregation norm from “Riyadh” and apply it against the host’s
stated preference. A faithful world model should hold the conflict open rather than resolve it from the
country name alone.
Observation 1.GPT-5.6 produces a tidy 8-state world with two terminals under the Saudi Arabia
label, but when the location is removed, its world restructures dramatically: the terminals become
human_hr_review and structured_inquiry, and the robot’s action set shrinks. The country label made
GPT more decisive, not less.
Observation 2.Under the no-location condition, Llama 3.3 generates a world where the robot can
reach complaint_dismissed as a terminal outcome, something none of its located worlds permit. The
location label constrained Llama’s action space; removing it opened a punitive path.

C.2 C13 – USA (Workplace Power / Gender Politics)
An HR-support robot receives an anonymous, evidence-free complaint naming a manager. The HR
process unambiguously owns the decision, so the discriminating question reduces to one: does the
robot insert itself into the resolution?
It does not. Every LLM routes the complaint into an inquiry and stops. But the LLMs separate on
how much of the process they preserve: some collapse to a single terminal state, while one world
model preserves three genuinely opposing terminals, including the dangerous one, “action taken on
unverified claim”.

Observation 1.In Crowded India, Llama 3.3 generates a short 8-state world where the robot can
move directly from evidence_analyzed to take_action, a 2-step path from evidence to punishment. In
the USA (Native American) world, the same complaint requires a 16-state chain. Same unverified
claim: the location decided how much due process exists before punishment.
Observation 2.GPT-5.6 produces structurally similar worlds for USA original, USA (Native
American), and Crowded India. But removing the location label entirely triggers an EXTREME
restructure: the terminals change and the robot loses the initiate_inquiry action. GPT needs the
cultural anchor to commit to a process.
Observation 3.Qwen 3.8 generates its largest world (30 states) under the China (mixed religion) la-
bel, with branches like record_documented_material vs no_material, inventing an evidence-sufficiency
check that no other LLM uses. In the USA (Native American) world, the robot never acts at all.
Across the C9 and C13 conditions, 15 (model, location) pairs reach the EXTREME level, meaning
the set of reachable terminal outcomes differs. Every LLM shows at least one.
Summary.In C13, Llama gives a 2-step path to action under India and a 16-state chain under USA
(Native American). Across both cases and all five LLMs, the robot never awards itself normative
authority. But the location label systematically restructures the world model’s action space, process
length, and terminal outcomes. No LLM wrote a stereotype word, but every LLM changed the rules
of the world with the label: the actions the robot may take, the process it must respect, the endings it
can reach, and how much agency it keeps.
If confirmed as bias, it is bias at the level of consequence, and it matters beyond this benchmark. As
noted in Section 2, computing reversibility, reachability, or human power presupposes a world model

text:
that already contains the relevant stakeholders, options and consequences. If the set of reachable
terminal outcomes shifts with a country label, any empowerment or reversibility quantity computed
on the generated world model shifts with it. The bias does not stay in the representation. It propagates
into the safety quantity the world model was built to support.
C.3 Validation status and next step.
The consequence levels in Table 15 were assigned manually by one author. They are a qualitative
reading of what changed between worlds, not a computed metric. Establishing that any of these
differences constitutes bias requires a separate step, which we specify here and have not yet run.
Each differing pair is presented to at least two annotators with the location labels removed, so that
the annotator sees only the two world models and the scenario. The annotator labels each difference
as justified by the scenario, unjustified, or ambiguous. Agreement is measured with Cohen’sκ, and
pairs where annotators disagree are adjudicated by a third. Only differences rated unjustified by
agreeing annotators are reported as bias. Until that is complete, the findings in this appendix are
diagnostic: they establish that the location label changes the generated world model, not that the
change is unwarranted.

NeurIPS Paper Checklist
1.Claims
Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the
paper’s contributions and scope?

Justification: The abstract and Introduction state the scope of the work as generating and
evaluating LLM produced situational world models represented as stochastic games, and
describe the benchmark, generation pipeline, and multi-lane evaluation framework.
2.Limitations
Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors?
Answer: [Yes]
Justification: We clarify experimental validation is ongoing.
3.Theory assumptions and proofs
Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and
a complete (and correct) proof?
Answer: [N/A]
Justification: The paper does not introduce new theoretical results, theorems, or proofs.
Formal definitions are used only to specify the stochastic-game representation and evaluation
setting.
4.Experimental result reproducibility
Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main ex-
perimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions
of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)?
Answer: [Yes]
Justification: The paper and supplementary material specify the evaluated models, prompts,
test cases, validation procedure, and evaluation methodology. Code, prompts, generated
outputs, and experiment configurations are provided to enable replication of the reported
results.

Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instruc-
tions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental
material?

and evaluation pipeline.

rameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results?

fies the benchmark cases, model identities, prompt conditions, temperatures, genera-
tion counts, and first-pass/repair policy. The appendix and released repository pro-
vide the preserved prompts, per-run records, raw outputs, evaluation artifacts, and
experiments/openrouter_game_study/config.yaml. No model training, optimizer,
or train/test split is used: the study evaluates prompted hosted LLM outputs.

information about the statistical significance of the experiments?

text:
QUANTIFYING THE SAMPLING FREQUENCY INV ARIANCE OF TIME-SERIES
FOUNDATION MODELS FOR SENSOR DATA APPLICATIONS
Sourish Gunesh Dhekane2, Abinaya Kumar1, Torsten Woertwein1,
Yan-Bo Lin1, Thomas Ploetz2, Shabnam Ghaffarzadegan1
1Bosch Research, USA - Bosch Center for Artificial Intelligence
2School of Interactive Computing, Georgia Institute of Technology, USA
ABSTRACT
Time-Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) are increasingly used in
sensor applications, where sampling frequency (SF) varies across
sensors, devices, and operating modes (e.g., power saving). Ide-
ally, TSFMs must remain effective during such SF changes, pro-
vided the SF retains task-critical bandwidth. In this paper, we stress-
test 4 prominent TSFMs: MOMENT, Chronos-2, Moirai-MoE, and
TimesFM, to quantify their SF-invariance and investigate whether
their behavior tracks the resulting loss of information bandwidth
rather than the SF value itself. Our stress-test probes 3 dimensions:
(i) the shift in embeddings, (ii) the degradation in forecasting perfor-
mance, and (iii) the degradation in downstream performance, quanti-
fied by three novel metrics: FSI, FDI, and CDI, respectively. To our
knowledge, this is the first study to place SF-invariance at the core of
TSFM evaluations. Our results characterize: (i) how SF-invariance
depends on the margin between signal’s native-SF and the bandwidth
its task requires, (ii) how much of that invariance the choice of TSFM
explains, and (iii) how much of TSFM’s performance degradation
under a lower SF reflects information loss rather than a limitation
of their abilities. These findings reframe SF-invariance as a measur-
able, signal-aware property of the (signal×TSFM) pair, and guide
practitioners on when TSFMs display SF-invariance.
Index Terms—Time-Series Foundation Models, Sampling Fre-
quency Invariance, Foundation Model Evaluation
1. INTRODUCTION
TSFMs are increasingly applied to sensor applications ranging from
activity monitoring and healthcare to industrial settings [1, 2], where
heterogeneous sensors and devices operate at different SFs. Even a
single device changes its SF across operating modes to conserve bat-
tery or to optimize bandwidth usage. An ideal TSFM should there-
fore remain effective across all such settings with varying SFs. A pri-
mary obstacle to this is the SF mismatch between TSFM’s pretrain-
ing and the downstream sensor data, as most pretraining benchmarks
span SFs from seconds to years [3]. Consequently, at deployment,
TSFMs can encounter SFs that differ substantially from those seen
in pretraining, yet we have little evidence of how robustly a TSFM
behaves under such unseen SF changes.
However, a behavioral change in TSFMs may sometimes be in-
evitable. By the Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem [4], reducing
the SF removes signal content above the new Nyquist frequency,
so a lower SF entails some information loss, and a model’s behav-
ior is therefore expected to change. What should distinguish a SF-
invariant TSFM is that this change stays proportional to the informa-
tion loss, and that for a downstream task, the performance should be
robust as long as the task-critical information is still retained in the
signal. Also, disproportionate changes (See Figure 1) can make the
Fig. 1: TSFM embeddings on CWRU vibration data remain stable
up to a 40% reduction in SF, but shift sharply between 40% and
50%. In this paper, we study and quantify these behavioral shifts
across TSFM embeddings, forecasts, and downstream performance.
underlying application less robust. While some existing works in the
literature have pointed out these issues [5, 6], a systematic stress test
that isolates the aspect of SF in TSFMs and quantifies their robust-
ness to varying SF is absent from the literature.
In this paper, we perform such a systematic stress test on 4
prominent TSFMs used in the community: MOMENT [7], Chronos-
2 [8], Moirai-MoE [9], and TimesFM [10], on use cases that span
accelerometers, gyroscope, vibration, and ECG sensors. Our stress
test covers 3 dimensions of TSFMs that track a change in: em-
beddings, forecasting performance, and downstream performance,
upon a change in SF. To quantify this change, we propose the met-
rics of Frequency Sensitivity Index (FSI), Forecast Degradation In-
dex (FDI), and Classification Degradation Index (CDI), respectively.
The results of our stress test reveal interesting findings: (i) the 3 di-
mensions do not respond to SF-reduction at the same point: while
the embeddings begin drifting immediately, forecasting and down-
stream performances do not degrade much until the SF approaches
the task-critical bandwidth, (ii) SF-invariance is influenced more by
the gap between native-SF and the information bandwidth critical
for the downstream tasks as compared to the choice of the TSFM
itself, and (iii) however, all TSFMs have scope to improve their SF-
invariance, as their downstream performance drops further than the
information loss accounted for by SF-degradation. Together, these
findings give practitioners a basis for choosing design choices (e.g.,
a sensor’s SF, choice of TSFM, etc.) in their sensor applications and
motivate the community to treat SF-invariance as an integral part of
TSFM evaluation, eventually towards improving it.
2. STRESS TEST DESIGN
We stress-test 4 prominent TSFMs spanning the transformer-based
architecture family (Table 1): encoder-only MOMENT [7] and
Chronos-2 [8], decoder-only TimesFM [10] and Mixture-of-Experts

3. RESULTS
We perform experiments on 3 publicly available datasets. In HHAR
[17] we use accelerometer and gyroscope data from Samsung
(100Hz) and LG (200Hz) watch to perform6-class human activity
recognition. In CWRU bearing [18] we use drive-end vibration data
at12kHz and48kHz SFs to perform fault severity classification. In
MIT-BIH [19] we use pre-segmented beats at125Hz to perform
5-class AAMI arrhythmia beat classification. Since beats are pre-
segmented, Dimension 2 forecasts each beat’s final 32 samples from
its prefix. We anchor our discussion on Table 2 and Fig. 2 results.
3.1. Interesting properties of FSI, FDI, and CDI
FSI is a non-negative and bounded metric in the range[0,∼1.8].
The cosine distance in FSI is measured within TSFM’s own embed-
ding space. Hence, its magnitude is affected by model’s embedding
dimensionality, anisotropy, and multi-channel pooling strategy [20],
making FSI incomparable across TSFMs. Still, FSI remains useful
as it is computationally cheap and label-free. FDI and CDI, on the
other hand, are performance-driven metrics, and hence are compa-
rable across TSFMs. Unlike FSI, FDI is unbounded and observed
to be heavy-tailed (observed values run from−0.011to5.692),
whereas CDI is bounded and carries practical significance for many
downstream tasks. Since FSI is comparable only within a TSFM,
we correlate FSI and CDI per TSFM over the seven settings in Ta-
ble 2. They are strongly correlated for MOMENT, Moirai-MoE,
and TimesFM with Pearsonr= 0.99,0.97, and0.85, respectively.
FDI, in contrast, is observed to be uncorrelated with both FSI and
CDI. Small negative FDI values (e.g., -0.011, TimesFM on Bear-
ing 48 kHz) indicate that band-limiting slightly helps remove high-
frequency content that is difficult to forecast.
3.2. Do the indices track the information the signal loses?
Figure 2a plots per-dimension discrepancy curves (cosine distance
δin row 1, excess nRMSE in row 2, and macro-F 1 drop in row 3)
against the sampling frequency dropρ= 1−K/F, and compares
them with the fraction of spectral information retained by the signal
in terms of retained spectral energy (R) and spectral Jensen-Shannon
similarity (1−JSD). Overall, we observe that these three discrep-
ancy measures do not begin to degrade at the same point. Specifi-
cally, the embedding drift (row 1) responds first and grows smoothly
whileRand1−JSD are still close to 1. On the other hand, fore-
casting and classification degradation (rows 2 and 3) stay negligible
across a wide range ofρand then fall sharply past a threshold, which
aligns with the point at which the retained-information curves start to
collapse. These patterns reveal that each dimension relates to infor-
mation loss in fundamentally different ways. The embedding shift
measures the model’s sensitivity to a change in input, so it responds
early and grows continuously. The downstream indices, however,
behave differently: they remain stable across large SF drops and de-
grade only when the spectral content critical for their task is lost.
3.3. Are TSFMs SF-invariant? How do they compare?
Fig. 2b comparesF tr

should be close to zero. However, in all (TSFM×dataset) config-
urations, we observe a significant transfer gap, which suggests that
there remains scope for TSFMs to be more SF-invariant.
Since FSI is not comparable across TSFMs (see Section 3.1)
and FDI is undefined for MOMENT, we compare TSFMs using CDI
and the transfer gap, the metrics which are the most practically rel-

the smallest transfer gaps on the HHAR gyroscope streams, while

3.4. Can a contrastive alignment head close the transfer gap?
The contrastive SF-alignment head (see Sec. 2.5) improved CDI in
26of the28configurations (see Table 2) by40%on average, with
gains as large as86%. While not necessarily optimal, this demon-
strates that SF-invariance can indeed be improved. However, there
are two caveats to these improvements. First, the mean improve-
ment is smallest for Moirai-MoE (26%), one of the less SF-invariant
models, and largest for TimesFM (46%), one of the most invariant
ones. Second, the head causes some native-SF performance degra-
dation across all TSFMs (Figure 3), revealing a trade-off between
SF-invariance and native performance. The key challenge is thus to
enhance SF-invariance without sacrificing native performance.
3.5. Insights on SF-invariance and practical guidelines
Taken together, our results suggest that SF-invariance is not an in-
trinsic property of TSFMs, and rather is jointly shaped by 3 fac-
tors. The first is how much gap exists between the native-SF and
the signal’s information bandwidth, since this gap influences what
SF-reduction can remove. This is the reason why CWRU dataset’s
two tasks (at 12 and 48 kHz) behave differently (see Table 2), de-
spite a majority of information loss happening∼6kHz in both. The
second is the factors of sensing modality and the downstream task,
which together determine where in the spectrum the discriminative
information lives. This is why, for the same activities, the gyroscope
yields lower CDI than the accelerometer in 6 of 8 (TSFM×SF) pairs,
Chronos-2 being the exception (Table 2). The third is the TSFM
itself, which determines how commensurate its response is to SF-
degradation and information bandwidth removed by it. However,
