These insights guide practitioners in using TSFMs for sensor ap-
plications. First, an estimate of how much SF-degradation the sys-
tem can expect should be made considering cheaper sensors, power
saving, and heterogeneous devices. Then, the native-SF should be
set high enough to provide sufficient margin above the signal’s in-
formation bandwidth to ensure that the expected SF-reduction stays
within the safe range. Second, the choice of TSFM should be driven
mainly by task and engineering constraints (compute availability,
model size, and throughput), because although the 4 TSFMs studied
here differ in their SF-invariance, that difference matters less than
the gap between native-SF and information bandwidth.
4. CONCLUSION & FUTURE WORKS
In this paper, we present, to our knowledge, the first study to place
SF-invariance at the center of TSFM evaluation, quantifying it along
embeddings (FSI), forecasting (FDI), and downstream classification
(CDI) for 4 TSFMs. Our results show that TSFMs are not inher-
ently SF-invariant; however, the invariance is governed more by
the gap between native-SF and task-critical information bandwidth
than the choice of TSFM itself. These findings turn “is this TSFM
SF-invariant?” into a measurable, signal-aware question and guide
practitioners in anticipating when a TSFM will transfer reliably
across SFs. This study can be extended to more TSFMs and sensing
modalities for more robust generalization. Moreover, our analysis
acts as a motivation for training TSFMs to be more SF-invariant.

Abstract
Branch-and-Bound (B&B) andA∗ are popular exact search methods originating from Operations
Research and Artificial Intelligence, respectively. Although the two methods share fundamental
search principles, their different ways of exploring the search space can lead to substantially different
computational performance. We investigate these differences using the Resource-Constrained Project
Scheduling Problem (RCPSP) as an exemplary problem setting. We first establish the relationships
between mixed-integer linear programming, state-action, and timed Petri-net representations. Since
B&Band A∗ admitnumerousalgorithmicenhancements, wefocusonrelativelybasicimplementations.
This allows us to examine the fundamental differences between the methods rather than compare
the performance of state-of-the-art solvers. By using the same lower bound and best-first node
selection, we isolate the effects of the search mechanisms, particularly the identification of equivalent
states reached through different scheduling decision sequences. Experiments on 480 benchmark
RCPSP instances show that graph-basedA∗ substantially outperforms the B&B variants considered.
With additional pruning rules,A∗ proves optimality for all 480 instances, compared with 445 for
best-first B&B under the same time and memory limits. Depth-first B&B uses less memory and can
find feasible solutions even when the search does not finish within the time limit. Stronger linear
programming relaxations reduce the search space but introduce considerable computational overhead.
Our findings highlight the importance of duplicate-state detection and clarify the computational
trade-offs between the search approaches. These insights can help researchers select an appropriate
method and identify opportunities to incorporate effective mechanisms from one approach into the
other.

1 Introduction
The Resource-Constrained Project Scheduling Problem (RCPSP) seeks a schedule that minimizes
project completion time while honoring interdependencies among activities and limits on requested
resources (see, e.g., Artigues et al., 2026, for a recent overview). The problem itself and its extensions
model a common challenge in construction (see, e.g., Zhang et al., 2024), manufacturing (see, e.g.,
Čapek et al., 2012), maintenance (see, e.g., Chen et al., 2024), healthcare (see, e.g., Yousefzadeh and
Harati Motlagh, 2026), software development (see, e.g., Li et al., 2024), and other project-based settings
in which activities that could otherwise run in parallel must compete for scarce resources. Because
even moderately sized instances can be difficult to solve optimally, the RCPSP is important both as a
practical scheduling problem and as a benchmark for exact optimization methods.
Two mature research traditions approach this problem from different perspectives (details are
presented in Section 2). In Operations Research (OR), exact methods commonly explore a tree of
restricted subproblems or partial schedules using Branch-and-Bound (B&B). Lower bounds are used
to eliminate subproblems that cannot improve the best complete schedule found so far. In Artificial

Intelligence (AI), the problem can instead be represented as a state-space graph and solved usingA∗,
which expands states in best-first order according to an admissible evaluation function and merges
equivalent states reached through different decision sequences. At a sufficiently abstract level,A∗ can
be represented within general formulations of B&B (Nau et al., 1984). This theoretical relationship,
however, does not explain how the concrete algorithms used in OR and AI differ when applied to the
same scheduling problem. In practice, B&B in itsordinaryvariant (see, ordinary B&B in Nau et al.,
1984) explores a tree of subsets of feasible solutions implicitly defined by partial schedules, whereas
graph-basedA∗ systematically searches a graph, detecting and merging duplicate states reached through
different decision sequences. B&B may also use the best feasible solution found so far to prune nodes.
Existing comparisons are often affected by differences in problem representation, lower-bound strength,
node-selection strategy, or algorithm-specific enhancements. Consequently, it remains unclear how
much of the observed performance difference is caused by the different search mechanisms themselves.
This study aims to explain the fundamental computational trade-offs between these two widely used
exact-search paradigms and to provide a basis for selecting, improving, or combining them. Its purpose
is therefore not to determine whether a basic implementation of either method outperforms state-of-
the-art RCPSP solvers. Instead, our contributions are threefold. First, we develop a common modeling
foundation for the comparison by presenting mixed-integer linear programming (MILP), state-action,
and timed Petri-net representations of the RCPSP and establishing the relationships between their
schedules, states, and search graphs. Second, we provide a mechanistic and formal comparison of B&B
and A∗ under identical lower-bound information and best-first node selection. The analysis identifies
how duplicate states, pruning, repeated heuristic evaluations, and memory requirements affect the two
searches. Finally, we conduct a controlled empirical study on benchmark RCPSP instances, comparing
computational time, generated and expanded nodes, lower-bound evaluations, and memory use. The
experiments examine how instance characteristics and the search mechanisms influence the relative
performance of the two methods.
The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the relevant literature
and identifies the gap addressed by this study. Section 3 defines the RCPSP and introduces a
running example. Section 4 presents the MILP, state-action, and timed Petri-net representations and
establishes their connections. Section 5 describes the B&B andA∗ algorithms and compares their
search mechanisms. Section 6 reports the empirical study. Finally, Section 7 concludes the paper and
discusses directions for future research.
2 Related Literature
Thissectionreviewsthreerelatedresearchstreams: B&BmethodsfortheRCPSP(Section2.1), heuristic
state-space search for scheduling (Section 2.2), and theoretical studies on the relationship between
B&B andA∗ (Section 2.3). Together, these streams position our comparison of optimization-based
B&B and graph-basedA∗ (Section 2.4).
2.1 Branch-and-Bound Methods for the RCPSP
Exact RCPSP solution approaches in OR have mainly focused on MILP and specialized B&B algorithms.
Early exact approaches were compared by Patterson (1984). Subsequent B&B algorithms introduced
delay alternatives, schedule schemes, memory-efficient enumeration, and constraint propagation (De-
meulemeester and Herroelen, 1992; Brucker et al., 1998; Sprecher, 2000; Dorndorf et al., 2000). Their
performance depends on the branching scheme, lower bounds, dominance rules, node-selection strategy,
and the early discovery of good feasible schedules (Brucker and Knust, 2003; Coelho and Vanhoucke,
2018; Guo et al., 2023). In parallel, MILP formulations range from classical time-indexed models
(Pritsker et al., 1969) to event-based formulations (Koné et al., 2011). Surveys document the continued
development of these approaches (Brucker et al., 1999; Artigues et al., 2026).
In this OR interpretation, B&B is an optimization framework. Each node in the search tree
represents a subset of feasible schedules, encoded either by a partial schedule or by a restricted
optimization subproblem. Branching decisions partition this subset into smaller subsets. A valid lower

dominance rules may remove some of this redundancy.
2.2 State-Space Search for Scheduling
In A∗, nodes are selected according toˆf =g +h, whereg is the cost accumulated so far andh is an
admissible lower bound on the remaining cost (Hart et al., 1968). As originally defined,A∗ performs
graph search: itsOpenandClosedstructures detect when a state is regenerated along a different
path, and only the cheapest path to each state is retained. This mechanism’s effect depends on the
state representation. Ordinary B&B, in contrast, may retain the corresponding decision sequences as
distinct nodes unless a dominance rule detects their equivalence.
Timed Petri nets have long been used to model scheduling problems, including job-shop systems
(Hillion and Proth, 1989), manufacturing systems (Proth and Sauer, 1998; Lee and DiCesare, 1994; Mejía
and Odrey, 2005), and data-driven project planning (Cohen, 2024). Scheduling through reachability-
graph search, particularly usingA∗, is a well-established approach in this literature (Lee and DiCesare,
1994; Huang et al., 2023).
Bell and Park (1990) developed an exactA∗-based algorithm for the RCPSP. Its nodes are subprob-
lems obtained by adding precedence constraints to resolve resource conflicts, so equivalent project states
reached through different repair sequences are never identified. Accordingly, Nazareth et al. (1999) later
interpreted the method as a best-first B&B procedure formulated as anA∗ tree search. More recently,
Lublin et al. (2026) formulated the RCPSP as an optimal search over a Petri-net reachability graph
and showed that graph-basedA∗ can compete with general-purpose MILP solvers. That comparison
demonstrates the potential ofA∗, but it does not isolate the algorithmic differences betweenA∗ and
B&B under identical lower-bound information and search conditions.
2.3 Relationship between B&B andA ∗
Earlier studies related B&B to dynamic programming and state-space representations (Morin and
Marsten, 1976; Ibaraki, 1978), while Kumar and Kanal (1983) proposed a broad B&B formulation
for AND/OR-tree search. Nau et al. (1984) introducedGeneral Branch and Bound(GBB), defined
through abstract representation, goal, selection, splitting, and pruning functions. These functions
are deliberately general enough for both ordinary B&B andA∗ to be represented as special cases.
We argue that this common abstraction should not be interpreted as showing that graph-basedA∗
and ordinary optimization B&B are the same practical algorithm. In the terminology of Nau et al.
(1984), ordinary B&B selects one active subproblem at a time and prunes using a lower bound and
an upper bound which is given by the best solution found so far.A∗ is embedded in GBB through a
different choice of representations, selection rules, and pruning functions. Similarly, Labat and Pomerol
(2003) concluded that heuristic search and B&B apply the same principles and differ mainly at the
interpretation level within an abstract view of B&B. Thus, the AI literature compares the methods
within a highly general search abstraction, rather than comparing the concrete optimization-based
B&B used in RCPSP research with graph-basedA∗.
2.4 Research Gap
Taken together, the existing literature does not provide a controlled, practical comparison of the two
introduced search paradigms for the RCPSP. An admissibleA∗ heuristic and a B&B lower bound serve
the same mathematical purpose and may be computed from the same relaxation. Therefore, differences
in bound strength should be controlled when comparing the methods. To the best of our knowledge,
no study compares ordinary OR-style B&B and graph-basedA∗ on identical RCPSP instances while
holding the lower-bound function and node-selection conditions fixed. This paper addresses that gap

3 The Resource-Constrained Project Scheduling Problem
A project consists of activities that must be executed subject to precedence relations and limited
resources. In the RCPSP, the goal is to choose activity start times that minimize the makespan while
satisfying all precedence and resource constraints. This section gives the formal problem definition
(Section 3.1) and introduces the running example (Section 3.2) used throughout the paper.

4 Problem Representations
The RCPSP can be modeled from several computational perspectives. A MILP formulation (Section 4.1)
represents complete schedules through decision variables and supports ordinary OR-style B&B. A
state-action formulation (Section 4.2) represents scheduling as transitions between timed system states
and supports graph-search methods such asA∗. A Petri-net formulation (Section 4.3) provides an
explicit token-based model of precedence, timing, and renewable-resource availability, whose timed
reachability graph is equivalent to the state graph. This section introduces the three formulations and
formalizes their relationships (Section 4.4).
4.1 Mixed-Integer Linear Programming Formulation
The RCPSP can be formulated as a MILP by introducing binary decision variables that encode the
scheduling decisions. Several MILP formulations exist in the literature; here we present a standard
time-indexed formulation.

4.3 Petri Net Representation
A Petri net can be viewed as a directed bipartite graph with two types of nodes: places and transitions.
Petri nets provide a formal mathematical framework for modeling concurrent systems, capturing
synchronization, precedence relations, and shared resources (Murata, 1989). We use them to model
concurrent project activities and resource availability, and to establish a formal correspondence between
their timed reachability graph and the state graph used byA∗. Places represent conditions, intermediate
project states, or available resources. Transitions represent activities or events. Directed arcs connect
only places to transitions or transitions to places. Therefore, there are no direct arcs between two
places or between two transitions. A token is a marker residing in a place, and the distribution of
tokens over the places represents the current state of the system. The movement of tokens through
the net naturally represents synchronization and parallelism among activities. Petri nets can also

4.4 Mapping between Representations
The three representations, MILP, state-action, and Petri net, describe the same underlying RCPSP
from different viewpoints. The MILP formulation encodes complete schedules, whereas the state-action
and Petri-net representations encode intermediate execution states and their transitions. In particular,
the state-action representation records explicitly which activities are completed, ongoing, or not yet
started, while the Petri-net representation records the same information implicitly through timed
control-flow and resource tokens.
4.4.1 Mapping between State-Action and Petri Net Representations
For the RCPSP-inducedTTPNR considered in this paper, the reachability graphRG = (SRG,ERG)
of Section 4.3.2 is already defined atdecision states. Each node is a timed state represented by a timed
marking and the current system time, and each outgoing edge corresponds to choosing one activity to
start next, with the clock advancing by the smallest amount needed to make the required control-flow
and resource tokens available. Therefore, the Petri-net reachability graph and the state graph use the
same transition granularity, differing only in how states are represented.

5 Solution Approaches
In this section, we describe the two exact solution methods B&B (Section 5.1) andA∗ (Section 5.2)
and provide a structural comparison of the two approaches (Section 5.3). We first present each method
in a generic form and then specialize it to the RCPSP. Both methods use lower bounds on the best
achievable project completion time to guide their search. For the baseline comparison, we use the same
critical-path lower bound and best-first (BF) node-selection rule for both methods. This design controls
for the common lower bound and search order while retaining the algorithm-specific mechanisms that

5.1 Branch-and-Bound
In the field of OR, B&B is an exact solution framework for combinatorial optimization problems that
systematically explores the solution space while avoiding exhaustive enumeration. In the context of
the RCPSP, it is naturally applied to the MILP representation and corresponding partial schedules.
Within B&B, the explored solutions can be represented by a rooted search tree, in which the
root nodeN0 corresponds to the optimization problem to be solved, i.e., its objective function and
constraints. Each other nodeNj of the B&B search tree is implicitly defined by the objective function
of the problem to be solved and the constraints of the problem corresponding to its parent nodeNi, as
well as an additional attribute (usually a constraint) that every solution to the problem atNj must
satisfy, whereas this need not be the case for all solutions to the problem atNi. A path in the search
tree from the root nodeN0 to a leaf node thus corresponds to the initial problem inN0, successively
extended by the constraints added along the branches of this path. Consequently, the set of feasible
solutions can only shrink from a nodeNi to its childNj, while the best achievable objective value
of the corresponding subproblem cannot improve. Hence, B&B relies on partitioning the solution
space (branching) and eliminating problems (nodes) that cannot lead to an optimal solution (bounding
and pruning). The overall search is typically guided by strategies for selecting the next node to be
evaluated.
Since the best achievable objective value of a node is hard to calculate in general, bounds are
computed at the nodes of the search tree. First, a global upper bound is the objective value of a
feasible solution of the problem inN0, which may be improved several times during the search as
new, better feasible solutions ofN0 are found. Second, a local lower bound of the problem inNi is
computed at each nodeNi, i.e., a value not exceeding the best-possible objective function value that
any feasible solution inNi can achieve. The computation of this bound can, for example, be performed
by solving a relaxed (simplified) version of the optimization problem considered inNi that can be
solved efficiently. If this bound indicates that no better solution can be found within the corresponding
subtree originating inNi, the node is discarded (pruned, fathomed).
5.1.1 Generic Framework for Minimization Problems
Consider a combinatorial optimization problemminx∈XF (x)with the set of feasible solutionsX and
objective functionF :X→R . Assume thatX is too large to be enumerated explicitly, so that it is
systematically explored by means of B&B. The root nodeN0 represents the original problem. The
remaining nodesNi are associated with subsetsX (Ni)⊆X of feasible solutions. Hence, the branching
of a nodeNi corresponds to partitioningX (Ni)into smaller disjoint subsetsX (Ni) =⋃k
j=i+1X (Nj),
where Ni+1,...,N k are the child nodes ofNi. This partitioning is typically induced by fixing decision
variables or imposing additional constraints.
The algorithm maintains a global upper bound¯F, which corresponds to the objective value of the
best feasible solution of the original problem found so far. Additionally, for each nodeNi, a lower
bound F(Ni)≤min x∈X(Ni)F (x)on the objective value of all solutions inX (Ni)is computed. The
quality of these bounds affects the efficiency of the algorithm.
A nodeNi is pruned if one of the following conditions holds:
•F (Ni)≥ ¯F, since no solution inX(Ni)can improve the current best solution.
•X(N i) =∅, i.e., the subproblem atNi is infeasible.

The order in which nodes are explored is determined by a search strategy. Common strategies
include DF search and BF search. DF search completely explores a single branch before backtracking.
It aims at quickly determining feasible solutions, and thus global upper bounds, to the original problem.
BF search, in contrast, selects the next node to be explored based on the lower bounds of the not yet
fathomed (active) nodes.

In summary, a generic version of B&B can be described as follows:
1. Initialize the set of active nodes with the root node (corresponding to the original problem).
2. Set ¯F:= +∞, or ¯F:=F(x 0)if a feasible solutionx 0 is known in advance.
3. While there are active nodes:
(a) Select a nodeNi according to the search strategy.
(b) Compute F(Ni), e.g., by considering and solving a relaxed version of the problem inNi.
(c) If F(Ni)≥ ¯F or if the problem inNi has no feasible solution, pruneNi, i.e., deleteNi from
the set of active nodes, and continue.
(d) Else, if the solutionxi of the relaxed version of the problem inNi is feasible for the original
problem, set ¯F←min{ ¯F,F (xi)}, potentially update the best solution toxi, pruneNi and
continue.
(e) Otherwise, branch onNi, i.e., delete it from the set of active nodes and add its children to
the set of active nodes.
The correctness of this generic version of B&B follows from the fact that only nodes that cannot
contain better solutions than the currently best known solution are pruned. Therefore, an optimal
solution is never discarded if no optimal solution is yet known. The efficiency of the method critically
depends on the strength of the bounds, the effectiveness of the branching scheme and the search
strategy. In the worst case, the algorithm may still explore the entire search space. However, in
practice, strong bounds and good branching rules can lead to substantial reductions in computational
effort.

5.2A ∗ Search
A∗ is a well-known BF graph-search algorithm for finding a minimum-cost path from an initial state to
a goal state (Hart et al., 1968). We first describe the genericA∗ framework and then specialize it to
the RCPSP state graph defined in Section 4.2.
5.2.1 Generic Framework
Consider a directed state-space graph with an initial state, a set of goal states, and nonnegative
transition costs. For each generated states, A∗ uses the evaluation functionˆf(s) =g(s) +h(s), where
g(s)is the cost of the best path currently known from the initial state tos, andh(s)estimates the
minimum remaining cost froms to a goal state. The heuristich is admissible if it never overestimates
this remaining cost. If, in addition,h is consistent, the standard graph-search version ofA∗ guarantees
that the first goal state selected for expansion lies on an optimal path.
A∗ maintains two sets:Open, containing generated states that are candidates for expansion, and
Closed, containing states that have already been expanded. Initially, the initial state is inserted into
Open. At each iteration,A∗ selects a state fromOpenwith minimum ˆf-value. Ties may be resolved
using a secondary rule, such as preferring the state with the largerg-value.
The selected state is expanded by generating its successor states, i.e., the states reachable through
its outgoing edges. A newly generated state is inserted intoOpen; if the same state has already been

5.2.2A ∗ for the RCPSP
We now apply this generic framework to the RCPSP state graphG defined in Section 4.2. Its initial
state iss0, its goal states are the states inSf, and each edge corresponds to selecting one activity to be

For the RCPSP, the evaluation function is thereforeˆf(s) =g(s) +h(s), whereh(s)is an admissible
lower bound on the remaining time to project completion. When a scheduling decision is made, time
advances to the earliest moment at which the selected activity can begin, namely when its precedence
and resource requirements are satisfied. We use the same tie-breaking rule as for B&B: among states
with equal ˆf-values, we select the state with the largestg-value and remaining ties are resolved by

provides an admissible lower bound on the remaining time to project completion. We also consider
the two pruning refinements introduced at the end of Section 5.1: lexicographic pruning of alternative
orderings of activities starting at the same time, and active-schedule pruning of scheduling decisions
that could have been made earlier without delaying previously scheduled activities.

5.3 Structural Comparison of Branch-and-Bound andA∗
Although B&B andA∗ both systematically explore alternative scheduling decisions using lower bounds
to guide the search, they differ in several fundamental respects. In this section, we identify the key
structural differences and discuss their implications for solving the RCPSP. The results are summarized
in Table 1.
The B&B algorithm searches a tree whose nodes are generated by sequences of scheduling decisions,
whereasA∗ searches a graph of timed project states. Every B&B node induces a timed state containing
the information required to determine the remaining feasible scheduling decisions. Different branches of
the B&B tree may induce the same timed state and therefore represent the same remaining scheduling
problem. Tree-based B&B retains such branches as separate nodes. For example, the decision sequences
⟨0,a,c⟩ and⟨0,c,a⟩ generate different paths in the B&B tree, although they may result in the same
scheduled activities, current time, ongoing activities, and resource availability. Graph-basedA∗, in
contrast, identifies nodes by their timed-state representation. When a generated successor is already
present inOpenorClosed, it is recognized as a duplicate and is not retained as a separate search

merging nodes that induce the same timed project state. Consequently, under otherwise identical
search conditions, tree-based B&B may generate and evaluate the same remaining scheduling problem
several times, whereas graph-basedA∗ represents it once. The potential redundancy increases with
project concurrency, because independent activities can be selected in many different orders while
leading to the same timed state.
We now turn our attention to the bounding mechanisms of the algorithms. In their RCPSP
specializations, both methods use the same evaluationˆf =g +h, but they differ in how this bound
affects the search. B&B maintains a global upper bound¯F, updated whenever a complete schedule is
found, and explicitly prunes any nodeNi with ˆf(Ni)≥ ¯F. The interplay between the improving upper
bound and the lower bounds of individual nodes is central to its effectiveness. OurA∗ implementation
does not maintain an upper bound. Instead, BF expansion with an admissible and consistent heuristic
guarantees that the first goal state selected fromOpenis optimal. Hence,A∗ does not exploit an
incumbent solution for pruning in the way that B&B does.
The methods furthermore differ with respect to the heuristic computation efficiency. With state-
based duplicate detection,A∗ retains a single search record for each distinct state, and with a consistent
heuristic, each state needs to be expanded at most once. If duplicate detection is performed before
evaluatingh, the heuristic is therefore computed only once per distinct retained state. In B&B, distinct
tree nodes can induce the same timed state, soh may be evaluated multiple times for the same
remaining scheduling problem.
B&B permits flexible node-selection strategies such as depth-first, breadth-first, or hybrid. This
choice interacts with the upper-bound update mechanism.A∗, on the other hand, requires BF selection
for its optimality guarantee. When both use BF selection with the same heuristic, their expansion
orders are closely related but not identical sinceA∗ may expand fewer nodes due to duplicate detection.
With respect to the memory requirements,A∗ stores all expanded states in aClosedlist and all
frontier states in anOpenlist. DF B&B avoids most of this cost because it only keeps the children of
the nodes on the current path from the root in memory. However, when B&B uses BF selection, it
has to maintain all unexpanded nodes, resulting in memory requirements comparable toA∗. In this
setting, theClosedlist is an additional cost ofA∗ that can also save memory by preventing duplicate
states from entering theOpenlist.
6 Empirical Study
The purpose of this section is to examine the differences between the ordinary B&B andA∗ algorithms
presented above across a broad range of instances. To this end, we consider the 480 instances in the
J30 benchmark from PSPLIB (Kolisch and Sprecher, 1997), which consists of RCPSP instances with
30 activities and varying precedence structures and resource requirements. Note that we do not aim to
establish that the algorithms are competitive with state-of-the-art RCPSP solvers.
All methods were implemented in Python 3.13.13, and experiments were conducted on a single
core of an Intel Xeon Gold 6354 @ 3.00 GHz, without parallelization, with a time limit of 2 hours
and a memory limit of 64 GB. All code, data, and results are available athttps://github.com/
ShimShtern/rcpsp-astar-vs-branch-and-bound(version v1.0).

7 Conclusions and Future Research
This paper investigates the computational differences between B&B andA∗ using the RCPSP as a
common problem. We establish the relationships between MILP, state-action, and timed Petri-net
representations and compare basic implementations of both methods. By using the same lower bound
and BF node-selection rule, we examine the effect of their different search mechanisms. In particular,
tree-based B&B may repeatedly explore the same remaining scheduling problem through different
decision sequences, whereas graph-basedA∗ identifies equivalent states and avoids their repeated
exploration.
Experiments on 480 PSPLIB J30 instances demonstrate the importance of this difference. With
lexicographic and active-schedule pruning,A∗ solved all 480 instances to optimality, compared with
445 for BF B&B under the same time and memory limits. Although these pruning rules substantially
improved B&B, they did not eliminate the performance gap. DF B&B required less memory and found
feasible schedules for many instances where the search could not be completed within the time limit.
Stronger LP relaxations reduced the number of generated nodes but increased computational time,
illustrating the trade-off between bound strength and evaluation effort.
These results highlight the importance of how the search space is represented and explored. They
also illustrate different advantages of the two approaches: duplicate-state detection can considerably
reduce redundant exploration, while DF search and incumbent-based pruning offer opportunities to
control memory use and obtain feasible solutions early. Such insights can help researchers select
appropriate search methods according to the characteristics and requirements of the problem. However,
our findings concern the implementations and benchmark instances considered here and do not claim
the general superiority of either method.
Several directions for future research arise from this study. Since both approaches admit numerous
algorithmic enhancements, an important direction is to investigate the transfer of effective mechanisms
between them. Examples include introducing duplicate-state detection into B&B, incorporating
incumbent-based pruning intoA∗, applying constraint propagation to restrict scheduling decisions and
strengthen bounds, and using lazy heuristic evaluation to reduce unnecessary computation. Finally,
extending the analysis to other combinatorial optimization problems would help quantify the findings
across additional problem domains.

better lower bound than both LP variants on at least 98 instances. For DF B&B, in contrast, the LP
relaxations present a trade-off, which is why their lower-bound profiles cross that of the no-LP variant.
The no-LP variant proves optimality on more instances, since solving an LP at every node is two to
three orders of magnitude slower, but the LP variants obtain considerably tighter lower bounds on the
instances that remain unsolved. This trade-off is sharper for the strong LP, which proves optimality on
69 fewer instances than the no-LP variant, compared with 52 for the weak LP, but also yields tighter
lower bounds. Specifically, on the 40 instances that the no-LP variant does not solve, which the LP
variants do not solve either, the median relative gap between the optimum and the final lower bound
drops from 39.0% without LP relaxations to 34.2% with the weak LP and 28.1% with the strong LP.
On these instances, the final lower bound of DF B&B usually remains at the root bound, as shallow
open nodes are never revisited. The strong LP therefore benefits mainly from its tighter root bound,
whereas the weak LP also raises its bound above the root bound on about a third of these instances,
as its cheaper LPs allow more nodes to be processed. This suggests that, for DF B&B, it may be
preferable to solve the strong LP only once at the root, to obtain a global lower bound, and to use the
cheaper critical-path bound at all other nodes. Such a hybrid would retain most of the lower-bound
advantage of the strong LP while preserving the speed of the no-LP variant.

Sprecher, 1997). The network complexity (NC) is the average number of immediate successors per
activity. The resource factor (RF) is the average fraction of the resources required by an activity, so
that a higherRF means that each activity uses more of the resources. The resource strength (RS)
measures how scarce the resources are relative to the demand, where a lowerRS means more scarce
resources and hence a more constrained instance. The unresolved instances concentrate in subclasses
with low resource strength (RS = 0.25) and high resource factor (RF≥ 0.75), and the LP-based
variants leave considerably more instances unresolved than the variants without LP relaxations.

text:
One Policy for 100 Household Tasks:
Our Solution for the 2026 BEHA VIOR Challenge
Ilia Larchenko Gleb Zarin Atindra Nair Keerti Manney
ilya.larchenko@gmail.com zaringleb@gmail.com atindra.nair@gmail.com keertimanney@gmail.com
Vitaly Kleban Mirko Kiefer Anjana Yodaiken
vitaly.kleban@gmail.com mirko@blackbeltlabs.com anjana.yodaiken@gmail.com
November 11, 2026
Abstract
We describe our solution for the 2026 BEHA VIOR Challenge: 100 long-horizon household tasks in the OmniGibson simulator.
We placed 9th on the final leaderboard, the only independent team in the top 10. The core of the solution is a single vision-language-
action (VLA) model, one checkpoint for all 100 tasks, built on our 1st-place 2025 solution [1], which is based onπ0.5 [10]. On the
50 tasks shared with 2025, its Q rises from 0.260 to 0.371; across all 100 tasks it scores 0.392.
Our main conclusion from 2025 was that the model was undertrained, so most of the 2026 work went into training the model for
longer, optimizing some training parameters, making each training step slightly faster and reducing the gradient noise:
• migration from 50 to 100 tasks: semantic stages built from the demonstrations’ skill annotations, task and stage embeddings
of new tasks warm-started from similar old ones, and a 21-dimensional action space matching the teleoperation controls;
• variance-reduced multi-sample flow matching: stratified flow times and antithetic noise, and a simple noise-vs-compute
model that picks the number of action-expert samples per observation without ablations;
• a 200k-step training run(one B300, then 8 ×H200 at batch 2048), about one pass over the 211M frames of the demonstra-
tions;
• a cloud evaluation infrastructure: a shared evaluation record across local machines and two cloud platforms, with
provenance, episode diagnostics and restorable simulator states for follow-up experiments, with six simulators on one GPU
together running faster than real time.
On top of the learned policy we developed LLM agent control with GPT-6 Astra [29] for 14 tasks that we routed to the agent after it
outperformed the policy in our own trials:
• an agent route: on these tasks a GPT-6 Astra coding agent controls the robot through observation and motion tools, starting
every episode from a frozen copy of its own practice session on training instances. We also explored a learned policy
monitored by GPT-6.1 Sol [30] with bounded Astra interventions, which we did not submit;
• result: across the 14 agent tasks, Astra’s mean Q is 0.639, against 0.108 for the learned policy. The public submission
included only part of the Astra results and scored 0.446 Q with 27.3% full-task success.
1 Introduction
1.1 The 2026 BEHA VIOR Challenge
The BEHA VIOR Challenge [4, 3] evaluates robot policies on
long-horizon household activities in the OmniGibson simu-
lator, built on NVIDIA Isaac Sim. The 2026 edition doubles
the 2025 task set: 100 activities, from turning on a radio to
cooking a meal, each with 200 teleoperated demonstrations
(20,000 episodes, 211M frames or about 1,950 hours, in the
LeRobot [6] format). The robot is the same Galaxea R1Pro:
a holonomic base, a 4-joint torso and two 7-DOF arms with
parallel grippers, observed through a head camera and two
wrist cameras plus proprioception. An episode is a full success
if all goal predicates are satisfied, which scores 1. Otherwise
its q-score (we also call it Q) is the fraction of satisfied predi-
cates. Scores are averaged over instances and then over tasks.
The time limit of an episode is 1.5× the mean duration of the
human demonstrations of the task (2× in 2025). The 50 tasks
of 2025 are included with the same demonstrations; the other
50 are new.
1.2 Vision-language-action models
Vision-language-action models (VLAs) fine-tune a pretrained
vision-language model to output robot actions [ 8]. The π0
family [9, 10] pairs a PaliGemma VLM [ 15] with a smaller
“action expert” trained by flow matching [ 18] to generate
chunks of continuous actions, optionally co-trained with dis-
crete FAST action tokens [ 12]. Many alternatives have ap-
peared since, such as GR00T [13] and, increasingly prominent,
MolmoAct2 [14]. Yet more than a year after its release (paper
in April 2025, code and weights in September 2025 [11]),π0.5
is still widely used as a base for fine-tuning: both top 2025
BEHA VIOR solutions were built on it [1, 7]. We built our
2026 solution on top of our 2025 one, so we kept itsπ0.5-based
1
arXiv:2611.14432v1 [cs.RO] 10 Nov 2026
title: One Policy for 100 Household Tasks: Our Solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge

text:
architecture. For this reason, in parts of this report we call our
learned policy simplyπ 0.5.
1.3 LLM agents as robot controllers
A second line of work uses large language models to control
robots directly: by choosing among learned skills [27], writing
control code [28], or orchestrating a low-level policy. With
frontier models that can use tools for hours, this has become
a practical option in simulation. GPT-6 Astra [ 29], released
in September 2026, was strong enough to solve some BE-
HA VIOR tasks that our learned policy could not, so our final
submission routes 14 tasks to an Astra-based agent (Section 9).
1.4 Our starting point
Our 2025 solution [1] won the first BEHA VIOR Challenge.
It took π0.5 and changed the following: trainable task em-
beddings instead of text prompts, correlated noise for flow
matching, a learnable mixture of all VLM layers’ keys and
values for the action expert, a stage-prediction head with vot-
ing (“System 2”), a FAST auxiliary loss, several flow samples
per VLM forward pass, and correlation-aware inpainting at
inference. The 2025 checkpoints were clearly undertrained:
the loss was still falling when the deadline came, and four
checkpoints split the 50 tasks between them. The LeHome
Challenge solution [2] of one of our team members was built
on top of the 2025 BEHA VIOR solution and introduced sev-
eral engineering fixes and improvements that we inherit here
as well. The 2025 runner-up [ 7] also starts from π0.5 and
studies the effect of image resolution, of the training data and
of rejection-sampling fine-tuning.
1.5 Contributions
• A recipe for growing a task-conditioned VLA from 50
to 100 tasks without retraining from scratch: semantic
stages from skill annotations, similarity-based initial-
ization of new task and stage embeddings, and a 21-
dimensional action space matching teleoperation controls
(Section 3).
• Registers, scratch tokens and attention sinks at several
levels of a VLA; moving the pretrained SigLIP attention-
sink outliers into the registers by parameter surgery on a
running training made the attention maps readable (Sec-
tion 4).
• Variance-reduced multi-sample flow matching and a way
to choose the number of flow samples from one gradient-
noise measurement (Section 5).
• An evaluation infrastructure that makes cross-cloud roll-
outs inspectable and reusable through provenance, di-
agnostics and restorable simulator states, and runs six
simulators per GPU faster than real time in aggregate
(Section 7).
• An LLM agent route with GPT-6 Astra for 14 tasks where
the learned policy is weak and the agent performed better
(Section 9).
Code and models.Code: https://github.com/R
obot-Learning-Collective/behavior-1k-s
olution-2026 . Checkpoint: https://huggingf
ace.co/IliaLarchenko/BEHAVIOR2026VLA . The
2025 checkpoint we start from: https://huggingfac
e.co/IliaLarchenko/behavior_submission .
Project page, including evaluation videos and visual examples:
https://robot-learning-collective.github
.io/behavior-1k-2026/.
2 Overall Solution
2.1 What carries over
From our 2025 solution we keep the model and most of the
serving logic [1]:
• Task embeddingsinstead of text: each task has a learned
embedding, and the prompt is never tokenized.
• System 2 stages: the model predicts the current stage of
the task from the base task token and is conditioned on
a stage embedding; at inference the stage is tracked by
voting.
• Correlated flow noise: the flow-matching noise has the
covariance Σβ =βC+ (1−β)I (β= 0.5 ), where C
is the empirical correlation of normalized action chunks,
both in training and at inference.
• KV mixing: each action-expert layer attends to a learn-
able mixture of the keys and values of all VLM layers.
• Multi-sample flow matching: the VLM prefix is com-
puted once, and the action expert is run forK flow sam-
ples (Section 5).
• FAST auxiliary loss: the VLM also predicts the FAST
tokens of the target chunk during training.
•Correlation-aware inpaintingat inference: the actions
already committed from the previous chunk anchor the
next one, and the action correlations carry the correction
over to the free actions.
From the LeHome solution [ 2] we take the training side:
a weighted multi-dataset loader, corrected state scaling (in
2025 many normalized state values fell outside the range of
the state bins and were clipped), loss masking of padded steps
at episode ends, and the augmentation set (crop, rotation, color
jitter, cutout, camera and state dropout). New in 2026, the
frames after the task is complete (the idle tail of each demon-
stration) are never sampled for training.
2.2 Model
The backbone is that of π0.5 in its openpi release [ 11]:
PaliGemma (SigLIP So400m [ 16] and Gemma 2B [ 17]) as
the VLM and a 300M Gemma action expert with adaptive
RMS-norm conditioning on the flow time (Figure 1). Images
are 224×224 (256 tokens per camera). The prefix holds the
image tokens with their SigLIP registers, VLM scratch tokens,
the base task token, four task/stage fusion tokens, a continuous
state token and 21 quantized state tokens, and in training the
FAST tokens of the target chunk. The expert’s suffix holds
four scratch tokens, the 30 noisy actions and two conditioning
tokens.

robot state; the smaller action expert (right) denoises a 30-step action chunk and reads the VLM through a learnable mixture of the keys and

of both transformers has a learnable sink. FAST tokens are used only in training.
State tokens. π0.5 embeds each state dimension as one
of 256 bin tokens of the language model’s embedding table,
so “left shoulder at bin 120” and “right wrist at bin 120” are
the same vector, and values outside [−1,1] are clipped. We
expanded each of the 21 state tokens to
tokj =E bin[bin(xj)] +ej +Wϕ(x j),
so that the same bin maps to a distinct token for each
joint, whereej is a learned per-joint embedding, ϕ is a 256-
dimensional sine/cosine encoding of the unclipped value, and
W is a learned projection matrix shared across joints that maps
ϕ(xj) to the token width;ej andW are initialized to zero. In
addition to these 21 per-joint tokens, a single continuous state
token is a linear projection of the whole unclipped state vector.
Task and stage inputs to the action expert.In π0.5 the
expert sees the task only through the VLM’s keys and values.
We add two tokens at the end of the suffix that carry zero-
initialized projections of the task embedding and of the task-
stage embedding, a direct conditioning path into the expert.
Attention structure.Figure 2 shows the attention mask.
The images, registers, VLM scratch tokens and the base task
token form one bidirectional block that cannot see the stage or
the state; the stage head reads the output of the base task token,
so the stage is predicted from the images and the task alone.
The stage and state tokens see that block and each other; the
FAST tokens are causal. The action expert’s tokens see the
whole prefix except the FAST tokens and attend bidirectionally
among themselves. Every query can also attend to the sink.
Inference.The serving loop is the 2025 one with re-tuned
parameters; Appendix A lists the changes.
3 Migration from 50 to 100 Tasks
The 2025 solution served four checkpoints, each fine-tuned
on a subset of the 50 tasks. In 2026 one checkpoint serves all
Figure 2:Group-level attention mask in training (rows: queries,
columns: keys; colored: can attend). Rows above the dashed line are
VLM tokens, rows below are action-expert tokens. FAST tokens are
causal among themselves and are removed from the cache the expert

100 tasks. It is warm-started from the 2025 checkpoint that
carried the largest share of the 2025 score; a single conversion
script maps it to the new task set, stage layout and action
space. All parameters added in 2026 are zero-, identity- or
small-normal-initialized, so the converted model starts close
to the 2025 function.
3.1 Semantic stages
In 2025 the System 2 stages were equal slices of each episode
in time (5–15 per task), because we did not use the skill anno-
tations. With 20,000 annotated demonstrations we could check
how well these time slices match the actual steps of the tasks,
3
title: One Policy for 100 Household Tasks: Our Solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge

text:
and they match poorly. On average only 50% of the frames
of a time stage belong to its most common annotated step
(0.17–0.82 per task); 57% of the 1,093 time stages of the 100
tasks have no step that covers more than half of their frames;
and the borders of the time stages are no closer to the real
step borders than random borders would be. Episode lengths
within a task vary by 20%, so in an 11-stage task a fixed time
grid can be off by about two stages in either direction.
We replaced them with semantic stages built from the anno-
tations (Figure 3):
1. each episode is cut at the frame where the task is com-
plete, and its sequence of annotated skills is aligned to
the typical sequence of the task (the medoid); retries and
extra steps are assigned to the current step;
2. the steps are grouped into stages at points where the
demonstrations agree; parts that demonstrators do in vary-
ing order (e.g. sorting items) become order-free progress
stages;
3. a few rules then adjust the grouping: a grasp and a press-
type action (press, switch, toggle) are never in the same
stage, so that the gripper rule (Appendix A) can tell a
missed grasp from a press; similar-looking states of the
same appliance are kept in separate stages; repeated steps
in a row become one stage; very short stages are merged
into a neighbour unless they are a distinct final action.
The result has 413 stages (2–9 per task) instead of 1,093 time
stages. Every label is regenerated from the dataset annotations
by deterministic scripts.
3.2 Warm-starting new tasks and stages
Tasks.The 50 tasks of 2025 keep their trained embeddings.
We could initialize the 50 new ones randomly, but many
new tasks are similar to old ones, so instead each new
task starts from a weighted average of the embeddings of
1–5 similar 2025 tasks (most have three), with weights
1,0.7,0.5,0.35,0.25 by rank. The average is rescaled to
the average norm of its sources, because averaging makes
vectors shorter. The similar tasks were proposed by a
similarity search over task names, skills and object categories
and then reviewed by hand and by Claude models. For
example, freeze_fruit starts from freeze_pies,
clearing_food_from_table_into_fridge and
storing_food.
Stages.The same idea is used one level down. A semantic
stage of an old task starts from the average of that task’s 2025
time-stage embeddings, weighted by how many of its frames
fell into each time stage. A stage of a new task starts from
the matching stages of similar old tasks (e.g. “open the fridge”
from the old tasks that open a fridge). The output weights of
the stage head are converted in the same way.
3.3 Minimal action space
The 2025 model predicted 32 dimensions, of which 23 were
real (base 3, torso 4, two arms of 7, two grippers). We changed
the action representation to match the degrees of freedom used
in teleoperation:
• the 9 padding dimensions are gone;
• the JoyLo teleoperation system [ 5] does not move the
four torso joints independently. It has two torso controls:
translatemoves the torso along a fixed path through three
key poses, from upright to fully bent down, andtiltadds
an offset to the third joint; the fourth joint is always
zero. Every torso command in the 211M frames of the
dataset has exactly this form, and translate and tilt can
be recovered exactly from the four joints. The model
therefore predicts translate and tilt, and its outputs are
mapped back to the four joints.
The result is a 21-dim action and state space: [base 3, translate,
tilt, left arm 7, left gripper, right arm 7, right gripper]. Four
correlated, partly redundant torso dimensions became two
meaningful ones, and the policy can no longer produce torso
configurations the demonstrations never visit. The shared con-
trol space also lets a JoyLo operator smoothly take over from
the policy during an episode. The weights of the remaining
dimensions are copied, and the two new torso rows start at
zero.
The same principle applies to the vocabulary: the model
only ever embeds the 256 state bins (FAST tokens have their
own embedding table), so we keep 256 of Gemma’s 257,152
embedding rows. This removes 526M parameters that received
no gradient but were stored four times in every training check-
point (weights, EMA and the two Adam moments): about
8 GB per checkpoint.
4 Sinks, Scratch Tokens and Registers
This part of the work started as debugging. To understand
failures we render the attention of the action tokens over the
three cameras for every step of a rollout. For the warm-started
2025 model these maps were nearly useless: the same few
cells lit up in all three cameras, in every frame of every episode
(episode-mean maps correlate at 0.97, Figure 4, left).
The cause was the pretrained SigLIP position embeddings:
a few cells have outlier norms (cell (12,1) has norm 313 against
a mean of 22, mostly in one channel), so their tokens act as
content-free “parking spots” for attention. The 12 hottest cells
took 31.9% of all image attention, and cell (12,1) alone up to
29% of the right-wrist camera. This is the artifact described
by Darcet et al. [ 24] in vision transformers and by Xiao et
al. [25] in language models: the softmax needs somewhere to
put excess attention, and the model repurposes some tokens
for it, losing whatever information they carried. Beyond the
lost information, it made the attention maps unreadable.
We gave the model dedicated places for this at four levels:
• SigLIP registers[ 24]: 8 learnable tokens inside the vi-
sion tower of each camera, without position embeddings.
Their outputs pass through the same projection as the
patch tokens and join the prefix (24 tokens), masked
together with their camera.
• VLM scratch tokens: 8 learnable tokens in the prefix,
attended bidirectionally with the images.

We also added a linear projection per camera after the shared
SigLIP encoder, initialized to the identity.
Surgery on a running training.The new tokens start neu-
tral in the converted 2025 checkpoint, and fresh registers did
not take over the sink role by themselves: early in the produc-
tion run the outlier cells were unchanged and the registers had
barely moved. We therefore moved the sinks explicitly, by
parameter surgery on the running training: registers were ini-
tialized from the position embeddings of the hottest cells, each
such cell’s position embedding was replaced by the mean of its
neighbours, and the Adam moments of the edited parameters
were reset. The surgery cost a brief loss bump that disappeared
within a few hundred steps. After the surgery the attention
maps follow the objects and the grippers (Figure 4, right),
and the attention-mass breakdown per token group became a
useful diagnostic.
We did not ablate these changes. The loss fully recovered
after the surgery, so we do not think they hurt, but apart from
making debugging easier we have no evidence that they im-
prove the success rate. The numbers of registers, scratch
tokens and sinks were chosen fairly arbitrarily.

All inputs are cheap to measure:cp andck from two 50-step

5.5 Other optimizations
Per-group learning rates.We experimented with several
per-group multipliers, applied to the final updates so that they
do not touch the optimizer state and can change between
resumes. The final recipe uses 2× for the action expert, the
action and time projections, the KV mixing and the task/stage
embeddings and 1× everywhere else, including the vision
tower, with the gradient clipped at 2.0.
Efficiency.Capping the FAST target at 68 tokens instead
of 200 (the mean is 37 per chunk) saved about 9% of the
step time, and choosing the token counts so that the attention
keys are multiples of 16 another 4–5%. Removing the un-
used vocabulary (Section 3) shrinks the optimizer state and
checkpoints by about 8 GB.
Augmentation.Head camera: random crop (98%) and
rotation (±2◦); all cameras: color jitter and a cutout rectangle
(probability 0.3, up to 10% of the image); each wrist camera
is dropped with probability 0.05 and all state tokens with
probability 0.02.
6 Training
The submitted checkpoint is step 200k of one run on all 20,000
demonstrations, warm-started from the converted 2025 check-
point. The run had two phases:
• 1×B300, batch 480 (the largest that fits), 130k steps,
peak learning rate 2.24·10 −5; a step took about 10.5 s
(46 samples/s);
• 8×H200with FSDP, batch 2048, 70k steps, peak learning
rate 4.63·10 −5 (= 2.24·10 −5p
2048/480), continuing
the same cosine schedule; a step took 11.9 s (172 sam-
ples/s, 3.7×the B300).
The first half of the B300 phase doubled as a testbed: we
tried a number of training parameters and model changes on
the live run, resuming from its checkpoints, and kept what
worked. For most of the run the optimizer was AdamW with
β= (0.95,0.99) and an EMA of 0.995, the cosine schedule
had 5k warmup steps, and the loss weights were 1 for flow
matching, 0.1 for the stage head and 0.05 for FAST. In total
the model saw about 200M training samples, roughly one pass
over the 211M frames of the demonstrations.
7 Evaluation Infrastructure
Evaluating 100 long tasks is expensive: an episode runs for
up to tens of minutes of wall time, and a simulator takes
6–9 minutes to boot. Over the competition we ran around
9,000 evaluation episodes, about 100M environment steps
or nearly 1,000 simulated hours; we saved each run with its
provenance, diagnostics and restorable scene checkpoints, so
we could compare models, inspect failures and start follow-up
experiments from recorded states.
7.1 Cloud infrastructure
One record across clouds.We ran evaluations on local ma-
chines and two cloud platforms (RunPod, then Nebius); all
runs were uploaded to one cloud bucket. A web portal indexes
them automatically. Each run carries a manifest with its full
provenance: code revision and diff, simulator and package
versions, all evaluator and serving arguments, and the check-
sum of the served checkpoint, which links the run to a model
registry.
Rich data.Recorded evaluations retain video and resource
telemetry, plus per-step actions, observation and policy diag-
nostics, inference timing and BDDL goal progress. We save
the robot and all initialized scene objects, including sleeping
and non-task objects, at the start, every 30 steps, and at ter-
mination. This gives recovery experiments a restorable scene
near a failure while limiting storage and evaluation slowdown;
the tradeoff is that we can restore only saved steps. When an
action creates new objects, as slicing does, we also save the
scene description needed to rebuild them.
Restoration and review.These saved states can be loaded
into a fresh simulator to replay part of a rollout or start a tar-
geted recovery experiment. The portal lets people and coding
agents find any model and episode, compare outcomes, watch
the video next to the goal progress and leave timestamped
comments. Agent rollouts (Section 9) use the same store and
viewer (Figure 7).
Scaling large evaluations.In the cloud, each GPU machine
ran one policy server and six simulators, and a shared job
queue, longest jobs first, kept all machines busy until the end,
also when spot machines were preempted. A CPU-only head
node requeued jobs after worker interruptions and uploaded
completed runs. This mattered most for full evaluations: 100
tasks× 10 instances took about 20 hours on eight machines
and cost about $300. Between full evaluations, a local driver
sampled the least-measured tasks for each newly published
checkpoint.
7.2 Faster than real time on one GPU
Simulation is CPU-bound, so the gains came mostly from
keeping the CPU busy with useful work:
• Persistent simulators.Each simulator boots once and
runs many episodes. The scene and random generators
are saved at boot and restored before every instance
(about 10 s instead of a 7.6-minute reboot), so each
episode starts exactly like the first episode of a freshly

8 What We Tried and Dropped
Scripted recovery in an agentic loop.A single failed grasp
ends many episodes, and the demonstrations contain almost
no recoveries. We developed a small declarative DSL in which
a recovery is described as a sequence of primitives (approach,
grasp, rotate, release, hand back to the policy) with tolerances,
and used coding agents to write recipes for selected failure
modes. Recoveries are generated from full simulator-state
checkpoints of failed rollouts (Section 7), so every recovery
episode starts exactly in a state the policy actually reached.

On turning_on_radio the recovery data raised the spe-
cialist’s success rate from about 50% to 60–75%, i.e. roughly
+0.1 Q for that task; on hanging_pictures it fixed the
targeted failure but not the full task. Writing and validating
recipes for new tasks took too long for the process to become
autonomous, and at the scale of 100 tasks the expected gain
for the final model was negligible.
Manual DAgger.We also collected human corrections [33]
by restoring failed rollouts and teleoperating from the failure
state. For set_up_a_coffee_station_in_your_
kitchen, we compared fine-tunes from the same checkpoint:
one used the 200 task demonstrations, and the other sampled
70 reviewed teleop recovery segments (16,904 frames) at 5%
of training samples. Mean Q was 0.367 with recoveries versus
0.267 without them (one-sided paired permutationp= 0.131 ),
a difference that was not statistically significant.
Astra-generated recoveries.In exploratory experiments,
we found that nearly every policy failure could, with mod-
est manual oversight, become a 15–30 s recovery task with
a verifiable goal, such as satisfying one BDDL goal predi-
cate or grasping or releasing an object. Astra solved all the
mini-tasks we tested (100% success) in multi-turn sessions
using the RoboICL [31] harness, suggesting a way to generate
demonstrations for imitation learning.
Scripted recovery data and human corrections improved
single tasks at small scale, and both were probably most useful
for undertrained models: as the main run progressed, the base
policy closed most of the gap on its own. We lacked the time
and compute to scale recovery-data collection and fine-tuning
to 100 tasks, or to distill Astra-generated trajectories into the
policy, so we used Astra directly as a policy for difficult tasks
(Section 9).
9 Agent Route: GPT-6 Astra
We used GPT-6 Astra in two ways. In the first, the learned
policy controls the robot and Astra takes over only for a short
recovery. In the second, Astra controls the robot for the whole
episode and starts from a saved copy of its own practice on that
task. Only the second is in our final submission. We describe
both, in the order in which we built them.
9.1 Sol monitoring and bounded Astra intervention
In the intervention system, the learned policy stays in control.
A GPT-6.1 Sol [30] monitor watches the three camera streams
at 1 FPS and writes visual notes on the progress of the task.
When the policy makes no progress for some time, for example
when it fails the same grasp again and again or the robot falls,
Sol writes a text description of a recovery, grounded in the
task and in its notes. GPT-6 Astra then controls the robot for
a bounded recovery: at most three interventions per episode,
each of at most 900 actions. After the recovery, the learned
policy continues from the new state.
The length of the window that Sol looks back over mattered.
We started with 10 seconds. This was too short, because the
failures above develop over a longer time. We increased the
window to 30 seconds, which Sol reviews every 10 simulated
seconds.
We found no gain that we could attribute to the interventions.
On one task, two monitored runs scored a Q of 0.67, against
0.17 for the learned policy alone, but one of the two runs
contained no Astra action. The monitor also costs money
when it does nothing. We did not submit this system.
9.2 Historical failure comments as context
We also used agents to review all our earlier rollouts and to
annotate where the learned policy failed. For each task we
collected these comments in one file, ANNOTATIONS.md,
and gave it to the Sol monitor, so that it knew which failures to
look for and could give Astra better guidance. We had to trim
the files as training progressed, because the policy changed
and its early failures stopped occurring.
The comments did not change the result. With them, the
intervention system scored a Q of 0 on all 8 instances that
we tested of two attachment tasks: attaching a camera to a
tripod and making cabinet doors. The learned policy alone
also scored 0 there. These tasks give no credit for a part that
is almost attached, and after a recovery the control goes back
to a policy that cannot do the precise step.
This work gave us the idea for the next step. The comments
were feedback that we prepared before the episode, with offline
compute. Astra could prepare such feedback for itself, from
its own attempts at the task.
9.3 Practice on training instances
In the final design, Astra learns each task by practice before
evaluation, in the spirit of automated research loops. A prac-
tice session is one long conversation of GPT-6 Astra, running
in the Pi coding agent [32], with one simulator. The simula-
tor holds a training instance of the task, never an evaluation
instance. It uses the same robot configuration, physics and
cameras as the official evaluator, because earlier practice with
a lighter robot base and different cameras did not transfer. As-
tra receives the task instruction, the goal definition, the human
demonstrations of the task (camera images, robot state and
actions) and the lessons that earlier practice sessions wrote
down on other tasks.
The session follows a fixed loop. Astra first lists the hard
parts of the task, such as grasps, presses, insertions, doors
and hand-overs. It then practices one part at a time: it saves
the scene just before the part, tries the part, and reads which
goal conditions hold. When a part fails several times, Astra
steps through two or three human demonstrations of the same
part, compares the human motion with its own, changes what
differs, restores the scene and tries again. When a part works,
Astra writes a short recipe with the exact commands and mea-
surements. After the parts, it runs the whole task from a fresh
reset, without restores and within the official step limit, and
writes a procedure for a later copy of itself.
Reset, save, restore and goal feedback are privileged tools
that exist only in practice. No weights are trained. What Astra

text:
learns stays in its conversation, which grew to 29–395 MB per
task, and in its notes and recipes.
To test if practice transfers, we moved sessions to training
instances that they had not seen, each with a different layout
of the scene. The first attempt on a new instance used only the
notes, without saved states, goal feedback or demonstrations.
Over the final two days, 8 of 17 such first attempts succeeded.
After a failed attempt, Astra studied the failure and practiced
on the new instance. On cook_a_brisket, for example,
the frozen session scored a Q of 0.33 and 1.0 with the official
evaluator on two instances held out from practice. The learned
policy scores 0.07 on this task.
9.4 Observation and motion tools
Practice and evaluation use the same three calls and the same
controller (Figure 9). observe returns one image with the
left wrist, head and right wrist camera views, and the robot
state as text. xyz returns the position of every pixel in the
robot frame, computed from the depth image of the official
observation. act is the only motor command: one call is one
full goal, for example a gripper pose, a gripper opening and
a base motion. At every simulator step (30 Hz) a controller
takes one inverse-kinematics step toward the goal and limits
the joint and base speeds. It stops when the goal is reached,
when the motion stalls or at a step limit, and returns a new
image and what was achieved. Nothing reports contact or
force, so Astra must judge from the images and the finger
positions if a grasp holds.
We rebuilt these tools several times in the ten days before
the deadline, and three iterations mattered most. First, we
replaced short open-loop chunks of actions, after which Astra
could not tell what had happened, with one goal per call and a
loop that closes at every step. Free motions then reached their
target within 0.83 mm, and a blocked motion is reported as
stalled. Second, we replaced positions estimated from pixels,
which missed grasps by centimeters, with positions from depth.
Their worst error against the simulator was 1.06µm over 3,598
samples. Third, long base motions made the robot fall, so we
limited the base speed to 0.20 m/s and stop a motion when
the measured velocity does not follow the command. In our
experience, these iterations mattered more than the wording
of the prompts.
9.5 The final Astra policy
At the end of practice we freeze the session: we save the
conversation, the notes and the recipes, and do not change
them again. In evaluation, the task of an episode decides
which policy controls the robot. On 14 tasks, Astra controls
it from the first step to the last. On all other tasks the learned
policy plays alone. Unlike in the intervention system, control
does not pass back and forth.
Every agent episode starts from a fresh copy of the frozen
session of its task (Figure 10), so nothing carries over from
one episode to the next. The privileged tools are gone. As-
tra receives only the official observation: the head and wrist
camera images with depth, and the robot state. It does not
produce low-level actions. It writes short programs that call
the tools of Section 9.4: they look at the scene, measure po-
sitions from the depth images, and send one goal at a time,
such as a gripper pose, a base motion or a gripper command.
The controller converts each goal into one action per simulator
step and returns the result together with a new image. While
Astra thinks, the simulation waits.
If the agent fails at runtime, the learned policy plays the rest
of that episode. This happens after three consecutive answers
that exceed the time limit for one query, after an API error,
or when the session reaches its cost limit or the episode its
wall-time limit. A motion that does not reach its goal is not
such a failure: Astra receives the result and plans again.
We practiced 27 tasks and routed 14 of them to the agent.
These are tasks on which the learned policy is weak (mean
Q of 0.108) and on which either the agent did better in our
tests or the policy scores about zero, so that there was little
to lose. The agent route worked only one to two days before
the final deadline. Practice, task selection and tuning were
therefore short, and some tasks were routed without a complete
successful practice run.
Across the 14 tasks, Astra’s mean Q was 0.639, against
0.108 for the learned policy alone (Figure 11). Due to time
constraints, the public results contain only part of the agent
episodes, 106 of 140. The agent is also slow and expensive:
an agent episode took a median of 0.63 hours of wall time,
about 17 times longer than real time, and cost tens of dollars
in API fees.
10 Results
We placed ninth overall and first among independent teams in
the 2026 BEHA VIOR Challenge. On the public instances, our
submission achieved a Q of 0.446 and a success rate of 27.3%.
The organizers re-evaluated only the top-ranked submissions
on the private test set; ours was not among them, so our score
is self-reported from our own evaluation of instances 301–310
with the official evaluator.

were hard for the policy, Astra achieved 0.639, compared with
0.108 forπ0.5. The public submission included only part of
the Astra results due to time constraints.
The per-taskπ0.5 scores span the full range (Figure 11): 13
tasks score at least 0.75 and 8 score zero.
10.1 Comparison with 2025
On the 50 tasks from 2025, Q rose from 0.260 to 0.371 (Fig-
ure 12). We think continued training, demonstrations from
50 additional tasks, model improvements, and bug fixes con-
tributed to the gain. One checkpoint now covers all 100 tasks,
compared with four checkpoints for 50 tasks last year (we
did not have the resources to fine-tune multiple checkpoints).
This gain came despite a 25% shorter episode time limit (1.5×
demonstration duration versus 2× in 2025). The evaluations
used different simulator versions, but we did not observe a
meaningful performance difference between them.

10.3 Astra failure modes
On the selected tasks we reviewed, Astra struggled mainly
with precise and efficient robot control. Pouring and other
dynamic movements were difficult; placement lacked preci-
sion at times; Astra occasionally knocked objects out of place
or moved the robot inefficiently. It could also loop when a
task appeared complete but was not. We believe limited prac-
tice time explains most failures and that more practice could
improve performance substantially.

10.4 Emergent behavior
Last year, we demonstrated that single-task policies made
no attempt to recover, while the multi-task policy showed
tentative attempts despite having no recovery demonstrations
in its training data [1]. The 2026 policy, also trained without
recovery examples, attempts recovery more often and with
less hesitation; these attempts often let it continue the task
successfully. Training across 100 tasks rather than 50 gave
it a broader range of actions and situations to draw on when
recovering. The policy also adapts familiar actions to the state
it reaches, sometimes using the other arm or changing the
action sequence after an earlier mistake (Figure 14). We find
it promising that such goal-directed behavior can be learned
from demonstrations alone across many tasks.
11 Discussion
One policy on 100 tasks.After 2025 we assumed that our
model was undertrained, and this year we trained one model
for 200k steps, about one pass over the 211M frames of the
demonstrations. On the 50 tasks shared with 2025 it scores
a Q of 0.371 against 0.260 for our winning 2025 submission
(Section 10). The migration recipe (Section 3) let us continue
from the 2025 checkpoint instead of starting from scratch.
One checkpoint now covers all 100 tasks (we did not have
the resources to fine-tune multiple checkpoints). We cannot
attribute the gain to longer training alone: the policy also saw
demonstrations from 50 additional tasks, and we made model
improvements and bug fixes. The 2026 episodes had a shorter
time limit; the evaluations used different simulator versions,
but we did not observe a meaningful performance difference
between them.
Recovery data helps a little, but we could not scale it.
Extra recovery data had a small positive effect on under-
trained models: scripted recoveries raised the success rate
on turning_on_radio from about 50% to 60–75%, and
human corrections raised Q on one task from 0.267 to 0.367, a
difference that was not significant. We found no efficient way
to collect such data for 100 tasks, and we did not test it on the
final, better-trained model.
A practicing LLM agent solves what the policy cannot,
at a high price.After practicing on training instances in
an automated research loop, GPT-6 Astra reached a mean
Q of 0.639 across 14 selected tasks, compared with 0.108
for the learned policy on those tasks (Figure 11). On
installing_smoke_detectors it scored 1.0, where
the policy scores 0.10. This in-context learning from its own
practice is the most striking result of our work. It is also expen-
sive and slow: an agent episode took a median of 0.63 hours
of wall time, about 17 times longer than real time, and tens of
dollars in API fees, while six simulators served by the learned
policy together run faster than real time on one GPU, and a
full 1,000-episode evaluation costs about $300. We had the
agent route working only one to two days before the deadline,
so it is far from tuned. Making such agents cheaper and faster,
or moving what they learn into the policy, remains open.

A Inference Details
The serving loop is the 2025 one with re-tuned parameters:
predict 30 actions with 20 denoising steps, execute a prefix,
keep the next actions as the inpainting anchor of the next
prediction, and update the stage by voting. The changes:
• Soft inpainting.As in 2025, each denoising step moves
the anchored coordinates 70% of the way to the an-
chor; the correlated correction of the free coordinates
(ΣUO Σ−1
OOδO) is now capped per step instead of being
dropped.
• Faster playback.The first 26 predicted actions are exe-
cuted in 13 environment steps by cubic resampling, and
each new chunk is shifted to start at the last executed
action with an offset that decays by 0.7 per step.
• Stage votingover a fixed window of 120 environment
steps, and a minimum stage duration of 0.67× the short-
est duration of that stage in the demonstrations.
• Gripper rulemined from the data: a gripper may stay
fully closed in a (task, side, stage) only if more than
15% of the demonstrations close it there for at least 0.5 s
(pressing a button or switch). Elsewhere a fully closed
gripper has missed its grasp, and it is opened.

RE-SEARCH: Dissecting LLM Ideation
Through a Two-Player Questioning Game
Muhan Gao1 Hangxiao Zhu1 Xinqi Su1 Yu Zhang1
Daniel Khashabi2,† Kuan-Hao Huang1,†
1Texas A&M University 2Johns Hopkins University
Abstract
Research ideation is iterative: researchers re-
fine their ideas step by step based on feed-
back. Yet existing evaluations obscure this
search process, making it difficult to under-
stand how LLMs explore the space of research
ideas and what limits their progress. We intro-
duce RE-SEARCH, which adapts the format of
Twenty Questions to research ideation: given
only the research problem of a published pa-
per, a model must rediscover the paper’s core
idea by asking yes-or-no questions. Built from
200 ICML 2026 papers, RE-SEARCHtracks
how a model’s idea evolves as it asks ques-
tions and receives binary oracle feedback, iso-
lating ideation from execution. Across six re-
cent LLMs, nearly all progress happens within
the first 30 of 100 questions, which largely de-
cide how the game ends; after that, most mod-
els plateau. Through controlled interventions
on the candidate questions and the hypothesis
space, we find that the bottleneck is generation,
not judgment: models recognize a good idea or
a good question when one is offered, but often
cannot produce it on their own. We further ana-
lyze the ideation traces and find that models fail
by either over-exploiting one direction or over-
exploring too many. These findings point to
concrete design principles for autoresearch sys-
tems: since models can judge candidates they
cannot produce, enriching the search with exter-
nally sourced ideas and questions may be more
effective than improving any single model’s
generation ability.
1 Introduction
Research ideation is not a one-shot proposal but
an iterative searchinterleavedwith every stage of
a project: researchers form hypotheses, test them,
and refine them based on feedback. This process
can be viewed asadaptive information seekingover
a space of plausible yet unverified ideas (Klahr

provide limited visibility into this iterative search.
Ideation benchmarks evaluate one-shot proposals
using LLM judges (Guo et al., 2025; Chen et al.,
2025), overlooking how ideas evolve through feed-
back. End-to-end benchmarks involve iterative
search but entangle it with coding, debugging, and
experimentation (Wijk et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026;
Rank et al., 2026; Lupidi et al., 2026; Garikaparthi
et al., 2026; Chan et al., 2025), making it difficult
to distinguish failures of ideation from failures of
execution.
In this work, we aim to isolate the information-
seeking process from the rest of autoresearch. To
this end, we introduce RE-SEARCH, a two-player
questioning game that makes every step of this
process observable and measurable (Fig 1). The
setting is a scientific variant of Twenty Ques-
tions (Mosher and Hornsby, 1966; Siegler, 1977),
a classic paradigm in cognitive science for study-
ing human reasoning and problem solving (Coenen
et al., 2019). Given only the research problem of
