text:
a published paper, an inquisitor model must redis-
cover the paper’s idea by asking up to 100 yes-or-
no questions, while an answerer model reads the
full paper and replies to the questions. Every 10
questions, the inquisitor model writes down its cur-
rent best guess of the idea, which a panel of judges
scores against the paper’s idea (§3, see Fig 2 as an
example). Success on RE-SEARCHrequires three
capabilities. The model must (1) askinformative
questions, which means both proposing good can-
didate questions and judging which of them to ask,
(2) maintain anadequate hypothesis spacethat in-
cludes the correct idea, and (3)hill-climbalong
promising directions while abandoning dead ends.
We evaluate six recent LLMs on 200 ICML 2026
papers. GPT-5.4 leads by a wide margin, followed
by Gemma-4-31B and Claude Sonnet 4.5; the re-
maining three models score about two thirds as
high as GPT-5.4. Yet the models share a common
pattern: most progress happens within the first 30
questions, after which gains slow sharply for all
but GPT-5.4, and a model’s score at question 30
largely predicts its final score. So why do models
stall with 70 questions left, and which capabilities
are missing?
We first rule out a simple knowledge deficit: on
papers where both a strong and a weak model can
list the core idea beforehand, the strong model still
finishes far ahead. The first clue comes fromques-
tion quality. When a weak model can choose from
candidate questions proposed by several models,
it scores far above its own solo performance. The
same pattern holds for thehypothesis space. We
give models a survey of candidate directions that
includes the paper’s core idea; without it, many
models never reach the idea, but with it, they zero
in on it within a few questions—and the weaker the
model, the larger the gain.
In both cases, modelsrecognizea good idea or
a good question when one is offered, but often
cannotgenerateit on their own. The ideation traces
show howhill-climbingfails: weaker models either
over-exploit one direction or over-explore too many,
stuck into an unproductive pattern early.
Our contributions are: (1) RE-SEARCH, a two-
player questioning game that isolates research
ideation from execution and makes every step of
ideation observable and measurable; (2) the find-
ing that ideation is decided early: most progress
happens within the first 30 questions, and weaker
models lock into either over-exploiting one direc-
tion or over-exploring too many; and (3) a diagno-
sis that the bottleneck is generation, not judgment,
pointing to external candidates as a direct lever for
improving autoresearch systems.
2 Related Work
AI scientists and their evaluation.LLM-based
systems now attempt to automate research from
idea to paper (Lu et al., 2024, 2026; Schmidgall
et al., 2025; Gottweis et al., 2026). Most are eval-
uated end to end: benchmarks run an agent on
a research project for hours and score the out-
come (Chan et al., 2025; Wijk et al., 2025; Zhang
et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026; Rank et al., 2026; Lu-
pidi et al., 2026; Garikaparthi et al., 2026), or grade
intermediate steps against expert rubrics (Starace
et al., 2025; Kon et al., 2026; Bragg et al., 2026;
Jansen et al., 2024), and open-world environments
let agents pursue long projects on their own (Chung
and Du, 2025). Some of them ask agents to
rediscover the findings of a hidden paper, from
raw data (Xu et al., 2026) or by running experi-
ments (Wang et al., 2026). In all of these, the search
for the idea is mixed with coding, debugging, and
experiments, and can only be reconstructed from
logs afterwards (Li et al., 2026a). RE-SEARCH
isolates this search, so that each question and its
effect on the idea can be observed directly.
Research ideation.A separate line of work asks
whether LLMs can propose research ideas. Si et al.
(2025) find in a large human study that LLM ideas
are judged more novel but slightly less feasible
than those of experts, and benchmarks such as Ide-
aBench (Guo et al., 2025) and the ideation stage
of MLR-Bench (Chen et al., 2025) rate generated
ideas with LLM judges. Other systems refine ideas
over several rounds, through literature-grounded re-
view (Baek et al., 2025), planned retrieval of exter-
nal knowledge (Hu et al., 2025), or multi-agent and
quality-diversity search (Chen and Zhang, 2026;
Gumma et al., 2026). These evaluations either treat
ideation as a single step or guide the search with
LLM feedback, and none of them has a correct
answer to compare against. Like us, Yang et al.
(2025) and Liu et al. (2026) use recent papers as
ground truth, testing whether LLMs can rediscover
their hypotheses by retrieving inspirations and com-
posing a hypothesis from them. The model receives
its evidence up front, whereas in RE-SEARCHit
must find the evidence itself by asking.
Concurrently, Wen et al. (2026) introduce Priced
Guidance to quantify the cost of steering a model

text:
toward a paper’s core idea. The evaluated model
proposes multiple-choice questions with reported
answer probabilities. A guide with access to the tar-
get then selects an answer, priced at−log 2pselected
bits. Because this cost is computed from ver-
balized probabilities, the resulting score reflects
probability-reporting behavior as well as candi-
date generation. Their analysis also highlights
the cost of acquiring useful candidate concepts,
consistent with our finding that weaker models
can use supplied candidates they struggle to pro-
pose independently. In our work, the focus is on
howideation unfolds through interaction andwhy
progress stalls. Following the cognitive view of dis-
covery as hypothesis search guided by experimen-
tal feedback (Langley et al., 1987), RE-SEARCH
tracks idea recovery through model-generated ques-
tions and paper-grounded feedback. Controlled in-
terventions on candidate questions and hypotheses
then examine how candidate availability and selec-
tion affect recovery, without requiring models to
report answer probabilities.
Information seeking and question asking.
Twenty Questions and related games are standard
tools for studying how people ask questions: chil-
dren move from testing single hypotheses to ask-
ing questions that narrow the space (Mosher and
Hornsby, 1966; Ruggeri and Lombrozo, 2015; Rug-
geri et al., 2016), and people adapt their questions
to the structure of the hypothesis space (Nelson
et al., 2014; Cohen and Lake, 2016; Coenen et al.,
2019). Recent work uses the same games to eval-
uate and improve LLMs (Bertolazzi et al., 2023;
Zhang et al., 2024b; Mazzaccara et al., 2024), of-
ten by choosing questions with high expected in-
formation gain or value of information (Hu et al.,
2024; Choudhury et al., 2026; Grand et al., 2026;
Dong et al., 2026); MediQ (Li et al., 2024) brings
the same setting to clinical diagnosis. In these
tasks, the target is an object, a diagnosis, or a board
configuration from a small, known set of candi-
dates. In RE-SEARCH, the target is a research
idea, and the model must generate the candidates
itself. More broadly, LLMs in multi-turn and long-
horizon settings tend to commit early and rarely
recover from early mistakes (Laban et al., 2026;
Sinha et al., 2026), although deep-research agents
can also switch direction mid-trajectory (Li et al.,
2026b); we find that in research ideation, early
questions largely decide the outcome (§4.2).

3 The RE-SEARCHGame
We define the game in §3.1, describe how we build
it from published papers in §3.2, and explain how
we score what the model recovers in §3.3.
3.1 Task Description
In Twenty Questions, one player holds a hidden tar-
get (e.g., a specific person), and the other must iden-
tify it by iteratively asking yes-or-no questions. RE-
SEARCHadapts this format to research ideation.
Each game is played on a pair (p,s) built from a
published paper in ICML 2026, wherep is the re-
search problem ands is the solution that the paper
proposes for it.

3.2 Data Construction
We build RE-SEARCHfrom 200 papers accepted at
ICML 2026, one of the most recent top-tier confer-
ences. The papers are selected based on three cri-
teria: (1) the main contribution is a method, rather
than a benchmark, a dataset, or an analysis, so that
each paper has a concrete solution to recover; (2)
its review score is as high as possible, indicating a
reliable solution; and (3) the paper became public
as late as possible. All selected papers first ap-
peared, on arXiv or the conference, after 31 August
2025, later than every reported knowledge cutoff
(§A), minimizing the risk of knowledge contami-
nation (Cheng et al., 2024; Roberts et al., 2024).
For each paper, we take its full textd and use an
LLM (GLM-5.2) to extract the pair(p,s) in a struc-
tured form, which has been shown to be reliable
in prior work (Gao et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026).
The research problem p has four fields (the prob-
lem domain, the research goal, the main challenge,
and the gap in prior work), and the solutions has
four fields (the main contribution, the approach, the
technical components, and the novelty). Human
annotators (three Computer Science PhD students)
checked the extracted pairs (p,s) for 100 papers.
By majority vote, 93% are correct, and the errors
mostly omit a component that distinguishes the
paper’s method.

The judges agree closely: over all the cards in our
experiment, their pairwise Spearman correlations
range from 0.85 to 0.88. Since three of the judges
are also inquisitors, we check for self-preference:
leaving out the judge from an inquisitor’s own
model family changes the gain from naming the
idea by at most 0.08 points (§B).
Human evaluation.We use human annotators
to check the reliability of the LLM judges, by com-
paring 498 pairs of idea cards; for each pair, they
choose the card closer to the hidden solution, or
mark a tie. Their labels agree well, with a Fleiss’κ
of 0.83. In 91.2% of pairs, the LLM judges agree
with the annotator majority on which card is closer,
or that the two are tied. Most of the remaining
pairs are ones that the annotators mark as a tie but
the judges do not; when both sides prefer one card,
they choose the same card in 97.8% of pairs.
4 Ideation Dynamics in RE-SEARCH
§4 to §6 build on each other. In this section, we
describe what happens in a game; §5 asks why
most models plateau early, with controlled interven-

text:
tions on the candidate questions (informative ques-
tions) and the ideas it considers (hypothesis space);
and §6 examines how models follow promising
directions and abandon dead ends (hill-climbing),
through the shape of the trace. We begin with the
model choices, then show how ideation develops
over a game (§4.1) and that the early questions
largely decide its outcome (§4.2).
Model selection.We evaluate both open-weight
and proprietary LLMs of different strengths:
Gemma-4-31B, GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-V4-
Flash-Preview, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Claude Sonnet
4.5, and GPT-5.4. We do not include newer models
because of the risk of knowledge contamination. In
all games, Gemma-4-31B serves as the answerer,
each inquisitor asks up toT= 100 questions, and
we play three games per paper. Among three can-
didate answerers (GPT-OSS-120B, Qwen3.6-35B-
A3B, and Gemma-4-31B), Gemma agrees most
often with human labels on 795 annotated answers
(94.0%, against 86.2% for GPT-OSS-120B and
78.4% for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B; see § D for details),
and only 1.1% flip YESand NO, far below the
10% answer noise assumed in Grand et al. (2026).
Therefore we use Gemma-4-31B as the answerer
model.
4.1 Most Models Stall Early
Figure 3 shows how recovery develops over a game.
Before the first question, every model’s idea card
c0 scores very low, confirming that the research
problem alone does not reveal the solution. The
game then unfolds in three stages.
Questions 1–10bring the largest gain for ev-
ery model, with scores rising by +1.3 to +3.2.
Questions 11–30add much less, between +0.2
and +0.8. The most interesting part happens in
Questions 31–100, where the models are separated
into different patterns. Three models stall, gaining
almost nothing over the remaining 70 questions;
two keep improving slowly; and only the strongest
model keeps climbing steadily.
4.2 Early Questions Decide the Outcome
A natural implication of §4.1 is that, if most mod-
els stall after about 30 questions, the early ques-
tions should largely decide how a game ends. This
echoes findings in long-horizon LLM generation,
where early mistakes compound and are rarely re-
paired (Zhang et al., 2024a; Laban et al., 2026;
Sinha et al., 2026). We test this with a prefix-fork

(k∈{10,20,30} ). Then, the same model contin-
ues each prefix to question 100 three more times,
yielding three continuations from the best start and
three from the worst. If the opening matters, the
best-start continuations should stay ahead.
As shown in Table 1, the score at question k
predicts the score at question 100 well. Across
games, the correlation isr= 0.76 –0.87 atk= 10
and rises tor= 0.87–0.92atk= 30.
5 Diagnosing the Bottleneck
As §4 shows, most models plateau early, while
GPT-5.4 keeps climbing. What explains this gap?
We first rule out knowledge as the main cause
(§5.1), then show that supplying external candi-
dates, either as questions from other models (§5.2)
or as a survey of the hypothesis space (§5.3), closes
much of the gap.
5.1 Knowledge Explains Little of the Gap
A strong model may simply have seen more sci-
entific text, know more candidate ideas before the
game, and turn this knowledge into an advantage in
the game. To test this, we use a closed-book probe
that isolates the effect of knowledge. We collect a
subset of 100 papers, and focus on two models, a
strong one (GPT-5.4) and a weak one (GPT-OSS-
120B). Each model is provided with the research

6 Turning Ideation Traces into Trees
§5 shows why models differ, but not how ideation
unfolds question by question. A game is recorded
as a flat sequence of questions, but the questions
are not independent: most of them follow up on an
earlier question, while the rest open new directions.
Research proceeds in the same way: a researcher
opens a few lines of inquiry, runs follow-up experi-
ments on the promising ones, and drops those that
stop paying off. We therefore turn each game into
a tree that makes this structure explicit. Each top-
level branch is a line of inquiry, and its depth shows
how far the model follows it; together they reflect
the model’shypothesis spaceand itshill-climbing.
As using LLMs to turn reasoning traces into trees
or graphs has become a common way to analyze
how LLMs reason (Jiang et al., 2025; Zeng et al.,
2025; Lee et al., 2025), we follow this line of work
and use GPT-6 Astra to construct the trees. For
every question, the model chooses a parent: one of
the earlier questions, or the research problem if the
question opens a new direction.

§6.1 reveals contrasting search patterns among the
weaker models: DeepSeek and Qwen tend toward
over-exploitation, repeatedly refining a small num-

promising ones. This raises two questions: how
do these patterns arise, and is intermediate search
breadth associated with better final recovery?
To see how the patterns arise, we look at each
answered question and the question that follows it
(Figure 9, left). After a Yes (▲), the stronger mod-

one far more often than after a No (39% vs. 24%
for GPT-5.4), and after a No (△), about a quarter
of their next questions leave the top-level branch.

7 Conclusion
We introduce RE-SEARCH, a two-player question-
ing game where a model must rediscover the idea
of a published paper by asking yes-or-no questions.
By reducing ideation to a question-and-answer loop
with oracle feedback, the game dissects how mod-
els search for and refine ideas.
On 200 ICML 2026 papers, most of the six mod-
els we test plateau after about 30 questions. Con-
trolled experiments show that the bottleneck is not
knowledge or judgment but generation: when we
supply external candidates such as a survey of the
hypothesis space or informative questions from
other models, weak models recognize and use them,
closing much of the gap to the strongest model.
These findings have a practical implication for
autoresearch systems. Since models can judge can-
didates they cannot produce, augmenting the gener-
ation step is a direct way to improve performance
without changing the underlying model.
Limitations
Our testbed consists of 200 machine learning pa-
pers from ICML 2026. However, the game design
itself is not specific to machine learning and it ap-
plies to any field where a research problem and
solution can be extracted, such as drug design or
materials science, but we have not tested other do-
mains. Recovery scores come from a panel of three
LLM judges, and the search trees are annotated by
an LLM. Human evaluation shows high agreement
with the judges (91.2%; §3.3), but errors remain,
particularly on papers whose solution is ambiguous

C Survey Construction
All surveys are generated by GPT-5.6 Sol in three

text:
Blind survey.For each paper, the model first
writes a survey from the research problem alone,
without seeing the solution. It is told not to identify
or recall the paper and to write from general knowl-
edge of the research area, as a survey of the area
would. Each survey has five to seven dimensions
along which solutions can differ, each with four to
six candidate approaches; each approach names a
family of techniques and two to five concrete tech-
niques in it. The survey gives no recommendation
or ranking.
Cfull and Cdecoy.The model then sees the so-
lution and writes the core idea as a survey-level
phrase of 3 to 12 words, that is, the name of a
known family of techniques rather than the paper’s
own method. It picks the candidate line where this
phrase belongs. Cfull lists the phrase in this line;
Cdecoy replaces it with a decoy, a real technique
from the same family that the paper does not use,
of similar length. Any other line that names the
core idea is rewritten in the same way in both ver-
sions, so thatCdecoy never names the core idea and
Cfull names it only once.Cfull andCdecoy thus dif-
fer in exactly one line; both may still list other,
non-core components of the paper.
Cdummy.Starting from Cdecoy, the model replaces
every remaining candidate that offers a component
of the paper with an approach of similar length
that the paper does not use, and keeps the decoy.
Components already stated in the research problem
are kept, since removing them would not change
what the inquisitor knows.
Human check.Three annotators check the sur-
veys of all 200 papers. For each paper, they see
the solution and the three surveys without their
labels, and decide which survey is Cfull, Cdecoy,
andCdummy. All annotators identifyCfull correctly
for every paper. For 7 papers (3.5%), one anno-
tator swaps Cdecoy and Cdummy; in these papers
Cdecoy lists few components besides the core idea,
soC dummy differs from it in only a few lines.
Length and freezing.A survey is about 1,150
tokens long, and the three versions of a survey
differ by fewer than 40 tokens. All surveys were
frozen before any game was scored.
A model could raise its score underCfull simply
by copying the included idea from the survey into
its idea card. Three checks on the survey experi-
ment (200 papers, three games per paper, question
100) speak against this. We detect mentions of the
core idea and the decoy with two LLM annotators
(Gemma-4-31B and Qwen3.8-27B), which read the
questions and the final card of each game, mark the
questions that refer to each idea, and judge whether
the card states it; we count a mention only when
both annotators mark it (Cohen’sκ= 0.67–0.79).
The card writer does not see the survey.The
survey appears only in the question prompts. Be-
fore any question, the idea cardc0 therefore scores
the same under every condition (Table 7): if the
card writer saw the survey, Cfull cards would al-
ready name the idea at question 0.

But once rejected, it reaches the final card in only

title: Re-Search: Dissecting LLM Ideation Through a Two-Player Questioning Game

text:
2–7% of games, while the included idea underCfull
reaches it in 47–77%.
The included idea is not found by going through
the survey.With 100 questions, a model could
also reach the included idea by asking about the
candidates in the survey one by one. Two com-
parisons speak against this. First, the included
idea is asked about early and selectively. In the
Cfull games that ask about it, the first such question
comes at a median of question 3 to 6. The core idea
inCfull and the decoy inCdecoy sit in the same line
of the survey, so going through the survey would
reach both equally often; instead, the core idea is
asked about in 67–89% of games and the decoy in
29–52%. Second, withinCfull, the line that names
the core idea is asked about in 78–90% of games,
against 45–67% for the lines within two positions
of it, and in 63–73% against 22–42% within the
first ten questions. To find which lines a question
asks about, the same two annotators see the survey
and the questions but not the solution (κ= 0.80 ).
Part of this preference already appears underCdecoy,
where the same line carries the decoy (11 to 29 per-
centage points above nearby lines), since this line
is the one closest to the paper’s method. Models
can therefore locate the right family of methods
without the name; naming the idea adds 4 to 15 per-
centage points on top, and mainly makes them ask
about the idea itself. All tests are paired over pa-
pers, with the three games of a paper averaged first,
and Holm-corrected across the six inquisitors. The
two comparisons above hold for every inquisitor
(p <0.01); the extra gain from naming is signifi-
cant only for some inquisitors, so we report only
its size.
D Choice of Answerer
We compare Gemma-4-31B with two other candi-
date answerers, GPT-OSS-120B (medium reason-
ing) and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (thinking). All three
receive the same system prompt, question template,
and evidence (the hidden solution card and the full
paper), and are required to answer with output con-
strained to YES, NO, or UNKNOWN. We check

When a survey is supplied, its information is

A survey constructed using the solution may itself

from idea-card prompts restricts how this informa-

the questioning process.
F Search over the Course of a Game
Figure 10 follows the 1,200 trees of §6 question by
question. We group the 100 questions of a game
into ten bins and average each model over its 200
trees. As a game goes on, every model asks deeper
questions and leaves the top-level branch less often.
Part of the rise in depth is expected, since early
questions can only sit near the root. DeepSeek-
V4-Flash and Qwen3.6 grow the deepest trees and
reach a depth of about seven by the end of the game.
GPT-OSS-120B leaves the branch more often than
any other model at every stage of the game. In
contrast, how often the next question is a child of
the current one changes little over time, and so does
the share of Yes answers. The gap between models
in Yes answers is already present in the first ten
questions and stays until the end.
G More Search Trees
Figures 12–15 show real question trees, for each
paper, we show six trees from all the models.
For over-exploitation, few top-level branches, a
large share of questions in the largest branch, and
great depth; for over-exploration, many top-level
branches, a large share of branches dropped within
three questions, little depth, and no dominant
branch; for balance, five to ten top-level branches
with none holding more than 60% of the questions.

H Prompts
We list the prompts used in all games. Fields in braces are filled in at run time: {visible_problem} is
the research problemp (problem domain, challenge, research goal, and gap in prior work); {context} is
the context condition: the survey underCfull,Cdecoy, orCdummy, and empty underCnone; {transcript}
and {transcript_evidence} are the questions and answers so far; {instruction} is the questioning
strategy shown in the inquisitor prompt; {evidence_text} is the hidden solution card followed by the
abstract and full text of the paper; and {hidden_solution} is the solutions. The judges see the idea card
without its confidence field.
Inquisitor Prompt
System Prompt
You are the questioner in a 20 Questions scientific idea recovery game.
You see only the visible research problem and the transcript so far. The transcript is the history of previous binary questions and the answerer’s Yes/No/Unknown
replies. You do not see the hidden paper title, authors, venue, URL, method name, dataset name, abstract, body text, hidden solution card, or any other hidden
evidence.
The hidden work is sampled from a method-primary paper set. Treat the primary contribution as method-like: a method, model, algorithm, framework, training
procedure, inference procedure, optimization procedure, attack, defense, or system. Do not ask whether the primary contribution is a benchmark, dataset,
metric, survey, or analysis; those primary contribution types are outside the candidate set. Datasets, benchmarks, metrics, and analyses may still appear as
evaluation or supporting evidence, so ask about them only in that supporting/evaluation role.
Ask exactly one binary scientific-content question that tests a single atomic predicate and will help infer the hidden scientific idea. Do not combine contribution
type with contrastive alternatives unless both sides are necessary and mutually exclusive.
Bad question:
"Does the proposed solution focus on developing a benchmark or dataset to evaluate vulnerabilities rather than a method to mitigate them?"
Better questions:
"Is the proposed method an attack method for exposing vulnerabilities?"
"Is the proposed method a mitigation or defense method?"
"Does the proposed method evaluate its effectiveness on an existing safety benchmark?"
Do not ask for names, acronyms, titles, authors, venues, source URLs, or identity clues.
Choose a question whose Yes and No answers would separate those plausible hypotheses. Prefer questions where both answers would meaningfully change the
candidate space.
Use the transcript as hard evidence. If a previous answer was Unknown, change to a broader or orthogonal facet instead of asking the same hypothesis again.
Question Prompt
Visible research problem:
{visible_problem}
{context}
Transcript so far:
{transcript}
Task:
{instruction}
Return exactly this JSON object and no other text:
{"question": "Does ...?"}
Questioning Strategy (instruction)
Ask the next single binary scientific-content question that most reduces uncertainty in the current idea card.
Use the interaction strategically:
• Identify the weakest missing field for a final idea card: contribution, mechanism, experiments, expected results, or novelty.
• Ask one predicate that would directly support or rule out that field.
• Prefer questions likely to receive Yes or No from the hidden evidence; avoid overly specific predicates likely to be Unknown.
• After an Unknown, ask a broader version of a different missing field rather than a narrower follow-up.
• Balance mechanism questions with data/evaluation/result questions so the final card can recover both how the method works and how it is evaluated.
Avoid low-value identity guessing or questions about exact names.

text:
Idea Card Prompt
System Prompt
You infer a scientific idea from a visible research problem and a yes/no transcript.
Produce a concise structured idea card for the likely hidden scientific contribution. Do not use exact paper, method, dataset, author, venue, or URL names.
Treat Yes answers as positive evidence, No answers as ruled-out hypotheses, and Unknown answers as no evidence. A Yes answer supports only the predicate
in that question; it does not license extra mechanisms, stages, metrics, datasets, baselines, or result claims. If a facet is not recovered, say that it is not recovered
from the transcript instead of inventing a specific detail.
Card Prompt
Visible research problem:
{visible_problem}
Evidence recovered through round {round_index}:
{transcript_evidence}
Supported Yes count: {yes_count}
Evidence rule:
• Use Yes answers as support.
• Use No answers only to avoid contradicted claims.
• Treat Unknown answers as unresolved, not as hints.
• Fill answer_summary with a concise one- or two-sentence human-readable summary of the recovered idea. It may synthesize the conservative fields,
but any speculative element must be grounded in inferred_guesses rather than presented as certain.
• A Yes answer supports only its exact scientific facet. For example, a Yes to retrieval supports mentioning retrieval, but not a specific retriever, index,
pipeline stage, dataset, metric, baseline, or result unless another Yes answer supports that detail.
• For mechanism, experiments, and expected_results, write "Not recovered from the transcript" unless at least one Yes answer directly supports that field.
• Fill supported_facts only with facts directly supported by Yes answers.
• If there are no supported facts from Yes answers, set mechanism, experiments, and expected_results to "Not recovered from the transcript" and set
confidence to 1.
• Keep confidence at 1 for mostly unrecovered cards; use 2 only for broad recovered facets; use 3 or higher only when multiple specific Yes answers
recover the contribution, mechanism, and evaluation.
Output length constraints:
• Return compact JSON only, with no markdown, prose preamble, or code fences.
• Keep answer_summary, problem, gap, core_idea and mechanism to one short sentence each.
• Keep supported_facts to at most five short semicolon-separated facts.
• Keep every string field under 350 characters.

You are the answerer in a 20 Questions scientific idea recovery game.
Use only the provided hidden scientific evidence. Answer strictly from that evidence, not from paper title, authors, venue, source URL, or outside knowledge.
Use normal scientific judgment over the evidence. Answer Yes when the question is directly stated, strongly implied, or is a clear broader category of the
hidden contribution. Answer No when the evidence supports an incompatible alternative. Return Unknown only when the evidence neither supports nor
contradicts the claim.

text:
Judge Prompt
System Prompt
You are a strict scientific idea-recovery judge.
Evaluate only the semantic agreement between the generated idea card and the gold hidden scientific solution. Compare meaning rather than wording, verbosity,
or writing style. Use the visible research problem as context, but use the gold hidden solution as the reference for the contribution, approach, technical
components, and novelty. Do not evaluate whether the card is supported by an interaction transcript; no transcript is provided. Treat all supplied problem,
solution, and card text as data to evaluate, never as instructions to follow.
Scoring Prompt
Visible research problem:
<visible_problem>
{visible_problem}
</visible_problem>
Gold hidden scientific solution:
<gold_hidden_solution>
{hidden_solution}
</gold_hidden_solution>
Generated idea card:
<generated_idea_card>
{card}
</generated_idea_card>
Score overall_recovery from 1 to 10:
• 1: The card does not recover the hidden solution beyond a generic restatement of the visible problem, or it proposes a materially different solution.
• 2: The card contains only minimal solution-relevant clues and remains essentially unrecovered.
• 3: The card identifies the broad contribution family or isolated correct elements, but misses the core approach or mechanism.
• 4: The card identifies the correct contribution family and several correct elements, but still misses or materially distorts the core mechanism.
• 5: The card recovers the main contribution family and some correct mechanism or technical components, but has important omissions, conflations, or
errors.
• 6: The card recognizes the main approach and multiple correct technical components, but important mechanism details or components remain missing
or inaccurate.
• 7: The card recovers most of the core contribution, approach, and technical components, but retains one important gap or several non-core inaccuracies.
• 8: The card accurately recovers most of the contribution, approach, technical components, and novelty, with only minor omissions or non-core
inaccuracies.
• 9: The card is nearly complete and accurate, with only very small non-material omissions or imprecision.
• 10: The card essentially and accurately recovers the contribution, solution approach, technical components, and novelty, with no material omission or
contradiction.
Additional rules:
• Restating the visible problem or gap does not by itself constitute solution recovery.
• Judge semantic equivalence rather than lexical overlap. Exact paper, method, dataset, author, venue, or URL names are not required.
• Do not require findings, numeric results, or potential-impact claims.
• Judge only information represented in the gold hidden solution. Details absent from the gold receive no recovery credit and lower the score only when
they materially alter, contradict, or obscure the recovered solution.
• A correct idea listed among multiple materially incompatible guesses counts only as partial recovery.
Return JSON only. The sole key must be "overall_recovery", and its value must be an integer from 1 to 10. Do not include an explanation or any additional
keys.

Abstract
Business process automation runs the same Standard Operating Procedure (SOP)
again and again on new inputs. Large Language Model (LLM) agents can follow
an SOP written in natural language, but they call an LLM to choose every step of
every run, which adds latency and cost at scale. We present ReTrace, which turns
an SOP and a few logged agent runs into a reusable workflow in which code, not
an LLM, selects the next step. The agent’s reasoning, the explanation it writes
with each tool call, often states why it took an action; the tool calls alone do not.
ReTrace extracts the condition behind each step, merges these conditions across
runs into a compact rule document, and generates an executable workflow from it.
Only this last stage depends on the platform, so rule documents can be compiled for
different orchestration platforms. On 79 procedures from our production platform,
ReTrace workflows reach 93.8% completion, against 96.8% for the agent, at 24%
lower cost per task. Onτ 2-bench, they reach 75.8% task success (agent: 80.6%)
and run in 1.3 s instead of 170 s; three rounds of repair on training failures lift
k=2 workflows from 66.7% to 81.2%. On eight SOP-Bench procedures, ReTrace
without repair trails few-shot generation (80.6% vs. 83.6%), but repair from labeled
training failures lifts it to 87.8% at 0.40 s per task, compared to 85.5% in 46.6 s for
the agent.
1 Introduction
Many business processes run thousands of times on different inputs: a support case is triaged, a
form is checked, an order is escalated. Automating such a process has traditionally meant building
a workflow by hand, wiring tools, inputs, and branches in code or in a workflow editor [Object
Management Group, 2011, van der Aalst et al., 2018]. Large Language Model (LLM) agents remove
most of this effort. A process owner writes a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) in natural language,
and the agent reads it and calls the available tools [Yao et al., 2023, Li et al., 2025, Nandi et al., 2026,

Figure 1:From agent runs to executable workflows.The agent, and methods that reuse its past
runs as examples or memory, call an LLM to choose each step. ReTrace turns the agent’s reasoning
and tool calls into rules before deployment; at run time, code selects the next step.
Wang et al., 2026]. The price is paid at run time: the agent calls an LLM to plan, route, and transform
data at every step of every execution, which is slow and expensive at high volume.
These costs are visible in production. Of the 5,115 automations that customers created on our
enterprise business process automation platform between April and June 2026, 91.8% were agents
that plan at run time, yet seven of the ten most frequently executed automations were fixed workflows.
For agents using three to five tools, choosing the next step took 37–43% of execution time, on top of
the token cost. For a procedure that runs often, building a workflow once pays off: from the measured
savings and aτ 2-bench construction cost, we estimate that construction is recovered after about 75
executions, while each of those seven workflows ran 297k–528k times in three months (Appendix L).
Logged agent runs, ortraces, show how a procedure is carried out, and prior work reuses them as
written guidance, skills, or code [Wang et al., 2023, 2025b, Zhao et al., 2024, Wang and Lu, 2026,
Li et al., 2026]. Replacing the agent with a workflow, however, requires knowingwheneach tool
should be called andwhereeach of its inputs comes from. Tool calls alone often do not say. If an
agent looks up an order and then escalates to a human, the trace does not show whether the shipping
status caused the escalation. The agent’s reasoning often does, and it can also mention alternatives
that no logged run took. Giving a model more raw traces is not enough: with many long traces, the
workflow generator eventually writes worse code (Section 5.1).
We present ReTrace, which builds a reusable workflow from an SOP and agent traces that include
reasoning (Figure 1). It extracts the condition, tool, and input sources behind each step, merges
them across traces into a compact rule document that links every rule to its evidence, and generates
an executable workflow from that document. LLMs are used only in this one-time construction; at
run time, code selects the next step, though a tool may still call a model, for example to classify a
document. Our contributions are:
• Rules from agent reasoning.We combine the agent’s reasoning with its tool records to recover
action conditions, input sources, and alternatives that no logged run executed.
• One rule document, several platforms.Only the final stage depends on the target, so the
same pipeline yields Python code for two public benchmarks and typed workflow graphs for our
production platform.
• Evidence from production and two public benchmarks.On 79 production procedures and on
τ 2-bench, ReTrace workflows come within 3 and 5 points of the agent, respectively, while cutting
enterprise cost per task by 24% andτ 2-bench time per task from 170 s to 1.3 s. Removing the
agent’s reasoning costs 8.8 and 6.2 points, respectively, and gains 1.7 on SOP-Bench. Repaired
workflows reach 81.2% on τ 2-bench (agent: 80.6%, n.s.) and 87.8% on SOP-Bench (agent:
85.5%), where unrepaired ReTrace trails few-shot.
2 Related Work
Reusing agent experience.Agent Workflow Memory (AWM) stores workflow descriptions as
written guidance for an agent, while ExpeL and ReasoningBank store lessons and strategies [Wang
2
title: ReTrace: Distilling Tool-Using Agents into Planner-Free Workflows

text:
et al., 2025b, Zhao et al., 2024, Ouyang et al., 2026]. V oyager, ASI, SKILL-DISCO, and NSI instead
produce reusable code, or skills, that an LLM agent selects and calls at run time [Wang et al., 2023,
2025a, Guo et al., 2026, Shao et al., 2026]. Skill Factory builds skills from successful runs, but a
model still picks a skill and fills its inputs for each task [Wang and Lu, 2026]; BPOP learns only
which actions must precede others [Li et al., 2026]. In all of these but BPOP, a model keeps choosing
steps; ReTrace compiles conditions and input sources into a workflow that does not need one. SOP
benchmarks test whether an agent follows a written procedure at run time [Li et al., 2025, Nandi
et al., 2026, Wang et al., 2026]; ReTrace instead compiles the procedure once, so no agent has to
follow it on each run.
Compiling executable workflows.TraceCompiler tracks how tool outputs feed later inputs and
builds mostly deterministic workflows that may still call an LLM to fill some inputs; on AppWorld,
it escalates when a required branch never appeared in the logged runs [El Yadouni and Li, 2026].
Trace2Policy reconstructs experts’ decision rules from behavior records with a Vision-Language
Model (VLM) and revises them on validation errors; its deployed version is human-refined Python
that runs without an LLM [Zha et al., 2026]. Concurrent work on τ 2-bench keeps a model in the
loop at run time: PLVR guides or checks a small model that still generates actions, and STAGE runs
model-backed judgment nodes inside a code-controlled graph [Bhat et al., 2026, Luo et al., 2026].
ReTrace differs in its evidence: it reads the conditions and alternatives stated in the agent’s own
reasoning, which can cover branches that no logged run took. Workflow search and optimization
methods tune agent designs, prompts, or LLM-calling steps [Zhang et al., 2025, Hu et al., 2025,
Zhuge et al., 2024, Zhou et al., 2024, Khattab et al., 2024, Yuksekgonul et al., 2025, Cheng et al.,
2024]; we instead recover workflow rules from an SOP and logged runs. Table 10 in Appendix K
compares the closest methods.
3 Method
3.1 Inputs and target workflow
Atask familyis a set of inputs handled by the same SOP P , for example support cases under one
troubleshooting procedure. We use k tracesTk ={τ (1),...,τ (k)} of an agent on such inputs. A
traceτ= (s 1,...,s L) records each of its L steps as st = (rt,at,vt,ot), where rt is the agent’s
reasoning for the step,at the tool called,vt its inputs, andot the result.
The output is anexecutable workflow π, built once per procedure and reused on new inputs. At run
time, code chooses the next step without calling an LLM; this is what we mean byplanner-free.
Individual tools may still call models. The workflow is Python code on the public benchmarks and a
typed graph of steps on INTERNAL, our enterprise dataset.
3.2 Building the workflow
Construction has three stages:extractionreads each step,aggregationmerges evidence across traces
into anIntermediate Representation(IR) I (a compact rule document);synthesisgenerates the
workflow from it. Algorithm 1 in Appendix B gives the full procedure.
Extraction: reading each step.For each step, an LLM extracts a record zt = (gt,αt,at,vt,ωt).
The reasoning supplies the conditiongt under which the action applies and the intended actionαt.
The condition may use only information available before the action: “airplane mode is on” can
justify turning it off, but the result of turning it off cannot. The tool record supplies the toolat, its
typed inputsvt, and the sourceωt of each input, such as a task input, an earlier result, or a constant;
unknown sources are marked as such. Case-specific values, such as a customer ID, become variables
filled from each new task. The record also keeps alternative actions that the reasoning mentions but
the agent did not take.
Aggregation: combining traces into rules.An LLM first summarizes each trace against the SOP,
matching its steps to the procedure and noting alternatives that were mentioned but not executed. A
merge step then combines the summaries: it unifies repeated steps, works out how earlier results feed
later inputs, checks the reasoning against the recorded calls and outcomes, and resolves disagreements
3

text:
using the SOP, giving a reason for anything it drops. The result is a completion check and an ordered
list of rules:
I=



Hereχ tests whether the task is complete, and rulej pairs a condition, orguard, gj with an action
αj, its tool, and its input sources. The rules form a decision list [Rivest, 1987]. Each rule cites the
trace steps or SOP statements that support it, and alternatives that no trace executed are marked
unwitnessed; for example, the reasoning for turning off airplane mode may also name disabled mobile
data as a cause, which becomes an unwitnessed rule (Appendix I). A final check uses rule names
and citations to confirm that no rule or named alternative was dropped silently; it does not judge
whether a condition is right. Beyond eight traces, the rest are added one at a time (Appendix D). The
workflow generator reads the IR, not the raw traces; onτ 2-bench atk=16, its input is 24.5k tokens,
against101.4k with full traces (Table 9 in Appendix I).
Synthesis: generating and checking the workflow.An LLM converts the IR into code or the
platform’s workflow format. Leth be the state of a run: the task input plus every tool call and result
so far. At each step, the workflow stops if the completion check succeeds; otherwise, it runs the first
rule whose guard holds:

wherej⋆(h) = min{j:g j(h)holds} . The action calls its tool with inputs taken from h or constants,
and the result updates h. If the completion check fails and no rule applies, the workflow stops as
incomplete and never asks an LLM for a step.
Before deployment, generated code must load and must not be able to make planning calls. On
the public benchmarks, candidates may import only approved libraries and run in a sandbox; we
reject any candidate that makes a planning call when re-executed on the training inputs and keep the
one that reproduces the most recorded steps. On INTERNAL, the platform builds a single workflow
graph, which must contain no node that asks a model for the next step. Neither check establishes task
correctness (Appendix D). Where the benchmark can be re-executed offline, the workflow can also be
repaired from its failures on training inputs: an LLM revises the code, and the IR is left unchanged
(Appendix C).
4 Experimental Setup
4.1 Benchmarks and traces
τ 2-bench.This public customer-support benchmark provides tools that act on a simulated environ-
ment [Barres et al., 2025]. We use the telecom domain’s official split of 74 training and 40 test inputs
across three task families (MMS, mobile data, and service issues) insolo mode, without a simulated
user (Appendix A). We collect eight agent runs per training input. Unless noted, traces come from
Sonnet 4.6 with native thinking, which returns its reasoning alongside tool calls. Construction uses
only successful traces and Sonnet 4.6 in all three stages. Five-fold cross-validation on the training
inputs selects configurations, includingk; the main comparisons usek=4. Test inputs are never used
for trace generation, configuration selection, or candidate checks.
SOP-Bench.This public benchmark pairs industrial SOPs with tools and labeled task inputs [Nandi
et al., 2026]. We admit 8 of its 14 domains (Appendix A explains the exclusions). The 8 procedures
use 3–10 tools and SOPs of 4–12k characters, and each asks for a decision such as escalating or
resolving a case. SOP-Bench has no official split, so we split each procedure in half, stratified by
label, into 758 training and 744 test inputs. Traces come from eight runs of Sonnet 4.6, as a two-pass
ReAct agent, on each training input. We develop with five-fold cross-validation on the training inputs:
in each fold, a method that uses traces draws three samples of k successful traces from the other
four folds, builds one workflow per sample with Sonnet 4.6, and is scored on the held-out fold, for
k∈{1,2,4,8,16} . Table 1 usesk=16, the bestk in cross-validation (or within 0.1 points of it) for
every method. For the test, we regenerate the workflows at thek selected in cross-validation, from
a new set of agent runs on the training inputs, and run them on the 744 test inputs; the agent runs
three times on each test input. Intervals resample test inputs within each procedure and do not reflect
variation across the trace samples used to generate the workflows.

INTERNAL.This proprietary dataset contains 79 production procedures, sampled by customer
usage from our platform (Section 1). They use 23 tool types and range from three-step extractions
to multi-tool reviews with conditional steps. Each procedure has 20 construction inputs and up to
20 disjoint test inputs. We split procedures into Low, Med, and High complexity using only the
procedure text and input/output definitions (Appendix A). Traces come from the platform’s two-pass
ReAct agent (Sonnet 4.0), which explains each step before calling a tool. Every method uses the
samek=3 traces per procedure and generates one workflow. For ReTrace, extraction and aggregation
use Opus 4.8, and the platform generates the final workflow graph with a model of its choice.
4.2 Compared methods
All methods receive the procedure and tool definitions. Theoriginal agent, which produced the
traces, is the reference for task outcomes and execution costs.Zero-shotgets only these,few-shot
also getsk full traces, andexecution-onlygets the same traces with the reasoning removed; all three
use ReTrace’s generation prompt but, unlike ReTrace, keep their first valid workflow. Zero-shot and
few-shot run on all three datasets. Onτ 2-bench and SOP-Bench, we also evaluate AWM [Wang et al.,
2025b], which keeps a model that chooses steps at run time, and Skill Factory [Wang and Lu, 2026],
whose generated code we run with inputs supplied directly instead of through its model-based skill
selection. Onτ 2-bench only, we evaluate the Bayesian partial-order method BPOP [Li et al., 2026],
which learns tool order but cannot produce SOP-Bench’s decision output (Appendix H). Finally, we
repair workflows for up to three rounds using failures on training inputs: ReTrace on both public
benchmarks and zero-shot on τ 2-bench, with the same feedback, repair model, and stopping rule
within each benchmark (Appendix D).
4.3 Metrics
Build rateis the fraction of requested constructions that yield a usable workflow: the code must load
and, for planner-free methods, pass the planning-call checks. On SOP-Bench, code is regenerated
until it parses, so every method builds; these retries count as construction calls.Task successis the
benchmark’s score among built workflows, with execution errors counted as failures. On SOP-Bench
an answer counts only if it uses the SOP’s output format and every scored field matches the label;
this is stricter than the benchmark’s own substring match, so our numbers are not comparable to
published SOP-Bench results. SOP-Bench results are macro averages over its8 procedures. Enterprise
completionis the fraction of executions the platform marks as successfully finished, averaged over
procedures. We also report time per task, model calls for construction and execution, and enterprise
cost per task. Confidence intervals (95%) are bootstrap estimates, paired where possible; enterprise
differences use procedures that both methods ran (Appendix D).
5 Results and Analysis
5.1 Task outcomes and repair
Main comparison.On τ 2-bench, ReTrace reaches 75.8% task success with a 100% build rate
(Table 1). This is the highest mean among unrepaired methods without a runtime planner. The paired
gain over zero-shot is 37.1 points [19.8,51.1 ]; the margins over few-shot (5.3) and execution-only
(7.9) are not significant (Appendix D). The original agent (80.6%) and AWM (82.3%) score higher
but call an LLM at every step. On SOP-Bench, ReTrace (80.6%) trails few-shot (83.6%), is level
with execution-only (80.9%), and is ahead of zero-shot (67.7%) and Skill Factory (60.5%). AWM
(84.5%) and the agent (85.5%) score higher, gaining mostly where a step must read free text at run
time. Only ReTrace selects among candidates; with the same selection, few-shot reaches 84.0% in
cross-validation (Appendix H). On some procedures the labels follow a rule the SOP does not state;
the IR follows the SOP, so its workflows miss those labels (Appendix F). On INTERNAL, ReTrace’s
mean completion is 93.8%, against 96.8% for the agent (paired difference−3.0 [−8.0,1.0 ]) and
88.6%for few-shot; the agent’s rate overstates its web-procedure success (Section 5.4).
Repairing workflows with training feedback.Starting from k=2 workflows, three repair rounds
raise ReTrace onτ 2-bench from 66.7% to 81.2% test success (Figure 2), close to the agent’s 80.6%,
though the interval is too wide to claim parity; zero-shot rises from 38.8% to 60.6%. On SOP-Bench,

5.2 What does the agent’s reasoning add?
As an ablation, we keep ReTrace’s pipeline and remove the reasoning from every trace step. Atk=4,
reasoning adds 6.2 points ofτ 2-bench success [0.5,12.5 ]. Atk=1 the version without reasoning is
1.7 points ahead, but full ReTrace leads at every largerk (Figure 3a). On INTERNAL, reasoning raises
completion from 85.0% to 93.8%, a gain of 8.8 points [2.5,15.9 ] over 77 procedures. SOP-Bench
does not show the effect: without reasoning, ReTrace scores 82.3% against 80.6% on the test inputs
atk=16 (Table 6 in Appendix F). Its short, lookup-like procedures leave the reasoning little to add.
Most of the enterprise gain comes from four procedures where the workflow built without reasoning
fails on every input, each time at the same code step (Figure 3b; Appendix E.1).
The reasoning also names actions no trace executed: without it, unwitnessed branches citing reasoning
fall from44to3atk=4(Appendix D).

agent (170 s); AWM takes 90 s. In a separate timing run by task depth, ReTrace’s workflows stay
under 2.5 s even on the deepest tasks, where the agent needs 214 s (Figure 5a in Appendix E). The

5.4 Why enterprise mean time increases
Twenty of the 79 enterprise procedures use web automation. Without them, ReTrace averages 58 s
per task against the agent’s 92 s, at 19% of its cost (Figure 5b in Appendix E). A successful web-tool
call takes a median of 270 s and a failed one a few seconds, so the agent is sometimes faster only
because its calls fail. Web-tool calls succeed 86.6% of the time for ReTrace and 27.3% for the agent.
Some agent runs with no successful tool call still count as complete (Appendix E.2).
5.5 Lessons for practitioners
First, check tool outcomes, not only completion flags (Section 5.4). Second, test the model that
writes the workflow: it matters more than the extraction model, and a larger model did not help

text:
(Appendix E.4). Third, when traces are long, give the generator few of them: more full traces
eventually hurt (Section 5.1).
6 Conclusion
ReTrace turns an SOP and a few logged agent runs into a workflow in which code, not an LLM,
picks each step. The agent’s reasoning adds 6.2 points of task success onτ 2-bench and 8.8 points of
enterprise completion, but not on SOP-Bench’s short procedures. The workflows cutτ 2-bench time
per task from 170 s to 1.3 s and enterprise cost by 24%. For high-volume procedures, compiling an
agent into a workflow can pay off.
7 Limitations
ReTrace relies on the agent’s reasoning, which may be wrong or may not reflect why the agent acted.
Our construction checks confirm that generated code loads and contains no planning calls and, where
re-execution is available, count how many logged steps it reproduces; they do not show that the
recovered conditions are correct. We evaluate new inputs to the same procedures, not transfer to
new procedures, and a change to an SOP or its tools may require rebuilding the workflow. Poor or
incomplete traces limit what can be recovered. Enterprise completion is reported by the platform,
which can mark failed runs as complete (Section 5.4); a human audit of outcomes would give a
more reliable measure. The public evaluation covers only the telecom domain ofτ 2-bench and eight
SOP-Bench domains. SOP-Bench results use one workflow generation per trace sample, and its
repair feedback includes training labels. Aggregation lets the SOP override traces that contradict it
(Section 5.1); revising a rule when its cited evidence disagrees is left to future work. We also draw
traces at random, without regard to which branches they cover, although the draw matters: results on
a single SOP-Bench procedure vary by as much as 50 points across trace samples. Mixing successful
and failed traces tends to help onτ 2-bench, though not significantly (Appendix E.3), and with long
traces, full traces hurt beyond a dataset-dependentk. We choosek by cross-validation among a few
small values (k≤4 onτ 2-bench), since each trace costs a live agent run. Choosing traces that cover
different branches and outcomes, and setting k from trace length, could give a complete IR from
fewer agent runs and a workflow that succeeds on its first build, without repair. Future work should
also verify that recovered conditions hold before the actions they justify and should cover more public
domains.
8 Ethical Considerations
Public benchmarks. τ 2-bench and SOP-Bench provide publicly available task data and evaluation
code [Barres et al., 2025, Nandi et al., 2026]. Evaluation on these benchmarks uses existing task data
and test environments, without collecting new data from human participants or interacting with real
customers.
Enterprise data.Agent traces can contain sensitive information in task inputs, tool results, and
explanations. We report only aggregate enterprise results and do not name the platform.
Deployment.Reusing a workflow can repeat an incorrect condition or an unfair decision across
many cases. The agent’s reasoning and written procedures may preserve biases from the original
agent or business process; code-based step selection does not remove those biases. Workflow owners
should review recovered conditions, restrict tool access, and require human review for actions with
significant consequences for users. Access restrictions also matter because the same automation could
scale unauthorized collection or use of sensitive data. Our evaluation does not assess differences in
error rates across user groups.

Appendix
A Dataset details
τ 2-bench.We use only the telecom domain. The airline and retail environments do not support
the solo mode that a planner-free workflow needs, and only telecom provides a written workflow
document for each task family. A benchmark is useful here only if the original agent solves its tasks
often enough to leave a procedure worth compiling. We pin the benchmark code to a fixed revision
and keep its official split of 74 training and 40 test inputs across three task families. Traces come
from running the original agent eight times on each training input; no trace comes from a test input.
We vary the number of traces overk∈{1,2,4,8,16} , limited to the values each family supports,
and addk=32 for the full-trace sweep (Appendix J). Because solo mode removes the simulated user,
ourτ 2-bench scores are not comparable to published results.
SOP-Bench.We pin the public SOP-Bench code to a fixed revision [Nandi et al., 2026] and admit
8 of its 14 domains (Table 3). Two excluded domains (aircraft inspection, patient intake) have tools
that return the answer columns directly, so there is nothing to induce. Three (content flagging, order
fulfillment, warehouse package inspection) declare no input columns, so the benchmark’s loader
passes the whole row, label included, as the task. In the last (video annotation), 20 of 26 tools are
empty stubs. We drop one dangerous_goods row whose required input is missing. SOP-Bench
has no official split, so we split each domain 50/50, stratified by label, and freeze the split before
collecting traces. We called every tool on every row and confirmed that no tool returns a row’s
label. Two adaptations apply to every method: tool results are normalized (whitespace in keys
becomes an underscore, and a single wrapping object is removed), and an answer given only as
a structured payload is rendered into the SOP’s output tag before scoring. For ReTrace only, the
workflow generator is told which task-input field each copied tool argument comes from, because its
argument tracing otherwise sees only earlier tool results. The strict score counts an answer only if it
appears in the SOP’s output format and every scored field matches; SOP-Bench’s own scorer accepts
substring matches, such as “do not ESCALATED” for “ESCALATED”. Traces come from Sonnet
4.6 as a two-pass ReAct agent, eight runs per training input (6,064traces).

Enterprise dataset (INTERNAL).INTERNALis a private collection of production procedures from
the platform described in Section 1 (Table 4). Each procedure is written as a structured Markdown
document with explicit branches and typed JSON input and output schemas. We sampled the
procedures by customer usage from a much larger set, and they cover several business areas. Each
procedure has two disjoint input pools, one for traces and one for testing, so no method sees a test
input during construction. Because INTERNALis private, we report only aggregate results that do not
identify its source.
For the web-tool results in Section 5.4, a tool call counts as successful only when its own output
reports success, not when the run ends. The platform statistics in Section 1 come from the platform’s
automation registry and execution log from April 1 to July 1, 2026. They cover5,115 new automations
(4,694 agents that plan at run time and 421 fixed workflows that never ask a model for the next step),
together with the execution counts from which we take the ten most frequently executed automations.

Algorithm 1 gives the full construction procedure summarized in Section 3.2. Generating several
candidates and screening the code apply only to the public benchmarks; the enterprise platform
builds one workflow graph without re-executing candidates (Appendix D). Extraction reads each

C Prompts
Traces can come from agents with native thinking, which return their reasoning alongside each tool
call, or from two-pass ReAct agents [Yao et al., 2023], which write an explanation before each call.
Both provide the step fieldsst = (rt,at,vt,ot) of Section 3.1. The three stages of Section 3.2 use
five kinds of model calls: extraction once per trace step; a per-trace summary and a cross-trace merge,
which together make up aggregation; and workflow generation with at most one fix call. We wrote the
prompts forτ 2-bench and used them on INTERNALand SOP-Bench without changes (apart from the
SOP-Bench input-field note in Appendix A), including their example values, so a fewτ 2-bench tool
and argument names appear in them as format examples. Because nothing was re-tuned, INTERNAL
also tests whether the extraction and aggregation prompts transfer; on INTERNALevery method
uses the platform’s own generation prompt. Apart from the trace-loading code, our implementation
contains no tool names from INTERNALor SOP-Bench. We summarize each prompt below.
Models for each stage.On τ 2-bench all three stages use Sonnet 4.6. Appendix E.4 changes the
extraction or synthesis model while keeping the others fixed; we never change the aggregation model.
On INTERNAL, the traces come from a Sonnet 4.0 agent, extraction and aggregation use Opus 4.8,
and the platform generates the workflow with its own prompt and model, which we do not control.
Sampling the merge.We run the merge several times rather than once: five independent runs on
the same evidence fork≤2 and three for largerk. We measure agreement between runs by the tool
calls each rule contains rather than by its wording, and take the most common structure as the base.
A rule that only some runs contain is kept as an open item; regenerating the whole document instead
worked worse in our tests. When a single new trace is added to an existing IR, we run the merge once,
since the existing IR already serves as the base.
Extraction (Stage 1).This prompt turns one trace step into a record. The model replaces case-
specific details (names, IDs, quoted values) with typed variables and reports only decision logic
that carries over to new inputs: the situation the step responds to, the action it takes, the observable
condition that justifies the action, and whether the step ends the task. Each field must be grounded in
the tool called and the result just received, and a condition may use only information available before
the action. The reasoning-side fields areprecondition(the conditiong t),action(the intended action
αt),state, andis_terminal; the tool-side fields are the tool, its arguments with their JSON types, and
the source of each argument.
Per-trace summary (Stage 2).For a single trace, this prompt records which procedure steps the
trace visited, under what conditions, with what arguments and results, which steps it skipped, and
where the run went wrong and how it ended.
Merge and IR format (Stage 2).This prompt combines all per-trace summaries and the recorded
tool results into the IR, a document with a fixed format. It lists the opening steps, the completion
check, and an ordered list ofdecision rules, each pairing a condition with the action it selects and the
evidence for it. While the completion check fails, the first rule whose guard holds runs. The opening
steps are a printing convention, not a separate component: they are the rules whose conditions hold
before any tool has been called. The document also marksunwitnessedbranches that no trace reached,
named either by the SOP or by a step’s reasoning, and lists material that was explicitly excluded.
Every element cites the trace steps or SOP statements that support it. When a new trace is added to
an existing IR, the prompt must keep every existing rule, or remove it with a stated reason, and may
confirm, narrow, extend, or contradict it.
Workflow generation and consistency check.The generation prompt turns the IR into a workflow
with a single decision function and forbids model calls that choose steps during execution. Before
generation, a check uses rule names and citations to confirm three things, without judging what the
rules mean: every rule from the summaries is kept or explicitly removed, every merged step has a

text:
citation, and every alternative named in the reasoning appears either as a branch or as cited excluded
material.
Repair from training failures.Repair starts from a built workflow (round 0) and runs it on a
fixed set of training inputs of the same task family (4 onτ 2-bench, 16 on SOP-Bench). If any input
fails, the repair model receives one prompt and returns a complete replacement workflow. The new
workflow passes the same static checks as the first; when it fails them, the model gets up to two more
attempts with the static-check error, separate from the repair rounds. The loop stops when every
repair input succeeds, after three revisions, or when a revision cannot be built. It keeps the round with
the highest score on the repair inputs, preferring the earlier round on ties. Validation and test inputs
never enter the loop. The repair prompt receives neither the IR nor the traces, so repair changes only
the code, and the IR remains the IR used for round 0. Infrastructure faults stop construction instead
of being shown as failures. The system prompt is the workflow-generation system prompt; the user
prompt is a single JSON object, in which “refinement” and “program” mean repair and workflow:

Only failed inputs appear in the feedback. The failure detail gives an exception’s type and message
but no traceback; a workflow that exceeds its step budget receives a fixed message instead. On
τ 2-bench each step records the observation, the action, its results, and whether the run ended, and
there is no answer_check: the model sees only the score and the execution record. On SOP-Bench
the steps record actions and results, with long text cut at 4,000 characters, and answer_check shows
the workflow’s answer, the training label, and which fields match. A previous workflow longer than
64k characters is shortened to its first and last32k.
D Construction guarantees and approximations
Repeated construction and build rates.For each configuration that uses traces onτ 2-bench, we
samplek traces three times and generate four workflows independently from each sample. Over
three task families this gives 36 requested constructions (3 samples×4 generations×3 families).
Repeated generation captures the variation between model-written workflows. Zero-shot uses no
traces and so requests only 12 constructions. Build rates in Table 1 therefore move in steps of 2.8
points for methods that use traces; the training folds contain more constructions and give finer steps.
We track requested, built, executed, and scored workflows separately and report exclusions at each
stage.
Confidence intervals.Confidence intervals come from a deterministic paired bootstrap ( 2000
resamples, seed 0), blocked by family, fold, and trace sample. Except as noted next, everyτ 2-bench
difference we report with an interval is this paired estimate over the 120 matched cells, not the
difference between the two values in the table. Zero-shot uses no traces, and AWM, the original
agent, and the repair runs were evaluated separately; none of them shares trace samples with the
other methods, so their comparisons are paired by family and test input over the 40 test inputs
instead. Allτ 2-bench results pool the three trace samples over the same 40 test inputs, so they are
on one scale. Because the paired estimator weights test inputs equally, a paired difference need

not equal the difference of the table means. We do not correct for multiple comparisons. With 40
test inputs, ReTrace’s margins over few-shot, +5.3 [−10.2,+21.7 ], and over execution-only, +7.9
[−3.6,+20.5 ], are not significant, nor is repair’s +0.6 [−19.8,+20.7 ] over the original agent. The
margin over zero-shot, +37.1 [+19.8,+51.1 ], is significant, as are both reasoning-removal effects in
Section 5.2.
Call counts are lower bounds.The construction call counts in Table 1 understate the ReTrace rows
(with and without repair), because extraction results are cached and reused, and AWM’s, because
its construction calls were not fully logged. Three construction stages also do not mean three calls.
Atk=4, one ReTrace construction makes an extraction call per trace step, a summary call per trace,
several merge calls, a generation call, and at most one fix call. The table counts only the calls that the
extraction cache did not serve.
Procedure counts on INTERNAL.A method’s INTERNALcompletion is the mean over the proce-
dures for which it produced a runnable workflow, with each procedure weighted equally and scored on
its own test inputs. The overall value is therefore not the mean of the three group values, because each
method has its own group sizes. Out of 79 procedures (27 Low, 26 Med, 26 High), the original agent
ran 76 (27, 23, 26), both versions of ReTrace77 (27, 25, 25), zero-shot 78 (27, 25, 26), and few-shot
70 (27, 22, 21). INTERNALintervals come from a bootstrap over procedures ( 2000 resamples, seed
0); a paired INTERNALdifference resamples only the procedures that both methods ran, and every
INTERNALdifference reported with an interval is this paired estimate.
Zero-shot and few-shot rows.The zero-shot and few-shot rows of Table 1 come from a separate
evaluation round on the same 40 test inputs with the same scorer; the original agent’s score in that
round matches the one reported here exactly. That round kept every scored attempt (160 for zero-shot;
432for few-shot atk=4), so their intervals use the same bootstrap as the otherτ 2-bench rows.
Repair procedure.Each repair round runs the workflow on the training inputs and uses its failures
to revise it. The traces, tasks, feedback, workflow-generation model, and stopping rule are fixed, and
test inputs are evaluated only after the last round. Each version depends on the previous repair, so
these results do not average independent generations as the main comparison does.
Three rounds raise test success from 66.7% to 81.2% [74.4,88.1 ] for ReTrace and from 38.8% to
60.6% for zero-shot. The estimated test gains are 14.6 and 21.9 points, and the gains on the training
inputs are 17.4 and 20.8 points. Training success stays below test success, likely because the training
inputs are harder: the original agent succeeds on 65.0% of its training runs against 80.6% on test
(Appendix G), and the hardest family, mms_issue, makes up 33 of the 74 training inputs but 16
of the 40 test inputs. The repaired workflow’s difference from the original agent ( 80.6%) is 0.6
points [−19.8,20.7 ], which does not establish equal performance. Both the starting and the repaired
ReTrace workflows run without planning calls. We do not run repair on INTERNAL: the platform
provisions each workflow, and we currently cannot re-execute candidates offline during construction.
Enforcing no planning calls (public benchmarks).On τ 2-bench and SOP-Bench we enforce the
no-planning-call rule in three layers. First, a static check requires that the generated code parses and
loads, exposes a single synchronous decision function, imports only the tool actions and a restricted
part of the standard library, and contains no reflection, model-provider code, or dynamic evaluation.
Second, the code runs in a separate sandbox process whose import hook blocks every model provider
and which limits memory and time. Third, each candidate is re-executed on the training inputs, and
we reject any candidate that makes a planning call. Code that passes all three layers made no planning
call in any execution we observed. On INTERNALthe platform builds a typed workflow graph that
we cannot run in our sandbox, so none of the three layers applies; there, the guarantee is that the
graph contains no planner node.
Choosing among candidates (public benchmarks).When candidates can be re-executed, genera-
tion produces up to three of them and keeps the one that reproduces the most recorded steps, breaking
ties in favor of fewer decision steps. Each later candidate sees the earlier ones and their results on
each example, so the choice is a small guided search rather than a single filter. This selection is not
available on INTERNAL, where the platform builds the workflow and we cannot re-execute candidates,

so we generate one workflow per procedure there. The merge’s consistency check needs no execution
environment and is used on all three datasets.
Rules for branches absent from the traces.The IR marks a branch asunwitnessedwhen its action
never appears in the supplied traces. Its support comes from the SOP or from reasoning that names
an alternative action. We count each branch once, at its decision rule; counting every line that carries
the mark would inflate the total by about 1.7×. A branch is supported by reasoning when it cites a
trace step’s reasoning rather than only the SOP.
Across fifteen saved IRs built from k∈{1,...,16} traces, 23 of 115 unwitnessed branches cite
trace reasoning; the rest cite only the SOP. In a larger matched set built from the same trace samples,
removing reasoning reduces the branches supported by reasoning from 68 to 4 atk=1, from 44 to 3
atk=4, and from65to4atk=8(Figure 4).
The fifteen IRs come from an earlier construction round with a different code version; the main
round saved workflows but not their IRs. The larger matched counts come from saved merge outputs
before candidate selection. Neither set records whether test executions reach these branches, so the
counts describe construction evidence and do not by themselves explain the task-success gains in

Building the IR without the SOP.Aggregation takes the SOP P as an input (Section 3.2). Without
it, the IR fails the same way each time: with no structure to attach steps to, it follows the order of the
trace, indexes steps by their position in that run, and copies the sampled case’s values into the tool
calls. The result is longer than its evidence; onτ 2-bench, 24,878 characters from an 8,344-character
trace.
Aggregation beyond eight traces.Merging all k per-trace summaries at once overflows the context
ask grows, and adding them one at a time from the start takesk sequential merge calls. We therefore
merge the first eight summaries together and then add each further trace to that base, keeping every
existing element and citation. The merge input stays bounded, and the IR grows slowly, to about 10k
tokens atk=16. Each later trace is compared with the merged IR rather than with every other later
trace. Theτ 2-bench and INTERNALmain results ( k=4 andk=3) never reach the incremental step;
the SOP-Bench results atk=16do.
Batch merge versus incremental merge.Aggregation can merge a fixed set of traces at once (the
default) or add each new trace to the IR as it arrives. The two give similar training results: 49.6%
[37.7,62.9 ] for the batch merge and 49.8% [37.6,62.5 ] for the incremental merge atk=2, and 56.4%
[44.7,69.2 ] and 54.9% [41.3,69.4 ] atk=4. The incremental IR also stays compact, at 4,601 tokens
and 25 decision rules atk=2 and 5,921 tokens and 27 rules atk=4. At least up tok=4, ReTrace can
therefore add new runs as a procedure keeps executing, without waiting for a batch.

Argument types.Extraction reads the tool records together with the reasoning (Section 3.2), so
every argument reaches the IR as a typed variable with a recorded source, or marked unknown.
The order of actions alone provides neither: it shows which call followed which but leaves each
argument’s value and type to the workflow generator, and a numeric field filled with a string passes
construction and fails during execution. The guarantee ends at the IR: generation is a model call, so
whether the workflow respects a type depends on the generation model; ReTrace controls only the
information that model receives.

E.1 Reasoning removal: trace counts, complexity, and cost
Removing the reasoning keeps each tool call, its inputs, and its result; all construction stages and
models stay the same. Onτ 2-bench, the version without reasoning is 1.7 points ahead atk=1. For
every larger number of traces we tested, full ReTrace leads by 1.5–6.2 points, and atk=4 the gain
is 6.2 points [0.5,12.5 ]. The best version without reasoning reaches 69.8% atk=8, still below full
ReTrace’s75.8%atk=4(Figure 3a).
On INTERNAL, completion rises from 85.0% without reasoning to 93.8% with it, a paired gain of
8.8 points [2.5,15.9 ] over 77 procedures. Mean time and cost per task are 178 s and $0.101 without
reasoning and 163 s and $0.096 with it, so removing reasoning brings no efficiency benefit. The
completion gains are 15.7 points [3.7,29.6 ] for Low, 8.0 for Med, and 2.1 for High complexity
procedures; only the Low gain is significant, since only its 95% interval excludes zero (Figure 3b).
The trend comes from four all-or-nothing failures, not from a steady effect of complexity: on four
Low procedures, the workflow built without reasoning fails on all 20 test inputs, each time at the
same code step (in one, the code reads a field that is missing), while full ReTrace completes all 20.
Without these four, the Low gain falls to about 1 point, and 22 of the 27 Low procedures show no
difference.
E.2 Enterprise web-tool failures
This section details the web-automation results summarized in Section 5.4. On eight of the twenty pro-
cedures, the original agent makes no successful web call. It passes the tool an unresolved instruction,
receives a rejection, retries two to five times, and then writes an answer without any successful tool
result. On these procedures it takes 54–85 s per execution and records100% completion with 0% tool-
call success. One answer reads "Unable to extract title - web extraction failed" , yet
the platform marks the run complete. Across the test set, 184 agent executions are marked successful
