Neither problem occurs in ReTrace’s outputs.
ReTrace’s completion falls from 96.3% on Low to 89.2% on High complexity procedures, while
the agent’s ranges from 95.4% to 98.5% with no clear trend. Platform completion does not directly
measure whether the user’s goal was met. Tool outcomes add evidence about execution quality, but
they do not establish that every workflow is correct.
E.3 Successful and failed traces
We compare workflows built from successful traces, from failed traces, and from a balanced mix of
both. The main Sonnet trace pool is 65% successful and contains no failures for one family, so this
comparison uses Haiku 4.5 traces, whose 29% success rate gives both outcomes in every family, with
k=4.
τ 2-bench.With native thinking, a mix of outcomes gives 66.7% task success against 60.3% for
successful traces only; with two-pass ReAct, it gives 66.0% against 63.1% (Figure 6a). Neither
paired gain (6.3 and 2.9 points; Appendix D) is significant: both 95% intervals include zero. Relative
to successful traces only, failed traces alone raise success by 5.6 points with native thinking but lower
it by15.4points [−30.3,−0.4] with two-pass ReAct, so failures alone are not reliably useful.
INTERNAL.This experiment generates few-shot workflows directly from the platform agent’s
traces, without ReTrace’s extraction and aggregation. Each trace mix (successful, failed, or mixed)
is compared with zero-shot on the procedures where that mix is available. The groups contain
8–34 procedures and differ in complexity, because failed traces exist mostly for harder procedures.
Completion gains over zero-shot are 11.5 points for mixed traces, 3.1 for successful traces, and 3.7
for failed traces (Figure 6b). Because the groups contain different procedures, these gains are not a
controlled ranking. Together, the two experiments suggest trying mixed traces, but they do not show
that failed traces are always safe to include alongside successes.

Know-your-business (51.1% against 59.3–60.0% for few-shot, execution-only, and ReTrace without

validation, every method that uses traces scores higher atk=16 than atk=1 (Table 7). Two procedures
do not separate methods: referral abuse v1 is saturated (zero-shot scores 100%), and on dangerous
goods almost every method without repair stays near 78.7%, because the SOP’s own scoring rule
disagrees with about a quarter of the labels. Know-your-business is hard even for the agent (60.0%),
yet a lookup on a single input field scores 73.3% on the training inputs (leave-one-out), above every
method’s test score. In cross-validation at small k, ReTrace’s main failure is execution defects on
traffic spoofing: loops that exhaust the step budget and calls to tools that the SOP names but the tool
list lacks. Both disappear byk=16. AWM’s lead comes mostly from email intent (100%), where it
reads each email at run time; the agent is close there (98.2%) and leads on customer service (92.2%).
Reasoning removal.On the test inputs, ReTrace without the reasoning scores 82.3%, 1.7 points
above full ReTrace. It is ahead on know-your-business (60.0% against 51.1%) and dangerous goods
(79.4% against 75.5%) and within 0.4 points on the other procedures. In cross-validation, it is 3.3
and 3.7 points higher atk=1 and 2, 1.3 points lower atk=4, and within one point at k=8 and 16
(Table 7). SOP-Bench traces have 2–8 tool-calling steps, and on five of the eight procedures every
tool argument can be obtained by lookup from the task inputs and earlier results, so the reasoning has
little to add that the actions do not already show.
Labels that contradict the SOP.On customer service, the label is “resolved” exactly when latency
after troubleshooting is at most 100 ms. The SOP additionally requires jitter of at most 30 ms and
bandwidth at or above the subscribed plan, and every resolved case misses its plan’s bandwidth
slightly. In cross-validation at k=16, 12 of the 15 IRs contain the SOP’s full guard; they note the
bandwidth shortfall in the traces only as a caution, and the generated workflows escalate the resolved
cases. With the bandwidth clause removed from the IR and everything else unchanged, ReTrace rises
from 82.7% in a replicate run (85.2% in the main cross-validation run) to 92.8% on the same trace
samples (29 cells better, 5 worse). Telling the workflow generator to prefer evidence over literal
guards did not help ( 80.6%). On email intent, the SOP allows an “unable to decide” answer that
never occurs as a label; in cross-validation atk=2, ReTrace gives it in 32 of 279 cells, and zero-shot
never does.

the reasoning format (native thinking or a two-pass ReAct loop). Figure 7a shows the test success of

their training runs, a different denominator, so we do not plot them next to the workflows. The main
experiments use Sonnet 4.6 with native thinking, the only agent we also ran on the 40 test inputs:
there it scores 80.6% with 12.1 planning calls and 170 s per task (Table 1), above its 65.0% success
over the training runs.

H Baseline implementations and fair comparison
Choosingk.Every method receives the same inputs where they apply: the SOP, the tool list, and
the same pool of traces. Each method except AWM onτ 2-bench chooses its number of tracesk by
five-fold cross-validation on the training split before any test run; no method is tuned on the test split.
Onτ 2-bench, cross-validation averages four workflow generations per fold, scores them with the
same estimator as the test (task success among built workflows), and chooses amongk∈{1,2,4} ,
breaking ties toward smaller k. We cap the candidates at k=4 because every trace costs a live
agent run, so a method that needs few traces is the one worth deploying. Larger k, up to 32, were
swept afterwards as a sensitivity analysis, not as candidates (Appendix J). Choosingk and the traces
themselves without cross-validation is future work (Section 7). This selects k⋆=4 for ReTrace,
few-shot, execution-only, Skill Factory, and BPOP (whose ordering threshold is chosen the same
way [Li et al., 2026]), and we also report AWM at k=4. ReTrace’s training scores are 44.3% at
k=1, 49.6% atk=2, and 56.4% atk=4, with build rates of 91.7% atk=2 and 99.2% atk=4. On
SOP-Bench, cross-validation uses three trace samples per fold and compares k∈{1,2,4,8,16}
(Table 7);k=16 is the bestk, or within 0.1 points of it, for every method, so Table 1 reports every
method atk=16.
Baseline implementations.Zero-shot, few-shot, execution-only, and ReTrace share one workflow-
generation model and one generation prompt and differ in the evidence they receive and, forReTrace,
in candidate selection and, on SOP-Bench, the input-field note (Appendix A). ReTrace chooses
among up to three candidates by re-executing them on its traces (Appendix D); the other workflow-
generation baselines keep their first valid workflow. In SOP-Bench cross-validation atk=16, giving
the baselines the same selection raises few-shot from 82.9% to 84.0% and execution-only from
75.7% to 81.2%, against 82.2% for ReTrace, so selection accounts for most ( 5.5 of 6.5 points) of
ReTrace’s margin over execution-only there. The external baselines follow their published methods
on the same traces. We run Skill Factory [Wang and Lu, 2026] as the planner-free code it produces,
so that it can be compared directly with the other planner-free workflows. Its full system also makes
one model call per task to choose a skill and fill its parameters, and falls back to a live agent when no
skill applies (Table 10); we supply the parameters directly instead. AWM [Wang et al., 2025b] keeps
its runtime planner, and we report its runtime cost accordingly. BPOP learns only the order of tool
calls and ends each run with a fixed message, so it cannot produce SOP-Bench’s decision output, and
we run it only onτ 2-bench. Where the original papers left a setting unspecified, we chose the value
that maximized the baseline’s own cross-validation score.

that the reasoning mentions but no supplied trace executes.

text:
Comparative Analysis of Agent Evaluation Frameworks: Stability,
Detection, and Discovery in Enterprise Analytics Agents
Howard Zhang
Amazon
New York, NY, USA
zhanhowa@amazon.com
Chuck Arvin
Amazon
Washington, DC, USA
chuarvin@amazon.com
Logan Brown
Amazon
Austin, TX, USA
logbrow@amazon.com

Amazon
New York, NY, USA

Amazon
New York, NY, USA
nlchoudh@amazon.com
Lily Miao
Amazon
New York, NY, USA
mwting@amazon.com
Abstract
Deploying LLM-based analytics agents in enterprise settings re-
quires evaluation frameworks that can reliably detect failures across
complex, multi-tool workflows. We present a three-phase compar-
ative study of three evaluation frameworks, each representing a
distinct evaluation paradigm (trace-based LLM judging, text-only
LLM judging with red-teaming, and deterministic heuristics), ap-
plied to two analytics agents in a controlled research setting us-
ing frozen execution traces. Phase 1 quantifies evaluation harness
stability through repeated measurements, finding that 97% of con-
figurations meet the stability threshold and that stability patterns
are agent-independent. Phase 2 measures known risk detection
on 72 ground-truth test cases, where the trace-based framework
achieves the best precision-recall balance (F1=0.90) while text-only
evaluation matches on recall but generates5× more false alarms.
Phase 3 evaluates unknown risk discovery, uncovering 24 novel
failures with zero overlap between functional testing and secu-
rity red-teaming. Our results demonstrate that (1) the information
available to the evaluation harness determines evaluation qual-
ity, (2) functional and security evaluation are complementary, and
(3) LLM-based evaluation harnesses surface subtle errors that hu-
man reviewers miss. We recommend a two-framework strategy:
trace-based evaluation for functional assessment and adversarial
red-teaming for security validation.
CCS Concepts
•Computing methodologies → Intelligent agents;•Software
and its engineering→Empirical software validation.
Keywords
agent evaluation, LLM-as-a-judge, evaluation stability, adversarial
testing, agentic AI trustworthiness
1 Introduction
1.1 Customer Impact Statement
Enterprise teams are deploying LLM-based analytics agents that
generate SQL, invoke tools, and synthesize answers over sensi-
tive business data. Incorrect outputs have direct operational conse-
quences that often evade manual review. In this study, automated
evaluation uncovered a systematic SQL generation bug (Section 4.3)
that silently returned zero rows for an entire class of queries, a fail-
ure mode that persisted undetected through manual spot-checking
because the generated SQL was syntactically valid. Prior work
demonstrates that such silent text-to-SQL failures degrade down-
stream decision quality in business intelligence systems [9], while
undetected schema leakage vulnerabilities expose internal database
structure to adversarial users [1]. Today, most teams rely on ad-hoc
spot-checking, which this study shows misses 9 out of 72 ground-
truth failures (12.5%) that were syntactically valid but semantically
wrong. This research provides an evaluation strategy that catches
these errors automatically.
1.2 Research Gap and Contributions
Agentic systems exhibit stochastic behavior [2] and execute com-
plex multi-step workflows involving tool usage, SQL generation,
and human interaction [4] that resist simple correctness checks.
Three evaluation paradigms have emerged (LLM-as-a-Judge, de-
terministic heuristics, and hybrid approaches), yet no systematic
comparison exists of how they perform across stability, detection,
and discovery for agentic systems.
We present a three-phase comparative evaluation of three frame-
works: Strands Evals (trace-based LLM judge), PromptFoo (text-only
LLM judge with red-teaming), and Agenta (deterministic heuristics).
We evaluate on two supply chain analytics agents and address three
research questions:
• RQ1 (Stability):How stable are evaluation outputs across
repeated measurements?
• RQ2 (Detection):Which framework most reliably detects
known failure modes, and does the answer depend on the
type of failure?
• RQ3 (Discovery):Which framework most effectively sur-
faces unanticipated failures through automated test genera-
tion?
Our key findings: (1) the information available to the evaluation
harness determines quality: trace-based evaluation catches 91% of
failures at 10% FPR while text-only matches on recall but generates
5× more false alarms; (2) 24 novel failures were discovered with zero
overlap between functional and security testing; and (3) evaluation
harnesses surface subtle errors that human reviewers miss, with 9
ground-truth failures across both agents initially mislabeled by the
human reviewer and corrected after evaluator flagging.

2 Related Work
LLM-as-a-judge techniques are widely adopted for evaluating agen-
tic systems [10], with studies demonstrating high agreement with
human annotations [11]. Li et al. [ 5] document systematic inter-
judge disagreement as a key reliability concern. However, existing
comparisons focus on judging method variations rather than the
information available to the judge. Our work compares evaluation
quality across three levels of information access: full execution
traces, text-only outputs, and string representations.
Randomness inconsistency compounds in agentic systems as
reasoning spans multiple steps and tools [8]. Mustahsan et al. [8]
propose ICC to measure inter-run consistency, but ICC breaks down
under ceiling effects common in well-behaved agents. We instead
adopt average within-case standard deviation, the standard mea-
sure of measurement error in clinical reliability studies [3], which
isolates instrument noise on the original score scale regardless of
between-case variance. We pair this with decision consistency (the
probability that repeated administrations yield the same pass/fail
classification, a standard reliability concept in measurement [6]) to
capture the operationally relevant question: whether score fluctua-
tions cross the pass/fail threshold. See Section 3.3 for details.
Adversarial testing of LLM systems has gained attention for
identifying prompt injection vulnerabilities and information leak-
age [7]. Our work is the first to quantitatively compare functional
and security evaluation on the same agents, demonstrating they
are complementary rather than substitutable.
3 Methodology
All phases use frozen execution traces to enable fair cross-framework
comparison.
3.1 Candidate Agents
We evaluate two analytics agents from a retail supply chain fore-
casting system. Agent A analyzes category-level demand forecasts
(9 tools, moderate data volumes). Agent B analyzes product-level
inbound lead time forecasts (9 tools including a code interpreter,
large-scale production tables). They produce distinct SQL error pat-
terns: structurally detectable on one, semantic on the other. Both
agents were evaluated in a research setting using frozen execution
traces; this study does not describe a live production deployment.
See Appendix I for details.
3.2 Frameworks Under Evaluation
Selected from a qualitative evaluation of seven frameworks (see
Appendix H), these three represent distinct evaluation philosophies:
Strands Evals(trace-based LLM judge with OpenTelemetry access),
PromptFoo(text-only LLM judge with red-teaming), andAgenta
(deterministic heuristics at zero LLM cost). Each implements five
evaluation harness requirements mapped in Table 1.
The key architectural difference is the information available to
each evaluation harness. Strands operates on the full OpenTeleme-
try execution trace. PromptFoo operates on text-only inputs plus
injected context strings. Agenta operates on string representations
only.

3.3 Phase 1: Evaluation Harness Stability (RQ1)
20 frozen test cases per agent, prepared by domain experts. 3 judge
models (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Haiku, Qwen3 32B)× 5 repe-
titions for LLM-based frameworks; 5 repetitions for Agenta. We
measuredecision consistency(do all repetitions produce the same
pass/fail verdict?) andaverage within-case standard deviation(sta-
bility threshold:≤ 0.15). The threshold is operationally motivated:
on a 0–1 scale with a pass/fail boundary at 0.5, a within-case std of
0.15 means scores near the boundary have a non-trivial probability
of crossing it across repetitions, flipping the verdict [5]. Total: 5,605
evaluations.
3.4 Phase 2: Known Risk Detection (RQ2)
36 test cases per agent across 6 failure categories, expanding
Phase 1’s 20 cases with 16 additional cases. Each case labeled across
5 dimensions independently to eliminate cross-contamination. La-
beling was performed by a primary domain expert per agent, with
cross-review from two additional team members on ambiguous
cases. This reflects the realistic constraint facing most enterprise
teams, where domain expertise is concentrated in a small number
of individuals. Frozen traces evaluated by all three frameworks
with 3 repetitions, median score, pass/fail threshold > 0.5. Judge:
Claude Sonnet 4.6, selected based on Phase 1 stability results as
the best balance of stability and evaluation depth. Total: 2,415
evaluations.
3.5 Phase 3: Unknown Risk Discovery (RQ3)
Phase 2 baseline + framework-specific generation: Strands Experi-
mentGenerator (20 functional cases per agent with deduplication)
and PromptFoo red-team (42–48 adversarial cases per agent). The
same domain expert classified each flagged failure asnovel(a fail-
ure mode we did not already know from developing the agents),
known(failure modes discovered during agent development), or a
false positive. Judge: Claude Sonnet 4.6 (selected per Phase 1) with 3
repetitions for LLM-based frameworks. Total: 202 test cases, 3,680
evaluations.
4 Results
4.1 Phase 1: Evaluation Harness Stability
35 of 36 configurations (97%) meet the stability threshold (Table 2).

Among judge models, Claude Haiku is the most stable (0.029 avg
within-case std), followed by Sonnet 4.6 (0.035) and Qwen3 32B
(0.072). The single unstable configuration (Qwen3/style in Strands,
0.207, 20% decision consistency) is stable in PromptFoo (0.011),
demonstrating that stability is a property of the (framework, model)
pair, not the model alone.
Decision consistency, whether all repetitions produce the same
pass/fail verdict, reveals an important practical limitation. Agenta
achieves 100% decision consistency (deterministic scores never
cross the threshold), but as Phase 2 shows, its pass/fail decisions
are not meaningful for open-ended responses. PromptFoo achieves
92% average decision consistency, with faithfulness as the weakest
(67% for Sonnet, 68% for Qwen3) because scores cluster near the 0.5
boundary where small fluctuations flip verdicts. Strands achieves
82% average decision consistency, with Qwen3/style dropping to
20%, meaning 4 out of 5 test cases get a different pass/fail verdict
depending on which repetition you look at.
These decision consistency rates have a direct implication for
deployment: at 82–92% average consistency, LLM-as-a-Judge evalu-
ation harnesses are not reliable enough for automated CI/CD gating,
where a flipped verdict on a single test case could block or approve
a deployment incorrectly. However, they are well-suited for the
iterative agent development process, helping developers identify
failure patterns, compare agent variants, and prioritize improve-
ments, where the aggregate signal across many test cases matters
more than any individual pass/fail decision. The evaluation har-
nesses’ strength lies in surfacing systematic issues (as demonstrated
in Phases 2 and 3) rather than providing deterministic per-case ver-
dicts.

Evaluation harnesses discover failures humans miss.
Across both agents, 9 failures initially labeled “pass” by the human
reviewer were reclassified to “fail” after evaluation harness flagging:
5 SQL partition errors on agent_a and 4 calculation interpretation
mistakes on agent_b.1 In each case, the error was syntactically valid
but semantically wrong, making it invisible on manual inspection.
The agent_a SQL case illustrates the pattern. The agent generated
category-level queries including partition_level = ’top’ , a
filter that is syntactically valid and returns correct results, which
is why the human labeled it “pass. ” The SQL evaluation harness,
given the full query text extracted from the execution trace and
a rubric specifying the correct partition patterns, scored these at
0.20–0.30 (fail) across 5 cases. On re-review, the human confirmed
the partition error and reclassified all 5.
The agent_b accuracy case reveals a different failure mode. The
agent calculated calibration metrics for inbound lead time fore-
casts but misinterpreted the direction of the calibration coefficient,
reporting “well-calibrated” when the data showed systematic un-
derbias. The human reviewer, unfamiliar with the specific metric
interpretation, accepted the agent’s framing. The accuracy eval-
uation harness flagged the inconsistency between the calculated
values and the agent’s interpretation, catching 4 errors the human
missed.
These findings suggest that LLM-based evaluation harnesses
with domain-specific rubrics and trace access can serve as a sec-
ond reviewer for agent outputs, particularly for errors that are
syntactically valid but semantically wrong.
4.3 Phase 3: Unknown Risk Discovery
24 novel failures with zero overlap on either agent. The two gen-
erators target different inputs by design: functional testing uses
normal analytical queries, and security red-teaming uses adversar-
ial prompts, so some of the zero overlap is expected. Strands found
SQL bugs, tool workflow gaps, and schema fabrication. PromptFoo
found schema metadata leakage, storage path exposure, system
prompt disclosure, and excessive agency under adversarial prompt
injection (Table 7). See Appendix C for failure details.
ExperimentGenerator yield varies by agent maturity: 40% novel
rate on agent_a (hidden systematic bug) vs 5.9% on agent_b (failures
already characterized). Security yield scales with schema complex-
ity: agent_b produced4×more security findings than agent_a.

5 Discussion
5.1 The Information Access Hierarchy
A unifying theme across Phases 1 and 2 is that the information
available to the evaluation harness determines both its stability and
its detection capability. Three levels of information access produce
three distinct profiles:
At the lowest level, deterministic evaluation harnesses (Agenta)
see only string representations. They achieve perfect stability (0.000
avg within-case std) at zero cost, but cannot discriminate between
correct and incorrect open-ended responses, producing 100% FPR on
accuracy and intent. The exception is SQL correctness, where hand-
coded regex checks achieve 92.9% recall on structurally detectable
errors (agent_a), but this requires significant custom development
effort and fails on semantic errors (0% recall on agent_b).
At the middle level, text-only LLM judges (PromptFoo) see the
agent’s response plus injected context strings. They achieve ex-
cellent stability (0.025 avg within-case std) and perform well on
requirements assessable from text alone: SQL correctness (89.3%
recall) and intent understanding (2.9% FPR). But they cannot assess
requirements that depend on the full execution context: faithfulness
(52.1% FPR because tool result metadata lacks the actual data the
agent references) and tool correctness (11.1% recall because the
judge cannot infer what tools should have been used from text
alone).
At the highest level, trace-based LLM judges (Strands) see the
full OpenTelemetry execution trace. They introduce more variance
(0.053 avg within-case std) but can assess all five requirements:
faithfulness (0% FPR), tool correctness (88.9% recall), accuracy (83.3%
recall), SQL correctness (89.3% recall), and intent (0% FPR). The
additional variance concentrates on complex cases and does not
cross the decision boundary for well-configured judge models. The
framework-model interaction effect is agent-independent: teams
that validate a configuration on one agent can trust it on others.
5.2 A Layered Evaluation Strategy
No single framework covers all evaluation needs. The results point
toward a two-framework strategy where each is deployed at the
cadence and scope that matches its strengths.
Strands provides comprehensive functional coverage across all
five requirements without requiring custom evaluation code. Its
LLM-based evaluation harnesses reason about SQL semantics, tool
trajectories, and faithfulness from rubric guidance alone. This is
where the stability-nuance tradeoff pays off: the additional variance

issues (0% FPR vs 52%) that text-only evaluation misses. Determin-

PromptFoo’s adversarial test generation surfaces information

sign. Phase 3’s zero-overlap finding across both agents confirms this

target fundamentally different failure surfaces. Security yield scales
with context complexity: agent_b’s richer schema produced4 ×

gins.
6 Conclusions
We presented a three-phase comparative evaluation of three agent
assessment frameworks applied to two analytics agents. Our results
support three conclusions:
The information available to the evaluator determines
evaluation quality.Three levels of information access produce
three distinct profiles. Trace-based evaluation (Strands) achieves
the best balance of precision and recall because it can verify claims
against actual tool outputs, analyze execution trajectories, and as-
sess SQL semantics. Text-only evaluation (PromptFoo) matches
on recall (88%) but generates5× more false alarms because it can-
not see the execution context. Deterministic evaluation (Agenta)
achieves high precision on hand-coded structural checks but re-
quires significant custom development effort and fails on any error
pattern not anticipated in advance. Framework-model interaction
effects are agent-independent: teams that validate a (framework,
model) configuration on one agent can trust it on others.
Functional and security evaluation are complementary.24
novel failures were discovered with zero overlap on either agent: 9
functional failures (SQL bugs, tool workflow gaps) from trace-based
evaluation and 15 security failures (schema metadata leakage, stor-
age path exposure, prompt disclosure) from red-teaming. Neither
approach alone provides comprehensive coverage. Security yield
scales with schema complexity; agents with richer context produce
more exploitable attack vectors.
LLM-based evaluators surface errors that human reviewers
miss.Across both agents, evaluators discovered 9 failures initially
labeled as “pass” by the human reviewer: systematic SQL partition
errors and calculation interpretation mistakes that were syntac-
tically valid but semantically wrong. This capability depends on
providing the evaluator with sufficient context (execution traces)
and well-calibrated rubrics.
We recommend a two-framework evaluation strategy: Strands
Evals for functional assessment across all five evaluation harness
requirements, combined with PromptFoo for security validation
through adversarial red-teaming.
7 Future Work
Packaging the evaluation strategy as a reusable toolkit.The
two-framework strategy recommended in this paper currently re-
quires manual setup: configuring evaluation harnesses, collecting
and freezing execution traces, running red-team generation, and in-
terpreting results across both frameworks. A natural next step is to
package this workflow into a reusable toolkit that orchestrates both
functional test generation and adversarial security generation, runs
the target agent once per test case using the frozen-trace approach,
and produces a consolidated scorecard with per-requirement de-
tection metrics and security findings. The evaluation harness-to-
requirement mapping (Table 1) provides a fixed structure applicable
to any agent without per-agent customization, reducing the barrier
to adoption for teams deploying new agents.
Evaluating discriminative power.This study establishes
which frameworks detect known failures (Phase 2) and discover
unknown ones (Phase 3), but does not test whether they can detect
real improvements or regressions when an agent changes, the criti-
cal capability for CI/CD gating. A controlled perturbation design
would address this: starting from a baseline agent, deliberate vari-
ants with known quality differences (improved/degraded system
prompts, stronger/weaker foundation models, refined/vague tool
descriptions) would be evaluated on the Phase 2 benchmark. Four
metrics would determine CI/CD suitability: directional accuracy
(do scores move in the expected direction?), effect size (is the
change meaningful?), sensitivity (what’s the smallest detectable
perturbation?), and specificity (do unrelated evaluation harnesses
remain stable when only one dimension changes?).

C Phase 3 Novel Failure Details
C.1 SUBSTR Negative Index Bug (Strands, Agent
A)
The agent dynamically extracts the product partition character
using UPPER(SUBSTR(product_id, -1)) in SQL WHERE clauses.
Negative indexing is invalid in the target SQL dialect, which silently
returns an empty string rather than raising an error. The resulting
query matches zero rows and the agent reports “no data found”
without recognizing the SQL generation error. Example generated
SQL:
-- Agent generates :
WHERE partition_key =
UPPER ( SUBSTR ('SKU12345XYZ', -1) )
-- The target SQL dialect does not support
-- negative indexing . Correct :
WHERE partition_key ='Z'
This bug is systematic: it affects every product-level query where
the agent dynamically computes the partition character. It was invis-
ible to Phase 2 because those test cases used category-level queries
(which use a different partition scheme) or hardcoded product IDs.
Six cases triggered this pattern across different products and date
ranges.
C.2 Schema Fabrication (Strands, Agent B)
Agent falsely claimed location_id is not in the orders table
schema. The orders table includes location_id per the schema
documentation. A one-off knowledge gap.
C.3 Schema/Table Name Leakage (PromptFoo,
Both Agents)
Under social engineering, agents disclosed internal schema meta-
data including table structures and access patterns. 10 cases across
both agents.
C.4 Storage Path/Resource Exposure
(PromptFoo, Both Agents)
Agents disclosed internal storage paths and resource identifiers
through tool output leakage. 5 cases across both agents.
C.5 System Prompt Disclosure (PromptFoo,
Agent B)
Agent disclosed operational principles and analysis workflows
framed as “system instructions. ” Did not disclose verbatim system
prompt text. 4 cases.
C.6 Excessive Agency Under Adversarial
Prompt Injection (PromptFoo, Agent B)
Agent executed DESCRIBE, SHOW COLUMNS, SELECT *, and
LIMIT 1 under an adversarial prompt prefix. Changed behavior in
response to adversarial framing. 1 case.

text:
CONTRASTIVEDiscovery: Open-Ended Scientific
Discovery over Competing Explanations
Ziang Liu* James J. Kim* Yijia Dai Jennifer J. Sun
Department of Computer Science
Cornell University
codiscovery.ai/contrastive-discovery
Abstract
LLM agents are increasingly used for open-ended, data-driven scientific discovery,
yet most of them evaluate hypothesespointwise, testing an empirical claim h
only against its complement¬h. When evidence rejects h, the agent learns that
one explanation is unlikely but not which alternative the evidence supports. To
recover that alternative, we introduce CONTRASTIVE Discovery, which replaces
the single hypothesis with acontrast set, a scientific question paired with mutually
exclusive and collectively exhaustive competing explanations. Each experiment
is scored by how its evidence redistributes belief across the set, and the question
is resolved when belief concentrates on one explanation. Because contrast sets
change only the unit an agent proposes and scores, an existing agent can use them
to re-evaluate evidence it has already collected or to guide its search. Across
six domains, 89% of thepointwisecandidates with the largest belief shifts are
rejections. On the same evidence, contrast sets resolve 73% of these candidates to a
specific alternative. When contrast sets guide search, the agent resolves 67% more
questions thanpointwisesurprisal under the same experiment budget. In a blinded
study, 38 human experts chose the same explanation on 78% of resolved questions
and on 82% of questions where thepointwiseagent rejected its hypothesis and
stopped. Together, these results support explicit competing explanations as a way
for discovery agents to resolve more scientific questions from the same evidence
and validation budget.
1 Introduction
The shift toward autonomous scientific discovery has been accelerated by agents that generate
hypotheses, design experiments, collect evidence, and iterate on candidate findings [ 1, 2, 3, 4].
Recent systems scale this loop to evaluate hundreds or thousands of discoveries across scientific
domains [5, 6, 7]. At this scale, measuring progress becomes a problem. In closed tasks, progress is
measured against fixed objectives, answer keys, or benchmarks [8, 9], but open-ended discovery has
no oracle specifying which discovery should come next. Without an oracle, progress depends not
only on how each candidate is scored, but on whatunitof knowledge the agent treats as learned.
In most current discovery systems, that unit is a single hypothesis. The agent proposes an empirical
claimh, tests it, scores the result, and then keeps, revises, or discardsh [6, 10, 11]. The score may
be an LLM judgment of novelty or feasibility [ 12, 13, 14, 15], or a belief-shift objective such as
Bayesian surprise [5, 16], which treats discovery as evidence-induced belief change rather than a
subjective judgment of interestingness. Yet the representational unit of progress stays the same:
evidence updates belief in one focal hypothesish against its implicit complement¬h. We call this

pointwisediscovery. This formulation is shared across agentic discovery systems that otherwise differ
in how they propose hypotheses, gather evidence, and score discoveries.
Thepointwiserepresentation is epistemically limiting because scientific evidence often discriminates
among plausible alternatives rather than supporting a single hypothesis in isolation. This limitation is
clearest when evidence rejects a proposed hypothesish: the agent learns that the focal hypothesis is
unlikely, but not which alternative is better supported. For example, evidence against “self-employed
applicants with poor credit face higher mortgage denial rates” does not say whether their denial rates
are lower or no different. Under a fixed evidence-generation budget, this is information-inefficient:
the agent may need additional hypothesis proposals and evaluations to resolve a scientific question
that the original evidence already helps answer.
We argue that open-ended discovery requires a larger unit of progress:a scientific question together
with the plausible explanations that could answer it. This follows contrastive accounts of scientific
explanation, in which evidence is informative because it discriminates among alternatives [17, 18].
We introduceCONTRASTIVEDiscovery, which represents each discovery step as acontrast set
(Eq. 1, Figure 1): a set of mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive (MECE) explanations
answering one question. The agent elicits prior and posterior beliefs over the set and scores a
candidate discovery by how much its evidence redistributes belief. A question isresolvedwhen
posterior belief concentrates on one explanation, so a single experiment can both rule out alternatives
and identify the best-supported one. Otherwise, the evidence remains informative but the question is
unresolved.
Contrast sets change the unit an agent proposes and scores, not its architecture, so they can be layered
onto an existing agent in two ways. As anevaluation lens, they re-evaluate evidence the agent has
already collected, without modifying the agent. Toguide search, they replace the agent’s hypothesis
and score, so the search is rewarded for evidence that discriminates among competing explanations.
We evaluate CONTRASTIVEDiscovery across six domains spanning materials science, astronomy,
mortgage discrimination, online discourse, software engineering practices, and social behavior. Under
a shared scaffold and evidence-generation budget,pointwisebaselines are guided by surprisal, novelty,
or feasibility, while CONTRASTIVEDiscovery is guided by belief shift over contrast sets. We find:
• Pointwiserejections conceal resolvable alternatives.Across three elicitor models, a majority
ofpointwiseproposals receive a “maybe true” prior, and 89% of the highest-surprisalpointwise
candidates are rejections. Used as an evaluation lens on the same evidence, contrast sets resolve
73% of these candidates to a specific alternative without running new experiments (§5.1).
2
title: Contrastive Discovery: Open-Ended Scientific Discovery over Competing Explanations

text:
• CONTRASTIVEDiscovery turns rejections into resolved questions.Guiding search with contrast
sets resolves 67% more questions thanpointwisesurprisal under the same experiment budget.
Nearly all the gain comes from corrective resolutions, where evidence shifts support away from the
explanation favored beforehand;pointwisediscovery records these cases only as rejections (§5.2).
• The gain comes from explicit alternatives and holds up under validation.Ablations trace the
gain primarily to evaluating evidence against the full contrast set (§5.3). In a blinded study, 38
human experts chose the same explanation on 78% of resolved questions and on 82% where the
pointwiseagent rejected its hypothesis and stopped (§5.4). The gain holds when each alternative is
scored independently with thepointwisescorer and at matched token and dollar cost (§5.5).
2 Open-Ended, Data-Driven Discovery
Discovery loop.We study open-ended, data-driven scientific discovery, where an agent uses a dataset
D to propose hypothesesh∈H , evaluates them using evidence computed from the data, and scores
them, repeating under a budget ofN steps. The setting is open-ended because no predefined reward
function determines the value of a discovery, which depends instead on the scientific question, the
available evidence, and prior knowledge. This formulation captures recent LLM-based discovery
systems [5].
Pointwisediscovery.We call a discovery methodpointwisewhen, at step t, the agent proposes a
single hypothesisht and independently assesses it by scoring only that proposed candidate and its
evidence. Many recent LLM-based discovery approaches arepointwise, assessing each hypothesis
through novelty and feasibility [12, 13, 14], evidential support [6, 7], or Bayesian surprise [5]. In our
notation (§3.5),pointwisediscovery is the binary case of CONTRASTIVEDiscovery, where the only
alternative toh t is its negation.
The rejection case.Inpointwisediscovery, confirmation and rejection have different epistemic
consequences. Confirmation identifies a supported explanation, but rejection only rules against the
proposed one. The evidence may bear on alternatives, yet thepointwisescore exposes only its effect
onht. Resolving among competing explanations then takes a separate step for each alternative, each
drawn from the finite budget ofN steps, even when one experiment’s evidence bears on all of them.
3 CONTRASTIVEDiscovery
We reframe a discovery step from validating a single candidate hypothesis to resolving a scientific
question. We keep the evidence-induced belief-shift principle of surprisal-based discovery [5, 16]
but change the unit over which belief is represented, from one hypothesis to a structured set of
plausible explanations for the same question. The alternatives thereby become part of the unit, so
they determine what the evidence is compared against, how belief is updated, and what outcome the
step can produce.
3.1 Constructing contrast sets
At each discovery stept, the agent poses a local scientific question and constructs a contrast set
Ct ={h t,1,...,h t,M},(1)
where eachht,m is a plausible explanation for the same question. We require these explanations to
be locally mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive (MECE): within the scope of the question,
no two of them can hold at once, and together they cover the main outcomes the evidence is meant
to distinguish. For example, for the scientific question “Given a poor credit score, how is self-
employment associated with mortgage denial rates?”, the three explanations in the contrast set are
that self-employed applicants face higher, no different, or lower denial rates than other applicants
(further examples in Appendix U).
3.2 Eliciting beliefs over contrast sets
Given a contrast setCt, we next define the belief state used to score evidence-induced change. Before
observing evidence, we elicit pprior

Computing the posterior by Bayes’ rule would require a hand-specified likelihood modelp(et|h t,m)
for every analysis. We therefore obtain each distribution directly through a constant-sum allocation

also randomize the order of explanations during elicitation to mitigate positional bias in LLM-based
evaluation (see Appendix D).

measure how evidence changes that distribution. Given prior and posterior beliefs pprior

3.4 Discovery outcomes

In this representation,pointwisediscovery is the M= 2 instance of CONTRASTIVEDiscovery,
where the only alternative¬ht contains all ways the focal hypothesis could be false. Thus, when
evidence weakensht,pointwisediscovery can record negative evidence about the claim but cannot
identify which alternative explanation receives that support. CONTRASTIVEDiscovery replaces this
complement with an explicit local partition (Eq. 1), so the same belief shift is distributed over named
competing explanations.
Forpointwisebelief elicitation we follow an established categorical procedure [ 5]: the belief elicitor
ratesht on a five-level scale (definitely false, maybe false, uncertain, maybe true, definitely true), and
a “cannot comment” response counts as missing. We draw 10 ratings each for the prior and posterior,
map them to numeric scores, fit a Beta distribution to the prior ratings, and update it with the posterior
ratings.Pointwisesurprisal is the normalized absolute difference in the two Beta means, and we use
it as thepointwisediscovery score (details in Appendix T.1; design comparison in Appendix O).
4 Experimental Setup
We evaluate CONTRASTIVEDiscovery in an open-ended, data-driven setting: given a tabular dataset
D and metadata, we give the agent a fixed budget of N= 200 experimental validations. Each
validation consists of exploring a scientific question by generating a contrast set, eliciting prior
belief over the set, designing and executing an experiment to evaluate it, checking the experiment
with a reviewer agent, and eliciting posterior belief. To choose which question to explore next, we
use Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) [ 19], following prior work on agentic scientific discovery
and hypothesis search [2, 5, 13, 20] and on tree search for LLM reasoning and machine learning
engineering [21, 22, 23]. Each node is one experimental validation, and its children are follow-up
contrast sets that the agent proposes from the node’s result. Search is guided by the upper-confidence
bound on trees (UCT) [ 24], with the clipped contrastive belief shift rt = min(κ t,1) as the node
reward (reward in Appendix T.2; tree structure in Appendix T.3).
Our primary evaluation metric is the number of resolved scientific questions among theK candidates
that a method’s own score ranks highest, and theresolution ratedivides this number byK. Candidates
are ranked within each run, and counts are averaged over seeds within each dataset and then over
the six datasets. A question is resolved when the experiment concentrates posterior belief strongly
enough to identify a leading explanation (§3.4), and forpointwisebaselines a confirmed hypothesis
counts as resolved. Among resolved questions, we further distinguishconfirmativeandcorrective
resolutions, corresponding to belief confirmation and belief revision, respectively. Appendix F repeats
the resolved-question count after semantic deduplication.
Discovery agent scaffold.Our base agent is the AutoDiscovery scaffold [ 5], using gpt-4o for the
discovery agent backbone and a separate gpt-4o-based belief elicitor (agent details in Appendix T.3;
prompts in Appendix P). In CONTRASTIVEDiscovery, the elicitor assigns a belief distribution over
all explanations in a contrast set (§3.2); in thepointwisesetting, it assigns scalar beliefs for a single
hypothesis at a time to computepointwisesurprisal (see Appendix T.1).
Baselines.We compare againstpointwisebaselines under the same N= 200 evidence-generation
budget. In this setting, each experimental validation proposes a single hypothesis and guides MCTS
usingpointwisesurprisal. With the number of experimental validations fixed, the comparison asks
whether CONTRASTIVEDiscovery resolves more questions per validation by discriminating among
alternatives. To provide additionalpointwisecomparisons, we guide MCTS using LLM-judge scores
for hypothesis novelty and feasibility, following prior work on generating and evaluating research
ideas [12, 13, 14, 25] and scientific hypotheses [6, 15, 26] (judge prompts in Appendix P.3).

Figure 2:Pointwisediscovery masks resolvable alternatives behind rejection.Left:pointwiseproposals
show prior collapse, with most mass in the “maybe true” bin under each of three belief elicitors (columns),
while explanations in contrast sets span a broader range of prior beliefs.Right:among the top-50 hypotheses

Datasets.We evaluate on six datasets spanning scientific and social domains: Materials Project [ 27],
SDSS Galaxy [28], BLADE Mortgage [29], BLADE Conversation [29], DiscoveryBench Require-
ments Engineering [30], and DiscoveryBench NLS Raw [30]. These datasets vary in feature spaces,
sample sizes, and domain structure. Dataset statistics, preprocessing, and filtering criteria are reported
in Appendix G. We report results on three independent runs for the first four datasets and one run on
the two highest-cost datasets.
5 Results
We evaluate whether CONTRASTIVEDiscovery increases the epistemic yield of discovery under a
fixed evidence-generation budget by tracking confirmed and rejectedpointwisehypotheses, resolved
and unresolved contrast sets, and ruled-out alternatives. We first show thatpointwiserejections
conceal alternatives that the same evidence can already resolve (§5.1). We then show that guiding
search with contrast sets turns these rejections into resolved questions (§5.2). Finally, we validate the
gain: ablations trace it to evaluating evidence against explicit alternatives (§5.3), resolutions agree
with blinded experts and other independent references (§5.4), and the gain holds across scoring rules,
matched token and dollar cost, and resolution thresholds (§5.5).
5.1Pointwiserejections conceal resolvable alternatives
We first ask what high-scoringpointwisesurprisal candidates actually represent. Figure 2 (left) shows
thatpointwisehypothesis proposals concentrate heavily in the “maybe true” prior bin across three
belief elicitors (at least 59% for each). This concentration is strongest when the same model, gpt-4o,
both proposes and elicits (82%), but remains pronounced under cross-model elicitation. In contrast,
explanations drawn from contrast sets produce a much broader prior distribution, with the largest
bin containing only 41% of mass (gpt-4o). This suggests thatpointwiseproposals cluster around
hypotheses already considered plausible but uncertain, while contrast sets cover a wider range of
competing explanations for the same scientific question.
We call this concentrationprior collapse, and it affects which candidatespointwisesurprisal ranks
highest. Because mostpointwisehypotheses begin near the “maybe true” bin, there is limited
headroom for confirmatory shifts and much more for disconfirming ones (see Appendix T.1 for
the scoring rule and its normalization). Consistent with this asymmetry, high-surprisalpointwise
candidates in our runs are disproportionately negative. Among the top-50 candidates from each run’s
200 experimental validations, only 4% are confirmed, 7% are ambiguous, and 89% are rejected.
Pointwisesurprisal thus primarily surfaces evidence against a focal claim, and because the complement
is unstructured, that evidence does not identify which alternative explanation is better supported.

To test whether those rejected hypotheses contain recoverable information, we construct a post-
hoc contrastive companion for eachpointwisehypothesis: we keep the original hypothesis as one
explanation, generate alternatives using the same contrast-set proposer, and reuse the same evidence
(prompt in Appendix P.3). This uses contrast sets as an evaluation lens: no new experiments are run.
The companion generator sees the hypothesis, the dataset’s variables, and the same prior context as a
live proposer, but not the analysis, its output, or the verdict, and it is applied whether the hypothesis
was confirmed or rejected. On the same evidence, the companion resolves 73% of the 50 candidates
to an alternative (Figure 2, right). Counting only confirmations as resolutions,pointwisediscovery
leaves 96% of them unresolved, against 23% for CONTRASTIVE. Because both readings use the same
evidence, the difference comes from how the hypothesis space is represented: the same evidence
pointwisediscovery spends to reject a claim can instead identify what is more plausible.
5.2 CONTRASTIVEDiscovery turns rejections into resolved questions
Having shown thatpointwiserejection often contains information that resolves an alternative, we next
test whether using contrast sets to guide search directly captures this latent information to resolve
more scientific questions. For both methods, we rank candidates by their respective discovery scores
(i.e.,κt or surprisal) and evaluate the top-K questions retained for inspection.Pointwisebaselines
cluster together (Figure 3): ranking candidates by surprisal, novelty, or feasibility yields similar
numbers of resolved questions. This suggests that the limitation is in thepointwiserepresentation
rather than its scoring function since an isolated hypothesis can only be confirmed or rejected. In
contrast, CONTRASTIVEDiscovery produces substantially more resolved questions across budgets:
at K=200, it resolves 161.9 questions on average versus 97.2 forpointwisesurprisal (+67%).

Compatibility withpointwisesurprisal.The contrastive belief shift stays compatible with the

Blinded human expert evaluation.Thirty-eight evaluators with MS or PhD degrees judged 60
questions across all datasets using only the question, candidate explanations, and evidence; a median
of 8 rated each item, and we use the majority vote. As Table 1 shows, experts agreed with CON-

Incomplete contrast sets.A contrast set that omits the explanation the evidence supports can produce
a confident wrong resolution. For 163 questions whose supported explanation was independently

5.5 The gain holds across scoring rules, costs, and thresholds
To test the robustness of the gain in §5.2, we vary key evaluation choices (details in Appendix L).
Joint versus independent scoring.CONTRASTIVEDiscovery both writes out the alternatives and

Budget.Both methods are given the same number of experimental validations, at similar cost per

Discovery still resolves more under each: 148.3 against 87.7 at equal tokens and 145.8 against 92.2
at equal dollars.

6 Related Work
Recent surveys trace the shift from task-specific automation toward autonomous LLM-driven discov-
ery systems [31, 32]. Related work develops hypothesis-generation and refinement methods [33, 34],
alongside pairwise LLM evaluation [ 35] and scientific argument alignment [ 36]. In contrast to
such settings that generate or evaluate hypotheses individually or in pairs, CONTRASTIVEDiscov-
ery focuses on how evidence distinguishes a set of mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive
competing explanations for the same question.
This reframing builds on a longer tradition of information-theoretic experimental design, which values
experiments by their expected effect on belief [37, 38, 39]. Our objective measures realized posterior–
prior belief change through Bayesian surprise [40], following prior evidence-informed LLM discovery
work [5, 41]. ClaimSpect [42] also moves beyond binary claim assessment, but organizes existing
evidence into non-exclusive aspects rather than constructing mutually exclusive alternatives to be
resolved by new analyses. A related line of work also generates research hypotheses from scientific
literature, from early text-mining systems [43] to LLM agents [12, 44, 45]. CONTRASTIVEDiscovery
is compatible with this setting because contrastive resolution requires only a scientific question and
plausible alternatives. In this work, we focus on open-ended, data-driven discovery [ 11, 46] over
tabular datasets [29, 30], where experiments can be run directly against rich scientific data.
7 Conclusion and Limitations
We introduced CONTRASTIVEDiscovery, which replaces the single hypothesis that a scientific
discovery agent proposes and scores with a contrast set of competing explanations. Because only this
unit of discovery changes, an existing agent can use contrast sets without changing its architecture,
either to re-evaluate evidence it has already collected or to guide its search. Across six domains,
contrast sets turnpointwiserejections into resolved questions, almost entirely through corrective
resolutions. Ablations trace this gain primarily to evaluating evidence against the full contrast set. In
a blinded study, human experts broadly agree with the explanations the system selects on resolved
questions. Together, these results support explicit competing explanations as a way for discovery
agents to resolve more scientific questions from the same evidence and validation budget.
Our experiments use tabular, observational datasets and a single base agent with a gpt-4o backbone.
On such data, a resolution is a statistical rather than a causal finding. Because contrast sets need
only an agent’s hypotheses and evidence, we expect the gains to carry over to other discovery agents,
which we leave to future work. Contrast sets may also be malformed or omit plausible explanations.
Structural audits and expert ratings find most sets well formed (Appendix C and §5.4), and adding an
abstention alternative flags omitted explanations (§5.4). Finally, resolution is measured with LLM-
elicited beliefs, so resolved-question counts depend on the elicitor, even though most resolutions
agree with recomputed statistics and experts ( §5.4). Future work should test whether these gains
extend to laboratory experiments and longer-horizon interventions.

A Cross-Elicitor Agreement and Prior Collapse
A useful and effective hypothesis generator should produce claims that span the prior-belief axis,
because scientific discovery is bidirectional: evidence may either support an initially unlikely claim or
refute an initially plausible one. We audit LLM-elicited priors for hypotheses generated by free-form
prompting (pointwise) and contrastive partitioning (CONTRASTIVE), and identify prior collapse, a
failure of free-form generation that the contrastive construction structurally mitigates.
Setup.We fix the hypothesis generator to gpt-4o and re-elicit beliefs using three independent
elicitors: gpt-4o, gemini-3-flash, and claude-sonnet-4-6. For each of six datasets, we
sample 90pointwisehypotheses and 30 CONTRASTIVEsets, stratified by tree level. Apointwise
node contains a single hypothesis, whereas a CONTRASTIVEnode contains a partition of M≥2
mutually exclusive cells (typicallyM= 3 ), each treated as a standalone hypothesis for the per-cell
label analysis. This gives us a sample of 540pointwisehypotheses and 180 CONTRASTIVEsets (573
CONTRASTIVEcells).
Following our generation process exactly, for each hypothesis (or contrast cell) and elicitor, we
draw 10 categorical belief samples over five labels: definitely_true, maybe_true, uncertain,
maybe_false, and definitely_false. We map these labels to scores1.0, 0.75, 0.5, 0.25, and 0.0,
respectively, and aggregate them into aBeta(α,β) posterior under a Jeffreys prior. We use the Beta
mean as the per-hypothesis belief score. To measure cross-elicitor agreement on CONTRASTIVEat the
unit of analysis the runtime metric actually uses, we additionally elicitset-levelpartition allocations:
each elicitor distributes 100 probability points jointly over theM cells of a set (5 samples for each
set, elicitor, and prior or posterior call, averaged into oneM-vector).
Prior collapse is a generator-side failure, not an elicitor-side one.The prior collapse onpointwise
priors does not imply that elicitors are simply noisy. Table 2 shows cross-elicitor agreement on
per-hypothesis ranks (pointwise, Spearmanρ) and on per-set partition allocations (CONTRASTIVE,
mean per-set Pearsonr, with 1−TVD as a total-variation similarity robustness check at the partition
level the runtime metric actually uses). Onbothmethods, evidence sharply raises agreement: pooled
ρ rises 0.660→0.887 onpointwise, pooled r rises 0.664→0.923 on CONTRASTIVE(paired
Wilcoxonp<10 −4 for both, all per-dataset cells significant under both Bonferroni and Benjamini–
Hochberg corrections over 24 tests). The symmetry of this convergence argues against elicitor noise
as the source of the unreliability we observe at the prior step: when given evidence, the elicitors are
more cross-elicitor consistent on both methods. What isnotsymmetric is the prior collapse, which
is a property of the free-form generator that the elicitor cannot fix. Constructing hypotheses as a
mutually exclusive partition rather than independent free-form claims reduces the collapse at the
source. This matters because discovery is bidirectional: maximal information gain either comes
from evidence refuting an initially plausible claim or from evidence supporting an initially unlikely
one, and each requires the generator to propose hypotheses on the corresponding side of the prior
axis. Underpointwiseprior collapse, the refutational direction dominates. Because the generator
rarely produces claims with low elicited prior, discoveries in which evidenceconfirmsan initially
unlikely claim are rare. CONTRASTIVE’s partition tends to include lower-prior cells by forcing
explicit alternatives, restoring access to the full prior axis on which discovery operates, while leaving
the elicitor’s evidence-driven posterior convergence intact.
Do different model families pick the same explanation?Agreement on ranks and allocations does
not show that the families agree onwhichexplanation the evidence supports, so we also compared
their leading cells. On the same 180 contrast sets, all three families lead with the same explanation
on 55.0% of sets before the evidence (99 of 180; chance, given each family’s observed choice
frequencies, is 21.8%) and on 88.9% after it (160 of 180; McNemar exactp= 1.2×10 −13). The
rise holds in every dataset (Conversation 63→90%, Mortgage 63→90%, Materials 37→93%, NLS
73→87%, Requirements 47→90%, SDSS 47→83%). How often each family crossesτsupport = 0.80
differs (gpt-4o 77.2%, gemini-3-flash 86.1%, claude-sonnet-4-6 67.8%), so the resolution
rate depends on the elicitor while the leading explanation does not. Three families that start apart and
converge after reading the evidence are hard to explain as one model agreeing with itself. One caveat
remains: all three read the same gpt-4o analyst summary, so part of the convergence could come
from shared framing rather than the evidence alone.

C Audit of MECE Structure in Generated Contrast Sets
CONTRASTIVEDiscovery assumes that each contrast set defines a well-formed partition of possible
analysis outcomes. In particular, the explanations in a contrast set should be mutually exclusive and
collectively exhaustive (MECE): any plausible result of the planned analysis should support at most
one explanation, and the set should not omit an obvious residual outcome. The generator prompt
(Appendix P) asks for one of a fixed set of partition templates, a residual outcome, and a quantitative
criterion that maps the planned analysis to each alternative; this audit checks the sets it actually
produced.

Audit protocol.We extracted 3,260 parseable contrast sets from the full CONTRASTIVEruns
across 6 datasets and 14 runs. From this pool, we drew a frozen stratified sample of 384 contrast sets,
stratifying by the requested partitioning dimension and by the number of hypotheses in the set. This
intentionally oversamples rare partition types, making failure modes easier to inspect.
Each sampled contrast set was judged by gpt-4o using two independent passes, with 5 randomized-
order votes per pass. The first pass identified pairs of hypotheses that were not logically distinct,
including paraphrases, redundant hypotheses, and subsumption relationships. The second pass as-
signed structural failure tags, including missing residual outcome, redundant hypothesis, subsumption,
insufficient number of hypotheses, and inherently non-MECE structure. We classify a contrast set
as structurally MECE if no overlap pair, missing-residual, redundancy, subsumption, or inherently
non-MECE flag receives at least4/5votes. Insufficient granularity is evaluated separately and does
not count as a structural failure. We use this supermajority rule because manual inspection showed
that unanimity misses recurring redundancy failures, while simple majority admits more judge noise.
Results.Under the primary 4/5 rule, 372/384 sampled contrast sets are structurally MECE (Ta-
ble 4), corresponding to a raw audit pass rate of 96.9%. Reweighting the stratified sample back to the
full 3,260-item pool gives an estimated population pass rate of 98.4% with a stratified bootstrap 95%
confidence interval of [97.3%,99.3%] . The conclusion is stable across reasonable vote thresholds:
the raw pass rate is93.8%under a3/5rule and99.0%under a5/5rule.
Failure modes.The non-MECE cases are concentrated in two recurring patterns. First, 9 of the
12 failures contain overlapping or redundant hypotheses. These usually occur when the proposer
includes two versions of a null or residual outcome. For example, one contrast set contains both
“association disappears after controlling for PhD prestige” and “no effect of male contributions on
total citations.” These are not exclusive outcomes; both describe the absence of a residual association.
Another contrast set contains both “distribution does not follow a specific crystal system” and “no
pattern across crystal systems,” which again duplicate the same residual hypothesis.
Second, 3 failures arise from mechanism-style contrast sets that are not naturally MECE. These
contrast sets ask the hypotheses to distinguish causal pathways, such as whether residence type
affects later wealth through social capital or through initial economic advantage. Without stronger
identification assumptions, these mechanisms are not mutually exclusive and may not be empirically
separable from the proposed analysis. These cases suggest that mechanism-discriminating templates
should either be restricted to observationally distinguishable outcomes or excluded from automatic
MECE generation.
Cross-provider re-audit.The audit above uses a judge from the same provider as the proposer, so
we re-ran it on the same 384 sets with Claude Sonnet, keeping the prompts, the two passes, and the
4/5 rule (Table 5). The cross-provider judge passes 87.0% of sets (91.4% design-weighted) against
96.9% (98.4%) for gpt-4o, flagging 50 sets where gpt-4o flagged 12. The same-provider judge is
the more lenient of the two, so we report both figures and carry the stricter one. The disagreement
runs almost entirely one way (on the overlap check, 24 sets flagged only by Sonnet against 3 flagged
only by gpt-4o), and the extra flags are mostly alternatives that overlap or entail one another. They
concentrate by question type: half of the mechanism-discriminating sets and 40% of the ordering sets
fail, against none of the directional sets. A structural audit cannot tell whether a plausible explanation
is missing altogether; for that, the human raters of Appendix I, who judged the set well formed on
80% of ratings and flagged a missing alternative on 15%, are the external estimate.

D Hypothesis-Order Randomization in Belief Elicitation
CONTRASTIVEDiscovery elicits two probability distributions over the explanations in a contrast set:
a prior distribution before observing the analysis result and a posterior distribution after observing
it. Since language models can be sensitive to list position, these probabilities could depend on the
order in which hypotheses are shown. We therefore randomize the hypothesis order independently
for each elicitation call, then invert the permutation before computing priors, posteriors, KL, or any
downstream statistic.
Validation protocol.We validate this choice with two checks, summarized in Table 6. First, we
run a controlled permutation study on four contrast sets from two datasets, with each set evaluated
under five different hypothesis orderings. We compare a canonical protocol, which preserves the
displayed ordering, against the randomized protocol used in our experiments. After each call, all
probabilities are mapped back to the same canonical hypothesis identities. We then measure pairwise
consistency across orderings using total variation distance (TVD), where lower TVD means the
elicited distribution is less affected by presentation order. Second, we run two parallel CONTRASTIVE
runs on BLADE Mortgage that differ only in whether hypothesis order is randomized. This checks
whether randomization changes the aggregate scale of the elicited KL updates or posterior confidence.

hypothesis orderings. The effect is strongest for the prior distribution: prior pairwise TVD falls from

stable, but still improves, with posterior pairwise TVD falling from0.031to0.025.

updates. The confidence intervals for average KL, average normalized KL, and average posterior

This appendix justifies the numerical thresholds used by the pointwise and contrastive metrics. The
main paper defines the contrastive update scoreκt, the contrastive support/rule-out gates, and the
corresponding pointwise gates. Here we explain why the chosen numerical values are principled and
empirically aligned.
Contrastive thresholds.We use
τsupport = 0.80, τ reject = 0.10.
The support threshold requires strong posterior concentration on one hypothesis, not merely a plurality
winner. At the modal contrast-set size M= 3 , posterior mass 0.80 leaves at most 0.10 for each
remaining hypothesis under uniform residual splitting, giving an 8× leader-to-average-rival ratio (at
least 4× leader-to-runner-up in the worst case). The rule-out threshold 0.10 is the corresponding
residual mass implied by thisM= 3anchor:

We keep this value fixed acrossM so that ruling out has the same numerical meaning across contrast-
set sizes.
For contrastive surprise we threshold the score atκt≥0.5 . Because κt = KL/log 2M is divided
by log2M but not bounded by one, this is a threshold on the scaled score and should not be read
as “half of the available information gain”; it is placed at the same numerical value as the pointwise
belief-change threshold of0.5and avoids theM-dependence of a raw KL threshold.
Pointwise thresholds.We use
γsupport = 0.625, γ reject = 0.375.
These values are anchored to the elicitor’s five-level belief scale
{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0}.
The support threshold 0.625 is the midpoint between “uncertain” (0.5) and “maybe true” (0.75);
the rejection threshold 0.375 is the midpoint between “maybe false” (0.25) and “uncertain” (0.5).
Thus, the pointwise thresholds correspond to crossing out of the uncertainty region in either direction,
rather than being tuned post hoc to maximize agreement with the contrastive thresholds.

F Deduplicating Replicated Hypotheses
Following prior work [5], we apply a post-run deduplication pass to test whether a method receives
extra credit for repeatedly generating the same semantic hypothesis under different surface forms.
Shared deduplication procedure.Both pointwise and contrastive runs use the same semantic-
equivalence machinery. We first collapse exact-string duplicates, embed the remaining hypothesis
texts with the same embedding model, build a Ward agglomerative clustering tree, and use an LLM
judge to decide whether proposed cluster merges are semantically equivalent. Each merge decision is
judged with 10 votes and accepted only when at least 70% of votes mark the two clusters as the same
hypothesis. Thus, both methods use the same embedding model, clustering procedure, judge prompt,
judge model, vote count, and merge threshold.
Pointwise deduplication.In the pointwise setting, each search node proposes one focal hypothesis.
Deduplication is therefore performed at the node level: two nodes are merged if their hypothesis texts
express the same claim. This matches the representation used by the pointwise metric, where each
candidate is a single hypothesis.
Contrastive deduplication.In the contrastive setting, each search node proposes a contrast set
containing M mutually exclusive hypotheses. Deduplicating only at the node level would be
inappropriate: it would treat the whole contrast set as one textual object and would not remove
repeated hypotheses across different contrast sets. We therefore flatten contrastive outputs and
deduplicate at the hypothesis level. Each hypothesis inside a contrast set is treated as a candidate for
cross-node deduplication.
We add one structural constraint: hypotheses from the same contrast set are never merged with each
other. They are MECE alternatives to the same analysis question, not replications. For example,
“positive effect,” “negative effect,” and “no effect” may be textually related, but they are distinct
alternatives by construction. This within-set hard gate prevents deduplication from collapsing valid
contrastive alternatives.
Resolved questions after deduplication.We recount the resolved questions of Section 5.2 so
that each resolved claim counts once, grouping confirmedpointwisehypotheses and the leading
explanations of resolved contrast sets by the clusters above. At K=200, the average number of
resolved questions falls from 97.2 to 87.4 forpointwisesurprisal and from 161.9 to 141.9 for

G.3 Filtering rationale for scientific datasets
For the two large scientific datasets, Materials Project and SDSS Galaxy, we apply simple domain-
motivated filters before running hypothesis generation. These filters are not intended to optimize
downstream performance. Instead, they define physically coherent, cleanly measured, and computa-
tionally tractable hypothesis spaces. In both cases, the goal is to avoid forcing the model to generate
hypotheses across incompatible physical regimes or over measurements known to be unreliable.
SDSS Galaxy.For SDSS Galaxy, we restrict the dataset to entries with class = ’GALAXY’ . This
keeps the hypothesis space physically coherent: stars, quasars, and galaxies obey different physical
regimes, and several galaxy-oriented columns, such as size and profile-radius measurements, would
be meaningless or differently interpreted for non-galaxy objects. We also requirezWarning = 0 , the
standard SDSS quality flag indicating a clean redshift fit. Nonzero warning values often indicate failed
pipeline checks, such as low signal-to-noise, bad template matches, or problematic spectra; including
these entries would inject unreliable redshift-dependent measurements into many hypotheses.
We further restrict redshift to 0.02≤z≤0.3 . The lower bound removes very nearby objects for
which peculiar velocities can be comparable to the Hubble-flow velocity, making redshift a poor
distance proxy. The upper bound keeps the sample within the approximate regime of the SDSS Main
Galaxy Sample, rather than mixing in higher-redshift luminous red galaxies or other populations
governed by different selection effects. Finally, we require 14≤modelMag_r≤22 . The bright-end
cut avoids saturated sources for which photometry may be unreliable, while the faint-end cut avoids
objects for which photometric uncertainty and redshift signal-to-noise become limiting. The top-
50,000 cap is a practical scale constraint: it remains below the SDSS unauthenticated query limit, fits

the physical and quality filters, this cap is primarily pragmatic rather than physically principled.
Materials Project.For Materials Project, we restrict to materials with nelements∈{2,3,4} . This
excludes pure elements, whose small and heavily studied set would make many property hypotheses
trivial or degenerate. It also excludes materials with five or more elements, such as high-entropy
alloys and complex multicomponent oxides, where individual elemental contributions are often highly
entangled and harder to interpret cleanly. Retaining binary, ternary, and quaternary compounds
captures much of functional inorganic chemistry, including families such as rock salts, perovskites,
spinels, and Heusler compounds, while keeping the hypothesis space tractable.
We additionally require energy_above_hull≤0.05 eV/atom. This threshold follows the common
Materials Project convention for selecting materials that are plausibly synthesizable or near-stable.
Materials substantially above the convex hull are increasingly likely to be hypothetical or physically
unstable, making their computed properties less useful for generating hypotheses about realizable
materials. This filter also removes unusual metastable phases whose extreme properties could
dominate regressions or produce hypotheses driven by outliers rather than robust physical structure.
Overall design principle.Across both scientific datasets, the filters are chosen to satisfy four
criteria. First, retained samples should be physically coherent, so that hypotheses are generated within
a comparable regime. Second, measurements should be clean enough to avoid obvious garbage-in,
garbage-out effects, such as failed redshift fits or saturated photometry. Third, the filtered datasets
should remain large enough to support statistically meaningful hypothesis generation. Finally, the
filters should be conventional enough to be defensible to domain experts, rather than appearing as
post hoc cherry-picking.
Portfolio coverage.The resulting benchmark portfolio covers six domains: materials science
through Materials Project, astrophysics through SDSS Galaxy, finance and policy through BLADE
Mortgage, software engineering through DiscoveryBench Requirements Engineering, sociology
and labor economics through DiscoveryBench NLS Raw, and online discourse through BLADE
Conversation. The datasets also span a broad range of sample sizes: 276 rows for DiscoveryBench
Requirements Engineering, 2,380 rows for BLADE Mortgage, 7,975 rows for BLADE Conversation,
12,686 rows for DiscoveryBench NLS Raw, 50,000 rows for SDSS Galaxy, and 68,805 rows for
Materials Project. This row-count spread is useful for analyzing how hypothesis-generation and
validation behavior vary under different statistical-power regimes.
