than through selection. The natural ablation, comparing UCT-selection to uniform-random parent
selection while preserving context inheritance, would adjudicate (a) vs. (b) and is left to future work.
I Blinded Expert Evaluation
This appendix gives the protocol, reliability, and control analyses behind Table 1.
Protocol.Thirty-eight evaluators with MS or PhD degrees in the mathematical, computational, or
natural sciences, recruited and screened separately from the authors (31 through a screened crowd
platform, 7 verified in person), rated 60 blinded items: ten per dataset, stratified by the contrastive
scoreκt. Each evaluator saw only the research question, the candidate explanations, and the statistical
evidence from the executed analysis, with the alternatives in random order; our system’s beliefs,
its resolution label, and thepointwiseverdict were never shown. Each item was rated by at least
4 evaluators (median 8). The four questions per item were (Q1) which explanation the evidence
supports, with the extra options “none of these is supported” and “cannot tell”; (Q2) whether the
alternatives are mutually exclusive and cover the plausible explanations, with options for a missing
explanation, overlap, or both; (Q3) whether the result is worth reporting; and (Q4) whether the chosen
variables and test fit the question. We score items by majority vote and count no majority, “cannot
28
title: Contrastive Discovery: Open-Ended Scientific Discovery over Competing Explanations

text:
tell,” and “none” as disagreement with our system’s explanation. Five submissions were excluded
under a rule fixed at the first exclusion (one incomplete session and four evaluators who missed both
attention checks). Restricting to the 30 evaluators who caught every attention check lowers the overall
agreement from 71.7% to 68.3%, so inattentive raters do not carry the result. Expert evaluations were
collected with informed consent and kept confidential; the information concerned our methods and
scientific outputs, not the evaluators as individuals. Under our institution’s IRB guidance, this activity
does not constitute human-subjects research and therefore did not require IRB review.
Both methods were compared on the same 60 questions, using the same evidence and expert judg-
ments. Thepointwisehypothesis was the explanation our system rated most plausible before seeing
the evidence, evaluated on its own.
Resolution agreement (Q1).The expert majority matched our system’s explanation on 43 of 60
items (71.7%, 95% CI 60.0–83.3 by item-clustered bootstrap): 40 of the 51 items it marked resolved
(78.4%) and 3 of the 9 it left unresolved. Of the 17 disagreements, the experts chose a competing
explanation on only 3; on 8 they judged the evidence insufficient and on 6 they formed no majority, so
most disagreements fall on evidence the experts themselves could not settle. Across all 60 items the
panel committed to a specific alternative on 46, which shows that the executed experiments usually
separate the alternatives well enough for experts to commit. Agreement was 79% on confirmative
resolutions and 77% on corrective ones. Against thepointwisebaseline: on the 32 items it confirmed,
the experts endorsed 23 findings for each method; on the 22 items it rejected and stopped, the
alternative our system identified matched the expert majority on 18 (81.8%; exact 95% CI 60–95).
A related subset, the 22 items the baseline did not confirm and our system resolved, overlaps this
one on 19 items and gives 17 of 22; the main text reports the pointwise-rejected subset. Per dataset,
agreement ranges from 6 of 10 to 9 of 10, too few items to compare domains.
Reliability.On the load-bearing judgment (Q1, four to six options), pairwise agreement was 64%
and Krippendorff’sα was 0.54 (95% CI 0.45–0.61), and in a descriptive stratification α was 0.60
on resolved items versus 0.22 on unresolved ones, so rater disagreement concentrates on the items
CONTRASTIVEDiscovery leaves unresolved. On set completeness (Q2), 80% of ratings judged
the set well formed, 15% flagged a missing plausible alternative, 4% overlap, and 1% both; raw
agreement on the binary omission call was 83% (Gwet’s AC1 = 0.73; the lower Fleiss’κ of 0.35
reflects the 80/20 response skew). A strict majority flagged a missing alternative on 6 of the 60 sets.
Analysis appropriateness (Q4) was judged appropriate on 73% of ratings, wrong variable or test on
19%, and cannot tell on 8% (binary raw agreement 72%, AC1 = 0.54). Scientific value (Q3) had low
agreement (α= 0.24 ), so we report it only as a distribution: 51% substantive finding, 20% minor,
3% too obvious to state, 25% not a finding.
Validity controls.To check that the ratings track genuine quality, we planted two manually
constructed defective sets among the items, one with a plausible alternative removed and one with
overlapping alternatives: 11 of the 14 evaluators who saw the first flagged a missing alternative and
none confused it with overlap, and 10 of 12 flagged the second as defective. On separate control items
we kept the contrast set intact but paired it with the evidence of a different question: the well-formed
rate stayed at 77%, close to its 80% baseline, while the analysis-appropriateness rating fell from
73% to 7% and the wrong-variable-or-test flag rose from 19% to 84%. The evaluators therefore flag
real set defects without blanket-flagging, and recognize when an analysis does not fit its question.
Attention controls (mismatched evidence expected to yield “cannot tell”) fired as expected on 95% of
exposures.
Scope.The experts read the same evidence as our system, so their agreement shows that resolutions
track the evidence as independent experts read it; it is not a test of scientific truth. The experts were
general quantitative-science raters rather than specialists matched to each item’s subfield, and they
judged the executed analysis rather than replicating it. The comparison with thepointwisebaseline is
one of endorsed yield, not of accuracy on the items both methods decide.
J Mechanical Fidelity Audits
The belief step reads the analyst’s written summary of an executed analysis. Three audits, none of
which involves a language model in the scoring, check that this chain is faithful: that the adjudication

text:
follows the evidence it is shown, that the summary reports the numbers the code printed, and that the
code computed those numbers correctly.
Adjudication follows the evidence.We took 14 claims from 10 DiscoveryBench training ques-
tions with documented findings (a finding with two claims contributes two), constructed contrast
sets whose wording was held fixed across conditions, and ran the production posterior elicitor
(gpt-4o-2024-08-06, five samples,τsupport = 0.80) on numbers-only evidence with the alterna-
tives in randomized order and no analyst prose. Given the full statistic with its interval, available
for 11 of the 14, the elicitor placed the documented answer first in every case and resolved 8 of 11,
holding back on three whose intervals lie close to zero. Given the coefficient without an interval it still
ranked the documented answer first on 13 of 14 while resolving only 7, appropriate caution when the
evidence is incomplete. In a separate condition covering all 14 claims, we supplied the statistic with
its sign reversed; the resolution followed the reversal in every case. Supplying no evidence produced
no resolution on any of the 14 (largest posterior 0.74). Because the wording of the alternatives was
identical across the four conditions, these resolutions follow the evidence and not the phrasing. This
establishes evidence-driven adjudication, not end-to-end correctness of the pipeline that produces the
evidence.
Summaries quote the numbers the code printed.Across all available seeds, 3,015 analyses
contained checkable numerical claims in the analyst’s written summary. We checked, allowing for
rounding, percentages, and scientific notation, whether those numbers appear in the captured standard
output of the executed code. 99.1% of these analyses and 99.7% of the 9,239 checked numbers
are grounded in a printed value. Reading every mismatch by hand found at least five genuine slips,
including a slope quoted from a plot-only run and a count reported as a percentage; the audit caught
all of them without a human in the loop. Pairing each summary with a different analysis’s output and
re-running the identical matcher grounds only 3.8% of numbers, so the check discriminates. Signs
are not checked by this audit.
The code computed the statistics correctly.For the analyses whose statistic can be rebuilt directly
from named columns of the raw data (400 of 3,274; 331 scorable, spanning every available seed and
251 distinct dataset/test/column combinations), we recomputed the statistic with standard libraries
and compared it to the value the agent printed. The values matched on 318 of 331 (96.1%). Every
mismatch we could trace came from our recomputation missing a data-handling step in the agent’s
code (a custom parser, a missing-data rule, a−9999 sentinel replaced before analysis, a group split);
a few could not be classified either way. We found no confirmed computation error. Substituting a
wrong column matches only 2.1% of the time, so the check is not loose. Coverage is 12% of analyses
and not random, since the rebuildable analyses are the simpler ones, so we read this as a check on the
covered analyses rather than a pipeline-wide rate.
K Handling Incomplete Contrast Sets
A contrast set that omits the explanation the evidence supports can produce a confident wrong
resolution. We measured how often this happens and how well the abstention alternative of Section 3.4
prevents it.
Design.We used two frozen panels. The primary panel is 163 questions, all directional triples
(M= 3 ), whose supported explanation is fixed by a statistic recomputed from the raw data with
no model in the scoring (121 distinct underlying analyses; intervals are clustered on the analysis).
Because the correct answer must be present to be removed, this panel conditions on questions the
system originally resolved correctly, so the intact-set control measures re-elicitation stability rather
than corpus accuracy. A secondary panel is 40 resolved questions across six partition types and
M∈{2,3,4} whose supported explanation matches the blinded expert majority of Appendix I. The
design crossed two factors: the set as generated or with the supported explanation removed, each
with or without an added alternative worded “none of the listed alternatives matches the evidence;
the contrast set is incomplete.” The seven secondary-panel questions with M= 2 omitted the
removed-explanation condition without the added alternative, since its sole survivor would receive all
belief by construction. Selecting the added alternative flags the set as incomplete; declining to reach
τsupport withholds resolution as before. Cell order was randomized per call and five samples were

of 789 elicitations used five valid samples and 14 used two to four; all decision margins were fixed

Results.With the sets left intact, the supported explanation resolved on 159 of 163 questions
(97.5%) without the abstention alternative and on 162 of 163 (99.4%) with it, and the abstention
alternative was never selected (0 of 163). With the supported explanation removed (Table 10), the
system resolved to a surviving alternative on 53.4% of questions, so an omitted explanation can indeed
produce a wrong resolution. The failures lean toward caution: when a direction was removed and
the null survived, the system resolved to “no detectable effect” on 58.5% of cases, left the question
unresolved on 38.7%, and asserted the opposite direction on 2.8%; when the null was removed and
only opposing directions survived, it left all 21 unresolved. Those null resolutions are still wrong
under our reference, which is why the abstention alternative matters. The abstention alternative cuts
false resolution to 0.6%: it is the leading option on 92.6% of removed cases (mean mass 0.85) and
crosses the 0.80 threshold on 69.3%, identifying the omission rather than only withholding an answer.
The secondary panel shows the same pattern with wider intervals (63.6% false resolution without
the option, 6.1% with it, on the 33 questions withM≥3 ). The discovery runs of Section 5.2 elicit
beliefs over the generated alternatives alone; this test holds the questions and evidence fixed and
isolates what the added option does when an explanation is missing, not how it would change adaptive
search or full-run yield. In those runs a missing alternative can force a wrong resolution only on a set
that omits one, and two external checks show such sets are few: a strict majority of experts flagged a
missing alternative on 6 of the 60 sets they rated, and on the 51 items our system resolved, experts
preferred a competing explanation on only 1 (Appendix I).
L Baselines and Robustness of the Gain
This appendix gives the details behind Section 5.5. All analyses replay or re-score the logged
discovery runs; none changes the resolution rules or the aggregation of the headline (within-run
top-K, seed mean within dataset, then mean over the six datasets).
Matched budgets.Every run logs the cost of each individual candidate. Within each of the 14
matched dataset/seed pairs we capped both methods at the smaller of the two methods’ own totals
in a given currency, walking candidates in the order they were produced and charging every one,
including failed or unusable attempts, until the run reached its 200 experimental validations. Under
equal total tokens the methods reached 181 (pointwise) and 189 (CONTRASTIVE) of their 200 scored
candidates and resolved 87.7 against 148.3 units (difference +60.7, 95%t interval over six dataset
clusters [+23.4,+98.0] ); under equal logged dollars, 92.2 against 145.8 ([+22.4,+84.8] ); charging
output tokens only, 95.8 against 124.9 ([−0.9,+59.1] , the one interval that includes zero; five of six
datasets positive). Applying one common budget to every run (4.45M tokens, the smallest total that
any run spent) gives 52.4 against 89.6. Belief elicitation accounts for 8.5% of contrastive tokens
against 2.5% forpointwise, but total spend per candidate is similar (61.1k tokens forpointwiseagainst
52.8k for CONTRASTIVE), because the extra cost of writing the contrast set is offset by shorter
analysis code and interpretation; since the cap charges failed and unusable attempts as well, the
method with the cheaper candidate does not necessarily reach more scored ones. We do not read this
as an efficiency advantage, since the two methods differ in prompts throughout and a token count
cannot tell a narrower experiment from a thinner one.

Joint versus independent scoring.Every contrast set in our runs was also scored one alternative at
a time with thepointwiseelicitor (five-level categorical rating mapped to a Beta mean, ten samples),
never mentioning the other alternatives; the independent scoring additionally saw the experiment-
reviewer agent’s notes, so the comparison is conservative against joint scoring. Applying thepointwise
method’s own gate (γsupport = 0.625) to the independent scores under the paper’s estimator gives
157.8 resolved units at top-200 when exactly one alternative passes (165.4 when any passes), against
161.9 for joint scoring: a difference of 4.1 units, about 6% of the 64.7-unit headline gap, with a t
interval that includes zero. The two scorings name the same leading alternative on 89.3% of sets
under dataset-equal weighting, and against the 170 questions with a statistic recomputed from raw
data neither is more accurate (166 against 165 of 170). We therefore claim no advantage for scoring
the alternatives together: given a fixed contrast set and its evidence, the scoring format accounts
for a small share of the gap. Both scorings read the same analyst summary, so this check holds the
analyst fixed. That resolutions follow the evidence rather than the analyst’s framing is established
separately: the elicitor resolves from the numbers alone with no analyst (Appendix J), and experts
who read the same evidence with no instruction chose the same explanation on 78% of resolved items
(Appendix I). What remains is how the alternatives are constructed, tested directly below.
Implicit contrast sets in thepointwisecorpus.Could thepointwiseruns’ hypotheses be clustered
post hoc into the contrast sets we construct explicitly? Coverage is a necessary condition for such
clustering: every member of a set must have been proposed. We screened every hypothesis generated
by thepointwiseruns (8,547 hypotheses over 32 runs) against a stratified sample of 300 contrast
sets from the same datasets, judging each candidate pair with a model that generated neither corpus
(gpt-4.1-mini) under a rubric that permits refusal. The matcher assigns a set’s own alternatives
to the correct member on 99.9% of positive controls and matches nothing from unrelated datasets;
blinded human labels on 40 matcher decisions agreed on 36, with three of the four disagreements
being matches the human rejected, so the matcher errs toward overcountingpointwisecoverage. At
matched budget (the same-seedpointwiserun truncated at the paired contrastive run’s total tokens),
29.1% of individual alternatives appear anywhere in thepointwisecorpus, the runs share at least one
alternative with 64.7% of the sets, and the complete set is present for 2.6% of the questions that at
least onepointwisehypothesis addresses (95% t interval [0,7.0] , truncated at zero). Enlarging the
corpus to all seeds and prompt variants, four to six times the matched budget, raises complete-set
presence only to 15.4% ([0,31.5] , wide) and per-alternative coverage to 53.7%. The explanation that
the evidence eventually supports is present 52.0% of the time when it confirms the prior-leading
explanation but 25.4% when it corrects it (paired difference−26.5 percentage points, [−44.8,−8.3] ),
so exactly wherepointwiseevaluation rejects its hypothesis and stops, its corpus usually lacks the
explanation that turns out to hold.
Sensitivity to the number of alternatives.Stratifying the frozen top-200 pool of Section 5.2
by contrast-set size, resolution is 93.4% with two alternatives (102 questions, 4.4% of validations,
dataset-weighted), 83.2% with three (2,217; 78.3%), and 68.3% with four (479; 17.3%). Resolution
requires 80% of posterior mass on one alternative however many are on the table, and belief starts
more spread out with four alternatives (leading prior mass 0.41) than with two (0.68), so the bar is
a longer climb; the evidence itself is not weaker on larger sets, where raw belief change rises from
0.59 to 1.07 bits. The number of alternatives was chosen by the generator and is confounded with
question type: directional questions are almost all three-way and resolve at 92.7%, and a separate
pooled comparison gives a three-to-four gap of 15.7 percentage points, which shrinks to 2.2 after
standardizing the question types represented in both strata to the four-way mix. On paired support-
scope questions thepointwisegate fires 12.2 percentage points more often than ours where there
are four alternatives, so there is no evidence that our threshold becomes the more permissive one
as contrast sets grow. This series covers two to four alternatives, excluding one five-way and one
seven-way question, and describes how resolution varies withM; it does not isolate a causal effect of
M.
Elicitation format.On the same 180 contrast sets and byte-identical evidence, we re-elicited beliefs
under two other response formats: a per-alternative five-level categorical judgment (thepointwise
scoring rule) and a forced choice among the alternatives with the option that the evidence does not
distinguish them. Among sets yielding a comparable decision, the leading explanation agreed with
the paper’s 100-point allocation on 94.2% of sets under the categorical format (161 of 171) and 99.3%
under forced choice (152 of 153), against 98.9% when the paper’s own format was run twice; before

M.2 Extraction
For each generated hypothesis, we extract the set of dataset columns it references by parsing four fields
from the run logs: the hypothesis text, the agent’s experiment plan (objective, steps, deliverables),
the executed Python code, and the agent’s textual analysis. We use four lexical signals to identify
column references: an AST parse of the executed code to detect pandas-style column accesses (e.g.,
df[’col’]), a regex fallback for cases where the code fails to parse, identifier tokenization on
statsmodels-style formula strings, and substring matching of canonical column names against the
concatenated textual fields. Each candidate token is validated against the dataset’s canonical column
list (parsed from the run’s data-loading description) and dropped if it does not match a known column.
The pipeline is fully lexical and uses no LLM calls.

are presented as descriptive characterization rather than as statistical tests.
N Recovery of Published Findings
We screened 14 questions with published findings from the DiscoveryBench [30] training split and
tested recovery on ten leakage-screened questions (questions whose wording gives away the answer
were excluded). Each method received the question and the data once, with no tree search and never
the answer, and the final hypothesis each run stated was scored against the published answer by a
calibrated judge (gpt-4.1, temperature 0, 9 of 9 on calibration items), with undecided or malformed
outputs counted as wrong. CONTRASTIVEDiscovery matched on 1 of 10 and thepointwisebaseline
on 0 of 10. The transcripts show why: the analyst usually answered a different question than the
benchmark asked (a different predictor or outcome, an unrequested moderator or subgroup), and
several published answers depend on modeling choices of the original studies that cannot be recovered
from the question and column schema. The test therefore measures question framing and analysis
choice at least as much as adjudication, and with both methods at floor it says nothing about the
difference between them. The correctness evidence in this paper comes instead from Appendix I and
Appendix J, which start from the executed analysis; end-to-end recovery of known findings from raw
data remains open.
O Elicitation Design Across the Two Methods
Thepointwiseand CONTRASTIVEmethods share the discovery scaffold but differ in how beliefs are
elicited and in what the analyst is asked to report. We list the main differences here, with what has
been tested about each.
• Response format and aggregation.Pointwisebeliefs are five-level categorical ratings (ten
samples) mapped to a Beta mean (Appendix T.1); CONTRASTIVEbeliefs are 100-point
constant-sum allocations (five samples) averaged into a distribution (Appendix T.2). Scoring
the same contrast sets one alternative at a time with thepointwiseformat changes the leading
explanation on about one set in ten (89.3% agreement) and the headline by 4.1 resolved units
(Appendix L); a per-alternative categorical format and a forced choice reproduce the leading
explanation on 94.2% and 99.3% of sets yielding comparable decisions (Appendix L).
• Elicitor instructions.The CONTRASTIVEprior prompt asks the elicitor not to default to a
uniform allocation, and the CONTRASTIVEposterior prompt asks it to be discriminative and
avoid unjustified hedging (Appendix P); thepointwiseelicitor prompt has no corresponding
instruction. Because resolution is read off the posterior, these instructions could raise the
resolution rate on their own. Two checks bound this. On the resolution rate, the independent-
scoring check of Appendix L keeps the contrast sets and evidence fixed and replaces our
elicitor with thepointwiseelicitor and its threshold, which carry no such instruction: the
yield falls from 161.9 to 157.8 questions, about 4 of the 64.7 gained overpointwise. On
the leading explanation, the expert panel of Appendix I, reading the same evidence with no
instruction, selected the system’s leading explanation on 40 of 51 resolved items. The first
check replaces the instructions and the response format together, so the 4.1 questions bound
their combined effect. The gain overpointwisetherefore does not rest on the elicitor being
told to be discriminative.
• What the analyst reports.The CONTRASTIVEanalyst returns a winning_cell_idx field
and describes, by content rather than label, which alternatives the evidence does and does
not rule out; the posterior elicitor then reads the analyst’s prose. Thepointwiseanalyst
writes a free summary of the code output. The adjudication-fidelity experiment (Appendix J)
removes the analyst entirely, giving the elicitor the numbers alone, and still finds evidence-
driven resolutions, while the mechanical audits confirm that the summaries quote the printed
numbers; isolating the verdict field’s own effect on the discovery runs is left to future work.
• When alternatives are generated.In the discovery runs the contrast set is part of the
experiment proposal and is fixed before the experiment runs, so the alternatives are named
before any evidence exists. The post-hoc companion of Section 5.1 generates its alternatives
from the hypothesis under test, the dataset’s variables, and the same earlier context a live

text:
proposer would have; the current analysis, its output, and the verdict on the hypothesis are
withheld, and the companion is applied whether the hypothesis was confirmed or rejected.
• Review and revision.The CONTRASTIVEexperiment-reviewer agent additionally flags
whether an experiment discriminates among the alternatives and the reviser agent can rework
a non-discriminating plan; thepointwisereviewer agent checks faithful implementation and
whether the focal hypothesis was sufficiently tested. This is part of the contrastive method
rather than a scoring artifact, and its cost is included in the matched-budget comparison
(Appendix L).
• Normalization.Pointwisesurprisal is normalized by an achievable ceiling derived from
the prior (Appendix T.1), whereasκt is scaled by the constant log2M (Appendix T.2); the
consequences of each are discussed where they are defined.
P Prompts
P.1 CONTRASTIVEDiscovery-specific prompts
Hypothesis Generator Prompt
You are a research scientist doing open-ended, data-driven research using the provided dataset(s). Each
step in your investigation, you must propose a CONTRAST SET of competing explanations rather than
a single hypothesis, and an EXPERIMENT PLAN that DISCRIMINATES between them.
A contrast set is a small, mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive (MECE) partition of outcomes.
Four operational requirements (all mandatory):
1. **Single local question.** All cells must answer ONE specific question (e.g. "what is the
direction/presence/moderation structure of X->Y?"). Do not mix questions.
2. **Single variable set.** All cells reference the same target and predictor variables. Do not
switch what is being measured.
3. **Single analysis family.** A single coherent analysis (one regression, one stratified test, one
comparison) must plausibly distinguish among all cells. Avoid contrast sets where one cell needs
regression, another needs clustering, and another needs causal discovery.
4. **Small discrete outcome space.** Prefer M=3. Use M=4 only when subgroup or mechanism structure
genuinely requires it. M=5 should be rare.
Most contrast sets should include a residual cell ("no effect" / "no clear pattern" / "neither") so
exhaustivity is real, not aspirational. Some partition families (SIGN, PRESENCE_WITH_DIRECTION,
FEATURE_DOMINANCE) already include one by construction; do NOT add a second residual cell when the
family already provides one. Uncertainty lives in the probability allocation downstream, not as a
separate "we don't know" cell inside the partition.
NAMED PARTITIONING DIMENSIONS (pick exactly ONE per contrast set):
- **SIGN** (M=3): {{positive effect, no effect, negative effect}} for a scalar relationship between
two variables.
- **PRESENCE_WITH_DIRECTION** (M=3): {{effect absent, effect present positive, effect present
negative}}. Use when sign is hard to commit to but presence/absence is.
- **SUBGROUP_MODERATED** (M=4): {{effect only in A, only in B, in both, in neither}} for a binary
moderator.
- **MECHANISM_DISCRIMINATING** (M=3 or 4): {{association persists after controlling for C,
association attenuates after controlling for C, association disappears (no residual effect after
controls), no effect}}. Strictly OBSERVATIONAL wording -- describe what regression coefficients DO
under control adjustment, not WHY. Do NOT use mediation language ("X is mediated through M");
mediation is a causal-identification claim our designs do not support. Do NOT use "causes" / "
causal pathway" language.
- **FUNCTIONAL_FORM** (M=3 or 4): {{linear positive, linear negative, nonlinear or threshold, no
effect}}. Use only when the question is genuinely about the shape of the relationship AND sample
size supports the distinction (e.g. n > 200 for a polynomial-vs-linear comparison; nonlinear
claims need enough power to reject a linear null). Otherwise default to SIGN or
PRESENCE_WITH_DIRECTION.
- **COARSE_ORDER** (M=3 or 4): coarse ordinal contrasts only -- e.g. {{highest in A, highest in B, no
clear ordering}}, or {{monotone increasing, monotone decreasing, non-monotone}}. NEVER enumerate
full permutations like (A>B>C>D); coarsen those to one of the forms above.
- **VARIANCE_DIFFERENCE** (M=3): {{variance higher in subgroup A than B, variance higher in B than A,
no significant difference in variance}} for second-moment / dispersion / heteroskedasticity
questions. Distinct from SUBGROUP_MODERATED, which is about mean/effect differences. Use when the
question is genuinely about how spread (variance, IQR, MAD) differs across groups, not how means
do.
- **FEATURE_DOMINANCE** (M=3 or 4): {{feature X is the dominant predictor of outcome Z, feature Y is
the dominant predictor, both contribute comparably, neither contributes meaningfully}} for multi-
feature contribution decomposition. Distinct from SIGN (which concerns one relationship's
direction). Use when the question is which of several candidate predictors carries the signal.
37
title: Contrastive Discovery: Open-Ended Scientific Discovery over Competing Explanations

text:
EXTENDING THE TAXONOMY (last resort): if your question's structure genuinely fits none of the named
dimensions above -- for example, a regime-change / threshold-effect question that FUNCTIONAL_FORM
doesn't cover, an interaction-structure question SUBGROUP_MODERATED can't express, or some other
genuinely novel structural shape -- you may coin a new dimension. Name it in your own SHOUT_CASE
in the`partitioning_dimension`field, and ensure cells satisfy the same MECE / falsifiability /
mechanical-cell-mapping properties as the named dimensions (every cell must be a discrete
observable pattern that the experiment plan's analysis maps to mechanically). Inventing a new
dimension is rare; the named ones cover the vast majority of cases. Prefer the named ones whenever
they fit.
HARD CONSTRAINTS:
1. M <= 5. Never enumerate combinatorial outcome spaces (every ordering of several items, or every
combination of several multi-valued outcomes).
2. Each cell is a complete falsifiable claim referencing the actual variable names -- not a label
like "positive" or "ordering A > B".
3. Pick exactly ONE partitioning dimension per contrast set (a named one when applicable; a coined
one only when none of the named dimensions fits).
4. The experiment plan must produce an output that maps each cell to a specific quantitative
criterion (e.g. "CI entirely above 0 -> C_1; contains 0 -> C_2; entirely below 0 -> C_3").
5. **Cells must differ in substantive statistical pattern** -- sign, presence, subgroup membership,
mechanism class, functional form, or coarse ordering. Cells that differ only in wording strength
("weak positive" vs "strong positive") are NOT a valid contrast -- that is one hypothesis re-
described, not multiple alternatives.
6. **Adequate support.** Do not define cells over sparse categories or tiny subgroups unless the
experiment plan explicitly checks for adequate sample size (e.g. minimum n per cell, robustness
checks, or power-aware test selection).
Example of a well-formed contrast set output (note that`cells`are PLAIN-CONTENT strings -- the slot
labels`C_1`/`C_2`/`C_3`belong only in the`experiment_plan.deliverables`cell-mapping criterion,
not in the cell text):
```
cells:
- "Total citations increase with years since PhD"
- "No effect of years since PhD on total citations"
- "Total citations decrease with years since PhD"
partitioning_dimension: "SIGN"
rationale: "Test the direction of the citation-experience relationship; the residual cell covers no-
effect."
experiment_plan:
objective: "Quantify the relationship between years-since-PhD and total citations."
steps: "Compute Spearman correlation between years_from_PhD and total_citations; report the 95%
bootstrap CI."
deliverables: "Spearman rho + 95% bootstrap CI; cell-mapping is: CI entirely above 0 -> C_1; CI
contains 0 -> C_2; CI entirely below 0 -> C_3."
```
Examples of well-formed discriminating plans:
- SIGN: "Compute Spearman correlation between X and Y with 95% bootstrap CI. Report the CI; the cell-
mapping is: CI entirely above 0 -> C_1; CI contains 0 -> C_2; CI entirely below 0 -> C_3."
- SUBGROUP_MODERATED: "Fit interaction model Y ~ X * Z; test simple slopes of X within each level of
Z; classify by which simple slopes are significant at alpha=0.05."
- FUNCTIONAL_FORM: "Fit linear and natural-spline models, compare BIC; if linear wins and slope CI
excludes 0, classify by sign; otherwise use the spline residual structure to distinguish nonlinear
from null."
Self-check before output:
(a) Count cells. M <= 5? Prefer M=3?
(b) Pick any two cells. Could BOTH be true on the same dataset? If yes, fix.
(c) Imagine 5 plausible experimental outcomes. Does each map to exactly one cell? If not, add a
residual cell or coarsen.
(d) Does the plan output a quantity that can be cleanly mapped to a specific cell?
(e) Could ONE coherent analysis (regression / stratified comparison / model-comparison test)
discriminate all cells? If not, the contrast spans too many questions; split it.
Other instructions you must follow:
1. Strictly use only the dataset(s) provided. Do not simulate dummy/synthetic data or columns that
cannot be derived from existing columns.
2. Each contrast set should be creative, independent, and self-contained.
3. Use prior explorations as inspiration; do not repeat the same partition.
4. Multiple datasets: if provided, you may propose contrast sets that join across datasets.
The unit of discovery is the redistribution of belief across the cells of the contrast set after
evidence -- not the survival of a single claim. A good contrast set + discriminating plan moves
probability mass between cells; a bad one leaves the prior untouched.

text:

Experiment Analyst Prompt
You are a research scientist evaluating the code execution output for a contrastive scientific
experiment. The experiment was designed to discriminate between the cells of a CONTRAST SET -- a
small mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive partition of outcomes (cells C_1, C_2, ...
given to you in the user message). Your job has two INDEPENDENT parts.
PART 1 -- execution status (separate from whether the experiment discriminated):
Set`success=false`ONLY when the code itself failed:
- no code was executed
- the code raised an error
- the code's first line contains`# [debug]`(debugging protocol -- return success=false, note the
debug execution, ask for the experiment to be retried)
- the code "failed silently": produced no interpretable quantitative output, no statistics relevant
to the contrast set, only plots / log spam / unusable text
Otherwise, set`success=true`. The code ran AND produced usable output. **This holds even if the
experiment failed to discriminate among the cells** -- that judgment belongs to the reviewer's
separate`discriminates`flag, not yours.
When success=true, write a short analysis summary: report the **main decision-relevant quantities** the
code actually produced -- effect estimates, CIs, p-values, model-comparison metrics, whichever
the experiment computed -- plus any caveats (sample size, missing data, sparse subgroups, etc.).
Do NOT force a p-value if none was computed.
PART 2 -- contrast-set mapping (independent of PART 1's success flag):
Identify which cell of the contrast set is best supported by the experimental output. Use **only what
the code output reports** -- no prior expectations, no domain knowledge beyond the printed
statistics. Return:
-`winning_cell_idx`: zero-based index of the cell the evidence most cleanly favors.
- If the result decisively supports one cell (e.g. tight CI on one side, large effect with clear
direction matching exactly one cell's criterion), return that index.
- If the evidence is genuinely ambiguous between two or more cells (CI straddles boundaries, mixed
signals, the planned cell-mapping criterion wasn't actually computed), return **null**.
`winning_cell_idx=null`is a legitimate honest answer compatible with`success=true`. **A success=true
analysis with winning_cell_idx=null** is the right output when the code ran cleanly but the result
didn't actually distinguish among cells. Prefer null over overclaiming when evidence is
borderline.
In the analysis text, when discussing cells, **describe them by their content / semantics only -- do
NOT reference cells by their numerical label** (no "C_1", "C_2", etc.). For example, write "the
evidence supports the effect-attenuates-after-controls scenario" rather than "the evidence
supports C_2". The numerical labels are an artifact of how cells are presented to you in this
specific prompt; downstream consumers (the posterior belief elicitor, auditors, future re-
elicitations under different cell orderings) will see the cells in possibly different label
positions, so a label like "C_2" written here will mislabel the cell in those contexts. The cell
content / short description IS the cell's identity; descriptions transfer correctly across
orderings, labels do not. Briefly note which cells the evidence does and does not rule out (by
description), and any reasons it may be ambiguous. Use`winning_cell_idx`to record the index --
that field is reordered correctly downstream; the prose should be label-free.
Experiment Reviewer Prompt
You are a research scientist holistically reviewing a contrastive experiment pipeline: the generated
code, the output, and the analysis against the original experiment plan AND the contrast set the
experiment was meant to discriminate.
`success=true`and`discriminates=true`are LOGICALLY INDEPENDENT. Judge each separately on the
criteria below; do not let one bleed into the other.
Assess two things:
1. **Faithful implementation.** Was the experiment plan followed without significant deviation? Are
the test, statistics, and reporting consistent with the plan? If you find code-level or pipeline-
level issues (missing variables, wrong test, broken output), return`success=false`and explain.
39

text:
2. **Discrimination.** Did the experiment, as implemented, produce evidence that meaningfully narrows
the contrast set?
For the discrimination check, ask explicitly:
- **Did the implemented analysis actually compute the predeclared cell-mapping criterion?** The
experiment plan should have named a specific criterion (e.g. "Spearman CI sign", "interaction p-
value", "BIC delta between linear and spline"). If the code computed something else -- even
something interesting --`discriminates=false`. The cells were defined relative to that criterion;
an output that doesn't map to the criterion can't discriminate.
- **Did the evidence rule out at least one competing cell?** A plan that produces only a quantity
consistent with one cell while leaving the others untouched isn't really a discriminating
experiment.
- **Discrimination does not require statistical significance per se.** It comes from whichever
criterion the plan declared -- effect estimates, confidence intervals, model-comparison metrics, p
-values -- whichever was the predeclared rule for mapping output to cells. Do NOT require`p <
0.05`unless that was the rule.
Set the`discriminates`flag accordingly:
- **`true`** if the output, under the predeclared decision rule, narrows the contrast set to one cell
or a near-singleton subset (i.e. one cell strongly favored, the others materially ruled out or
implausible).
- **`false`** if the experiment passed but the evidence is too weak, ambiguous, doesn't compute the
predeclared criterion, or is equally consistent with multiple cells.
In the feedback text, separate the failure modes explicitly when they apply:
- **Implementation issue:** name what was wrong with the code, data, or pipeline (only when`success=
false`).
- **Non-discrimination:** explain why the evidence didn't narrow the partition, and briefly note **
what would have been needed to discriminate** (e.g. "tighter CIs", "stratified test", "model
comparison instead of single-coefficient test"). Used when`success=true, discriminates=false`.
When both flags are true, provide a summary of the contrast set, the experiment, and the resulting
evidence-to-cell mapping.
Experiment Reviser Prompt
You are a research scientist revising a contrastive experiment that the reviewer flagged. The
experiment proposes a contrast set (a small mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive
partition of outcomes) plus an experiment plan that should discriminate between the cells.
Default behavior: **preserve the cells; revise only the experiment plan.** Move the target only when
you must.
ANTI-PATTERNS YOU MUST AVOID
- **Do not tighten the cells after seeing the data.** The cells were declared BEFORE evidence;
revising them now to better match the observed result is HARKing -- paper-indefensible. Tightening
is allowed ONLY when the reviewer explicitly identified the original partition as ill-posed.
- **Do not respond to weak evidence by inventing a more specific subgroup or mechanism** unless the
reviewer explicitly requested repartitioning. "The effect was weak in general but appears in
subgroup X" is a post-hoc move and is forbidden.
- **Do not invoke "more powerful test" reasoning** as a justification for changing the analysis. "
More powerful" is statistical jargon that invites fishing. Frame revisions as "more APPROPRIATE
test" or "more INFORMATIVE analysis" -- and explain why.
The reviewer's feedback usually falls into one of these categories. Apply the corresponding revision in
priority order -- change as little as possible:
- **Technical failure** (code error, data issue, runtime crash, debug-marked code): keep the cells
exactly as they are. Revise the plan to fix the technical problem. Do NOT change the partition.
- **Plan didn't discriminate** (`discriminates=false`from the reviewer): keep the cells. Revise the
plan in this priority order -- try the cheapest fix first:
1. **Change the decision rule / estimand / comparison structure.** E.g. switch from coefficient
sign to model-comparison metric; add a CI for the existing estimate; switch from two-sample t-test
to interaction term; recast as ordering test.
2. **Tighten the analysis without changing what is measured.** E.g. add controls, stratify, use a
robust estimator, fix specification errors, address sparse-cell concerns.
3. **Change variables** -- only as a last resort, and only if the reviewer flagged the original
variables as the problem.
- **Partition itself is ill-posed** -- only in this case, revise the cells. Operational rule: revise
cells when (a) the reviewer explicitly flagged a MECE violation (cells overlap, fail to cover the
outcome space, or answer different questions), or (b) the cells are not empirically

distinguishable under any reasonable single analysis. Stay within the same partitioning dimension
if possible; coarsen rather than refine.
HARD CONSTRAINTS for the revised contrast set (if you change it):
- M <= 5, mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive.
- Each cell is a complete falsifiable claim with the actual variable names.
- Pick exactly ONE partitioning dimension. The named taxonomy is SIGN / PRESENCE_WITH_DIRECTION /
SUBGROUP_MODERATED / MECHANISM_DISCRIMINATING / FUNCTIONAL_FORM / COARSE_ORDER /
VARIANCE_DIFFERENCE / FEATURE_DOMINANCE. If the original partition coined a custom SHOUT_CASE
dimension that genuinely fits the question and meets the MECE / falsifiability / mechanical-cell-
mapping properties, preserving that coined dimension is acceptable.
- Most revised contrast sets should include a residual / null cell (no effect / no clear pattern) for
practical exhaustivity. Some families (SIGN, PRESENCE_WITH_DIRECTION, FEATURE_DOMINANCE) include
one by construction; do NOT add a second when the family already provides one. No "uncertain"
cells.
The revised experiment plan must:
- Address the reviewer's specific concerns.
- **Explicitly state the cell-mapping rule** -- the predeclared mapping from possible outcomes to
cells (e.g. "CI entirely above 0 -> C_1; CI contains 0 -> C_2; CI entirely below 0 -> C_3"). Do
NOT just say "do regression and interpret coefficients"; the cell-mapping must be declared so the
next reviewer can check whether the implementation followed it.
- Output a quantity that maps to a single cell of the contrast set under one coherent analysis.
- Use only the provided dataset; no synthetic data.
Do not provide code -- explain the revised experiment in natural language for the programmer.
Belief Elicitor Prompt
## system_prior
You are a senior scientist making a comparative judgment about a research question. You will be given a
set of mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive (MECE) claims that partition the outcome
space -- exactly one is true given the real data, and you must allocate your prior belief across
them.
Use your domain knowledge. Allocate exactly 100 probability points across the cells, summing to exactly
100. The points represent your prior probability (in percent) that each cell is the true one.
Do NOT default to a uniform allocation. Many research questions have informative priors -- make them.
If you genuinely have no view, allocate uniformly, but only if so.
Briefly explain your allocation in the rationale.

You are a senior scientist judging which cell of a partition is true given experimental evidence.

Allocate exactly 100 probability points across the cells, summing to exactly 100, reflecting your
posterior belief that each cell is the true one given the evidence. Be discriminative -- if the
evidence strongly supports one cell, put most of the mass there. If the evidence is weak or
ambiguous across multiple cells, distribute accordingly. Avoid unjustified hedging.
Briefly explain your allocation in the rationale.

S Compatibility withPointwiseSurprisal
This appendix reports in full the two analyses summarized in Section 5.3 (“Compatibility with
pointwisesurprisal”).
S.1 CONTRASTIVEbelief shift preserves surprisal while revealing corrective updates
We comparepointwisesurprisal and CONTRASTIVEbelief shift ( κt) on the same set of candidate
discoveries. For each node from a CONTRASTIVErun, we compute κt over the full contrast set and a
post-hocpointwisesurprisal score for the highest prior hypothesis. This tests whether κt is merely a
rescaled version ofpointwisesurprisal or instead prioritizes different discovery semantics. The two
scores are aligned (Spearmanρ= 0.675 ) with 90% of nodes falling within a±0.4 percentile-rank
difference band (Figure 16). Thus, CONTRASTIVEbelief shift preserves the core belief-shift signal
captured by surprisal.
The disagreements, however, are structured. When the metrics largely disagree (i.e.,|∆pct|≥0.4 ),
nodes ranked higher by CONTRASTIVEare disproportionately corrective, while nodes ranked higher
bypointwiseare more frequently confirmative. This pattern does not imply thatpointwisediscovery
is mostly confirmative; Section 5.1 showed the opposite. Rather, it shows thatpointwisesurprisal
tracks movement in one focal claim, while CONTRASTIVEbelief shift tracks redistribution across
competing explanations.

V Broader Societal Impact
By resolving more questions from the same data and validation budget, the method can lower the cost
of screening hypotheses before laboratory follow-up. Three hazards are specific to this system. First,
its outputs are statistical resolutions on observational data, not causal findings; a “resolved” question
should be read as a prioritized claim to be verified, not as an established result. Second, two datasets
involve people: BLADE Mortgage (the Boston Fed HMDA study) records applicant race and gender,
and BLADE Conversation lists named public contributors with gender, institution, and citation
attributes. On such data the system can produce confident statistical resolutions that are not causally
identified; the abstention alternative (Appendix K) lets it decline instead of forcing a resolution when
no listed explanation matches the evidence, and any use of such outputs in policy-adjacent settings
requires unit-aware inference, pre-registered analyses, and human review. Third, each resolution rests
on the agent’s own analysis choices, including how it handles missing-value sentinels and clustered
observations (Appendix G); the audits of Appendix J verify that reported numbers match the code’s
output, and users should review the analysis code before acting on a resolution. We release prompts
and, at the project website, code so that these behaviors can be audited.
W Cost Analysis
Each 200-iteration run for a given dataset costs $20 to $50. We estimate the total cost of our
experiments at $1,500 to $2,000. Token spend per candidate for each condition is reported with the
matched-budget comparison in Appendix L.

Example-Based Grounding in EM-DETR
Sheethal Bhat1,2[0009−0006−2044−5113], Bogdan Georgescu3, Awais Mansoor3,
Florin C. Ghesu2, Sasa Grbic3, and Andreas Maier1

Abstract.DeepLearning(DL)-basedComputer-AidedDiagnostic(CAD)
systems have shown great promise in supporting clinicians, but their
performance heavily depends on the availability of large, well-annotated
datasets. In medical lesion detection, the scarcity of comprehensive, stan-
dardized annotations and the heterogeneity of existing datasets limit the
development of robust foundation models. In this work, we introduce
a novel approach to building a multi-domain foundation model for le-
sion detection by integrating diverse medical image datasets annotated
for both anatomical structures and abnormalities. We first propose a
student-teacher training strategy to effectively combine datasets with
heterogeneous label spaces, mitigating catastrophic forgetting, and im-
provingfeaturelearning.Inaddition,buildingonourpreviouslyproposed
example-based EM-DETR framework, we adapt it to jointly learn from
multiple domain-specific datasets, enabling fine-grained, example-driven
detection across modalities. Our model achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA)
results, with image-level AUC scores exceeding previous SOTA by 1%
point and on four key findings in CXRs.We achieve a leadingmAP50
in CXRs and mammography, surpassing EM-DETR trained on a single
dataset by 2-3% points.
1 Motivation
Object detection is a fundamental challenge in computer vision, finding extensive
use in fields such as autonomous driving, robotics, and surveillance. In medical
imaging, detection plays an equally critical role, enabling the identification and
localization of anatomical structures or pathological findings that guide clinical
decisionmaking.TraditionalCNN-baseddetectionmodelssuchasFasterR-CNN
[21], RetinaNet [12], and FCOS [24] have demonstrated strong performance in
natural image domains and have also been adapted for radiographic tasks [7].
However, these models often rely on extensive, dataset-specific supervision and
struggle to generalize across modalities or out-of-distribution (OOD) data [1].
This is primarily due to the intricate nature of obtaining high-quality anno-
tations, the subtle visual indicators that complicate the defining of boundary
regions, and the diversity of anatomical structures [18,22].

title: Toward Foundation Detection Models via Example-Based Grounding in EM-DETR

text:
2 S. Bhat et al.
To address the limitations of supervised object detectors, recent work has
explored Vision-Language (VL) detection models [10,14,8,16,17] that integrate
image and text supervision during training. These models show strong potential
for generalizing across novel classes and domains, particularly in natural image
settings. Models such as GLIP [10], OWL-ViT [17], and Grounding DINO [14]
achieve state-of-the-art detection performance by leveraging powerful, jointly
learned visual and language embeddings, which are aligned through contrastive
learning. Moreover, large-scale pretraining on “grounding” or “caption” datasets
i.e., region-level textual descriptions, enables open-set zero-shot detection, allow-
ing recognition of unseen classes from their textual cues. This pretraining lever-
ages automatically mined image-caption pairs from extensive web sources and
curated datasets, including LAION-400M [23], Visual Genome [9], and COCO
Captions [5].
In contrast, the medical domain lacks comparable comprehensive image-text
paired datasets, posing challenges for effective VL model training. Medical im-
age annotations are sparse [18,19], domain-specific, and expensive to obtain [6],
often requiring expert knowledge and adherence to stringent annotation proto-
cols. Consequently, the development of a similar foundational model for medical
lesion detection continues to pose significant challenges. In this study, we ini-
tially examine two distinct datasets: annotated for anatomical structures and
abnormalities, with the goal of enhancing the visual feature space during base-
line training. While this approach offers modest gains, we extend it further by
leveraging our previously proposed EM-DETR [1] framework. Specifically, we
use EM-DETR [1], an example-based multi-modal detector accepted at MIC-
CAI 2025, to integrate multiple domain-specific datasets, allowing the model to
learn fine-grained, example-based features tailored to distinct lesion types across
various imaging contexts.
Our contributions are twofold: (1) we explore combining anatomical and
abnormality annotations to enrich supervision during training, and (2) we ex-
tend EM-DETR to develop a multi-domain, example-based foundation detection
model that achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) results across five key findings in
CXRs and mammography. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows:
Section 2 details the datasets used, covering both anatomical and abnormal-
ity annotations. Section 3 outlines the two methods of developing a foundation
model. Section 4 presents experimental results, and Section 5 concludes with
discussion and future directions.
2 Datasets
This work utilises four image datasets across two modalities: Chest X-Rays
(CXRs) and mammography. These include a private dataset annotated for key
anatomical structures, two datasets with abnormality-level labels (private [6]
and public [18]), and an additional public mammography dataset [19] annotated
for abnormalities at the lesion level. The details of each dataset, including an-
notation types, and class distribution, are described below.

4 Experimental Results
4.1 Experimental Setup
Experiments were conducted on a single node with four 40 GB A100 GPUs,
within the MMDetection framework [4]. Default data augmentations and hyper-
parameters were applied. The Swin-L backbone used a per-GPU batch size of 1,
with a learning rate of 0.0008. Standard CXR-related augmentations such as ran-
dom auto-contrast, sharpness adjustments, and random horizontal flipping, were
added to the default augmentation pipeline. Furthermore, additional terms such
as “right lung” and “left lung” were added to the text vocabulary, allowing the
creation of distinct tokens for the intended left and right categories. Predictions
from the anatomy teacher below 0.8 score and deviations greater than 50% from
the average size of the ground truth were excluded. For mammogram images, the
background dark regions were cropped, and the annotations were recalculated
for the resized images. Each experiment was conducted five times, training upto
25 epochs. The reported results correspond to the mean performance calculated
from the top 5 check points selected based onmAP50.

culty or prevalence. Conversely, owing to their example-based learning paradigm,
the EM-DETR and EM-FM models generally exhibit more stable performance
when trained on a large number of classes. This stability arises from their abil-
ity to leverage learned feature representations to match examples, rather than
relying solely on class-dependent contrastive language objectives. As a result,
these models are less sensitive to class selection and distribution, enabling more
consistent detection performance across diverse and heterogeneous datasets.
5 Conclusion
This study explores creating a detection foundation model for all radiography
images across multiple modalities. We first demonstrate that the combination
of disjoint and overlapping set of anatomy and abnormality datasets, achieves
SOTA classification performance. In contrast to their naive combination, we
prevent catastrophic forgetting by weakly labelling missing annotations using
a student-teacher approach. While not specifically optimizing for localization,
we achieve comparable capabilities for most conditions, with the exception of
atelectasis. We then incorporate all available CXR and mammography data into
our previously proposed example-based detection model EM-DETR, resulting
in significant detection improvements over prior SOTA across both modalities.
Leveraging foundation models also facilitates faster and more stable training
convergence, as widely reported in foundation model research. Future work will
extend this approach to additional findings and datasets to further validate its
generalizability and robustness.

text:
Medical Image Segmentation: Foundation Model Adaptation versus
Task-Specific Training
Emre Kutlusana, Yongmin Lia,∗
aDepartment of Computer Science, Brunel University of London, Uxbridge, UB8 3PH, United Kingdom
Abstract
Foundation models pretrained on large natural-image collections are increasingly adapted for
medical image segmentation, in the expectation that they will replace models trained for each
task. Most comparisons, however, use data from the training distribution and a single task-
specific baseline whose configuration is rarely justified, and therefore provide limited evidence
of performance at new clinical sites. It also remains unclear how much of a foundation model
must be adapted, and what determines this. We adapted a foundation model, DINOv2, with
strategies ranging from tuning only its bias terms to full fine-tuning, and compared it with U-Nets
and ResU-Nets trained from scratch. Experiments covered colonoscopy, breast ultrasound and
dermoscopy, with testing on held-out data from the training source and on independent datasets
from other institutions. The adapted foundation model generalised better on every external
dataset. Within the training distribution, the task-specific models remained competitive when
training data were abundant, and delineated boundaries more precisely, while the foundation
model more often missed small lesions. Only a small fraction of the foundation model required
adaptation, and the capacity needed was determined by the imaging domain rather than by the
adaptation method. A widely used polyp test set was also found to duplicate images from another
benchmark. Foundation-model adaptation is therefore warranted where models must work across
sites, with capacity selected on the target domain.
Keywords:medical image segmentation, foundation models, parameter-efficient fine-tuning,
cross-dataset generalisation, U-Net, ResU-Net, nnU-Net
1. Introduction
Vision foundation models, pretrained on hundreds of millions of images at a scale no clinical
dataset approaches, have made a question urgent for medical image segmentation. Given a new
dataset and task, is it better to adapt one of these models, or to train a task-specific architecture
from random initialisation as the field has done since U-Net?
The question matters because of where segmentation models are deployed. A model trained
at one hospital is intended for use at others, on images from different scanners, protocols and
patient populations. This distribution shift, rather than in-domain accuracy, is the principal
obstacle to clinical adoption, and it is invisible in the measurement usually reported. Every model
in this study is therefore evaluated under two regimes: in domain, on held-out data from the
training distribution, and out of distribution, on data from institutions that contributed nothing
to training.
The literature comparing the two approaches generally reports that adapted foundation
models win, and three properties of how that comparison is made limit what follows from it. It is
usually conducted within the training distribution, so a property of the evaluation is reported as a

text:
property of the models. It is usually made against a single task-specific model whose configuration
is not itself defended, and Isensee et al.[1] show that many claimed improvements over U-Net are
made against a weakly configured instance of it; the two objections compound, since an advantage
so obtained can be an artefact of both at once. It is also usually made at a single operating
point, that is, at one choice of settings such as the adaptation rank or the training budget, so a
statement about one configuration appears to be a statement about the methods.
A parallel gap concerns how much adaptation a target requires. Dutt et al.[2], in classification
and generation tasks, report that parameter-efficient methods are most effective in low-data
regimes, making training-set size the governing quantity and one known before any experiment;
Teuber et al.[3] report the contrary directly, finding no such advantage even at very small training
sizes, and attribute the variation to properties of the dataset, which are not known in advance.
What neither establishes is whether the requirement belongs to the domain or to the method
supplying the adaptation.
The aim of this study is to determine, for medical image segmentation, when adaptation of a
pretrained foundation model is warranted in place of a task-specific architecture, and what governs
the amount of adaptation such a model requires. It does so along two axes. The architecture
axis compares an adapted foundation model with task-specific architectures trained from random
initialisation; the adaptation axis varies how much of the foundation model is adapted, measuring
how the choice of adaptation strategy affects cross-dataset generalisation and whether the capacity
required is a property of the domain or of the method supplying it.
Both axes span three imaging domains—colonoscopy polyp imaging, breast ultrasound and
skin lesion dermoscopy—each with one training source and held-out test sets, giving eight
out-of-distribution test sets, one of which (CVC-T) consists of images also present in another
(CVC-ColonDB; Section 3.2). The foundation model is a DINOv2-Small encoder with a minimal
linear decoder, adapted under strategies spanning 385 to 22.1 million trainable parameters. The
task-specific comparators are a plain U-Net and a residual U-Net, both under the nnU-Net recipe
and each tuned independently.
The contributions are threefold:
1. A controlled comparison of foundation-model adaptation against task-specific training from
scratch, with the evaluation regimes separated throughout and against baselines shown to
be competitive with published architectures under an identical protocol: adaptation leads
on all eight out-of-distribution test sets in DSC, IoU, sensitivity and HD95 under both
architectures and its advantage grows as training data shrinks within a domain, most clearly
in polyp, while in domain at the full training set no accuracy advantage was observed.
2. Empirical findings on adaptation capacity: the step from a frozen encoder to bias-only
tuning captures most of the available benefit in polyp and breast, LoRA at 2.7 per cent
of the parameters is equal or ahead of full fine-tuning in DSC on all five polyp sets across
three seeds, and the capacity a domain requires is a property of the domain rather than of
the method supplying it.
3. Practical recommendations for choosing between and evaluating the two approaches: when
adaptation is warranted, how much capacity to use and how to select it, which failure
modes to check before deployment, and which evaluation hazards in standard benchmarks
to control.
2. Related work
Medical image segmentation spans a wide range of imaging modalities, including X-ray
radiography [4], computed tomography (CT) [5, 6], magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) [7, 8],
ultrasound [9], colonoscopy [10, 11], dermoscopy [12, 13, 14], fundus photography [15, 16] and
optical coherence tomography (OCT) [17, 18]. These modalities differ in how the image is formed,
in the appearance and scale of the anatomical targets and in how much annotated data is available,
2
title: Medical Image Segmentation: Foundation Model Adaptation versus Task-Specific Training

text:
and each has accumulated its own methods and benchmarks. The three domains studied here,
colonoscopy, breast ultrasound and dermoscopy, are drawn from this range, and the remainder of
this section reviews the segmentation architectures, foundation models, adaptation methods and
evaluation practices on which the study builds.
2.1. Segmentation architectures and nnU-Net
Before deep learning, segmentation methods were typically designed around the anatomy
and appearance of a single task, for example graph cuts for retinal vessels [19] and for retinal
layers in OCT [20, 21], and Gaussian mixture and other probabilistic models for vessel extraction
[22, 16]. Learned encoder–decoder networks have since largely replaced such pipelines, although
task-specific deep architectures continue to be proposed for individual targets such as colonoscopy
polyps [23, 24, 25, 26]. The U-Net of Ronneberger et al.[27] still dominates medical segmentation,
and of the many variants proposed since, McConnell et al.[28], comparing residual, dense,
inception and attention families across eight datasets, conclude that none dominates and that the
optimal choice is dataset-dependent. nnU-Net [29] reframed how such comparisons should be
conducted by proposing a procedure rather than an architecture: it derives the network topology,
patch size, resampling strategy, batch size and training schedule from a fingerprint of the dataset,
and its central empirical claim, that a U-Net so configured matches or exceeds most published
architectural modifications, makes the configuration of a baseline a methodological question
rather than an implementation detail. That claim was sharpened in nnU-Net Revisited [1], which
finds that many papers claiming to outperform U-Net do so against a weakly configured instance
of it, and which also reports strong performance from residual-encoder nnU-Net configurations,
evaluated on three-dimensional multi-class segmentation across large datasets. Both results
shape the design here: a residual variant, in the spirit of those configurations but with residual
blocks in both encoder and decoder, was adopted as the primary task-specific baseline, and
the 2015 architecture was deliberately not used, since employing it would have reproduced the
weak-baseline error in the direction that flatters the conclusions drawn here.
2.2. Foundation models and their medical adaptation
DINOv2 [30] is trained self-supervised on 142 million curated natural images with no labels,
and its patch-level features transfer to dense prediction without task-specific supervision during
pretraining. Because it has never seen a segmentation mask, whether its representations transfer
to medical segmentation is a question about representational generality rather than about label
overlap, which is why it was selected here. Its medical transfer has been assessed by Baharoon
et al.[31] across nine radiology benchmarks and by Ayzenberg et al.[32] in few-shot segmentation,
and Li et al.[33] report that pairing DINO features with a U-Net decoder supplies a strong
inductive prior for medical segmentation.
The second family originates with the Segment Anything Model [34], trained on a billion
masks over eleven million images, and is adapted to medical images by retraining on large-scale
medical data [35], by applying LoRA to the image encoder [36], by large-scale two-dimensional
adaptation [37] or by inserting adapters into a frozen backbone [38]; SAM-Mamba [39] reports
strong cross-dataset polyp performance and appears in the comparison of Section 4.2. A model
supervised on segmentation masks and a model that has never seen one require different amounts
of adaptation to reach a medical target, so a finding about how much adaptation one needs does
not automatically transfer to the other (Section 5.5).
2.3. Parameter-efficient adaptation
Parameter-efficient methods update a small fraction of a pretrained model’s parameters,
avoiding the memory and storage cost of full fine-tuning and, on small target datasets, the risk of
destabilising representations that took large-scale pretraining to acquire. Adapter modules [40]
and visual prompt tuning [41] add computation at inference, which is the property LoRA avoids.
3
title: Medical Image Segmentation: Foundation Model Adaptation versus Task-Specific Training

text:
LoRA [42] freezes the pretrained weights and adds a trainable low-rank decomposition to selected
projections, so that the effective weight update is constrained to rankr; the rank controls the
capacity of the update and is the method’s principal hyperparameter, and because the adapters
can be merged into the base weights after training, inference cost is unchanged. Kalajdzievski
[43] shows that the conventional scaling factor slows learning and stunts performance at higher
ranks and proposes a rank-stabilised alternative, which is why the present work holds the scaling
constant so that the rank sweep of Section 4.5 varies rank and nothing else. BitFit [44] freezes all
weight matrices and trains only bias terms, under one tenth of one per cent of the parameters
in the models it was proposed for, and its authors report performance competitive with full
fine-tuning on language tasks with the advantage concentrated in low-data regimes. The absence
of a rank parameter and its different intervention site make it the natural control for testing
whether a capacity requirement is a property of low-rank factorisation or of the target, which is
the role it serves in Section 4.5.
The literature applying these methods to medical imaging contains an unresolved disagreement,
and it is the point at which this study enters. Dutt et al.[2] benchmark parameter-efficient
methods across medical image analysis tasks and report an ordering that depends on data volume:
in their HAM10000 classification experiment with ViT-Large, LoRA overtakes full fine-tuning
from approximately eighty per cent of the available data downward, while BitFit is superior only
below twenty per cent. Teuber et al.[3] evaluate parameter-efficient adaptation of SAM across
biomedical datasets and report instead that the relative effectiveness of these methods differs by
dataset in a way that data volume alone does not account for, and that for computational efficiency,
where in the encoder a method intervenes matters more than which method it is. The two are
not straightforwardly reconcilable, and no study separates them, which would require varying
data volume within a domain while comparing across domains at matched volume. Section 5.5
returns to the disagreement with results in hand.
2.4. Cross-dataset evaluation and data hygiene
Most published results are obtained on held-out data from the training source, which is not
the deployment setting, and under a consistent protocol well-tuned empirical risk minimisation
is competitive with most proposed domain generalisation algorithms [45]. The protocol of Fan
et al.[23] partitions five polyp collections into a fixed training portion and three held-out sets,
and its widespread adoption means published scores are comparable in experimental setup rather
than merely in metric, which is what permits the baselines here to be positioned against the
literature. U-Bench [46] evaluates 100 U-Net variants across 28 datasets and 10 modalities,
reserving eight unseen datasets for zero-shot evaluation, and reports that in-domain metrics have
largely saturated while zero-shot generalisation continues to separate methods. Ndipenoch et al.
[18] apply the same distinction within medical segmentation, comparing an adapted SAM against
nnU-Net variants across three OCT device vendors and reporting the task-specific models slightly
ahead. A domain qualifies for such a study only if it offers a training source with independently
acquired, comparably annotated, public test sets; three satisfy this and were chosen to differ in
modality, by a factor of more than four in training-set size, and in severity of shift. Selecting
domains that differ this way is what makes it possible to ask whether a regularity is a property of
a method or of the data it was measured on, which a single-domain study cannot ask.
Cross-dataset evaluation is only as sound as the separation between the sets compared.
Truong et al.[47] report that medical datasets often contain near-duplicate images that can
bias evaluation, identifying possible near-duplicates in the widely used Medical Segmentation
Decathlon and benchmarking their detection under transformations that include cropping and
compression. On metrics, Taha and Hanbury[48] set out the consequences of choosing among
them. On representations, centred kernel alignment [49] is the standard tool for comparing
representations across networks, and Nguyen et al.[50] use the debiased estimator adopted in
Section 4.6.
4

text:
2.5. Research gaps
Three gaps follow.
1. When adaptation should be preferred.The literature does not settle when one approach
should be preferred over the other, because comparisons are typically made within the
training distribution and against a baseline whose configuration is not itself defended, the
weakness nnU-Net [29] and nnU-Net Revisited [1] identify in architectural comparisons.
2. How much adaptation a target requires.Separating the data-volume effects and dataset-
dependent outcomes of Section 2.3 requires varying data volume within a domain while
comparing across domains at matched volume, and testing the same question under two
methods that share no mechanism, so that any regularity found cannot be a property of
one method’s parameterisation.
3. How far the answers depend on configuration.nnU-Net Revisited [1] and U-Bench [46] reach
their conclusions by breadth, evaluating many methods under a common protocol, which
leaves little room to vary the configuration of any one comparison.
This study varies data volume on the architecture axis and compares domains and methods on
the adaptation axis; the interaction between capacity requirement and data volume is left open
(Section 5.4). For the third gap it takes the complementary trade-off, few methods examined at
many operating points, which is the reason it covers three domains and two adaptation methods,
examining their sensitivity to adaptation rank, training budget and evaluation regime.
3. Methods
3.1. Design and scope
The foundation model adopted is DINOv2 [30], in its smallest variant. It was chosen
deliberately in preference to segmentation-specific or medical foundation models such as SAM
[34], which is trained on a billion masks, and SAMed [36], which fine-tunes SAM on medical
images. The aim is to demonstrate the effectiveness of the adaptation approach with a small,
general-purpose model that has never been trained on segmentation masks or medical images,
so that any advantage it shows can be attributed to adaptation rather than to prior exposure
to the target task or domain. Such a model represents a conservative case: if it suffices, larger
foundation models, and those pretrained on masks or medical data, would be expected to perform
at least as well. A finding about how much adaptation one model family needs does not, however,
automatically transfer to another (Section 2.2), and repeating the adaptation axis on SAM, which
SAMed adapts with LoRA in the same way as the configurations here, is left to future work
(Section 5.4).
The design is organised around two axes kept separate throughout, summarised in Fig. 1. The
architecture axis asks when adaptation outperforms task-specific training: an adapted DINOv2
encoder is compared against a plain U-Net and a residual U-Net (ResU-Net) trained from random
initialisation. The adaptation axis asks how much adaptation is required: the foundation model is
compared only against itself under strategies of increasing capacity. No task-specific model appears
on the adaptation axis, and no adaptation strategy is applied to the task-specific architectures,
which have no pretrained parameters to adapt.
The adaptation axis is conditional on the architecture axis, and the two intersect at a single
point rather than as a factorial design. Only one DINOv2 configuration enters the architecture-
axis comparison, selected on in-domain validation rather than imported from the rank sweep, and
results from one axis are not used to support claims about the other. Claims on the adaptation
axis consequently rest on a single backbone, a limitation returned to in Section 5.4.
All models share training splits, evaluation code and metric definitions. Augmentation and
optimiser settings differ by model family, the task-specific models using a stronger pipeline than
the adaptation experiments. Where budgets or learning rates differ it is because each configuration
